Valheim isn't just a game. It's an experience. A way of life. A Viking simulator that somehow manages to make chopping down trees, building a house, sailing across an ocean, and getting absolutely obliterated by a giant angry mosquito some of the most memorable moments in gaming.

The world is breathtaking. The soundtrack is phenomenal. The atmosphere is unmatched. The building system is dangerously addictive. You start with a tiny wooden shack and a dream, and 100 hours later you're constructing an enormous Viking fortress at 3 AM because that roof beam is slightly off-centre and you cannot live like this.

And the exploration? INCREDIBLE. Every new biome feels like an adventure. Every boss feels like an achievement. Every expedition feels like a story you'll be telling your friends afterwards. And when you're sailing home across the ocean, watching the sun set over the waves while the music kicks in? Gaming doesn't get much better than that.

But what truly makes Valheim special is the freedom. You can spend your entire evening fighting terrifying creatures, or you can spend six hours building a cosy little village, farming carrots, cooking meals, and pretending you're living a peaceful Viking retirement. Both are equally valid. Both are equally brilliant.

Playing with friends takes it to another level entirely. Nothing brings people together quite like sailing halfway across the world, losing the boat, dying in a swamp, spending two hours recovering your equipment, and somehow deciding that was the best gaming session you've had all year.

The developers have created something genuinely special here. It's challenging without feeling unfair, relaxing without being boring, and rewarding without constantly holding your hand.

Valheim is proof that you don't need photorealistic graphics, battle passes, or a £70 price tag to create one of the greatest survival games ever made. It has heart, personality, incredible atmosphere, and that magical quality that makes you say "just one more thing" until suddenly the sun is coming up in real life.

If you enjoy survival games, exploration, crafting, building, or simply getting lost in a world that feels alive, do yourself a favour and play this game.

And if you've already played it, you already know.

What makes Baldur's Gate 3 so special is the sheer amount of love and effort Larian Studios put into it. It feels like they thought of everything, down to the smallest details. Everywhere you go, there is something new to discover, and even the smallest decisions can have consequences you might not notice until much later. The attention to detail is incredible, and it really shows how much passion went into making this game.

I wasn't sure whether I should compare it to Divinity: Original Sin 2, but since I absolutely loved that game as well, I think it's worth making the comparison.

Compared to DOS2, I found BG3's main story more complex and intriguing. The story unfolds over three acts, each with its own locations, characters, and quests, while the world design makes exploring a joy. The side quests are just as enjoyable as those in DOS2, with plenty of interesting stories and meaningful choices. Your decisions can have consequences far beyond what you initially expect, sometimes becoming apparent much later in the game.

The combat is good and offers plenty of options, with a wide variety of spells, abilities, classes, and equipment to experiment with. However, personally, I preferred the combat in DOS2. While BG3's combat is certainly enjoyable, it didn't quite reach the same level for me. This is one of the few areas where I think DOS2 has the edge.

One of the biggest strengths of BG3 is its presentation. The cutscenes, character animations, and dialogue make you feel much more involved in the world. You don't just feel like you're controlling a character in a story; you feel like you're actually part of it. Combined with the memorable companions and their personal stories, this makes the entire experience incredibly immersive.

And then there is the amount of content. You can easily spend 100–150 hours on a single playthrough, and there is still so much you could experience differently on another run. With so many choices, alternative approaches, and things to discover, the replay value is enormous. You get an incredible amount of content for your money.

Larian Studios really outdid themselves with this game. Even though I prefer certain aspects of DOS2, BG3 offers an incredible RPG experience with a fascinating story, memorable characters, a beautifully crafted world, and an almost ridiculous amount of detail.

I was very excited after first trying this in early access in 2021 and I returned after launch to find that while they've added new biomes, enemies, items, etc. the fundamental issues with the core gameplay loop remain unimproved. Even basic confusing UI seems completely unchanged after 5 years in development. It took us 25 hours to get out of the second biome because the resource grind is so intensely long and unfun. The world generation is often buggy, breaking immersion (tall mountains sloping steeply into the ocean with a repeating texture on the flat, undecorated slope, etc.) and the variety of interesting things to find in the world is low. You'll find the same 3 small ruined buildings over and over and over again as you explore. We'd often work hard to kill a new enemy or find a new resource only to get a single unlock, a cosmetic for our base. Combat is frustrating and unintuitive and most of our deaths were from getting stuck on the environment while fighting instead of being bested by the enemies.

The setting is interesting and a lot of the basics are there, but 5 years in development has landed this game in a place that seems to want you to play hundreds of hours doing the same few basic tasks over and over again and it just isn't fun once you come to this realization. I wish they had spent more of their time making the world more interesting to explore instead of adding so many nearly identical pieces of gear and base building components that you have to grind relentlessly to afford to construct.

I had a friend focus on exploration, research, and collecting upgrade items around the map. While I pretty much just stayed in the base and brute-forced progression and expansion. Not deliberately,  just as a result of the things each of us were interested in.

It really felt like both playstyles were a meaningful contribution to beating the game, and I can imagine other playstyles beyond just "the factory must grow" would also get something out of a group playthrough.

Um universo inteiro para explorar. Simplesmente incrível.

No Man’s Sky é um daqueles jogos em que você começa querendo fazer uma coisinha e, quando percebe, já perdeu horas explorando planetas, descobrindo criaturas, coletando recursos, melhorando sua nave ou simplesmente viajando pelo universo sem rumo.

A sensação de liberdade é absurda. São tantos planetas para explorar, lugares para descobrir e coisas para fazer que parece que sempre existe alguma novidade esperando por você. Quer explorar o espaço? Construir uma base? Melhorar sua frota? Sobreviver em planetas hostis? Ou só sair voando por aí e ver o que encontra? O jogo te deixa fazer tudo isso no seu próprio ritmo.

E o mais impressionante é a escala de tudo. Você olha para o espaço, escolhe um planeta e simplesmente vai até lá. Essa liberdade de viajar, pousar e explorar é uma das coisas mais legais que já experimentei em um jogo.

Claro, ainda existem alguns bugs e problemas técnicos aqui e ali, mas, na minha experiência, raramente chegam ao ponto de estragar de verdade a diversão. São pequenos tropeços em um jogo que oferece tanta coisa que fica fácil relevar.

No Man’s Sky é um jogo gigantesco, cheio de possibilidades e com uma liberdade absurda. É aquele tipo de experiência em que você pode criar seus próprios objetivos e jogar por centenas de horas sem sentir que está fazendo sempre a mesma coisa.

É simplesmente foda. Um universo praticamente sem fim para explorar, milhares de possibilidades e aquela vontade de continuar viajando só para descobrir o que existe no próximo planeta.

Se você gosta de exploração espacial, sobrevivência e jogos que deixam você jogar do seu jeito, vale muito a pena!

Project Zomboid is a stinking mess of a software that's been stuck in development hell since 2013 with no signs of the end in sight. It is a 'decent' game at its core with lots of mods/custom difficulty but all the cool thing this game does gets thrown out the window when you have to interact with it through its atrocious UI system. Do you want to cook ? Right click your stew 5 times and navigate a drop down that covers the entire screen to add an ingredient which gets consumed by a random amount depends on how the game feels that day. Want to level car mechanic skills ? Right click the car parts to take out and reinstall from a dropdown menu 100 times until you develop RSI. Want to build a cool house ? Not only you have to navigate the atrocious UI to find the stuff you want (which is like, one step up from the shitty drop down), you also have to repeat the process like 10 times while shuttling between storage and build sites as if deploying blueprint and depositing resource isn't the standard across these kind of game for like a decade. Every single item you right click in this game have like 50 billion option in its drop down that you will legit use only 2. 

I have other qualms with how janky the game is or how it seems to love implementing features that exists solely to make you miserable BUT they are either not that bad/can be played around or straight up turned off so it's a miniscule issue compared to the UI. 

I think it genuinely has the potential to be the single most comprehensive and fun zombie survival game out there that can range from bleak apocalypse simulation to casual friendslop experience but the only thing that holds it back are the jank and that's not going anywhere soon after 13 years.

I've played Terraria for about ten years now, on every device and platform I've ever owned. It's always been filled to the brim with cool things to collect, monsters to kill, things to build, places to explore, goals to pursue. I liked the GBA and DS Castlevania games growing up and Terraria to me is those, with metric tons more content and building. 

Every time I come back I learn something new. Every time I hop into a new world I spend dozens of hours needlessly mining and collecting shiny things to sort into chests back home, like a loot goblin with OCD. I recently realized not only can I paint walls and furniture and trees, but that I can dye clothes and armor and accessories. 

It's like the collection and exploration aspect of Skyrim, but the game loop of Minecraft, and the graphics of GBA/DS era pixel graphics side scrollers. 

There is enough content by itself to last a lifetime if you're like me and enjoy world hopping and plundering and building. If you mod it, you'll have to pass your save down to your kids and their kids after them because that well runs deep.

It also runs on potatoes. I have a 10 year old office laptop with no gaming guts to speak of and Terraria runs smooth on it. This laptop starts to sweat if you so much as open Youtube and a Reddit sub at the same time. I know that's not saying much as Terraria literally has GBA era pixel graphics, but you'd be surprised how many extremely low res games stutter and lag on this thing. Not Terraria though. 

100/10 would recommend. Play it solo or drag a friend or two into it. It plays good no matter how you come at it.

Path of Exile is an outstanding free-to-play action RPG that delivers an incredibly deep and demanding adventure through a world consumed by darkness, corruption, and supernatural horrors. Developed and published by Grinding Gear Games, it distinguishes itself through extraordinary character customization, challenging combat, and an enormous collection of interconnected progression systems. Set on the hostile continent of Wraeclast, the game places players in the role of an exile fighting to survive against terrifying creatures and powerful adversaries. Its greatest achievement is the freedom it provides to experiment with different playstyles, although that same complexity can make the experience intimidating for newcomers. For players who appreciate intricate mechanics and long-term character development, it offers one of the most substantial experiences available in the genre.

The atmosphere immediately establishes a grim and unforgiving identity. Abandoned settlements, corrupted wildernesses, ancient ruins, and grotesque monsters create a convincing world where danger feels ever-present. The narrative gradually reveals the disturbing history of Wraeclast through quests, dialogue, environmental storytelling, and encounters with memorable characters. Although the lore is extensive and fascinating, its presentation sometimes takes a secondary role to relentless combat and equipment progression. Nevertheless, the dark fantasy setting remains compelling, supported by excellent environmental design, unsettling sound effects, and atmospheric music that reinforces the feeling of exploring a civilization devastated by supernatural forces.

Combat is fast, destructive, and remarkably flexible. Players can specialize in melee attacks, ranged weapons, elemental spells, summoned allies, traps, and numerous unconventional combinations. Defeating large groups of enemies with carefully developed abilities creates an immensely satisfying sense of power, while challenging bosses demand awareness, preparation, and appropriate defensive strategies. The skill gem system is particularly impressive because abilities can be modified through support gems, allowing seemingly ordinary attacks to evolve into devastating combinations. However, encounters can become visually chaotic when numerous projectiles and effects overwhelm the screen. Certain character builds also encourage repetitive ability usage, making extended grinding sessions occasionally monotonous.

Character progression represents the game's most distinctive accomplishment. Its enormous passive skill tree provides an astonishing degree of freedom, allowing players to construct highly specialized characters without being completely restricted by traditional class identities. Ascendancy specializations introduce additional layers of customization, while equipment modifiers and skill interactions create countless opportunities for experimentation. Discovering effective combinations can be incredibly rewarding, especially when a carefully planned build begins overcoming previously impossible challenges. Unfortunately, the learning curve is exceptionally steep. Newcomers may struggle to understand complicated mechanics, and poorly distributed passive points can significantly weaken a character. The game rewards research and patience but offers comparatively little forgiveness for inexperienced decisions.

Equipment acquisition and crafting provide another compelling foundation for progression. Defeated enemies frequently drop weapons, armor, accessories, and valuable crafting materials, encouraging constant experimentation with different combinations of attributes. The unconventional currency system gives numerous resources practical crafting functions, creating a fascinating relationship between item improvement and trading. Finding a rare piece of equipment or successfully crafting a powerful upgrade can feel genuinely exciting. However, randomized outcomes occasionally make progression frustrating, particularly when substantial resources disappear without producing worthwhile improvements. Inventory management also becomes increasingly demanding as players accumulate enormous quantities of equipment and specialized materials.

The endgame offers exceptional longevity through the Atlas of Worlds, challenging maps, formidable bosses, and numerous specialized activities. Completing the main campaign opens the door to increasingly sophisticated progression systems that encourage players to refine their characters and pursue more difficult encounters. Challenge leagues further enhance replayability by introducing fresh mechanics and opportunities to begin new adventures. These features make the game particularly appealing to dedicated players who enjoy optimization and continuous improvement. However, the sheer amount of available content can feel overwhelming, and reaching the highest levels of progression often requires considerable grinding and detailed mechanical knowledge.

Multiplayer adds another dimension through cooperative encounters, trading, and community interaction. Players can collaborate against dangerous enemies or participate in an extensive economy where valuable equipment and crafting resources are exchanged. The game also supports independent progression, although a persistent internet connection remains necessary. Its free-to-play model is commendable because the core adventure and substantial endgame content are accessible without mandatory purchases. Most optional transactions involve cosmetics, while additional stash tabs provide meaningful storage convenience. These purchases are not required to enjoy the campaign, but dedicated players may find them increasingly useful.

From a technical perspective, the game delivers impressive environmental detail, distinctive monster designs, and spectacular combat effects. Its visual presentation successfully captures the brutality of its setting, although performance can fluctuate during encounters involving numerous enemies and elaborate abilities. Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable, meaning the game can be enjoyed on Valve's handheld system but is not fully Verified. Controller support makes combat accessible, although navigating complicated menus, managing inventory, and examining detailed equipment descriptions can feel cumbersome on the smaller display. Graphically demanding encounters may also require reduced settings for smoother performance.

Ultimately, Path of Exile is a remarkable achievement in action RPG design, offering exceptional customization, rewarding combat, and almost overwhelming replayability. Its greatest weaknesses are its intimidating complexity, occasional performance problems, demanding inventory management, and reliance on repetitive grinding. Nevertheless, these shortcomings rarely diminish the satisfaction of mastering its elaborate systems and developing increasingly powerful characters. It is particularly recommended for players who enjoy strategic character building, challenging encounters, and extensive endgame progression. Those seeking a casual adventure may find its demands exhausting, but dedicated enthusiasts will discover an extraordinarily rewarding experience.

I don't even know where to start, this game has gotten me through insanely difficult times and has been an incredibly safe and overwhelmingly fun experience. When I was first eyeballing it I was deeply interested but hesitant to get it because I've never played any automation game or deep-systems based game before, especially one that requires quite a bit of math to truly get the most out of it. I was particularly concerned I wouldn't be able to keep up with the demand the game puts on players deeper in the game given how big factories would become in mid-game and beyond; Especially given I have a learning disability with math called dyscalculia which is, functionally, dyslexia with numbers and symbols. That disability has caused a lot of strife in my early years, and pretty much made me despise math of any kind as a result, but Satisfactory has changed that.

 At first I was building semi organized spaghetti factories, gridded ones, but still spaghetti nonetheless, but when I started to really put in the time to properly plan out factories, learn what does and doesn't work, developing the skills to troubleshoot, I actually began to really take the game seriously. This game genuinely has as way of rewiring your cognition in a way no teacher was able to when I was in my schooling days. Through an indirect but still hands on approach, it taught me necessary organizational and planning skills I desperately needed in my life given I also have ADHD and it actually made me find math FUN. I've never in all my years found a single thing that could make math fun. At first I found water planning tedious and annoying, but by the time I got to oil and started working on my very first off-shore style on-shore oil rig/facility, I was genuinely getting excited at number-crunching and getting a huge dopamine hit off seeing my math actually working correctly. In school (at least American schooling), you don't see physical tangible results from your math in your formative years and it can all be so dull and mind-numbing to the point of pain, but in this game you get tangible visual feedback for all of your hard work and planning, and the /Satisfaction/ of seeing it all work and unlocking new technology and milestones is a feeling no other game has provided to me before.

On top of the math skills the game helped me develop and refine, it also wired my brain to be more geared toward logistics and planning, which (without getting into too many personal details) when I went homelessness in '25 became functionally life-saving. I was able to organize and plan financial details and action plans that not only saved myself but my partner and my household from being stuck on the streets, whereas in previous years I was an absolute mess in terms of planning and logistical needs. During this time frame, while I was without access to my computer, all I could think of besides keeping those I loved safe, was playing this game again and working on my factory that I had put so much of my life into the previous months. This game gave me goals, motivation, and critical thinking skills that genuinely kept me out of an incredibly dark place and kept me safe. Oh, and on top of that, it helped me stay sober (I straight up couldn't play the game when zonked out of my gourd on the green stuff).
*
*
*
Outside of the personal stuff, the game is a masterpiece in game design, from the atmospheric music, how sound reverberates based on different conditions and spaces, to how addictive yet educational it can be. I literally haven't even gotten past the halfway point of the game (after which nuclear becomes available and the game really takes off) because I've been obsessed with upgrading and rebuilding my factory in better and more efficient and grand ways. I'm currently on Phase 3 and I've spent a vast majority of the hours you see working on a Cyberpunk 2077 inspired Megabuilding which houses an Iron all in one factory that consumes 5 Gigawatts of power and 6750 Iron Ore per Minute. This game WILL consume your life, but it can even improve it if you're someone like me. If you need a game to lose yourself in for an unholy amount of time and aren't resistant to math/developing your math skills, love architecture and design, or just want the *perfect* automation experience this is the game for you.
Got a touch of the 'tism? You got every kind of tool for expressing it here, and yes, that includes *trains* which is a whole game within itself.

11/10 would spend 1000+ more hours on it without hesitation.

(Also I really think this game should be used as an educational tool in schools)

Well, I figured it was finally time to leave a review after playing this game multiple times and finally "finishing" it with the 1.0 release. Would I recommend it? Absolutely.

Valheim is a fantastic game for anyone who enjoys a mix of exploration, base-building, and combat. The combination works really well, but personally, the building is where the game really shines. The building system gives you tons of freedom, but also rewards planning and understanding how its mechanics work if you want to create something truly impressive. And when everything comes together? It's just beautiful.

The game can be fun solo, but it's so much better with friends. I'll never forget the first big city we built, the long journeys to haul back all the iron and other materials we collected, or the countless deaths caused by... cutting trees. So many great memories. And in my book, that's a pretty good sign of a game well done.

That said, as much as I love this game and as many hours as I've put into it, it's certainly not perfect.

Over the years, I feel like some areas, particularly quality-of-life features, have taken far too long to improve. Considering the game spent 5 years in Early Access, it's VERY disappointing to still be missing so many basic features. Things like crafting directly from nearby chests, a quick way to stash items, and a better-organized personal inventory might sound like small things, but they make a huge difference in a game where you're constantly juggling mountains of materials from start to finish.

Thankfully, there are TONS of mods that can make the experience much better. Honestly, I can say with confidence that I probably wouldn't have played Valheim nearly as much as I did without the incredible modding community.

So, a massive shoutout to all the modders out there creating SO MANY INCREDIBLE MODS! You guys are absolute legends. Thank you!

And a big thanks to the devs as well for creating such a great game and allowing the community to do its thing instead of trying to shut down or restrict what players and modders create.

Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing short of a monumental achievement in modern gaming. Its meticulously crafted open world, breathtaking visual fidelity, and extraordinarily immersive atmosphere set a benchmark that few titles can even aspire to reach. Night City is not merely a backdrop for the narrative; it is a living, breathing metropolis, teeming with moral ambiguity, social stratification, technological obsession, and the haunting consequences of unchecked corporate power.

What truly distinguishes the game, however, is its narrative sophistication. Beneath its dazzling neon lights and futuristic spectacle lies a profoundly human story about identity, mortality, freedom, and the desperate pursuit of meaning in an increasingly dehumanised world. Its characters are remarkably nuanced, its dialogue often incisive, and its most emotionally resonant moments linger long after the credits roll.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing less than extraordinary. The interplay of neon illumination, atmospheric fog, intricate environmental detail, and sophisticated lighting techniques creates an aesthetic that is simultaneously mesmerising and unsettling. Night City feels as though it has been ripped from the darkest, most compelling visions of the future and brought to life with astonishing technical precision.

Ultimately, Cyberpunk 2077 transcends the boundaries of conventional entertainment. It is an ambitious, thought-provoking, and occasionally heartbreaking exploration of what it means to remain human in a world that increasingly treats humanity as a commodity. Few games manage to combine such artistic ambition, narrative depth, and technological brilliance so convincingly. Cyberpunk 2077 is not merely a game worth experiencing; it is an experience that exemplifies the extraordinary artistic potential of the medium itself.

Let me paint a picture for you: You launch this game thinking, "Oh, neat, a cozy little Viking survival game with retro graphics."
Fast forward 60 hours.
It’s 3:00 AM. You are screaming into your mic because a giant blue troll just smashed your beautifully crafted, OSHA-violating longhouse into splinters. Your friend is running for his life naked through a swamp, and you just died trying to transport four pieces of copper ore across an ocean during a thunderstorm.
And you know what? You’ll log right back on tomorrow to do it all over again.
Valheim is an absolute masterpiece of survival gaming. It perfectly balances the brutal, unforgiving nature of Norse mythology with an incredibly satisfying gameplay loop.
Why you should buy it:
• The Building: You start with a leaky shack and end up building a massive, sprawling Viking citadel (just make sure you build a chimney, or you will literally suffocate on your own campfire smoke).
• The Atmosphere: The lighting and music are so breathtakingly beautiful that you’ll forget you're playing a low-poly game. Sail into an ocean sunset just once, and you'll see what I mean.
• The Progression: Every boss you defeat unlocks a whole new era of tech and completely changes how you play.
• The Physics: Trees are the most dangerous enemy in the early game. If you chop a tree down and it falls on you, you die. If it falls on another tree, it triggers a domino effect of wooden destruction. It's glorious.
Whether you want to play it solo as a serene, peaceful farming simulator, or grab 3 friends and treat it like a chaotic, high-stakes Viking raid simulator, this game is worth every single penny.
Pros: Incredible co-op, deep crafting, immersive exploration, epic boss fights.
Cons: Mosquitoes. If you know, you know. 🦟

This game is one I started back roughly when it first launched as basically nothing more than a demo.   I tried to enjoy it and just absolutely couldn't.

The learning curve was just too difficult, but I watched others play and learned tips and tricks with excitement rather than annoyance.

Then about 5 years ago, I picked it up again.  This time I went deep.   I learned how to survive, I learned how to accept loss, and I loved the customized experience I could make for myself.   Zomboid finally felt like a game that was without question the best zombie survival experience I could have.   Did it still have frustrating issues with direction aim?  yes.   Is it a perfect experience?  no.   But it's absolutely the best I can enjoy without question compared to other zombie survival experiences out there.   Others have tried, and some have done very well in their own experiences.   But this game is probably the ONLY true zombie survival experience that I truly and completely enjoyed.

Over 2000 hours later, and I'm STILL hooked, and I'm STILL amazed by the developer's care and focus on developing the game further.    It absolutely helps that The Indie Stone, make just about every single new addition a customizable experience in the custom sandbox option.   Add a modding community that makes incredible additional tailored experiences and you basically get Skyrim but zombies with infinite replayability.

The game IS a difficulty curve to learn.  I recommend you start simple, and work your way to harder difficulties.   I still don't think I can handle 100% sprinters, but that's ok, for me the experience is wonderful without them.  For those that want a challenge you can absolutely and always find it.

I really wanted to love this game on release. I spent over 900 hours in Valheim throughout the Early Access. I built massive bases, conquered every biome, and two years ago put the game on hold to wait for the complete product, hoping Iron Gate would polish the core mechanics and give the game the grand finale it deserved. That full release finally arrived, and I have never been more disappointed. What they slapped the "1.0" label on is still strictly Early Access quality, and the final biome - the Deep North - feels like a lazy conclusion to a once-promising journey. 

It took the development team two years to deliver a vast, empty, and utterly lifeless biome, which is in large part just recycled assets from the Meadows, Black Forest, and Mountain biomes mashed together. The biome has barely any mob spawns to keep you engaged, and points of interest are mostly useless. Chests from villages and ship graveyards contain the same junk you already got tired of in the Meadows. Feathers and arrows. Very rewarding.  There is zero sense of survival or threat in this final area. It feels completely hollow. You barely meet any enemies, with half of those being good old skeletons, greydwarfs, fulings, and dvergrs.  And then there are seals—whether by mistake or intent, the devs forgot to attach behavior to them. They just sit on the ice like inert sacks while you walk up and whack them for resources. 

But the most disappointing part is building. Building used to be the main reason I dumped hundreds of hours into this game, but 1.0 does almost nothing for builders. No scaling or free rotation of building pieces. No new stone building pieces. No new metal building pieces. No new cloth decorations. Boring wood pieces & furniture. The only good addition is the wardrobe.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is, without a doubt, the best game I have ever played.

It’s been a long time since a game has completely taken over my mind the way this one has. When I wasn’t playing it, I was thinking about it. It was all consuming in the best possible way, and I honestly can’t remember the last time a game had such a hold on me.

For context, I have over 600 hours on console, and I’ve since started two runs on PC. One of those is my first time playing alongside someone else rather than playing solo, and I genuinely didn’t think this game could get any better than it already was. Somehow, it has.

Playing alongside someone else has opened up an entirely new side of the experience, and I’m enjoying it just as much, if not more, than I did the first time around.

That’s what makes Baldur’s Gate 3 so special to me. It isn’t just a game you finish and move on from. It’s a game you can return to, time and time again, and still find something new to love. The freedom, the choices, the characters, the stories, and the sheer number of ways you can experience the world make it feel like there’s always something waiting to be discovered.

This game deserves every positive review, every award, every recommendation, and every bit of praise it receives. Games like this are rare, and I feel genuinely lucky to have experienced something that has brought me this much enjoyment.

Three years on, hundreds of hours in, and I’m still not done. I don’t think I will be for a long time.

I'll start the review completely honest, I originally refunded this game. It later went on sale, and I picked it back up again to give it another shot. It was an incredible decision. When you get through your head that you will inevitably die, the experience becomes far more enjoyable than your expectations. This game has a steep learning curve, lots of systems to learn and manage, and tons of items with even more interactions. This makes every run essentially a roguelike experience with your meta progression being permanent knowledge of the game and it's core loop. Each time you go back out to die again, you'll pick up new tidbits of information, map knowledge, potentially new gear/weapons/resources, and gain the opportunity to deploy different strategies and tactics. 

It was several runs later that I figured out you can keep making new characters from your dead ones to keep a persistent world and progression continuing. That added whole new layers of depth I couldn't wait to explore. I was using pretty failed runs to just drag corpses off the highways, go fetch vehicles and bring them back to base, and clean up some stray walkers. You can take even your worst runs and make them mean something if you learn to manage your time wisely.

All in all, this game is truly special. It really forces you to adapt and try to outsmart the process, just for something completely unexpected to happen for better or most likely worse (but in a good way, if you've played, you know).  Always keeping you on your toes, giving you tons of different situations, maps, buildings, threat levels to deal with adds near infinite levels of replay-ability. Not to mention the insanely outstanding community and it's mod support as well. This game will be eternal and I'm here for it in this life and the next and the next and the next and the.....

Not even 1 hour in Johnny immediately hijacks the story and the rest of the story is basically V being taken along for the ride in Johnny's story, hell one of the endings are literally just johnny taking over at the end and V not even being aware of what's going on. V themself also is a very selfish and shallow character, what else does V wanted out of their life other than becoming a legend, get rich, or survive; I really can't find anything else that V values even towards the end. The game does not give me a reason to root for V, and there is also no sense of urgency to V's condition beyond the cutscenes, I just doesn't care about V at all as a character, let alone engage with their story. 

The world building is also extremely generic. Hell it's name literally is just it's genre + 2077, you could not find a game that is more of a parody of cyberpunk than this game. "Oh no! AI will take over!" Yeah like I haven't seen this story already in Terminator, 2001 a Space Odyssey, The Matrix, I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, Dune, exc... all of them have a deeper exploration into the topic than this game does. And the concept of Rogue AI is also so dumb, like the writer don't understand how technology works, they think AI programs can just "exist" in the magical realm that is the net, without requiring a hardware to run on, like human's can't just locate the server that contains the rogue AI and cut it's power source. And don't even get me started on "Capitalism Bad" and how even more generic and milked to death that topic is. Night City also don't give my any desire to explore it, when basically 95% of the building is just a shell with no interiors, filled with pedestrians that are dumber than a squirrel. Fallout 4 gives me better motivation to explore it's world than this game, and it's literally just a wasteland. There just isn't anything interesting in night city to explore and discover, most of the lore are basically shards with text messages for me to read telling the same generic miserable story about, you guess it, "Capitalism Bad". There is also very little philosophical exploration on the nature of identity, in a game where the story is literally about one person's identity overriding the other, which is just another massive waste of potential in a mountain of wasted potential that is this game. Like imagine V contemplating what it means to be yourself, and questioning rather or not merging with another person's identity is really that bad, like what if instead of Johnny taking over, their identity merges and becomes a whole new person that is neither Johnny or V, imagine the potential of the premise of transferable consciousness and identity, but NO, this game doesn't explore ANY of those possibilities! Ghost in the Shell explore a lot of these topics, so I don't know why they didn't even study one of the most popular cyberpunk franchise out there and learn from it, like I'm not even asking you to have original ideas, at least match the depth of other stories in the same genre! 

I can use two words to summarize this game: Wasted Potential. Valheim, on release, was an innovative and fun take on the genre. It came up with (or at least, was the first popular game with) several concepts that ended up being copied by most other open world survival crafters. Unfortunately, Valheim suffered from its obscenely slow development which didn't even implement half of its old roadmap. Those games that copied its systems have all done them better by now and, in general, have way more quality of life and less overall jank. Valheim was easily a game I would recommend years ago. But now that it has finally released while barely making any changes and taking years to add less content than what modders could release at higher quality in a few months? No, I don't recommend it. A less jank, more fun Valheim experience that can compete with other games in the genre requires heavily modding the game now, and I'm basing this review on the vanilla game as a final product released in 2026, not its potential with mods nor my enjoyment of it earlier in development before the developers released such a disappointing 1.0.

But also, let me be positive for a moment here. To this day, there is still no other game in the genre that has as satisfying sailing and logistics. I absolutely love loading up a cart with a ton of wood or metal and slowly hauling it back to base. I am in love with the sailing mechanics and have happily spent dozens of hours sailing in this game either to explore or to haul metals for myself or friends. Not a single other game has made the logistics side of thing as enjoyable as Valheim. Of course, I'm apparently the weird one for loving this side of Valheim, because it seems like the vast majority of the community prefers enabling metal transport via portals and absolutely despise using the cart.

I also like the graphics. Yeah, they make the game look old, but it's stylistic and helps set it apart from others.

Unfortunately, that is where my praise ends.

Fighting on slopes is still cancer due to hit detection even after the developers "fixed" it. Enemies can frequently hit you through gaps despite you not being able to hit them (a major pain in the ass going through swamp crypts). The difficulty scaling--oh my fucking god the difficulty scaling. My friends and I love playing games on the highest difficulty, but Valheim handles difficulty in such a stupid way. All Valheim does is increase enemy health, speed, and damage. It's extremely artificial difficulty. Not only is it artificial, but it completely breaks some "class" options and forces you to either cheese or dodge-roll and abuse immunity frames to survive.

You know those shields, especially tower shields, available every single tier? That are good for nothing but blocking? Hah, guess what? It doesn't matter how much you minmax your armor and health. Trying to actually be a tank and block things in this game on anything other than the normal difficulty (which is disgustingly easy) is worthless and will get you killed. The game scales up enemy damage while leaving shields balanced around normal damage, so the shields are literally just worthless. Even parrying becomes mechanically impossible on the hardest difficulty. The extremely simple solution to this (possible with mods) is to increase the block power of shields to match the difficulty. This way, shields don't become literally useless on anything above normal while still punishing you for making mistakes or getting in over your head. But if the developers knew how to balance this game instead of set the stats once five years ago and then never touch them again, this review would probably be positive.

Not being able to craft or build from nearby chests is annoying, but that on its own is not that much of an issue. But then there's no sorting option and, far worse, building requires stamina. Do you want to just chill at your base and do some building? Have fun having to stop every 15 seconds to wait for your stamina to recharge. Change your mind about how something looks and want to tear it down to try again? Have fun waiting for your stamina to recharge. Waiting on stamina just to *build* is extremely unfun.

Resource rates are extremely unbalanced as well. There are a good few resources you will get infinite amounts of that have next to zero uses, and then the things that are actually useful several times over require hours and hours of grinding for. And this is just if you don't even want to build a lot. If you get inspired seeing some huge build someone posted online, you need to either increase the resource rates by a huge amount (which will also flood you with a disgusting amount of the resources you don't want that are already too common) or cheat.

Another issue is skill balancing. Some skills level up pretty fairly. Other skills, like farming, cooking, crafting, blocking, etc, make Runescape skilling feel fast. But don't worry, if you die, you lose progress in all your skills equally.

And then. And then! What do the developers add in 1.0 as an attempt to make it so that any weapon or piece of armor in the game can potentially be useful throughout the entire game? Korean MMO gacha upgrade mechanics designed to waste time and keep people playing a game for months to years! Someone did the math and, on average, a world should have around six iron battle idols across every single swamp-tier chest. That's disgusting. And on top of that, there's a 35% chance every single time you upgrade a weapon using these idols that the weapon just straight up breaks and you lose all your upgrades while only getting a tiny fraction of materials back. That's really what the game needed after half of its roadmap was abandoned while taking 5 years without adding any quality of life or fixing jank. Gacha upgrade mechanics reliant on RNG upon RNG. Oh, and they also broke the rare drop system (mainly noticeable when hunting for trophies of rare enemies) because... I don't know, they wanted to try and fix a system that wasn't broken and ended up releasing their new system in a broken state for their big ol' 1.0 release and it still hasn't been fixed even after a month?

There is far more I can bitch and whine about, but other reviews have already got most of my other complaints covered, and a review can only be so long. I've lost any faith in these developers to ever make Valheim good (in comparison to other, more recent games of the genre), and I sure as fuck won't ever spend money on any early access title from them again.

What a ride. The worldbuilding in Cyberpunk is great—it immediately sets the tone for the world you will soon be let loose in, showing the rawness and dystopian nature of Night City. The game covers a lot of subjects, such as politics, the economy, corporations, history, the loss of a loved one, depression, PTSD, and more.

I initially dropped this game somewhere around the end of Act I and returned months later. I decided to start a completely fresh playthrough since I had forgotten a lot of the story. It wasn't until this playthrough that I got the opportunity to appreciate how dynamic the gameplay can be. The Skill Tree allows for a plethora of choices on how YOU want to play Cyberpunk 2077. Want to be a Cyberpsycho with a katana and a Sandy (Sandevistan) to slow down time? Sure. Prefer to be a brute with Gorilla Arms and land explosive punches? Go ahead. Want to be a Skyrim-like stealth archer, but with a silenced pistol? It's here. The gameplay really is GREAT!

I wasn't here when the game was the infamous dumpster fire we all know. But I can testify the game is great now and runs smoothly, especially on a mid-tier setup like mine (specs attached). Easily getting 130-160 FPS.

However, there's something that bugs me, and it's the story pacing. Act I is phenomenal. It introduces the main character, their backstory of your choice, the heist, and [spoiler] Johnny Silverhand—showing the consequences of raw ambition for fame, glory, and riches. [/spoiler]

Personally, the game carries the story well... until the end of Act II. Suddenly, everything just feels very rushed and lackluster once you reach the Point of No Return. I also found, disappointingly, Act III to be extremely short in comparison to the others. I played multiple endings and found most of them just... meh? Like, c'mon. The game kicks off with a bang... literally. But towards the end, it feels like a slow-burning candle with an almost exhausted wick.

Aside from that, I really have nothing negative to say about Cyberpunk 2077. The creativity that went into this is WILD. Props to CD Projekt Red for not doing an Anthem and instead standing behind this project.

I have REALLY tried to love this game. And to be fair, I played a LOT of hours in it, that made it worth the money... I guess.

The game can be beautiful and spectacular - even thought provoking at times.
But the game is also riddled with - sometimes game-breaking - bugs that have been around for YEARS.
The interface often tries to fight you. Some keys are mapped to multiple competing functions BY DEFAULT, while some functions can't be remapped at all. The game often glitches and causes you, NPCs and/or buildings to spawn in impossible locations or even out of bounds. Mission targets can get lost, causing the missions to be stuck and need you to abandon them. Cinematics appear on EVERY interaction and on EVERY travel, with no way to turning them off. Even simple things like turning in requested materials to a quest giver can take the better part of a minute to finish, because the game would rather have you watch a marker animate over the screen, instead of quickly updating your mission status. No joke: It takes almost 10 minutes to accept 5 salvage missions - that you already have the resources in your inventory for - and hand them in "immediately"...

Some features of the game are completely outdated by newer additions of the game, but kept in game for no reason - like the various exocraft, that most players build once for tutorials or missions and then never use again, because they are frustrating and useless for the majority of gameplay.

The main story is also very short and convoluted with no real conclusion - well there is, but also isn't...

Most of the time I played the game, I made up my own goals or targets. If that is your thing and you want to experience a vast galaxy that appears... mostly empty while you work around bugs and outdated irrelevant features, then go for it - when the game is at a discount. Otherwise get a game with a non-procedurally-generate world.

The building is fantastic, the world is beautiful, and the atmosphere is about as good as it gets. Every biome feels different, and exploring the world is genuinely enjoyable. The music and sound design deserve a mention too. They do a lot to make the world feel alive.

Building is probably my favorite part. There's a ton of freedom to get creative, and unlocking new building pieces as you progress through the biomes gives you something to work toward beyond just getting stronger equipment. There's a lot of content here, especially for new players. I enjoy a good grind, so the resource gathering and progression don't bother me much.

The game is also perfectly playable solo, but playing in a shared world with friends is where it's at. Working toward the same goals, building things together and getting into trouble along the way make for some great memories. It's the kind of game where the stories you end up telling your friends can be just as good as the game itself.

My biggest complaint is the combat. It's pretty shallow. You hit things, then dodge, block or run away. Fighting multiple enemies can be a pain, and the lack of target lock doesn't help. The bosses aren't particularly challenging either. Honestly, combat and difficulty are the weakest parts of the game, and I'd love to see more depth added here.

But even with those shortcomings, I keep coming back. The world, building, and co-op experience make up for a lot, and the value for money is ridiculous. 800 hours in, I'm still looking forward to what's next.

An Incredible Survival Game Full of Adventure and Possibilities!

Rust is one of those survival games that keeps you coming back for more. I love the freedom it gives you to explore, gather resources, build your own base, and find your place in a dangerous open world. Every time you play, you can have a completely different experience, which makes the game incredibly replayable.

One of my favorite things about Rust is how satisfying progression feels. Starting with almost nothing and gradually working your way toward better equipment, stronger defenses, and a more impressive base is a rewarding experience. There's always something to work toward, whether you're exploring the map, collecting materials, crafting items, or expanding your home.

I also love how unpredictable the world can be. Other players add an extra layer of excitement because you never quite know whether an encounter will turn into a friendship, a trade, or a fight. Working together with friends to survive, defend your base, and gather resources makes the experience even more enjoyable.

The base-building aspect is another huge highlight for me. I love being able to design and customize a place of my own while figuring out how to protect everything I've worked hard to collect. The combination of creativity, strategy, exploration, and survival makes Rust stand out from other games in the genre.

Overall, Rust is a fantastic survival game with tons of freedom, exciting encounters, and endless possibilities. Whether you're playing solo or teaming up with friends, there's always a new challenge waiting around the corner. If you enjoy open-world survival games where your decisions matter and every adventure creates its own story, Rust is absolutely worth playing!

[h1] Potential: The Game [/h1]

I wanted to enjoy Valheim. My group of friends played up to the plains biome prior to 1.0. The building is really satisfying, the graphics are gorgeous, and simply existing in the world fills me with a sense of relaxation and nostalgia. The developers created an amazing system to build on and expand in coming updates. And they did, but...

[h3] Issue #1 - Update Integration [/h3]

Your character levels certain skills through usage that you lose upon death. The system seems to promote weapon specialization - the only way to level up a weapon skill a decent amount requires either a lot of fighting or mindless training. As the game grew, the developers added new weapon types. I was excited as more styles of fighting were added; fist weapons were added later in development and sprinkled throughout progression. The problem is that the devs didn't stick to this system. Greatswords, both forms of magic, and crossbows are all fully locked until the last stretch of the game, and knives don't get any upgrades past the 2/3 mark of the game. This bizarre spread forces the player to farm experience for any level of proficiency with some of the most interesting weapon types, while also disincentivizing a mixed arsenal.

[h3] Issue #2 - Balancing [/h3]

If a player is forced to commit to a weapon type, it would be safe to assume every weapon type would be decent. In Valheim, this simply isn't true. Some players found it easy to defeat bosses with bows early on. Instead of developing the bosses around this (i.e. add in ranged attack patterns, better pathfinding, etc), the bosses were  [b] all [/b] given resistance to piercing damage. This heavy-handed response nuked the usefulness of bows, but also caught spears and other weapons that deal piercing damage in the crossfire. Tower shields, similarly, have been left in the dust with the parry-/dodge-centric combat, making the most expensive shield type worthless in any fight.

Bosses themselves aren't very fun. I enjoy how each shrine makes the player explore their biome, and the anticipation was thrilling as the world shook with every summon. Then I would stare at the side of the boss for upwards of half an hour, stabbing pinpricks into its health. The "difficulty" of most bosses comes from their sponginess. The unique gimmicks were never fun to interact with. (Boss Spoilers) [spoiler] The Elder's roots are stationary and mostly non-threats, Bonemass' poison is nothing more than a potion-brewing tutorial, Moder just forces waiting around, Yagluth's big AoEs "test" the player's ability to run around like a headless fuling, the Queen's endless enemy spawning was frustrating, Fader's slow lingering attacks waste time, and the final boss just summons all these disappointments over again. [/spoiler] These fights throw a damage sponge at you, give it some quirk that will either waste your time with no counter or not be a threat at all, and call it a grand battle.

The Shrine of Potential is used to infinitely upgrade a weapon past its prime with a flat 35% chance to destroy the item - already a system most players never touch due to the exorbitant risk-reward ratio. This is made worse by the fact that it must be found in a biome halfway through progression, while the altar itself is made to be used on weapons of all tiers. The player has no need to upgrade old equipment with their gathered upgrade idols as their new gear will be more powerful, and there's no reason to upgrade the new gear when they risk losing a large portion of materials they've recently fought to gather for a tiny boost.

[h3] Issue #3 - Design [/h3]

Valheim is made to be slow. Smell roses, bask in beauty, cherish moments, seize days, and all that. Why, then, does the player home randomly get attacked with ever-more-dangerous raids of enemies? These raids don't provide the player with any unique challenge, reward, or spectacle past the sudden surprise of a few enemies that have already been surpassed. In practice, these raids only serve to disrupt whatever chore the player is doing. Building, farming, and crafting are all harried by a constant small pressure that keeps the player on edge. This same problems extends to the meadows, which grow more dangerous as the game continues yet is likely where the player built their first home.

Base-building, while on a great foundation, has been tarnished by the rest of the game. Material costs are exorbitant, and many materials in the world are limited. Trees will eventually stop dropping seeds, and the player risks eventually having to sail between islands just for a new shed. Stone building, which adds a massive layer of depth to the system, is locked until mid-game. When the stonecutter is brought home, not many players are going to want to tear up their wooden house to completely redesign their base in a slightly different building system.

Exploration, while fun when discovering a new biome, quickly grows old and boring. While there are some small sub-biomes, the world is dotted with only a few visually distinct biomes. After exploring one, the player will know exactly what to expect in every other similar biome across the world. After finding the 3 traders in the world (usually by sailing around the edges of islands for hours), there's no more reason to explore.

The sailing itself hardly counts as exploration; the ocean itself only has one uncommon creature and one small formation only useful for a few niche early game items. Every time the player sets out to sea, they can expect half an hour of sailing in one direction with no real obstacles or difficulties. The biggest opponent on the water is, ironically, the wind. The wind system in Valheim adds nothing to gameplay - not arrow drifting, not blowing the player around, not some unique storm-related enemy. The wind system instead serves to waste the player's time. The player is at no risk on the water, so when the wind starts blowing the wrong direction, the player simply raises the sail and starts drifting slowly along their same course. It's obvious the developers thought the sailing was some marvel, because the end of the game forces you to sail half the world before ending. It's not.


[h3] Overall [/h3]

Valheim had so much potential. There were so many directions the game could grow, yet instead we have a jumbled mess of disconnected and time-wasting mechanics and seemingly unfinished game design. I have so many little complaints that would take too long to type - I mean seriously, why is the Barka (a simply better-designed Abomination) given almost no purpose? And it's because of all these little issues that Valheim just wasn't fun for me.

I've heard many players claim that modding can supplement the systems already in place and server settings reduce the grind, but base Valheim 1.0 disrespected my time and didn't offer enough of worth to me as a player. Maybe I'll come back in a few years to give it another try with fresh eyes, but I simply can not recommend Valheim right now.

Rainbow Six Siege is one of the most intense tactical shooters out there. Destructible environments, unique operators, strategic gameplay, and sound-based decision-making make every round feel different. Winning a round because of smart positioning or a perfectly executed strategy is incredibly satisfying.

But let's be honest, Siege can be absolutely brutal. You get headshot from an angle you didn't even know existed, your teammates make questionable decisions, and every death somehow feels like a personal attack. The learning curve is steep, the toxicity can be exhausting, and sometimes you need a degree in architecture just to understand where you got shot from.

1600 hours ago, I downloaded Warframe because being an unkillable ninja backflipping off walls sounded fun. I am now a warehouse employee in a spaceship full of roombas. Steam says 1600 hours played. I’d say forty of those involved being a ninja. The rest were spent checking if I had enough of a resource whose name sounds like a prescription medication.

[h2]The power fantasy[/h2]
Warframe lets you become a walking extinction event. I enter a room, everything dies. Somewhere, a Grineer supervisor is watching employee numbers decrease faster than he can update the excel spreadsheet.
“Stay focused, there's a Heavy Unit approaching.”
Lotus, I just deleted everyone in this postal code. [b]If this man is carrying the orokin cell I need, you are announcing a donation.[/b]

Meanwhile, the Corpus are clocking in for minimum wage, unaware that today's workplace hazard is a glowing skeleton moving at Mach 4 with a gun that violates mathematics. One of them gets issued a helmet, a laser rifle, and instructions to stop me while I have twelve buffs active and a dog that desecrates corpses for loot. [b]This man needed a miracle, not a shield.[/b]

[h2]The farming & foundry[/h2]
I want a weapon. Every crafting recipe begins reasonably. Then, at the bottom, one resource appears that changes the entire course of my evening. Cryotic. I am now operating industrial refrigeration equipment for Cryotic while armed men interrupt my shift. “Excavator needs power.” Of course it does. I have enough energy to make the sun uncomfortable, but this machine requires a very specific battery carried by a man who has apparently called in sick. Three excavators are waiting. Nobody has a power cell. My teammate is defending a hole where an excavator used to be. At this rate, the weapon will be ready shortly after the Earth becomes uninhabitable.

When I finally get the parts, the game congratulates me by asking me to leave. Apparently the chassis and systems need time to get to know each other. I open the foundry six times that evening to confirm that time is still passing. Then I get a 75% platinum discount. Five seconds ago, I was a person with a budget. Now I am a mentally ill hamster who has learned how to enter credit card information.

[h2]The RNG[/h2]
Relics are containers full of things somebody else wants. We upgrade four identical relics. We are coordinated. Statistically, this should work.
We stand at extraction looking at the same Forma blueprint. [b]Four radiant relics. One unanimous “go fck yourself.”[/b] 

On the next run, a stranger brings an intact relic and gets something worth actual platinum. I select his reward with the dignity of a raccoon accepting bread.

[b]The part I need remains unavailable because the game has detected that I need it.[/b]

Then there are Archon shards. I want red. That is apparently a controversial request. Blue. Yellow. Blue. Yellow. My inventory looks like IKEA is preparing to sponsor my fcking Warframe. I see other people's builds. Five red shards. Beautiful. Coordinated. Exactly what they wanted. Mine looks like a gender reveal where the only thing being revealed is that I’m not getting ability strength.If a red shard finally drops, I will stare at it long enough for the game to ask if I am still connected. [b]I am not using it. I am taking a photograph and hanging it on my wall.[/b]

[h2]The missions[/h2]
I load into a public squad. Then Volt gives me speed. I attempt to move forward and immediately enter a relationship with the doorframe. Then there's Vauban. His build involves constructing a second sun indoors. He throws something, the room becomes white, and the enemies disappear. So does the room. So does my ability to identify objects.
Brother, I turned away from the monitor and [b]the flashbang followed me into the kitchen.[/b]
My GPU fans start making the noise of a plane denied permission to land. [b]The enemies are taking radiation damage. I am taking it through the screen.[/b]

[h2]The objective.[/h2]
Warframe players can calculate damage interactions involving six separate multipliers, ask them to stand inside a circle and society will collapse. In Survival, someone activates life support almost immediately at ninety-seven percent. Thank you, I was beginning to worry about the missing three. In Spy, the teammate who enters the vault with absolute confidence sets off every alarm ever manufactured. I was halfway through carefully avoiding a laser when this fcker arrived to demonstrate that the shortest route between two points is mission failure.

[h2]The trading[/h2]
Warframe.market turns you into a small business owner. Eventually, someone invites me to their dojo. It looks like an AI bedroom video with relaxing music, indoor waterfalls, and a bed overlooking a galaxy.
[b]“Which bathroom are you shtting in the hardest?”[/b]
Apparently this one. It has a dragon above the toilet and a direct view of Saturn. I follow the seller through six impossible Airbnb thumbnail rooms just to spend twelve platinum.

Then Baro Ki’Teer arrives like he returned from an expedition that will change civilization. I check his inventory: an ankle bracelet, a mod I own, and a weapon confiscated from a gas station robbery. [b]You cannot sell me disappointment and then complain that I arrived looking disappointed.[/b]
See you in two weeks, you duty-free airport motherfcker.

[h2]Unfortunately, I love it[/h2]
Because eventually everything works. The weapon I thought was useless starts deleting things. I clear a room, launch myself across a ridiculous distance, land exactly where I intended, and briefly become the person the trailer promised. Honestly, this is the best gaming community I've ever seen. I ask a question and a veteran appears with the answer, three spare mods, and a willingness to restructure his evening around my problem. Here, a man with thousands of hours invites you to his dojo, gives you what you're missing, refuses payment, and disappears.
[b]He has completed everything in the game. Apparently I am the next quest.[/b]

[h1]Recommended. 1600 hours played.[/h1]
Get some slots. Learn to mod. Start the foundry before bed.
[b]At my funeral, lower me into the ground slowly. There might be a rare resource down there.[/b]

...you probably enjoy an extremely meditative experience focused on strolling around leisurely holding that W button (because you either want it,

[*]or ... [i]well you get an idea now[/i]).
[/list]
If you have another dozen of hours you would probably enjoy farming those Trophies of mobs as well as other mats for your cool armour, another dozen for farming mats for building and building itself. Generally, Valheim is worth around 100 hours of meditation per playthrough.

  | [i]For those, who doesn't find that quite appealing, I have a confession[/i]

[h3]Father, I've sinned[/h3]

and desecrated this game with 25ish mods to make it playable and enjoyable. Dedicated slots for amour, sort/deposit/quickstack for storage, [b]a dedicated button for dodge[/b], crafting from containers or looking into one simultaneously with your friend ('das crazy), being able to lift your leg 10 cm to step over the last step of the  staircase while being overcucumbered or filling gaps in tiers where a specific weapon is missing etc. Is that much to ask for?

If not for mods I would have dropped Valheim long before finishing it for the first time. If you want to [i]play the game[/i] you have to build it yourself first. And when you break free from those shackles and don't spend more time sorting sh*t and start focusing on exploration you actually start to understand how shallow and empty the world is. There's very few POIs and those present mostly have nothing valuable in them. Procedurally generated map, it big, but what purpose does it serve? Reinforces your primal urge to sail for hours?

For 5+ years of development it has surprisingly little content and mechanics, some being underdeveloped, poorly designed and often frustration inducing. I don't even gonna get started on combat of this game. You get used to it, but it's definitely far from good. And that so funny how dev [b]straight up refuse to improve their game[/b]. A so-called "substantial" update once a year, and it's barely anything. Last big biome? More than 2 years ago. How many new mechanics, improvements of old ones were there in recent years? Exactly. UI/UX? Just some random letters.

[h3]Overall[/h3]

Personally, I would consider this game an okay(ish) filler arc when there's nothing else to play. And only with mods and at least one friend. Finishing Valheim doesn't bring a lot of satisfaction, but rather disappointment.

Satisfactory is an exellent game for people with an interest in the crafting and automation genres. There is little to no narrative and the premise is deceptively simple, but the gameplay loop is both challenging and compelling. 

Setting up a factory is a rewarding experience because no two factories are exactly the same. The geography and availability of resources encourage you to exercise innovation and creativity. Seeing your plan come together and watching your factory come to life gives you a sense of pride that compounds as you build outwards and find ways to create synergies and connections between factories.

There are enough building pieces and customization options to ensure that you have a good amount of creative freedom. With a little bit of elbow grease and out of the box thinking, you can transform your factories into visual delights and architectural marvels. Alternatively you can let chaos reign with spaghetti belts and convoluted systems that resemble Rube Goldberg machines.

The game has little to no political messaging and is fun for all ages by today's standards. There is some cartoon violence in the form of combat with alien flora and fauna, but there is no blood, gore, or vulgarity.  All in all it is a relatively tame and inclusive game. The game also has some educational merit since it consistently provides the player with opportunities to use applied mathematics (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, ratios, percentages, etc). Elementary level math skills aern't required, and the game does include a built in calculator, but I do think that the opportunity to get a mental workout here enriches the experience. 

As of now Satisfactory is comprised of one large open world with multiple biomes as opposed to seperate instanced levels. Multiplayer allows you to play with friends and visit thier saves, but it is always great to come back to your own when you know that there isn't another like it.

Lastly the game has alot of support in the form of youtube videos, production planners, and mods. The community is alive and well and is a great resource for inspiring your next build. 

PS The game runs great on Linux using Steam's Proton compatibility layer.

Sea of Thieves is a best-in-class pirate experience, and generally a good time. There are some unfortunate drawbacks: Namely that development has largely slowed to a crawl, and following this development team in particular has been very disappointing in recent years for verteran players like myself.

However, what does exist is a really solid experience with a plethora of content. For the new player who wants a fun pirate experience, I recommend this game wholeheartedly. The story missions are fun, and you can get some real enjoyment from doing the open world content with all the uncertainties and challenges of running into other players.

On the community: There are toxic sweaty crews, crews that play like chickens with their heads cut off, pirate roleplayers who will Parlay with you to share in the wealth just as often as they try to go for a sneaky betrayal, and everything in between. The community is a mixed bag, but if you stick with it in the open world mode, you'll have some genuinely amazing stories to tell, even if sometimes you just frustratingly sink or get sunk.

Overall I recommend Sea of Thieves. It's far from perfect, but it's still a great time and a gold standard in the Pirate game genre.

You can build everything out in the ocean or up in the sky, or carefully fit your factories within the existing terrain.  You can play nice with nature, or chop down everything and replace it all with concrete, metal, and glass.  The movement is fun and fluid, it's super fun just to spend a day exploring, especially after you unlock new movement options.  

My only complaint is that I wish there was more variety to the wildlife, both the aggressive and passive kinds, and some way to tie them into the gameplay more besides getting in the way.

I think it's both easy and difficult to describe just how good of a game Cyberpunk 2077 turned out to be from the way I experienced it. In one sentence, Cyberpunk 2077 is probably one of the most well-made, wholeheartedly complete games that exists out there. The entire world of Cyberpunk basically lived by its code of making a name for yourself that it itself spawned a majorly successful anime, collaborations, comics and books, a whole new fandom out of it. Just the CD Projekt effect maybe. 

Else, Cyberpunk 2077 certainly has some flaws that to others may have been the arrow to the knee for them, but I'm going to be describing how I felt. And in spite of the minor flaws it had, as a whole, I felt very, VERY content with it all. 

I spent the past year and a bit playing this game, on and off, taking breaks that were months long before picking it up again, and every time I did, I got right back into the groove of completely absorbing myself into the world of Night City like I never left. Some games when I've played after a certain time away from it, I end up struggling to reconnect. But with Cyberpunk, it never felt like that at all. 

Every character actually had depth. I sympathised with more than one character and wanted to learn of their back stories more than ever. Learning characters back stories? Who would've thought. The side gigs - sure, some of them got repetitive - but they at least were different in that each gig occasionally had motives. They had clues, evidence of something else going on, and at some point Cyberpunk 2077 the action RPG turned into a mystery thriller game. The combat is extremely versatile. I mostly played a Netrunner build for my V with quickhacks and non-confrontational attacks, but when I restarted and decided to go for a mostly Mercenary frontal assault V, it was just as smooth of a transition to be a ruthless killer slicing enemies with katanas and shooting everybody down with the spray of your machine gun.
