[b]Terraria[/b] 🌳 – 200 Hours, Two Friends, One Unforgettable Adventure. ❤️

Some games are just games. You play them, enjoy them, finish them, and eventually forget about them. But then there are games that become something much more. Games that create memories, turn ordinary evenings into unforgettable adventures, and make you wish you could experience everything for the first time again. For me, [b]Terraria[/b] is one of those games. ❤️

This is the story of Steve and Alex. Two friends, one enormous world, countless adventures, and over 200 hours of absolute greatness. 🌎

Our journey started long before May 2023. Back then, we decided to give [b]Terraria[/b] a try on Xbox. Unfortunately, things didn't exactly go according to plan. Maybe it was the controls, maybe we didn't understand the game, or maybe we simply weren't ready for what it had to offer. Whatever the reason, we eventually gave up. At the time, I thought that was it. But our real adventure hadn't even begun.

Fast forward to May 2023. We finally had PCs, and one day we had a brilliant idea: "Bro, we have PCs now. Why don't we give [b]Terraria[/b] another try?" And just like that, everything started. 🎮

I created Steve, and my friend created Alex. Two incredibly ordinary names for what would become an extraordinary adventure. We entered our world with practically nothing. A few basic tools, absolutely no idea what we were doing, and a whole lot of enthusiasm. But this time, something clicked.

Suddenly, the game that had confused us on Xbox became one of the most fascinating experiences we'd ever had. We explored caves, collected resources, built our first home, and slowly discovered just how ridiculously massive this little 2D game actually was. Before we knew it, we were completely addicted. ⛏️

Our early days consisted of getting lost underground, falling to our deaths, discovering enemies we were nowhere near prepared to fight, and constantly asking ourselves, "What the hell is that thing?" Every chest was exciting, every weapon felt like an achievement, and every time we thought we'd figured everything out, [b]Terraria[/b] surprised us again.

The progression is genuinely incredible. You start as two clueless idiots with questionable equipment, and suddenly you're preparing arenas, crafting potions, upgrading weapons, and developing strategies because some enormous monstrosity has decided your existence is personally offensive. 💀

Every victory feels earned. You fail, improve, try again, and eventually defeat something that seemed impossible just hours earlier. And experiencing that with a friend makes everything ten times better. You celebrate together, panic together, scream at each other, and occasionally die in the most embarrassing ways imaginable.

From our first bosses to the absolute madness of Hardmode, every encounter felt like another chapter in our adventure. And when we finally reached the Moon Lord, it felt like everything we'd accomplished had led us to that moment. Steve and Alex had come a long way. 🏆

Here's the thing about [b]Terraria[/b]: you never notice how much time you're spending on it. You tell yourself you'll play for another hour. Then you discover a weapon, need another material, realize you must defeat another boss, and suddenly you're building an arena at four in the morning. 🕓

That's basically how our entire journey went. What started as giving an old game another chance became approximately 200 hours of unforgettable memories. And not a single one of those hours felt wasted.

Sometimes we progressed through the game. Sometimes we explored. Sometimes we simply messed around, doing completely unnecessary things because we thought they were funny. That's what makes games like this special. They don't force you to create memories. They give you the tools to create them yourself.

Even after finishing our adventure, the journey wasn't entirely over. New achievements were added over time, and naturally, I wanted my beautiful 100% completion back. I'll admit that I used the Steam Workshop to make some of those newer achievements easier. After experiencing the game properly for around 200 hours, I think I've earned that little shortcut. 🏅

Now I've once again unlocked every achievement, and seeing that 100% feels incredible. Not just because of the achievements, but because of everything they represent.

I also have to appreciate the unbelievable amount of love Re-Logic has put into this game. The weapons, armor, bosses, biomes, secrets, music, and countless updates are genuinely impressive. It's incredible how a game that looks so simple can offer such an enormous experience.

There. I said it. 😂

Minecraft will always hold a special place in my heart. But that doesn't take anything away from [b]Terraria[/b]. Both games are masterpieces in their own ways, and constantly comparing them doesn't do either justice.

What makes me emotional looking back is realizing we'll never experience that first adventure again. We can create another world, try different classes, and defeat every boss again. But we'll never be those same two clueless guys entering that world in May 2023, completely unaware of the incredible journey waiting for them.

We'll never discover everything for the first time again. We'll never recreate every ridiculous conversation, spontaneous decision, or unforgettable evening exactly as it happened.

And maybe that's what makes those memories so special. ❤️

It's funny to think we almost missed out on all of this because our first Xbox attempt didn't work out. Sometimes a game deserves a second chance. And sometimes that second chance becomes one of the greatest gaming experiences of your life.

To Re-Logic, thank you for creating something this special. Thank you for the countless updates, the passion, and the unbelievable amount of content. Thank you for giving two friends a world they could lose themselves in for 200 hours.

And to Alex, thank you for being part of this journey. From two idiots struggling to survive their first nights to two idiots eventually conquering the Moon Lord, it was one hell of a ride. 🤝

[b]Terraria[/b] isn't just a game I completed. It's a game I experienced, a game I shared, and a game I'll always associate with a particular time in my life, a particular friend, and hundreds of hours of pure happiness.

Somewhere out there, in a little pixelated world, Steve and Alex's adventure has finally come to an end. The bosses have been defeated, the treasures collected, and the achievements unlocked.

But the memories? Those aren't going anywhere. ❤️

[b]200 hours. Two friends. One unforgettable adventure.[/b] 🌅

Thank you, [b]Terraria[/b]. 10/10. ❤️

Of all the MMOs in the world, I chose the original Guild Wars as mine. So naturally, when Guild Wars 2 came along, I expected an evolution of the game I loved. Instead, ArenaNet decided to make something almost entirely different.

Don't get me wrong, I've had plenty of fun with GW2 over the years. There are moments where the worldbuilding, environments, and sheer creativity genuinely shine. But it never really managed to capture what made the original Guild Wars so special to me.

The story is often painfully corny, with dialogue and plot developments that feel like they were lifted straight out of someone's amateur fanfiction. Meanwhile, PvP and WvWvW, two modes with enormous potential, have spent far too much time feeling neglected.

And then there's the endless grind. Every new map, dungeon, and piece of content seems to need its own special currency, progression system, or collection of arbitrary chores. Instead of feeling like you're exploring a living fantasy world, you often feel like you're working through an ever-expanding spreadsheet of things to collect.

What frustrates me most is the sheer inconsistency.

One moment, you're exploring an absolutely breathtaking environment filled with atmosphere, personality, and incredible attention to detail. The next, you're stumbling through something that feels like it was hastily cobbled together by an intern on their first day.

It's almost impressive how a game can swing so wildly between brilliance and mediocrity.

I can count the things I genuinely love about Guild Wars 2 on one hand, but the things that frustrate me would require a considerably longer list.

Counter-Strike is the only game I know where I can have the worst 40 seconds of my life, get called every insult known to mankind, witness a teammate attempt to defuse a bomb with the spatial awareness of a confused goldfish, and immediately click "Play Again."

And I wouldn't have it any other way.

There is something genuinely special about this game. Every round is a new opportunity to prove that you're either a tactical genius or the single greatest liability ever assigned a keyboard.

One moment, you're lining up the cleanest shot of your life. The next, you're staring at the killcam wondering how someone with the reaction time of a particularly sleepy houseplant just deleted you from existence.

The beauty of Counter-Strike is its simplicity. The mechanics are easy to understand, but the skill ceiling is absolutely ridiculous. Every map has a thousand little details to learn, every gunfight can teach you something, and there is always someone out there who will make you feel like you've never touched a mouse before.

And the sound design? That single footstep around a corner can trigger more psychological damage than an entire horror game.

You stop breathing.

You stop moving.

You begin reconsidering every decision that led you to this moment.

Then your teammate kicks open a door, misses every shot, and dies instantly.

Beautiful.

Counter-Strike isn't always fair, and it certainly isn't always friendly. But when everything clicks, when the impossible clutch lands, when a perfectly timed play turns a hopeless round into a victory, there are very few games that can match that feeling.

It's frustrating. It's addictive. It's occasionally a test of whether you can remain civil to another human being.

But there's a reason people keep coming back.

One more round.

Just one more.

I'm nowhere near as qualified to leave a review as someone who has spent more than 365 days playing this game, but I can honestly say that I have loved my time it. I have had so many positive experiences with this game and hardly regret any of the 800 hours I have put into it, but like many other people in the community, I have grown tired of it. There are three things I'd like to talk about in this review gameplay, community, and developer effort.
Before I dive into these subtopics I would like to preface this by saying I have a bit of a unique take on gameplay ethics. If I do not like when something is done to me, I will not do it to other people beyond the scope of testing it out. For example, I do not like to be tunneled, so I refuse to do it.
     
Gameplay
     To start with gameplay, I have to say that this game is the best in the genre. You can't find any other game in the horror space that allows you to play as such a diverse roster. Whether you're looking for cult classics like Michael Myers and Jason or modern masterpieces like Kaneki and Springtrap, Dead by Daylight has it all. In addition to an absurd roster of licensed characters, there are tons of Dead by Daylight originals here to draw your attention. While the roster is truly something to behold, I believe that this is where a lot of the novelty ends. In regard to playing Killer, I have grown increasingly bored and frustrated with my recent experiences. On one hand there is a severe lack of build diversity in the survivor teams I play against. In a game with 179 survivor perks, you might see 5-6 unique perks each game. This is because the meta survivor perks have not changed in Dead by Daylight since 2016 with the addition of the Halloween license. Additionally, what once felt like a game where material management was integral to survival, survivors now have drastically increased pallet density on almost every map. This change makes basic attack killers extremely hard to play. So if you are coming to Dead by Daylight for a killer that released earlier than 2022, I wish you the best of luck. Additionally the maps that the game have to pull from are decisive in deciding which side wins against which killer. One additional point is that playing against a full team of survivors that are communicating with each other can often times be unbearable. They are aware of your location constantly which makes getting the jump on them impossible, as well as allowing them to avoid you almost effortlessly. As long as survivors have functioning brains they can knock out your first three generators in under 4 minutes, and make the game impossible for you to win from there on out. From a survivor standpoint the game can get very old very quickly as well. No matter how much or how little you do, your fate is never truly in your hands. Dead by Daylight presents survivor players with a unique experience of gambling every time they load into a match. Your teammates can be the greatest players you've ever seen or bottom of the barrel players that seem like they haven't graduated from kindergarten. Another point of interest is that playing against new killers on release is a hellscape. Killers often get added in severely strong states that make playing against them utterly dreadful. You'd think that a game with a Public Test Build, there would be a lot more polish on updates when they come out. If you do think that, you'd be wrong. 
     
Community
     The community is by far the worst element that Dead by Daylight has to offer. It is simply mind boggling how absurdly toxic this game is. I won't even mention the unwritten rules. No matter how fair you attempt to play, there will always be someone to say something to you in endgame chat. People will t-bag and stall out games for as long as possible because you did something completely normal. I would love to tell you that it is improving, but it isn't. It is getting much much worse. In a world where people do not have to take accountability for anything, Dead by Daylight is an ideal location for them to vent all their frustrations from their real lives without fearing the repercussions of their actions. There has been a faction war between killers and survivors since this games inception and it shows no signs of slowing down. I could go on about the horrible community for another 2,000 words but for the sake of brevity, I'll leave that out.

Developer Effort     
     As far as developer effort goes, Behavior is one of the worst studios I have ever encountered. Balance changes can take years to release or may never even release at all. I doubt that they care very much about the state that the game is in because they already know that nothing can take this position away from them. Blight is a killer in this game that took years for them to tone down. This killer could stomp lobbies like Mario stomps Goombas and they refused to change him for years. On a similar note, old killers are so power crept that there is essentially no reason to play them. The majority of killers before 2020 have become so outdated that you would have better results playing a 2025/26 killer blindfolded with no perks, than running a full meta build on an old killer. Behavior does not care about rebalancing old killers to hold their own in the modern era. Dead by Daylight's killer selection feels like a museum of all the things that once were. In a way, it is beautiful to see the way the game has evolved and all the new killer gimmicks they have come up with, but the more time I spend playing the more it haunts me. A game so focused on pumping out new content that it fails to balance the content that is already in the game and is already loved by players. My last grievance with the developers is that they seemingly do not use the PTB results. I cannot quantify the amount of times where updates get released onto the main branch and there are tons of bugs of very strong perks or killers. Surely the people playing in the Public Test Build are informing Behavior of this but there never seems to be a change. If you are looking for a game with developers that have a desire to do right by their own content, Dead by Daylight isn't the game for you.

Conclusion
     Overall I think Dead by Daylight is one of the most tragic gaming stories that I have seen. Dead by Daylight used to be a game with so much passion behind it from the community and the developers. However it has become a ravenous self-hating ecosystem where one of the most dominant motives is to harm the playing experiences of others. Occasionally Behavior will step in but more often than not, they sit back in their chair with a crown titled No. 1 Horror Developers, and watch the community wish death upon itself. The worst part of the whole thing for me is my own toxic attachment to the game. As much as I hate getting on and playing a couple matches, there is something that keeps me here that I can't quite place my finger on.
Two final questions to answer:
1. Is this game the best in the genre? Absolutely
2. Is it worth playing in 2026? Not if you value your sanity.

Hunt: Showdown 1896 is an absolutely phenomenal game. Unfortunately, it sometimes feels like it was developed by three raccoons in a trench coat,

The atmosphere? 10/10. The gunplay? Amazing. The sound design? Incredible. The performance? A ******* coin toss.

Roughly 50% of the time, my game decides to run like a PowerPoint presentation, despite having a perfectly good PC. Nothing quite captures the immersive Wild West experience like dying because reality itself decided to buffer.

And the matchmaking? Oh, boy.

I'm a 1-star player. A genuine bottom-of-the-barrel, eats-dirt-for-breakfast, probably-loses-a-gunfight-against-a-scarecrow kind of player. I'm just out here trying to figure out which end of the gun goes bang, and the game keeps matching me against people who have more hours in Hunt than I have hours of sleep in my entire life.

These people don't play Hunt. They ARE Hunt. They can hear me blink from three compounds away, headshot me through six walls, and know what I had for breakfast based on the sound of my footsteps.

Meanwhile, I'm crouched in a bush having a panic attack because I heard a twig snap.

I don't mind losing. Losing is part of the game. But there's only so many times you can get your ass handed to you by a 6-star sweatlord while your game runs at 14 FPS before you start questioning whether you actually enjoy video games or just enjoy being bullied by Louisiana.

I also wouldn't say no to a few more accessibility options. When you're blind as a bat and about as sharp as a bag of wet cement, the fifty-seven shades of beige that make up this game's colour palette aren't exactly doing you any favours. Sometimes I genuinely can't tell if I'm looking at an enemy, a tree stump, or a particularly threatening shadow. More visual clarity options, better colour customization, and accessibility settings would go a long way. I love the atmosphere, but apparently being able to SEE things is considered an optional DLC.

And that's the frustrating part: **Hunt is genuinely fucking fantastic.** There's nothing quite like it. The tension, the atmosphere, the gunfights, the sheer terror of hearing someone cough in the next building. I WANT to play this game.

But between the technical jank and matchmaking that apparently thinks I'm secretly a professional esports player, the game is doing its absolute best to make me reconsider.

Deep Rock Galactic – Great with friends, a lonely grind without them!

Deep Rock Galactic is an absolute blast when you've got a group of friends to play with. Exploring caves, fighting off hordes of bugs, and getting into all sorts of ridiculous situations together makes for some genuinely great gaming moments.

But then your friends move on to other games, and suddenly you're left with a rather repetitive gameplay loop. The seasonal events, Christmas decorations, and endless reward tracks don't really do much to change that. It's still the same thing over and over, just with a few new carrots dangling in front of you.

If you've got three friends looking for a fun cooperative adventure shooter, absolutely pick this one up. If you're lost and alone in the mines, however, maybe think twice.

That being said, the core gameplay loop is still far more enjoyable and comfortable than something like Helldivers 2. And unlike some developers, the people behind Deep Rock Galactic seem to genuinely care about their game and actually put effort into improving it.

Nine hundred hours in, and I’m still coming back for more. Dead by Daylight is one of the most unique multiplayer games out there: a tense 4v1 game of cat and mouse where every match plays out differently. Whether you’re a survivor sweating through a last generator or a killer hunting down the final survivor, the adrenaline never gets old.

What it does best:

Two completely different experiences. Survivor is all stealth, teamwork, and clutch escapes. Killer is about pressure, mind games, and map control. Switching sides keeps the game fresh.
Huge variety. With dozens of killers, survivors, perks, add-ons, and maps, there’s always a new build to try. No two trials feel quite the same.
Licensed chapters. Horror icons and original characters sit side by side, and each new chapter brings new powers, perks, and playstyles.
Skill ceiling. Looping, mind-gaming, tracking, and macro decisions take real time to master. After hundreds of hours I’m still learning new tricks.
Best with friends. A coordinated survivor squad or a good group in voice chat is where the game really shines.

What could be better:

Matchmaking and balance can be hit or miss, and some matches just aren’t fun.
The learning curve is steep for new players, and the first few hours can be rough.
Some DLC and cosmetics are pricey, though the game is fully playable without all of them.
Toxic players exist, as in most competitive games.

Dead by Daylight isn’t perfect, but it delivers something no other game quite matches. The thrill of a close escape, or of a hard-earned 4k, is why I’ve sunk this much time into it. If you like horror, tension, and a challenge that keeps rewarding you the more you learn, give it a try. Just don’t be surprised when you look up and see your playtime in the hundreds.

War thunder, is a "game". It's typically played for suffering, competition, or development of depression.
Now you may think this is one of those "Oh no please don't touch this game I have played it for so long" kind of meme review, but I do actually want to give new players a relatively objective review and viewpoint of the game. I want to note that most of my hours are in air realistic battles, and therefore my comments are ground battles are from what I hear from others.

War thunder is a game that has an extremely long learning curve. The best diagram I can put here would be inserting the "Dunning Krueger Effect" diagram. Your first few hours in the game will be a lot of fun, in fact this will be the most fun you will have in this game. Then you go into realistic battles, and you dip your feet into water that's way too deep or cold than you have anticipated. You're thrown into the world of wild animals where there is no such thing as skill based matchmaking. You will fall quickly into the valley of despair and realize that the game is a lot of pain and suffering.

The skill floor of war thunder is high, and the skill ceiling even higher. Even if you feel like you're good at the game, you'll find yourself humbled if you play against an Esports team player. Their plane seems just that bit better, their reaction time just that bit better, but it's all because they have understood the game for far more competitive reasons and to a depth that's way greater than what casual players are willing to dedicate.

So, what about the fun? Between hour 5 to hour 2000, you don't get to have fun. The only way you get to "have some fun" in this game, is when you treat it very lightly and laugh it all off. However, it's difficult to laugh it all off when the game's economy is unforgiving, the grind is extremely long, and over time in order to actually have fun, you have to buy some sort of premium vehicle to aid in your learning curve.

Pay to win factor? You can buy some of the most powerful vehicles in the game with just money, at a ridiculous price tag that you would believe is crazy if it was a whole triple A game. 80 dollars. Only buy premiums when they are on sale, please, do yourself that favor. If you plan on buying a premium to grind, I would recommend the: F-18 premiums, the Su-30 premiums, and the BMPT, as those are vehicles that will minimize your suffering and maximize the suffering of others. War thunder is a fair market after all, you having fun means others will lose it.

So why would I ever play this game? The dopamine addiction and the feeling of progress. "target destroyed" sound, is an "A" note. A very satisfying sound that you'll begin to get clicker trained on. The game is difficult enough you feel proud of yourself when you actually do well and wants to play more. Your favorite vehicles are just out of reach, why wouldn't you keep going? The fear of missing out in this game is what drives it so far, and why it has so many grinding players.

Is this game any good? In my personal opinion, yes. There's nothing that feels like war thunder out there, and it feels like the controls of the game are extremely well polished. Damage is modeled relatively well and it feels pretty good to play. The game does gets problems once in a while with gaijin making weird changes that are unpolished into the game but it usually gets fixed, so it's not really that big of a concern.

How is the balancing of the game? As of currently, it's "okay". The whole game suffers a lot from BR compression, that is, vehicles that have extremely big capability differences face each other. Matchmaking in WT works by having a full up or downtier limit of 3 BR brackets. Ex: If you have a 4.0 vehicle, your full uptier is 5.0 and full downtier is 3.0. The brackets are: 4.3, 4.7, 5.0. 3 brackets, as I talked about. However vehicles that are just a bit better than another vehicle is given a 1 BR bracket bump, and as vehicles with better and better capabilities stack on top of each other, those 3 BR brackets start to feel rather suffocating. Common examples of poor balancing is the 13.3 SU-30 premiums having 8x fox-3 missiles while everyone at 13.0 either doesn't have any or have 4 fox-3s at max (if you're a really bad airframe). The Spitfire Mk.24, J6K1, as well as a bunch of 6.7 battle rating prop planes will face at 7.7, the Me-262 C2b, which is a jet aircraft with two rocket boosters that basically triple its normal jet thrust. Completely impossible to touch by those prop planes unless the jet player plays it really poorly. This is just the Air RB situation, and ground from what I heard is even worse. However you eventually learn to cope with it, though it's not good, doesn't mean it's impossible to adapt to.

Finally I want to point out that this game is NOT free to play. You either pay with money, or you pay with your soul... as for me, I paid with both. Before you start playing this game you should consider some other significantly easier to get into, and much more fun and relaxing games that does not cause this much financial pressure and frustration. It's simply not "worth your time".

If you wanna play your favorite jets, may I refer you to "Project Wingman", if you want something with a high skill ceiling but is still super fun to play, may I refer you to "Ultrakill", if you want a vehicle simulator similar to war thunder but without a significant part of the pain, may I refer you to "IL-2 Shturmovik", If you're a big fan of mil-sim combat, may I refer you to "Arma III", and if you are a real hardcore flight sim enjoyer, may I point you to "DCS World". For every aspect of this game that it offers there is one that does it just a bit better that's easier to get into.

As for me... why do I still play it? Because I already have so many hours in it, I finally got ahead of the curve. I'm finally having fun, but it's never as fun as the first innocent arcade battles can offer... Do you think it's worth it? I believe for most people the answer will be "no", but if it is worthwhile for you, be my guest and please contribute to my 14 thousand air targets destroyed when I meet you in a match one day.

Tldr: It's fine to have a punishing game. It's not fine to have a punishing game with some mind boggling terrible game design decisions. 

Your progression is entirely based around your gear. In addition, you have skills for everything (running, jumping, blocking, using swords, using bows, using axes, chopping wood, etc) that reduce the stamina cost of your actions, these skills increase as you use them. If you die, you lose all your gear that is equipped, AND you lose 8% of your skills (across the board). 

You then get a 10 minute death timer that prevents skills from reducing further if you die again. 

This incentivizes you to run to get your stuff back before the 10 minute are up. But if you died to some enemies, those enemies will sit and camp your body because nothing draws them away or back to their spawn location. So good luck getting your body back unless you craft 2x of all your gear. Now you are left to try and run in, and grab it and then run out and try and equip everything again. The mobs, almost never de-aggro you, so if you get one that is faster than you are, and you have no armor on (say because you died) they will just hound you until you die again. 

You do have food that you can craft, that increases your health and stamina, which is great. That food is consumed on use, and if you die, it resets to zero. this leads to an ongoing failure cascade where you use your good food to get your body back, but if you fail, your food then starts to run out, forcing you to then use worse food, which gives you less health/less stamina. Making the whole point of just getting your stuff back, even harder. 

No big deal, make more food, but wait, you have that 10 minute timer to think about. It's not challenging, its just frustrating and punishing. 

The crafting is great, no notes, the building is fun. If you have friends who like the combat and can run out and get you crafting materials, have at it, you'll have a blast. 

The sailing is a large section of the game, and it is boring as hell. Have a second monitor ready so you can sit in a boat for 20 minutes at a time going one direction to get where you need to go. There's no interaction, you just sail and hope the wind helps rather than goes against you. Water and being in/around it is a large section of the game. So you would think there would be some mechanics that involve it. Nope, none. Most loot falls straight to the bottom. It's also very easy to drown (swimming uses stamina and if you run out while swimming you have no way of getting it back outside standing on something, so naturally you just drown, and your gear/body then stays where you died, in the middle of the ocean. swimming in general is half baked and feels terrible.  How did they manage to build a game around water, and making swimming onto a ladder this difficult? Your character can't grab anything, so you just wait until the water lifts you onto the latter. and try to jump, except your jump height and moment is reset when you exit the water for some reason. So you end up doing this weird jump fall motion over and over just to try and get 1m up a surface. Did you sail to an island and die? Well now you get to build a second boat, and sail back to it. 

There are teleporters that help with this, but if enemies destroy it, its gone. Also you better remember what you named it, because teleporters link based off of what you name them, and only 2 can be linked at a time with the same name. This leads to having giant teleporter rooms where you keep all the shortcuts to different islands, all so you can avoid interacting with sailing, which as said, is awful. This also leads to fun moments where you die in the process of setting up a portal on a new island, so then you lose your gear, your portal materials and the boat that is over there. Get cracking on crafting a whole new boat. 

Maybe the bosses are fun? I mean...meh. Every enemy kills you in 1-3 hits anyway, so the bosses just continue that trend but add in some new attacks, and also bring in other enemies to fight (ads). It's just more of the same except now you die, respawn, portal back in, get your stuff, try and get a few hits in, and then die again. The bosses health only regenerates, but doesn't reset. So it ends up being you throwing bodies at it over and over until it dies, and hope you can out damage its health regen. You do have a health potion (that you can craft, naturally) but you can use it once, and then even if you have more, you're prohibited from drinking it again for 2 minutes because...I guess the game was too easy. 

I'm 200 hours in, and my favorite moments are just building and crafting in it. The combat is just okay and each new biome you enter has some new and awful way of being "challenging". Finally got a grasp on trolls and large monsters? Well welcome to the swamp where it constantly rains and your stamina regeneration is reduced in addition to new monsters that can kill you in one hit. I hope you got a hang of that arrow timing to parry it, because the block mechanic is entirely dependent on your max health, which is largely dependent on the food you eat. Or the mountain biome, where your health constantly drains, your stamina regeneration is halved, and your health regeneration is negated. Surely there's some interesting ways to work around that right? No, you just make some freeze resist potions, until you get a new cape and the freezing is negated entirely and you never interact with it again. Or the mistlands, where the fun new mechanic is just literally you can't see anything. You have to build little torches to push the mist away, or rely on a lamp that follows around you.

On that note, there is no brightness slider in this game. If you play during the night, you have to bring a torch or head lamp (using either a shield slot, or a helmet slot). And it gets to a point where you just cannot see anything around you in some biomes. What they were thinking in making the night time this dark, is beyond me. Good luck trying to see what is attacking you in the dark of the ashlands at night while trying to retrieve your body. 

lastly, there are quality of life things that you would think are here, that are not. Crafting materials and loot must be carried in your inventory to craft with, and you end up having giant rooms of chests for all your stuff because there's no sort or loot dump function. If you want to repair your gear, you have to click repair for each item, because apparently a repair all, which would be like, the second thing you would design after a weapon durability/repair feature, was too much work. 

See what I mean? It's not punishing and challenging, it's punishing and terrible user design. There's a fun game in here somewhere, but right now, do not recommend. My group and I will likely play through and beat it, but I am can't wait to move on to something else.

The factory-building genre has no shortage of excellent titles, but Satisfactory stands out as an absolute masterpiece of automation, scale, and design. Developed by Coffee Stain Studios, this first-person factory builder takes the addictive, complex logistics of games like Factorio and seamlessly translates them into a breathtaking, fully 3D world.
Here is why Satisfactory is one of the most rewarding and beautifully crafted simulation games on the market.

🌌 An Immense Scale in First-Person

Most automation games place you high in the sky with an omniscient top-down view. Satisfactory forces you onto the ground as a pioneer for FICSIT Inc. Building in a first-person perspective completely changes the weight of the experience. Walking through a multi-story mega-factory that you designed—listening to the rhythmic hum of dozens of assemblers, watching miles of conveyor belts weave over your head, and seeing massive freight trains snake through the sky—provides an unparalleled sense of architectural awe.

⚙️ Flawless, Addictive Progression Loop

The game excels at making you feel like a genius while keeping you constantly hungry for the next tier of technology. The progression loop is exceptionally well-paced:
• The Routine: You start manually mining copper and iron on a gorgeous, hand-crafted alien planet.
• The Automation: Within hours, you build your first automated miners and basic constructors.
• The Complexity: Just as you master basic assembly lines, the game introduces fluids, oil refining, nuclear power, and advanced orbital mechanics.
Every time a milestone feels slightly overwhelming, the tools you unlock—like hoverpacks, jetpacks, and blueprints—give you exactly what you need to scale up your operations.

🪐 A Beautiful World Worth Exploring

Unlike procedurally generated survival maps, Satisfactory’s world is a massive, meticulously hand-crafted planet spanning diverse biomes, from lush fields to barren deserts and glowing, treacherous swamps. Exploration is heavily rewarded. Foraging for alien flora, hunting down power slugs to overclock your machines, and searching for crashed drop pods to unlock powerful alternate recipes turns the game into a thrilling exploration adventure between stints of heavy factory planning.

🛠️ Respect for the Player’s Time

One of the game’s greatest design triumphs is its lack of punishing survival mechanics. There are no base raids, no decaying structures, and no penalty for tearing down an entire factory floor to redesign it. If a layout doesn't work, you get 100% of your resources back when you dismantle it. This creates a stress-free environment that actively encourages experimentation, perfectionism, and creative architecture.

🎮 Seamless Multiplayer Integration

While building solo is a deeply satisfying, meditative experience, playing with friends elevates it to chaos and comedy. Subdividing tasks—where one player handles the complex logistics of an oil refinery across the map while another designs a brutalist concrete hyper-hub back at base—makes massive late-game projects feel incredibly rewarding to complete together.

🏆 The Verdict: 10/10

Satisfactory is a triumph of engineering and game design. It balances deep, mind-bending logistics with accessible, highly satisfying building mechanics. Whether you want to build a perfectly efficient, math-optimized factory matrix or a sprawling, chaotic web of "spaghetti" belts over a scenic alien waterfall, it is a game that will easily swallow hundreds of hours of your time.
It isn't just a game about building factories; it’s an immersive sandbox where you tame a planet, master logistics, and construct your own mechanical empire. Highly recommended.

This game is one of the most fun games I ever played. First person shooters can be pretty hit or miss for me, but this game starts off incredibly fun and it only gets better as you level up. There are a LOT of ways to customize your character, from weapons, to skills, to clothes, and to cyberware, and you can really create some interesting combinations. Plus, there is so much leveling! Normal leveling, plus skill progression, plus street cred! By the end of the game, I'm a powerhouse with armor, health, weapon damage, and resistances, mowing my way through whatever crosses my path.

The main issue is the story SUCKSSSSSSSS. There are fun and interesting parts of the story, but a lot of it is slow and unskippable. I've done the main story all the way through twice, and there are so many dead moments. There is also a lot of slow walking behind someone, sometimes while they explain something you can't skip. There are a lot of times where you have to [spoiler]fight as Johnny, removing any and all upgrades/cyberware/weapons you've gotten but keeping the level difficulty. You get thrown into a completely new playstyle at a high level with no way to manual save! It's the only part of the game I really die in.[/spoiler]

Plus, [spoiler]I love Keanu Reeves, but Johnny is ANNOYING. I liked him the first playthrough, but he actually lies to you/misleads you/misrepresents things a LOT and he shames you for things you have no control over. Plus he bothers you all the time. And your relationship is applied inconsistently. Why am I being forced to say I hate him when I spent the entire game building rapport? Why am I forced to say I like him around when we have no relationship to speak of? There are times where he tells you to do something, and if you don't do it, you're treated like an idiot by the game, and there are times where you are treated like an idiot if you DO listen to him. It's all very confusing and jarring. [/spoiler]

Speaking of characters, Judy and Panam are fine, but the male romance options are TERRIBLE. You have a [spoiler]corrupt cop who tries to play puppy after dragging you through corrupt cop shit[/spoiler] and then you have [spoiler]the 80 year old rockstar who is still in love with the man in your head who tries to destroy three girls careers because he's a bitter washed up asshole.[/spoiler] Plus, both male romance options are side quest locked, so completely missable, while Judy and Panam are met through the main plot.

Heck, even Judy has her problems. Judy [spoiler]is left sad in all endings except one that has nothing to do with her. Why am I becoming distant and shitty to her in the mansion ending? My V wouldn't do that?[/spoiler] I haven't finished the Panam romance yet, but it's... weird so far too.

Also, the gigs. There are so many gigs with secret requirements that aren't communicated in anyway. Sometimes it will say "Don't be seen (optional)" but a LOT of times, the game expects you to be stealthy or not kill people or whatever and you only find out at the end of the mission when the fixer is disappointed in you. It happened with EVERY fixer, to the point that I dropped a save before EVERY gig so I could go back and do it again in case of secret expectations.

The biggest sin of the story has got to be the extreme cynicism. By the time I was getting to the end of the game, I knew that if I was going out of my way to save someone, there was a pretty high chance they would [spoiler]kill themselves.[/spoiler] It literally just kept happening. There are so many times where you try so hard to do good things, and it almost feels like the game is laughing at you for trying. I actually really like grimdark, gritty, and cynical media, but this was almost unpalatable in some cases because instead of "everything is literally as bad as possible, but you can do something" it very much has the feeling of "everything is bad and you're stupid for thinking you could make ANYTHING better." There are a couple places where you can do something, but it's mostly punished in my experience.

All this to say, the story is frustrating and mean and painful. There isn't a single ending [spoiler]where you don't die,[/spoiler] which has some foreshadowing, but it really feels like the last f u to [spoiler]give you hope and then show you that it's hopeless.[/spoiler]

There is honestly a lot I like about this game. The environment, building, and combat are all pretty fun. However, it feels like a lot of different game mechanics were not fully finished or thought through. The following is a list of my issues, ordered from game-breaking to mildly annoying.

1. The 1.0 Anticheat – I've been playing again since the 1.0 release with a group of friends. We decided to build a large town, and one of the players went to his own world to spawn stone, making it count as a "cheated item." This alone is fine; I can understand the point of labeling "cheated-in items." However, this has spread across the server like an infection, and now items we pick up from enemies count as "cheated" too. This prevents us from getting achievements if we want to progress. The amount of frustration and headache this caused is unreal, and it inspired me to write my first and worst Steam review. The owner of the server had to give all of us admin status so we could use console commands just to use the command /yesiuseddevcommandsbutiwantmyachievementsanyway. This is infuriating and a slap in the face from the devs after we had to fix their mess. Why implement something so half-baked that it ruins playthroughs for achievement-hunting players?

2. Absurd punishment for dying – Yes, I know there are settings to limit this, but by default (the intended way to play), when you die, you lose 5% of your levels in skills on top of dropping all your items at the location you died. You have a ten-minute timer that prevents skill loss after you die, but it can easily take more time to reach your corpse unless you set up portals for nearly every adventure you take from the base. Dying also resets your food, health, stamina, eitr, and rested bonus. So if you don't have decent food at the base and rest before running back to your items, you'll likely struggle greatly to retrieve your items without help from another player (depending on the biome). In most cases, the enemies that killed you stand at or near your items, making it much harder to retrieve and equip your gear without dying again. You can say "skill issue" all you like, I don't care.

3. Enemies spawning within the base – My group has built a moderately sized town, and even with workbenches and numerous other constructs that should stop spawning within a radius, we still have enemies spawning in the center of town, inside buildings, and in the middle of our farms. Time and time again, we have built workbenches all over the town to stop this, to no avail. I'm honestly wondering if this game has broken code or something. My point is this should not be happening, and yet it is.

4. Adding content without reworking the old – It's nothing new when it comes to devs of early access games only pushing out new content and never touching up older content. The Meadows, The Black Forest, Swamp, and Plains should be reworked or touched up. It's obvious how much work went into the later biomes. Different skill descriptions are inaccurate, like the crossbow skill. A lot of building items from earlier biomes don't place as well as later ones. It really looks like they only want to push content to pull players in or bring them back. It's like a child "picking up" their room by throwing everything under the bed and into the closet.
I would honestly avoid buying this game until they polish up and fix their game, if they ever do. I say check back in 6 months.

I like this game. It's a good game compared to where it was multiple years ago but there are still so many issues with the game, and some of that has come from it being worked on for so long. 

Nothing in this game is fully fleshed out. There are a lot of things that are tried, and to a various degree even succeed at keeping me engaged for a while. Most of the game mechanics are like this for about 2 hours, then you kinda top out and get bored. Let's rapid fire through game mecahnics that aren't fully fleshed out. 

Units are the worst. Either you are a slave to the navigation maps that provide almost no units, you do some trade system stuff that doesn't make that many units, you can have an S tier settlement to make almost no units, or you can just scan stuff through a visor after eating a magic donut and you make billions per hour. 
Nanites? By far the best way to make nanites is to farm mold. Is it fun? no. but if you want to progress at anything other than a snails pace, you don't have many options that are fun.
the fix: nerf mold farming, make the best way to get nanites to be exploring the galaxy. the nanites you get from discovering creatures and fauna just needs a small buff to be more viable, and raiding outposts needs to be harder but more rewarding.

Settlements is a big pain point for me as they have so much potential but are completely left to dry in so many ways. When you get an S tier settlement you have options of what gets produced for you, but since units don't matter unless you are exploiting mechanics, it's almost worthless. It provides no other real benefit for all the time you put in. 

Combat is good until you realize when you are fighting a pirate dreadnought for the first time thinking "this will be what the combat is like in this game?" then you warp to another system, get that same fight again, realize it's the same fight again. And once you have good modules it's just over for anybody you see.

Corvettes are cool. I spent a lot of time to make a pretty good one. I'll give hello games that but even that system isn't fully fleshed out. 

The main mission is just a bunch of fetch quests with dialog about being alone, and honestly I think the game would be better without a main story at all or the option to skip it. 

Your characters movement is horrible, you bump into everything that is tiny and it makes your camera move pretty violently if you are clipping, the quests make me upset because there are permanent side quests that you cannot get out of the "side quest" page. 

If you take every major update, you see that this game has "transformed into something new" and that's true, it has, but it's also a mess that needs to be cleaned up. it's overwhelming at first when you learn there is a whole cooking system put in the game, but once you get a few pretty basic ingredients you can cook almost anything in the game. 

I hope the next few updates for a while calm down the new features and expand on the existing ones.

I started playing Destiny 2 back when Bungie brought the game over to Steam. After experiencing firsthand everything this game has gone through over the years, my bottom line is this: I only recommend Destiny 2 if you can get the full collection on a steep discount.

If you pick up the complete bundle on sale with its campaigns, dungeons, and expansion content included the sheer amount of gameplay makes it worthwhile. Otherwise, it is extremely hard to recommend.

Bungie's Missteps & Why the Score
- My final rating is heavily impacted by the history of poor decisions made by Bungie throughout the game's lifespan:

- Removed Paid Content (Vaulting): It is unacceptable that Bungie removed entire story campaigns that players originally paid for, such as the Red War, Curse of Osiris, Warmind, and Forsaken.

- Misleading Free-to-Play Model: If you download the game for free, there is barely anything meaningful to do besides basic patrol zones. Almost all core endgame content, raids, and story arcs are paywalled behind DLCs.

- Microtransactions & Silver: While it leaned close to Pay-to-Win mechanics in the past, you can at least earn decent cosmetic items through Bright Dust nowadays without spending real money on Silver.

-Massive File Size: It is simply not worth downloading over 100 GB for a game where free-to-play users barely get a fraction of playable content.

Final Verdict
- Final Score: 6.5 / 10 (Weighted down by years of controversial publisher decisions).

Recommendation: DO NOT download it if you only intend to play free-to-play. Only consider it if you find the Expansion Collection heavily discounted and want a polished sci-fi shooter experience with friends.

Alright. It's probably about time that I review the game, considering I have over two hundred hours in it.

The first question that'll probably pop up is: why do I not recommend it? To be honest, I wish I could have a mixed review, or a purely informational one. Because my opinion is much more gray than it is negative, but if I had to choose between only positive and negative, it is sadly negative.

The game is a mixed bag. From the very start I've always gotten the feeling that the developers are more artists than they are designers, and over the course of my time in their realm that thought has only been reinforced. The game mixes various different styles of gameplay. Survival, crafting and building, souls-like combat. And from those, only the building aspect is something that is in my opinion actually well done.

The biggest gripe I have with the game is the fact that its combat... honestly is just not well designed. It's Dark Souls on a budget. The weapons, each and every single one, has damage types. Some have multiple, others only one. Not bad on its own, but it becomes bad when certain damage types are just kind of useless. Bows all have pierce damage. The vast majority of enemies are all resistant to pierce. Spirit damage is thrown around every now and then. Chuck it in the bin. Only enemies it is worth using on are enemies that you can take on just as easily without it. Almost every boss is immune to it, and if not that they are neutral. There are more examples, but these are the most egregious ones that I can think of.

Then we have weapon classes. Some just... don't have end game counterparts or skip areas entirely. On one of my playthroughs the iron mace stuck with us all the way up to the Ashlands where an upgrade finally became available. Again, not that bad. There are other classes. But we also have skills which take ages to level! Like this, you'll have acceptable skill in a weapon and the game forces you to abandon it because the area is too strong for it.

The combat itself is simple. You hit, you shoot, you roll, you block, you parry. That's it. Not bad. But a lot of enemies do not respect pacing. In Souls games, the designers take care to make every enemy have its own "dance". This game does not. The enemies have no real dance. They simply do one move after the other. And a lot of the time, it does not allow proper breathing room. Graydwarf Brutes for example just hit, and once you come out of the roll they hit again. There is no space to retaliate. Sure, a shield would probably help. But that funnels the player down a certain playstyle, something the areas themselves are already guilty of and which the skill system actively punishes. And if you do not listen to the game when it funnels you like this, you'll encounter bosses like the Queen that can take over half an hour like that.

See what I mean? Lots of features, and a lot of it counteracts itself. The areas funnel which promotes variety, but the skill system punishes variety by weakening you until you build it back up. The weapons have damage types, but enemies and especially bosses nullify certain weapons to the point of uselessness. And more.

Then we get to sailing. The world is massive, and it is too massive for its own good. And how do we traverse? By sailing. Problem with that is that sailing is literally just doing nothing. Sure, sometimes there's a sea serpent, leviathan or a change in the wind. But none of those are, in my opinion, deserving of my continued attention. Sailing can take a long time. And since we're on the topic of travel, the game does have portals. Cool right? Well, by default valuable items like ores cannot be transported through portals! Now thankfully the game lets you change this setting (we'll get into settings) but the default way to play the game funnels you into sailing, an activity largely synonymous with doing absolutely nothing.

Then we get into stamina management, arguably the single most important aspect of the game. And for me it's abysmal. Lack of stamina is debilitating, and about every status effect that doesn't affect health affects stamina instead. Being cold handicaps your stamina regeneration speed. Being wet handicaps your regeneration speed. This makes being well rested as good as mandatory with how often you find yourself out after dark or in the rain. This is a massive time waste if you need to get back to your friend who's in trouble after you died because you first have to sit on the ground for half a minute every time. And being cold in the night doesn't get solved until your fourth area, so you already need to have gotten through three bosses before you can finally dress warm.

Then we get to actually dying itself. The default death punishment is severe. You lose a good chunk of skills and your entire inventory. The game does not let you reduce the death punishment to nothing. You will always lose skills, no matter how low you set it. Again an artificial time waster because skills take ages to gain and make a sizeable difference in your performance.

Now raids. Raids add literally nothing gameplay-wise. Raids do not consist of unique enemies, do not supply unique resources and only serve to again either inconvenience you and waste time or at best fatten up your resources. And if your base is not well defended, it can destroy your pretty structures! Since the building has a stress system, high strung buildings can easily succumb to a chain reaction. At no point have I ever been excited about a raid. Again, thankfully something the game lets you turn off.

We also have resource management which is also very grindy. Maybe you're not supposed to upgrade everything all the way. But I can remember literally becoming completely sick of the swamp because it took crypt after crypt and swamp after swamp across like a third of the world just to get and upgrade our gear. That... cannot be intentional.

And my last major gripe is the soundscape. The quality of the sounds is fine. I have no problem with that. But the placement of the sounds also add no value to the gameplay. Often games use sounds both to add to ambience, but also to provide additional player feedback. There is feedback, but nothing that actually warrants its existence in my opinion. What you hear, you can also always see. Playing as a deaf person brings as good as no disadvantages. Now this I recognize likely only irks me. But for me the sound has become very repetitive so I've turned it off completely. Now, make no mistake. I am not arguing for its nonexistence. But when we play games, I do argue that good design means proper utilization of the senses players have available to them which I find especially important in games that feature souls-like combat. We only have sight and sound, after all.

Now the settings. Basically I would just like more customization. The possibility for zero death punishment, no wind mechanics, weather chances, etc. Weather can be damn annoying at times and fog is absolutely debilitating (looking at you Mistlands. You look gorgeous, and show none of it)

And for a few technical aspects. The game allows commands. There is a console which you can use to alter your game. Day cycles last I checked are not server side, and neither is the weather. Making it day on one end does not make it day on all ends, effectively desynchronizing player's ability to sleep since everyone needs to be able to sleep to skip a night. And weather is also not server-side. The host being able to see clearly does not mean it is not foggy on another person's screen.

That's basically my thoughts on the game. The reason I keep playing and returning to it is because when the game is not actively trying to inconvenience you, it's relaxing. Building is fun, exploring is fun. Most of these qualms are related to the combat. But if I must draw a conclusion? I would not play it if I had no one else to play it with.

I'm trying to figure out why I don't like No Man’s Sky. I find this game boring. Which surprises me, since in other games I like the core gameplay loop: the locust. The locust can be described as taking anything that isn’t nailed to the floor. So why can I sink hundreds of hours into games like Starfield or The Last Caretaker, but I zone out after only 25 in No Man’s Sky?

I think the answer is context. No Man’s Sky doesn’t give me anything to care about. There is a story, but it’s told in such a way that I can’t be bothered to engage with it. 

You are dropped on a random planet, and go figure it out. And in the first few hours, I had my fun, but then I asked myself a very obvious question: Why am I doing any of it? In a normal game, I would have narrative to lean on, or interesting characters, set pieces, or visuals. But this game doesn’t really have any. Any interesting visual will get drowned out by how many times it occurs, and it will happen on all the planets you will visit. All (well, almost all) characters are procedurally generated, and those that aren’t might as well be. And narrative, while it exists, is told in such a way that I didn’t care.

And without anything else to lean on, the locust is just a chore. Gather more resources to go to the next planet. Will there be anything interesting there? Probably turns to no, and no turns to I don’t care. Will we do anything interesting there? We will gather more resources…

Developers added more content over the years and ironed out multiple rough edges. But the gameplay loop is boring. If the primary gameplay loop is boring, I won’t be motivated to engage with the other loops. And guess what? I was bored.

I read online that this game is a sandbox, and I need to remind people: the game doesn’t promise that anywhere on its Steam page. It explicitly names “exploration” and “survival”. And exploration sucks, mainly because of repetition, and survival is just meh. 

Also, the UI is bad; I don’t understand how a 10-year-old game can have UI that sucks. You would think that it's one of the first things developers would fix first. But apparently the UI in the original game sucked even more.

Would I recommend this game? For the current price: fuck no. With a big enough discount? Only if you treat this game as a sandbox and can find your own fun. Personally, when I pay for entertainment, I'd rather games be more structured than “find your own fun.”

Act 1: Absolutely amazing. The absolute peak of RPG gaming.

Act 2: Still good, but the cracks are starting to show.

Act 3: An incomprehensible clusterfuck where everything pretends to matter, but somehow nothing feels particularly impactful anymore.

Baldur's Gate 3 starts off as one of the most incredible RPG experiences I've ever had. Act 1 is genuinely fantastic. The exploration, the companions, the choices, the feeling that you're just a bunch of adventurers trying to make sense of the world around you. It's everything I want from an RPG.

Act 2 is still good, but things start feeling increasingly railroaded. Misinterpret one little thing, make a decision without fully understanding its consequences, and suddenly something massive happens that can sour the rest of your campaign. Player agency starts feeling less like freedom and more like trying to guess what the writers intended you to do.

And then comes Act 3.

Good lord, what happened here?

Suddenly you're drowning in supposedly world-shattering revelations, grand conspiracies, and characters with increasingly ridiculous ambitions. Everything is presented as the most important thing imaginable, yet very little of it actually feels meaningful.

It's like starting out reading The Fellowship of the Ring, embarking on this wonderful, grounded adventure with a group of companions, only for the story to slowly transform into some American Gods-style drama where the biggest, strongest, most important beings in existence all have the biggest, meanest plans.

And of course, you and your merry band of increasingly overpowered superheroes are the only ones who can stop them.

Somewhere along the way, the grounded RPG adventure turns into a comical superhero flick.

And perhaps the funniest part is that, in doing so, Baldur's Gate 3 stays remarkably faithful to D&D 5e.

Because it suffers from exactly the same progression problem: you start out as a bunch of nobodies worrying about goblins stealing someone's chickens, and before you know it, you're fighting gods, dragons, and the equivalent of World War III because apparently every adventure needs to escalate into a cosmic catastrophe.

Bigger stakes, bigger villains, bigger explosions. But not necessarily a better story.

I wish Baldur's Gate 3 had remained the adventure it was in Act 1. A wonderful, personal journey where your companions, discoveries, and smaller decisions felt like they mattered.

Instead, it trades that magic for an increasingly bloated spectacle that seems convinced the fate of the entire universe is inherently more interesting than the fate of a handful of adventurers.

An absolutely phenomenal beginning, a decent middle, and a final act that completely lost me.

Sometimes saving a village from goblins is a far better adventure than saving the entire world from gods.

There's a great game hidden somewhere in Valheim. It's just such an absolute chore to get to it.

So much of the game revolves around backtracking, gathering resources, preparing food, and getting ready for the part that's supposed to be fun, that eventually the most enjoyable moments are simply the ones where you don't have to do all those things.

And you'd think that with all those materials you've spent hours collecting, you'd at least be able to build increasingly amazing settlements. But the building system feels frustratingly limited. Most of the meaningful building freedom is already available with the starting materials, while everything you unlock afterwards feels more like another stepping stone to bridge the power gap to the next boss.

And then the next boss. And the next boss.

I really wish they'd spent more of their Early Access development time expanding the building systems, making settlements more meaningful, and streamlining the tedious parts so you could actually spend more time enjoying the game.

Instead, it feels like they've fallen into that increasingly common trap of game design where progression simply means escalating everything until you're practically playing a shoot-'em-up.

Every new boss needs to be bigger, badder, and more ridiculous than the last, until eventually you're fighting something that might as well be blasting a thousand lasers out of its eyes.

But is that really what a Viking survival and building game needed?

I'd much rather have more reasons to build, explore, and actually live in the world than another boss that requires another dozen hours of preparation just to overcome the next artificial power gap.

Valheim has an incredible foundation, but it feels like the developers keep building upwards when I wish they'd build outwards.

The game also requires a ton, and I mean a TON of grinding. With vanilla settings, be ready to be mining for hundreds of hours, and travel for double that. But it's arguably the most boring part of the game, oceans are empty and you're just semi-afk waiting for your ship to reach your destination.

I understand friction is a big, important thing in game design, but this game just does it too much. It's like it doesn't want you to enjoy the really cool things the game has to offer.

What saved the game for us was the modifiers and mods. We finally found a good balance : 2x resource rate, allow items through portals, limit death penalty and add a few QoL mods that let us focus on things we enjoy.

I also want to talk about the building in this game : the support system is actually really strong and interesting to play with. At first, you might be annoyed and think this limits your creativity but I think it pushes it even more, forcing you to solve architecture problems, it's really satisfying.

Please note, the following is purely my personal and also very subjective view on Project Zomboid, and I understand and respect that many players will see it very differently. And this is fine.

However, in my opinion, the biggest strength and weakness of Project Zomboid is its complexity. At the beginning, I loved it. There were so many things to find and try out. Especially the first hours in the game were so exciting: Waking up in an apartment, with barely any clothes on, while the undead start populating the streets outside. And I need to sneak to my neighbor's house to find some food and water, only equipped with a butter knife from my kitchen cupboard. And any sound or wrong movement can betray me and lead to disaster.

When the power was cut for the first time, I was in shock. And the pizza and ice cream I had stacked in my freezer started to rot.  
I built a water barrel to save any drop of the precious rain. When my hygiene was severely lacking, I broke into a barber's shop and stole some scissors, hair gel, and a razor. I finally looked like a decent guy again, albeit shortsighted and with two holes in my hoodie and my muddy boots.

I barricaded my windows. I built strong fences around my house, because some wandering zombies had trampled my zucchini that I had so carefully planted. When the canned mushroom soup was running out, I managed to catch a rabbit. And a racoon. The latter was still a baby though, and I was unable to cut his throat in spite of really looking forward to a hot meal again. So I petted him, and he became visibly less stressed over the next days. This is probably thankfully also because of the 10 chicken I stole from one of the nearby farms, transporting each carefully one by one to my house and dropping them on my lawn. The unfortunate part, however, is that I need to pick up their droppings every two days and clean their hutch. And I just can't force myself to eat another egg. I had so many of them over the last two weeks!

Having survived for 2 1/2 months, my life feels like an endless routine and worse than my previous day job. This warehouse a few blocks down still looks like an attractive target that I should absolutely visit. I just don't find the time anymore though between all this cleaning, cooking, tailoring, and yes, I admit, watching videos about woodcraft!

I was thinking about leaving my chicken behind. Moving to the forest and leading the simple life. I have a sixpack of beer in the trunk of my old Chevrolet, ready to go. But it would mean giving up so many hours I invested into building all of this up. And then starting from fresh again, just to do the same.

I know those are probably my crazy thoughts, because I haven't eaten for 6 whole hours again, and I am starving. However, the apocalypse... I wish it was a bit more fun! Less tedious. And more exciting. 

I never wanted to become a chicken farmer. And collect all that poop. If this is how life should be, is it really still worth living?! The old lady from next door didn't survive her first two hours after the news of the outbreak had come in. I wonder who had the better fate after all.

Let's get one thing out of the way before I say anything: I adore this game. I adore the combat, the story, all the characters, and that I'm still finding new things in every playthrough. I'm on my 8th playthrough right now. You can see how many hours I have in this game. At the time of writing this review I have three more playthroughs planned not including the one I'm currently on. None have been boring and every single one has been different. I've played this game every three months since its release.

Now, would I recommend this game to other players? It depends.

Do you enjoy an intricate story with lots of character customization and role playing possibilities but don't care for intricate combat? Play this game and play it on the easiest difficulty. Look up builds so you know which abilities to pick and what gear to buy. Get mods to make your player character look even wackier or make them nigh invincible so the combat is peanuts. Romance your favorite companion and then make a new character and romance them again. Explore what happens when you fail a roll. Save scum if you don't like the outcome. Play your favorite character's origin and make them smooch another origin character, or your guardian. Make their guardian look like your player character. Take screenshots. Frame your favorites. Go wild. 

Do you enjoy strategy turn based combat that has a variety of ways to solve fights, challenging bosses and hours of enormous battles with 20+ participants, but don't care for elaborate party management, pesky approval ratings and their consequences, and don't care for role playing in general? Play this game on Tactician and only use hirelings, don't recruit any companions. Try honor mode and enjoy the adrenaline rush. Min-max your heart out. Do a challenge run. (Also definitely try the previous game from Larian; Divinity Original Sin 2 if you enjoy this type of combat.)

However. Do you not care for elaborate roleplay worth hundreds of hours over multiple playthroughs, long cutscenes and romance mechanics, or any form of turn-based strategy games? Then there's thousands of other games for you out there. But probably not this one.

Or, you know, get it on sale some time and give it a go anyway. Broaden your horizons.

I bought Cyberpunk because everyone keeps saying how good the game has become, and honestly, I was just bored out of my mind.

The entire gameplay loop feels like:

Dialogue → walk for 30 seconds → dialogue → walk for another 30 seconds → dialogue → shoot some enemies with some of the worst gunplay I've ever experienced → dialogue → walk for 30 seconds → repeat.

It's just so unbelievably boring.

Don't get me wrong, some of the dialogue is actually interesting, and I can see the appeal of certain story moments. But especially during gameplay missions, the conversations feel incredibly shallow. Characters keep talking at you while you're walking from one objective to another, but most of it feels like filler rather than anything genuinely interesting.

And then there's the dialogue system. You get multiple dialogue options, but most of them feel completely pointless. If you don't pick the obvious main story option, you don't discover anything interesting, unlock a side quest, or get any meaningful alternative outcome. You just get a few extra lines of dialogue before the game forces you back onto the one option that actually progresses the story.

Why even give me the illusion of choice if nothing meaningful comes out of it?

I genuinely don't understand why people enjoy this game so much. Maybe the story gets better later on, but if the gameplay is this tedious, the gunplay feels this bad, and so many dialogue choices feel superficial, I really don't see the appeal.

Then comes Phantom Liberty—the ultimate cherry on top. Easily ranking among the best expansion packs ever created, it kicks off with a bang and maintains non-stop momentum straight through to the end.

Seeing where Cyberpunk 2077 started compared to where it sits today is nothing short of incredible. CDPR delivered a legendary gameplay experience, and getting to step into the shoes of V is an journey no RPG fan should miss

The most detailed Zombie survival game to date.  Not really my cup of tea, but it is a good game.

PROS
- Very deep game-play that keeps getting better with each new build of the game.
- health, hunger, hydration, & psychology systems.
- Destruct-able environments, eventually.
- Building and Crafting and maintenance.
- Mountains of items of varying degrees of usefulness.
- Large Skill Tree with positive and negative traits to custom craft your character.
- You can improve skills as you play.
- Excellent tutorial.
- Lots of mods for the game.

CONS
- You can't win.  Get used to dying all the time.  Some people believe this is a PRO, but not me.
- Freedom of choice is mostly an illusion.  Yes you can do what you want in this game, but if you want to survive for very long you are forced into only a few playstyles.
- The Devs don't want you to survive and they nerf working strategies every update.  When they flash "This is how you died." at the start of each run, they are serious about it.
- There is a crazy lack of food in houses the week after the 4th of July.  There should be leftover BBQ all over the place, not to mention the rest of the food that's normally there.
- Guns seem overly scarce.  Not that I recommend using them in game, but I should think small towns in Kentucky would have more than you find.
- The default modes are too difficult.  The "Builder" mode sells itself as easy to let you experiment with building and crafting, but in reality you are starving to death and constantly fighting zombies and have no time or energy to build anything.  Seriously, Easy mode should be Easy.
- Any objection is rebuffed with "Just Play Sandbox" which is a bit much to ask for new players that don't understand what all the options do.  If that is your response, then they players are likely to just go play something else.
- Item durability is very low.  Crowbars eventually break, somehow.
- Moodles are deliberately vague.  Moodles are status indicators for your character.
- You need some mods for necessary QoL in game.

It's a midpoint between three genres:
1. Terrain and environment building/resource extraction (minecraft, valheim)
2. Exploration and tech progression (subnautica, Ark)
3. Space sim (elite dangerous, space engineers)
It does some of everything but not as good as the other, more focused games above. 

You might like it a lot. But I can't make myself go back to it for several reasons:
- Nothing you can gain is particularly appealing, visually. The design style seems to be going for a Star Wars-esque aesthetic (your starting ship is reminiscent of an X-wing, your exosuit is similar to a rebel pilot outfit, etc.) but it just doesn't hit the mark. Everything is so BUSY, like the art director thinks the final step to looking cool is vomiting a bunch of flaps, bumps and angles onto every surface.
- Progression is VERY sluggish. What accounts for the extended tutorial is well over 2 hours and I still feel the leash holding me back. Why do I need ancient blueprints to unlock commonplace technology? Why are storage crates locked behind >12 hours' worth of missions, story or otherwise? Holy shit, get to the point.
- Resource gathering is unfun. The game revolves around mining and such but getting to, harvesting, and storing material is tedious. And you can only build ten crates! In the entire game! Bases share the same storage space, the chests just access those spaces.
- The game is presented as a space combat simulator, but the primary gameplay loop is resource extraction. Four hours in and I don't have any idea when the fighting - when the FUN - begins to start.
