Stardew Valley is one of those games that I will always come back to, no matter how much time has passed. I have over 200 hours on PC alone, and I couldn't even begin to guess how many more I've spent playing on Switch! No matter how many times I start a new farm, there is always something new to discover, another goal to work toward, or another reason to fall in love with the game all over again.

The amount of content is genuinely incredible. Between the overarching story, the countless quests, the secrets to uncover, and the individual stories and relationships of each NPC, there is always something to do. Every character feels unique, with their own personality, struggles, interests, and growth. Getting to know the villagers and seeing their stories unfold makes Pelican Town feel like a real community rather than just a setting for a farming game.

And the farming itself? There is genuinely something for every type of player! Whether you love growing crops, fishing, mining, raising animals, ranching, crafting artisan goods, decorating, or focusing on relationships and exploration, the game gives you so much freedom to play however you want. You can spend an entire day optimizing your farm, disappear into the mines for hours, or simply wander around town talking to everyone. There's no single right way to play, and I love that.

What makes Stardew Valley especially special to me is how comforting it is. It's the kind of game you can pick up when you need something familiar and relaxing, lose yourself in for hours, and return to months or even years later without losing that feeling of coming home. There's always another season to experience, another project to finish, or another little detail to appreciate.

And I genuinely cannot praise ConcernedApe enough for what he has created. The love, care, and attention to detail that went into this game are so evident, and the fact that he continues to support it and bring more content to players makes it even more impressive. It's amazing to see a game made with so much heart continue to grow and bring joy to so many people.

Stardew Valley is so much more than a farming simulator. It's a comfort game, an adventure, a community, and an experience that never really gets old. If you haven't played it yet, I cannot recommend it enough. And if you have? Well, I'll probably see you back on the farm.

Another game that makes me wish there was a "down the middle" option. I don't really recommend this game, despite having over 200+ hrs in it at this point. A large chunk of this time came from before 1.0 release, and a majority of it was spent building structures on multiple friends new worlds/sessions to see what the hype was about in EA.

The game just gets progressively.. worse. The first two areas of progression feel fine, then you hit the swamp and realize that's the entire loop of this game with virtually no variation beyond adding more excessively grindy ways to achieve the same goal of find new area > make new material > spend the rest of your time in the area trying to find a boss/boss locator. Maybe make a new weapon that you spent the last 30 minutes gathering materials for just to make it and find out it's a complete dud.

Enemy AI is absolutely atrocious. This is a low point from the beginning when you realize enemies will attack you then run circles around you trying to find a new spot to begin an attack, and unsurprisingly it only gets worse with enemies that quite literally amplify the issue. But, at the same time, enemy AI is also smart enough to know when you're chopping a tree on the other side of the forest from it and will bring a small party to "investigate" the exact spot you chopped at. Fighting in this game is more often than not waiting for the AI to reposition itself so it can execute its attack. One on one this isn't a problem, but as with the nature of this game you're assailed by multiple enemy types at the same time in your encounters later on, meaning more often than not every single encounter is you dancing around the enemies trying to barely regain just enough stamina just to attack. 

Progression, as mentioned before, is the same blueprint through every biome. New trees, new ore, move on. To keep this fresh, instead of unique and meaningful gameplay elements to keep things fun, choose to directly hinder the player with little to no resolve beyond the specific intended interactions. The swamp requires constant micromanagement of your rested stamina buffs and forces you to create poison potions. The mountain forces you to make frost potions. While they're only suggestions, they are borderline required. The plains gives you reprieve from the formula only to realize they're an even bigger "blink and you miss it" biome as it appears the plains biome from EA release was truly their final vision for the biome, because it feels largely unfinished and more like an after thought. As for the latter biomes it really feels like they just lost all creativity they were running low on and thought "lets just say these areas are war torn" because they're utterly boring and tedious to navigate.

There's a large amount of QoL missing from this game too, even for modifiers you're able to change. Storage is an absolute nightmare with the amount of materials required for things at all times, the building is this games greatest strength and simultaneously has the worst building out of any survival crafter I've ever played. Simple things like area storage, area crafting, building free-cam, and easing acquisition of commonly needed material are either introduced outright or steadily incorporated into your gameplay, not in this game. Your equipment takes up physical inventory slots so no matter what you're always feeling strapped for inventory space. The in-game provided solution to transport materials short distances is cool for about 5 seconds untill you realize the cart is virtually worthless without more preparation than it's worth. This and other tiny things just constantly compound on themselves to the point where the latter half of the game just feels like a tedious endurance sprint rather than wanting to see what cool things are waiting at the end of the finish line.

For all the people reading the pretentious reviews and jabber from the devs saying "Ohh you only made it to the swamp and rage quit huh?" please ignore their drivel, the Swamp quite literally sets the expectations for the rest of the game. Most decisions/interactions in the game post-Swamp are all detrimental to the player giving them workarounds in the form of micromanaging 30 minute potion crafts. It just steadily becomes not fun and not worth the effort, and the lack of any real changes from pre-1.0 areas to now just feels like the developers had the same sentiments.

This game has a lot of content and it took me a long time to beat.  When I say "beat," I mean "perfect."  Because the only way to really beat the game is to 100% it, which is very time-consuming.

There's not really much of a story except for at the beginning.  Otherwise, you basically just build up your life, family, friends and town.  There are really only two mutually exclusive choices to make, but they mostly lead to similar outcomes, and the rewards are different.

When starting the game, you can choose what kind of farm you want between a regular farm, beach farm, a forage farm, a farm with monsters, etc.  The goal is still the same; sow, harvest, get paid.

I lost track of how many quests there were, mostly because a lot of them repeat.  If I were to summarize it into different parts, I'd limit it to the following:  Farming, mining, relationships and community.

Farming is what you would think; grow crops, build coops and stables, care for animals, produce artisan goods, craft stuff, cook dishes, etc.

Mining is more of the adventurous and combative part of the game where you explore the floors of mines, fight enemies, find rare resources and artifacts, forge, find and upgrade weapons, etc.

Relationships involve the local and non-local citizens.  Talking to them, gifting them things they like or completing quests for them increase your relationship.  In contrast, saying mean things, hitting trashcans in front of them, or gifting them things they don't like will decrease your relationship.  There are events that happen at various times and places once you've reached a certain relationship threshold with a particular person and it reveals a little more depth to their lives and develops their character further.  There are bachelors and bachelorettes that can be romanced and eventually married, after which they move in with you, enabling you to have/adopt up to 2 children.  Some of this cannot be done until you've upgraded your house sufficiently.  There are a number of characters that are either already married or cannot otherwise be romanced.  There are mods that can change this, FYI.  I didn't use any of them, for the record.

The community-related part of the game involves developments that improve things around town, like fixing buses, boats or bridges that lead to new places, fixing the greenhouse on your property for indoor farming, removing rocks so that ore and minerals flow through the town's water, etc.  This is the part where there are two mutually exclusive ways to go about it.  The developer has made it very apparent that one of these ways is their preferred way, and is a lot more in-depth and time-consuming in nature.  The other way is more efficient, but is made to feel more empty in the end. Valheim is terriffic. It is frustrating. It is cozy. It demands huge time commitments. It is challenging. It is relaxing. A lot of those may seem contradictory, but Valheim manages it. It's best played with friends and at a slow pace, because chasing improvement will lead to burnout fast as you grind through resources at breakneck speed. The combat can feel gruelling and the biomes intimidating, yet the base building lends itself to cozy quiet villages with a relaxing atmosphere (until besieged by monsters of course). It can wind up feeling like the perfect Viking fantasy, setting off in a longboat to face perils unknown in uncharted lands, fighting for glory, then sailing home victorious, armour dented and blades dulled, boat low in the water loaded down with spoils, arriving to a cozy village with roaring fires, warm beds, a feast on the table, and barrels of mead. 

TLDR: This is not Minecraft. You are a Viking on a final trial to enter Valhalla. By the same token, it is not Dark Souls. Be ready to fight, do not expect constant action.

Oh, and it's a lot more demanding than it looks. Don't try to run this on a cheap laptop or an email machine just because of the PS1 graphics, it wants CPU and VRAM in abundance.

Project Zomboid is one of the few games I've put this kind of time in. I do not regret it. If you are a fan of zombie movies/tv shows/books/games etc this is a no brainer. Growing up one of my favorite books was The Zombie Survival Guide by Max Brooks and this game has the same brand of insane attention to detail the book has when it comes to the minutiae of surviving in a hypothetical apocalypse where the dead rise. The game does not pull it's punches. A bite is a death sentence, your character can grow tired, depressed, hungry, sick, panicked, etc. You aren't a badass main character with infinite stamina. You are a weak everyday person not a killing machine. Having to meet basic human needs when leaving your house could mean a quick and painful death which keeps the game exciting. Every playthrough is a new adventure to get lost in. Trying different character set ups with unique abilities that can give them a jump start in different skills like starting the game with the knowledge on how to hotwire a car, or already knowing how to use firearms effectively can drastically change how each run goes. You can customize your own style of zombie scenario too. The ability to change difficulty like loot scarcity, weather, zombie lore (such as them being able to run or bites not being lethal) empowers the player with more options to diversify their experience. Throw in a fully functional online mode with other players and a really dedicated mod community means the game is nearly limitless in what it can offer. If you want a hyper detailed zombie survival game where killing zombies isn't the only goal and find enjoyment in the everyday trials of day to day survival this is the game for you. Cannot recommend this game enough.

Recommended, but there's a lot of wasted potential.

First off, Cyberpunk 2077 is a genuinely enjoyable game. The atmosphere, visuals, combat, and overall design of Night City are impressive. However, the longer I play, the more I notice just how many opportunities were missed.

On the technical side, I've experienced some rendering issues that may or may not be related to my PC. I've lowered my graphics settings considerably, but the problems persist. I've also encountered a handful of bugs that required me to save, completely close the game, and restart it. Annoying, but nothing that has ruined the experience.

My biggest complaint, however, is Night City itself.

For a city that looks so alive, it feels surprisingly dead.

There's an incredible amount of detail throughout the world, but very little of it actually responds to your existence. You can spend hours completing side activities, fighting gangs, and building your street cred, but it rarely feels like any of it carries meaningful weight in the world around you.

Take the gangs, for example. If I spend my time hunting down members of a particular gang, eventually they should recognize me as an enemy and attack me on sight. On the other hand, if I've consistently avoided conflict with another gang, maybe their members should acknowledge that. Even something as simple as different dialogue, attitudes, or reactions based on your history with a faction would make the world feel significantly more immersive.

Street cred could have been so much more than a number. Imagine having separate reputations with different gangs, where your actions determine whether you're respected, feared, tolerated, or hated. That alone would give side activities a much greater sense of purpose.

Cyberware customization is another missed opportunity. For a game centered around a society obsessed with body modification, installing cyberware has surprisingly little impact on your physical appearance. Being able to customize the color, style, or design of your implants would have added another layer of immersion and personal expression.

But all of that ties into my biggest issue with the game:

You never really feel like you're part of Night City.

At times, it almost feels like The Truman Show, except nobody is actually watching you. Nobody seems to care who you are, what you've accomplished, or what you've done to the people around them. You can be an absolute menace to a particular gang, and the next group you encounter acts like they've never heard of you.

The city is beautiful, flashy, detailed, and full of people, yet somehow manages to feel strangely lifeless. It's almost like exploring an incredibly elaborate movie set rather than living in a functioning world.

And that's what frustrates me the most. The foundation for something truly incredible is already there.

Despite all of this, I still recommend Cyberpunk 2077. I've had a lot of fun with it, and there's plenty the developers got right. I just can't shake the feeling that Night City could have been so much more.

This is a wonderful game well worth your time to play whether solo or in a group. I played the game entirely solo. It is quite a simple game when you boil it all down to its constituent parts, but when those parts come together, they form something so much more. You are not going to be wowed by any individual system to the game, but taken together you have this vibrant experience even after 100 hours of playing can still feel satisfying to engage with. And this experience puts you into that world and you become immersed in it. 

I had some major misgivings with the game before I really gave it a chance. The idea that procedurally generated worlds could be compelling was a preposterous proposition. There’s no way some randomized seed could create a majestic, intriguing world in my eyes. And I was wrong. I was flatly wrong. Maybe they figured out the secret to procedural generation. Maybe the fact that this is a relatively primitive world plays a part. Perhaps it is the wonderful artistry of the game. Maybe all three combined. Nevertheless, there are so many times I found myself in awe of the world around me.

I have trekked to the highest peaks. I have descended into the deepest of delves. I have capered across dark, foreboding forests engulfed in an eldritch energy.I have trudged through the muck and mire of infested swamps loomed over by primeval evil. It has been a grand adventure that has seen me desperately scrambling for survival amidst a blizzard hounded at every step on a treacherous mountaintop. And there have been moments of supreme tranquility as I built my home while crickets and frogs chirped in the fog at night. 

There is an energy to this game that I have seldom found in other games and it is not a quality you can quantify. Plenty of other games have distinct areas that you venture in, but I cannot think of any game that has done them as well as this game has. It is what sets Valheim apart and if you and it get on that wavelength together, you will get Valheim. 

And if you like building things, fuhgeddaboutit. This is the game to do it in. There’s seemingly endless possibilities for you to construct whatever your heart desires. The only quibble I have is that so much of the coolest building materials are locked by progression.

It is not without faults, though. There’s some design decisions that are just baffling. I have larger bones to pick below, but some of my nitpicks are: enemies being able to freely attack you from water while you cannot do the same, taming and riding being irritating, tacked-on systems, attacking things above or below you.

The incessant noises from animals/monsters can be extremely grating. It’s fine when you are running about and helpful obviously because it helps you find them. Where it isn’t helpful is being in your home just trying to relax and do stuff. I won’t even keep tamed animals because of how much noise they generate constantly. And sometimes animal noises can happen so frequently and with each animal staggering its calls, an endless cacophony can occur. I had to hunt down 3 crows once because there was a non-stop ‘CAW CAAAAAAAAAW’ every second. 


It is a survival game and inventory management is to be expected. You have very limited carrying capacity. And that’s fine; however, what isn’t fine is the chest management. The chests can also only stack as much as you can personally, which means you end up with an absurd amount of chests that require signage to even be manageable. It is troublesome even with upgraded chests. That really shouldn’t be necessary. Chests should be able to stack far more than they do. 

While I had a wonderful time solo, the game world is perhaps too big for a solo player. It is fine if you have a group because it gives everyone tons of resources and a lot to explore, but if you are doing it all on your own, the world is almost insurmountably large. It would have been nice to make smaller worlds to accommodate being solo. 

The Mistlands are well and truly a complete grind. It isn’t even that they are difficult. I found the jump to it from the last biome to be pretty small honestly. Finding seals takes way too long. Finding sources of soft tissue likewise takes way too much time. Clearing the mists takes way too much time. And the mists along with the extreme terrain means you can never see anything except that which you have cleared and isn’t obscured by rocks. There’s various ways to somewhat mitigate it all, but not entirely and it is still unenjoyable. It was a neat idea at first, but I soured on it quickly. I hadn’t felt that way with any other biome. They all felt good in their own ways. I want to replay the game some time and the thought of trudging through this biome again fills me with dread. The mist should have just been like a regular intense fog and the terrain should not have been so extreme. I will say that I actually quite like its boss battle, though. And Gjalls are cool.

There are other ways in which the game is oddly hostile to the player, like hunting Ocean monsters where everything they drop but their trophies floats to the surface. So you either have to be extraordinarily quick to get the trophy or drag them to the shore. And it is one of those needless acts of anti-player behavior that does nothing to make the experience better. It’s just there to make things more tedious. There’s various instances of that kind of friction.

Weapon types missing entirely from certain biomes is also a real misstep with my favorite one being entirely absent in the final biome. I don’t really understand that at all. 

It feels like the game had the potential to be so much more than it is, though. Despite being as wonderful as it is, there’s just so much about the game that feels like it was just shipped as ‘Good enough.’ And that’s a shame because I could envision a Valheim where everything was more fleshed out and interesting, like revamped Sunken Crypts or the Ocean.

All and all, it is a truly great game with a bunch of shortfalls. It is an amazing experience and an adventure like no other. It could have been much more than it is, but for what it is, it is still something truly worth experiencing whether alone or with friends.

I immediately fell in love with Night City. The futuristic design, technological advancements, cyberware, and the whole question of what it means to be human. Everything comes together beautifully. The Asian inspired aesthetics give certain parts of the city an almost Japanese atmosphere, making Night City feel unique and unforgettable.
And the story... absolutely incredible. I genuinely grew attached to the main and side characters, especially those with their own relationship storylines. Even the NPCs make the city feel alive, as if everyone has their own life beyond your own. CD Projekt Red did an outstanding job creating a world that feels like it actually exists.
And those endings... damn. Some of them genuinely made me emotional, and a few even made me cry. Not many games can make you feel that connected to their characters and their stories.
I also have to mention Phantom Liberty. This DLC could easily stand on its own as a separate game set in the Cyberpunk universe. The story, the characters, the quests, the atmosphere... it's an intense experience from beginning to end. Calling it just a DLC almost feels unfair.
I've also heard rumors about an upcoming Cyberpunk movie, and I'm curious to see how it turns out. Though, honestly, the game has set the bar incredibly high. It's going to be difficult to capture the same depth, atmosphere, and emotional impact in a movie.

No Man's Sky is one of the best video games ever made. Most people have heard about its rocky start but Hello Games stuck with it, relentlessly pursuing their vision and beyond. For years now it has been a masterpiece that just keeps getting better. There is so much to do in this game and so much personal creativity you can express. It's largely a sandbox game but with some directed goals here and there where you can put your focus if you like. The visuals are often quite stunning and you strongly feel drawn into the universe of No Man's Sky. 

The experience elevates to a whole other level if you play the game in VR. That VR experience of hopping in a spaceship and flying into space, or walking the corridors of your corvette, or plundering a haunted derelict freighter in space all from the perspective of "being there" is incredible. The VR experience isn't intensely kinetic. You won't be doing manual reloads on your weapon or scaling walls with your hands. in fact, I play the game seated. Yet it is extremely immersive and there are plenty of little touches that make the VR experience come home, such as grabbing the cockpit hatch and lifting it to leave your spaceship. Also, for a game with a lot of moving parts the controls are very well done.

No Man's Sky is largely a chill and relaxing game. Fights with the Sentinels can be intense. Pirate freighter battles are frenetic and not entirely simple to win. Much of the game, however, is about exploration, harvesting resources, improving your gear, and building functional & appealing bases, corvettes, and space platforms. There's even some light management sim elements in dealing with Settlements.

The bottom line is that this is a great game for anyone, but especially for those who like sci-fi, exploration, sandbox games, or who want to lose themselves in another place and have the feeling that they can go anywhere and do nearly anything. When a game is still pulling in brand new players ten years after release, its clear that the experience is something special.

Valheim is a slow survival game of upkeep and exploration. The focus is the journey. If you go into it expecting a non-stop action game, or even a great fighting game, you'll be disappointed. The other aspects—farming, dungeon delving, cooking, building, sailing—are all integral to the experience. You need to make sure you get a grasp of what the next biome has to offer before you can safely fight the boss of that biome.

If you aren't into slow burns, this game is probably not for you. You WILL be bothered by half an hour of sailing, or constant assaults from weaker enemies from previous biomes which only are weak because your new norm as far as gear goes is so much further beyond them, you will be toiling in a pit digging out every nugget of ore you can. But in spite of those faults, you'll be exploring an interesting world and fighting new and challenging monsters as you gain the strength to face the new normal.

# No Man's Sky – 97 Hours Played and Still Exploring!

**Recommended – An Incredible Space Exploration Experience**

After spending 97 hours playing No Man's Sky, I can safely say this is one of those games where you can easily lose track of time. There's always something new to discover, another planet to explore or another objective to complete.

**Graphics and Atmosphere**

Playing at 4K on my RTX 4090, No Man's Sky can look absolutely stunning. From colourful alien planets and vast oceans to enormous space stations and impressive starships, the sheer variety of environments is one of the game's biggest strengths.

Flying through space, landing on an unexplored planet and discovering what it has to offer never really gets old. The sense of scale and freedom is fantastic.

**Exploration and Gameplay**

What makes No Man's Sky special is the freedom to play however you want. You can explore planets, discover new star systems, build bases, trade resources, upgrade your equipment, fight space pirates or simply travel around the galaxy.

There isn't just one way to enjoy the game, and that's what keeps it interesting.

The procedurally generated universe is enormous, and even after 97 hours, I feel like I've only scratched the surface of what's available.

**Progression and Upgrades**

One of the most addictive aspects is improving your equipment, expanding your inventory and upgrading your starships, multitool and exosuit.

There's a real sense of achievement when you finally obtain that upgrade you've been working towards.

The missions, guilds and reputation systems also provide plenty of reasons to keep exploring different star systems.

**Performance and Optimisation**

On a powerful PC, No Man's Sky offers a visually impressive experience, especially at 4K.

With a Ryzen 7 7800X3D, RTX 4090 and 64GB RAM, I have plenty of hardware available to enjoy the game's detailed environments and impressive space scenery.

**Things That Could Be Improved**

The inventory management can sometimes feel unnecessarily complicated, particularly when juggling resources, upgrades and storage.

Some missions can also become repetitive, and the game doesn't always explain certain mechanics particularly well. I've occasionally found myself having to work things out through trial and error.

However, these are relatively minor frustrations compared with the sheer amount of content and freedom the game provides.

**Final Verdict – 97 Hours Played**

No Man's Sky is an excellent example of a game that offers tremendous freedom, exploration and long-term enjoyment.

After 97 hours, I'm still discovering new things, upgrading my equipment and finding reasons to visit another star system.

If you enjoy open-world exploration, space travel, upgrading equipment and games that allow you to progress at your own pace, there's an enormous amount to enjoy here.

**Overall: Highly Recommended – 9/10**

*97 hours played | PC | RTX 4090 | Ryzen 7 7800X3D | 4K Gaming*

Valheim is not a bad game, but it suffers from mediocre Gameplay and some bad design decisions.

The good parts:
- The lighting, the music and the ambience is very atmospheric. Sometimes I just sit there and watch the epic sunrise over the dark forest or listen to the ambience sounds of the various biomes.

- Interesting lore and different biomes with different creatues and resources.

- The Building System is good and let's you create very unique Buildings and other structures.

The bad parts:
- The progression system is mediocre at best. Upgraded bronze gear is on par with unupgraded iron gear. Why? It doesn't feel like an upgrade as it should be. And this goes on from biome to biome.

- The movement is very clunky for a survival game and it feels like you are playing a game from before 2005... Every slight slope will send you sliding downwards if you are not running, every single stone and bush will block your movement, it just feels bad.

- You can build ships to travel fast distances, but besides the beautiful scenery there happens absolutely nothing in such a voyage and the ships are not much faster than running. But the most annoying part is, that you can get your boat stuck on underwater rocks and sandbanks. And if you are unlucky you can't get the boat out because you cannot just deconstruct your boat like everything else in the game. You have to destroy it and on water some resources fall on the Ground where you can't get them because you can't dive.

- You are playing a viking, but somehow this "viking" has catastrophic endurance. Everything you do costs stamina and after a few seconds of running, your entire stamina has vanished. Even if you eat enought buff Food. I don't get it why do I always have to play some seemingly asthmatic guy in a Survival game that can't even run for 10 seconds?

- You can build portals to traverse vast distances in a second, but on standard settings every second resource you find cannot be teleported (Although you can change that in the cettings at least). So you have to travel an hour over seas with your boat (and hope you don't get stuck on the way) to just bring some ores back home to craft two new items. Which leeds to the next point:

- The grind in this game is massive. I like grinding personally, as long as the gameplay loop is satisfactory to play. But when your character slides away as soon as he stands on a slight slope or when every single pixel is blocking your way than it soon becomes tedious. Especially when you are playing alone.

- At some point some of my portals stopped working. I had to manually deconstruckt them and build them anew. Which takes time when you have to sail over half the world to a broken portal. I don't know why Valheim has such a primitve portal system were only two portals can be connected instead of just choosing a portal in the map to teleport to, but it just feels bad.

- The user interface (if you want to call it that) is the worst I have ever seen in a survival game. Nothing about this interface is good or informative. It just looks like a prototype from a very early alpha build of a game. For a 2026 release this is just lazy.

- No crafting from chest, which is a quality of life feature since at least 10 years in the survival genre.

Without mods I couldn't dare to finish even the second biome as the clunkiness was very annoying. I installed some mods to fix that and it instantly felt way better. But still, the broken portals, the (anti)progression system just don't feel rewarding or fun. I played the game 5 years ago and it felt way better back then, maybe because everything was new and exciting. But now after so many hours I can see the flaws of the game.
I can see why people like this game, and I liked it also, but at this point there is just to many annoyances to be fun for me.

I’ve played this game for a long time and put many hours into it, but it has only gotten worse over time. I can no longer recommend Apex Legends, especially not to new players.

Broken Ranked System & Smurfing
The Ranked system is completely out of touch. In lower ranks, you get paired with players who are either totally new or barely know how to play. But as soon as you reach Diamond, you are thrown into lobbies with players who have thousands of hours or even Top 750 Predators, depending on the time of day. Because Ranked becomes virtually unplayable at Diamond, an absurd number of people create smurf accounts and hop on alts, making the experience terrible for everyone in lower tiers.

Horrible Legends Balancing
The legend balancing is frustrating. Some legends are left completely underpowered for years, while a select few remain blatantly overpowered for multiple seasons in a row. It genuinely feels like you are trolling your own team in Ranked if you aren't picking from the meta Top 3.

Persistent Bugs & Poor Optimization
Despite being out for so many years and having a massive player base, the game’s technical state is atrocious:

Visual / Animation Sync Issues: Enemies shoot at you while their character model is facing completely away from you on your screen.

Hit Registration: You get clear blood splatters and hit effects, but the game registers zero damage ("no-regs").

Audio Bugs: Footsteps and enemy audio cues fail constantly—people can run right up behind you without making a sound.

Server Instability: Frequent server crashes, heavy lag, and issues during season launches and regular updates.

Greed Over Community Feedback
In recent years, it feels like Respawn and EA have stopped listening to community feedback altogether. Their main priority has shifted entirely to pushing overpriced skins and cosmetics no one asked for, while fundamental gameplay issues, quality-of-life updates, and proper balancing are ignored.

Final Verdict:
Do not waste your time—and especially do not spend your hard-earned money on this game. There are plenty of other games out there where the developers actually care about providing a good player experience. Pass on this one.

It's "OK" fun with friends, but the game has serious issues, and is rather empty as a whole. It's basically a sandbox game with a light layer of progression through some interesting zones. But as a solid stand-alone game this is not very good.

Here's a fun list:
- can't save server passwords
- players who only play on servers instead of single-player worlds will always be prompted to create a new world when they go to play, forcing extra dialogue dismissals before being able to connect to the server.
- many dialogues don't have confirm or back buttons, just a border and a text box.
- the game doesn't allow choosing your output audio device, so if it picks up the wrong one from the OS you're using, you need to tab out of the game and change your system-wide settings, then restart the game.
- in-game sorting options are hidden behind cryptic chat commands
- networking does not scale due to bad architectural choices causing NPC pathing and collisions to misbehave in multiplayer settings.
- server configurations are poorly documented and use archaic parsing that is prone to breakage without proper error logging to console.
- crossplay impact on server listing TTL is undefined in any documentation, forcing crossplay enabled server to ocasionally need re-creation by the user in the saved section.
- configuring server parameters (e.g. difficulty) locks achievements off from player character because that is considered cheating by the developers.
- re-enabling achievments after nonsensical and badly chosen criteria requires an obnoxiously long variable toggle in the developer console in-game --because the developer thinks you should play the game they want.
- skill drain is a contrived option that wastes time. it should be changeable per-character or chosen at creation time for runs where that is important --though it appears the devs will consider you some kind of lesser vermin for thinking this.
- difficulty options are untuned, and instead apply a coefficient to spawn rates, health, damage output, instead of actually making the game more difficult in meaningful ways mechanically. This also leads to breakage of game mechanics during raids, like duplication.
- the game material progression system is contrived and forces re-trodding the same swamp zone many times for basic ingredients, making the gameplay loop monotonous. It's fun at the start when the zone is difficult and can result in interesting interactions, but later on it's frankly a waste of time.
- Much of the game difficulty can be cheesed with hammers through doors, or by partially opening rooms in dungeons to deal with enemies. The combat in general is quite boring in enclosed spaces, being just a hack-and-slash fest. Larger rooms could've helped with that.
- land-height is limited arbitrarily based on the location (and biome?), making building impossible above sea-level near the coasts. This limits creativity for no good reason. This is true for building up (raising land) and digging down.
- The sea is implemented so that it effectively mandates a lower limit for digging in the game, which is boring from gameplay perspective and limits map and gameplay design, and creative building.

And much more, but that's all from the top of my head...

# Sea of Thieves – A Disappointing Pirate Experience

Honestly, *Sea of Thieves* is one of the most frustrating games I have played. At first, it looks like an amazing pirate adventure where you can explore the ocean, discover treasures, fight other players, and sail with your friends. The graphics are beautiful, the water looks fantastic, and the idea of being a pirate sounds exciting. Unfortunately, after spending enough time playing, the experience starts to feel repetitive, annoying, and unnecessarily time-consuming.

One of the biggest problems with this game is how repetitive the gameplay becomes. Most missions involve sailing to an island, digging up treasure, fighting some enemies, and returning to an outpost. At first, this can be fun, but after doing the same activities over and over again, it quickly becomes boring. There is not enough variety to keep the experience interesting for long periods of time. It often feels like you are doing the same task for hours just to earn some virtual gold that does not even feel rewarding.

Another major issue is the PvP experience. Nothing is more frustrating than spending an hour collecting treasure, only to have another crew attack your ship and steal everything. While I understand that piracy is the main idea of the game, it does not make the experience any less annoying. Sometimes you just want to enjoy the game and complete a few missions without constantly worrying about being attacked by random players. Losing all your progress because another crew decides to ruin your day can make you want to uninstall the game immediately.

The solo experience is also terrible compared to playing with a full crew. Managing the ship, steering, adjusting the sails, repairing damage, fighting enemies, and navigating the map alone becomes exhausting. The game seems designed around teamwork, but playing alone often feels like doing several people's jobs at once. Finding reliable teammates is not always easy either, especially when random players refuse to cooperate or have no idea what they are doing.

The progression system is another disappointment. You spend hours completing missions and collecting treasure, but the rewards often feel meaningless. Most of the items you unlock are cosmetic, which means that all your grinding does not really make your character stronger or give you a significant gameplay advantage. While cosmetics can be fun, the lack of meaningful progression makes the whole experience feel unrewarding after a while.

There are also moments when the game feels unnecessarily unfair. You can spend a long time sailing across the map, only to encounter an enemy ship, get sunk, and lose your loot. The long travel times make these situations even more irritating. Instead of feeling like an exciting pirate adventure, it sometimes feels like wasting your evening doing chores on a virtual ocean.

Overall, *Sea of Thieves* has a great concept, beautiful visuals, and plenty of potential, but the repetitive missions, frustrating PvP encounters, tedious solo gameplay, and lack of meaningful progression make it difficult to enjoy consistently. It can be fun with friends, but that does not excuse its many frustrating aspects. For a game that promises adventure and excitement, it often delivers more boredom and irritation than anything else.

**Rating: 4/10.** A fantastic idea buried beneath repetitive gameplay and frustrating mechanics. I wanted to become a legendary pirate, not spend hours sailing around just to lose everything to someone who has nothing better to do.

[h2] Unplayable without mods, and tedious with mods [/h2]

I really tried to like Valheim, but I couldn't. It started out as fun survival crafting game, where exploring and building are genuinely satisfying. Then I reached the Swamp, and the game started to become increasingly tedious.

Inventory management is my biggest gripe. Quick-depositing into existing chests and quick-crafting from resources in nearby chests are quality of life features that the game industry has long learnt to be essential, yet Valheim doesn't have that. Coming back from an excursion and having to go through every chest to deposit items, and going through them again to take items out for crafting is utter mindless boredom that no-one should be forced to do. Of course, there's a mod to handle this.

Combat is sluggish and clunky, with animation locks, frustrating terrain, punishing stamina management, and questionable weapon balance. Items have little meaningful stats outside damage and armor, so the whole party rocking the same setup to fight bosses means the game has little room for build diversity and player creativity. Of course, there're mods to improve this.

Exploration feels more like a chore than joy in discovery. Terrains from Swamp onwards are stamina-intensive, and often getting yourself Cold or Wet means an extra 10s standing around waiting for your stamina regen every 20s. Biomes have next-to-none interesting areas or landmarks beside boss arena and dungeons. Materials are heavy and often scattered, and the dev-intended way of transporting them by cart is nigh impossible with the terrains, making farming them miserable. And god help you if you mistakenly land on Plains with Iron gear and get 2-shot by a Mosquito, because you'll be spending multiple depressing hours for those corpse runs. Unfortunately, no mods can help with this.

Building remains the only excellent feature Valheim has. It offers a lot of freedom, albeit clunky, in the ways you can place the building pieces to create the most extensive building system in any games I've played. Creating your own structures and terraforming are genuinely rewarding, despite occasional frustrations with materials and structural integrity.

One last problem I want to mention is the serious lack of quality of life features that for some reasons weren't addressed in the game's 5 years in early access. From the aforementioned essential quick-stack-to and quick-craft-from chests, to other smaller but numerous issues like: monsters take a while to drop loot after death, going up a ladder is clunky, cannot sort items, going up from water don't re-equip your weapon, cannot trash items, cannot teleport tamed creatures through portal, ballistae shooting at own players, cannot rename a pair of portals, etc. Of course, there're mods to handle all this.

Ultimately, Valheim starts as an inviting Viking adventure but gradually becomes a logistics simulator with clunky combat and increasingly hostile, unbalanced biomes that I don't recommend to anyone unless they want an immersive experience where you waste time doing chore like in real life with little fun rewarded

I even did an evil playthrough, which is usually really hard for me because I always end up feeling bad and making the “good” choice in games. 😂 The fact that Baldur’s Gate 3 actually got me to commit to an evil character says a lot about how much freedom the game gives you to play a completely different story.

After more than 230 hours, I still feel like there are things I could have done differently or storylines I could have missed. Definitely recommend it, even if you’ve never played D&D before.

The game started really fun. I love building my home then upgrading it gradually, it truly did feel immersive and cozy. The stamina system is rediculous, though; the guy runs 10 feet then is out of breath—too much so to even draw a bow? Come on. This guy is supposed to be some viking? He's unfit to serve jugs of mead. And don't even get me started with being cold. Like, jog bud, it'll warm you up. The combat is what it is. There's some nuance, but overall is just baiting attacks then sluggishly striking. Meadows was a pure joy to play, as it should be thematically, then Black Forest is a great progression: the trolls and bears are menacing yet rewarding to take down, the mood is darker, the mining and smelting of copper and tin is extremely satisfying. I enjoyed scouting for nodes then carving a path for my cart. Getting my first sword and buckler with the troll armour was awesome. Then you finally get a boat; this is the peak of Valheim. Setting sail on the ocean in this game is unparalleled for exploration. It truly felt like I was sailing to a new world. It was such a thrill following the coast, mapping different biomes, spying for natural harbours and plotting my next base whereby I'd place down a portal. Magical. I'm not gonna knock the wind system, it's suitably realistic, but this is where the game just starts straight wasting your time. Like, give me a fucking break with the wind man, half the time the wind was blowing off the mainland in the complete opposite direction I needed to go. Like, if you're with 3 buddies, you can ham it up in the boat while waiting for the winds to change, but solo it's pure waste of life. Literal waste of life. Like, it's a video game, at the end of the day, and the balance between realism and fun is a broad balance from player to player. I LOVE sailing in games, I LOVE the sense of adventure, but here? It just felt so annoying dude, at the end of the day. I quickly changed settings to allow metal through portals after my first voyage because there was no recapping the first experience. The Swamp was actually pretty thrilling the first time around. A monstrosity spawned, I dealt with it eventually. Rating: 10/10 – Would willingly sacrifice my social life, career, and physical hygiene to the glorious cause of optimal logistics.

The Setup: A Gentle Descent Into Madness
It starts so innocently. You crash land on an alien planet, told by a corporate overlord named ADA that your only purpose is to exploit the local ecosystem for "Project Assembly." You think, “Ah, cute. A little casual crafting, maybe build a quaint little copper wire shack, touch some alien grass.”

Three hundred hours later, you haven't slept, you are sweating over an Excel spreadsheet at 4:00 AM, and you are actively screaming at a digital conveyor belt because it’s carrying 3 fewer iron plates per minute than your mathematical calculations demand.

The Gameplay Loop: Just One More Line
The Architecture of Despair: The game tricks you into thinking you are an engineer. You start by hand-crafting items like a caveman. Then you unlock a biomass burner. Then coal power. Before you know it, you’ve paved over half a lush alien continent with towering monoliths of concrete, steel, and pipework that would give an environmental inspector a fatal aneurysm.

The Spaghetti Stage vs. The Enlightenment: Every player goes through the dark, shameful phase known as "The Spaghetti"—where your factory looks like a plate of ramen noodles dropped from a third-story window. You swear you'll fix it later. You won't. You will just build another layer of spaghetti right on top of it, crying softly as your frame rate plummets into the single digits.

The Time Dilation Effect: Einstein’s theory of relativity has nothing on Satisfactory. You sit down at 8:00 PM to "fix a slight bottleneck in the heavy modular frame line." You blink. Birds are chirping outside. The sun is up. Your coffee is ice cold, fossilized in its mug, and you have successfully automated the production of reinforced iron plates, but at the catastrophic cost of your grasp on linear time.

Why It’s Dangerous
This game doesn't just hook you; it rewires your brain chemistry. You look at a highway traffic jam in real life and your eye starts twitching because you aren't utilizing a smart splitter to divert the congestion into an awesome sink. You start viewing your household chores in terms of “throughput optimization.”

Furthermore, you will inevitably find yourself neck-deep in third-party planning tools like the Satisfactory Calculator Interactive Map, meticulously plotting out your supply chains like a paranoid cold-war general.

The Verdict
If you value your sleep, your job, your relationships, or your sanity, do not install this game.

If, however, you’ve ever wanted to spend six hours agonizing over whether a conveyor belt should turn left at a 90-degree angle or curve gracefully across a canyon just to feed a machine that makes useless plastic trinkets—welcome home. FICSIT does not waste.

First played on PS4 back in 2018. This was my go to game for years until around Angels of Zariman, when the PS4 started to really struggle. The constant disconnects made the game unplayable.

Then cross save came out and on day two of getting back into things I lost 3 gold drops from a endless relic mission on, you guessed it, the Zariman (I have an irrational distaste for that area of the game now). Dropped it again for about a year.

Finally started playing again back in late 2024. Why? Because it is one of the best games ever made.

The movement is lighting fast and buttery smooth. The different playable Warframes each have a unique look, playstyle, and lore. The level of customization is incredibly deep in both in terms of build-crafting and aesthetic appearance. The music, gameplay, and story are all top tier.

I've been playing this game off and on for almost a decade now and I can still count the number of bad interactions I've had with other players on my hands. The only other game I've played with as welcoming a community as this one is Deep Rock Galactic.

The developers really care about making the game as enjoyable as possible, and to prove that, they play it themselves. I don't mean they play one choreographed level to showcase something; I mean they actively play the game with people from the community live on stream, as well as on their time off. They love this game, and it makes the players love them all the more.

Does the game have problems? Of course. Is the early part of the game thin on story? Yes. Does the game do a great job of explaining how to play it? Not really. Can the networking be buggy? Certainly. Is RNG the bane of my existence? You betcha.

None of that should stop you from trying the game though. This game is easily the best live service game out there, and it's free. If you haven't played it yet, do yourself a favor and give it a try. Hop in the Q&A chat and ask questions. Join a clan. Do your quests. There is something in this game for everyone. What do you have to lose?

10/10 - A must play for all gamers

GAMEPLAY
--------------

As close to perfect RPG gameplay as we have ever seen. Every single situation can be resolved in what feels like thousands of ways. Whether it's ridiculous cheese or clever party tactics. The roleplay potential is incredible, with every race, class, and then subclass having unique dialogue/in-dialogue action options in many conversations. The build variety is amazing, especially with multi-classing. You can go the traditional Warlock/Wizard caster or Barbarian Bruiser route; or whip out the excel sheet and create a multi-class demon that excels at your ultra-specific playstyle. Considering you can have 3 other party members, this adds so much gameplay/combat potential that it'll make your head spin if you try to consider all the possibilities. You can approach encounters in pretty much anyway you want; whether that's teleporting targets in-between your damage dealers, going invis for stealth, shapeshifting, sending someone to talk to the target while you attack their allies, dropping 50 fire barrels from your inventory on their head, spamming arrows from the high ground, cheesing them with CC, the list goes on forever. There is definitely a learning curve if you have never played D&D or the like, but starting the game on "Easy" and watching a YT video is really all you need. I recommend playing a little first, then watching a video, as the terms and info dump are hard to contextualize without exp in-game.

STORY
--------------

But a massive RPG is dependent on it's story and companions. BG3 has excellent female companions, with Lae'zel and Shadowheart being the most interesting and with the best questlines. The other recruitable female companions are good too, with interesting backstories and dialogue options. And this is all without their romance questlines, which are all quite well-done. But the male companions are where the game kind of suffers. Gale, Astarion, and Wyll especially, are just kind of annoying. Their questlines are all pretty interesting so it is worth completing them, but I found myself leaving them in camp in further runs. They come on to you pretty quickly as well, even if you are already progressing another party members romance. These companions never really hinder the game, but I definitely would have preferred a few more stoic, less quippy type male characters. There is a companion you can recruit who is a bit more serious, but that is late into the game. Regardless, completing your parties questlines and hearing their interactions with you and others were some of my favorite moments in the narrative. There is a very immersive element to hearing your party members talk to each other and mention their surroundings or past events without your input. 

The main story is great, with the voice acting and character models being stellar. I would have preferred a slower or more grounded start to the game and overall story, but that is just personal preference and others might enjoy a more epic fantasy tale which the game has. The ending cutscenes feel a little rushed and it would have been great to have more options when it comes to who you have to fight, but these are pretty excusable considering the rest of the games story. 


OVERALL
------------

This game has lots of fun elements but is absolute dumpster fire of broken bug crap, horrible menuing, and pathing.  If you enjoy falling through the floor, fighting with cameras, watching your attacks not hit because of invisible walls, and watching your characters path through known traps and hazards, then you'll love this buggy mess.  If the game were $20 it might be worth it.  It's not worth it in it's current state and at this point I doubt they'll actually try to fix it.  The menus are miserable to navigate,

Do I recommend this game? Yes, with some caveats attached.

[h1] The Combat [/h1]

The combat honestly feels clunky, and on top of that, it feels like you're punished for it if you dare move away from sword and shield or bow. The fact that there is no way to cancel animations for attacks causes a great deal of frustration when enemies can deliver 2 or 3 blows to you as you're swinging your weapon.

[h1] The Difficulty [/h1]

This game's difficulty curve is [i]brutal[/i]. The first biome isn't too bad, nor is the second, but the later ones feel actually unfun to explore without careful preparation. If you're going to go exploring, stay armed and equipped for the biome you are exploring in, and be prepared to make several corpse runs.

On top of this, the game prevents you from transporting certain materials in it's fast travel system by default, which means unless you change the world modifiers: Get ready for a lot of sailing. Get ready for it anyway. You'll be doing a ton of it.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Why am I still recommending it in spite of my grievances? Because with friends, and on solo with some of the more merciful/easy world modifiers on, I've had a lot of fun. Just understand that the intended experience can be very frustrating for all involved if you aren't prepared for it.

I've been playing World of Tanks for 15 years, and it's certainly had its ups and downs.

On the negative side:

-The company behind it is incredibly greedy. Frankly, I wish the game were run by someone else.

-It barely listens to its player base, even when the community raises perfectly reasonable concerns.

-The game has been drifting further and further towards a Russian-style pay-to-win model, where money increasingly buys you a competitive advantage.

-The company openly promotes gambling-like mechanics through loot boxes, which, in my opinion, ought to be regulated just like lotteries. It's astonishing that a game accessible to young players can get away with monetization practices like these.

-The matchmaking system is another major source of frustration. I strongly suspect that the algorithm manipulates team selection to artificially increase difficulty without ever telling players what is happening. This is particularly unfair to newcomers, who can lose ten battles in a row and end up blaming themselves, never knowing whether the system itself is working against them. At the very least, the lack of transparency makes it difficult to trust the matchmaking process.

-I've become so frustrated with all these practices that I've finally stopped spending money on the game altogether.

On the positive side? Just one thing, really, but it's a big one: World of Tanks is a genuinely great game.

It's addictive, it sparks an interest in military history, and every now and then it delivers moments of sheer brilliance and excitement that few other games can match.

And that's the frustrating paradox of World of Tanks: a fantastic game trapped inside an increasingly exploitative business model. I still love playing it. I just wish I could feel the same way about the company running it.

I played this at launch when it had many graphical and bug issues. I was disappointed with the product at the time, having pre ordered it and was anticipating its release for months. I didn't pre order any game for probably 4 years after that. I came back to this years later after getting the Phantom Liberty deal on sale and sunk over 160 hours into it, played every single gig except for all the NCPD content. 

CDPR have accomplished creating an open world that feels truly lived-in. A lot of open world games have the problem of creating too large a sandbox with not a lot to do outside the more closely designed points of interest. There's something to do on pretty much every street corner of Night City. Storytelling, characterization and performances are top notch. There's many side quests to get involved in, with great characters the player can decide to help or hurt. A lot don't have impact on the end of the game but they're entertaining nonetheless. Main quest follows a similar path where certain choices within them impact the final few missions of the game and give the player up to 7 endings with the Phantom Liberty DLC. 

One complaint about the base game versus the Phantom Liberty DLC is the quality in gigs. Base game gigs are formulated mostly by a short call from a fixer introducing you to a contract that often involves stealing something, killing someone or escorting someone to safety at a particular location. The worldbuilding and storytelling for these side gigs are often limited to reading a shard that you can find on the ground or in buildings. I find the Phantom Liberty gig content having more variety and in depth storytelling than the base game, with a lot more dialogue and player choice on the outcome. Many moderm games do these lore reading dumps and thats fine, but I just wish the quality and delivery was as good in the rest of the game as it was in the DLC.

In terms of player choice, combat is like a Deus Ex/Fallout lovechild. Cyberware, netrunning, stealth and skill trees give the player freedom to defeat enemies however they want. First playthrough i played as a melee heavy cyberpsycho, and on my recent replay I mostly focused on stealth, netrunning and pistol headshot damage multipliers.

 I kinda hated the Johnny character at first but after playing alongside him for 100 hours I started to feel for the guy, especially during Phantom Liberty. I look forward to the sequel and wonder where CDPR will take the world of Cyberpunk next. Its preem content, choom. You should try it. 9/10

This game is amazing. It all started when my friend recommended this game to me. I am so glad he did. When I watched the trailer, and looked at the pictures, it honestly didn't look good. The graphics didn't look good, and the gameplay looked extremely grinding. I was completely wrong. If you like Open-World Survival & Strategy games, this is the perfect option. I have a list of info below about the game.

What to know before you buy:
1. If you are looking for a good Open-World Survival Sim, this is
perfect for you. It's procedurally generated maps and resources are perfect.
------------------------------
2. If you are looking for an easy building sim with a big storyline, this game
is not for you. It doesn't have that much of a storyline to it.
------------------------------
3. The game is set in the Viking era, set in Norway, Greenland, and Iceland.
With different biomes, each with new creatures, and resources.
-------------------------------
4. The game requires lots of grinding, and each biome is different.
You can't get every material in one biome. You need to travel.
-------------------------------
5. Each biome in the game has a boss.
Every biome you travel to has its own unique boss you have to beat. 
You can travel to the other biomes without defeating the bosses, but it will
be hard. Each biome gets more dangerous and harder to beat.
-----------------------------------
6.  Yes, there are monsters.
Each biome has different monsters that you have to worry about.
Think the meadows are nice, meet the trolls and skeletons
Think the Black Forest is nice? Meet the trolls, wolves,bears, and drakes (dragons)
Think the Swamp is cool. Wait until you meet the human-sized leeches, zombies, and
skeletons!
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If you really like open-world survival games, then this is for you. Chop trees, build bases from
cozy log cabins to huge castles, this game is the ultimate open world game. Each world is procedurally generated, like Minecraft, it is inspired by Norse mythology, with gods like Odin and the Vahalia Realm involved in the game. Some of the bosses and monsters are inspired from the Viking folklore and mythology. There is also a really good ambient soundtrack, with different music in each biome.
All in all, it is a great game that I really like to play. it is also really worth the price as well. i hope this review helped you.

After roughly 110 hours with this game, I finally feel justified in sharing my thoughts.

First of all, I wouldn’t recommend playing this game solo. With a team it can work, because there’s a certain fun factor, and that’s the only thing that saves it. Solo, though, it’s going to be your worst nightmare.

The game stopped being satisfying for me after the first 20 hours. The gameplay loop became clear and repetitive, and it turned into an annoying routine with the same pattern every time. I played on Normal difficulty with two friends and without the teleport restriction. I can’t even imagine what the developers were thinking when they banned metals from being teleported, given how stretched the gameplay loop already is.

Here are some issues that I consider pure developer negligence:
- Poorly balanced progression. Even after crafting the best weapons available for a biome, you can suddenly get surrounded by a horde of enemies and die. Additionally, in multiplayer with top-tier gear, some mobs are still a struggle to kill.

- Poorly designed skill system. What’s the point of skills that barely do anything? Maxed levels don’t give you much of an advantage, and you lose progress with every death. As a result, you end up stuck at around level 20 in most skills for the entire game.

- Bad optimization. I can’t speak for solo play, but in multiplayer it’s a bit awkward to even have to mention this for a game like this. The problem is real, though: especially toward the end of the game, the server was freezing terribly.

- Chests can’t be used by multiple players at once. This can’t be serious. A game with this budget simply disabled the feature because the developers couldn’t fix a loot duplication bug, which we still occasionally ran into in multiplayer. Almost every decent game nowadays has this feature. It’s a shame.

- Poor admin command support. Why can’t I give other players admin rights or teleport them to me? At the very least, let them teleport to me. The textures can be so bad that you get stuck out of nowhere.

I've been playing Warframe since mid-2024. Overall, I see many flaws of the game, but for every flaw there are 20 compliments I could give to the game. However, I am sure there are many general reviews that say "DE has lost the plot" or "DE is great" but neither review tells a story with enough depth. I want to be clear here and now that Warframe is worth your time and is fun. Admittedly, for people who are like me (someone who is familiar with looter-shooters) I think Warframe's biggest flaw at attracting players is a lack of a good in-game tutorial and early game pacing. Also, I'll admit most of my hours are inflated as for leaving the game open. I have less than half of my hours.
That being said I noticed recently (as in 2026 leading up to TAU) that Warframe has had admittedly bad update launches consistently. I think DE does need to be criticized for not delaying updates as a whole when they need it clearly. It feels all so disappointing to see a Warframe update come out and know its an aggravating experience the first few days sometimes, as the first half of the year has felt like that. I believe Icebind the new 6 player gamemode is a  fantastic addition that needs tweaks and adjustments but overall is pretty great. 
At the time of this review I have done 3 runs and got most of the side objectives as something I needed to do. I can see the frustration of this gamemode being that you are reliant on randoms, but many of the side objectives are incredibly intuitive that they can be done the first time you see them and require no knowledge before hand. I think ultimately that should be the goal for a gamemode like this as if the side objectives are too demanding I fear that KWTD for Icebind will become too common. A lot of complaints about this gamemode I believe are unwarranted as they tend to say the mode is unfun and feels too random, but the complaints about the loot are more than justified as truthfully the side objectives have a good chance to give meager scraps for loot. I trust the developers will continue to add to this mode as from the grand-scheme of Warframe the mode is admittedly not finished due to their not being enough variety and different gamemodes do not feel balanced as survival and disruption seem to be the best modes to pick. As a whole I believe the issue for many players with Icebind is that it forces you to have builds geared at such a high level of game-play that many are not familiar with as it felt like the enemies were tougher than level cap runs in my experience: granted that is impart due to the modifiers. As a whole this is a significant upgrade from Archimedea.
To address that "DE has lost the plot" in relation to how Warframe's story has been expanding, Warframe has never had a more clear vision than it does now. Keep in mind that I only saw Warframe's story from playing it in a few months or so and missed out on some FOMO events for story telling, but nevertheless there are many great videos that showcased that Warframe has always had a messy story that would change on the whim's of the previous developer team. While I have only played what Rebecca's team has been producing they're storytelling has been far more clear and consistent, but Warframe has never been a story driven game. Warframe is as fun as it is due to it being a sandbox for gameplay and fashion. Fashion framing is a serious task in Warframe as well as build crafting. That is what Warframe has been primarily about from my experience and DE keeps releasing massive changes to the game that shake-up these aspects and add so much variety to build-crafting. For example, Riven Splicers from Icebind allow many primary weapons to achieve 100% ammo efficiency. And a lot of new fashion choices with Ephmeras, SIgnas, and Sigils being expanded out far more than before. This is to say at the core Warframe is making the adjustments it needs to. While I don't think Warframe is particularly good at storytelling and I would say it is similar to Destiny in that regard, Warframe knows what changes it needs to make mostly and it doing so.

It had a rough beginning, no doubt about it. However, since then, this game has become an absolute masterpiece. There is no game on this Earth that has ever made me feel what this game has. It is a masterclass example of what exceptional story writing should be. There are no happy endings in Night City, and no game has ever made me, as the main character, feel so powerless. 

When Phantom Liberty was released, I was expecting a simple DLC that added a few extra hours of gameplay, but man was I wrong and I couldn't be happier about that. This DLC alone is better than 99% of the full-fledged games I have played throughout my entire life.

Aside from the story and the writing, the characters are exceptional by themselves, especially Johnny, the other main story characters, the romance options, and honestly, all the character of Phantom Liberty. No matter what you do in this game, whether it be focusing on the main story, doing side quests or gigs, or simply exploring, you will find gems hidden away at every corner of this map.

The combat is phenomenal. It is highly responsive, bloody, and gritty. There are dozens upon dozens of builds you can do, focusing on melee, snipers, blades, netrunning, drugs, spray and pray, stealth, and on and on. There are various types of weapons such as the basic ballistic firearms, but also power firearms that pack a greater punch and can be increased via certain builds, smart weapons whose ammunition locks onto targets and can be more effective with a netrunning build, explosives, burning, poison, blades, dildos (yes, I'm serious, you can beat people to death with dildos), hammers, etc. You can also forgo weapons altogether and focus purely on netrunning hacks which permit you to do various things such as spread viruses, knock enemies out, force them to commit suicide, and so on and so forth.

You could replay this game a dozen times and have a different build each time. How many games offer that much freedom?

Sunsetting and premium. Apparently most everything that was in the game at any time can be gotten again. There are apparently a few warframes that are permanently gone which means they do in fact remove things from the game, but even if you want to be charitable the system they have in place is sunsetting light. The big play is to vault warframes and gear and no longer provide a set in game path to acquire these items. How do you get around this? Well give them money for platinum, and then go to the Warframe ebay-like website that is not affiliated with them and trade other players for their crap. Huzzah. See something in the shop that isn't available anymore, or is rare, if its a warframe you better hope you have the cash because a single warframe costs 20 dollars for their premium currency exchange. Just getting started? Start actually enjoying the game and getting stuff to build weapons and warframes...too bad. Inventory is full. Pay up kiddo. You want more than three warframes or like ten weapons, well open up that wallet. What's that? Oh well, platinum please. 

Gameplay loop. This one is more of a pet peeve of mine, but it's found in this game so I'll mention it if you happen to share my view. Games like Warframe, Diablo, POE. They don't show you how to play it. They give you a game to play, but that isn't the game. The game is dungeons, and specific grinding. Everything is hella complicated and in my opinion, complicated for the sake of being complicated. They could just as easily keep things simple while keeping their nested systems and in universe language. It doesn't make you smart for googling how to make a key to enter into a dungeon to grind the materials you need. You could just keep it simple and cut out the middle man of googling it and get the same return. I'll add onto this for this game they add a bunch of modes. You like the warframe mode? Well I hope you like not playing it sometimes. You have a darks souls like, a space shooter, a normal guy with low resources mode and probably more besides I haven't unlocked yet. That's kind of cool to me honestly, except every time I have played these modes I spend a good amount of time being annoyed, and I know I can't be the only one. Do a mission as your low resource guy and spend twenty minutes fighting your resource regeneration. Destroy this object, you have 100 energy. That object takes 50 energy to destroy, there are three of them, so enjoy waiting watching your bar recoup...it's that level of bad design where it feels malicious rather than accidental. 

Overall. I don't recommend this game unless your willing to be honest with yourself about it, which I'm learning from my own issues is not as easy as it sounds. This is an MMO and has all the same MMO trappings of timed and limited stuff. It's free to play which means that there is heavy emphasis on getting your money even if the community swears up and down that it's not that bad. It isn't, but you just got to be willing to not get what you want sometimes for the sole reason they want you to pay money for your happiness. If you care about the story you might get frustrated. It's not a masterpiece, but it's present enough to be interesting and their mangling of it is purposeful and strange. So if your okay with all of that and you just want to slice dudes in half and parkour around maps then I recommend it highly.  The gameplay loop is fun. Bullet jumping and parkour are legitimately easy and fun. I could never bunny hop in counter strike, this takes all the skill out and makes it a simple and fun experience for all. Don't be sucked in because it's free. People lose their minds when they see the free tag and are not objective about their experience at all. The good news is there is no barrier to entry, try it, see if you like the movement, the gameplay, and find out for yourself.

I've been playing this game since the beginning. I thought it was good back then. Just the thought of going from planet to planet across a seemingly endless galaxy was unheard of back when this game came out. It was a little bare bones back then, but it was still fun. 
I kept coming back to it on and off, and each time it got better, with more stuff to do. They just keep expanding. I don't have any other game like this that just keeps adding fun stuff to do without making me pay for another season pass or expansion pack. 
This game is a grind, but its one you want to do. I'm just going to list out some of the many things you can do in this game: Build your own starship, buy a starship, or find a crashed one. Build a bigger starship that's a mobile base and take your friends along for a ride. Fly from planet to planet, star system to star system, even discover new galaxies. Look for different minerals, scan different flora and fauna. Recruit your own animals, feed them, challenge other animals in a mini game. Like geology? enjoy finding strange rock formations. Paleontology? find bones and assemble them to make a fossil. Build a farm and grow some crops, collect milk and eggs from strange creatures, cook strange dishes. Go fishing. Build bases across the galaxy. One base for farming, one for mining, one on an asteroid, one on a nice beach planet with a chair so you can sit down and enjoy the view.  Find stuff in space, find stuff on varied planets, find stuff underground, find stuff underwater. Learn language word by word by talking to different aliens. Customize your character, your multitool, your spaceship, your bases, your space freighter, your star base. 
I'm getting tired of listing stuff, but it goes on and on. I have games that do one or two of these things, but none of them with the depth of this game. Almost ever time you play this game you will see something new. 
If you don't have this game yet, why not? This game continually grows and unlike others, so far I have never had to buy an expansion pack or season pass or in game currency.
