Counter-Strike 2: A Song of Smoke and Betrayal
Hear ye, hear ye, Lords and Ladies of the Competitive Realm!

Counter-Strike 2 is a battlefield worthy of legends. A game of steel nerves, cunning strategies, and glorious headshots. Here, friendships are forged in fire, rivalries are born in blood, and every round is a tale worthy of the bards. The thrill of clutching a 1v5 is sweeter than victory at the Iron Throne, and the sound of an AWP firing is music to the ears of even the coldest lord of Westeros.

The skins? Oh, what a splendid treasury! From crimson blades worthy of House Lannister to dragon-lore rifles fit for the Targaryens, one may adorn their arsenal in magnificent fashion. For in this realm, it is not merely how you slay your foes, but how gloriously you do so.

The competition is fierce, the stakes are high, and when both teams are evenly matched, the battles are glorious. Every smoke is a scheme, every flash a deception, and every defuse a race against the Stranger himself.

BUT LO, A DARKNESS GATHERS BEYOND THE WALL.

For this realm is plagued by a most vile affliction: the poison of cheaters.

Wallhackers, who see through stone as if blessed by the Three-Eyed Raven. Aimbotters, whose arrows never miss, whose bullets find skulls with the certainty of a prophecy. Suspicious lords who turn corners with knowledge no mortal ought to possess. They roam the servers like White Walkers, corrupting the living and extinguishing the joy of honest warriors.

And what of the honourable player who trains for countless hours, perfects their aim, studies the maps, and fights with all the skill they possess? They are left wondering whether they were bested by a better warrior or struck down by some foul sorcery beyond the laws of the realm.

'Tis a cruel fate, to enter the arena seeking glory, only to discover that the enemy has brought a dragon to a knife fight.

Still, when the stars align, the teams are fair, and the cheaters are banished beyond the Wall, Counter-Strike 2 remains a magnificent contest of skill, teamwork, and nerve.

My verdict, therefore, is this:

A glorious game with the heart of a champion, the soul of a warrior, and the potential to rule the Seven Kingdoms of competitive shooters.

Yet its throne is besmirched by treachery, and its kingdom weakened by those who forsake honour for hollow victories.

Valve, the realm cries out for justice! Sharpen thy anti-cheat, strengthen the Watch, and cast these foul sorcerers into the frozen wastes!

For a kingdom cannot thrive when its honest warriors grow weary of fighting shadows.

Would I recommend it? Aye.

But I would sooner trust a Lannister with my gold than trust every death replay in this cursed realm.

For us these helped a ton and made the multiplayer as enjoyable as it should've been from the start :)

It's sad you can't leave a "neutral" review, because the game is genuinely amazing, but also unnecessarily tedious and loves wasting your time at the same time. I'm at the boss of the second to last biome at this time, but i believe I experienced most of the game by now to leave a review.

Pros
- exploration is very rewarding and fun
- the game is beautiful, love the plains and mountain biome
- building in this game is very detailed and you can make a lot of cool looking buildings if you know the knowhow.
- sailing is fun, especially sailing during the night and thunderstorms
- sophisticated combat, like the parrying and roll system. Weapon diversity is also great.
- the grappling hook, nothing else to be said

Cons
- stamina system can be very annoying, everything you do eats stamina and regen is slow. Certain buffs are a necessity
- skilling certain skills, like farming or cooking takes an ungodly amount of time
- swimming is awful, and also apparently enemies are blessed by Njord and they can swim indefinitely, but you can not
- combat branching out is late game, you gain access to magic, crossbows and some twohanded weapons in the last third of the game. way too late in my opinion
- talking about crossbows, what's the point of having a crossbow if you can't arm your crossbow and also store it on your back or inventory. you have to rearm it everytime you take it out of your inventory or from your back. why design it like this?
- trophy hunting is tedious, some accessories or base upgrades need trophies, but the trophy system is bugged now from what I've heard, so it takes a very, very long time to farm trophies of bears and other starred enemies
- game has almost no basic QoL what you would expect from a surivival game, like crafting from chests or a separate equipment slot for your armor
- portals take a really long time to use for some reason
- performance is sometimes terrible
- some bosses are an endurance challenge, but are very boring and have no interesting movesets at all
- raid mechanic needs to get reworked, getting raided WHILE I'm not even at my base is bad game design. not only that, you get no timer, the enemies spawn everywhere around you and if you are unlucky you get swarmed by said enemies without having a chance to survive it

Overall the game is very fun, but also very tedious and can become very annoying at times when these annoyances add up over time. There were certain points that I just wanted to uninstall the game, not because the game is extremely difficult, but the game became so enormously tedious it felt like I wasting my time. No Man's Sky is a fun sandbox, and that's about it.

The progression loop is the best part. Building bases is genuinely fun, and maxing out your exosuit, exocraft and ship is weirdly addictive. But once you've got everything, there's nothing to use it on. No real endgame, so all that gear just sits there.

Nothing else picks up the slack. The story is okay and you can tell they tried, but it's too abstract, and digging through lore to make sense of it feels like homework. Maybe five NPCs are memorable; the rest are procedurally generated filler. Combat is bland on foot and in space, with almost no enemy variety.

Exploration is what keeps it going. There are tons of cool planets to land on, stare at, and leave. But that's the whole loop: see it, move on. Nothing makes you want to stay.

I think the problem is the procedural generation itself. A smaller, handcrafted galaxy with a tighter story and better characters would've given all those systems a reason to matter.

Worth playing if you want a chill sandbox. Just don't expect much more.

[h1]V Rising[/h1]

Is it a good game?

Yes, but it's slow. The first hour goes fast, but after a few hours of gameplay it gets slower and slower. The crafting part is solid. The game looks beautiful, with a large variety of enemies and environments. You can also set up your bases however you want, but the story progression is quite rigid. Sometimes the instructions the game gives you are basically "figure out a way to build X".

Let's take an example, and let's assume that you're following the main story quests and you even know where you need to go. You need a blueprint for a building, so you go hunting. Your target is very far away. So you start traveling when the night arrives, but by the time you're there, it's already daytime. So you go spanking a tree or mining some stone for resources in the meantime because you can't fight in the sun, can you?

The night finally comes, and you go clear a camp. If you play solo, you only need to fight like 20 or more enemies and one boss. The boss is called Keely the Frost Archer. So you beat the boss, collect the loot and explore the camp. Lo and behold, daytime comes and the game respawns every enemy instantly, including the boss. So you get killed, and then you go back to pick up your stuff, navigate to a teleporter, but then it says you can't teleport because you're carrying "certain items". You need to go to the settings and disable the restrictions. And then you travel in wolf form, but you still might have to stop for a moment and squat in the shade for a while because it's daytime, for Christ's sake!

The combat can be a slog. Boss fights are usually unique and challenging, perhaps a bit frustrating. When you try to get to a boss, you need to clear a lot of enemies before you can even reach it, sometimes as many as 50. If your equipment level is roughly the same as the boss's, you might have to whack the boss with your best weapon for several minutes before it goes down. And when you're raiding a camp, you get hit with different stun effects. Very nice to play solo when you get stunned in place for several seconds at a time.

There are some skeleton bosses that can spawn skeletons that can spawn skeletons. Yeah, it's nice when the enemy spawn rate is higher than your kill rate.

When you play this game, you see that some of the elements were made for co-op and some were made for PvP. But when you play solo, it just doesn't make sense how slow the game is, or that you can't even carry something like copper ore with you when you're trying to use a teleporter. You can't change form when you have a dominated human in tow, and the only thing it can do is follow you. When you're getting yourself just one new servant, you need to walk slowly back to the castle with it and fight packs of enemies on the way.

So my gripe with this game is twofold: I don't like the restrictions that the game imposes on me, and the progression system itself doesn't give me the freedom to do the things I actually want to do. So it feels like I'm just doing some arbitrary missions to mark all the checkboxes.

You might say that I'm just imagining it, but tell me why do I need to collect papers to unlock upgrades with like 40–60 papers for each upgrade schematic when I can unlock the Paper Press by beating a level 35 boss? Do you know how many camps you need to raid to get enough resources for Greater Blood Essences, equipment repairs and research desk upgrades? I'm just saying that after the first few hours, the game requires grinding way too much. I didn't even find the option to pin blueprints. It would've been easier for me to remember what I needed for my next upgrades and to make the grind less cumbersome.

I think this game is slightly overrated, but if you like to play co-op with friends, build a vampire castle and grind for resources, then this game is for you. If you don't like grinding, slow progression and building stuff just for the sake of building, then this game isn't for you.

If you play solo, prepare for a combat system that feels like you can't recover once you've lost the edge in a fight. There's a horde of enemies between you and the boss in most boss fights. You're too slow, so there's no going around them. The one skill you might wanna use has a two-minute cooldown. Once you've lost enough health or can no longer regenerate, you either flee or die. There's no middle ground.

One of the few games that can make you wait 2 minutes for the boss to spawn.

Final score: 6/10

[List]
[H1]Foreword[/h1]
[*]Loved Baldur's Gate 1 & 2 (Shadows of Amn & Throne of Bhaal), including Siege of Dragonspear - they are in my list of all-time best and favorite CRPGs.

[*]Never touched tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, but I considered myself an avid RPG-er (western ones). Advanced D&D 2nd edition and 3.5 D&D are some of my favorite systems.

[*]Played in 2-players co-op.

[*]Played on Balanced difficulty as to avoid excessive metagaming that will break roleplay.

[*]Explored every place and did every content (hence the hours) - as long as it didn't contradict roleplay.

[*]No achievements because of some cosmetic mods used and the absolute necessity of using the Item and Spell Bug Fixes mod. The game is almost unplayable without this imo. Imagine building your character with care and with roleplaying in mind to later finding out too late that half the skills, feats, and equipment your character is using don't work as intended.

[*]Held back from playing the game since its launch so that it could be enjoyed post bug-fixes, dlcs, and polish - biding literally 3 years of time thinking it the 'messiah' of CRPGs from the word of mouth and hype surrounding it.

[*]Played with keyboard and mouse.

[H1]The Good[/h1]
[*]The game is very aesthetically pleasing. The best looking CRPG to date. HDR support.

[*]No loading screen, unless you're changing regions.

[*]Co-op up to 4 players.

[*]Character models are excellent (not including custom-created player characters). The dialogue camera captures this beautifully.

[*]Fully voiced but there are odd fews which are not - probably due to time constraints.

[*]Very accessible and beginner friendly to anyone wanting to dip their toes into D&D or just fantasy CRPGs in general.

[*]Throwback to events from BG 1 & 2 with old characters returning. Jaheira and Minsc are brilliant in this and easily are the most interesting characters/ [spoiler]companions[/spoiler] in the game.

[*]Overall great OST, but somehow not as memorable as the classic ones for me.

[*]Massive amount of content you can sink hundreds of hours into. It is not one of those RPGs that end abruptly.

[*]Non-linear path on which you tackle the main quest and side quests, embark on an adventure of your own making.

[*]All the combat animations, spells, and visual effects are flashy and smooth, not janky.

[*]Pet [spoiler]owlbear[/spoiler].

[*]A conclusive ending.

[H1]The Bad[/h1]
[*]Bugs. Not worth all the wait. Just to list a few: Web (level 2 spell) useless, failed saving throw against it will instead free you. Shatter spell no AOE indication. Combat log showing wrong calculation of spell DC, shove DC, damage modifiers, attack rolls. Tooltips not accurate, Evasive Footwork not lasting one turn, Shield Master feat practically useless. There are many others that I can't possibly list the majority of them but the mod I mentioned in the foreword mitigated this problem to a bearable degree.

[*]Ability and skill checks don't detect who you bring into your party. Want to succeed an Arcana check even though you have a wizard just by your side? Tough luck.

[*]The stealth and surprise system made me want to tear my hairs out. Many unexplained intricacies/ bugs that will make a simple stealth attack fail. For example: successfully killing an enemy with stealth attack will result in the remaining enemies not being surprised.

[*]Master volume is too low. I needed to turn to my headphone external controller to crank up the volume.

[*]As per standard of today's game industry, no beautiful faces to choose from for your human female PC. Resolved this by using mods.

[*]Memory leak - constant micro-stutters - if your game session is on the longer side. Also two instances of buggy dialogue scenes that lock you up and require a restart of the game, only happened when the game's running long.

[*]Initial romance routes are too strict. Not choosing the correct 'thirsty' option in that particular time will make you unable to romance that companion for the rest of the game.

[*]Further into the game, there will be feats that are not listed in the enemies' abilities. E.g. darkvision not listed, [spoiler]Cazador cannot be disarmed despite not having Permanently Armed feat[/spoiler].

[*]The voice acting doesn't cover all the info that is given to the player - you need to consult the journal/ trust the journal more than what's being said to get the full picture. E.g. [spoiler]Investigator Valeria pledging the City Watch help for the final battle was never mentioned in dialogue[/spoiler].

[*]Some subclasses are clear dev's favorites. Assassin is lackluster compared to Gloom Stalker and playing Hunter subclass felt like you have a grenade launcher in your hand - its AOE capabilities far exceed a Fighter's.

[*]Many villain expositions. The villains bored me.

[*]Thematically, no subject deeply explored nor a hard question asked. The game is massive and coupled with high production value, but it is generic fantasy. It will not cause any restless night or contemplation.

[*]Camera controls using mouse and keyboard are janky. Oftimes, the environment will mess your camera up and rotating using Q and E has input delay if pressed successively.

[*]The ratio between combat and dialogue skews heavily towards the latter. Felt like the devs are allergic to trash mobs and encounters - even though BG 1 & 2 had those aplenty. It could last up to 30 minutes - felt like an hour - before the next combat encounter.

[*]Balanced difficulty is not it. It rests more on the easier side and even becoming too easy oftimes. The bosses we faced usually can only act one turn before dying, and the final one didn't even have a single turn.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[*]There are plenty of CRPG goodness here, especially for those not looking to bog themselves in the genre's usual complexities. But if you perhaps are looking for a CRPG that has a well thought-out system, way less bugs in its core mechanics, stays truer to the classics, and most importantly, ask deeply the questions regarding gods, faith, destiny, soul, philosophy, and morality, play Pillars of Eternity 1 instead.

It’s hard to clearly judge Destiny 2. The beautifully designed world clashes with the character models, whose faces look like they belong in The Sims. It seems to be a standard in modern gaming that every character has to look like a Ken or Barbie doll. The game is quite well optimized and has some interesting combat ideas, like battles during meditation that create a mirrored version of the real map in their dreamlike form. The vehicles are incredibly agile and fast, making travel over long distances a real pleasure (the shortcut tab+E after 4 hours of gameplay has carved itself into my mind as an instant dopamine trigger). Unfortunately, all these advantages are ruthlessly destroyed by the itemization system. I understand that nowadays games need to cater to mindless mobile gamers, but if you have to shove item power everywhere, at least let it mean something. In the first 4 hours of playing, I found about 250 items - almost all legendary (I don’t know how humanity could lose this war if under every rock there’s a legendary plasma rifle). All weapons had item power between 300 and 305... So what? Does that mean a legendary soup spoon deals as much damage as a quantum black hole launcher because both have item power 302? The game supposedly has something called damage potential, but its noticeable impact on damage dealt is minimal and you have to dig deep into weapon stats to find it. To sum up: another game trying to be Fortnite with a mobile vibe, and it turned out too well, but nobody needed it... I just feel sorry for the artists because they really made a beautiful world. Time to go back to ArcRiders.

I'm not a huge fan of Zombie type games, but Dying Light was certainly one I enjoyed due to the freedom of the movement mechanics. Project Zomboid though is a hidden gem isometric type that feels just as free, and just as dangerous. In short, fun game, will take a little time to understand how to play. 

Project Zomboid's [b]gameplay[/b] is awesome. It's been a long time since (maybe late 90s) since I've played a good isometric game, and this one certainly felt like a huge upgrade to what I used to play. The [b]controls[/b] are also easy and intuitive, though take a little to get used to. Thankfully, there is a solid [b]tutorial[/b] at the start with a wonderful twist at the end (honestly, have to say, classic). Players are able to run, climb, open and close windows and doors, break windows (beware of getting cut by glass - yes, this is how much detail there is in the game), drive vehicles, craft, deconstruct, build... it's actually pretty crazy how much this game has. The noise detection system and sneaking around is certainly one to pay attention to (and not recklessly just break every window in sight). The [b]combat[/b] system is also a wonderfully intuitive, easy, and fun. That being said, doesn't mean its completely easy to start fighting 5-10 zombies at once, again, unless the right equipment is equipped. Speaking of equipment there is no shortage of items, clothing, weapons, or anything else in this game. This domain was really well done.

The [b]graphics and visuals[/b] was another domain that was absolutely done right. There are animations for almost every action that the character initiates, and its wonderful. It's not annoying, it makes sense if it takes a little in the game (especially if the character is lacking certain skills), and it's so fluid that it makes it hard to go back and play Commandos again. Running, hitting with weapons, picking up items, disassembling items... like it was just all well done and done with attention. The user interface is also awesome, just wish the text size could be a little bigger! The [b]sounds and music[/b] are absolutely suitable to the environment. It can get quiet with some quiet but suspicious music, all is okay, then all of a sudden there is something banging or there is a weird breath-ey growl. It honestly amazes me how from top-down this game has been fine tuned. 

Overall, would highly recommend on a sale, and even not on  a sale if this is something that really interests you. It just feels so well developed and so well made. Top it off with the ability to play online, and boom, solid game.

I recommend this, but I don't think it will ever be finished. Compared to indie titles that released around the same time, Project Zomboid has barely seen any updates for what it has promised in its development roadmap. It has been many years and still we have no signs of human NPCs coming back to the game. As someone who has been playing since the days of the Bob and Kate tutorial, it feels like the developers removed that so we forget they even attempted NPCs to begin with. We're on build 42, NPCs are expected to be finished on build 47. I understand when the laptop was stolen there were months of progress lost but it has been *years* and development has been moving at a snail's pace. 
The game is quite good on realism, except in regards to anything that would benefit the player. 
For Kentucky 1993 there is a dramatically low amount of alcohol, cigarettes, and firearms even on the highest loot settings. This is something that can be fixed with mods, but it feels like the developers want the player to rush to agrarian medieval life simulators where you can lose dozens if not hundreds of hours of progress to bad geometry building taller structures if your character ever gets to a high enough level to do build stairs or more advanced construction. With no saves of any kind in the base game it just feels bad to kill your old character and start at 0 after the water and power are cut. Even if it was seasonal checkpoints or something that would strongly incentivize longer term playstyles but as it stands I just start a new game rather than play farming simulator with the occasional zombie jumpscare. I enjoy the fact sandbox mode allows for players to disable mechanics they don't find fun and enable unrealistic things like unlimited gas stations or water never shutting off. 
For most of my complaints about the game the solution is either tweaking sandbox settings or mods, The Indie Stone needs to get some of these modders on their team because evidently they have the capacity to get things done well in a timely manner. Mods like Week One NPC are a perfect example of what this game is capable of, and new innovations with perspective mods have transformed a once isometric game into a 1st/3rd person one which blows my mind. This game has a ton of potential, I just wish TIS would put out more regular updates, there are studios like Hello Games that have completely transformed their games in the time it has taken for TIS to add livestock and blacksmithing, with a few additions to the map.  I also dislike the idea of the basements being RNG related when the rest of the world was all designed bespoke, a more thoughtful approach to hiding stuff like the bunker basement in certain homes would give more room for worldbuilding and natural story telling. I understand procedural generation makes developing large areas easier, but quality is superior to quantity and designing areas to be dense with stuff to explore and do is better than having large swathes of wilderness to add a few more cities. 
TL;DR: I like the game but development is painfully slow. The modding community rocks.

I have given 832 hours of my life to Planet 4546B—wait, no, Massage-2(AB)b. See, my brain is so fried from conveyers and splitters that I don't even know where I am anymore. But ADA knows. ADA always knows. ADA is in my head, reminding me that every single second I spend sleeping, eating, or having a "life" is a second that humanity, puppies, and kittens are paying for. If I don't squeeze another 0.4% efficiency out of my screw production, a golden retriever somewhere suffers. That is basic corporate math. I didn't want to let mankind down. I turned a beautiful, pristine alien paradise into a concrete smog-filled nightmare of pure, unfiltered productiveness, all under the gentle, passive-aggressive encouragement of a computer voice telling me I am inadequate compared to a well-oiled copper wire assembler.

I have been in the trenches since day one launch day. I remember when the world was young, the grass was green, and I didn't see conveyor belts when I closed my eyes to sleep. Now I see pasta in my sleep. Not the food, the belts. Infinite, tangled, clipping-through-walls spaghetti that haunts my dreams while ADA whispers in my ear that my factory layout is an insult to the FICSIT pioneer training program. I spent hundreds of hours trying to make straight lines, failed, embraced the chaos, and then spent another two hundred hours replacing it all with nuclear power plants just so I could power more constructors to make items I don't even fully understand.

Anyway, I finally logged off today. Eight hundred and thirty-two hours later, I walked out of my computer room and met these strangers sitting on the couch in my living room. Turns out they are my family! Really chill people, honestly. My wife is pretty nice, and my kid has grown like two feet. They asked me where I've been and I told them I was saving the planet by exploiting its natural resources at peak operational capacity. They didn't really get it, but ADA would be proud of my brevity. 10 out of 10 game, would abandon my loved ones for coal power again.

While I have not played a ton of Project Zomboid comparitively I can safely say with the amount of time I have played that: It is the BEST zombie simulation game on the market. If you wanted to simulatre surviving a zombie apocalypse then Project Zomboid is the ONLY way to do it.

You count callories, you have to bathe, sleep, rest, deal with muscle pain, sickness, everything from running to picking up items is some form of a chore that you need to look at from a realistic stand point. In a normal game running into a wall does nothing; In Zomboid you can and will knock yourself out when you hit a wall. If you crash your car, the engine will take percentile damage and start to get a failure to start chance or randomly shut off, progressively getting worse. You need to maintain said vehicle as well by checking the tires, headlights, windows, making sure the door locks work and if you left a stray water bottle on the floor. You can eat dangerous food: Rotten, spoiled, uncooked. And each of them have they're own values and dangers. Eat too many fatty foods and well, you get fat. Don't get enough calories and your body will get weaker. Taking damage as well isn't just a case of managing a health meter; you have cuts, breaks, bleeding, bites, infections (of various degree) and each one needs to be tended to differently or they WILL KILL YOU. 

There's a lot more to go over, but this game is Zombie Survival Simulation PERFECTED.

Finally fully released, but still full of bugs and issues from early releases.

The crafting UI is horrible and gets super bloated towards endgame. Every craft from the specific workbench is just added to the list in random order. You can't search, filter or organize this list and there is no logic to the order.

A ton of bugs, invisible mobs, moose can't be hit from the side etc.

Multiplayer lags like crazy. Insane lag and rubber banding at random times. We have had dedicated servers since many patches, crossplay is off, we have fast internet 1 Gps and have run them on separate machines. The only thing that kind of helps is a combination of three mods, but even they don't completely remove it or solve the issues let alone fix the combat related bugs. (No real performance issues, we have not had any major framerate issues now or in past releases)

If the combat actually worked, crafting UIs would be decent, there would not be so many bugs and multiplayer would not have giga lags the game would be fun.

Now it is just a massive grind which gets interrupted by great one shot deaths from rubberbanding mobs, which your arrows just fly through without damaging them and who are hitting directly forward, but strike you behind them.... 

Also the inventory management is an absolute chore with 2+ people. You cannot open chests at the same time, and the largest capacity chests are built on the third last biomes, so all the new items from the last two biomes need more chests or you just give up and dump them in random chests around. There is no multi-chest auto stack/sort or locking inventory slots. You can only auto-stack by holding down E and having the chest open, so if you have a chest for "Wood" "Stone" "Metal" "Bones" etc. you have to go through each chest separately in order to empty out your inventory. Due to the inability to lock items in your inventory, you will also autostack all the consumables and extra gear which is not equipped, if the chest has the same item. You cannot craft gear using nearby chests inventory, so you have to manually go to each chest to pick up the right amount of items for the crafts, you cannot pin the recipe either so you have to remember each material and quantity, this is especially fun when crafting multiple items and with multiple people trying to do this at the same time.

MUTLIPLE PEOPLE STILL CAN'T OPEN THE SAME CHEST AT THE SAME TIME!!!
Maybe sounds minor, but with 4 people, 20+ massive chests and such poor inventory management systems, this will drain hours of your life in a playthrough.

There are much better and more fun survival crafting games like Abiotic Factor, which respects your time and the devs actually care about the playerbase and introduced many QoL features so you can focus on playing the game instead of wasting hours fighting the UI and low capacity cluttered chests.

Honestly, this game is crap. It hit EA at a particular time, when the genre had basically nothing else in it worth looking at. The graphics were fresh and interesting, the gameplay loop was simple. Punishing, but it was novel. The base building was pretty good, and most people hadn't seen sailing with waves in a game, so it got tons of attention.

You need to be constantly farming every resource out there to keep abreast of build materials, upgrade materials, food, meads, etc. There's a lot, and it just gets more and more. 90% of this game is preparation. Don't go anywhere until you're fully kitted, mead, enough materials to build a house and a portal, etc. The slightest degree of impatience is brutally punished. Factorio is the weird one out of every game on this digital storefront. This is THE game that I binged for 50 hours within the first 72 hours of buying it. This is THE game that I installed and play on my school computer instead of learning PHP and MySQL. This is THE game that I just... can't let go for some reason. And I'm not really sure why that's the case. I don't like automation games, yet turns out I enjoy Factorio more than anything, and I still didn't find the answer why Factorio is the one that hooked me in. Maybe it's the gameplay loop of:
1. find a problem,
2. solve that problem,
3. automate it,
4. automate it some more
5. reach flow state,
or maybe it's the little squares, representing the logistics bots, flying around on my map screen. I just can't figure it out. 

But here's this one thing that I figured out about Factorio: this game is worse than drugs. Like, this game literally hits better than an 18 year old's first legally bought liquor. It's THAT good. Like I said at the beginning, I spent 50 hours in this game, 3 days into the purchase. I remember that I played through the entire first night of my purchase, figuring stuff out in my little newly built spaghetti factory. This game is filled to the brim with content, even without the DLC (It took me like 125 hours to discover everything in the tech tree) and it's a little bit too easy to get lost into everything that surrounds you in this drug-game. I didn't even catch the fact that it's already 6:30AM on the clock, and I just spent my entire night playing an overpriced (I bought the game before it got discounted in Poland) ugly automation game.

There's this one thing that's been bugging me the entire time I've been playing on my singular save since the beginning - the biters. The first time they came running straight into my pollution emitting factory, I immediately searched up a tutorial on how to turn them peaceful (this is the sole reason why I don't have any achievements despite playing this game for 220 hours as of  writing this review), and while I understand that making them not attack you if you don't attack them first basically cuts 25% of the base game's content, I honestly just wanted to play a sandbox, not a tower defense game, and I found the biters simply annoying. but now with the experience I got through my last 220 hours on my save, I think I'll try to keep them on when I buy the Space Age DLC and start a new save. 

Please, play this game, it's worth it, but don't make a spaghetti factory and learn about ratios, I beg you. Don't be like me when it comes to ratios. Use 1 offshore pump that will connect to 20 boilers, which will run 40 steam engines for power. I didn't know about ratios when I started, and i just did the 1 offshore pump > 1 boiler > 1 steam engine setup. Insanely inefficient.

Counter-Strike 2 is one of those games that can keep me coming back again and again. As a huge fan of competitive shooters, I really enjoy what CS2 offers: intense matches, constant action, teamwork, strategy, and an almost endless amount of room for improvement.
What I love most about CS2 is that every match feels different. Even when playing the same map for the hundredth time, situations can develop in completely unexpected ways. One round can be calm and tactical, while the next can turn into an intense clutch where every second and every decision matters.
🎯 Gameplay
The gameplay is the biggest reason I keep playing.
The shooting feels satisfying, and improving your aim, movement, positioning and game sense takes real time and practice. There is always something new to learn, whether it is improving your crosshair placement, learning utility lineups, understanding timings or simply making better decisions under pressure.
I especially enjoy the feeling of getting better over time. When something that used to be difficult suddenly becomes natural, it feels incredibly rewarding.
🧠 Strategy and Teamwork
CS2 isn't just about having good aim.
Communication, teamwork and decision-making are extremely important. A well-timed rotation, a good smoke, a successful retake or a coordinated attack can completely change the outcome of a round.
I really like that individual skill is important, but playing as a team can make an even bigger difference. When everyone communicates and works toward the same goal, the game becomes incredibly satisfying.
🔥 Competitive Atmosphere
The competitive aspect is what makes Counter-Strike so addictive for me.
Every round matters. Losing one round can change the economy, losing an important clutch can completely change the momentum, and winning a difficult round can give your whole team confidence.
There is nothing quite like being in a close match, hearing the final seconds of the round and realizing that everything depends on your next decision.
🎮 Maps, Weapons and Variety
Another thing I appreciate is the variety in how you can approach different situations.
Different maps require different strategies, positions and styles of play. You can focus on aggressive plays, patient defensive setups, utility usage or simply rely on your mechanical skill.
There are also many different weapons and playstyles to experiment with, which keeps the gameplay interesting even after hundreds of hours.
❤️ Why I Keep Coming Back
CS2 is not perfect, and like any competitive game, it can sometimes be frustrating. There will be bad teammates, unlucky rounds, missed shots and matches where absolutely nothing seems to work.
But even after a terrible game, I often find myself thinking:
“Alright, one more.”
And then another match starts.
That is probably the best sign of how enjoyable the game is.
Counter-Strike 2 has a unique combination of skill, strategy, teamwork and adrenaline. It rewards practice and patience, and there is always another level to reach.
⭐ Final Verdict
For me, CS2 is much more than just a shooter. It's a game where every match creates new memories, every mistake can teach you something and every victory feels earned.
If you enjoy competitive shooters, teamwork, strategy and games that reward skill and dedication, I definitely recommend giving Counter-Strike 2 a try.

[b]An enjoyable mess of a sandbox game full of tacked on ideas that only sometimes get improved upon, even after this many years of updates later.[/b]

Most everything in the game relies on its procedural generation so as to create its universe and entire galaxies that you can explore.
The amount of explorable planets in the whole game actually goes far beyond the trillions, astronomically far more than anyone can cover.

One of the game's main appeal is its exploration and discovery. It's definitely cool seeing certain things for the first time, like seeing extremely hot planets to frozen ones to the grassy paradises, and even the dead & barren ones are neat to see. That interest dies pretty quickly though, because if you've seen one part of a planet, then you've most likely already seen the rest of it, and there's a good chance you'll see that same kind of planet again as you're exploring, only it has more mountains or is flatter maybe. Most every unique thing on a planet can just be found with an item or a vehicle's scanner too, and these unique things you've discovered are most likely on every planet you've already been on and will be on.

As a sandbox game, there's definitely a lot you can do, and they've been adding new things to do since the release of the game that isn't just going from one planet to another, albeit with varying degrees of enjoyability. Much of these new features though barely get any polish or fixes, if at all, even to this day.
For example, it's only until a little after the release of the game that they added base-building. The base-building, ever since it's been released, is extremely bare and janky, and getting properly creative with it requires you to do some weird workarounds.
Making a starship sounds cool, but it takes forever because you have to buy or find starships that has the parts you MIGHT actually want, and also it's a much more restricted process as opposed to the corvette starship building feature, which you have way more open options for.
The concept of going to ocean floors is cool, but everything down there is either exactly the same or extremely similar to what you find on the surface already, only you're swimming.
Gas giants are just big, normal planets with never-ending storms.
The game does have combat against real enemies, but it's extremely easy and only gets easier the longer you play the game, turning fights into chores for missions rather than something exciting to get into.
There are settlements you can be the overseer of, but they're massive idle time sinks with very little rewards and extremely inconvenient ways to interact with things.
Owning a space station takes a bit of effort even for late-game, but the only reward for it is just to say you own one, because you don't really do anything with it aside from decorating it using the extremely janky base-decorating feature, and using it as an actual base is far worse than the game's other options for bases.
The trailers and such like to advertise a lot of its features with multiple people going through them, but the truth is that the game has the potential to get even buggier in multiplayer to the point that it can severely slow down or lock players out of mission progress. It's so bad, this game's forums often advise you to turn off multiplayer to avoid potential problems; it's a shame because the game actually can be way more enjoyable with others.
There's a Pokemon-esque mini-game that's actually pretty fun and can get a bit in-depth, but getting to any kind of its meaningful customizations is a major grind, and barely any other player actually even dives into this mechanic.
...

The game's also lacking a bunch of basic QOL features, as well as general polish & fixes.
For example, there's no quick stack feature, so you have to manually put the items you want into the specific inventory you want.
You can't split stacked items by a specific number, only by halves at a time, ten at a time, or one at a time, so trying to take out 43 of an item or something specific for a mission from your storage is a bit of a pain every time.
Interacting with something near you will often prioritize interacting with what's further ahead instead.
Many missions/quests don't update until you have them selected to be active.
On keyboard & mouse, you can only use the mouse to move dialogue along.
The game has loads of things you can craft and that can be crafted into, but there's no real tooltip feature, so you just have to remember or constantly look up online what an item is an ingredient for.
You can't turn off the constant pop-up notifications.
The game can just decide to completely wipe your entire "favorites" category for teleport destinations without notification.
There are dozens upon dozens of starship parts you can use to put a whole one together, but there's no dedicated inventory storage for them like the corvette starship parts do. Also, the only time you can recolor starships is when you're in the middle of making them.
The surface color of the planets don't often match to how they look when entering their atmospheres, even the non-weird ones.
Every planet that has a particularly fancy weather category like "Echoes of Acid" or "All-Consuming Cold" actually all just have hot storms instead of blizzards or toxic storms, which actual cold and toxic planets have.
They added planetary rings two years after the game's release, but they're just planetary cosmetics that can actually hinder gameplay because they sometimes phase through a planet's moons, obscuring your vision as a result when exploring said moons.
Random people can just dump their inventory into yours without consent.
...

The story and lore is at least pretty interesting if you can or even want to follow it along. The lore is a bit of a grind to unlock, but they're all at least readily available to read online.

The game is full of things that "you just have to get used to" or maybe use mods for.
It's certainly much better to play than it was back when it originally released. Additions like the Freighters and corvette starships really add a lot to the long-term exploration of the game. However, after years upon years of updates, the entire game's still showing a lack of polish, is still lacking many QOL things, and has many implemented gameplay features that have only been good in concept and trailers, all while still having a base price of $60 USD. Getting it for free or at a really big discount is recommended if you even want to try it.

1,716 hours on Steam. Thousands more memories that no playtime counter could ever measure.

Destiny 2 is more than a game to me. It is a universe I have lived in, a community I have grown alongside, and a place that has given me memories I will carry for the rest of my life.

I've experienced the highs and lows. The excitement of discovering something new, the frustration of wiping endlessly during a raid, the adrenaline of finally defeating an impossible boss, and the absolute chaos of six Guardians shouting because somebody forgot a mechanic for the fifteenth time.

And somehow, those are the moments I treasure most.

Because somewhere along the way, Destiny stopped being about the loot, weapons, armour or next expansion.

It became about the people.

The random Guardians who stopped to help. The strangers who became fireteam members. The fireteam members who became friends. The people who patiently explained mechanics, revived you when things went wrong, and stayed for one more attempt when everyone was exhausted.

Some of us may never meet in person. Some have stopped playing years ago. Some usernames on my friends list might never light up again.

But I remember those moments.

There's something beautiful about gaming that people outside these communities don't always understand. You can spend hours fighting imaginary enemies in an imaginary universe and somehow create friendships and memories that are completely real.

And if there's one thing I will be eternally grateful to Destiny for, it is this: Destiny gave me a friend for life.

Out of millions of players, countless fireteams, random encounters, raids and adventures, this game brought someone into my life who became so much more than another Guardian on my friends list.

Someone I can genuinely call a lifelong friend.

Two people who might never have crossed paths in the real world found each other in a fictional universe and built a friendship that exists far beyond it.

Weapons get sunset. Seasons end. Expansions come and go. Servers won't run forever.

But that friendship? That is something no Content Vault can ever take away from me.

Even if I never launched Destiny again, I would still be grateful for every hour spent playing, because those hours led me to someone I hope will remain part of my life forever.

I came to Destiny for the game. I stayed for the memories. And somewhere along the way, I found a friend for life.

No exotic weapon, god roll, raid title or flawless achievement could ever mean more to me than that.

Of course, Destiny hasn't always been perfect.

I've been disappointed with Bungie's decisions, frustrated by the game's direction, monetisation, seasonal repetition, and especially the Destiny Content Vault.

Watching entire destinations, campaigns, missions and experiences disappear from a universe I loved was genuinely heartbreaking.

Not simply because we lost content, but because we lost pieces of our shared history.

The Red War. The destinations we first explored. The missions that introduced us to this universe. The experiences that newer Guardians never got to discover.

These weren't simply missions or destinations. They were places where memories were made, where friendships began, and where strangers became fireteams that would remain together for years.

For so long, I wished that Destiny could become whole again.

And now, seeing content finally being unvaulted, I cannot express how happy that makes me.

Thank you. Genuinely.

I know restoring older content isn't as simple as flipping a switch. I don't expect everything to return overnight. But seeing these steps towards restoring our universe gives me something I haven't felt this strongly in a long time.

Hope.

Hope that new Guardians will experience the journey that brought us here. Hope that veterans can revisit the places where their adventures began. Hope that Destiny's incredible history will be preserved instead of slowly disappearing.

Destiny deserves to be experienced as a living, connected universe, not merely remembered through YouTube videos and stories told by veterans.

I want the next generation of Guardians to understand why we fell in love with this game.

And despite every criticism I have, I want Bungie to know something.

I still believe in Destiny.

I wouldn't have spent 1,716 hours here if I didn't.

I criticise this game because I care. Because I know how extraordinary it can be. Because I've experienced those moments when the music, storytelling, atmosphere, gameplay and community come together to create something very few games can replicate.

There is something magical about standing beneath an alien sky, hearing that incredible soundtrack, and realising how much imagination and love went into creating this universe.

Destiny has given me wonder, challenges, laughter, frustration, excitement and companionship.

Most importantly, it reminded me that even in a universe built around endless conflict, the greatest thing we have is each other.

To the developers, artists, composers, writers and everyone who poured their hearts into Destiny, thank you. Your work has meant more to some of us than you might ever realise.

You didn't simply create a video game. You created a place where people from different countries, backgrounds and walks of life could find something in common.

A universe where strangers became teammates, teammates became friends, and sometimes, those friends became family.

To the Guardians who taught me, helped me, carried me, laughed with me, wiped with me and stood beside me, thank you for being part of my journey.

To the new Lights, I hope you experience the same wonder that made so many of us fall in love with Destiny.

And to the Guardians who have put down their weapons, moved on with life, or never returned...

Your Light was here. Your stories mattered. And somewhere out there, someone still remembers running alongside you.

I don't know what the future holds for Destiny or how many adventures await us.

Perhaps one day I'll log in for the last time without even realising it. No grand farewell. No final raid. Just an ordinary evening when I close the game, expecting to return tomorrow, only for life to take me somewhere else.

But when that day comes, I won't think about the hours I wasted.

I'll remember the laughter. The late-night raids. The impossible victories. The people who stood beside me.

And above all, the friend for life this wonderful, frustrating, beautiful game gave me.

Because I didn't just spend 1,716 hours playing Destiny. I spent 1,716 hours making memories.

And if the Tower needs defending again, if another impossible raid boss stands between us and victory, or if a new Guardian needs help through their first dungeon...

I'll be there.

Not because Destiny is perfect. Not because I agree with every decision.

But because, after everything, this universe still feels like home.

And a home isn't made special by the walls surrounding it.

It's made special by the people you share it with.

Eyes up, Guardian.

Per audacia ad astra.

Through boldness, to the stars.

Thank you, Bungie. Thank you, Destiny. And thank you to every Guardian who made this journey worth taking.

See you starside. ❤️

From one Guardian who still believes.

Якщо чесно, Counter-Strike 2 для мене — це гра, яку одночасно люблю і ненавиджу. Бувають моменти, коли після хорошої катки сидиш і думаєш: «Оце було круто», а бувають такі ігри, після яких хочеться просто закрити Steam і більше ніколи його не відкривати. Але наступного дня все одно запускаєш CS2. Думаю, саме в цьому і полягає головна особливість цієї гри.
Найбільше мені подобається те, що тут реально відчувається різниця між гравцями. Просто випадково перемагати постійно не вийде. Якщо хочеш ставати кращим — потрібно тренувати аім, вчити карти, розуміти економіку, знати гранати, працювати над позиціонуванням і вчитися приймати рішення швидше. І коли помічаєш, що те, що раніше не виходило, через деякий час починає виходити — це дуже приємне відчуття.

Особливо люблю моменти, коли залишається один проти декількох і потрібно самому вирішувати, що робити. У такі секунди реально відчувається напруга. Можеш виграти раунд завдяки одному правильному рішенню, хорошому таймінгу або просто швидкій реакції. А можеш програти через одну маленьку помилку. Саме такі моменти найбільше затягують.

Потрібно читати суперника, запам'ятовувати його звички, розуміти, де він може бути, правильно використовувати гранати та думати наперед. Чим більше граєш, тим більше починаєш помічати різних деталей.
Ще одна річ, яка мені подобається, — кіберспортивна складова. Мені взагалі цікаво розвиватися в цьому напрямку, тому CS2 для мене — не просто звичайний шутер. Мені подобається дивитися, як грають сильні гравці, помічати їхні рішення та намагатися переносити щось у власну гру. Через це навіть звичайний матч може сприйматися як можливість чогось навчитися.
Але без мінусів тут точно не обійшлося.
Найбільше мене дратують рандомні тіммейти та токсичність. Іноді трапляється команда, де всі нормально спілкуються, дають інформацію і реально намагаються перемогти — такі матчі приносять величезне задоволення. А іноді потрапляєш у гру, де хтось із першого раунду починає кричати, ображати інших або спеціально руйнувати гру. І тоді навіть хороша механіка CS2 не рятує.
Також буває дуже неприємно програвати через власну команду, коли ти намагаєшся грати серйозно, а хтось просто не хоче співпрацювати. Особливо коли розумієш, що потенційно міг виграти матч, але через відсутність командної гри цього не сталося.
Ще одна річ, яка мені не подобається, — іноді гра може здаватися несправедливою. Бувають моменти, коли ти впевнений, що все зробив правильно, але результат зовсім не такий, як очікував. Після таких моментів дуже легко почати злитися. Хоча з часом я зрозумів, що далеко не завжди проблема в самій грі — іноді потрібно просто прийняти, що ти десь помилився.
Не завжди подобається і система матчмейкінгу. Після однієї хорошої гри можна отримати дуже сильних суперників, а після невдалої — відчути величезний контраст у рівні. Через це деякі матчі відчуваються максимально нерівними.
Але попри всі ці мінуси, я продовжую повертатися в CS2.
Мабуть, тому що тут є те, чого мені не вистачає в багатьох інших іграх — відчуття особистого прогресу. Коли кілька тижнів тренуєшся, а потім раптом починаєш стабільніше стріляти, краще розуміти карту або вигравати ситуації, які раніше здавалися неможливими, це реально мотивує.
Для мене CS2 — це гра, де ніколи не можна сказати, що ти вже всього навчився. Завжди є що покращувати. Аім, реакція, рух, гранати, тактика, комунікація, психологія — все це можна розвивати практично без кінця.

Valheim is a fun game for the first hour or so, but the longer you progress, the less fun it gets. The devs really forget that a game is supposed to be fun, and then you start to see lots of issues. You do not get the cart until way later. The weight system and lack of inventory space do not expand until mid to late game, when it matters much less. The mountains and Mistlands terrain design is incredibly stupid and not made for the character to traverse in any fun way.
You can work super hard to get weapons and armor and upgrade them, and they become next to useless in the next area, and you never use them again. Building is fun, but you do not get any of the cool looking building walls and such until the last two areas of the endgame. Since there is no replace option like most other games have, you are very unlikely to use them.
The enemies in most areas have cool designs, but the AI is just dumb. They will walk away or run away and you have to chase them. They will spin in circles. They have trouble traversing the horribly designed biomes. Do not get me wrong, the biomes look good, but from a design standpoint and for the player traversing them, they are very poorly done. Even the AI has trouble with them.
There are lots of pointless items, like hats and weapons that you will never use. The power difference between weapons from one area to the next makes no sense. You could be using dual-fist melee weapons in one area, but the next area’s fist weapons do way less damage or are slower. The same is true of many weapons. The ebb and flow of weapons through the game is like this. Some armor is like this too. For example, the lox and wolf capes are basically the same thing, which makes it pointless to upgrade.
The raids would be fun to defend against until you realize the game is bugged and starts raids way before you have even touched the swamp or mountains, and your base gets destroyed. Yeah, I know it is a bug, but this is 1.0, so that stuff does not fly anymore, devs.
Let us move on to how you have to pick up an item to learn it. Even more so, your inventory weight never increases, short of using a Megingjord belt, which in the Mistlands is pointless because you replace it with a wisp. Whose idea was this? It is just dumb. Not only that, when you craft you cannot just pull from chests like many games allow. You have to go back and forth and constantly pick up items and fight the weight system. It is not fun.
For every fun mechanic in the game, there are double the unfun mechanics. I could go on for days about all the stuff that makes zero sense in this game and is just designed to waste your time instead of letting you have fun. I really did expect a lot out of this game for how long it has been in development, and it really lacks polish and any quality of life. The mechanics become punishing and a tedious grind. There are many survival games out there I would recommend before this one, and after grinding through this game I can honestly say it is not worth your time, nor does it respect it.

Counter-Strike 2 is still one of the best competitive shooters out there, and honestly, it’s hard to beat when you’re after that proper competitive gaming experience.

The gunplay is what keeps me coming back. It’s clean, responsive and actually rewards skill. Every shot matters, every decision can make or break a round, and there’s nothing quite like pulling off a ridiculous clutch when the odds are completely against you. It feels absolutely brilliant when everything comes together.

I also love how much depth there is to the game. On the surface, it’s simple enough: buy your gear, take the site and win the round. But once you get into it, there’s loads to learn — utility line-ups, positioning, timings, economy, map control, team communication and reading the enemy. You can play for hundreds of hours and still pick up something new.

The maps are another massive part of the experience. Learning the angles, common positions and little tricks takes time, but that’s exactly what makes CS so satisfying. There’s a proper sense of progression even when the game itself isn’t throwing levels and unlocks at you.

And, of course, there’s the sheer chaos of playing with mates. Nothing beats a late-night session where everyone starts taking the piss, someone buys when they absolutely shouldn’t, another bloke forgets to defuse, and somehow you still win the round. Absolute scenes.

CS2 isn’t perfect, and you’ll definitely have moments where you want to launch your mouse across the room. But that’s part of the charm. When you’re having a good game, communicating with the team and hitting your shots, very few shooters come close.

If you enjoy competitive FPS games and haven’t properly given Counter-Strike 2 a go, I’d definitely recommend it. It’s one of those games that’s easy to pick up, ridiculously hard to master, and somehow keeps dragging you back for “just one more game”.

Today, I barely recognize the game I fell in love with.

Hunt used to be a slow-paced, atmospheric, hardcore tactical extraction shooter where every footstep mattered, every gunshot revealed your position, and every decision could cost you your Hunter. The tension was incredible. The darkness was terrifying. Winning a fight felt earned, and extracting with a bounty was genuinely rewarding.

That identity is disappearing.

1. Bring Back the Original Atmosphere

The atmosphere of the 2018 Beta was something special. The dark nights, gritty visuals, oppressive shadows, eerie lighting, and constant feeling of danger made Hunt feel like a true horror experience.

The current game may have a newer engine, but better technology does not automatically mean a better atmosphere. I miss the old visual identity and the feeling that I was hunting — and being hunted — in a genuinely hostile world.

I want the Bayou to feel dangerous again, not bright, predictable, and visually disconnected from the horror experience that made Hunt unique.

2. Restore Tactical Gameplay and Meaningful Consequences

Modern Hunt often feels far too fast and forgiving. Excessive mobility, powerful traits, and repeated revives have reduced the consequences of mistakes and deaths.

The old Hunt rewarded patience, positioning, sound awareness, careful rotations, and smart decisions. You had to think before acting. You could not simply rush everywhere without considering the consequences.

I want those decisions to matter again. Combat should be tense, death should have consequences, and surviving a difficult encounter should feel like a genuine achievement.

3. Bring Back the Classic Gunplay

The classic weapon balance and the old Sparks + Uppercut quick-swap era created an unforgettable style of gunplay. Positioning, timing, precision, and knowing when to take a shot were essential.

Today, the overall combat experience can feel much closer to a generic fast-paced shooter than the distinctive tactical gunplay Hunt was known for.

I am not asking for every old mechanic to return without consideration. I am asking Crytek to recognize what made the original gunplay special and give players the opportunity to experience that style again.

4. Make Bounty Hunting Matter Again

The economy and progression should give players meaningful reasons to pursue the bounty and take risks. When money loses its value and teams can ignore the main objective without meaningful consequences, the entire purpose of the match changes.

Hunt should be about more than farming kills, chasing quick PvP encounters, and leaving the map. The bounty should be worth fighting for, and every match should create meaningful decisions about risk and reward.

5. Give Us a Permanent Classic / Legacy Mode

This is my main request to Crytek.

Please introduce a separate, permanent Classic / Legacy Mode inspired by the original Hunt experience.

It should focus on:

The darker, grittier atmosphere and visual identity of the early game.

Slower, more deliberate tactical gameplay.

Classic weapon balance and gunplay wherever technically feasible.

More meaningful consequences for death and revives.

Fewer mechanics that remove the need for careful planning and positioning.

The tension, sound awareness, and high stakes that made every match memorable.

This does not mean the current game must be removed or that modern Hunt players should lose their preferred experience. Keep developing the current version, but give longtime fans a genuine alternative.

The argument that a separate mode might divide the player base should not automatically end the discussion. A carefully designed mode, with appropriate matchmaking and queue management, would at least give the community an opportunity to show whether there is sufficient demand.

Crytek, please listen to the players who have supported this game for years.

After more than 15,000 hours, I am not criticizing Hunt because I hate it. I am criticizing it because I remember how incredible it once was, and I want to feel that way about it again.

I do not want Hunt to become another generic arcade shooter chasing trends. Its greatest strength was that it was different from everything else.

Don't replace the Hunt we fell in love with. Give us the choice to play it again.

Bring back the tension. Bring back the atmosphere. Bring back the tactical depth.

Bring back Hunt's soul.

Counter-Strike 2 — это эволюция классики, где сохранили дух CS:GO, но заметно подтянули визуал и физику. Особенно круто выглядит обновлённый дым: он теперь реагирует на выстрелы и движение, добавляет тактической глубины. Стрельба ощущается плотной и отзывчивой, каждый раунд строится на точных действиях и командной работе.

The game is definitely worth buying if you can get it at a massive discount, as in: single-digit price, being that one cannot deny that it is not a complete miss after the massive overhaul and fixes which polished what they could from the infamous initial version.

PROS:
The game obviously had a AAA budget and a fairly long story.
Someone poured their love for the Cyberpunk lore into the concepts and the pre-release marketing promised to deliver it.
If you want to end up with a mindless time-skip in the form of a semi-idle walk-and-click in your Library, this is a good choice. But again: only and only at a massive discount.

CONS:
1. Before anything else, the first thing that destroys the fun in this are the *unskippable* segments.
[spoiler] After Chapter 1 , you are thrown into an unskippable walking simulator with horrendous overeasy gameplay, that suffocates you with hopes of ending every time there is a fade-to-black, but no! At several points you have to literaly press the forward button several times to (!)crawl forward [/spoiler].
And the dialogue skip option is intentionally taken away at instances where you just sit and look at a character the developers deemed to be so important that you cannot skip.
Do you have choices? None that affect the gameplay.

And this can eat up to 15+ minutes of your life at several instances.

2. The gameplay is a an enormous tease and a letdown. You grow powerful incredibly fast and are given such a vast array of ways to combat that I had stopped upgrading my character a tad bit into chapter 2 because I couldn't find a reason to. The characters are unbelievable and the dialogues are cringe-inducing, with propaganda and forced perspectives infused with varying subtlety.

4. The game-breaking bugs that made it infamous are largely removed, but still present. At certain points the loading screen will shut down the game, there are untested spaces where you can get trapped and have to reload, the physics quirks are still present although rare, etc.

I really wanted to like the game and read online review promising the gameplay to get better as time progresses, but even this much time invested in it later, I cannot say that it is a win.

Valheim is an absolute masterpiece of survival crafting, blending atmospheric exploration with brutal combat. The building mechanics alone are worth the price of admission, offering incredible architectural freedom.

However, the game stumbles hard when it comes to quality of life and progression pacing.

Inventory management is a constant, frustrating chore, with arbitrary restrictions on metal transport that force endless, tedious backtracking. The world is massive, yet traveling across it often feels like a slow, unrewarding slog rather than an adventure.

Progression hits a brick wall with bosses that feel spongy and tedious rather than genuinely challenging. Too many encounters rely on artificial difficulty and repetitive attack patterns, dragging out fights well past their welcome.

Despite these glaring flaws, the core experience is too good to ignore. Iron Gate has crafted something special, but the grind desperately needs a modern, respectful pass on player time.

Review:

Baldur,s Gate 3 redefines systemic reactivity in computer role playing games, translating tabletop freedom into a digital space where player choice consistently reshapes narrative and mechanical outcomes.

Strengths:

Improvisational sandbox: The physics engine, surface interactions, and verticality allow creative problem solving that treats spells and environment as interactive tools rather than scripted events.

Reactive narrative branches: Companion arcs and main storylines adapt dynamically to player decisions, maintaining narrative coherence across vastly different playthrough paths.

Cinematic dialogue direction: Full performance capture elevates companion writing, grounding moral dilemmas and interpersonal conflict in genuine emotional stakes.

Weaknesses:

Third act pacing: Act 3 suffers from structural fatigue, dense urban navigation, and a noticeable drop in narrative focus compared to the tight pacing of Act 1.

Encounter balance: Combat scaling flattens in the mid game, where optimized builds easily break action economy limits and trivialize major encounters.

Verdict:
A monumental achievement in systemic role playing design that sets a new benchmark for player agency, tempered by pacing issues in its final act.

Where do I start with this.

Back in 2021. I was recovering from a particularly bad covid infection followed by an extremely strong reaction to the vaccine. While still at the uni, doing my degree one night one of my friends on discord mentioned this game. Within hours there was half a dozen of us playing it and having a fantastic time. Back then I was the only one to get through every biome in the end and finish the early access. I had dropped it after that, waiting for the full release, excited as to what it would bring. Sure it was a bit tedious and unpolished but it had so much charm and I was enamoured with it. 

Well, here I am five years later, with fresh eyes and as no man enters the same river twice, for neither he nor the river are the same, I feel as if both I and the game are something entirely different altogether. I have just beaten the game so here I am at 4AM trying to put my thoughts to electronic paper.

Let's start with the good. The game has beautiful art, biomes, environmental storytelling and in general an aesthetic I truly appreciate. The progression for the first few biomes feels just right. The combat can be quite enjoyable when it works well. I had a great time with my friends and the dedicated server was extremely easy to set up for which I am grateful. The game also has a natural flow to it. There is always something to do, some sort of a goal, and it is extremely easy to get lost and dragged in to accidentally losing an entire day to this game. I will give the dev team props for this.

This gets us to the flipside of that very same coin.

So many of the reasons for why you can get lost in this game kinda suck. You don't realise it at the time but the game has a very nasty habit of wowing you with the atmosphere and pushing forward to your next perceived objective that it obscures the reasons you have to do this and struggle so much. 

Would you like to level ground? Well you can, but only to a certain extent and never entirely flat no matter what you do. God help you if you build and try to level a something on a hill or a slope, as there is a max height and depth you can dig into and you can find yourself leveling the entire place only to find out at the end that some parts just cannot be leveled any further because of a height limit. This leads to some infuriating interactions with terrain when trying to build anything other than a shack in the woods, and you will need to build a relatively large base to fit every type of building in it that you get as you progress in the game.

Want to smelt some ores that you painstakingly found, mined and transported, whether via a cart (which sucks quite a lot and often gets stuck on the tiniest terrain with any even relatively small load) or shipped it with a boat to your base? I hope you enjoy holding down the E key as you manually handload every single piece of wood,coal,ore or crop into your machinery, sometimes loading as many as 50 items per one machine. If you are trying to smelt more than a few stacks then you can easily spend hours doing so while staying home. These sorts of features or to me missing quality of life options are present everywhere in the title.

Do you enjoy the combat and like seeing your character grow in skill? Make sure not to die or by levels 40-60 you will lose up to 3 skills per death for EVERY SKILL at the same time, losing hours of progress per skill and effectively forcing you to keep some skills below 10 because you do not use them often enough to recoup the losses from basic exploration and combat. I would consider myself average at best in this game regarding combat and even I have had at least a few dozen deaths accross my run. Many of my skills either hovered at 0 or were permanently at best around 20 unless I was really running them into the ground (pun intended, the running and swords skills were the only ones I managed to keep above 50 prior to mistlands). Some biomes like Mistlands do nothing less than serve as a complete difficulty spike and frustration mechanic that clashes with other bits and pieces.

Speaking of the Mistlands, this is one of those personal gripes, but by god this is a horrific biome through and through combining the worst of this game into one giant mess of hilly terrain with no visibility, enemy attacks that are faster than anything prior and also with little telegraphing (and god forbid there are more than 3 players in the zone increasing the enemy health by a total of 120% and their damage by 12% as well as introducing desync to half of the attacks meaning parrying becomes much more difficult. The boss also is the least fun I had had in the game. Or so I though until the last boss. Please heed my advice and turn camera shake off in the accessibility settings or suffer.

By now I think I have made my points clear. I want to love this game. I have 500+ hours in it. But the game fights me and hates me at every turn whenever I interact with any of the systems I like. Fundamentally the game has grown beyond its 2021 release but many of the flaws and mechanics never have. The lack of quality of life features that would be basic to implement but are not is infuriating. The lack of further development of many of the things that were there in the initial release like skills is depressing. The lack of a more fleshed out ocean biome, or farming improvements, or being able to craft 10x an item, or planting of some bushes but not others  all are problems that have me asking "Why is something so obvious always absent and always inconsistent". People say that this game has zero respect for your time and I feel that the most. So many of these mechanics do not really become a problem initially because you are still in the honeymoon phase. But they will grind you down eventually, piece by piece, until you are finding yourself wanting to finish the game but being so frustrated with what it has become that you no longer enjoy it anymore, you just press on.

I want to love the game, I want to be passionate about it. I just do not have faith in the developers fixing or improving so many of the long standing gripes and pacing issues and I am more inclined to believe this is actually their vision. And that breaks my heart.

I'm writing this negative review because I want to see this game improve. Since the forums are shutting down, what was once a feedback hub is now being taken away from us. Not that it matters, because the devs have never listened to the player base anyways. I don't believe this game is killer-sided or survivor-sided. If you believe one over the other then you ignore the actual problem. This game is MMR sided. Most important of all, this game finds the quickest match possible within the constraints of the hidden MMR metric each player has. But we can't ever see what that score is, nor will it ever be public. The community is already toxic towards each other as it is, seeing a number that determines our skill level would just incite more inflammatory responses towards each other.

I'm ignoring balance here. I'm ignoring bugs here as well. Both of those things change between patches. If this game didn't receive a consistent amount of updates then I would bring those up. But perk balance changes around often enough. I could very easily make arguments the game is killer sided but again that's not true. What's true is that I get the easiest killer matches possible while going up against some of the most brutal killers when I'm survivor. It just proves I play survivor more than killer. But when I say this game is MMR sided, I mean this game is essentially a free-for-all. What determines your score against survivors? What determines your score against killers? This game has so many variables to it.

For my last point I want to raise a problem bigger than the game itself. This game is not 1 killer vs 4 survivors. This game is 1 killer vs a free for all. There is very little to no incentive for survivors to cooperate in a match they deem losing. And this has historically been a problem with Survivors wanting to "Go Next", ie suicide on their first hook or intentionally run to the killer to get downed and hooked until death. The odds of escaping with all living survivors drastically goes down after 1 dies. Still possible but majority of the playerbase treats that as game over and the match dynamic changes. 2 deaths and now both survivors are pitted against each other hoping the other gets caught first so that they can be the last man standing to find the hatch. And all the while nobody is playing wrong here. The game incentives killers to tunnel a player out as soon as possible because of this very reason. The game does not force survivors to work together. You do not have to go for the unhook on the other survivor. The only reportable offense is working with the killer to sell out your other survivors.

I really don't see why people like this game.

The inventory system and item management are terrible. That seems to be a pattern in all these survival/crafting games, and valheim is by no means an exception. Having both a weight limit and stacking inventory slots results in nothing but tedium moving items around, and the game lacks the most basic of organization features such as stack to chests or build from chests. That much can at least be fixed with a mod.

Going further, the combat system feels wrong. The combination of not being able to cancel out of attacks, having very rough animations and very short hurtboxes on most of the weapons, and constantly getting stuck on terrain and objects while trying to maneuver make every part of fighting feel janky. Few, if any, fights aren't best done by getting enemies stuck with terrible pathfinding and shooting from outside their reach, and combat itself loses any threat as soon as you have armor appropriate for the region, at least on normal difficulty.

Worst of all, the traversal and mobility options in the game are nonexistant. No momentum sliding, no movement accessories, no flight, no mounts, not even paths speed you up. The game gives you absolutely nothing to work with to make getting around less boring than running in a straight line from A to B, or choosing to skip the process entirely with portals. At least that setting exists.

Basic options like turning off the death penalty aren't available without mods, discouraging risktaking. The exploration itself is directionless and often meaningless, since content is heavily siloed, with the player never having a reason to go back to old biomes, nor search a future biome since nothing can be done there anyway.

So much of the game needs mods to fix it, to provide basic features that are somehow lacking, that I genuinely cannot understand how this game even made it to a 1.0 release in this state.
