I'm going to be "One of those guys" that has over 1,100 hours into Valheim and does NOT recommend it. However, I'm doing so for the purpose of getting someone at IronGate to consider making some changes, because the potential of this game is incredible and although the "vanilla" experience is meh, a modded journey can actually be incredible. I strongly recommend playing with a few QoL mods, even on your first playthrough. There is a massive community of passionate modders out there that have really elevated this game much closer to a polished experience. 

Valheim overall has a bones of a phenomenal game and a LOT of things to praise. The building in this game is extremely well done and enjoyable, crafting is pretty good, and certain aspects of the combat are quite good (parrying with certain shields/weapons has very satisfying sounds and visuals, some weapons feel great to use). The art style of the game is terrific and strikes a great balance between low poly but still high quality assets. Some parts of progression feel good, and biomes like the Meadows and Dark Forrest are very enjoyable. 

That being said, the game has some major flaws that really feel bad and honestly could be fixed with just a little bit of effort. A lot of these flaws are fixed with mods as mentioned earlier, but some of them aren't (at least to my knowledge) and it's such a shame. In no particular order:
1. No dedicated player armor inventory is just lazy, bad design. It also makes zero sense, if my armor is ON my person, why would it occupy a slot in my inventory?
2. Utility items can't be stacked. Want to carry extra weight and also be able to actually navigate the mistlands with a wisp? Tough luck, sucks to suck. 
3. Stamina regeneration is PAINFULLY slow, even with Rested buff. Not Rested? Sorry, no stamina regen. Navigating some of the terrain in mountains or mistlands. 
4. Boss fights are unfathomably boring and poorly designed. Each boss after the first boss (who isn't even really a boss, he just dies), is a massive damage sponge with 2, maybe 3 mechanics that get spammed until your brain is liquid. It's some of the worst boss "design" you've ever seen. I would like to see bosses with multiple phases, telegraphed attacks, unique boss mechanics, etc. Whole system just needs to be rebuilt from the ground up.
5. Some of the biomes are miserable experiences. The jagged cliffs of mistlands are just awful, and the mist itself is bad design. Ashlands is a CONSTANT assault on your character, on your framerate, on your sanity, on your enjoyment,  Deep North is SO BORING and empty. You can run for 10+ minutes and encounter almost nothing of interest, it's so bad.
6. Super low visibility during storms and in Ashlands. Low visibility is a constant headache and makes for bad, unfun game design. 
7. Treasures found throughout the world, in dungeons and in abandoned settlements, are SO often utterly unrewarding. Instead of feeling happy that you found a super rare treasure box out in the world, you open it only to find a torch, some feathers, and some low level arrows. Like bro, what? What the hell is this?
8. Hexes (the flying enemies in Deep North) are so badly designed I could write multiple paragraphs about them. No effort or thought went into the programming of this enemy. 
9. Carts are so, so bad. They seem like they would be the way to transport heavy goods but in fact they're the opposite. 
10. Sailing is unfathomably boring and bad, wind is guaranteed to go against you 100% of the time unless you use the Moder power. The Ocean biome is almost completely void of anything interesting. No floating treasures, no way to explore the ocean depths, virtually zero dangers (easy to outrun or kill the serpents), leviathans are boring (no enemies on them).
11. Fishing is horrible and unfun, basically not worth doing ever.
12. Using mounts to travel is genuinely awful, very terrible controls.
13. Taming is messy and weird and badly designed. 
14. Feeding tamed animals is terrible, no dedicated feed boxes available. 
15. The new Forge system is the worst thing ever designed for a video game. 65% chance to upgrade your item by 1 level and 35% chance to DESTROY it completely, while consuming an INSANELY rare item, is about as braindead as it gets. It's like the developers don't actually play video games? Not one single human on earth likes this addition. Most players don't (and shouldn't) engage with this system at all.
16. The game absolutely DROWNS you in utterly useless items (bones, coins) for no reason. 
17. Can't build from containers.
18. Can't sort items in containers or inventory.
19. Many items are just flat out worthless (lots of trophies do nothing at all)
20. Poorly balanced items. Some items are just flat out miles better than others. Most noticeably, the heavy armor items are often just way worse because the tiny damage mitigation is obliterated by the speed penalty. 
21. Ashlands remains so badly optimized you'll have huge drops in FPS even with a beast machine at lowest settings. 

There are more positives and negatives that I'm forgetting, but this feels like a good list for now.

Valheim isn't just a survival crafting game; it’s an atmosphere machine that completely respects your time, patience, and curiosity. Playing through the entire journey completely solo was easily one of the most rewarding gaming experiences I’ve had in years.

From the quiet, misty mornings in the Meadows with acoustic guitar strings plucking in the background, to the terrifying adrenaline rush of sailing through open ocean storms, setting foot into the Plains, or surviving the sheer chaos of the Mistlands and Ashlands—the sense of progression never misses a beat. Every new metal tier, building piece, and biome feels genuinely earned through preparation and grit rather than tedious busywork.

The atmosphere is peerless. The lighting through the canopy, the smoke physics inside your hand-built longhouses, the howling wind on mountain peaks—it constantly pulls you into its world. And for anyone wondering if it holds up as a single-player journey: absolutely. Tackling the bosses, mastering parry timings, planning sea expeditions, and setting up interconnected outposts solo gives the world an incredible sense of scale and accomplishment. Even the food and cooking systems turn base-building into an art form.

If you enjoy deliberate, atmospheric survival games with gorgeous art direction, an unforgettable soundtrack, and deep progression mechanics, do not hesitate. Valheim is an absolute masterpiece.

as you can tell from my playtime, I really love this game. the game, for better and for worse, leans so heavily into realism to create a deeply immersive zombie survival experience. I say this because if you go into this game expecting a zombie SHOOTER, you're going to be disappointed. this isn't that. survival is the key, and oftentimes, that means you'll spend more time running away from zombies than actually fighting them. it is actually a pretty challenging game overall - I played on the default difficulty settings and found myself struggling often. a lot of the difficulty of the game can be overcome with experience, however. once you figure out how to fight and outpace the zombies without overexerting yourself or burning too many resources, even large hordes hardly become challenging.

the game offers a sandbox mode, which is where I think it truly shines. you can tailor your world to work exactly how you want in more aspects than I can name here. you can make a playthrough exactly the difficulty you want to be, save it to a preset, and use it over and over again to your heart's content. the game has a robust modding community as well, so if it doesn't offer what you want in vanilla (and believe me, in the current build, it will offer you a LOT), you can almost certainly find a mod that will add it in for you. excessive modding does sometimes lead you to disillusionment with vanilla when you realize that some small features could be easily implemented by the devs with a few small tweaks, but overall, you'll find yourself pleased with what the game has to offer and the flexibility you have to make your own changes.

if you want this game to shine, don't treat it like a game. there is no end goal, there is no set objective, and there is nothing to do other than survive. treat this like an experience - your character WILL die somehow, and your job is to give them a good life before then. sacrifice efficiency for the sake of immersion, and you'll find a truly beautiful game that you can sink days and weeks of your life into without even thinking.

The immersion of the world of Cyberpunk 2077 is the best and greatest aspect of this game. The word of a futuristic dystopia, but not a gray and desolate one - instead a colourful one full of distractions which are there to cover the real rot within. And for the third part I will add the wide variety of approaches in this game: You can play stealth, netunning, melee with berserk or grab your biggest gun and go full FPS - all of those options are available and all have their benefits and drawbacks and it is up to you to choose which of those to take.

Whatever had gone down with this game in the past, at this point the game stands as an example of what an RPG should be - a game when you play a role in a world that is foreign to you but is native and understable to its inhabitants - and becomes native to you through those characters and enviroments.

J’ai vraiment bien aimé Cyberpunk 2077. Au début, j’étais pas forcément à fond dans le jeu, mais plus j’avançais, plus j’ai accroché à l’histoire et aux personnages.

Le truc que j’ai le plus aimé, c’est clairement Night City. La ville est énorme et il y a toujours quelque chose à faire. Même quand on ne fait pas l’histoire principale, on peut faire des quêtes secondaires, des contrats, se balader ou juste découvrir la ville. Je trouve que l’ambiance est vraiment réussie, surtout la nuit avec tous les néons et les bâtiments.

L’histoire principale est aussi un gros point fort. J’ai bien aimé suivre V et surtout la relation avec Johnny Silverhand. Il y a pas mal de moments qui restent en tête et certaines missions sont vraiment excellentes. Les personnages secondaires sont aussi assez intéressants et certaines quêtes sont presque aussi bien que les missions principales.

Au niveau du gameplay, j’ai bien aimé avoir plusieurs façons de jouer. On peut utiliser des armes, des armes de corps à corps, le piratage ou jouer plus discrètement. Le système de cyberware permet aussi de rendre son personnage beaucoup plus puissant au fur et à mesure.

Graphiquement, je trouve le jeu encore très beau. Night City est vraiment impressionnante et certains endroits sont magnifiques. Avec de bons réglages graphiques, le jeu peut vraiment être incroyable.

J’ai aussi beaucoup aimé les quêtes secondaires parce qu’elles ne servent pas juste à gagner de l’argent ou de l’expérience. Certaines racontent vraiment des histoires intéressantes et permettent de mieux connaître les personnages.

Pour la durée de vie, je trouve qu’il y a largement de quoi faire. J’ai passé pas mal de temps dessus et je n’ai même pas terminé tout le contenu. Le jeu peut facilement occuper pendant plusieurs dizaines d’heures si on fait aussi les quêtes secondaires.

Pour Phantom Liberty, je ne peux pas encore donner mon avis complet parce que je ne l’ai pas terminé. Pour l’instant, j’aime beaucoup l’ambiance et les nouvelles missions, mais je préfère attendre d’avoir fini le DLC avant de donner une vraie note définitive.

Au final, je donnerais environ **10/10 à Cyberpunk 2077**. C’est un jeu que j’ai vraiment apprécié et dans lequel j’ai passé beaucoup de temps. Il n’est pas parfait, mais son histoire, son univers, ses personnages et tout ce qu’il y a à faire font que j’ai vraiment aimé l’expérience.

Pour Phantom Liberty, pour l’instant je partirais sur **9/10**, mais cette note pourra changer quand je l’aurai terminé.

Let me just start off by saying that I've played this game since the beginning. 

I pre ordered Destiny 2 and once it came out, I never really looked back. At one point, probably sometime before Forsaken, I had my Hunter, Titan, and Warlock all maxed out with pretty much every armor and weapon exotic unlocked. I have probably put over 1,200 hours into the game on PlayStation alone.

Destiny 2 was a huge part of my gaming life for a long time. The PvP was always a lot of fun and honestly still is. I remember putting together fireteams with friends on the weekends for Trials of the Nine, grinding Competitive Crucible, and just messing around in PvP for hours. Even when you were losing, there was always that feeling of wanting to play just one more game.

The raids are another thing that really stuck with me. I still remember how excited I was when my friends and I finally completed Prestige Leviathan, Eater of Worlds, and Spire of Stars. At the time, those completions felt like genuine accomplishments. You could spend hours wiping on the same encounter, getting frustrated, laughing at stupid mistakes, and then finally having everything come together. There was nothing quite like seeing that final boss go down after struggling with it for hours.

I think one of the biggest things Destiny gave me, though, was the people I met along the way. I've met some genuinely great people through this game, whether it was through Fireteam Finder, PlayStation Communities back when that was still around, raids, or just randomly joining up with other players. Some of those people I never would have met otherwise. That's something I don't think gets talked about enough when it comes to Destiny. You can log on expecting to play for an hour and somehow end up spending the entire night playing with a group of people you had never even met before.

Coming back after being away for three years or more has definitely been a little overwhelming. I logged in and immediately had what felt like 50 quests thrown at me. I'm still not entirely sure which campaign I'm supposed to start with or what order I'm supposed to be doing things in. I think Bungie could do a much better job of giving returning players some kind of direction because there is a lot to take in when you've been gone for that long.

At the same time, I do appreciate the freedom. Destiny has always been a game where you can kind of make your own path. You can chase a weapon, run strikes, play Crucible, work through a campaign, join a raid, or just wander around and see what you end up doing. I wouldn't want the game to completely take that freedom away just because it can sometimes be confusing for returning players.

The biggest disappointment coming back has probably been seeing how much content has been vaulted. There are locations, campaigns, and activities that I remember spending countless hours playing that just aren't there anymore. Makes it disappointing to come back to a game you loved and realize that parts of it are simply gone.

With Bungie talking about bringing those DLCs and locations back, though, I think that's a step in the right direction. I'm genuinely happy to hear that they're looking at bringing that content back because I think new and returning players should be able to experience it.

That said, I still don't think it should have been vaulted in the first place.

Despite all of that, coming back after so many years has made me realize just how much I missed Destiny. The gunplay still feels great. The worlds still have that same atmosphere. The music still hits in the same way. Even just walking around the Tower again brought back memories of spending countless nights playing this game with friends.

It's kind of like coming back to a place you haven't been to in years. A lot has changed, some things are gone, and there are plenty of things you don't recognize anymore, but there's still something familiar about it.

After more than three years away, I'm glad to be stepping back into the boots of a Guardian. I don't know how long I'll stick around this time, and I don't know what Bungie has planned for the future of Destiny, but I'm genuinely hopeful.

For all of its problems, there is still something about Destiny that keeps pulling me back.

[h1] From Absolute Frustration to Deep Appreciation (With One Major Caveat) [/h1]

If you had asked me about Valheim during my first ten hours with the game, my review would have been a scorching 2/10 rant. It felt punishing, clunky, and aggressively hostile to anyone with limited patience. But somewhere around the halfway mark, something clicked. The survival mechanics transformed from a frustrating chore into an atmospheric masterpiece.

That being said, if you hate grinding, proceed with extreme caution. Here is the honest breakdown of how this Viking purgatory won me over—and the parts I still despise.

[h2] Phase 1: Why I Hated It At First [/h2]
Let’s be honest: Valheim’s early game doesn't pull its punches; it kicks you squarely in the teeth.

[list]
[] Brutal Onboarding: Everything kills you. Wild boars are terrifying, dying to a falling tree is a rite of passage, and corpse runs back to your gear across half the map are soul-crushing.
[] The Clunk: The combat and movement felt rigid compared to modern action games, leading to plenty of unfair-feeling deaths.
[*] First Impressions: I was ready to uninstall it and never look back. It felt like another generic, tedious survival time-sink designed to waste my evenings.
[/list]

[h2] Phase 2: Why I Grew to Love It [/h2]
Slowly, the game’s true genius began to reveal itself beneath the rough exterior.

[list]
[] Masterclass in Atmosphere: The haunting music, the gorgeous low-poly aesthetic, and the dynamic weather system (there is nothing quite like a thunderstorm rolling in while you're out at sea) created an unmatched sense of immersion.
[*] Building Freedom: Snapping together timber cabins, smoke vents, and grand Viking longhouses turned out to be surprisingly therapeutic.
[/list]

[h2] The Elephant in the Room: The Grind [/h2]
Even though I fell in love with Valheim, I still despise the grind. And Valheim loves to make you grind.

[list]
[] Resource Bottlenecks: Upgrading your gear requires hoarding mountains of specific ores, and transporting those heavy metals back to your base (since portals won't let you carry them) can feel like a part-time job.
[] Repetitive Loops: Chopping down thousands of trees, mining endless copper veins, and farming crops one by one can test the patience of a saint.
[/list]

[h2] Final Verdict: 8/10 [/h2]
Valheim is an incredible, deeply rewarding adventure wrapped in a stubborn, old-school survival shell.

I’ve always heard and thought that Terraria was the 2D equivalent to Minecraft. After playing it, honestly I feel it has more in common with something like Stardew Valley or heck even Castlevania: Symphony of the Night once you progress far enough, which is a wild comparison I know.

I found that the game is largely about exploring and just continually upgrading yourself through your tools, weapons and your mobility so you can stand up to increasingly tougher enemies and challenges, eventually gearing up to fight the next boss.

The exploration and building elements are still there, but I think the best thing about the game is venturing out, discovering something new that you can test out. There’s a ludicrous amount of weapons to test out and they all play out in several simple and unique ways, it’s honestly impressive.

That said, I thought most of the combat is mostly done in preparation, rather than really doing anything interesting? Most boss fights I found is just a simple matter out-DPSing them before they kill you, and if you aren’t able to win, doing more research to find better gear and equipment. The combat itself I really don’t think has that much depth to it, but simple is fine.

Now while the discovery in this game is fantastic, I was warned that this is one of those games where you need to have a wiki on you at all times, and while I don’t think it’s always true… it really does help especially when you enter hard-mode, knowing what to do, when to do it, and what to look out for a specific build. It’s not always necessary but it can really help with progression being less overwhelming.

Admittedly I feel like SOTN, this game may have a couple of balance issues, especially towards the endgame? The weapons continuously get crazier and crazier and eviscerate the non-boss enemies before they even come on screen but for the actual boss fights, they are such bullet sponges and such heavy hitters that you can still feel underprepared for them. I played a Melee weapon focused build throughout most of the game, found it somewhat challenging but still rewarding, until the final boss, where everything was too chaotic. Then I swapped builds to a summoner and the fight was trivialised in just over in 20 seconds.

Despite that though, really good game to just get lost and just progress in.
It’s a huge game with lots of neat side stuff to do that can may or may not passively help with progression.

I don't even know how you're supposed to review Destiny 2 after putting over 2,500 hours into it.

At this point, I've spent enough time in this game that I should probably be paying rent in the Tower.

I've played through expansions, seasons, events, campaigns, dungeons, raids, Nightfalls, PvP, exotic quests, countless activities and an absolutely unreasonable number of hours doing things that I swore I wasn't going to grind again.

And somehow...

I keep coming back.

That's the weird thing about Destiny 2. It's a game that can simultaneously be one of the best games I've ever played and one of the most frustrating things I've ever played.

When Destiny is at its best, very few games come close.

The gunplay is incredible. The abilities feel amazing. The movement is satisfying. The raids and dungeons can be some of the best co-op experiences in gaming. And when you put together a build that completely clicks, there's something incredibly satisfying about watching everything on screen disappear.

Then there are the moments where you spend three hours farming for one weapon roll, get absolutely nothing useful, question every decision you've made in your life...

...and then log back in tomorrow and do it again.

The community is another huge part of the experience. Some of my best gaming experiences have come from playing Destiny with other people. Whether it's finally clearing a difficult raid encounter after hours of wiping, helping someone get an exotic, or just messing around with friends, those are the moments that make the grind worth it.

I've also watched this game change constantly over the years. Some changes have been fantastic. Some have made me wonder what Bungie was thinking. There have been incredible expansions, disappointing seasons, amazing weapons, terrible metas, content I never wanted to leave and content I was perfectly happy to see disappear.

But after 2,522.9 hours, the fact that I'm still here probably tells you everything you need to know.

Destiny 2 isn't perfect.

It can be grindy. It can be frustrating. It can waste your time. It can make you hate whatever activity you're currently playing.

And then you'll get the perfect drop, clear a raid you've been struggling with, discover a ridiculous build, or have one of those completely chaotic moments with your friends...

...and suddenly you remember why you play.

2,522.9 hours. 100%.

At this point, I'm not sure whether I play Destiny 2 or Destiny 2 plays me.

8/10. Would probably complain about it while continuing to play for another 500 hours.

I've put over 300 hours into Valheim at this point and it's still one of the best survival crafting games I've played.

Vanilla is already really good on its own. You go into a new biome thinking you're prepared, immediately get slapped by whatever lives there, then slowly work out what you actually need to survive it. The progression feels earned because you're constantly preparing for the next step rather than just watching numbers go up.

There's also something about building a base, sailing somewhere new, setting up portals and slowly expanding across the map that makes you actually care about the world you've made. Even the inevitable corpse runs become part of the experience, although some of them are considerably less fun at the time...

Then once you've played enough vanilla, modding gives you a ridiculous amount more to do with it. You can keep it fairly close to the base game and just add things like crafting from nearby chests and other QoL changes, or go much further with full RPG-style class systems, expanded magic, new progression mechanics, extra building pieces and larger gameplay overhauls.

That's probably one of Valheim's biggest strengths for me. The base game is strong enough that it doesn't need mods, but it's also flexible enough that you can change quite a lot without losing what makes Valheim feel like Valheim.

It's somehow both a really chill game where you can spend hours building and decorating a house, and a game where you sail into a storm, get attacked by something horrible, die miles from home and have to organise an expedition just to get your stuff back.

300+ hours later and I still keep coming back to it.

"Carried more animals than Noah" is a popular gaming slang phrase and insult used in multiplayer team games like Dota 2, League of Legends, and Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO).
What It Means
• The "Carry" Role: In tactical and multiplayer online games, a "carry" is a player who becomes powerful late in the match and is expected to lead or win the game for the team.
• "Animals": A slang term used by gamers to describe teammates who play poorly, make bad decisions, or act wild and uncoordinated.
• The Joke: To say someone "carried more animals than Noah" means a player had to single-handedly drag a terrible, underperforming team to a victory—mockingly comparing their effort to Noah carrying pairs of every animal on his ark during the biblical flood.

I've played this game since the first week it released in early access with friends back in 2021 and it was very enjoyable. Twice before full release, my friends and I got burnt out before Mid game because of the slight learning curve involved and to an extent, lack of direction. The game both benefits and suffers from this but upon its full release I returned on my own to set out to finish the full game. I have double my playtime and have only entered Mid game with a desire to still see the ending which is a good thing since I'm crossing 100 hours. The addition of achievements helps with the direction you're supposed to go in, at least for me, and if you ever get lost, the likely next thing you need to do is the next achievement based on % complete. This is a really good game and the building is one of its strongest features. As you progress more objects will become available to you and you can make some pretty complex builds, its really just up to you how long you want to wait to set up a big base, and adjust as more stuff is unlocked. I highly recommend this game with its only draw back to me and my friends being metal not going through portals with the player. They have modifiers that allow different functions of the game to change and this being one of them we turned it off, making the game increasingly more fun and less time consuming. The game will still be time consuming, to me, this is probably the longest survival game I've played without actually seeing the ending before 100 hours. You should definitely play this game if you like survival games and love to build buildings with real structural integrity.

     I just got back into this game after a while, but it seems like this has been an issue for a while. 

    Lastly as other reviewers have said, it seems like the dev team is largely focused on skins, and battle passes, much to the detriment of other aspects of the game, particularly in the last year. While I think it may have some netcoding issues in terms of hit detection, i think that issue is paired to some degree with bullet travel, drop, and drift which are varied across a pretty broad set of weapons and ammo types. 

So ultimately, as many other reviewers have said, at its core it has some really great elements, but has some long standing issues.

I've had a love-hate relationship with this game ever since I first started playing it on the PS4 back in 2018. That said, I always seem to end up coming back to it. If you're a new player considering getting into it, best advice I can give is to close the post-game chat and never open it again. You'll thank me later.

I’ll start with the positives.

There is an enormous number of Warframes, guns, companions etc to unlock. Each frame has its own unique set of four abilities and a passive ability. On top of that, you can equip two ranged weapons, a melee weapon, a companion, and a weapon for that companion. All of this creates an absolutely staggering number of possible builds and playstyles. Experimenting with different combinations and testing what works is easily one of the most enjoyable aspects of the game.

The amount of content is frankly astronomical. There is so much to unlock, explore, and learn that it can actually be intimidating or overwhelming, especially for a new player.
One of Warframe’s biggest strengths is that almost everything can be obtained for free. The premium currency, Platinum, can be earned by trading with other players. You can farm valuable items yourself and sell them to other players in exchange for Platinum, meaning that even premium cosmetics and other purchases are not necessarily locked behind spending real money.
Despite its age, the game still looks genuinely good. It also offers a huge number of customization options for your Warframe and other equipment, allowing you to change colors, cosmetics, attachments, and much more. There are also frequent limited-time events, which help keep the game from feeling static and often give players interesting rewards to farm.

Speaking of farming, this is very much a matter of personal preference. If you enjoy the classic MMORPG style grind, Warframe has more than enough of it. There are plenty of activities where you can repeatedly farm resources, weapons, mods, cosmetics, and other items. For some people this can become repetitive, but for others, having something to work toward and gradually improving their collection is a huge part of the appeal.
The game also offers a good variety of mission types and environments. While many missions take place in more traditional corridor-based tilesets, Warframe also has several open-world areas that provide a very different experience and give you more freedom to explore.

Figuring out which weapons work particularly well with a certain Warframe, which companions complement a specific build, or which damage types and status effects work best together is a big part of what makes experimenting in Warframe so enjoyable. There is a lot of room to test different ideas and discover combinations that you would not necessarily expect to work at first.

Cons

The biggest problem, in my opinion, is how poorly and sometimes not at all, many of the game’s mechanics are explained. This is especially noticeable with the modding system. The game gives you very little guidance on how to properly mod a Warframe or weapon, or even what the basic priorities should be when building one. The AutoMod function is almost completely useless and can even be actively harmful, because it may recommend mods that provide little to no meaningful benefit for the setup you are trying to create.

The problem is not that the game expects you to experiment. In fact, that is one of the things I enjoy most about Warframe. The problem is that it does not give new players enough basic knowledge to make those experiments meaningful in the first place.
How is a new player supposed to know when they should prioritize shields over health and armor, or vice versa? What determines whether a weapon should focus on critical hits or status effects? Which stats are important for a particular weapon, Warframe, or playstyle? The game rarely explains these fundamentals, leaving new players to figure them out through trial and error, external guides, the wiki, or questions in the in-game Q&A chat. The same problem applies to actually acquiring new equipment. For example, the game often does a poor job of explaining where to farm the individual parts needed to build a new Warframe or weapon, where to get all the resources required to craft those parts, and sometimes even how to obtain materials that themselves have to be crafted from other resources. For a new player, this can easily turn what should be a simple goal into a long chain of unexplained steps and a frustrating search for information outside the game.

To sum it up, the game is free, so just try it lol. What’s the worst that can happen? You lose a few hours of your life, get confused by 17 different currencies, open the wiki because the game refuses to explain anything, and somehow end up farming servfish in Orb Valis at 3 am XD

In succinct
Valheim is a very contrasting game. You’re either puckered or tuckered; there is very little content that lands between these two phases.
It is a very confused game. It doesn’t know what game genre it wants to be. You start out playing a comfycore sim-lite inspired by Nordic fantasy and mythology, and end up playing a wannabe horde-fighter with awkward controls.

Thick outer coating
Every single thing in Valheim is coated in a thick layer of tedium. This is where the genre confusion comes about; this game has an inventory, character skills (job-related levels; levels per weapon type; levels per different use of stamina, etc) and multiple partially scaling stat bars (heath, stamina, eitr - mana). All of this sounds absolutely ok from the outside looking in.
Unfortunately, all of this is meticulously crafted to create tedium. 

Upon death, you lose 5% of all character levels (levels are on an exponential curve). You also drop your entire inventory. Luckily, this death inventory stays within the game world permanently and does not degrade. The challenge arises in reclaiming your death inventory. Enemies do not despawn, and they typically do not move unless something catches their attention. This means you will always come back to your grave weaker, and to the enemies which killed you. Due to how the skills work, it may take hours, sometimes days, to get your skills back. Your skills make actions more efficient, and efficiency is the absolute key to Valheim. 
The game creates a large incentive to always be prepared for the worst, wherever you go, but it will punish you for doing so through this death system.

The inventory is tedious and illogical. The game has a large amount of materials and items you can interact with and use. All items (weapons, armors, materials, foods, buffing gears) stay within your inventory. Everything takes up your precious slots. There are no dedicated auxiliary slots, no armor slots. This can be upgraded later into the game, but, by that stage, there is also a larger quantity of drop variety. Materials can be stacked, but to a rather small amount (typically 30-50).

Your character does have a maximum carry weight. It is rather quite constricting. Many recipes require you to overburden your character with materials, considering the game lacks modern quality of life features, including building from stored items. You will find yourself going back and forth, back and forth, and back and forth. If you misplace something, you might as well not have it at all. The developers clearly state this is their intended “vision of the game” – the game is clunky by design, in other words.

The food system is also utterly disgusting. Food trickles down in its applied stats. Most food states that it gives around 30 minutes of buffs to your health, stamina, or mana. However, the amount it gives goes down rather quite quickly. Once your food reaches its half-life, it’s generally not going to be very useful to you, and you should replace it. The game balance is based around you being at peak preparation, so it is quite a pain to carry twice as much food as you would otherwise need. Decent food is fairly expensive to make.
The limited inventory size and the tight weight limit are pains and aches throughout the entire game. It doesn’t add enjoyment, just tedium. 


Base building
Quite fun. I enjoyed it a lot. Building a nice base is not cheap in terms of resources, but this is largely acceptable. Decorations can be a pain. They typically desire more premium resources – resources you’re better off using to upgrade some part of your gear; perhaps your armor, or your weapons, or to create buffs. The building in Valheim is largely good, although there are still many frustrations. Terraforming anything  slightly below sea level is a giant headache. Due to the lack of a free-roam camera while building, it is impossible to make a bridge over water deeper than a few meters. 


Exploration of an uninteresting world

This is rather ironic. Valheim should have an incredible, diverse landscape over many different biomes. It is based off Norse mythology, after all. 

The reality is quite simple, the world is very limited in terms of what it can/will generate. You might expect unforgiving, sharp coastlines made of sheer cliffs, beautiful fjords, large and long mountain ranges, thick alpine forests, but also rolling hills and flatland, and tons of rivers; thick and thin, and marshes, and rocky beaches – generally, you’d expect it to have more Scandinavian landscape features. 
The game doesn’t emulate these well at all. No area in Valheim in any biome I have come across or seen online really put any awe into me. It is immensely disappointing. Once you’ve seen one of each biome, you’ve seen them all. The diversity of world-gen is simply not good enough. The world is quite large, but it’s absolutely meaningless. The PoI’s are uninspired, and all very samey. The world is pointlessly large, and a smaller, more thoughtful, more wild, more interesting, more concentrated world would deliver such a more delightfully immersive game experience. 

One of the strangest oversights is the lack of seasons. All the mechanics to make seasons are already in the game, and they’d make the world feel much more dynamic, and much more alive. Seeing the game world go from the blinding stillness of winter and into the new, colorful growths of spring, signalling that you have lasted another year within this unforgiving world, and into the longer summer days, ending with the most fantastic autumn colors surrounding the natural world around you. 
The second half of biomes are uninspired, boring, and empty. One of the biomes in the middle of the game is an absolute pain due to poor design. 


Big boots
Valheim has so much incredible potential to be something magical. A significant amount of love and care was put into creating such an immersive world. 
This is the “puckered” part. Running away from a large, powerful enemy – or a group of enemies - will have your cortisol spike, and it has had me sweating many times. You’ll find yourself praying that your footing is perfect, doing your absolute best to use your precious stamina efficiently. The consequences of failure are, as previously described, very dire. Dying is very harshly punished, and it’s very easy to die. 


Combat
Clunky at best. There is an okay range of different weapons per tier to choose from, and they can generally all be upgraded. There is a chance to destroy your item if upgrading past a certain point. 
Animations are slow, and you’re typically fighting the terrain more than the enemies. Non-playable characters do not suffer from any terrain-related debuffs, and they do not suffer from combat-related terrain penalties; water will slow you to a crawl and render you fully defenceless – an enemy will be able to utterly destroy you because they can use their weapons in water. There isn’t always much you can do about this, considering how the building system works. 

Closing thoughts
Valheim has fantastic immersion, but the game is an inch-deep body of water. A little bit of rainwater, a bit of potable water, and a bit of untreated sewage. I could not recommend this game to play solo, unless you add some QOL and content mods and change some time wasting world settings. 

Valheim is a game that the developers expect you to play a fairly specific way, and there isn’t much wiggle room for personal touches. The geography in certain biomes makes the game simply frustrating, not challenging. This is why most people somewhat “cheese” the game; playing the game the way it’s intended to be played is not a good time. 

Even online, most of the general advice is spent on fighting the game mechanics and cheesing the game. Valheim could be a great game, but it really tries to fight you on every level. Most things feel pointlessly drawn-out.

5 years ago this was the only survival builder I knew that implemented falling trees, and the only one that had those trees be a death hazard, and the only one to be Norse Mythology based. Today in 1.0 it has 8 biomes and cinematic Lore! It has a unique skill, health, and stamina system. When you strip away the armor and the foods, the only thing that separates a novice and a seasoned player is character skills and the players experience in the game. Its very well designed and very good at keeping progression of the biomes uniform. Each biome boss grants you something you need in order to progress the next biome smoothly. Trying to skip bosses proves challenging enough to deter the idea. The difficulty of each biome gradually increases while bringing new challenges to overcome in unique ways. The variety of combat expands as you progress as well. There are buffs and weaknesses and another thing is the weight mechanic. It really makes you look at this game differently. Different armor sets and weapons give you different buffs and weaknesses as well, and even affect your movement speeds and concealment on top of armor ratings. There's plenty to do and no playthrough will ever be the same, making replayability VERY strong. Its a very beautiful game as well. the only thing I can recommend to new players is... turn down the volume in the settings. Also, dying is part of the game, so don't be too upset when you do. There's even an achievement for it called "First of Many"

As with a lot of games, it has a unique and beautiful artstyle, music, and story, but with some serious issues with the gameplay, the enemies in new biomes are far too powerful and often 1-hit kill you even with the absolute best food, potions, and equipment from the previous area, and they remain powerful until you have the gear from several biomes later. I'd describe it as the enemies x2 in power while your armor gets x1.8 more effectiveness, and I'd say this difficulty curve starts to get unreasonable at the plains and beyond. Most of the boss fights are amazing, there's really only 2 I'd complain about; the queen (mistlands) is extremely tanky but pretty fair if you can focus on her while ignoring the smaller bugs, while the emerald flame (ashlands) is both extremely tanky, spams massive spells that you physicaly can't outrun, and causes extreme lag spikes. Stamina management is painful, there is a full 1 second delay to regen after ANY action, and it recovers so slowly that most of the time I found myself forced to walk away from an enemy hoping they couldn't hit me, then dying because they in fact could. 

Getting new gear/food/potions is a tremendous grind, and by default you're not allowed to use portals to move ore so you're expected to build a new base for every biome (enemies past meadows [deathsquitos are pure evil] will absolutely wreck your base unless you raise the earth an make ugly but unpassable walls). Even enabling portals for ore and metal, they weigh way too much for you to carry- enjoy limping around at a snail's pace. Melee seems to be the only playstyle that actually does any damage, even post-ashlands spells do pitiful damage and I don't think bow and arrow was ever really good unless you were forced to use it on flying enemies. The deep north was a welcome change of pace, while it's very peaceful in open space, dangerous enemies lurk in the forest and if you fall through the ice you're just dead, no jumping out.

I started playing Valheim on September 9th, and today, October 6th, I have 225.5 hours on record, with 96.5 hours played in the last two weeks. So yeah... I definitely got my money's worth.
I finished the game playing mostly with one friend, and honestly, I barely went outside during these 28 days. I was almost always at home playing Valheim. I probably need to apologize to the sun at this point.
What makes Valheim special to me is that the game actually makes you enjoy everything you do. Gathering wood, fishing, farming, mining, exploring, building your base, sailing around, preparing food, even dying and having to go back for your stuff. Somehow, even the small things feel rewarding.
Nowadays, a lot of games are designed around giving you dopamine as quickly as possible. Valheim feels different. You have to slow down and actually enjoy the journey. You have to find fun in the little details instead of constantly asking "what do I unlock next?"
My friend and I even spent several days building a single house. Not hours. DAYS. We kept changing things, adding rooms, rebuilding parts and making it look better. And somehow, it never felt like wasted time.
Building a base with your friend, going out to collect materials, coming back with a full boat, getting completely destroyed by something you thought was easy, then going back and getting revenge... those moments are the game.
And that's what I think people need to understand before playing Valheim. Don't rush it. Don't treat it like a checklist. Enjoy the stupid little things. Enjoy cutting trees. Enjoy farming. Enjoy fishing. Enjoy building something that took you several days even though you could have built a wooden box in 10 minutes.
For me, Valheim is easily one of the best survival games I've ever played and definitely in my TOP 3.

Is No Man's Sky a bad game?
...Kinda?

I've strictly experienced this game in virtual reality, so I'm gonna review this game if it were a VR title. I know that games that are designed for PC that have VR capabilities can be very hit-or-miss, and may undersell the game itself. Do keep in mind that most of the negativity I have towards this title is largely in-part to the game itself, and not its translation into virtual reality.

Before jumping into the negatives, I want to first go over the positives. The game is actually translated into VR very well, integrating your camera, movement, and use of your hands to feel seamless, and as if you are actually completely enveloped in the universe. The navigation with the spaceship is by and large the best feature, since it really makes you feel like you're piloting a ship. The graphics for the game are decent, though admittedly they don't hold as well compared to games of today (credit where it's due, this game is already 10 years old). 

Unfortunately this is about where the positives end and the negatives start. To start, even though it's translated moderately well in VR, it's a game where you don't need to move whatsoever. So if you like a VR game that lets you sit down, then this game is a decent choice. I like my VR titles to integrate movement though, as that's a larger appeal to the system than just having 360° graphics. I WANT to be forced to punch air, jump around, reach my arm in strange areas. For most of the gameplay my arms could be entirely stationary, only needing to aim a scanner in the general area sometimes. 

Besides the VR stuff, the game is just... boring. An abundance of planets to visit, that hold virtually the exact same resources as every other planet, with similar life as every other planet, with the only real differences being the colors of the planet (is it more blue or green?) and shapes of plants. The tutorial seems to never end, but it's not like it matters since there are so many mechanics in the game you'll inevitably be confused by something eventually. Interacting with other alien species nets you a single word you can learn, and apparently a lot of them are nice and just give you stuff for saying a single word in their language (which, sure I guess?). The story is barebones and clearly not the primary objective of the game. Actually, I'm not really sure what the objective of the game is outside of simple exploration. Granted, a game doesn't need an objective to be good, nor does it need a good story (if any at all); it should at least give the player fun things to do or things to look forward to. No Man's Sky seeks to give the player a survival-like game with its focus towards space exploration; the game itself falls short on giving the player anything captivating, especially after the first hour of gameplay.

Frankly, the game feels like a sandbox that requires the player to waste a lot of time finding the actually interesting things to do, yet the player is somehow supposed to enjoy that process. Normally I'd add in stuff that they could do to improve the game, but it's already 10 years old. They've made the improvements to the game that they wanted to change. Not much else I can add.

...Though, if I were to make this game a lot better, I'd mainly make two changes:
1. Limited Solar System(s)
        -Create a select number of solar systems, I would say 2-3 would suffice
        -Design the planets to have very specific resources, and establish alien bases/cities on certain planets
2. Better Story
        -Ideally a story with voice acting would make the story a lot more engaging
        -Giving some sort of origin story to your character could be helpful
        -There doesn't need to be some villain group or person; just explain why or how all these alien species have come to be connected to one another, what started their desire to travel the cosmos, any history between them, maybe create groups of pirates or mafia-adjacent groups to have diversity within the aliens and unique interactions with the player

These changes will never happen to No Man's Sky, but if a VR title were to adopt these changes while designing gameplay similarly to what No Man's Sky has, it would be a pretty incredible game.

I doubt I'll keep playing this game. I'm not personally too sure what other people see in this title, but I guess the game just isn't for me.

Project Zomboid is a game that's ending has been set since the beginning. On every run, you are told, "This is how you died," and to many starting out this message may seem to be a grim reminder of an inevitable fate, but as time goes on it becomes a challenge to oppose. In my almost 200 hours of gameplay, i yet to even grasp the outer edges of what this game has to offer, and that is why it has become so special to me.

This is a sandbox zombie survival developed by the Indie Stone, and unlike typical triple AAA or indie games, it lacks a storyline, but it is what makes it so good. You get to create your own story, learning the mechanics of the game as you go on. Despite its isometric perspective, it is a pioneer of hyperrealism in gaming, including activities such as farming, fishing, foraging, construction, exploration, and more! It includes a wide variety of towns throughout the Kentucky area, and the main goal set by the game is to survive as long as possible in an apocalypse scenario.

On starting out, you will die a lot, but the learning curve is part of what makes the game fun. I have always felt that games were never a challenge enough, and while community-made challenges can be fun at times, they always feel so bland and repetitive for any game I play. Zomboid is an exception of this, with its intricate controls and environmental learning to be had, every experience you have playing this game will vary. Modding has also become a big part of the game as well, and with the recent addition of mods such as Project Viewpoint, even those not accustomed to the top down gameplay can experience it in their own preferences. 

It saddens me deeply that this game and its creators have not gotten the appraisal they deserve, especially upon learning of the threats received after inconsistent updating to the game. Things like this take time, and I'm sure Indie Stone would receive the same treatment if they just jammed whatever content they could into the game or turned it into a cash-grab. I would much rather play a high quality game made by people who actually care for the community than some of the recent slop I have seen. If you enjoy survival experience and want a challenge, I would highly suggest Project Zomboid as a game for you.

Valheim starts out great: a beautiful world, good atmosphere, fun exploration. But the further you go, the more the game turns into something it was never meant to be.

The Mistlands aren't a biome — they're a punishment. They're empty, boring, and the constant fog kills any joy of exploration. The shortage of soft tissue turns progression into endless grinding. The Ashlands are even worse: endless spawns of aggressive mobs that are faster than you turn the game into a job. You're not fighting — you're clearing a conveyor belt.

Technically, the game falls apart too. On a 9800X3D, 4070 Super, and 64 GB of RAM, both the Ashlands and the Deep North start stuttering. This isn't a hardware issue — it's an optimization issue. The game simply doesn't care how powerful your PC is.

Whoever designed the item collection for summoning the last boss should be permanently banned from game design. It's pure hell: you spend an hour in a dungeon where mages one-shot you, then you have to sail for 30 minutes to some godforsaken corner of the map — and you have to do it three times. And the problem is that the ocean has nothing interesting in it for the entire second half of the game.

The verdict: the first 50 hours are excellent survival. The next 50 are exhausting grinding. The final biomes are a slog and a disappointment. If I could leave a "mixed" review, I would. But after finishing it, there's only one feeling left — relief that it's over.

Not recommended for anyone who values their time.

Rust is one of those games that can be incredibly fun and incredibly frustrating at the same time.

You start with basically nothing and slowly build yourself up, gathering resources, making better gear and building a base. Then sooner or later, someone will probably come along and destroy everything you've spent hours working on.

And somehow, that's part of what makes Rust so addictive.

The PvP is what really makes the game interesting. You never know who you can trust, and even a simple encounter can turn into a fight, a betrayal or a completely unexpected situation.

Building and upgrading your base is also really satisfying, especially when you start getting better gear and more resources. There's always something else to work towards.

Of course, the game can be brutal. Losing hours of progress to another player can be incredibly frustrating, and the grind can get pretty intense if you're playing on a competitive server.

But Rust is at its best when you're playing with friends and creating your own stories. The game doesn't need to give you a scripted adventure because the players create one themselves.

🟢 MUST PLAY — Brutal, addictive and unpredictable. Rust can make you hate the game one minute and have the time of your life the next. That's part of the experience.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games that really grew on me the more I played it.

Night City is absolutely incredible. The atmosphere, visuals and soundtrack make exploring the city one of the best parts of the game. There’s always something happening, whether you're following the main story or just going off to explore and do random side activities.

The story is also one of the biggest strengths. The characters are memorable, the side quests are surprisingly well written, and there are plenty of moments that actually made me care about what was happening.

The combat and character progression are really fun too. There are plenty of different ways to build your character, whether you want to focus on guns, blades, hacking or a mix of everything.

It's not perfect, and the open world can sometimes feel a little too busy with things to do, but there's so much content here that it's easy to lose yourself in Night City.

After all the improvements the game has received, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely worth playing.

🟢 MUST PLAY — Great story, amazing atmosphere, memorable characters and a fantastic open world. Night City is a place I genuinely didn't want to leave.

It’s even better with friends, but playing solo is just as enjoyable if you like taking your time and building things your own way.

I had this game on the blizzard launcher before they switched over so my hours aren't exactly accurate. Back then I played the game with my dad and we both had a blast. The gunplay, spontaneous group content, movement, abilities, all fun as hell. I never transferred my account in time so I lost everything. I started playing again years later with a group of friends and again we had fun with the anniversary content and running through the dungeons, but all the nerfs, content removal and system changes put a hamper on things. The last expansion I played was Lightfall which added strand which is a ton of fun to use. The world content for Lightfall is decent but felt like a bit of a slog and was very repetitive while I was playing. The story had cool fight scenes and gameplay, but didn't have much substance to the narrative.

The story though. I don't even know where to start. Literally. Class stories and campaigns have been removed. They have removed key story content including the Red War, Curse of Osiris, Warmind, and Forsaken. Removed story missions are now only playable in random order in weekly/daily content that everyone speed runs. Exotic narrative quests like the old one for Drang and Sturm are just gone and remove any attachment you have to getting and using the unique weapons you have outside of how cool they look, the grind it took to get them, or how viable they actually are. I used to care about some of the characters, but they either wrote most of them to be completely incompetent or killed them off. New players have to go on you tube or forums to watch lore content or old gameplay videos just to get an understanding of how things started and why things are the way they are now. All of that should be provided in-game through normal gameplay or even optional missions that bring you back, but it just isn't. I'm all for intricacies and secrets being put in text and hidden throughout the world, but baseline understanding and world building should be established naturally through gameplay.

PvP has a clear meta that changes as things get nerfed/buffed for each mode, but if you're okay with that then you'll have fun.

I can't speak on the newer content as I haven't had a desire to come back to the game.

TLDR; If you want a game where you can just shoot shit, grind, and get stronger either solo or with friends it's fun, but content removal and bad decisions have removed the charm that once made this game and its world feel unique and special for me.

Helldivers 2 doesn’t just deliver chaotic cooperative gameplay; it elevates cinematic action to a whole new level. Visually, the game looks incredible, with impressive environmental effects, dynamic lighting, and orbital firemissions that light up the battlefield. The variety of enemy factions—from the overwhelming Terminid hordes and the relentless Automatons to the alien Illuminates—keeps combat scenarios fresh, diverse, and tactically demanding.

The real brilliance of the game lies in its weapon sandbox and iconic Stratagem mechanics. Call-ins feel punchy, responsive, and deeply satisfying, with calling down a 500kg bomb right in the middle of an enemy stronghold representing the absolute peak of the experience. On higher difficulty settings, this loop turns into an intense, adrenaline-fueled test of coordination, trigger discipline, and precise timing where every single decision counts.

While friendly fire and occasional chaotic spawns can lead to brief moments of frustration, Helldivers 2 stands as one of the most fun, cinematic, and addictive co-op shooters on the market. It offers endless replayability and an unmatched sense of scale when shared with a solid squad.

It's not my type of game. I mostly just kept playing to see what the hype was about, especially from a couple other people I know who have played for this game for a long time. I'll just be talking about the ground battles/tanks since that's what I've been playing for most of my time with it (and maybe touch on the air battles more another time).

I first had the game pitched towards me by someone as "cod with tanks," which I can kinda see but not really. It does have the same k/d style leaderboards, different loadouts, team domination/capture the point sort of game modes, and dopamine hitting kill confirmed pings/explosions. But to say it's just cod with tanks is really oversimplifying it since it's way more complex. I'm more used to the usual generic fps tanks (like halo or battlefield for example) where mostly you just blast on someone until they die. So that's how I, with very little knowledge of the game and being naively guided to, played initially. Then looking at the tutorial more and playing more games, I'd say it's more of a tactical sniperish game. You take cover a lot, you need to know sniping spots and push points while picking up on audio cues (like enemy engines), and have encyclopedic knowledge of ammunition and tank weak points/angling to really do anything. The maps (which there are a ton of) also change every time you go up a BR, so have fun doing that process all over again with stock tanks. It doesn't really help either that I'm not that big of a milsim guy and don't know a lot of the terminology, so a bunch of the jargon goes over my head when playing with more experienced friends. So slowly figuring out this game isn't that casual and way more complex than I thought made the painstaking steep learning curve very rough going through the first few hours on my own. The game is still kind of fun to play with friends and coordinate more than the random people you are matched with. And I guess speaking of matchmaking, it's similar to any other competitive shooter. You could be dominating one match with a couple newbie or braindead players and then the next you are up-tiered to another match where you're going against heavier tanks or experts who have be following this game since it's conception over a decade ago. It's nothing you can avoid really with a community that has lasted this long it's expected.

However, the biggest turnoff for me was the grind. The game is reeeeally grindy to get anywhere on the tech tree and leveling up your crews. I've been playing fairly causally for the last couple weeks and only reaching around BR 4.0, and it honestly gets a bit repetitive seeing the same roster of tanks each game. Some of my friends (who have long since unlocked a few tech trees) are saying wait until I get this BR or that BR which are way higher tier than where I'm at, but to be completely honest I don't want to tediously clock match after match, hour after hour until the game eventually gets fun. Again, there's nothing really wrong if you can tolerate that its just not my type of game. I find if you have a group of friends that are around your skill/BR or more experienced ones willing to downgrade to that BR to play with, you can still have somewhat of a fun time.

[h1]RAINBOW SIX SIEGE — The 2,000-Hour Vertigo, Ranked 2.0, & The Harsh Reality[/h1]
[b]Status:[/b] The most addictive tactical FPS ever made, slowly turned into a neon hero shooter | [b]Score:[/b] 8/10

[hr][/hr]

[b]THE 3 EDITIONS BREAKDOWN (BUYER'S GUIDE):[/b]
Ubisoft loves confusing store pages, but here is the actual breakdown of what you're paying for:

[list]
[*] [b]Free Access / Base:[/b] [i]THE RENOWN SLAVERY TRAP.[/i] You get a completely barebones roster and have to work a full-time job grinding in-game Renown just to unlock basic operators. Avoid unless you have endless free time.
[*] [b]Elite Edition:[/b] [i]THE GOLDEN SWEET SPOT.[/i] Unlocks a massive chunk of the attacker/defender roster right off the bat so you aren't stuck playing the same three operators every round. Best value-to-grind ratio.
[*] [b]Ultimate Edition:[/b] The corporate whale package. Gives you virtually all 70+ operators instantly plus bonus cosmetic bundles. Only grab this if it’s on an 80% sale or you despise grinding.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[b]THE UNFILTERED REALITY OF SIEGE (WHAT THEY DON'T TELL YOU):[/b]

[b]1. From SWAT Tactical Shooter to Sci-Fi Hero Shooter[/b]
Siege used to be a dark, realistic, SWAT counter-terrorism simulation in 2015. Today? It’s a fast-paced hero shooter where you play as Mozzie in a Pizza costume or Doc in a Rick & Morty skin, running around laser gates and holograms. If you are expecting a hardcore SWAT experience, adjust your expectations—it’s now a competitive esports twitch-shooter.

[b]2. The Brutal 500-Hour Learning Cliff[/b]
No other FPS has a map knowledge barrier this high. Floors are made of balsa wood, ceilings are killzones, and soft walls are just waiting to be blown open with C4 from the floor below. You will spend your first 100 hours dying to enemies you never saw, through holes in drywall you didn't know existed, from angles you couldn't imagine. 

[b]3. The Ranked 2.0 Nightmare[/b]
The current rank system is a complete illusion. Your displayed rank (Copper, Silver, Gold) means almost nothing because the game matches you based on a "hidden MMR". You can be stuck in Bronze and still get thrown against 5-stack Champion-tier sweats who haven't touched grass since 2019.

[b]4. Audio Bugs & Ghost Footsteps[/b]
The sound propagation engine in Siege is mathematically brilliant on paper (sound bounces through open holes/doors rather than passing through solid walls), but in practice, it bugs out constantly. Enemies will drop from hatches right behind you without making a single sound effect.

[hr][/hr]

[b]THE VERDICT:[/b]
Despite all its flaws, corporate greed, and toxic lobby culture, when you pull off a 1v4 clutch defusal with 2 HP remaining, no other FPS on Earth gives you this level of sheer adrenaline. 

[b]BUYING ADVICE:[/b] Grab the [b]Elite Edition[/b] on a deep sale, spend your first 10 hours in the Shooting Range practicing recoil patterns, mute toxic teammates instantly, and never sprint blindly around a corner. 8/10.

Valheim is a game that feels exciting, challenging and relaxing. From the moment I enter its world, it gives me a sense of nostalgia—like returning to an old adventure, even while discovering something completely new. Its calm atmosphere makes it easy to lose track of time, whether I am exploring a forest, sailing across the ocean, or simply sitting by a fire at home.

One of my favorite parts of Valheim is building. Building is incredibly relaxing, and the game gives players so many different ways to create homes, forts, villages, and anything else they can imagine. Every building project feels personal, and it is satisfying to slowly turn a simple shelter into a beautiful place to live.

The crafting and resource gathering are also very enjoyable. Grinding for materials never feels overly demanding; instead, it feels like a natural and rewarding part of the journey. Gathering wood, mining ore, preparing supplies, and crafting better equipment all give a real feeling of progress. Even food preparation is enjoyable, adding another cozy and meaningful layer to survival.

The enemies feel well balanced throughout most of the game. They can be challenging, but they usually do not feel unfair. Boss fights are especially memorable: they are not too easy, but not impossible either, so defeating them feels earned. The endgame bosses are much harder, which can be intense, but they also give players a true final challenge.

Visually, Valheim is beautiful. The landscapes are stunning, from misty forests and snowy mountains to open seas and peaceful meadows. Its graphics may not aim for realism, but that is part of what makes the game so special. Its unique visual style gives the world a magical, timeless look that is beautiful in its own way.

Playing with friends makes Valheim even better. Exploring, gathering resources, building together, and taking on dangerous enemies as a group creates many memorable moments. Whether playing alone for a relaxing experience or with friends for adventure and laughter, Valheim offers something truly special.

Overall, Valheim is a beautiful survival game with a nostalgic heart. It combines relaxing building, satisfying crafting, balanced combat, enjoyable progression, and breathtaking landscapes into an experience that is hard to forget.

The game starts out enjoyable, but somewhere around the midpoint of progression it completely stops being fun. Gameplay devolves into endless inventory management and sorting through dozens of tiny chests.
In version 1.0 they added a massive cupboard… and some absolute genius of a game designer decided to make its slots 5×10 vertical. Why not go full comedy and make it 2×25 horizontal while they’re at it?
The game is missing a ton of basic gameplay systems and quality-of-life features. Because of that, new content barely matters. I’ve been arranging chests and sorting items the exact same way since the beta, and nothing has changed.
Yes, mods fix most of this. But this is a review of the game, not the mods. There is no official mod support through the interface, so we can safely assume this inventory nightmare is the pure, intended vision of the developers: hunting for arrow feathers that are sitting in one of the 40 chests somewhere in your base.
They recently added the mountain forges with an absurd upgrade system that basically encourages save-scumming. The new method is “raise the weapon’s level or lose it completely.” In a sandbox game. Brilliant.
Building options are extremely limited. There are plenty of objects of various kinds, yet they feel strangely restricted and incomplete. It often feels like someone took away half of my Lego bricks and told me to build a model anyway. There is a serious lack of stone pieces, specific structural elements, and graphical consistency - especially noticeable with the wooden parts that just don’t match.
One more thoroughly terrible mechanic is the difficulty scaling. On higher difficulties enemies become nearly impossible to fight fairly without cheesing or looking for specific block interactions, because no shield in the game can actually block their attacks. A two-star Draugr Elite deals 116 base damage, which is then doubled on hard difficulty. No armor can protect you from that, and the hits go straight through blocks. Only armor from two or three biomes later even lets you survive a single hit. It perfectly illustrates how half-baked and uncommitted the RPG systems and stats are in this game.

Valheim is both a brilliant game, and a deeply infuriating one. The primary cause of irritation is with the grindy nature of the game which i'll go into later. But as of now, i'm leaving this as a negative review, purely in the hope that the devs will decide to go a little further with their QOL settings in the game.

Firstly, the game has a brilliant atmosphere and soundtrack. Its utterly absorbing and continues to impress through-out the experience. If you really want a deep and engaging experience, play with no map and learn the lay of the land yourself. Although the models are low-poly, the lighting and weather effects in this game are simply breath-taking, and it will drag you in if you let it.

Gameplay wise, this is a typical survival crafting sandbox, with a "buff don't nerf" approach to its mechanics. You will not starve to death, but you'll sure as hell wish you had a belly full of food when you're in a fight. Its stamina focused combat takes queues from soulslikes, with a parry, dodge and stagger system. Its basic, but it works and remains engaging enough through long gameplay sessions. Its building system is beautifully done, allowing players to create anything from their very first survival hovel, to trophy adorned castles that remind you of your journey. It weaves together lots of different, smaller systems to create a world that feels lived in. Some examples include the smoke system, where you'll need a chimney to vent smoke from fires, but rain puts out fires too, meaning you'll need to figure out how to have your fire in the rain too. Enemies are drawn to noise and mining or logging create a lot of noise, dragging enemies to your workspot. I have many fond enemies of midnight copper digs in the black forest quickly turning into a fight for our lives. Enemies even in-fight between groups, adding to that world sense and creating opportunities to make your opponants do the work for you. All these little things add together to make a compelling, fun and interactive world thats geninuely a joy to play in.

But the game suffers heavily from overgrinding. There absolutely is an experience to be had in going on your first iron mines and hauling a rickety cart back to your base with as much of the stuff as you can. But the 20th trip starts to feel a lot more like an exercise in frustration. Thankfully, you can edit your world settings and can directly increase the amount of drops! We've been playing on 2x drops and honestly feel the game is a lot better for it. We still need ever more iron and wood, we still need to grind to improve our settlement, but the pace is a lot more tolerable with double drops.

That may have been the end of the bad news but there is another grinding issue that has been on-going for three years now and the devs still haven't addressed it, which is the source of the unfortunately negative review. Crafting in Valheim works by picking up ingredients to unlock the receipes, but many of the mid and late game weapons/items are locked behind enemy "trophy" drops, which are rare drops from that specific enemy. For example, there are armour sets that unlock by picking up silver, but you only get the chest and legs - not the helmet. You only get the helmet reciepe by getting a certain enemies trophy. This particular example isn't to egegious, the enemy is very common. But there are powerful, gameplay defining items that are locked behind rare enemy trophy drops. The game supposedly has a pity system that kicks in to force a drop, but the requirements behind it are insane. I ran some maths earlier today to test it, and getting one particular trophy would require me to play 7-10 hours straight - no quitting and logging out because that resets the pity system - just farming that enemy to get a single trophy. Supposedly the drop rate is around 10% but i've killed 40 of those enemies and not had a single drop.

Locking content behind these weird, luck based grinds isn't something I approve of. Its deeply frustrating in much the same way as the resource grind can be. There are plenty of things the devs could do about this, between fixing the pity system to track between quits, to having a trophy always drop on first kill.

I absolutely adore this game when I feel like i'm progressing, building my hamlet and shaping the world around me. I absolutely hate this game when i'm throwing myself into a meat grinder to unlock more content that I should have had several hours ago.

If you have loads of time to kill and like survival crafty games, this is a no brainer. If you don't have as much time to game these days, there is still fun to be had here, but use the world modifiers. Don't listen to people telling you how to play the game their way. It will crush your enjoyment and waste your time.

Devs - Sort out your trophy drops. Just add more world modifiers. Not everyone can spend hundreds of hours on a single world. You did it for the resources and it made me fall in love with the game again. I will change this review to positive if trophies get addressed.
