I wanted to love this game. The first 15-20 hours are genuinely magical. But then, as you work your way through the biomes, you start to realize that the entire design philosophy is built around one thing: making sure you never stop doing chores for the sake of chores.

For context, I played through this back on its Early Access release in 2021 and cleared everything up to and including the Plains back then. But that was years ago. Coming back now, I expected the game to have grown not just a tad wider, but also a lot deeper, smarter, more respectful of the player's time. It hasn't. Not one of the core pain points I personally had has been addressed. The foundation hasn't been reworked or deepened in any meaningful way. All that's changed is the addition of three new biomes on top of the original five. Everything else is noise. And most of the QoL features people actually want are still only available through the modding community, not the developers.

And just to be clear: the critical parts mostly apply to the default experience on Normal or Hard, without the optional world modifiers that remove some of the unnecessary friction - but never all of it. And those sliders aren't a sign of UX work or balancing. They're a loud "fuck off" aimed at players who don't share the developers' vision, handed over instead of any actual work being done. Also, this game's not that great for playing it solo, in my opinion. Just something to consider.

Overall, after finishing the 1.0 release, this doesn't even feel like a videogame at this point. It's a glorified time-sink with a viking skin, posing as a realistic and so-called "brutal" survival game.

The selectively realistic mechanics are the worst offender. Your character can't carry ore through a portal, but you can teleport yourself - which is arbitrary bullshit if you ask me, since it's magic to begin with, and is only meant to draw out each iteration of the grind. You get crippling debuffs for being wet and/or cold, and you're stripped of all your health, stamina and mana if you forget to eat every 10 minutes. Considering that we play as some sort of revenant who already died on the battlefield and was brought back to slay some demigods or something along those lines, that's a bit rich. Thank god you don't get crippled even further if you forget to sleep for 8 hours each day, don't shower regularly, and relieve yourself in the outhouse. The "realism" is cherry-picked solely to waste your time, not to immerse you, and is applied specifically to your character while the same survival game logic is not applied to any of the NPCs.

Not to mention the constant corpse runs. You die, you lose your items, you lose a chunk of your skill progress on every skill, and you spend the next 20 to 60 minutes walking back in your spare set of equipment, if you have any at that given point. Otherwise you not only need to grind to get your skills back to where they were, so you don't waste half your stamina on a short sprint and a few attacks with a weapon, but also waste a ton of time to make a new set of equipment, which takes longer with each biome you go through. If you were carrying ore on a boat back to the main base and the boat sank due to an attack or some bad weather - everything sinks with it. You're losing hours upon hours of time spent on preparation each time you make a genuine mistake or die to some absolute bullshit, which happens more and more the further you go into the game.

Base-building is a treadmill, not a creative outlet unless you're REALLY into it. Your structures rot in the rain unless you build them from specific materials later on. Your fires eat wood endlessly, so you're constantly forced to haul fuel. And every few in-game days, a demolition crew shows up to trample your crops, slaughter your livestock, and try to level your base, whether you're ready or not. Meanwhile, producing anything - coal, ingots, mead, cooked food, honey - is chained to hard timers. One (!) production cycle can take anywhere from a couple of minutes to 20-30 minutes or more. The further you go, the more resources you need, and the longer you sit in front of your stations with your hand out, waiting for the timers to run out so the game lets you play itself at last.

But otherwise, credit where it's due - if you're here to build shit not just out of necessity, this game is a goldmine. If you're creative, there's more than enough building pieces and decoration options to make your dream viking dollhouse a reality. The community has done genuinely impressive things with them, and if your idea of a good time is spending hundreds of hours designing a castle or a village with a proper viking longhouse that has a functioning kitchen and a moat, you'll probably love it. But if you came to explore, fight, and collect gear, it's a much sadder story. There's not enough depth to sustain the combat, not enough variety to sustain the exploration, and again - not enough respect for your precious time.

The sailing is mandatory and feels tedious. I get why it's part of a viking fantasy, but it still has ways to go before it becomes fun. You spend hours sailing back and forth because you can't teleport metal until some point in the lategame. Sea serpents and other enemies may attack your boat. You run aground on rocks and terrain. Constant storms and high waves could keel over and straight-up sink your boat at any time unless you make yourself a drakkar, which only becomes available not too far from the end credits. Any vessel is slow and turns like a brick. And if you die out there, far from home, you get to grind for a new one to make that trip all over again.

Combat is a one-trick pony that makes earlier bootleg soulslikes seem overly complicated. In this case it literally just boils down to a dodge-roll and a swing with an optional parry if your gear overlevels a biome you're in and hence allows it. That's it. That's the whole game. Everything else - magic, archery, two-handers, stealth - is a self-imposed handicap or even an active detriment. Magic doesn't exist until the last two biomes, and when it arrives, it feels like an afterthought. Summons are made of glass and die to a stiff breeze, or, in the case of trolls, are quite tanky but attack everything including you. The only reason to use anything else but a sword and board is because the game is so shallow that having something else to do to prevent you falling asleep mid-fight.

Bosses are damage sponges with one-shots and constant AoE spam. They don't test your skill. They test your patience and your willingness to farm for upgraded gear, constantly grind the mats for the best foods available and for the meads that are basically either resource replenishing potions on a 2-minute cooldown or short-term status resistance buffs you're supposed to prepare well in advance since they require about an hour of real time get made. From the Plains onwards, every boss just spams AoE/DoT attacks and/or summons waves of adds - that's the entire moveset. The arena fills up with trash you can't sensibly despose of on vanilla from all the structures, rocks and trees breaking around you, the framerate drops, and you're just rolling around getting 2-3 hits in until one of you dies. Rinse, repeat. It's not a fight. It's a war of attrition against the game's performance consisting of chipping off the HP bars that are too long to keep the boss battles engaging.

Final verdict: if you really really want to - you'd be better off playing it with mods and tinkering with vanilla world modifiers on top of that. Lots of mods. Mods that fix the grind, mods that fix the balancing, mods that add some much-needed QoL and depth to the game's mechanics, so basically just mods that stop your time from being wasted like it amounts to nothing.

Previously a fantastic game, but devs intentionally broke matchmaking because higher MMR players were not finding lobbies fast enough. Now, low MMR and high MMR players get matched together wantonly with no regard for skill level, constantly creating lobbies where average players are getting steamrolled by skilled players. Valheim is a game all about the journey, which is fantastic. But it repeatedly does things for no reason other than to extend your play time, and it often contradicts itself in doing so. It's not insurmountable though, some quality of life patches would fix a lot of the problems I have with it. 

You are signing up for a grind, and that's a totally fine game design approach to take. But it feels like once they got to the Swamps, their design philosophy changed for the worse. It's around this time you start gathering iron, but you will need to travel for it. They introduce portals in the same moment, but (by default) you cannot take metal through portals. It feels like a contradiction or compromise: I would have respected it more for not having a portal network and encouraging travel, and then building a world that reinforces and rewards that travel. Instead it's got its foot in both places, punishing you for attempting to skip the tedium.

I found the lack of respect for my time frustrating, but it came to a head when I arrived in the mountains. You need frost resist here, and by the point we arrived the buff lasts 10 minutes. Then, you find yourself in snowstorms: these restrict your vision so much that, compounded with flying enemies, all you can do is take cover and wait it out. But these storms take at least 10 minutes to clear, meaning you simply sit around wasting time and precious resources twiddling your thumbs doing nothing. Reducing the time of these storms but incresing their ferocity, or allowing you to see better but at a cost, would cost the devs nothing and be far more fun. Instead, they remove your vision and you just have to wait.

I think there's a very specific group of people for whom Valheim is exactly their game. But right now, the grind and the frustrating design choices make it really hard to recommend to others.

On PC, you have a lot of battle royale games like Apex Legends, Call of Duty: Warzone, Fortnite, and many others. Some people may say they are the best in the business, and I’m not saying they’re wrong. But the thing about PUBG is that it feels genuinely different from most other battle royale games.

PUBG was one of the games that helped establish and popularize the modern battle royale trend, and even today, it stands out because of how grounded and realistic its gameplay feels. It’s probably one of the most realistic battle royale experiences you can play on PC.

If you’re used to fast paced battle royale games like Warzone, you might initially feel like PUBG is slow, clunky, or even a little rough around the edges. But honestly, that is also part of what makes PUBG special. The slower pace gives the game a more realistic and tactical feeling. You have to think about positioning, movement, weapon choice, recoil, timing, and when you should actually take a fight instead of constantly rushing from one gunfight to another.

Of course, a battle royale game doesn’t have to be realistic to be fun. Games like Fortnite, Apex, and Warzone have their own identities, and that’s completely fine. But PUBG has always tried to make its weapons and mechanics feel more familiar to how things work in the real world. For example, reloading a weapon can feel noticeably slower compared to some other battle royale games. You can’t just reload instantly and continue sprinting around like nothing happened. You have to actually think about when it’s safe to reload.

And if you don’t like that slower feeling, that’s completely understandable. Not every game has to be for everyone.

One thing I do think Krafton needs to improve though, is the number of bots. Depending on your matchmaking and region, you can sometimes encounter way more bots than you would expect in a match. I mean, getting a few easy kills as a free gift is always nice lol but when there are too many bots, it can take away from the feeling that you’re actually fighting for your survival against other players. I’d personally like to see fewer bots in matches, especially once the player has reached a point where there should be enough real players available.

That said, PUBG still has something that many other battle royale games don’t. The atmosphere, gunplay, sound design, vehicles, maps, recoil, movement, and overall pacing come together to create a completely different experience. A firefight in PUBG can feel much more intense because you know that making one bad decision can get you killed instantly.

And I also think PUBG deserves more recognition for what it achieved globally. It became one of the biggest battle royale games in the world and showed that a battle royale game developed outside the traditional American gaming industry could become a massive international success. That alone is pretty impressive.

PUBG isn’t perfect. It has its problems, and there are definitely areas where Krafton could improve the game. But after all these years, there’s still something special about dropping onto a map, finding a weapon, hearing footsteps nearby, and knowing that the next few seconds could completely change the match.

If you want a super fast, movement heavy battle royale, Warzone or Apex might be more your thing.

But if you want a slower, more tactical, grounded, and intense battle royale experience, PUBG is still one of the best choices you can make.

630 hours. Four different worlds. One actual completion.

I think that probably says more about Satisfactory than any normal review I could write.

This is one of those games where "finishing" it almost feels beside the point. I've restarted entire worlds because I looked at something I spent 40 hours building and decided I could do it better. I've torn down factories that technically worked because the belts annoyed me. I've spent hours solving a production problem that I created myself, only to realize the solution created three new problems somewhere else.

And somehow, that is fun.

Satisfactory gives you a ridiculous amount of freedom to decide how complicated you want to make your own life. You can throw together a horrible spaghetti factory where everything technically works, or you can spend an entire evening calculating exactly how many machines you need, balancing inputs, building infrastructure, making everything symmetrical, and then realizing you forgot to account for power.

There is always another project.

That is probably what has kept me playing for 630 hours. Every time I start a new world, I know more than I did the last time. The factory gets cleaner. The logistics get smarter. 🎧 Rust Review from a Music Producer's Perspective
For me, Rust isn't just a survival MMO. It's an underground recording session where heavy basslines vibrate from raid explosions, and every swing of a hatchet into a tree feels like capturing a raw, industrial sample.

As a music artist, I view this game as a brutal exercise in sound design and mastering under extreme conditions:

Structure & Composition (Base Building): Building a base is like sculpting an arrangement from scratch. You have to balance sub-frequencies (loot rooms tucked deep in the foundations) with a thick wall of sound (traps and armored walls). One wrong move in your structural mix, and the whole composition collapses after a single C4 raid.

Dynamics & Noise Floor (PVP & Steath): Audio in Rust is the absolute core of the mix. Footsteps on sand, grass, or metal have such precise selectivity that you can pinpoint an enemy with your eyes closed. Meanwhile, a bolt-action rifle shot echoes across the map like a massive kick drum dropping through club monitors.

Atmosphere (Lo-Fi & Survival): Desert winds, night ambiance, and the crackle of a campfire create a unique lo-fi texture that instantly shifts into a heavy, distorted drill beat the moment a copter rolls up on your base.

Verdict: Rust can wreck your mental health and waste hundreds of hours, but when you successfully pull off a raid after a week of sample-hunting (resource gathering) and secure the loot—it sounds sweeter than a platinum record.

Rust is genuinely one of the most shit games I’ve ever played, and somehow I still keep coming back to it. Ever since around 2020, the game has had a consistently bad updates, where every update somehow manages to make you wonder what the developers are on and yet despite all of that, Rust is like fucking cocaine—you start playing and there is  no stopping. You can tell yourself you’re only going to play for an hour, and suddenly it’s 5 in the morning, you’re starving, exhausted, your base has been raided, you’ve lost everything, and somehow your first thought is still, “Alright, one more wipe.” The game can be unbelievably repetitive, unfair, toxic, and infuriating, but that’s also what makes it so addictive. You can spend hours gathering resources, building a massive base, getting guns and gear, and feeling like you’re finally doing well, only for some random group to come out of nowhere and completely ruin everything you worked for. Then you get pissed off, swear you’re never playing Rust again, close the game, and somehow find yourself launching it again the next day. The updates may constantly leave me questioning the direction of the game, but Rust has this weird ability to keep you hooked no matter how much you hate it. It’s one of those games that you can genuinely have the worst experience imaginable and still somehow have a good time, which is probably the most annoying thing about it.  Despite all the problems, the questionable updates, and the amount of pain this game will put you through, I would still recommend Rust. If you have friends to play with, it becomes even better because half the fun comes from the chaos, arguments, stupid decisions, and completely unexpected moments that happen every wipe. Just be prepared to lose hours of your life because once you start playing Rust, there is genuinely no escaping it.

I purchased Valheim around its Early Access release in 2020 and did a full playthrough at the time. I thoroughly enjoyed it, but there were a lot of pain points around progression and QoL. I figured the game just needed time to be polished and have more content added.

Six years later, the game still lacks way too many basic QoL features, and progression feels like a drag. Valheim is already a very long grind, and seemingly every hiccup adds another 30–60 minutes to it. Stamina management is frustrating, the wind always seems to be against you while sailing, combat is simplistic—which is fine—but clunky, and inventory and weight restrictions are overly aggressive. On top of that, you still can't bring important items through portals without changing the game settings.

I also don't think fixing these issues should fall on the community. "Just play with mods" isn't a solution we should be letting developers get away with.

I gave the game the benefit of the doubt six years ago, but even after 1.0, a new playthrough doesn't feel meaningfully improved. The new zones are frustrating, progression somehow gets even slower, and so much of the game feels designed to waste your time rather than challenge you.

You're still spamming E to refill kilns, furnaces, blast furnaces, windmills, and other stations. The crafting menu doesn't even have a search function, items feel poorly organized, and when you unlock new recipes, you see them once and then have to hunt through menus to figure out what you actually unlocked. The building system is still clunky and feels almost exactly as I remember it from six years ago. There are plenty of other smaller complaints too, like having no innate eitr and food buffs immediately getting weaker after eating, but I won't list every minor annoyance.

A lot of Valheim's "difficulty" is really just a massive time sink. Farming trophies for important unlocks is a good example. Will there be a bear in the Black Forest, or a troll? Will I spend an hour looking for a single troll? Will it actually drop the trophy, or will I need to find another one? Combine that with the stamina system, sailing, inventory restrictions, and increasingly slow progression, and it becomes exhausting rather than enjoyable.

The amount of content added over six years is also severely disappointing. The 1.0 release focused on adding cinematics between boss kills when the game desperately needed more meaningful content, progression improvements, and polish. After six years, what was really added? Three new zones and a handful of smaller updates to the existing ones? It feels like updates get pushed out and then are barely revisited for QoL improvements or optimization. The Ashlands is still laggy in multiplayer two years after its release.

I played through the game with three friends, with 3x resources and unrestricted portal items. Even with those settings cutting down the grind considerably, and without getting into mods, it was still a pretty miserable experience overall.

There are some positives. I still really enjoy the music and art style, and I think the developers did a great job with that side of the game. Some of the armour sets and weapons look great, and there are some cool building options as well.

But ultimately, I don't recommend Valheim, and I'd actively steer friends away from it if they asked me about it. I loved the game enough

Terraria. What a game. Terraria is a 2d survival/creative game which is inspired by Minecraft, but way more complex. You spawn in with an NPC which tells you how to build him and other NPC's that decide to move in a house. You start with the basics and work your way up until you enter Hard Mode. There is two main sections of the game: Pre-Hard Mode and Hard Mode. Pre-Hard Mode has the basic enemy's that don't have too much damage and bosses of which shouldn't be too hard to beat. Hard Mode on the other hand, has much more stuff, but more difficult bosses and enemy's, and almost all the bosses you have to beat in order (Mechanicals, Plantera, etc.). 

       There is four different difficulty's that you can choose from, and I would encourage you to play on the more difficult ones (expert and master), as they offer more unique items, and a greater challenge. There is also a difficulty called "Journey" which you are essentially semi-god; you can control the weather, time, enemy spawn rate, and the unique feature, if you get enough of an item, you research it getting infinite of it. Your world that you spawn in always has unique features also, as you can choose if you world is corrupted by crimson or corruption. There is also special seeds where it does different things to your world like making you spawn in the underworld, making mobs do 4x damage, and having new vanity items.

         There are four main classes of which you can choose from, being melee, ranged, magic, and summoner. Melee is the best class by far, having multiple subclasses (Spears, True Melee) and dealing a lot more damage. Ranged is very useful for certain stages of the game, usually being Early Hard Mode, and having fun weapons like the megashark. Magic uses things like books to deal damage, and being usually the worst class to beat the game with, but it still has some fun mechanics, and some weapons in this class take moves from other enemy's. Lastly, the summoner class is usually the most fun, and not having to constantly attack while your summons do the work.  

        Learning the game is a very difficult task, as almost every person has to use the wiki to find out what to do next to advance to beat the final boss, the moon lord. Multi-Player in Terraria is pretty uncommon, as it doesn't add much to the game, but Terraria overperforms in single player, as it offers so much to do, there is no end to how much you can do. 

      As for the two main types of players: casual and competitive, Terraria offers endless things to do and think about. For casuals, you have main progression through moon lord, unique things to collect, and different classes you can try beating the game with only. For competitive, there is even more. Terraria holds about six thousand items as of writing this, and you can try to collect them all if you want! There is also a lot of achievements for the completists, like getting The Zenith (the omega post-game weapon), and finding/killing every critter or enemy in the game.

        For mods, there is a Terraria mod loader that you can install to have access to amazing mods. The most popular by far is calamity, which you can search up yourself. My favourite though is wrath of gods, because of the nameless deity.

       Overall, I think this game is worth the 10$ USD, and it's usually 50% off, so it's not too big of a deal. The soundtrack has absolute bangers, endless things to do, custom worlds, and different ways to play the game, makes it one of my all time favourites, and I strongly recommend it to anybody who likes Minecraft, or strong game design.

I am going to ground this review in my personal preferences and experiences because I thinka lot of my potential complaints are more likely a matter of taste.

Graphics - I love this game because it has the sandbox survival freedom feelings like that of Minecraft, but boosts immersion with decent graphics.

Multiplayer - Speaking of Minecraft, this game weirdly echoes anarchy Minecraft in the sense that the game is sort of a single-player with chat due to vast differences between real players, with the Anomaly acting like spawn to bring yourself around real people.

Quests - Transactionally, many quests are basically mini-tutorials for "doing a thing" for the first time like crafting an item or completing your first derelict freighter mission. This is what it is and fairly straightforward. Not good, not bad, serves its purpose.

Story - The main storyline is also a bunch of quests and quite frankly felt like a bunch of soulless World-of-Warcraft-style fetch 12 eggs because reasons, except instead of fetch 12 eggs, go to some planet to climb some tower that has ladders even though literally anyone playing it should just be jetpacking up. Dialogue-wise, it is riddled with "kzzt" to simulate comms interference, but until the game has actual voiced dialoge it just becomes tedious to read past. The dialogue itself tries to, I don't know, read like a space opera? But for me felt like said "space opera" was written by a 14-year-old trying the 'emo poet' schtick on for size using emotionally evocative techniques with the grace of an elephant in a window shop. It's cringe inducing and unfortunately major progression aspects are locked behind having to muscle yourself through it. To be fair, I haven't completely finished this storyline, specifically because of previously mentioned critiques.

Gameplay - It is easy to skip the story entirely because there is so much to do. I haven't even scratched the surface of the freighter, settlement, and space station parts as I've been keeping myself way too busy LARPing as a blood salts chain-snorting junker Gek loading salvage into his scrap-heap looking corvette while inbetween yelling anti-Vy'keen racial epithets as he raids their freighter convoys for easy loot. "Not so strong *now*, are ya, you flap-jawed pricks?" he would often say as he sadistically fires the last fatal rockets at an already crippled and stripped Vy'keen smuggling freighter.

Sruvival / Early-game - As someone who is experienced with survival games, I found everything easy. Which was nice at the beginning while learning. But, as I slowly evolved and learned, all of what I thought were "gentle reminders" that the world bites back turned out to be nerf-padded teeth that never actually get sharp. I decided to crank up the difficulty settings, but to not much avail. I particularly find a distaste in any modification to item stack sizes slapped on calling it "more survival." Interface-based friction without immersion isn't survival, it's just plain bad UX design masquerading as survival. I am perfectly okay with progression systems turning certain survival aspects into trivial matters, that's great. But. when I can raid cargo fleets with near certain impunity anytime I see one, without a second thought about the negative consequences of my actions, it makes certain actions feel like cheating without participating in a single gameplay exploit.

All that said, anything negative I have to say is because of how invested I've become in this game and disappointment about those parts. I don't know if it's a lacking on their part or preferences on mine. Either way, I see myself spending at least another 200 hours on this game, if not 1000+

People have said all the good things about this game, so I will just list out the things I didn't like about Valheim as it's a much shorter list.

1 Bow gameplay has no variety, especially when compared to Melee & Magic.
 Your first bow of the game will work exactly the same as the last bow you get in the game, one just has more damage over the other.

2 Certain skills level up abysmally slow, (cooking, crafting, dodging to name few) and if you want to level these skills you would completely stop what you are doing and active focus on leveling them for hours on end, and stop playing the game normally.

3 Stagger, the stagger system is in place to prevent you from just blocking everything and parrying everything, which is fine, but when you get staggered on any damage if you are blocking or not that is just bad game design, you already lose 50%+ HP from a big hit, and getting staggered on top so enemy can do a cheap followup felt bad the first time, and the last time before completing the game, garbage system.

4 Trophies being used in making weapons and gear sucks, random RNG preventing you from crafting items you want shoulnd't be in a survival game when everything else can be reliably obtained but 1 armor piece for a set bonus needs a RNG roll trophy, horrible game design.

5 Nearly everything gameplay wise in Deep North region is horrible, Boss, Gear, and Food progression are all random RNG, and me and my friends didn't even get the gear we wanted despite spending hours farming, horrible gameplay all around, the zone feels like the devs ran out of ideas, and had to artificially extend the last region in the game, the zone is pretty but that is the only good thing I can say about it.

6 Forge Of Potential Gacha Machine should be removed from the game, especially when trying to use it on gear needing RNG trophies, no reason to have a Chinese Mobile game mechanic in here.

(The forge is an altar that can upgrade your gear with 66% success chance, but if you roll the 33% failure it breaks your item and only refunds half the materials rounding down)

7 Merchant spawn logic, some peoples worlds get merchants very close, others at the end of the world east/west, and merchants sell important items and upgrades, so having their location be different so that other players get it 10 hours into a playtrough while others get to a merchant after 100 is not fun whatsoever.

8 Sea Serpents loot sinking, spawning a Water based enemy and making its loot sink into the bottom of the ocean was ass, 5 years ago, and its still not fixed.

---------
While these 8 things were annoying, and most of them should be removed from the game or changed during the past 5 years, Valheim is an excellent survival game, the Viking aesthetics are nice, the game runs fairly well 
(with SOME exceptions in last 3 biome types)
The pricepoint is more than fair.
And it has a very unique artstyle that makes it stand out from games like Dragonwils or Enshrouded.

Though I thorougly recommend playing with friends and preparing to spend 100-300 hours on a run depending how much want to invest in things like leveling skills, getting achievements, or if if you want to build a massive castle.

I do recommend turning the death penalty either off or to minimal, as the game hands out BS deaths more than once, and some of the skills level so slowly that even losing a single level can set you back hours, and the death penalty does not enhance the gameplay much to begin with.

But should you go the other way, you can absolutely crank all the difficulties up and have absolute sadist fest of a game if you REALLY want to put the word Survival in a survival game.

[h1] Simulador de costura medieval e desemprego profissional [/h1]

Entrei neste jogo a pensar que ia ser o herói de Tamriel, salvar o mundo de dragões, deuses malévolos e profecias antigas. Centenas de horas depois, dou por mim a passar 4 horas seguidas sentado numa cadeira numa taberna em Daggerfall a tentar decidir se o meu capuz combina com as minhas calças de couro de cabra.

[h2] O meu percurso até agora: [/h2]
[b]• Horas de jogo:[/b] 800 horas.
[b]• Tempo a salvar o mundo:[/b] 15 minutos.
[b]• Tempo a colecionar mobília, pescar peixes inúteis e farmar tecidos:[/b] 799 horas e 45 minutos.
[b]• Estado da minha conta bancária no jogo:[/b] Mais falida que a economia de Elsweyr após uma invasão de Skooma.

[h2] Pontos Positivos: [/h2]
[b]•[/b] Podes criar um personagem com proporções corporais tão ridículas que até os monstros sentem vergonha alheia antes de te atacarem.
[b]•[/b] O sistema de habitação ([i]housing[/i]) é tão viciante que vais gastar todo o teu dinheiro real em camas virtuais em vez de pagares as contas da luz.
[b]•[/b] A comunidade é tão simpática e prestativa que até mete nojo — se entrares numa zona de iniciantes, és capaz de levar com presentes de jogadores veteranos só porque sim.

[h2] Pontos Negativos: [/h2]
[b]•[/b] O inventário base é um teste psicológico à tua paciência; gerir o espaço de armazenamento dá mais trabalho do que um mestrado.
[b]•[/b] De vez em quando tens de parar a tua sessão de decoração de interiores para ir fazer uma masmorra e matar monstros chatos que insistem em interromper a tua paz.
[b]•[/b] As montarias começam a correr com a velocidade de um cágado com reumatismo até gastares meses a treiná-las todos os dias.

[h1] Conclusão: [/h1]
Se queres um MMORPG onde podes ignorar completamente a salvação do universo para te tornares o maior estilista e decorador de Tamriel, este jogo é para ti. 10/10, vou ali colher umas flores para fazer um chá.

Factorio is one of the greatest video games ever crafted by mankind. So much so that the game terrifies me a little bit. 

You can run this game on a potato, and it runs perfectly. The size is roughly 5GB. Every single building, every machine, every sprite looks extremely detailed and neat. The game is extremely moddable. There's options for world generation, so you can fine-tune your experience exactly how you want it. The music fits perfectly, especially for Space Age, which also roughly triples the amount of content Factorio has to offer. God help us all.

There's a reason people call it Cracktorio. Your intention will be to play for maybe an hour or two, only to realize you've spent the last 10 hours coming up with new layouts, optimizing your output ratios, analyzing your logistics, defending against the wildlife, optimizing your output ratios again, setting up a train network, creating yet another new layout that uses the previous layout as a mere input, realizing you're running out of resources so you're now looking for more. It's now been 12 hours. 

Factorio has had you within it's grasp that entire time, refusing to let you go. You can only leave when your body can't take any more, or when Factorio decides you deserve a break. Factorio is an endless loop that feeds back into itself, like a conveyor belt that never ends. Even after you've beaten the game, the factory yearns for more, siren-calling you back to the cycle of ever increasing expansion once again. You are becoming one with the machine. The factory is becoming, and you are. You are becoming together. Putrid black smoke rises from every kind of uncountable machine constructed from the flesh of the earth, it's blood, the very essence that gives life, now gives life to your factory, transformed. Mechanical whirrs in every direction, the crackling and sizzling of electricity, an inferno of sounds and objects and movements and object and sounds. You see nothing but input and output. You see nothing but production.

You temporarily break out of the trance, and lay eyes upon what you have created with newfound clarity, before you're dragged back to the industrial hellscape that you have created. This is your prison. A prison you can leave at any time. But you cannot.

The factory must grow.

Where the 1.0 Release Somehow Feels Like a Downgrade from Early Access

Valheim’s full 1.0 launch somehow manages to feel like a step backward from its early access days. Not only did the developers crank up the spawn rates of Greydwarfs and various other pests, they also dialed the aggression to eleven. Think you can just peacefully gather a handful of resources and call it a day? The game has other plans. Greydwarfs will descend on you with the same single-minded hunger Americans display at the grand opening of a new all-you-can-eat buffet—relentless, numerous, and deeply inconvenient.
I ran it with two friends, and every single one of us independently concluded the game is borderline unplayable on standard settings. The constant pressure turns simple resource runs into exhausting attrition battles.
On top of that, basic quality-of-life features are still nowhere to be found. Crafting directly from chests—my beloved, the one change the game has needed for years—remains absent. How do you ship a 1.0 without that? It starts to feel less like an oversight and more like a design philosophy: maximize friction, not player satisfaction.
Progression pacing took a hit too. What was already deliberate now borders on punitive.
A game this atmospheric and ambitious deserved a cleaner, more respectful launch. Instead, we got higher enemy density, the same missing conveniences, and a sense that the studio prioritized the finish line over the people who actually play it.

Across PS4, Xbox Series X, and PC, I’ve logged roughly 600 hours into Destiny 2. I haven’t played every season or expansion; like many adult gamers with real-world responsibilities, my playtime dropped off whenever the checklist grind started demanding life-consuming commitment.

But when Destiny 2 hits its stride, practically nothing else in gaming can match it.

Running the Leviathan Raid for the first time remains one of my all-time favorite gaming memories:

- S-tier gunplay and movement

- Clever raid puzzles and tight encounters

- Genuinely meaningful co-op communication

- Rewarding buildcrafting, lore, and secrets tucked into every corner

- Challenging but fair mechanics that respect player coordination

(And on a co-op wishlist note: while I know the entire universe is tuned around the sacred 3-player fireteam, expending it to 4-players would be incredible for balancing friend groups without forcing someone to sit out.)

Ultimately, it’s the treadmill grind that made me walk away, and it’s the exact same wall keeping me away. When the pinnacle of Destiny 2—optimizing stat distributions and hunting down essential build-defining Exotics—requires a massive, multi-week ramp-up just to catch up, the barrier to entry feels insurmountable.

Whether Bungie can rekindle that design philosophy in D2 with un-vaulted content or channel it into an eventual Destiny 3, my biggest plea is simple: stop designing the game exclusively for players with 200 hours of free time every month.

Design for the player who has 30 to 50 hours a month to give. It is completely fine if players reach a natural stopping point between content drops. It's OK for people to replay content simply because they love playing it—not because they're forced into an optimal chore loop just to hit the power cap and access end-game activities. Quality beats artificial engagement metrics every time—a game shouldn't have to feel like a full-time job just to be fun.

Project Zomboid is a zombie survival game where the real threat is time. You loot, fight, and build a base, but hunger, thirst, injury, and bad decisions kill you just as often as the dead. Combat is clumsy on purpose, noise matters, and one bite is usually the end of that character.

The isometric view and deep skills make it more of a slow sim than an action game. Power and water shut off, winter hits, and the longer you last the more the world falls apart. Multiplayer works if your group is patient. Mods fill in almost anything the base game does not.

It is bleak, janky in places, and the learning curve is steep. If you want a zombie game you can actually live in for dozens of hours, this is still the one. I have lost more characters to my own mistakes than to hordes, and I keep starting over anyway.

Rust is one of those games that can give you some of the most unforgettable gaming moments, but also test your patience like nothing else.

The survival mechanics, base building, PvP, raiding, and the constant feeling that anything can happen make Rust incredibly addictive. Every wipe feels like a completely new story, and the player interactions are honestly one of the best parts of the game.

That said, the game still has some frustrating issues. The learning curve can be brutal for new players, progression can sometimes feel repetitive, and performance/optimization could definitely be better. Some systems also feel like they need more polish rather than simply adding more content.

Overall, Rust is far from perfect, but that's exactly why I keep coming back. It has a unique atmosphere and gameplay loop that very few survival games can replicate. If you're willing to suffer a little, lose everything, and start over again… Rust is absolutely worth experiencing.

If you haven't played No Man’s Sky, YOU NEED TO!

This game has absolutely blown me away. And before anyone looks at my playtime and thinks, “Only 50 hours?” I know! I’m still relatively new to the game, but honestly, that’s part of what makes it so impressive to me. I’ve put around 50 hours into it so far, and I feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface.

I’ll be honest, I remember hearing about the rocky launch and all the criticism surrounding it back in the day. But seeing where this game is now compared to where it started is honestly incredible.

The developers didn’t just fix the game and call it a day — they kept building on it. Year after year, they’ve continued adding massive amounts of content, new features, improvements, planets, ships, bases, missions, multiplayer features, and so much more. The game has genuinely evolved into something that feels almost completely different from its original release.

There is just SO much to do. You can explore an essentially endless universe, discover strange planets and creatures, build massive bases, customize your ships, trade, mine, craft, fight pirates, explore derelict freighters, play with friends, and just get completely lost in the universe.

And that’s probably my favorite thing about No Man’s Sky — there’s no single way you’re supposed to play it. You can spend hours chasing a specific goal, or you can land on a random planet, start exploring, and somehow lose an entire evening without even realizing it.

The sheer scale of this game is ridiculous. Every time I think I’ve seen most of what it has to offer, I discover something new.

Huge respect to Hello Games for sticking with this game and continuing to improve it all these years later. Whatever your opinion of the launch was, I think it’s worth putting that aside and looking at what No Man’s Sky has become.

This isn’t just a game that recovered from a bad launch. It’s a game that kept growing. If you’ve never played No Man’s Sky, give it a shot. Seriously.

[b]tl;dr[/b] - Many times I've regretted giving Baldur's Gate 3 chances. Turn back... unless you're a masochist.

Buy only at deep discount if you're a CRPG fan. Accolades and the community's abusive attachment disorder aside, this is a still painfully janky game three years after release. It's not terrible, but... if you're bothered by poor UX or bugs, prepare to suffer death by a thousand little cuts.

[h2][b]The UI - frenemy at best:[/b][/h2]

*  The default camera constantly gets in the way. At times it's so disorienting you'll struggle to tell what's going on. Just to attack somebody the game keeps obscuring, you'll have to click this over here... then that over there... then that up there...(By Act 2 I had to install a mod just to make it playable).

* In a game where every other threat triggers turn based mode, do traps? Nope. Command low level parties perishing on the clock as you frantically try to button-press your way out of it. Worse - press wrong, and it's possible to start dialogue between characters _while they burn in real time_. Like some dark comedy, party locked behind a text based UI, you discuss whatever plot point Larian felt more important than characters gradually cooking into charcoal briquettes, their screams punctuating your mouse clicks.

*  Try to shoot a pesky goblin who hit you just a moment before and you begin a new mini-game: line-of-sight-wackamole. Spend many mouse clicks sleuthing exactly which spot will allow you to satisfy vague yet simultaneously strict conditions without yourself stumbling through acid, poison, or fire. Don't worry, when you give up, the auto-aim is still there to push you through things that hurt.

[h2][b]Bugs - so many still awkward or outright broken features:[/b][/h2]

*  Group pathing is excellent... at doing exactly the wrong thing. Click to go around or even jump over that obviously dangerous acid pool, and your party members follow you... stumbling through it like idiots anyway. Break group to avoid this? Enjoy 4x the number of keystrokes and mouse clicks.

*  Quests glitch, incompletable due to some decision you made hours ago, or not starting at all. You can try to hide finished items in your bloated quest log but that feature will turn itself off every new session.

*  Items for summoning assistance in tough battles... activate in the wrong place and your mercenary ogres just stand there, their AI pathing unable to navigate a giant room (looking at you, Goblin Boss fight). Then afterwards, they'll demand 500 gold for literally doing nothing.

[h2][b]Annoyances - plenty...[/b][/h2]

*  Encounters begin inconsistently, mobs seemingly ignoring combat right in front of them. Today a battle 'ended' within obvious view of an idle enemy. Then, instead of giving back control, said enemy just 'wakes up,' beginning a brand new fight ...cancelling all  prior-battle consumables and yanking me back to turn-based mode... despite neither pressing a button nor anybody moving. Oh goodie... guess I'll have to re-bless... and spend another charge of barbarian rage... and...

*  Enemies in the Baldur's Gate universe carry enough molotovs or acid bottles to make rioters jealous - AoE so rampant you don't dare position characters close for mutual support. D:OS2 explodium barrels(tm) return for several guest appearances too. Stand in the wrong place and... boom, sweep up your character's residue~

*  Action bars change without your consent, the logic dumping icons haphazardly. No action bar presets or import functionality - enjoy futzing with everything every new weapon type... every level...

[h2][b]And the rest...[/b][/h2]

How does Larian compensate for some of these issues? By shoving at you small mountains of consumables and vendor trash items until your bags nearly burst, becoming a tedious inventory. Rewards are... oddly paced, sometimes underwhelming, sometimes endgame gear in the first act. Resources go out of wack once you recognize camp supplies are basically limitless, allowing you to long rest after every battle, far more than any D&D campaign would allow.

Too easy? Turn up the difficulty so UI flaws become downright hostile. You'll struggle to consistently get characters to do what you want, gradually adopting all kinds of maladjusted coping mechanisms BG3 fans have Stockholmed as acceptable. Single mis-clicks frequently end battles in catastrophe. Eventually saving before every battle round isn't cheesing - it becomes... necessary.

Sigh.

In the game's defense, the story is remarkable for its many choices - no other title I've tried goes to these lengths (though expect cliche and forced moments - Shadowheart... I just met you and you're trying to jump my bones). And the piles of dialogue, well acted, making you feel like you're part of an actual world? Solid.

But even when the best parts rise to the surface, the jank buzzes back into your face like an aggravating fly, reminding you're just playing a messy CRPG that will never get the polish it desperately needs. There might be a good game... buried... under all this... somewhere... but it's frustrating to look (twice as hard if you're not familiar with D&D 5e).

Not sure I'll ever reach Act 3. Quit more than once, then blown the dust off months later while bored and had no other games to play. Why do I keep giving this game chances? Perhaps sharing the CRPG community's self-loathing, I've now modded the game so much it's... passable. Do I still believe in this negative review? With all my heart.

Thank you for reading. /rant

Valheim is an absolute blast whether you prefer spending hours building or heading out on adventures. You can easily sink hundreds of hours into this game and still find things to do.

That said, it still definitely lacks a few Quality of Life features that make certain mechanics feel more like a chore than they need to be. The developers could take a page out of older survival games (cough, Terraria) or look at existing community mods to fix some obvious friction points:

- Inventory & Equipment: Equippable gear desperately needs its own dedicated slots separate from the main inventory. 

- Menu & UI: The crafting and stats panels feel clunky. It would make much more sense if the full crafting window took over the middle of the screen, while stats replaced the smaller side panel.

Crop Planting: Farming is painful. There are no snapping zones, and every single crop has to be planted individually. If you plant carrots a millimeter too close together, half of them won't grow. Feeding a full group means sitting there clicking hundreds of individual seeds before you can actually go adventure.

Item Placement Smoke/Fog Effect: Placing items causes a cloud of smoke that partially hides the cursor. If you're trying to do intricate building work, you constantly have to pause and wait for the fog to clear.

As I said earlier, I know mods exist for all of these issues, but using them disables achievements. That might not matter once you’ve already hit 100% completion, but for a first playthrough, using mods just doesn't make sense.

Despite all of these flaws, I still love this game. I’ve logged over 300 hours and haven’t even finished it yet.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a story rich RPG featuring a beautiful open world, with the best character writing I've seen. The game covers themes such as freedom, identity, greed, and social inequality. It's an unforgettable experience worth playing. Jackie Welles & Johnny Silverhand are [b] GOATED [/b] support characters!

Story: You play as V, a lone merc in Night City, a futuristic violent dystopia dictated by greedy capitalist mega-corporations. You take on the most dangerous jobs trying to stay alive and make a name for yourself. There are 3 life paths to choose from: Nomad, Streetkid, and Corpo. They don't make much of a difference gameplay-wise, aside from unique dialogue options and shaping V's perspective on the world. After your biggest high stakes job goes FUBAR, the story truly begins as you race against time for your life! 

Gameplay: This game feels like a mixture of GTA and Borderlands because of the interactivity, stores, looting, class building, and the leeway to play however you like. Unfortunately, some elements are not well polished, but its not that bad because they can be fixed with mods. Majority of the cars handle terribly! I got around the map 90% of the time using motorcycles because they're really fast and consistently handle well. Another thing I did not enjoy too much was the early game. Enemies scale heavily to your level at all times, so the beginning is kind of rough because your guns aren't strong and targets feel tanky. Shotguns, revolvers, and snipers became my go to weapons. You'll be fine if your aim and positioning is really good. Mid to late game is when you can really start going crazy. 

Environment: Along with the story, this is another great aspect because of its visual storytelling. It shows you how bad things are, instead of telling you. The city is plagued with advertisements, some even reaching the sky! Gangs rule certain city districts, crime thrives more often in some places, and you can really see the poverty and flourishment of areas. What I truly did love were the small mentions of the 2076 Edgerunners crew. You can find iconic items left behind by a few members which is very cool, it makes the city's history feel more connected on a deeper level.

Side Quests: There are many to do and they give you really good rewards, but they aren't special because they follow a repetitive format. The only good quests are the character story missions, these deepen your bond with key characters, allowing you to learn their history and help them out with personal troubles. 

TL;DR Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best story rich RPG games you can ever play. It has some issues gameplay wise, but they're relatively minor and won't hurt your overall experience. Never stop fighting, my chooms!

Man, not sure where to start. This is probably one of the best games I've ever played. Story, Gameplay, Progression, Logevity, Depth and Breadth, Space-Magic, its all here. It has everything an MMO needs, social functions like clans, trading, squads, sharing xp and some loot, replayability, diversity of activities, customisation of literally everything on your warframe, weapons, ship, clan housing (dojo), pets, and even the UI. Great and vast story telling, from interpersonal stories, environmental stories to stories spanning millenia and dimensions of space and time. All of that on top of the satisfying gameplay and progression.

This game can be pretty grindy feeling at times, but i think thats also because of the depth of every single element in this game. Everything it does, it does it all in spades and that means learning and understanding over a decades worth of story, systems, game modes etc. It can be overwhelming for new or returning players because so much gets added each year and theres a lot of everything to do ahead of you. This isnt a 20hr one and done game. Its like 20x20hr games and the goal is to get as close to 100% completing each one as you can.
In saying that though, for the most part, no time ever seems wasted no matter what youre doing. If youre farming for materials for a new Warframe, other materials you find for a Warframe you already own have a secondary or tertiary function. You always have a different thing you could spend those currencies or materials on. It makes the grind less painful when you dont get what you want, something else is progressing regardless. So the word grind feels too punishing here, because the gameplay is so fun and rewarding in and of itself. I'd hardly use the word in a way that means its a 'slog', and more in a way where youre not on a single track but instead many tracks and youre constantly arriving at different stations and goals consistently. The momentum always has you ticking something off even when your main goal is still unfinished. And when I said for the most part, I mean in certain contexts, things could be scaled down in terms of progressing certain goals, especially after the main release of that Warframe. After a year or so of that unlock being available, scale back the requirements to obtain it once the hype has died down. No one wants to play countless runs of an activity to accumulate currency for a powercrept Warframe that released years ago. Especially having to run activities to acquire said Warframe solo because no ones grinding for it anymore. Thats the only issue I have regarding the game.

Its monetisation structure is very fair. You get everything for free, albeit for a longer grind. Its an easy sell for me to spend money on the game considering we get so much quality and fun out the gate with this game. No shady content vaulting or changing pay models every few eyars. Just play free, pay what you want and you get some QOL goodies for supporting the game. 

Theres years worth of well written and voice acted stories that can go from being silly and whimsical to heartbreaking and very dark to touching and sweet. The game isnt afraid to go deep and layered with the characters and the world actually feels alive and occupied by civilians. Makes you feel like youre fighting for something. The amount of freedom in buildcrafting is overwhelming, the damage system alone is incredibly complex but not in a confusing way, moreso in a "oh wow, i can modify that?" kinda of way. Projectile speed, audibility, fire rate, puncture depth, crit chance, status chance, elemental power can all be modified to suit your playstyle. Theres even the ability to combine elements to make new ones: e.g Fire + Toxin creates Gas. A cloud of lingering DOT damage. Theres a lot to master but that doesnt take away the enjoyment of just grabbing a kit and playing. Its all there for when you want to tinker with it and eventually when youll actually need it to progress in the game. Theres even weapons you can build from mixing and matching parts and creating unique combos and stats. The same can be done for pets/companions. You can even incubate specific breeds of pets based on what you want, to a degree you have to hunt down certain species and scan their DNA to cross-breed them. Not just a menu where you select your breed, but an actual game system based around it. Thats the essence of Warframe: A tonne of systems to interact with to progress you forward and keeping things feeling fresh.

And in that regard, It has parkour, hoverboards, space jetpack/exosuits for flying in the open world and for space battles, deployable mech-suits and even a space battleship thats customisable down to shields, engine type, armaments etc that you can pilot yourself with an active and hirable crew or board other ships to steal or loot and destroy. Theres even a darksouls like openworld game meshed with a roguelike mode, a street fighter arcade game based on Warframe, and even a bloody dating sim/ relationship builder for building rapport with characters in the game. And none of it cheapens the game or dilutes it, it all adds to the depth and breadth of the experience. No other game does what Warframe does, and not many do what it does on any front as good as Warframe does it. Its not a perfect game but man does it have heart and a killer team behind what theyre doing here. The community is also fantastic.

All in all, this game has made me laugh, cry, gasp, groan and all manner of wierd human sounds. I've been endlessly surprised at the variation and creativity over the last 1000 hours and despite taking breaks, I always come back to an experience that doesnt punish players for stepping away for a few months. And when I do, I'm also very quickly reminded of just how good this game is and thankful it exists.

Valheim is a brutal and cold survival game that feels as if it is designed for teams of 4+ players to suffer in the trenches together, between the amount tasks you must do and the friction making each task difficult. Once you settle in, it can be very cozy, but there are many game mechanics that are not explained very well and if you are even accidentally used to other games holding your hand you may think that this game is badly designed in some areas.

For instance, in my first few times playing, I got real fed up at hauling iron through the swamp to my boat to ship it back to my home. It just seemed like bad gameplay. But there are problems designed into this game and the solutions are there for you to find. Build infrastructure in the swamp. Build pathways, build a cart to haul the iron instead of walking through the mud back and forth 5 times. Or find a place to build a satellite base nearby the swamp and smelt it there, turn it into items, and you won't have to bring it all back to your main base. This idea rings true for many aspects of the game. Preparation, while not immediately rewarding, pays off ten fold, but it can require you to fumble and suffer for a bit until you realize the problems that have to be fixed.

Aside from that, I have to mention that Valheim has the single best building game mechanics of any game I've ever played. It is both simple yet complex, in that, the pieces you have to work with are pretty straight forward but each one has depth to it. A wood house is flimsy but cheap and easy to build. A stone house is heavy, expensive and difficult to build (literally it's heavy so you have to think about supports). You need fire, which also means you need to ventilate the smoke. Decorations actually have mechanical gameplay because they increase comfort. Valheim was the first game I found to introduce a lot of these mechanics that made building a base a game in itself.

The only bad part is that you don't really know what you're getting into at first. This game is very difficult to play solo and there is a lot of downtime designed into the game that is better filled with the company of friends. It really feels as if you are meant to run a small village with at least 4 players to split up all the work. But it's totally doable single player if you have a lot of time and enjoy the peace of lonliness.

Overall though, I find this game extremely unique, and while it is based on the open world survival craft genre of games, it is an absolute trend setter of a game and you can't find anything quite like it.

10 years later — and this game still manages to amaze me.

No Man’s Sky was an incredible game for me from the very beginning. I had been following it since its very first announcement, and back then I genuinely believed it was going to be a revolutionary game for its time.

The irony is that it actually became revolutionary… just not right away.

As we all know, the launch was far from what many players expected. People were understandably angry about promises that had not been fulfilled at the time, and the game simply could not live up to the enormous expectations surrounding it.

Back then, it seemed like the story of No Man’s Sky might end very quickly.

But Hello Games did something I honestly didn’t expect.

They didn’t just save the game.

They turned it into something far greater than it ever could have been at launch.

No Man’s Sky is like a good wine — it only gets better, richer and more enjoyable with age.

With every major update, the game gained something new. And most importantly, the developers kept doing this for years without turning the game into an endless stream of paid DLC, battle passes or constant demands for more money.

And now, this isn’t simply a game about space anymore.

There is an endless universe to explore, planets to discover, enormous oceans and depths that can feel genuinely terrifying.

And yes, I still sometimes hesitate to dive too deep because there is always that little thought in the back of my mind:

“What if something enormous swims out of there and eats me?” 😄

There is base building, exploration, trading, fleets, settlements, different kinds of ships and vehicles, resources, technologies, expeditions and countless other things to do.

And somehow, the game still manages to make you feel like there is something else out there that you haven’t discovered yet.

That is what I love most about No Man’s Sky.

You launch the game thinking, “I’ll play for an hour.”

Then you find an interesting planet.

Then you decide to explore the system a little more.

Then you realize you need to upgrade your ship.

Then you go looking for resources.

And suddenly you look at the clock and realize that four hours have disappeared.

No Man’s Sky constantly makes you want to stay just a little longer.

And then a little longer again.

And again.

I especially want to thank Hello Games for simply refusing to give up.

After a launch like that, they could have released a few updates, declared the game “fixed,” and moved on.

Instead, they kept working.

Year after year.

Update after update.

They kept adding new content, new mechanics, new possibilities and entire new layers to the game.

And they did it for years after release.

Ten years have passed.

TEN.

And the game is still receiving new content.

So today I simply want to say:

Thank you, Hello Games.

Thank you for not only eventually delivering on your promises, but for going far beyond what anyone could reasonably have expected.

Thank you for all these years of updates.

Thank you for not turning the game into an endless DLC store.

Thank you for continuing to make, make and make new content even ten years after release.

No Man’s Sky is a rare example where the story of the game itself has become almost as fascinating as the stories it tells its players.

I remember what this game was supposed to be.

I remember what it actually was.

And I can see what it has become.

And honestly, that might be one of the greatest redemption stories in the history of video games.

There is only one thing I genuinely wish the game had after all these years:

a Ukrainian text localization.

It doesn’t even have to be full voice acting — just a proper Ukrainian text translation would already mean a lot to Ukrainian players. After ten years of updates and an incredible amount of content, it feels like one of the few things still missing.

But even without it, No Man’s Sky remains an incredible experience.

Now excuse me, I’m off to explore another planet.

TLDR; Slow burn game to take your time with, relaxing environments to build in, minus one, and satisfying progression. 

This game evokes a great deal of emotion from me. I used to play with a friend, and honestly had such a good time before we decided to wait for the full release. I came back solo, and despite being alone, I still feel attached to this game. Every inch of progress is one I fought for, especially in the Ashlands, since I finally got to experience it during 1.0. It's slow and steady, and when I tried to rush, it tested me a bit. I'm not much of a base builder type, usually only having it be a drop-off for my loot and crafting, but not much else. Yet, somehow, I grew attached to this small, walled off settlement I built in the Meadows. It was after beating the fourth biome that I thought I would move, but when I sailed home and saw the smoke billowing out of my chimney and felt calm, the thought of leaving this house empty and abandoned made me feel genuine sadness. So I stayed, built a kitchen, built a second floor, dug out a basement, experienced peak fantasy: making a comfortable home to come back to after fighting for footholds in dangerous lands. 
The bosses aren't super difficult if you know what you're doing and are taking it slow. It's usually the hostile environments and other inhabitants that will get you. Dying is frustrating if you're running base settings. Take your time, if you get overwhelmed, back off and try to recuperate, assess what is stopping you from thinning the herd, and adapt. Good food is necessary if you want an easier time of it, use that cauldron, bake that pie, ferment your meads while you're out and about or doing work on the farm, feed the livestock, name some of them, have one of the ones you named accidentally run into the hearth you're in the middle of building and die, build a small grave, and store your ingredients. A lot of it may seem like chores to do before you continue exploring because that's what they are. However, to some, that is relaxing and what they play the game for. Relax a bit, progression will continue when you feel like it.
I rambled about how I've had it, but experiences may differ. If you want a slow burn game to take your time with for a long while, then I can recommend this. There are settings to lessen the friction if you want a more relaxing time, but also some to increase if you want more challenge. As always, a survival game is more fun with friends, but even solo, you can find the environments relaxing, except for the Ashlands, that place is oppressive and shouldn't be what you call home. If you don't like building or want something quick and to the point, I wouldn't say this game is necessarily for you. The game runs fine for me, but as always, mileage will vary. 

In my opinion, since it can make me frustrated, relaxed, and even spark a bit of sadness from me in specific circumstances, this is a good game.

[h1]An Absurdly Deep 2D Sandbox With Endless Exploration, Building, Boss Fights and Great Multiplayer[/h1]

Terraria starts off fairly simple. Chop down some trees, build a shelter, dig underground and try to figure out what you're supposed to be doing. Before long, though, the game opens up considerably.

There are countless weapons, accessories, enemies, biomes, bosses and things to discover, with progression constantly giving you a reason to explore a little further. Digging underground can turn into finding rare materials, which leads to better equipment, which opens up new areas and eventually leads to another boss. There's always something else to work towards.

The building system is just as flexible, whether you're putting together a basic house for your NPCs or spending hours making elaborate structures. And with multiplayer, the whole thing becomes even more entertaining, especially when everyone is exploring different parts of the world and bringing back whatever they've found.

What makes Terraria stand out is simply how much has been packed into it. It looks like a relatively straightforward 2D sandbox, but there's a huge amount of content underneath that surface. Even after all these years, there's still plenty to explore, build and fight.

This is yet another survival game that pads out playtime by making everything as tedious as possible. 

Your health and stamina are based around foods that you need to cook, but more than half of the ingredients aren't farmable, so you need to waste time wandering around looking for them, with nothing else in the area providing any real benefit. 

The boss of each area will drop something that will allow you to progress in the subsequent zones, but ores and some other materials can't be brought back with teleporters, so you'll have to either travel on foot or sail back for hours until you have enough materials to craft the upgrades and equipment needed to fight the zone boss, repeat.

If you die? Lose progress in all your skills, drop all of your equipment, lose food buffs, respawn at your base. Rebuff and hope you made a backup set of equipment to recover your first set of equipment with. 

The tedium can be cut down by sharing the load with other players, but it's still 95% farming for food, or drops from mobs, or chopping down trees, or mining, or traveling to bring materials back to base because they can't be teleported until the next to last zone in the game. 

The building mechanics are nice at least. 

The game has good bones, but the devs seem to have a certain gameplay length in mind, and they've not done much to make that time interesting, instead opting to prolong engagement by making almost everything inconvenient.

I'm not a player too concerned with graphics, extensive story, or multiplayer for my games in general. I quite enjoyed base building, dungeon delving, and early game exploring for Valheim. Prior to the Deep North release update I played through Valheim to Ashlands on three separate solo playthroughs so was fairly experienced and practiced at getting through the game. My issues with Valheim stem from lacking QoL features, slow mid/late-game exploration, and later zones frustrated me into writing this review.

This game by design is meant to waste your time with a lack of QoL features all over the place. Here's a list of features you either have to mod, change from default settings, or know going in to deal with:
- Default restrictive portal settings i.e. mandatory 30 min - 1 hr boat rides to shuttle metals and other resources back to your base for any reasonable progression.
- Default resource rate makes Valheim very grindy especially for necessary resources in each biome
- Wind direction mechanics that make sailing annoying and feel present to prevent afk sailing to destinations
- Boat speed limited so any main base to new biome trips take at least 30 min - 1 hr to do
- Mid/Late game exploration is painful requiring shore following and no possible way to expand the map radius for easier biome spotting
- Manual map pinning of interesting finds which gets tedious past the first two biomes
- Merchant and boss locations can be difficult to find from afar making use of the online map site very tempting
  -> Note: dungeon delving in Deep North update seemed to have many more boss runestones to highlight them on the map compared to previous updates
- No inventory sorting or storage management system, be prepared for at least 30 - 70 hrs of manual loot organizing
- None of the cooking stations, furnaces, charcoal furnaces, mead barrels, blast furnaces, spinning wheels, windmills, ovens, ice furnaces, or frost forges have automatic resource inputs and outputs
- No recycling mechanic so any items made are forever sinks for valuable metals and grinded materials you can't get back
- Several gear sets and very helpful items are trapped behind farming rare trophies and drops from mobs
- Several very good food items are trapped behind making worse food items to unlock which is means you have to waste time consuming resources checking if you missed anything
- Swimming is a nightmare to get back on boats and escaping out of water near shore, this is especially bad for the obvious first choice of ice mining in Deep North of the ice floats on the shore which has killed me through drowning during my last playthrough

Now with the QoL issues mentioned I will go into several frustration factors that add to my negative recommendation for Valheim below:
- Combat is generally poorly designed for irregular terrain, which is most of the game space, leading to several instances of WTF deaths or injuries that could have been avoided
- Combat is not good around groups of enemies leaving two strategies for dealing with the common groups of enemies: kiting them while poking away to kill them one by one or running away from the group which is non-viable for certain enemies that can chase players faster than they can run at certain game stages
- Boss fights don't disable random enemy spawns! This means you can get ambushed by mobs while fighting the bosses and get murdered because the game expects you to build a fortress around each arena
- Most of the bosses in Valheim are either slogs, annoying, or trivial. I used meads and buffs for them alongside knowing most of the fights and it still sucked:
  -> Eikthyr, Elder, and Bonemass are fine in terms of mechanics to deal with, moderate HP, and teachable movesets
  -> Moder effectively forces players to learn bows early game so you have the skill level to have her fight not be 30 - 45 minutes long excluding deaths. The majority of the fight is trying to use the poor bow mechanics to hit her and hoping her RNG crystal spray attack lets you dodge it rather than placing a death field you can't dodge or run out of w/o damage. Whenever she lands is a relief because you can just trigger her easy melee attacks and spam attacks to get her spongey HP down
  -> Yagluth is a exercise in patience where his explosion and meteor attacks force players away from him most of the fight while you come in and poke him to death slowly
  -> The Queen forces players to learn to handle group fights w/o running away. Her breath attacks, charging, summons, and teleports incentivize staying near her to deal damage and mitigating her mechanics to stay alive
  -> Fader is a terrible mixture of the prior two bosses with AOE magic attacks that force the player away from him most of the fight with summons that add pressure and irritation in the few windows to deal damage with more damage than previous bosses
  -> The final Deep North boss is trivial if you just block/dodge its spam attacks for adrenaline for trinket boosts while chugging meads with the Bonemass power. Its attacks are easily telegraphed, its summons are non-factors, and both phases are exercises in blocking/dodging than boss battles given the extreme screen shake and lag from the bosses animations
- Fishing is dead content where any benefits it brings can be provided with far easier alternatives, even for the weight and swimming meads, fooditems, and leviathan items
- Corpse runs can easily burn through your food stockpiles and drain your hard earned skills down into the low digits with death streaks as you try to get back to your body in dungeons, boss arenas, and dangerous regions. Generally a mechanic I feel is very player toxic.
- Skills level at a glacial pace so good luck getting value from them w/o excessive grinding and have fun when you lose whole levels from deaths that cost potentially hours of skill use
- The zone progression generally gets very frustrating at certain points and could easily be stopping points for many potential players
 -> I have no significant negative feedback for the Meadows, Black Forest, or Swamps besides already mentioned QoL and other comments
 -> The Mountains and Plains have mobs that you can't outrun so good luck if you run into them on a corpse run or a big pack with starred enemies
 -> The Mistlands "Mist" is awful

The Deep North update only solidified my negative recommendation for Valheim:
- The sheer time waste of Jotun invasions is insulting and aggravating compared to a simple portal or invasion at your spawn they could have done instead
- The requirement of armor molds from Jotuns and bloodgold from Gimmeltrolls can make progress in the Deep North glacial and frustrating compared to previous zones
- The RNG spawning of seed granaries in Ghost Villages meant you may only find the Deep North foodstuff as you are getting to the final boss. It is not at all like previous zone foods which had significantly more spawns
- The enemies are either are nothing burgers that you roll past or are multi attack spamming frustrations that can easily kill you
- The additions to previous zones continued previous issues of trophy locked items, frustrating grinding, or impossible to find interesting features
- The entire Altar of Potential feature is a toxic waste of time and should be removed or changed completely
