Nothing about this game is stable after 15 YEARS of development. Pick a bug, any bug. You will deal with multiple. You won't notice how bad they are until it is too late for a refund. For me, it's been the horrible "fog of war" bug in multiplayer. Your character is essentially playing in amnesia mode. See all those pretty buildings and lit-up visuals in the pictures/videos above? Your character will forget they exist entirely when you move to a new chunk or leave the game at all. It will be completely black. Imagine forgetting what your house looked like because you went to the gas station. Truly living in the moment, I guess. Well, until you die because it turns out that you're surrounded by zombies.

That's the level of stability we're talking about for a game that advertises "persistent player-run servers" and "in-depth visual systems" and "full line of sight system and real-time lighting" in the first five lines of its description. One could argue "but they re-wrote the entire lighting system for Build 42!" Yes, indeed they did. Almost 4 years ago, initially. Build 42's new lighting system was first discussed in February 2023. Build 42 launched to the "unstable" branch in December 2024, with NO multiplayer. It took another FULL YEAR for multiplayer to be added to Build 42 unstable, so December 2025. Build 42 was finally released to the stable branch in July 2026. I was suckered in September 2026 by all the hype around "stable". Indie Stone has seemingly invented their own definition of the word "stable".

The bug was first reported in February 2026 on their official bug report forums (go check those out and read all the lovely bugs for yourself). It took over 6 months and 3 separate bug reports for it to even be acknowledged, AFTER Build 42 stable was released. I do appreciate the QA team member that finally acknowledged and confirmed they were able to replicate the bug, but it's now been another month with zero further communication. If you check out the Build 42.21 Stable Release Notes, you'll see why: they had several OTHER critical bugs that they had to address first, like entire hoards of zombies de-spawning. Oopsies. No worries, it's not like this is a game about surviving hoards of zombies.

There's also several different character playstyles that you can try, and the difficulty levels are well designed. I first played Valheim with my husband in 2022 and we have followed the game's expansion and creative journey ever since. I had never played a video game before and the steep learning curve of this game was discouraging at first, but the story, the world, and the challenge kept me engaged and eager to see what was next. 

Building and terraforming were my favorite part of the game, and no other crafting-survival game I've played compares to its creative freedom. The brutality of resource gathering and the lack of QOL features won't be enjoyable for everyone, but for those willing to respect the grind, it is fun and rewarding. But there are plenty of ways to configure your game play to alleviate some of these problems (resource drop multiplier, passive mobs, no skill loss upon death, etc.), if they are truly having a negative impact on your experience. Beyond the survival elements, the world itself is breathtaking, and the developers' commitment to continuity makes the entire experience come together beautifully. 

After 5 worlds, 6 characters and several updates over the past 4 years, my husband and I finished Deep North today. As with any game, there will be things you wish you could change (Can we make early game foods useful in endgame? Add more things to increase the rested buff timer? Make one of the biomes allowed to grow all crops? Increase the Workbench range? Include all the weapon types in every stage of progression?) But looking back from where I started in 2022, I can honestly say that I enjoyed every minute of playing Valheim and it will always hold a special place in my heart.

Cyberpunk 2077 is, in my opinion, the best story-driven RPG I've played in years. What makes it so special is that every part of the game feels carefully crafted. The main story is emotional, gripping, and filled with unforgettable moments, but what truly surprised me was the quality of the side content. Unlike many open-world games where side quests feel like repetitive filler, Cyberpunk's side missions are so well-written and unique that they often feel like they could be part of the main storyline. Many of them introduce memorable characters, unexpected twists, and meaningful choices that make every mission worth playing.

The attention to detail is simply incredible. Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I've ever explored. Every district has its own identity, architecture, atmosphere, and people. The city constantly feels alive, with crowds walking the streets, traffic moving through highways, advertisements covering every building, and countless small details that make the world believable. Even the Badlands outside the city have their own unique atmosphere, making the contrast between the urban chaos and the empty desert feel natural and immersive.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely stunning. The lighting, weather effects, reflections, animations, and overall art direction make almost every location look like it belongs in a sci-fi movie. Whether you're driving through the neon-lit streets at night or watching the sunrise over the Badlands, the game is full of breathtaking moments.

The RPG systems are another reason why I love this game. The skill tree gives you the freedom to create completely different builds depending on how you want to play. You can become a deadly Netrunner who hacks enemies from a distance, a stealth assassin using throwing knives and silenced weapons, a cyber-enhanced samurai with katanas, or a heavily armored tank charging into combat with shotguns and LMGs. Cyberware implants, perks, iconic weapons, and countless equipment combinations make character progression incredibly satisfying.

Replayability is another area where Cyberpunk truly shines. Every new playthrough can feel completely different thanks to the different lifepaths, dialogue options, character builds, romances, endings, and even your character's gender. The choices you make throughout the game often change conversations, relationships, and the way certain missions unfold, giving you plenty of reasons to experience the story multiple times.

What really sets Cyberpunk 2077 apart is how all of these systems come together. The outstanding writing, unforgettable characters, meaningful side quests, incredible attention to detail, gorgeous visuals, deep progression systems, and the living, breathing world create an experience that feels unique from beginning to end. Very few games manage to combine storytelling, gameplay, exploration, and role-playing this well, which is exactly why I consider Cyberpunk 2077 the best RPG I've played in a very long time.

Project Zomboid is honestly one of the most ridiculously detailed survival games I have ever played.

At first glance, it looks simple. Then you actually play it and realize that basically EVERYTHING matters. Your character gets tired, hungry, stressed, bored, sick, injured, scared and exhausted. Your surroundings matter. Time matters. Weather matters. Light matters. Sound matters. The world itself changes around you.

And the craziest part is how many systems interact with each other.

You can have a perfectly planned day, go outside thinking you're just going to grab a few things, make one tiny mistake, attract attention, panic, run somewhere you shouldn't, crash into another problem and suddenly your entire situation has turned into complete chaos.

The game doesn't need scripted events to create memorable moments. The systems create them naturally.

You can spend hours preparing a safehouse, gathering supplies, improving your skills and making everything feel under control. Then one stupid decision completely ruins everything.

That's what makes Project Zomboid so god damn good.

It doesn't feel like you're playing through a story written by the developers. It feels like you're creating your own story while the game constantly throws unpredictable shit at you.

And the level of simulation is insane. The world doesn't just exist around you as decoration. Things actually change over time. Electricity can fail, the environment changes, hordes move, nature takes over, and your carefully built survival routine can slowly become harder and harder to maintain.

Even the smallest details can matter.

Project Zomboid is one of those games where you keep discovering another system and think:

"Wait... they actually thought of that?"

It's not just a zombie game.

It's a massive survival simulation disguised as an isometric indie game.

And every playthrough can turn into a completely different story.

The game's resurrection from its first release through Phantom Liberty is well documented. A bug filled failure, victim of greed and crunches. But instead of walking away with their tail firmly between their legs, CDPR took the complaints and criticisms to heart, and began a long-term renovation. By patch 1.61, the game actually was playable and you didn't wait for the inevitable crash. With patch 2.0, they rewrote everything from skill trees to fundamental game play. Phantom Liberty may be the only DLC released for the game, but it's one of the best, period. 

The game is based on Mike Pondsmith's TTRPG, and the influence of that game is all over the DNA of 2077. CDPR made changes to fit a video game better, but the fundamental story of living in a world under corporate oppression, the wealthy beyond the law's reach, and survival meaning sometimes giving up on your dreams, remains. The graphics, five years later, are still a benchmark. The story and the characters will draw you in, and your choices often make more of a difference than you think.

Instead, a lot of the progression feels like:
“Do this annoying thing so the game slowly becomes less annoying.”
Or:
“Make base building deliberately frustrating and limited, then use basic QoL features as progression.”

For example, Tired of constantly running back and forth for items? There’s cloud storage and more inventory space, but to improve it you need to go exploring caves.

If I wanted exploration, I’d rather play No Man’s Sky. If I wanted first-person combat, there are hundreds of games for that. 

Daisy chaining machines is locked away for some reason. Windows and lights are locked away. Getting a decent view while building is restricted because you’re in first person, the solution, the Hover Pack, is gated until much later. So you basically have to build in the more frustrating way first, then eventually unlock the ability to build properly.

Blueprints also feel unnecessarily restrictive. You can’t just select something you’ve already built and save it. You have to rebuild it inside a small Blueprint Designer.
That means you need prior game knowledge to know what designs you’ll want copies of later. It discourages experimenting and building naturally, and instead pushes you towards looking things up beforehand. 

Even late game you can never copy paste an existing design you did naturally. 
If I’ve already built a manifold or production block, manually placing the same machines, belts and splitters another 50 times isn’t interesting. 

Basically too much of the progression is based around removing frustration instead of giving you bigger and more interesting factory problems to solve.

What I wanted was a game about building large, visually appealing factories across different biomes while gradually increasing production, scale and complexity. This game seems like it got 70-80% there then got lost.

When playing solo, you are completely alone, surrounded by zombies that doom you to a slow death from a single bite, and the civilized world is crumbling around you, house by house, store by store, light by light. You fight the infected alone, you fight illness and hunger alone, and you fight yourself alone. The end of the world around you is not something to be happy about. 

I will probably never make it too far into this game. It's fun, but it is a deeply unsettling scenario for me. Still, if you are a fan of survival games and zombies, I highly recommend this one. Just beware: It does what is says on the package, this is weapons-grade downer.

After owning Valheim since the very beginning of early access, I honestly never thought I'd be saying this: I'm deeply disappointed with what the game has become.

I wanted to love Valheim. I really did. When I first played it, I could see an incredible survival game buried underneath the rough edges. The atmosphere, building system, world, and overall concept were fantastic, and I genuinely believed that, given enough time, the developers would address the game's shortcomings and turn it into something truly special.

Unfortunately, years later, I still find myself complaining about many of the exact same issues I had when I first started playing.

One of my biggest disappointments is the enemy AI. The enemies often feel rather lacklustre, with poor tracking and pathfinding that frequently causes them to get stuck on or around the environment. Combat could be so much more engaging if enemies had smarter AI, greater variety, and more interesting behaviours. Fighting the same predictable enemies over and over again simply doesn't provide the depth I'd expect from a game that's had this much time to develop.

I was also really hoping for better options when it comes to exploration and transportation. Travelling across the world can feel painfully slow and tedious, particularly when you're covering long distances. I had hoped we'd eventually see more mounts or other meaningful ways to travel and explore the world, rather than relying so heavily on the same methods of transportation.

More than anything, though, I wish there were simply more things to actually do. The world can often feel like a barren wasteland, and the gameplay becomes repetitive rather quickly. The constant grinding for resources can also become incredibly tedious, especially when there isn't enough variety or meaningful content to make that grind feel worthwhile.

And that's what makes this so frustrating: the foundation is already there.

Valheim has an incredible atmosphere, a brilliant building system, a fantastic premise, and a world that genuinely feels like it could support an amazing survival experience. That's precisely why it feels like such a massive missed opportunity. I don't think the game lacks potential — I think it has an enormous amount of potential that still hasn't been fully realised.

I genuinely wanted to love this game. I wanted to look back after all these years and feel that Valheim had grown into the survival game I'd always hoped it would become.

Instead, I find myself feeling that many of the same problems are still holding it back.

I really hope the game continues to evolve and eventually reaches the potential it so clearly has. I'd love to see more enemy variety, genuinely smarter AI and tracking, better transportation options, more activities, a world that feels more alive, and considerably less repetitive grinding.

As it stands, though, I'm unfortunately very disappointed with the direction of the game.

In my opinion, Valheim is massively overrated and overhyped, and that's incredibly frustrating considering how brilliant it could have been.

Good day.

[h3]A Timeless Sandbox Adventure Revisited – An Absolute Masterpiece for Every Player.[/h3]

I stumbled upon this gem many years ago but recently bought it yesterday – only to find my old nostalgia was still just as fresh when I dove back in. Terraria is an incredibly deep, endlessly rewarding experience that has defined the 2D action-adventure genre for nearly two decades.

Terraria offers perfect balance of depth and accessibility. The world generation creates unique landscapes from towering mountains covered in ancient trees to perilous underground caverns filled with creatures and ores. The progression system is incredibly satisfying – start as a vulnerable peasant wielding wooden weapons, survive dark nights against shadow creatures, mine deeper into the depths, craft better gear, defeat the first boss, progress through equipment tiers, unlock magic weapons at the dungeon altar, and eventually become an immortal being of pure power with advanced armor. Feel stronger as you ascend ranks with endless content.

The game's combat has a wonderful rhythm. Every class feels rewarding – ranged attacks can devastate from afar, elemental spells rain down upon enemies, summoners deploy armies to protect them, and melee fighters swing their swords like legends. The crafting system lets you build countless tools, weapons, and accessories using materials you gather throughout your journey.

The atmosphere is where Terraria truly shines. The vibrant colors of the surface world give way to ominous caverns beneath, creating a stark contrast that makes exploration even more compelling as you descend deeper into darkness – only illuminated by your little torch flame and surrounded by strange echoes from monsters above. The soundtrack is equally captivating, with calm piano melodies when walking gently through peaceful biomes, intense battle themes during raids, and haunting notes in the depths of hell itself. The game's art direction combines clean graphics with beautiful details that make every pixel count.

The multiplayer system makes Terraria even more fun – as friends join you, build together, explore underground caves collaboratively, craft powerful equipment collectively, and face bosses as a team. There is no better partner than playing alongside friends who will stand beside you during epic battles and celebrate victories together just as much as any single-player moment.

Technical Excellence Note: I tested Terraria on my [b]MacBook Pro with an M1 Pro chip[/b], and the experience was absolutely positive. Running this 2D masterpiece on Apple Silicon is a dream come true – smooth performance even when exploring vast worlds with hundreds of entities on screen, no loading screens or lag during intense boss fights, and beautifully crisp visuals that showcase the game's vibrant art style perfectly. The M1 Pro allowed me to experience Terraria without any technical friction while delivering stunning visuals on the Liquid Retina XDR display. It's a seamless experience that proves even games this charmingly simple can shine beautifully on modern hardware.

The boss designs are legendary – facing countless epic challenges, defeating mechanical foes in coordinated raids like clockwork, battling jungle guardians after traversing dense swamps below, and conquering everything that comes your way as a fully awakened hero who has proven their might.

For anyone seeking sandbox freedom, creative crafting possibilities, endless exploration opportunities, and a gameplay loop that has maintained its charm across multiple generations of players – Terraria is an absolute must-play. And yes, if you own a MacBook Pro with an M1 Pro chip – I highly recommend giving Terraria a try. It's simple in presentation yet infinite in depth.

[b]My verdict:[/b] An immortal masterpiece. Perfect for beginners and veterans alike. 10/10 for all players who value creative freedom, progression satisfaction, and timeless design.

After spending over 400 hours in this game, I can say that it is a game that sometimes, not often, but sometimes, actually brings me enjoyment. However, with every year that passes, I feel like the game becomes either more survivor-sided or simply more unbalanced for killers.

A killer realistically doesn't have much of a chance to win unless they're playing an S-tier killer, such as Blight or Nurse. Those are basically the only exceptions. Of course, if someone really masters a certain killer and knows how to play them at a very high level, they will have a better chance, but even then, it doesn't mean they are guaranteed to win.

The toxicity in this game, especially in Survivor with Friends groups, is, in my opinion, at an all-time high. I don't remember the last time I played on EU without getting teabagged or having survivors stare at me after I dropped a pallet. It's just these little things people do to humiliate you during the game and make you feel like you're simply terrible at the game.

And like I said, every year the game becomes more and more unbalanced. Killers such as Freddy Krueger, Trapper, or Hag are just not really viable in the current meta anymore. Survivors have over 400 perks, from what I know, while killers have 278.

Yes, of course, there are fewer killers and more survivors. That's a valid argument, because you can create more survivors, while you can't just keep adding killers forever. However, that doesn't change the fact that the meta keeps changing and becoming stronger, while more and more killers keep falling further behind.

The killers that stay at the top are mostly the ones with abilities that allow them to ignore the basic mechanics of the game. They can shoot across the map, teleport, ignore certain things, or completely ignore looping and pallets. A good example is Nurse, who can basically ignore the entire pallet-looping mechanic.

The game has simply stopped being enjoyable for me. Especially after the latest matchmaking change, which happened on August 25th alongside the release of the new killer, The Judgment.

MMR simply doesn't exist.

The first few days were chaotic, and that's understandable because a new MMR system needs some time to stabilize. The problem is that the new MMR, which, according to Behaviour, was supposed to make sure that players were matched with people around their own skill level, simply doesn't do that.

I remember what it was like when I had around 200 hours, and it is still the same for many people. A lot of players can confirm this. You can play killer and get matched against people with 3,000 or even 4,000 hours who know exactly what they're doing, while you're playing a killer you just bought and are still trying to learn. In that situation, you realistically don't have much of a chance.

And if you also get matched against a group sitting on Discord and communicating with each other, the situation becomes even easier for the survivors.

There is a very simple strategy. The game starts, and all four survivors work on separate generators. The killer finds one person on a generator and starts chasing them. That survivor can loop the killer while the other three work on their generators. During that time, three generators can get completed, leaving only two.

Then the next two survivors go to separate generators. The killer can still be chasing someone or move on to another survivor, and the whole process starts again.

And it just keeps going.

It's one of the easiest ways to win that you can imagine.

So, in short, the game is simply unbalanced for both sides, both from the killer's perspective and from the survivor's perspective.

From the survivor's side, the problem is that some killers can simply ignore almost every mechanic in the game. Flashlight saves, pallets, even looping itself. Nurse is a good example, as well as The Judgment, the new killer created by the community.

From the killer's side, the problem is that Behaviour keeps adding new perks and new things that strengthen survivors and create even stronger metas. You can obviously argue that there are significantly more survivors and that they generate most of the money, so Behaviour wants to keep adding more things for them.

There are far fewer killer players, even though sometimes it might seem like there are more, because someone has to play killer for survivors to be able to play the game at all. The truth is simply that there are more survivors, and that's probably not going to change.

So for now, I'm not gona play. Until the MMR changes, gets fixed, and actually starts working properly again, I don't really see a reason to play till my head explodes

I know that by saying this, I could just as easily be assuming that it will never happen. But even so, I think that, at the moment, this is probably the best decision I can make.

All I can really do is wait and hope that Behaviour eventually does something about it.

The game became boring for me during Act 3 (the biggest one)—including the stories, the vast majority of the quests, and the combat. Ultimately, there weren't enough good points to save the overall experience.
1) Character development is too diluted in political correctness. You can still choose to go down the evil path, but it brings no real sense of fulfillment. Most of the time, you just suffer penalties, and your choices don't truly impact the world around you. Nothing quite changes; the main story just runs its course. Character arcs are full of improbable, epic secrets, yet they still feel dull and flat. I felt no personal involvement.
2) Combat, on Tactician difficulty, is way harder at the beginning of Act 1—I would even say almost too hard, with archers insta-killing you from miles away. Then you start to mitigate things, and the end of Act 1 and most of Act 2 become enjoyable. Finally, it becomes way too easy in Act 3, with only a few hiccups here and there. It mostly becomes tedious (like enemies maiming your Mage Hand, "stun immunity" that doesn't actually work, or counterspell avalanches). Your powerhouse team breaks everything, and you just have to rest... often.
3) Quests are globally well-written but have no impact on the world. In the end, you just do them for the sake of it, like chores.
It's not the first time I've felt this way about a game that is obviously well-made. Maybe it's just me, and I can't feel the intensity anymore... or is it just gone, erased by today's lack of creativity?

Title: Never Fade Away...

A lot of time has passed since launch, and only now can I truly say it: this game is a masterpiece. The work CD Projekt Red put into turning this around is fantastic.

The plot tackles real, massive issues reflecting our own world. This isn't just a brief main quest that feels like a small add-on to a massive map—it’s a deeply human story filled with heroes, villains, and losers. It asks what it really takes for a "nobody" to become a legend, and more importantly, what price you pay for that success. This is pure, authentic Cyberpunk. To be honest, I wasn't sure CDPR could pull it off, but the voice acting and performances are fabulous. They brought Night City to life so convincingly that you instantly buy into its ruthless rules and struggles.

Gameplay at launch was okay, but weak. Today? It’s phenomenal. The world is packed with hidden details, easter eggs, and its own urban legends. As for bugs, I rarely ran into anything major—just the occasional floating car or clipping geometry. For where the game stands today, it plays great. It just needs a few tiny polish tweaks, but nothing that ruins the experience.

The map is huge, and the DLC filled in every empty space seamlessly. There are countless small stories to uncover and interesting places to explore. The level design and world-building deserve serious praise.

Summary:
Without spoiling anything: trust me, you won't regret playing this. It’s far from a typical video game story—it’s something much deeper. Accept the rules of Night City, jump in, and experience it. The writing and acting ensure this world never feels like a hollow cardboard set; the city is cruel, and you will feel every bit of it.

Valheim is really an awesome game, something like Minecraft but set in a much more magical world. The progression in this game is fantastic. I’ve always had a problem with games that have very fast progression, so this feels really refreshing.

What doesn’t feel refreshing or awesome, however, is the difficulty.

I personally love difficult games. I’ve beaten Elden Ring 3 times, Dark Souls 1 twice, Dark Souls 3 three times, and Hollow Knight. But this game isn’t difficult in the same way. Instead, it’s difficult because of frustration...
You farm for hours to make Bronze equipment, travel by boat for 1.5 hours to reach The Elder, only to get instantly killed by a mosquito before you can even make a portal. Then, randomly, a Swamp invasion happens, and the enemies are much stronger than the average monsters on the main island.

But there are things I really like, and one of them is the health system. Eating meat, vegetables, and berries to increase your HP and STAMINA?! That’s a really cool design, and I LOVE IT.

However, what I dislike is how this health system works together with the combat system. I need more HP to survive, but at the same time, I need stamina to dodge, run, attack, and fight effectively. The problem is that the early-game food mostly gives you one or the other. So I constantly feel like I have to choose between having enough health to survive or enough stamina to actually fight. I really like the idea behind the system, but in the early game, it can make combat feel more frustrating than challenging. Another thing that really frustrates me is how creatures constantly chase you. It doesn’t matter if you run half an island away — they can still be right behind you. If I’m gearless or already in bad shape, I sometimes can’t even lose them for a minute.

Despite all of this, Valheim is something else. It has a huge amount of content and so much time you can spend in a single game. There’s a lot to love here.

I honestly believe that if the combat mechanics and especially the way mobs behave were adjusted and balanced a little better, this game could absolutely rise to the sky. The foundation is already amazing — it just needs some improvements to make the combat feel challenging rather than frustrating.

The game itself is alright. Just alright. For an AAA title from people that made Witcher series this doesn't quite cut it, now does it? The original release of this game was a total mess, so I waited and waited till everything was done and patched to even try it. I like cyberpunky aesthetic and feel, if nothing else, experiencing that vibe in this game would be alright.

I must say, the strong suits of this title are the. . . Segments with Johnny. Stealth approach trying to not alert the enemies and using your 'magic' (quickhacks) to manipulate stuff in game.

The weak suits are the combat itself (it's too easy and not challenging at all), stories that don't involve johnny or his insights (he's a colorful character that while crude, has a proper main character energy), driving (it feels off), bugs that are still in the game - there are a lot.

While bugs themselves don't outright softlock you and aren't game breaking, there's a ton of them. From bad rendering, to enemies phasing through stairs and catwalks, to vehicles spawning and despawning while you look, vehicles with enemies falling out of the sky and exploding on impact with the ground because you walked out a bit too far from their rendering , the vehicle you own spawning in unreachable places or places it can't leave from. . . There's a ton. I played a 'vanilla' experience naively thinking I wouldn't see all that mess. I was wrong. Perhaps there are mods improving those aspects, there should be some at this point anyway. 

The game itself is rather boring. The moment you realize your build you locked yourself into doesn't utilize quickhacks but has to rely on some other cyberware (part of equipment you 'wear') it becomes extremely straightforward and frankly, way too easy. I couldn't for the love of me sit through all the extra side content. I would physically die of boredom, so to leave an honest review, I rushed to the ending.

It's a blessing I could stick with the game for 117hrs but that's just because of my willpower to see it through and perhaps find something that's suddenly making this 6/10 game into 8 or 9. Sadly, in my case there was nothing of the sort.

Play if you must or otherwise feel compelled to, but only after getting it on sale. Don't have regrets for wasting money on something that was hyped out of the orbit and underdelivers.

This -to me- is the greatest game ever made. Don't let the hour counter fool you - I have played Cyberpunk 2077 since half a year after the original release and have since then played over 1500 hours on Xbox. The story is great and very well told - Night City itself feels like a real, vibrant place with fascinating stories and discoveries at every turn. 

This alone would have been enough to lock me in for a descent amount of time, but the combat is the thing that kept me coming back year after year because there is nothing even close to the combat in Cyberpunk. The different cyberware augmentations and the massive skill tree allow dozens of different playstyles. You have a wide selection of standard and iconic weapons. The latter can be improved throughout the game in the crafting menu and also the cyberware can be upgraded. 

The driving is ridiculously fun, arcadey and allows for descent vehicular combat. The exterior of cars you own can also be customized. Additionally, you have a fast travel system, a subway, and self driving taxis  to be able to switch the means of traversal from time to time.

When the gameplay and the design of night city clicks, it is the best video game experience out there and one, that I will keep sinking hours into.

The immersion in No Man's Sky is top notch. The stylized art style looks amazing, and the soundtrack is fantastic. I actually turn down the volume for voices and sound effects just to let the music take center stage. There is always a ton to do and new goals to chase.

Do yourself a favor and play on Survival mode. It is pretty brutal right at the beginning, but once you get past that initial bump, it adds so much meaning to the journey. The updates keep making the game better, and right now I am completely hooked on corvettes. Expedition 23 in particular is awesome. I normally use guides to rush through these as fast as possible, but with this one I am taking my time and doing it on my own out of respect for the dev team's journey.

On the technical side, performance could be better. Frame rates take a hit during planetary storms, and there is noticeable shader compilation stutter. Also, fair warning if you tweak your hardware: the game really does not like undervolted GPU profiles. Entering or exiting a planet (or even just quitting the game) can crash the GPU driver. Even to a black screen sometimes, forcing a hard PC reboot.

Despite the stuttering and crash annoyances, the game is incredible. Wholly recommended.

A Gentle Dystopia

Ah yes, the promised land is finally here. After a botched release and years of updates improving, expanding, and stabilizing the game along with the release of the massive Phantom Liberty expansion. All is forgiven, Polish devs. But is it? As much as there is about Cyberpunk 2077 that I like and as much as I respect the support CD Projekt Red continued to put into it. We need to talk about the massive elephant in the room that never actually left. Borrowed time.

Majora's Mask is probably one of the most famous examples of making time itself part of the gameplay. Even though its three day loop, that doomsday clock is always ticking. The player constantly understands that time has value. For more modern examples, look at games like The Blood of Dawnwalker or Kingdom Come Deliverance II. Neither necessarily hangs one giant doomsday clock over the player in the same way. Instead, time becomes part of the player's agency. Dawnwalker gives you a limited amount of time before the endgame, with quests and major actions advancing that clock. Deliverance II takes a more situational approach, where certain quests and events will move forward without you if you wait too long. Personally, I think Deliverance II takes this idea a little too literally. Persona 5 is another great example. You have a limited calendar and have to decide how to spend it. Do you improve a relationship? Work on yourself? Explore the palace? Prepare for the next major confrontation? All of these systems are asking the player some variation of the same question. What are you going to do with the time you have? And Cyberpunk presents one of the strongest possible versions of that question. When you're dying, what do you do with your time?

Apparently nothing. Get up samurai, we're going drag racing. Get up samurai, we're clearing every gig and side mission on the entire map. Get up samurai, we're going bowling. This is the massive elephant that I don't think gets criticized nearly enough. The story presents V with a very simple and horrifying problem. You are dying. Your life is disintegrating in front of you. The writing becomes emotional. Relationships start forming. People begin attaching themselves to V. Johnny is slowly taking over. Every lead toward a possible cure should feel increasingly desperate. Your entire story is supposedly happening on borrowed time. And then Cyberpunk almost immediately throws that idea out the window. The clock doesn't actually exist. Take as long as you want. Do every gig. Help every fixer. Buy every car. Make every friend. Finish every companion storyline. Explore every corner of Night City. Eventually, whenever you finally feel like it, go choose your ending.

That's not meaningful agency. That's a story telling you that your time is valuable while the game design simultaneously tells you that your time is infinite. And that creates a massive disconnect. Your relationships with people begin to lose weight. Desperately taking gigs because you need money to upgrade your cyberware stops meaning anything because... why not just do everything? Eventually you'll be swimming in money anyway. The writing constantly asks for an emotional response from the people around V. Meanwhile, V suppresses the biggest problem in their life, another identity is literally eating away at their mind, their body, and eventually their entire existence. That should hang over everything. Every relationship. Every choice. Every job. Every conversation with Johnny. Instead, the uncertainty loses its weight. The confrontations with Johnny lose some of their urgency because, at the end of the day, who cares? Johnny, you and me are going bowling, again.

Once again, modders enter the scene. Modders add an actual doomsday clock, progressing V's deterioration according to the in-game passage of time. Other mods add life sim elements like eating, drinking, sleeping and generally maintaining yourself. The most baffling thing about all of this is that the foundations for these systems are already sitting inside the game. There are food vendors everywhere. Vending machines everywhere. You have a bed. You have showers. You can buy multiple apartments and living spaces. These places are presented like somewhere V can return to, decompress, sleep, shower, eat, and temporarily escape Night City. But for what? The game has all these little pieces suggesting that V is supposed to be living in Night City while simultaneously dying inside it, yet almost none of them carry any real mechanical consequence. And that becomes even stranger when you consider how heavily the writing emphasizes borrowed time. Every new person V grows attached to is potentially someone they're going to lose. Every relationship V builds is happening under the shadow of an approaching death. Every lead toward a cure should matter because another day wasted is another day gone. But without any meaningful passage of time, that shadow never really moves. And that's why, even after all the updates, all the fixes, Phantom Liberty, and everything CD Projekt Red poured into this game, part of Cyberpunk 2077 still feels half cooked to this day.

One of the biggest contradictions is still sitting there at the heart of V's story. Untouched. Unfixed. They wrote about a person discovering that their life suddenly has an expiration date, but never implemented the one element that could have made that premise truly meaningful. Your life is supposed to be on borrowed time. The grim story of a dystopian hell where one person is desperately trying to find some meaning in the trash heap around them loses much of its weight when the game refuses to make time matter. For all the work CD Projekt Red has done rebuilding Cyberpunk 2077, this contradiction has been sitting there since the beginning.

Cyberpunk 2077 is still in 2026 a gorgeous game. Night City looks absolutely stunning and on a modern PC you can crank the graphics settings all the way up and still enjoy an incredibly smooth experience. Your GPU may sound like it's preparing for takeoff, but hey, that's a small price to pay for pretty neon lights.

There are plenty of side quests to keep you busy, and some of them are genuinely great. That said, I still found myself wishing there were more. Apparently, I have developed an unhealthy appetite for wandering around Night City doing increasingly ridiculous jobs for complete strangers.

The biggest problem, however, is the main story. It's simply too short. If you focus mostly on the main quests, the game ends before it really feels like you've gotten your money's worth. You spend all this time building your character, exploring Night City and becoming murder machine, only for the main story to basically end too soon.

Thankfully, Cyberpunk 2077 has some solid replay value. You can approach the game with completely different builds, whether you want to be a stealthy hacker, a heavily armed psychopath, a katana-wielding lunatic, or some other combination of questionable life choices. Changing your stats and playstyle can make another playthrough feel surpprisingly different.

Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic-looking and incredibly smooth game with a huge amount of potential content, but I can't help feeling that the main story should have been significantly longer.

I'm one of those Destiny players that was looking for a new home after Sony killed my game. I had a Warframe account from a long time ago, and some friends convinced me to give it another try. After doing so, I've found myself really loving it. So here's the general gist for those looking to make the leap to another live service game. 

The Good: 

Playstyle Diversity: Initially coming over from Destiny 2 to Warframe, I was bored out of my mind running my Excalibur for the missions over and over and over again. But once I unlocked assassinations across Earth, Venus, Mars, and Mercury and got to farming other Warframes, I started vibing with Warframe a lot more. The ability to diversify your gameplay in Warframe through the various Warframes, mods, and weapons is a lot greater than in Destiny 2, whose rigid Class + Subclass system finds players inevitably limited in one way or another. I've adored getting to try out different frames and their skills as I progress through the story. Currently I'm quite enamored with Koumei; I find the synergy between her abilities and dedicated weapons to be fantastic. 

Dedicated Farming Missions: One of my biggest gripes with Destiny 2 has always been the resource farming required for upgrades. And while Warframe has a lot more resources, Warframe also introduces dedicated missions that allow you to endlessly farm said resources to your heart's content. It's a welcome upgrade from the Destiny experience, and one that allows me to try out my new gear as well. Bonus!

Engaging Boss Battles: You'll routinely run into Assassination contracts where you're hunting down some of the biggest bads in the Solar System. These bosses are a cut above your regular enemies, with unique mechanics that require you to solve puzzles or fulfill other unique mechanics in order to shatter health gates and progress the fight. While there are certainly a few that are frustrating, the majority of these fights are very engaging. They're a worthwhile challenge that tests your progressing skills as a player to see whether you're actually mastering what the game's given you, or whether your friends are just carrying you to victory. 

The Story: I won't say that it's not a weird story, it certainly is. But I've found what I've played of Warframe's story so far to be fascinating and engaging. I'm loving the lore, and the increased player choice the further the story progresses. I've gone from being a passenger to being an active participant, and it's a really cool evolution. 

Movement Tech: I really like the bullet jump, okay? As someone who doesn't do a whole lot of sword skating, I enjoy the sudden ability to zoom through levels. You can zip through levels with ease using the movement tech in the game, and every Frame has access to it. The omni-directional capabilities of the tech also means that you're never really stuck in any location either; the bullet jump is the ultimate movement tool. 

Everything is mostly free: The fact that I've not spent much of anything on Warframe is really cool. I've dropped maybe $15 on the game overall, and that's only because I got a really steep platinum discount offer as part of my daily log-in bonus a month ago. Warframe is incredibly affordable, and surprisingly good quality for a game that's free-to-play. 

Design Language: Warframe looks weird. But it's a good kind of weird. I love the designs of the characters in this game, especially the Warframes themselves. It's a unique style that I've not seen anywhere else. Warframe is incredibly distinct to a degree that other sci-fi games just aren't, and that design language is a clear labor of love. It's enjoyable from top-to-bottom. 

Clan Dojo: Coming from Destiny 2 where clans were essentially meaningless, the fleshed-out clan system in Warframe is incredibly cool to see. Having an entire Dojo where trades occur and research can be conducted and shared amongst all clan members is very cool. It's allowed me to grab some powerful gear that's assisted in leveling up more quickly, and enables some of my clanmates to share mods with me that they'd otherwise have scrapped. 

The Bad: 

Artificial Restraints: While everything in Warframe is mostly free, Warframe also does a lot to incentivize you to spend money on the game. One of the biggest ways it does that is by installing artificial caps on the number of Warframes, weapons, and loadouts you can have at once. You can unlock more these through rewards or rank-ups, or you can purchase additional slots with platinum, an in-game currency that you earn either by trading with other players or by purchasing with real money. When you hit that cap, it can be a real dissuader on playing. I was lucky it lined up with a steep platinum discount. 

Steep Level Curve: Warframe is designed very much like a Pokemon Fan Game. In the early hours of this game, it is a cakewalk. You steamroll over your foes and nothing poses a challenge to you. Then you hit Deimos and everything starts kicking your ass unless you're running Rhino. Certain frames, such as Excalibur, become useless for mid-to-late portion of the game because they don't have abilities that buff their defenses and you don't yet have access to endgame mods that buff them, nor weapons that deal enough damage to slay your foes quickly enough. Then, once you're over this hump, it's back to smooth sailing where things are mostly a cakewalk again until you hit the next cliff. Rinse, repeat. It makes grinding the game solo a little bit of a chore. 

New Player Experience is Sub-Par: While the game is addictive, it is very easy to get very overwhelmed very quickly. I was lucky to have my Destiny 2 clan with me, who were also a bunch of experienced Warframe players with endgame accounts. But without entering the game alongside a friend who has a PhD in Tennology, it can be very hard to navigate the game. Even now, as I've hit the mid-to-late game, I'm still finding mechanics that confuse me, or that aren't explained particularly well in-game, requiring me to either Google them, or ask my clanmates. 

Warframe is a better game tomorrow: Warframe has a foundry where you build things using materials and blueprints that you find across the solar system. This is super cool, but it quickly becomes frustrating when you realize that this foundry has build times that range anywhere from half a day to 3 whole days. I just got done building the Warframe Equinox, whose components altogether spanned 6 and a half days of  build time. It's a little ridiculous. You can spend platinum to speed this process up, but it's honestly a waste when there are better things to spend platinum on. Like more Warframe slots. 

Overall, Warframe is a solid experience. It's a lovingly crafted live service game with an engaging story, amazingly fun fights and mechanics, and an some solid quality of life improvements over its peers. It has its flaws as any live service game does, but unlike many other competitors, the beauty of Warframe is that it allows you to spend as much or as little as you want for the experience, and still have a great time. If you're a Destiny 2 player looking for a new home, I highly recommend giving this game a shot! I think you'll come to love it too!

Project Zomboid is an isometric zombie sandbox-survival game. It came out in 2013, and has since received many updates, and has evolved to a completely different game since the first version, which was a story game. I will now list some pros, and cons.

Pros:
================================
+ Has some of the most QoL features I've seen in any game.
+ Contains a unique and interesting artstyle.
+ Isn't an overly easy, or overly hard game, and includes about infinite freedom when it comes to building/crafting.
+ Steam Workshop
+ The modding community is efficient, and good at what they do.
+ The Zombie AI isn't overly dumb, or smart (but you can customize them to change it)
+ Almost every aspect of gameplay is customizable through settings, or mods.
+ Has a pretty good multiplayer experience in b42 stable.
+ Has a unique vibe compared to other zombie games.
+ Extremely expansive map (I'm still finding new locations)
+ So many different weapons, collectibles, and apparel items that you find new ones no matter your time. (such as the Luthex Wristwatch, or ALICE Gear)
+ Has an in-depth farming, and animal husbandry system.
+ ALSO contains an in-depth cooking system.
+ Looting feels unique and different every save you play, due to unique randomized houses, and areas, such as survivor houses, and camps, or unique zombies, such as soldiers, Jason Voorhees, prisoners, and more,
+ Cars actually require keys, and gasoline unlike some games.
+ You can remove zombies.
+ You can add sprinters.
There's more, but I want to list cons now.

Cons:
================================
- Cars seem to break down too easily sometimes, and too hard other times (can change in settings)
- With every few updates, your save/mods may not work.
- The Developers are very slow at updates.
- Melee Combat needs some work for PVE and PVP.
- PVP is terrible rn.
- Alot of workshop mods use AI for images, or code :(

That's about it, overall best zombie game (especially with the new 3D Mods (ik they use AI))

In order for me to describe Helldivers II, we first need to examine the mesocorticolimbic circuit. The mesocorticolimbic circuit is a group of neural stuctures responsible for incentive salience, associative learning, and positively-valenced emotions where pleasure is a core component. This is located in the ventral tegmental area of the midbrain, and is used to encourage exposure to positive stimuli and avoid exposure to negative stimuli for survival. Often times, certain stimuli can overload this circuit and result in compulsive and addicitve behavior. This is where Helldivers II comes in. This game does a really good job at stimulating the parts of the brain that processes pleasure becasue of its role-playing team based gameplay loop that makes you feel like a part of something larger than yourself. This is best demonstrated through the planet liberation mechanic where you can view how much of a planet is liberated, and how your actions and performance contibutes to its liberation. That's really the biggest part where this games addictiveness stems from, aside from the different stratagems you can use, and the different fronts you can fight on.  This game really makes it easy to immerse yourself as a Helldiver, and it really is a great time to just dive in, kill some bots and shoot the breeze with your friends.

Greatest Game of the 2020's. I am an old Bauldur's Gate veteran, and to be honest, I was afraid to try this one. It looked very different than 1 and 2 from the images with all of its new-fangled, 3d, fancy graphics. And from what I saw in videos and trailers, it just kinda looked like a dirty sex game. I was terrified to try it becasue I didn't want it to ruin my fond memories. But there was one Steam review that helped my confidence. It pointed out that this game is ALL about choice. The review amusingly stated, "You don't have to fuck the bear." LOL. So I bit the bullet and bought it. 
And boy am I glad.
Even on the character creation screen it was drawing me into the fantasy with its beautiful music. When the story started, I found that I liked Lae'zel. I liked Shadowheart. I could see that the writing and voice acting was decent, and I could see how those two didn't get along. I even liked Astarion when I met him—and I had even previously HATED the way he looked when no one would shut up about him on Youtube. I thought he looked like a sleazy Vegas magician lol. But It was all fine. 
I found that nothing bothered me as I played. The story held my attention—which is really saying something because I have been a BRUTAL writing critic ever since I became a writer lol. This game's story has my approval.
Yes, it's all very choice oriented, and that was a great thing. When there's various sex scenes getting isolated and showcased around the net, that would make any game look like a "dirty sex game" lol. So it's cool. I was able to play the narrative I wanted to see for my particular character.
Earlier, I mentioned that I was worried it wouldn't "feel" like Bauldur's Gate. Well turns out it did. Even though the graphics were heavily upgraded, it did still oddly feel like a continuation of the old games. I even feel like some of the old item-oriented sound effects were original. Not sure though.
Best of all was the battle system. Early on, I got to this one area that had a large party of enemies inside a building and it was very hard (I played on Tactician for my first play through because of my Bauldur's Gate history). It was SO hard, though, and I kept dying... And I noticed that I was hooked. I was determined to beat that battle and it was invigorating. I just loved the challenge! Too bad it will probably be a while before the next one comes out. DX.
This game put me through SUCH emotion though! I cried at the end. I cried at something at the middle too. This game really knew how to mess with me lol. Even when I came back to its Steam page, seeing the trailers made me feel something. ;_;
I ADORE the soundtrack, btw! I've been singing those songs and relistening to them on Youtube ever since that first day in the character creator lol.

Sea of Thieves is, quite simply, the best pirate simulator I have ever played, in virtually every category that matters to me. As it stands today, there is remarkably little to criticize. Not only is the game in the best state it has ever been, but it has also become one of my favorite games of all time.

The gameplay is practically perfect for what it sets out to accomplish. There is certainly nothing here for everyone, and I can understand why some players may find its structure too relaxed or its progression too unconventional. But if you're looking for a pirate power fantasy rather than a rigid combat-focused game or another meticulously optimized gameplay loop, Sea of Thieves is about as close to perfection as you can get. You sail the ship, you command the ship, you manage the sails, you navigate the seas, and you work together with your crew. There is something uniquely satisfying about simply *being* a pirate, and Sea of Thieves understands that better than almost any other game. There is remarkably little to criticize in what is otherwise an almost perfect pirate simulator.

The game is also beautiful to behold. Simply looking at the horizon, sailing across the sea, watching the sun set, or having your crew break into song while crossing the Caribbean can be enough to make the entire journey worthwhile. The game feels like a living pirate postcard, with gorgeous vistas and colorful environments around practically every corner. Its distinctive art direction is also unmistakably Rare, a developer I grew up loving as a kid. Seeing them return to the top of their craft with one of the most visually charming games I've ever played is genuinely special.

Sea of Thieves is, to me, the most perfect game in my library. Perhaps not mechanically, and certainly not because it is flawless, but because it combines so many things I have loved for years: Rare, pirates, exploration, cooperation, adventure, and simply having a good time with other people. It feels less like a game I was waiting to play and more like an idyllic dream someone finally turned into one. No other game comes remotely as close to delivering this particular fantasy for me. As far as I'm concerned, this is a perfect game in every manner that matters. Ahoy!

100 Hours: I am now the guy with the rock on the beach.

Core Gameplay Loop:

Collect wood and stone.

Suffer from extreme paranoia every time you hear a rustling bush.

Trust a guy who says he's friendly.

Get betrayed by the guy who said he was friendly.

Experience a sleep-deprivation-induced existential crisis.

Repeat.

Sea of Thieves is one of those games where I can understand why some people really like it and also why some people really hate it. It definitely has a lot of bad sides and there are times where the game can be really annoying, but honestly, after playing it for a while, I think it is actually a pretty good game overall.
The biggest thing about Sea of Thieves is that it can be really fun when you have the right people to play with. Playing with friends makes the game way better. You can spend hours just sailing around, doing random stuff, fighting other ships, looking for treasure, or just messing around. Half the time you don't even need to have a plan. You can get on the ship and somehow end up doing something completely different than what you originally wanted to do. The sailing itself is actually pretty fun too. At first I thought it was going to get boring really quickly, but there is something kind of relaxing about just being on the ship and sailing across the ocean. Then suddenly you see another ship and everything goes from being calm to complete chaos. You might be trying to finish a quest and then some random player attacks you and now you're spending the next 30 minutes trying to sink them. Sometimes you win, sometimes you lose, and sometimes you just end up running away because you don't feel like dealing with it. One thing I also really like is that the developers are actually working on making the game take up less space. They have said they are working on basically cutting the game size in half, which I think is a really good thing. Sea of Thieves is a pretty big game already, so having it take up way less storage is going to be really nice. Not everyone has a huge amount of free storage, especially on consoles, so making the game smaller without having to get rid of the actual content is a big positive in my opinion. That is also one of the bad things about the game though. Other players can either make the game really fun or completely ruin your mood. I know that is kind of the point of the game, but sometimes you just want to do your own thing without getting chased around the map by a crew that has probably been playing for 10 hours straight. You can spend a decent amount of time getting loot and then lose all of it because another crew comes along and sinks you. It can be really frustrating. The pvp can be fun when you are actually ready for it, but when you're not expecting it, it can be annoying. Especially if you are playing with people who are better than you. There are definitely times where I have been absolutely destroyed by another crew and just sat there thinking "well, that was a waste of time." But at the same time, those moments can also make the game more exciting. You never really know what is going to happen when you see another ship. Another thing I don't really love is the grinding. Some parts of the game can feel like you're doing the same thing over and over again. You get a quest, sail somewhere, collect something, bring it back, and then do it again. After a while it can start feeling repetitive. There are a lot of things to do, but sometimes it still feels like you're doing the same stuff just for a different reward. The rewards are also kind of weird because most of the stuff you unlock is cosmetic. I understand why they did this because it keeps the game more fair, but sometimes it can feel like you're working towards something for hours just to get a slightly different hat or ship decoration. It would be nice if there were more things that actually changed gameplay, but I also get why they don't want people who have played longer to have a massive advantage over new players. The game can also be pretty confusing when you first start playing. There is a lot of stuff going on and it doesn't always explain everything very well. You kind of have to figure things out yourself or look up what you're supposed to do. This isn't necessarily a huge problem, but it can be annoying when you're new and have no idea what you're doing. The community can also be hit or miss. You can meet some really funny and nice people, and then you can meet people who clearly woke up that morning just to make someone else miserable. Sometimes you get into a fight with another crew and afterwards everyone is joking around and having fun. Other times you get destroyed and then someone starts trash talking you like they just won a world championship. But honestly, some of the funniest moments in Sea of Thieves come from other players. There have been plenty of times where something completely stupid happens and it ends up being more memorable than any actual mission. Maybe someone falls off the ship, someone accidentally blows up the entire crew, or you get into a fight that lasts way longer than it should. Those random moments are probably one of the best parts of the game. I also really like the way the game looks. The art style isn't trying to be super realistic, but I think it works really well. The ocean looks great, the islands look good, and the whole pirate theme fits the game. Even after playing for a while, there are still times where I just stop and look at the ocean or a sunset because it actually looks pretty nice. The music is also really good. There are times when you're just sailing around and the music starts playing and it makes the whole thing feel like you're actually in some pirate movie. Then five minutes later you're screaming at your friend because they crashed the ship into a rock. I think that's what makes Sea of Thieves work. It doesn't take itself too seriously. You can have a serious fight with another ship one minute and then spend the next 20 minutes playing instruments on your ship for no reason. You can be trying to make money and then get distracted by something completely random. I also think the fact that the game is still getting updates is a good thing. Obviously not every update is going to be amazing and there are going to be things that players don't like, but at least it shows that the developers are still putting work into the game. The game has been around for a long time and there is still new stuff happening, which is pretty good to see. I wouldn't say Sea of Thieves is a perfect game. It definitely isn't. There are plenty of things that annoy me about it, and I can understand why people don't like the game. The grinding can get boring, losing your loot sucks, PvP can be frustrating, and sometimes the game just feels like you're doing the same things over and over. But even with all of that, I still think it's a good game. When you have a few friends with you and everyone is having a good time, the problems don't really matter as much. You can make some really funny memories in this game, and that's something that a lot of other games don't really have. I think I would recommend Sea of Thieves, especially if you have friends to play with. If you're planning on playing completely alone, it might not be as fun, but it is still worth trying. Just don't expect everything to go your way because there is always a good chance that some random pirate crew is going to come out of nowhere and ruin your entire day. Overall, Sea of Thieves has a lot of bad sides, but I think the good sides make up for them. It's not a perfect game and it can definitely be frustrating, but when you're having fun with your friends and something completely random happens, it's hard not to enjoy it. The fact that the developers are also working on things like reducing the game size is a nice bonus. Having the game take up way less storage is something that I think a lot of players will appreciate, especially if they can do it without removing the stuff that makes the game fun.

Overall: Good game. Not perfect, definitely has problems, but still worth playing.

NMS is one of those games that you have to be made for. It had a very bumpy start but the devs at Hello Games did not falter and managed to make it a quite impressive piece of work of an insanely huge galaxy that most will probably never explore to a 100% rate. In that manner it does the same like Star Citizen - or what Star Citizen wants to be if it was a complete game that is technically sound. We all know since the last live stream that even the devs at CIG now realized what they produced in 12 years is nothing but a joke. But thats another story.

What unites both games is they are highly immersive and they give you a lot of freedom. Only: there is no real purpose except "discover planet X, plunder resources, scan all fauna/flora, build base, leave, rinse and repeat" - at least it is like this for NMS. SC still has to find it's purpose if it will ever get to that level and someone will not be so reasonable and simply euthanize this project. I think I put some 70 to 80 hours into Star Citizen until 30k CTDs, missing quest objectives, OP AI infantry and senseless mining finally got the best of me and I gave up - because there is really not much more to get. Sure, server meshing is fine and such but it's all just the same in another color.

NMS on the other hand has no such issues - and is by far not coming along as pretentious as SC. And that's a good thing because if you are in games where you just build and trade without any deeper meaning, NMS is for you. I first thought I would not like this game because of the color palette (everything has this candy shop vibe going on) and the fact the whole appeal has a lot less serious approach than SC. But after a couple of hours I got used to it, in fact it really started to grow on me,

However, I found out that this game is what YOU make out of it, not the devs. So you have to know why you play. For me, I did not find this meaning and after 40 hours  I am annoyed and impatient: the base building gets really pointless the minute you realize you CAN do it, you don't have to because it really plays no role; salvaging shipwrecks just adds more to your bank account which will already burst after 20 hours if you know how to do it. Creating and managing your own fleet does  not add much depth but only more complexity. The planets look all more or less the same and as far as I can tell, none of them are seriously inhabited. The eco systems also do not make much sense if you e.g. realize that extreme heat storms that roast you at 150 degrees do nothing to fauna and flora. OK, imagination is unlimited and I can play along here pretending such resistant life forms exist. But it feels odd to me.

It's definitely a cool game if you like just sandboxing around and in that course it could even be a cozy game. But I expect something more. [b]Baldur's Gate 3 is my new favorite game of all time.[/b]

I picked it up during early access and it hooked me right from the start. After about four hours I shelved it, since the full launch was only four months away and I really wanted to play it from beginning to end. Now I have over 500 hours in the game, I've played through it more times than I can count, and I've 100% completed it. That's something I haven't done with any other game in my Steam library.

[b]The Characters & Story[/b]
The narrator is amazing. Her voice work and the writing behind her lines are so well done.

The story is decent, but what really makes the game for me is the cast. Every character you meet along the way is fantastic, and they make you genuinely want to help them. My favorite is Karlach. She is such a sweet, kind-hearted character, and her questline is really good. The best questline in the game, though, belongs to Shadowheart. Her story can go in multiple directions, and you get to influence who she really becomes in the end. The romance system is decent too, though some romances are far better than others.

[b]Combat & Builds[/b]
The builds are incredibly customizable. Honor Mode kicked my butt and I had to restart more times than I'd like to admit, but my Gloom Stalker/Assassin build finally got me through it. The most fun build I've played is a Monk/Rogue. You get so many attacks, and the movement is amazing. Between the build variety and the mod support, the game stays fresh even on a sixth or seventh run.

[b]Player Freedom[/b]
You can play it however you want. If you want to be the good guy and save everyone, you can. If you want to be the bad guy and take everyone out, you can do that too. The replayability is crazy.

[b]My One Criticism[/b]
Act 1 is top tier, above and beyond anything else, but Acts 2 and 3 just don't feel as fleshed out. Act 1 gives you so many places to explore, from the open world at the start, down into the Underdark, all the way to the Grymforge. The later acts don't quite match that. Don't get me wrong, they're still better than most games being made today, and I would rather play them than most AAA releases. The drop is just noticeable.

I can't say enough good things about this game. The characters, the storytelling, and the performances from every voice actor are outstanding. If you haven't played it yet, do yourself a favor and pick it up.

[b]Final Score: 10/10[/b]

Valheim is one of the most grindy, repetitive games of the 2020s.

It takes stamina to do everything, for some reason. Having to stop and wait for stamina regeneration to be able to level ground or build is infuriating and a useless waste of time. This means you have to eat max stamina food just to complete a build or a big terraforming project in a reasonable timeframe. Food alternates through the game from absolutely not worth to so easy to make you don't even have to farm the ingredients. Some recipes are stupidly expensive. You need 8 berries to make jam; that's 8 whole berry bushes because, despite looking bountiful, every bush drops ONE berry. Berry bushes cannot be planted or propagated in any way.

Even if berry bushes could be planted, farming is also a terrible experience. Planting a seed costs stamina, you have to plant one seed at a time and you have no grid or other reference to help you. For some reason, Iron Gate thought it to be intelligent game design to let you plant saplings too close together, knowing full well that they would wither because "plant needs more space"; they could have easily made the placement guide red or orange to signal an issue, but they didn't. The sickle, which should help you harvest large fields, is pretty slow and not even worth the walk to the chest to get, mileage may vary depending on field size.

Each biome has, on average, three things to do/see. The game is mostly walking AND sailing. Sailing is, probably, the worst part of the game; the developers chose to drop the ocean rework off the roadmap, probably because it already took them five years to add three biomes, meaning one of the biomes you'll spend the most time sailing in is completely uninteresting, and you'll probably doomscroll while the ship sails on its own. Biomes past the black forest are a continuous assault on the player, you will have no peace until you manage to break line of sight with the endless spawning hordes; since stone fortifications quickly become obsolete, and later stone upgrades aren't much better, I take it the devs fully intend for the player to just raise the ground itself as protection, a mechanic that I assumed was an exploit initially, but the lack of tools to defend structures leads me to believe they fully intend for you to do that.

The combat is basic but tolerable. You'll do plenty of this, especially if you're playing on 1x drops in multiplayer. This game does not respect your time and you shouldn't feel bad for playing on 1.5x or even 3x drops. You will still have more than enough grinding to do. Some weapons have no early game counterpart, meaning you won't be able to start farming experience for them until the Mistlands. Leveling anything is torture, with skills naturally plateauing around level 50, because the game doesn't give an option to remove XP loss on death, this can range from annoying to genuinely soul-crushing. The easiest skill to level is running, with your main weapon coming in second. Some skills are genuinely useless and exist only as a mockery of the player, leveling swimming or fishing is a complete time sink that, nonetheless, has achievements tied to it. Leveling magic will never happen naturally and I will not listen to liars pretending it can happen; the only useful way to level blood magic is by using an esoteric setup dreamt up by the utterly deranged on Reddit, look it up if you want to use summons.

All in all, Valheim's greatest contribution was inspiring similar games in the same genre, like Dragonwilds and Enshrouded.

I love this game, I can play it for hours and hours. I never seem to get tired of it.
Is it for everyone? No... it's actually a very difficult survival game. Although sometimes, it is calm and peaceful, if you let your guard down you can be ambushed by a horde of zombies. You will learn the hard way that taking risks is not a good idea when your life is on the line. 

- Base construction 10/10
Lots of choices for decorations, useful furniture, and practical items. It's really fun to plan and build up your base. Even if you die, you can return there with a new character.

- Combat 6/10
I wouldn't play this game specifically to fight zombies. Guns are very loud and attract hordes of zombies. You easily get overwhelmed if you focus on fighting all the time. Using your car for crushing zombies is also a bad idea because it gets damaged easily, just like a real car would. When a zombie is too close, it can be difficult to keep control and defend yourself. However, I consider this very realistic, so I wouldn't say it's bad... just not set up for fun and easy combat. Your character can improve and get better at fighting, but getting too confident will get you killed.

- Complexity 10/10
This game takes a long time to learn and things change overtime because of seasons. There is so much to discover and try that you can't really run out of things to do. There is a large number of skills and recipes to master. It would take months to complete all of it.

- Survival Realism 10/10
Out of all the zombie games I played, this one had the best realism. I like how detailed every system is, you can even reinforce your clothes by adding leather, cloth, or denim patches, and just like an attack dog training suit, it will protect you from bites.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game, and the story is amazing. Personally, I really liked playing as male V.
It is sad because this game had so much potential, but CD Projekt Red did not develop many parts of the world enough. For example, driving could be better, there could have been flying cars, more stores you can actually enter, and more NPCs with different voices and animations.
When you leave the main storyline and just explore the city, the game can still feel empty. It has improved compared to before, but I expected much more. The physics, cars, NPCs, and animations can still be very buggy and sometimes do not feel smooth. It is disappointing that even after almost six years, some of these problems are still there.
I think Cyberpunk 2077 could have been one of the greatest games of all time if it had received another five or six years of development, but CD Projekt Red made the choice to release it when they did.
The game is still worth playing and finishing, especially for the main story. The Dogtown/Phantom Liberty storyline is also very good. But if you like exploring the open world and paying attention to small details, you will notice many of the game's weaknesses.
I finished the game, experienced all the endings, and completed all the achievements. My favorite ending is “(Don't Fear) The Reaper.” I really enjoyed the idea of V and Johnny deciding to attack Arasaka Tower alone instead of risking the lives of their friends.
Even with all its problems, I recommend Cyberpunk 2077

Almost at 1,000 hours and it's safe to say that having been 6 star (the top rank) for a while, and then just playing for pure fun, this game will keep on giving and the content that the developers keep adding can't be argued with. 

If you want a game that's insanely fast-paced, then this isn't the game for you. It has a far more methodical, and honestly, satisfying form of gunplay that revolves around reloading, distance, and rotation based tactics. The game also doesn't rely on a 'better' gun (although there are "stronger" weapons) or a weird meta game to be fun or give you a fighting chance. 

Its strengths don't rely on what most extraction shooters do which is grinding and opening containers in an endless loop and dopamine cycling. Instead Hunt bases its gameplay around a wonderful mix of PVPVE that rewards players passively by clearing areas to make them safer to fight rather than endlessly fighting spongey npcs, thinking before firing, learning layouts of compounds and having patience.

I play solo, so I can't speak for how the team play feels with random people, but the game itself is mechanically super sound. The weapon variation is huge, and the custom ammunition means that you can play a huge variety of styles, so the game really can be played in the approach that you want. Sniper? Go for it. Melee only? Why not. Double poison bow? If you're a masochist, hell yeah! 

I have taken long breaks from the game, because when you've 1,000 odd hours you tend to end up playing out of habit, but whenever I come back to the game I find myself loving it because it has kept fresh in recent updates especially. Also, I'm decent at the game, so that helps - ha!
