Should you play Factorio? The simplest answer is, "Dear god, yes you absolutely must." Some nuance is involved, however, when you factor in things like relationships, responsibilities, and personal health & hygiene. You may want to reconsider playing Factorio if any of these three things is of any notable significance in your life as there will be little time for anything else besides playing Factorio if you start to play Factorio.

I first played Factorio 9 years ago (version 0.14) and it has been afforded a rent-free mansion in my head ever since. Don't let my low play-time fool you; when I first got the game I was the type of guy that had quite a lot going in terms of the aforementioned things; I was dating lots of girls, had a big-shot high-falutin' consulting job, and spent quite a bit of time and money on my wardrobe. But I never stopped thinking about Factorio. I recently got back into it, and would like to say one thing in particular that I believe is important.

Factorio is a shining example of what games used to be. An original idea, developed with love and deep personal commitment to their core concept. A whole-ass game that is actually completed, in fact it was complete on release. This is not Early Access slop that was rushed out to catch a content-creator wave and has since limped along on a starvation budget and skeleton team because the developers took their money and ran. This is not a Live Service money pit, designed entirely to exploit the consumer. Live service and Steam Early Access have bankrupted the soul of our industry, and Factorio stands as a testament to how to make a game that respects the people playing it.  Thus I support it, and so should you (if you care).

Almost 200h in. I bought the game after season 6 was released, so I started and finished season 6 first in around 100h. Then, I switched to season 3. The fact that you can replay past season, with amazing and different « seasonal events » (meteorites in season 3!) is amazing. The game is by far the best co-op multiplayer game ever — you can play solo, but really, it’s so much fun with others! I started playing alone with randoms before playing with a friend, but I still very often play with randoms. The community is amazing and the game has this superbe gameplay that makes it both engaging and relaxing at the same time.

You need to cooperate, and just pinging stuff around and watching over your mate is as easy as just thinking about it. The « Rock and stone! » shouting binds the whole community together, which is the sanest and most welcoming community ever, all game genres combined — trust me, newcomers are well welcomed and there is no feeling of misplaced ego.

For the rest, the gameplay loop is addictive. Procedural generation is probably the best I have seen so far — some caves and biomes create a poetic walking, as well as intense fights. You have primary and secondary missions, but the procedural generation variables (cave complexity, length, mutators — warnings and anomalies) make every run so unique that you will never feel completely at ease and will always have this amazing feeling of really exploring.

About exploration, the game is full of stuff to do besides the primary and secondary objectives (by the way, I haven’t said it: 10+ primary mission types, 12+ biomes!). You can find rare events, such as BET-C mini bosses, corruptors, etc. as well as seasonal events (the Bone Collector for season 6, meteorite and litophage outbreaks in season 3, etc.), dynamic/core events, climate and environment changes (blizzard, rain, etc.). It’s just fantastic. You will also need to collect hops to craft beer on the Space Rig to share a good time with your friend and benefit from buffs from special beer in the next run.

I rarely comment on Steam games I own, but this one hits special. I played many games for many hours, and I eventually get bored, but DRG is something special. You basically never run out of content, and I still discover stuff from time to time I didn’t know — chasm formation, enemy types, etc. With the arrival of season 7 in December 2026 and season 8 + expansion DLC in 2027, we have long days ahead to have fun.

FOR ROCK AND STONE!

PS: by the way, for those wondering, I play on Linux with Proton and the game runs flawlessly.

Satisfactory remains, so far, the only game of my 500-odd that I've 100%-ed. After two years of bouncing off other games in the genre, I've finally twigged why.

A common feature of management games, which often seeps into the factory sub-genre, is that you deal with unstable systems. Congratulations, you've supplied air, water, food and beds for your colonists. Grow. Do they still have enough air, water, food, beds? Now worry about comfort. Do they still have enough air, water, food, beds, comfort? Now worry about healthcare. Do they still have enough air water, food, beds, comfort, healthcare? Now worry about training. Do they still have enough air water, food, beds, comfort, healthcare, training? Now worry about luxuries. Do they st- oh, no, you took your eye off one of those balls while worrying about the next one, now you've got a crisis to deal with.

When I sit down at my PC ready for a gaming session, what makes me relaunch the game I played yesterday is excitement at the prospect of doing the next thing. If what's facing me instead is the prospect of spending half my time and attention babysitting the bits I've already done, that makes me want to move on. Satisfactory kept me booting it back up again day after day, week after week.

The key difference was that if I did things right, then I could get a factory, or section of a factory, to DONE - and forget about it. Great, my supercomputer factory is producing four supercomputers per minute; I will never have to worry about it again and can turn my attention fully to the next thing. If I DO have to go back to it, it's because it turns out I did something wrong and there's a problem to solve, not to tick a box of inevitable maintenance. For example - resource nodes aren't finite. The rate they can supply is capped, but you're never going to have to tear down and rebuild just because the local resources ran out.

Now, don't let me give you the wrong impression - you WILL go back. You will tinker, tear down, rebuild. But it's not because you have to. It's because you WANT to. It's because new tech you've unlocked, or new techniques you've figured out, or simply a grander vision you've come up with, mean that what you already built is no longer, ahem, satisfactory. You're gonna do it bigger, BETTER. It's a new project, it feels like a new project, it's just as fun second time round.

The factory must grow. NOT, the factory must be maintained.

Valheim is that rare survival game that respects your time while still demanding your attention. It drops you into a procedurally generated tenth Norse realm as a fallen warrior tasked with proving yourself worthy of Odin's hall—and from the moment you wash ashore with nothing but a rag tunic and a dream, it never lets go.

The Good

The atmosphere is unmatched. From the haunting Meadows at dawn to the oppressive Swamps at night, every biome tells a story through its sound design, color palette, and creature ecology. The music swells at exactly the right moments, and the first time a troll crashes through the trees, you'll feel genuine fear.

Combat is simple but satisfying. Blocking, parrying, dodging, and stamina management create a rhythm that rewards patience over button-mashing. Every boss fight feels like a genuine test of everything you've learned.

The building system is deep, flexible, and genuinely creative. Whether you're throwing up a quick lean-to or engineering a multi-tiered longhouse with a working harbor, the structural physics add a layer of problem-solving that few survival games match.

Progression is meaningful. Each biome feels like a real escalation—new resources, new threats, new tools. The moment you smelt your first bronze or forge your first iron weapon is genuinely rewarding.

The Not-So-Good

The grind can be brutal. Mining copper and tin, hauling ore, and smelting bronze is a rite of passage, but it's also tedious. The game respects your time in some ways but not others.

The UI and inventory management leave something to be desired. Sorting chests, managing weight, and navigating menus can feel clunky after dozens of hours.

The difficulty spikes hard. The jump from the Black Forest to the Swamp, or the Plains to the Mistlands, can feel like hitting a wall if you're not prepared.

The Verdict

Valheim is a triumph of atmosphere, progression, and player freedom. It's not perfect—the grind is real and the difficulty curve is steep—but it's one of the most immersive and rewarding survival games ever made. Whether you're sailing into the unknown, building a cathedral to Odin, or getting chased by a troll at 3 a.m., Valheim delivers an experience that stays with you long after you log off.

Starts out as a survival crafter until you eventually start automating more and more increasingly complex products. No survival mechanics like hunger or anything, but keep an eye on your power production at all times. You can get incredibly in depth with optimisation if you want to, but it's not really necessary to beat the game. I completed in around 300 hours, and never expected to enjoy this game as much as I did.

Be warned: if you have an addictive personality, this game will keep you up at night.

You can play the game how you want: you can build everything in a giant megafactory and import your raw resources for processing centrally, or you can build smaller, more focussed factories around the map and then use vehicles, trains or eventually drones to move things around between factories.

The game has great progression, and guides you well to learn how to build factories of increasing complexity without getting too overwhelming. Clear objectives are given at all stages (my main issue with these sorts of games is lack of a clear goal), and you get to decide how to progress toward and eventually accomplish them.

Highly recommended!

I think I've played enough hours to finally give this game my actual opinion now and even gave it a bunch of major updates to try to redeem itself as I have owned this game since 2017 and my 360+ hours have been divided across all those years of updates to be extremely fair:

1. This is forced competitive PvP at its core. If you came here expecting a relaxed sandbox to fly modern jets, sail warships, or enjoy physics-accurate combined-arms warfare at your own pace, be warned—the core loop is an aggressive, high-stress PvP meat grinder. I do not encourage CASUALS to pick up this game. Yes there is PVE but they are either seasonal or the wait queues are endless because nobody queues up for them almost EVER . . . Even if you do land one, it pays extremely abysmally reinforcing the WHY nobody plays them. This was designed on purpose to fuel the player frustration and paying model because Gaijin directly claims "it is to make sure PVP queues will stay populated" as if PVP frustration and player tilting is the ONLY way for a game to make money.

2. The sandbox experience is the ONLY THING I'd recommend but it is locked behind a pay-and/or-grind paywall. The most enjoyable way to play casually—Custom Battles with zero repair costs or penalties—requires you to ALREADY OWN AND FULLY UPGRADE the vehicles in your hangar. To fly modern jets or sail warships without touching public PvP, you HAVE TO drop hundreds of USD real money on premium packs and sometimes that's not even good enough because if you have any main tree vehicles you want, your ONLY option is to sacrifice hundreds of hours grinding through mandatory public matches.

3. About premium vehicles: Community gatekeeping and toxicity are rampant about them. If you DO purchase a high-tier vehicle to skip the multi-year grind and fly what you actually care about, a vocal segment of hyper-competitive elitists will actively harass and hunt you down as a "wallet warrior." They take pride in "sanitizing" matches of casual players who didn't spend ten years grinding prop planes. You WILL be painted with a star in a circle by your name to call you out that you bought a premium vehicle which paints a big target on you by these merciless fanatics who take this game far too seriously.

4. Matchmaking mechanics actively punish objective and casual playstyles. High-BR matches rapidly devolve into 4-minute supersonic missile furballs in ARB and vehicles with tech gimmicks you're never gonna be properly prepared for from radio-guided missiles against WWII to Korean War era mid-high BR ships or an 8 inch gun on a tank that guarantees one-shot deaths along with a tank that has barely the technology to have guided antitank missiles in a mid-high BR. Teams frequently collapse or wipe out the enemy before ground-attackers or bombers even reach their targets, triggering automatic match ends that slap you with 0% battle activity and zero rewards for your time. Then there are low-BR matches where if you have zero knowledge of proper dogfighting and aircraft stats memorized, you will get outmaneuvered and pilot-sniped in utter shock and confusion. 

War Thunder features unmatched vehicle models, damage models, and flight physics, and there is fun to be had if you strictly stay in user-hosted Custom Battles. However, Gaijin's predatory progression design and a toxic, gatekeeping player base make it impossible to recommend to casual gamers who just want to fly cool jets and sail ships in peace. There is so much potential, but currently Gaijin will never get their heads out of their hindquarters to ever stop and think if their predatory sales mechanics on how this game still somehow reels in money, albeit BLOOD MONEY from players only paying out of pure rage and frustration to get the upper hand or grind the trees a LITTLE faster, it is all just pointless and a waste of what colored hair you got on your scalp that did not turn gray yet . . .

Valheim has a great atmosphere, nice visuals, good music, and the first hours can be genuinely exciting. 

Exploring a new biome, building your first proper base, getting a better boat, preparing for a boss, all of that works.

The problem is that once the novelty wears off, you start noticing how empty and repetitive the game really is.

One of the strangest design decisions is the portal restriction on metals. Since metals are literally what you need to progress, the game forces you to spend an absurd amount of time carrying ore from point A to point B like a mule. Mine it, walk it to the shore, load the boat, sail for ages, unload it, walk it again, maybe transfer it to another boat, then finally reach your base.

This is not difficulty.
It is not skill-based.
It is not interesting decision-making.
It is just logistics and repetition used to artificially extend playtime.

When your main obstacle is not an enemy, a boss, a dangerous mechanic or a difficult dungeon, but simply “you are not allowed to teleport this item, so waste another hour transporting it”, that is not good game design to me.

The storage system also feels unnecessarily restrictive. Chests hold very little, inventories fill constantly, weight limits are annoying, and the game keeps generating huge amounts of materials. So instead of spending your time exploring or fighting, you spend a surprisingly large part of it sorting boxes, moving materials and doing repeated transport runs.

Combat is also fairly basic and can become repetitive quickly. Enemy variety is not amazing, many areas feel sparse, and once you understand a biome, there is often very little surprise left. The game sometimes feels much bigger than the amount of actual content inside it.

Building is probably one of the strongest parts of Valheim, but even that can become frustrating because of stamina, carrying limits and the amount of resource hauling required.

In solo, I honestly cannot recommend it unless you really enjoy slow survival games and repetitive logistics. The game constantly feels like it is wasting your time on purpose.

With friends, however, I can absolutely understand the appeal. Sharing jobs, sailing together, building a village, exploring as a group and laughing when everything goes wrong can make the same tedious systems much more enjoyable.

Solo: strongly not recommended.
With friends: probably a completely different experience.

Valheim has a very good foundation, but too often it confuses inconvenience with difficulty and repetition with content.

[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
In POE you are a criminal sentenced to death but instead shipped to the cursed continent of Wraeclast. You start with nothing and end up fighting Gods and other divine being. But to get there you will go through many beautifully crafted levels with many systems. At first it is intimidating and for your first run I highly recommend using a guide from for example [url=https://mobalytics.gg/poe/builds] Mobalytics [/url].

POE is an older game but can be measured against new releases as it has received and continues to receive updated. I've been an avid fan of Diablo and Diablo 2 since they were released (I was one of the first in D2 in Europe to hit lvl 99 back in the day). D3 was OK but not what I was looking into an ARPG and I've avoided D4 ever since the "don't you have phones" and all of the monetization; it's clear the Blizzard of old is no longer there.

POE is F2P but it doesn't mean P2W. Every couple of months new supporter packs are released that are time limited. But they are just cosmetics and the game comes with plenty. Only buy those if you want to support the developers. At most you probably spend about £30 to make your life easier with more inventory tabs but only gets those after you've played the game for a while and it's still not required for the first play through but it will help a lot managing all the loot you collect later on. Consider the campaign the trial or demo version to see if the game is for you.

You pick one of the available 7 classes when you start the game. As you progress you can then further specialise the class in the direction you like. There is so much to choose from that it will keep you busy for a long time. 

The campaign has 10 acts and those are really just the tutorial to avoid overloading you with the many systems POE has. After that the real game begins and it's all about completing maps at an increased difficulty for better rewards. Following that you arrive at the real end-game. It's a big game for sure :-).

It's great solo but multiplayer is good too. There is even PVP if you're interested in that. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
It has the most extensive systems I have ever seen in any ARPG. Just the skill tree alone is massive. This allows for a lot of experimentation to find the ideal setup. Your class is just a starting point and you can adjust how you feel fit.

I love the voice acting, the enemies and the graphical effects; GGG voice actors and artists are some of the best in class. 

There are many different leagues you can play (comparable to seasons in other games), including hard core and you can build even your own if you feel like.

The developers play their game and there are frequent updates. Tournaments are organised and if you watch them on Twitch you even get nice stuff from time to time.

The inner loot goblin is always satisfied when doing one of the many side activities in game. There is so much to collect and there is a variation of activities to keep it all fresh. 

You have your own hideout that you can decorate as you please. Later this becomes your central hub.

There is in-game trading with other players and multiplayer is supported. There is also a [url= https://www.pathofexile.com/trade ]trade post [/url] where you can buy and sell items you want or find.
The game plays really fast at times - much higher speed than D2; which is great it’s a constant adrenaline rush. The drawback is if your build has a weakness there is little room for error on the high end levels as it leaves you with little time to counter act.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
There is definitely a deep learning curve hence I advise using a guide for the first play through so you get an understanding of the basics. 

End game (lvl 90 - 100) can be really challenging depending on your build. Some require expensive (as in rare items they are player trade) to be effective and the AI will relentlessly punish you if you have a weak build to the point you want to give up. 

To counter this you probably want to start with a character that is less depended on gear and more on skills which are easier to come by. A second build could be one that is more depending on gear as you can use the first character to farm where necessary. In general: ranged class / skills are easier than melee especially later in the game.

For every new character you create you need to go through all 10 acts of the campaign; thankfully because of the stash, your hideout and all the other different game modes, including the progress in the second part (Atlas) is account wide it's not a major issue but it would be better if you would be given the option to skip the whole campaign after the first time that you've completed it (similar to like GW2 for example).

I disapprove of the lootbox mechanic introduced every season. It's not required, it's not in your face but it can cause serious issues for people that are vulnerable to gambling addiction. The positive maybe is that all the loot from the loot boxes are released later in the MTX store but still it should not be in the game.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are no DLCs other than supporter packs that only add cosmetics to the game. There is a microtransactions (MTX) store to buy cosmetics and QoL items. If you want to get any of those wishlist them and wait for a sale (every couple of weeks). Note that some of the MTX from POE is compatible with POE2 in particular most of the inventory tabs. 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is now. This is true for POE. I wish I had discovered it earlier but I'm happy I did eventually. If you're into ARPG it's one of the best games to get. Highly recommended.

I purchased this game on Steam along with a DLC, and after playing for approximately ONE HOUR, my account was banned by Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC).

I have NEVER used cheats, hacks, or any software intended to give me an unfair advantage. I had barely even started playing the game, yet I was suddenly banned without any specific explanation of what I supposedly did wrong. The ban notification simply states that I violated the rules, without identifying the alleged violation.

I contacted the developer hoping to get an explanation. Instead, they simply told me that EAC issued the ban, redirected me to EAC's appeal process, and closed the support ticket, stating that I would receive no further responses. So the developer takes no further responsibility for helping me understand what happened, and I am left trying to appeal a ban that nobody has properly explained.

I paid for the game. I paid for the DLC. I spent barely an hour playing. And now I have to spend my time appealing a ban despite never having intentionally cheated.

I understand the need for anti-cheat systems, but legitimate players should not have to deal with unexplained bans and such an frustrating support experience. If your system can ban a new player this quickly, at the very least, there should be a clear explanation and a meaningful review process.

I have submitted an appeal to EAC, but there is no guarantee that the ban will be lifted.

At this point, I cannot recommend this game based on my experience. I wanted to play the game I paid for, not spend my time chasing support teams just to find out why I was banned.

It's hard not to recommend NMS after putting in the time for a full loop and seeing what all they've done for the game over the time I've had it (for free).  They took the time to resurrect a product from the disaster it had at launch and create what truly feels like a passion project.  Regardless of your thoughts on it, that is something to be respected.  There's a lot here and, for the price, it's certainly worth it.

Granted, even with all the work this game has, it's definitely not a perfect product and I doubt it ever will be. I'm not the biggest fan of the plot or how same-y the game can get over time.  I feel like you could've eased off the throttle and let some of that happen a bit over time, let the user get to bits and pieces slower than this game decides to throw at you.

What it does excel at, for the most part, is being a good sandbox title for the genre...but there's plenty of things you will eventually run into that will get cyclical over time due to the nature of it.  The bases are definitely one of the worst offenders, since they tend to be similar in design just with random coats of paint and NPC placement.  Getting off the ground may be difficult for some as well, especially if you get a seed that generates you into hellfire or similar right off the bat, and I have seen a few situations of others getting frustrated at that and giving up not very long afterwards.

Still, if you can get past that, there's a lot to be had here.  It feels like a much simpler take on the space exploration genre and seems to be better suited to casual players than it would be if you took on something a little bit more advanced such as Elite: Dangerous, which I've put in quite a bit more time for.  I think this is actually a very good entry point into the genre in modern times, with that said.  Space sims aren't exactly the most straightforward games to get into and I think this one does that job quite well for what it is.  With friends, it's even better.

After 7,000 hours, I think I'm finally qualified to review Dota 2. This isn't a game anymore. It's a long-term commitment with occasional gameplay. The game itself is still incredible. The depth, strategy, hero interactions, itemization, and those completely insane comeback moments are things you simply dont get anywhere else. But the experience surrounding the game is what i would like to point out.

● The Report System
You can get reported for simply because someone didn't like your decision or yourself personally, not the gameplay you've given to the team as contribution. And sometimes losing a game apparently gives people enough motivation to investigate your entire steam profile and somehow involve your family tree.
Bro, I missed one stun. I didn't insult your ancestors.

● Behavior Score
Honestly, i like the concept. It actually gives toxic players consequences, and restricting certain features for extremely low behavior scores makes sense. It's basically dota saying: “𝘠𝘰𝘶'𝘷𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘮𝘪𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘱𝘩𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘦𝘴. 𝘗𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵.” 
But sometimes it still feels like you're maintaining a credit score for your personality.

● The Great MMR Reset
After all the MMR inflation and resets, matchmaking can sometimes feel like opening a loot box. You don't really know what you're getting. You just pray that your four teammates are locked in, awake, and emotionally present.
If someone is already AFK, feeding, or typing “gg” before the horn, you already know where this is going.

And yet, somehow, dota is still dota, -everything can work (cr:BigDaddyn0tail)
There's always something new to learn. A better ward, a better timing, a new interaction, a different item build. You can play the same hero for hundreds of games and still discover you've been playing it wrong for five years.
Someone makes the perfect initiation, another buys back, the carry gets the crucial item, and suddenly a completely lost game becomes the greatest match you've ever played. ONLY THEN, you queue again because apparently 7,000 + 1000 hours wasn't enough suffering.

Dead By Daylight what is it like to play this game as a killer? the community has constantly complained and moaned about killers over the years. Their abilities then get nerfed, as do their perks, more often than survivor perks, and you aren't allowed to slug or tunnel without receiving death threats or profanity. Survivors get what they want. Killers do complain as well however, I'd say killers don't get what they want or complain nearly as much, based on my experiences. In summary, survivors have always been prioritized.

2v8 queue times are like 30+ minutes, give or take. Killer queue times are around 5 minutes. Meanwhile, if you want to play survivor, you can expect to load into a game within 1 minute in either 2v8 or standard 1v4.

You have to play on top of your game as killer and make seemingly no mistakes. If you do, or you don't, it can make or break your game. You feel severely handicapped as killer, even with the stronger ones. To have genuine competition, you need to play superbly, while playing as survivor often feels much more easy and laid-back in contrast. It's much more accustomed for them, and this isn't even really referring to high-level MMR where every game is sweaty and you're going against tryhard SWFs. These high level survivor players have to work hard for their result; it's just killers have to work harder.

There's like a 1 in 3 chance that when you get stunned in chase, they teabag and deliberately choose to be toxic, often times because they are insecure of the fact that they suck. Of course, this and teabagging at the gate, which happens A LOT too.

When I used to play, I used to be able to have a good shot at winning most games with killer, but now it's much harder to win as killer. You're actually seemingly more likely to lose than win, not even getting 3 kills.

There is an element of bias, of course, because I think most of my playtime has been playing killer. However, that's not to say I haven't played survivor. I have in fact, played hundreds of hours of survivor, so I know what it's like. If you're solo queuing as survivor, I will say it can probably go either way, but that's also because my survivor MMR is super low since I never had a fantastic win rate. If you're with a competent group and you're tryharding, this will make it much more difficult for the killer to win in most cases. You also don't count a win if you only kill 2 survivors it's a draw.

The game can be fun. Maybe it's more fun for you if you don't take it competitively, idk. There's no fixed rank system in this game and probably never will be, but getting better and improving usually makes the game more fun, at least for me. But I know that some people find fun in just hanging out with their friends and are more casual.

In the lobby as killer, you now can't see the survivors' prestige. This should be an option to turn off instead of removing it altogether, in my opinion. This keeps everybody happy from complaining and gives grinding prestiges more worthwhile and motivating.

If you love playing DnD for an equal mix of roleplay and optimizing for combat, and you have a decent idea of how DnD works you'll be set to know what you're doing in building a character and playing in turn based combat. If not, there is a learning curve at the top of the game, you're going to have a lot of options thrown at you and it's a lot to learn all at once. On the other hand as well if you are expecting an exact 1:1 replica of 5e tabletop play, you'll probably be grumpy too, but if you can accept that they had to jigsaw 5e rules to work in a video game because they can't possibly account for every single subclass, spell, or feat the way you can on table top then you'll learn to love the off center replica of DnD.
All of the romances have different weights, but you don't HAVE to romance any of the characters if you don't want. Your decisions do actually effect the way your companions view you as well, so not everyone will take an interest in your character, some may be antagonistic towards you, but it is possible to keep everyone pleasant with you without too much going out of your way. That being said there is also lots of replay ability, you can zig zag all over the place with choices, explore different paths, go wild with it. If you're set on one specific way of things going, you're going to have to save scum a lot, but it's not impossible to get your ideal outcome.
Of course the voice acting is amazing, the writing is excellent and varied, the locations are stunning, the story arc is great, so on so forth.

My only complaint is the multiplayer is a little janky. Ran into so many glitches playing with friends that I never have in my solo runs. Save often if you play with friends over distance so you can reload as needed.

Other than that, I love the game top to bottom, I will still be playing this decades from now I am sure.

Been a huge fan of the farming/life game genre since the OG, Harvest Moon on the SNES, the first game that started the farming genre afaik.  It may seem weird to some people, a game about doing chores... Played many other Harvest Moon, Rune Factory, and the subsequent Story of Seasons/HM split games along with some other titles to death and tried many others before and since SDV.  Despite all my forays, SDV remains the best farming game ever made imo, even now 10 years later.  

It helps that the fanbase is so huge and it was such a ridiculous success.  Hard to imagine only one man built this masterpiece.  Because of its popularity there seem to be thousands of mods, some being expansion mods which drastically change the game and story, others utility and QoL, others visuals, theres even a pron mod (XXX) that I would never get due to morality and silliness....so that you can create your own new experience.

I had spent about 200 hours in it 7 years ago, 7 years later I came back to experience the updates I had missed out on in the Vanilla over that time period.  I did get a few mods but mostly utility, QoL and visual mods.  Still as addictive as the first time I played it. 

I guess its not for everyone, but this is one of the greatest games ever made even if you dont like this niche.  Have not been playing anything else for a few weeks now again...from reading update/patch notes there was a ton added since my last playthrough and an endgame that is much more fleshed out as it seems.

Compared to other big name farm titles, like Fields of Mistria, this game just has such a richness and depth, and a charm with the beautiful pixel art, that other games which are touted as being equals pale in comparison.  I was disappointed with Fields of Mistria, and some others; SDV just seems so massively superior in so many ways.

Highly recommend, even if you are into hyper realistic violent shooters or something, I trust many people are eclectic gamers and should at least try it.  One of my all time faves and its a blast to come back to it.

This is definitely not a game everyone likes. The points that make me quit this game:

---Highly not recommended if you usually play alone, without a friend. It's mostly a torment for a single player.
---The death penalty and respawn mechanism may be very frustrating. You may need to run for a long time to recover important gears, and the monsters may kill you again before you get your gears back.
---Terrain interaction and edition is rough to walk on and difficult to work with.
---Port system and mining system are intentionally designed to be inconvenient. Some key resources cannot pass the port, and it will waste a lot of time to carry and run back and force. Meanwhile, you need too may minerals to upgrade and cannot skip this. This process takes too much time, and may be a very boring part, and may exhaust your interest in this game. 
---The early game may be boring for some friends. However, the middle and later game experience may become very harassing and frustrating for some others.
---From beta to release, the game mechanism has little improvement. It's basically just adding more and more loathly monsters to torture you. Again, the sheer number of monsters is not suitable for a single player. You will be chased around by groups of monsters very often.
---Whenever you enter a new region, they will kill you multiple times, even if you finish and farm everything in the last region, and think yourself prepared. The feeling of rewarding and getting stronger may be very little, and the feeling of frustration and suffering may grow. This can make you quit.

If you enjoy all above, go ahead and play this. It will be a good game for you.

No Man’s Sky behaves as two completely different games, delivering a masterclass in sandbox mechanics while simultaneously subjecting players to one of the most frustrating narrative campaigns ever designed. When treated purely as an open-world exploration simulator, the game achieves something genuinely impressive. The sheer scale of the universe, the seamless transition from walking on a planet's surface to breaking through the atmosphere into deep space, and the freedom to build bases and manage fleets create a compelling sandbox environment.
However, the moment a player attempts to follow the main story paths, this sense of wonder is entirely replaced by a miserable and tedious chore. The campaign is fundamentally a sequence of artificial roadblocks designed to force the player into a repetitive cycle of jumping from system to system without any meaningful payoff. Instead of providing an engaging narrative, the story serves as a shallow excuse to trap players in endless warp animations, which are nothing more than hidden loading screens that completely destroy the pacing of the game.
Progress is constantly halted by aggressive time-gating, requiring players to mine hyperdrive fuel or hunt for obscure minerals just to endure yet another warp jump. The narrative itself is a pseudo-philosophical mess that fails to offer any real motivation, turning what should be a liberating space odyssey into a deeply annoying experience. Because the story adds virtually no value and only serves to frustrate the player, the developers would arguably improve the experience by removing the campaign entirely, allowing the impressive core exploration elements to stand on their own without this unnecessary narrative drag.

## Not New-Player Friendly — Ban Evasion Appeal Denied With No Explanation

I’m a very new Rust player. A couple of friends convinced me to start playing, and so far I’ve only played about two wipes, mainly on Rusticated EU Trio. Despite how brutal Rust can be, I actually started really enjoying the game and learning how everything works.

Unfortunately, my experience with Rusticated completely changed over the last few days.

During the wipe, a player named Avokados started repeatedly accusing me of cheating after I killed him several times while he was farming or carrying loot. He claimed that I was doing things such as killing Missile Silo scientists without entering the area, going through walls, and hacking.

None of those accusations were true.

He also kept claiming that I was somehow associated with another player named “123.” I have no idea who that person is. I never teamed with him, never knowingly interacted with him, and have no relationship with him whatsoever.

Then, on September 30, when I tried joining Rusticated EU Trio Monday, I discovered that I had been banned for **“Ban Evading #217243.”**

This confused me even more because this is my first Steam account and my first Rust account.

I immediately submitted an appeal and explained everything in detail. I specifically asked the admins to review my gameplay, server logs, team history, recordings, spectating evidence, or anything else they had available.

The administrator handling my appeal, KoЯn, then asked me:

- How long I had been playing Rust
- Whether I had any other Rust accounts
- Whether I had any other Steam accounts
- How long I had used Steam
- Where I was connecting from
- Whether I had connected from any other locations
- My Discord numerical ID

I answered all of those questions.

I explained that I am a new player, that this is my only Rust account and Steam account, and that I had been playing from New York.

He then responded:

> “I will provide you a SINGLE chance to be straight with me so we can work something out. Please link me ANY and ALL Steam account(s) you may be associated with you or your location.”

Once again, I told him that I genuinely did not have another account.

The next response I received was simply:

> “Appeal denied.”

Followed by:

> “Best of luck playing elsewhere.”

That was it.

No explanation of what account I was supposedly evading a ban from.  
No explanation of what evidence linked me to another banned account.  
No explanation of what information I supposedly lied about.  
No additional questions that could help me identify what was causing the issue.

That is what I find most frustrating.

If Rusticated believes that I am connected to another banned Steam account, I would at least like to know what caused that conclusion so I have an opportunity to explain it. I cannot provide information about an account that I genuinely do not know exists.

I understand that servers need strict rules against cheaters and ban evasion, and I understand that admins cannot necessarily disclose every detail about their detection methods. But there is a major difference between protecting anti-cheat methods and simply telling someone “appeal denied” after they answered every question honestly.

As a new Rust player, this has been an extremely disappointing experience.

I was willing to cooperate, answer questions, provide my Discord ID, explain who I played with, and have my entire gameplay history reviewed. Instead, it felt like the decision had already been made and there was nothing I could possibly say to challenge it.

I’m not asking Rusticated to blindly believe me. I’m asking for a fair review based on actual evidence and, at minimum, some explanation of what I am supposedly being accused of evading.

If there is legitimate evidence connecting me to another banned account, then tell me what I am being accused of so I can respond to it.

But permanently banning a new player for ban evasion, asking them repeatedly about accounts they say they do not have, and then denying the appeal without explaining anything feels extremely unfair.

It's a well-made game for sure, no doubt about it. If it weren't for the great expectations, there might not have been such a great disappointment. I've enjoyed Larian's previous works, loved them even, but there was almost nothing about BG3 to inspire similar feelings.

The story was boilerplate D&D plot, stretched to 100+ hours. Meaningless, emotionless, drawn out tropes and cliches. Only Act 2 made me feel something. I put off wrapping up Act 3 for years from sheer boredom, and felt nothing but tedium by the end.

The characters were as uninteresting as they were horny, I couldn't care about them with the obvious exception of Karlach, who was an actually well-written character. Shadowheart and Astarion were ok-ish. The rest were forgettable. Couldn't decide if the late shoehorning of Jaheira and Minsc was welcome fanservice or a way to distract from the voidness Gale, Wyll and Halsin.

The 5e ruleset is not a good fit for such a game, and Larian's attempts at patching it, while valiant, were not sufficient. Some made it actively worse. The combat was plodding, the interface clunky and annoying, the abilities and items both overwhelming in number and underwhelming in the choices they presented. 5e was never meant to be a lootfest, but the magic items the game showered you with created perverse incentives and boring micromanagement. The gear-juggling was made so much worse by the abysmal stash and inventory system. That they were this bad really boggles the mind.

In the end, the game had nothing to say, nothing to offer but a fun romp that degraded into tedium by the end, Almost nothing about this game is truly memorable, artistically profound or genuinely touching. It was a 150 hour fast food meal served on a really nice and shiny plate. For all its bugs and failures, I will forever remember and cherish Owlcat's glorious mess that is Wrath of the Righteous over the slog that was BG3. Even Larian's own Original Sin games were superior.

Edit: I'm sorry for all the feelings I hurt.

[b]TLDR:[/b] 

No Man's Sky is visually stunning with an endless amount of procedurally generated worlds to explore.  More often than not you are the first to have ever set foot there .... that feeling never gets old.

If you have any interest in space exploration and sci-fi this is a game you need to try once.  There's bound to be something in the game that keeps you occupied for a good amount of time.

Available activities in game:

[list]
[*]Resource gathering
[*]Catalogue discoveries - planets / flora / fauna / minerals
[*]Learn deep lore
[*]Learn alien languages
[*]Points of interest
[*]Fossil hunting
[*]Trading
[*]Farming
[*]Cooking
[*]Fishing
[*]Creature pets
[*]Creature battling
[*]Ground & space combat
[*]Base building
[*]Ship building
[*]Ship hunting
[*]Solo or Multiplayer
[*]Expeditions
[/list]

This is not an exhaustive list.

[b]Pros:[/b]

Endless exploration, visually stunning worlds, deep lore, engaging gameplay, game customisation.

[b]Cons:[/b]

Procedural generation 'patterns' become increasingly noticeable, poor narrative delivery, shallow gameplay mechanics.

If you want more please read on.


[b]Detailed info:[/b]

No Man's Sky is a procedurally generated, exploration sandbox game.

The main storyline is light and linear.  What choices it offers will largely lead to the same outcome with a few exceptions.  The narrative style is, in my opinion, the weakest part of the game.  The deep lore and worldbuilding is interesting but the delivery of this through the main storyline is cryptic, garbled, vague and ambiguous.  Sadly this devalues it.  More recent additions and updates to the canon lore have improved it slightly but my issues with it still remain.

After about 30+ hours, once you've completed the main storyline and the secondary missions, you may wonder what you're supposed to do next.  This is where the 'sandbox' element kicks in.  In fact, in the game 'Log' it explicitly tells you to go off and explore the rest of the universe.  If you're the sort of player that needs constant direction and a concrete 'ending' then this isn't that game.  From now on you're on your own and you will require some imagination to enjoy what the universe has to offer.

Some decide they want to try creating havoc as a pirate or engage in black market trading as a smuggler.  Others prefer a more chilled vibe like creature or fossil collecting becoming a xeno-biologist or exo-archaeologist.  It's cliche but, as they say, you're only limited by your imagination.  The game provides the universe and the tools .... you make your own story.

There's something for everyone here.  You want to roleplay you can, if you prefer to play it casually when you have a free half hour it's perfect for that too.

The gameplay mechanics can feel shallow but is something that is constantly being improved upon.

One of the best additions in recent years has been game customisation.  You don't want to deal with sentinels attacking you every five minutes .... turn combat off or dial it down.  Don't fancy grinding for parts .... start a creative save or keep your normal save but toggle all purchases to free.  It really is very flexible.  You play how you want to.

If you've been hiding under a rock this summer then you may have missed the fact that the game has just entered it's eleventh year and there is no sign yet of the developers slowing down.  They release new content every few months ... for free!

[b]In summary:[/b]

I still get that same buzz every time I enter the atmosphere of a new world, break through the clouds and land in my ship on a planet that the game has randomly generated and has never been seen before.  Even with its flaws I can't recommend this game highly enough.

This game has kept me coming back to it like no other for the last 5 years.  So yeah, I like it .... a lot.

If you are looking at Warframe, ignore the reviews calling it an impenetrable grind. Here is the unvarnished reality after 1,000+ hours:

The In-Game Tutorial is Non-Existent (How to Bypass the Cliff)[/b]
The game never explains damage formulas, status priorities, or modding math. In the past, this meant drowning in 15 open wiki tabs. 
Today, there is a vastly smarter way to play: use an AI model as your personal ship Cephalon to instantly organize drop tables, explain mission requirements, and draft builds. 

THE CRITICAL CAVEAT: AI models will hallucinate outdated patch data and bad mod math. Never spend Forma, Catalysts, or Endo on an AI suggestion alone. Use AI to do the tedious data scraping, then post the build into our clan Discord for human verification. Experienced clanmates will spot bad math or dead synergies in ten seconds. AI drafts it; veterans validate it.

Premium Currency is Earned, Not Bought
Warframe does not lock power behind a paywall. The premium currency (Platinum) flows entirely through a peer-to-peer player market. Almost every core game mode prints trade value:

    Fissures & Relics: Crack open relics on the Star Chart and sell Prime parts.

    Arbitrations: Farm Vitus Essence to buy Galvanized mods that every mid-to-late game player buys for Platinum.

    Nightmare Nodes: Quick two-minute runs for rare mods like Hammer Shot that sell instantly.

    Syndicates: Passively earn standing while running normal missions, then sell Warframe Augments to other players.

    Endgame Modes: Railjack, Archon Hunts, , Steel Path etc provide steady streams of Rivens, arcanes, and rare drops to fund your cosmetics and slots.

The Verdict
The movement is the fastest of any shooter on the market, you will never hit a hard paywall, and you can play entirely at your own pace. If you join, hop into our clan so you don't wander through the Star Chart alone. Highly recommended.

Dota 2 is one of the deepest competitive games ever made, and it is completely free.

Every one of the 120+ heroes is unlocked from day one. You never pay for power: the only things for sale are cosmetics. Few free-to-play games are this fair.

The depth is unmatched. Every match is different because of the hero picks, item builds, map control, and how your team works together. Even after years, you still learn something new: a better item timing, a smarter rotation, or a hero interaction you never knew about. When your team executes a perfect teamfight, nothing else in gaming feels quite like it.

Valve still supports it. Big patches regularly change the map, heroes, and items, so the meta never feels stale. The Linux version runs natively on Vulkan, which is a nice bonus.

It is not for everyone, though:
- The learning curve is brutal. Expect your first 100 hours to feel like a tutorial. Play bot matches and Turbo mode first.
- Matches take 35-50 minutes, and leaving early gets you penalized.
- The community can be toxic. Mute early and focus on your own game.

If you have the patience to learn it, Dota 2 rewards you like almost no other game. Highly recommended for players who enjoy strategy, teamwork, and constant improvement.

No Man's Sky launched with basically nothing.  Ten years and dozens of free major content patches later, it has an immense amount -- but that fix-it-in-post approach has come with the downside that the game is nowhere near as deep or cohesive as some might wish.

Ten years of exceptionally active (and free) development have added dozens of major activities.  If you want to land in an ocean and fish, you can.  If you want to go diving for sunken treasure, you can.  If you want to dig up dinosaur fossils and make your own museum (after mixing and matching excavated bones from different planets into novel skeletons, which I'm pretty sure is how archeology works), you can.  And if you find particularly stunning vistas in the procedurally generated ocean and want to make your fossil museum underwater, you had better believe that you can.

The key phrase there is "if you want to."  The game has no real overarching economy; currency is easily obtained and unappealing to spend, so there's no mechanical incentive to catch rare fish or collect exotic materials or do anything else.  If you don't want to engage with any of these activities, you'll likely wind up uninstalling and leaving one of the (many) Steam reviews concluding that the game is boring -- and that's perfectly fair.

It should also be noted that none of the game's systems aren't as deep as they could be.  There is an admirable variety of parts to use to build your bases and ships, for instance, but glaring gaps remain.  Spaceships only mount several types of weapons, and only a few are competitive -- and ships' shields, maneuverability, and every other statistic essentially boil down to "bigger numbers gooder."  Just as the lack of a balanced economy limits the game's ability to incentivize you to play, the game's focus on breadth over depth imposes a limit on how much each activity will grab you.

Perhaps all that sounds good to you, though.  Maybe you're happy to play around in a vast, bizarre, and beautiful sandbox even knowing that the sand only goes so deep and no one's paying you for your sandcastles.  If that's you -- and especially if you want some of your sandcastles to be underwater, or on an asteroid in deep space, or capable of interstellar flight, or filled with Frankensteinian mismashes of dinosaur fossils -- then No Man's Sky might just be the game for you.

The road feels like butter
And most of the side gigs aren't that diverse since it just makes you go to one place and slime everyone out with little to no consequences
No faction systems (I mean as if joining gangs and such)

I've been playing on and off for 10 years now, and the game is still being updated with new content, activities and events. I'm generally not an MMO fan, but ESO lets you explore at your own pace, with or without others. Most people I've met on the EU server are lovely, and ESO players remain the best gaming community I've met so far.

Overland content gets easy fast, sure, but ZOS has addresses this by allowing you to set a higher difficulty for greater rewards, which was a brilliant move. Most group content can also be done solo with a good build and a lot of gumption, for those looking for a greater challenge. Anyone who complains of the game just being button pushing has never completed VMA.

The world is rich and beautiful, and there are so many fully voiced NPCs and townspeople to talk to, random houses and shops to explore, and scenic points. Just exploring and wandering the many cities will bring you to fun secrets, funny dialogue, treasure, and easter eggs that would easily be missed just by doing quests.

There is also a couple of PVP zones that are fun, dynamic, and include some unique mechanics such as siege weapons and keep repair. People are more toxic there obviously, but it's easy enough to ignore. PVP is a more challenging game, and you'll have to keep up with the latest class updates and sets to stay on top.

My only real gripe is that the inventory management system is pretty bad without ESO plus - ESO plus is all but required if you want to be a crafter. I do have ESO plus and think the benefits are worth it, but for those that can't afford it or don't want it, I reccommed travelling with someone who has a merchant and banker, and being very selective with what you pick up.

Overall, this game just keeps on giving, and I would fully recommend it for anyone who loves TES games, or wants to try out an MMO. There are some great addons that improve gameplay a lot, and most people are happy to help out new players and give out tips. 10/10

As much as I completely adore Hunt Showdown's atmosphere, gunplay, and overall worldbuilding. There's simply too many grievances I have with it. 

THE GOOD:
- Fantastic Weapons and wide Variety of applicable playstyles
- Intriguing Monsters and a loop that rewards understanding them 
- Genuine value to having extensive Weapon, Map, and Monster knowledge
- Challenging and Rewarding

THE BAD:
- Horrible Matchmaking, 6 and 5 Star Players get coddled when they choose to play solo and get to fight 2 and 3 stars. Even in Duo cue, 6 and 5 star players get treated as if they aren't some of the best. They should be fighting other incredibly skilled players, not seal-clubbing the divorced 30 year old who wanted to play after his 9 hour shift. 
- Dwindling Variety, Crytek is capable of rapidly expanding the game by adding new enemies and bosses. Instead, we have the reskinned Assassin(Bloodskin) with a unique 2 stage mechanic. Cool, but they can do better. And they can do better in shorter periods of time. 
- Smurfing, Smurfing is a MAJOR issue from what I've seen. Level 100 without prestiging? Guaranteed Smurf. 

Overall. Hunt Showdown is infuriating. Its good at times. Its bad at others. Its middle of the pack, and if you can look past its multiple problems with matchmaking and content release timing. Then yeah, its fun. 

On the other hand, when you get insta-headshot by the guy who's played this game for 700 Hours and literally gets paid to do it? Yeah it's not fun at all. 5 and 6 stars need to stay in their own lobbies. Not get to bully new players.

TL;DR Rust is a game with a simple survival crafting premise that confront the player with the sociopathic nature of the human war for resources and withering entropy by rejecting structural ownership and subjecting every aspect of gameplay to decay or reversion to its natural state.

- Rust The Game -
Rust, despite the marketing, is not a game about survival. Its not about crafting or exploration either. Rust is  a game about staking your claim, taking what you want and protecting what is yours. The thing about rust is nothing you can get is permanent, you can and will lose all that that was ever 'yours'. Your structures decay, your items despawn, eventually the server map wipes and the tech tree gets reset. The forces of nature are not the only aspect of this game that will grind your things into dust, other players are the greatest threat. Everything you build or craft can be destroyed or taken by another player with sufficient time and motivation to do so. The joy to be found in this game are the times you are able to wrestle control from the persistent entropy. The game will however always win in the end, victory is always temporary in Rust.

- Basic Gameplay -
Rust has the normal survival crafting fair. Items go in your inventory in slots, some items can stack some items stack to different sizes. Your hot bar is an extension of your inventory that lets you use the weapons and tools you are carrying. Hot bar slots are their own slots in your inventory, they don't mirror an inventory slot. Similarly you have armor slots that let you equip cloths and armor to wear. Armor and cloths give certain resistances and abilities. You gather basic resources from nodes, trees and plants and animals. You can build a base out of square or triangle foundations with walls and floors that snap into place. Building pieces start out at tier 0, twig, and can be upgraded to higher tiers. Higher tiers are stronger but more expensive to build and maintain. You can craft tools weapons and armor. Crafting has 4 levels, level 0 is items that don't need any workbench to craft, levels 1-3 need the corresponding workbench or better to craft. Some crafting recipes are locked, these can be unlocked by learning from a one time use blueprint for that recipe or by researching them in the workbench tech tree. Blueprints cant be found in the world, you have to make them at a research bench from an example of the item that you found as loot as well as some scrap, this will destroy the item. Loot is a wide range of resources and items that cannot be gathered from the world at large. Instead Loot spawns in containers around roads and monuments. Loot also tends to build up in the bases and on the persons of other players and can be obtained from them in a multitude of less than consensual manners.

- Singleplayer, The Environment -
Rust is a multiplayer game but it [i]can[/i] be played alone. You can find an empty server or simply host your own for free. If you don't port forward the server, no one can find or join it, you can have a rust island all to yourself. Rust's world is an island lost in the open ocean. the island has four biomes, Grasslands, Jungle, Desert and Arctic. Grassland, Desert and Arctic have forested and non forested varieties. Roads railroads and powerlines span the island. Roads connect different monuments with a larger ring road around the island. Railroads always form a track ring around the island with branches for the train yard monument and two tunnels to the underground railroad. Power lines are random strings of somewhat connected towers. Monuments are a variety of structures around the island that along with roads are the main sources of loot. Further from spawn beach the monuments get hard and more rewarding. On the topic of spawn beach, one side of the somewhat square island is spawn beach, this is this side of the island with the jungle. You can always spawn at spawn beach by hitting the respawn button after death. Rust's environment is fairly benign. Temperature and radiation are the environmental effects to consider. Temperature is extreme in the Desert and Arctic. The Desert is hot during the day and cold at night, the Arctic is always cold. Heat causes thirst and Cold causes hunger. Either can reduce your health directly if extreme enough. Generally cold is a bigger threat than heat. Radiation only occurs at some monuments, its effect is cumulative. As radiation accumulates the rate at which it damages you increases. Like cold or heat, minor radiation is a mild annoyance but sufficient doses will kill you rapidly.

- Multiplayer -
Multiplayer is the intended way to play Rust. Public server will have tens to hundreds players living together on the same island. Resources, land and loot are limited and everything is first come first served. Starting out your goal should be to place a sleeping bag near where you want to live. You will die. A lot. An uncountable number of times. Remember that land is valuable to players, a naked player with nothing but a rock and a torch will be killed, not for their loot, but just to get them off the land. Placing a sleeping bag lets you spawn in the same place giving your presence in an area. Sleeping bags can be placed outside but can be easily destroyed. you should build either a base or place a shelter. A base is stronger than a shelter and can be expanded and upgraded but a shelter is cheap. Others player can be expected to fight for control of an area killing players and raiding bases near them to the extent they are able, you are advised to do the same. Push out other groups near you and control nearby monuments and events. Every player can be expected to use every tool at their disposal to claim land, gather resources and protect their stuff. Tactical efforts like wining fights and raiding are and obvious means to this end. There are other less obvious means as well. Be aware of the social aspect, players can be expected to manipulate and exploit you as much as possible. If someone comes up to your door to talk to you, odds are they don't want to be your new friend, they want info on your base or they want to kill you and put you on bag timer or they want to sneak in and disrupt the inner workings of your base. An example of a social victory would be befriending a player who lives near you, getting access to their base and robbing them when they log out or aren't home. Your base's tool cupboard is a critical part of your base. This deployable item prevents the decay of your base and grants building right to those with access. Don't let other player access your tool cupboard, gaining access is an easy attack vector. It can let them modify your base and lock you out of it. Any one with tool cupboard access can control others access, so giving someone rights to your tool cupboard can allow them to revoke your rights and seal you out of it. There are also long term strategic actions you can take to secure your resources. Build in an area with a balance of player population and resources that match your skills to control. Some areas may be too competitive or to poor in resources to make for good living. Grief other players and defend yourself from being grieffed. A common strategic grief is to place sealed tool cupboard around another players base. This blocks their building rights and can keep them from expanding their base. It is also recommended to operate from a different base then the one with your best loot. This serves to keep attention off your main base and can even bait a raid to the wrong base. Trick and confuse other players as much as possible. As an example don't run to your home after wining a fight, run to an enemies base as if you live there and then return home more secretly. You don't want player to know where you live or the size of your team, this information helps them size you up for a raid.

During the time of writing this, I would not consider myself a "skilled" or even "alright" player. 

    That being wrote, the experience in learning it is more like a journey. If you are not willing to go for a ride, then the game is not willing to include you.

    If you can be patient in learning (and playing) the game, you will find more than expected when browsing the game store. It's mechanics, teamplay and included items, are all so intricately woven into the game to make it a diverse experience. In most games, there is an obvious choice with an obvious answer. If you come across a powerful build extremely frequently in this game however, you simply came across those who had a similar way of playing the game, like a playstyle. I have seen characters in this game I tried and thought were terrible on the opposing team who constantly defeated me. 

    The gameplay is slow. It takes almost an hour to play a single match. This gives the players a sense of what path they might want to pursue within the game. This means not only are you able to play the same loadout every game, but you it may be better to switch things up depending on your team and your opponents. That is why having patience is so important in this game. You are in it for the long run.

     Despite having patience and being in it for the long run, the game constantly has you on your toes. Dota is very much a strategy game and one move could make or break the game. Now think of that move, but in every minute of the game, that is Dota. It's a 5v5 team game, with a balance of farming, buying, crafting and fighting, with plenty of downtime while also keeping you guessing, "what happens next?" It's complex systems tie well together so well, and each aspect of the game made me desire to explore it in depth. All of this complexity, and yet all to accomplish a single goal: make the enemy base fall.

    Now, like in every online game, all the players might not be enjoyable to play Dota with, but I am reviewing the game itself. I have met pleasant and unpleasant players during my time on Dota, but the points I made still stand.

    So, If you like a game that has pieces of it to learn and constantly improve upon despite their complexity, and how all those pieces come together to form the painting that is Dota, all while planning with a team, planning ahead, and planning your path for your character's power progression, while 
simultaneously improvising your moves and character layout, then this is a game for you.

An unmatched experience, despite the quirks.
War Thunder is easily the most comprehensive military vehicle game available. The sheer variety of tanks, planes, and ships from different eras is incredible, and the realistic modular damage system makes every battle intensely tactical. "When" everything is working smoothly, the combat loop (will be nice more game mods/maps) is addictive and visually spectacular.
That being said, the game definitely has its frustrating moments. There are times when the projectile registration feels completely off, leading to "ghost shells" that pass right through targets or critical hits that inexplicably do zero damage. Server performance can also be unpredictable, occasionally hitting you with sudden lag spikes or high packet loss in the middle of a firefight. Combined with the notorious progression grind and compressed Battle Ratings, it can test your patience.
Ultimately, the game is flawed, but its core mechanics are so unique that no other title can truly compete. It is absolutely worth playing, just be prepared for the occasional server-side headache!

You can. Want to be more of a stealthy ninja with tactical camo(invisibility) and speed to bypass or rush your enemies? You can. Want to be a netrunner, spamming foes with quickhacks, applying effects ranging from various debuffs and DoTs up to making them attack their allies or straight-up one-shot themselves? You can. You can even do all that from distance via a camera you hacked. Want to combine any of these playstyles and more? You can. There's also a wide variety of weapons from katanas and clubs to pistols, rifles, SMGs, sniper rifles, shutguns, etc. All of them feel different and satisfying to use.

I don't want to get into too much of a detail here, as I think it is worth playing through by yourself, but there is plenty of iconic characters and twist and turns to keep you entertained for dozens of hours, even if you barely do any side quests. And man, many of those are pretty good, too, and serve to flesh out the world.

I heard that the game was full of bugs on release, but I only played it after the release of Phantom Liberty and the big patch that fixed those issues, so aside from a very few visual glitches, I never experienced any performance issues nor bugs. I would honestly recommend Cyberpunk 2077 to anyone who enjoys a great action gameplay with an awesome story.

[h1]Project Zomboid[/h1]

[h3]First Impressions[/h3]
Ever since I can remember, I've been a huge fan of zombies. When it comes to zombie media, I've always been especially into The Walking Dead, as well as the entire series of The Walking Dead games developed by Telltale Games.

So when I first saw Project Zomboid, I immediately thought that this was a game made for me, mainly because of the atmosphere of a brutal zombie apocalypse that Project Zomboid presents.

I don't remember exactly when I bought the game, but from the moment I launched it for the first time, I was completely hooked. Of course, I've played it with some breaks in between, but the game really captivated me with its atmosphere and the feeling of a spreading and progressing infection.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Moving on to the gameplay. When it comes to the gameplay, it generally depends on what kind of experience you want to create for yourself.

As with every new playthrough, we start by creating our character and choosing their occupation. They can be unemployed, a firefighter, a police officer, or pretty much anything you want them to be in the game. After that, we choose our traits, both positive and negative, and then we're thrown into the game.

We're simply a civilian living in this world, and suddenly, out of nowhere, the zombie apocalypse hits, and you have to deal with it. We're not some kind of superhero or someone with extraordinary abilities who can kill everything around them. We're just a regular person trying to survive.

And that's exactly the point. When it comes to survival in this game, it is genuinely hardcore. You can die at any moment, and one stupid mistake can cost you your life. So, when it comes to that aspect, I'm really satisfied with the gameplay.

The gameplay is also very repetitive, but in a good way, because there are so many things you can do. I'm not going to go through every single mechanic because this game has so much to offer that I simply wouldn't have enough space to describe everything in this review.

You really have to buy the game and experience it for yourself.

On top of that, we have the Steam Workshop, and the Project Zomboid community does a great job creating all kinds of mods for the game. The game is already great in its vanilla state, without any modifications, but all you have to do is take a look at the Workshop and you'll see that you can basically turn the game into whatever you want it to be.

So, when it comes to gameplay, I think you'll be satisfied with what Project Zomboid has to offer, just like I am.

[h3]Graphics and Audio[/h3]
When it comes to the graphics, they are really good. I personally like them a lot. They're simple, but they fit the game perfectly. We have an isometric top-down view, so we see our character from above, and I think this visual style works really well for the game.

As for the audio, it also plays a big role here. The game is mostly quiet, which makes the atmosphere even stronger. You can hear zombies wandering around the streets, groaning and making noises, while the weather changes around you. You can hear leaves rustling or even something moving through the grass.

All of these little sounds really add to the atmosphere and make the world feel much more immersive.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
To sum up, Project Zomboid is a really well-made survival game when it comes to the zombie apocalypse genre. I consider it one of the best games on the market in this category.

No other game, in my opinion, manages to create a world like Project Zomboid does or deliver the same level of atmosphere and immersion.

If you're a huge fan of zombies, just like I am, then this game is really made for you. I highly recommend it.

The game works perfectly well as a solo experience, but if you have a group of friends to play with, you can easily spend countless hours in this game together.

So, for me, I would give Project Zomboid a 10 out of 10 without hesitation.
