As a pre-order and day 1 player, and now after 100%ing it and the new DLC, I think this game is significantly better, and great in some respects, but still rough around the edges, and straight up bad in some respects. I did a ~90 hour playthrough on release (pain and suffering), and I just finished my 2.0 + DLC fresh playthrough which took ~40 hours. I still have a lot of complaints but I think it's at least a worthwhile experience now.

[hr][/hr]

[h2][The Bad/The Mid][/h2]
- I have a hard time with calling games like this a role-playing game, the only choices that ACTUALLY matter are the last few relating to your ending. Nearly every single quest and event in the world is linear,  barring a few rare exceptions you really don't have a say in the end result. For a world with this potential, I want to be able to explore around, be immersed, and be able to make my own decisions and see how they impact the world around me, to me that is what a good rpg is and I don't think this is one. 
- Tying in to that, the world is pretty much uninteractive, you can't talk to anyone that's not a key npc, you can't go in a random building, you can't really do much of anything if there isn't a map waypoint there. So the majority of the game is just running from waypoint to waypoint, a lá Ubisoft, which I'm not a fan of. 
- The vast majority of the world's jobs/gigs are repetitive and uninteresting, which is annoying because there are a few good ones scattered throughout so you kinda have to do all the mid/bad to get the good
- The base game's story is just bland to me, the characters are mostly uninteresting, maybe I'm just a heartless animal, I don't think enough time was spent with Jackie to really care about him. All you get is a 30 second montage at the start of the game to build your 'relationship' and everyone talks about how close you were but I don't really buy it, and I feel similarly about others.
- The romance system felt half-baked, buggy, and unnecessary to me
- The new component/crafting system is... fine? It sort of clogs up the loot and feels tact-on and not useful to me
- This may be a personal one, but I think the game balance isn't great. Which can not necessarily be a bad thing in a singleplayer game, but when there's a few extremely strong strategies that dominate gameplay, its easy to just play through large chunks of the game with your brain off playing like that. 
- With the amount of build variety now, I wish it was easier to swap between different builds. The game is artificially restrictive in that you have to choose between netrunning/sandestivan/berserk key cyberware and there's no way to swap on the fly. Also I can't fathom why they would only allow 1 respec per run.

[hr][/hr]

[h2][The Good/The Improved][/h2]
- First of all, the gameplay and gameplay progression is massively improved, the builds are much more interesting and perk tree actually relevant and interesting. I also think the cyberware system is significantly better and more thematic, and clothing not being tied to armor value is a no brainer good change. The variety of builds now are really great, special props to the new throwing knives because they are not only usable now, but actually really cool, maybe my favorite new build. Maybe this is preference, but I only found the Tech/Body trees to be uninteresting, the rest are great. 
- Phantom Liberty (PL): oh do I have so much to say about it. Its like they hired all new writers that know how to write an interesting spy thriller with good character motivations all of a sudden and makes me even sadder when thinking about the base game. Songbird and Reed are both extremely compelling for different reasons, without going too crazy into spoilers, f*ck Reed. There are fantastic themes and symbolism throughout the story and its really a very well written tragedy sort of unfolded non-linearly.
- PL: The new Dogtown area is leaps better than any base game district. First of all, this is what the density of events/gigs/stuff to do that should be going on in all of Night City, the base game feels ridiculously sparse after all this. The random airdrop events give you something interesting to do in between gigs, and even if you don't do them (which you should bc their loot is crazy) they are great world-building and and an example of interactivity with the world which I really like. The gigs are hit or miss for me in Dogtown, maybe 50/50 between good/bad ones (excluding the sleeper vehicle deliveries those suck), but is wayyyy better than the base game which is maybe more 10/90
- PL: The story and levels, actually change in Act 3, depending on a key decision you make. Which is still far from the RPG I crave but a step in the right direction. The paths are significantly different, I HIGHLY recommend doing the 'bad' path even if you reload later, even though I knew I was doing So Mi wrong, the set pieces afterwards were insanely unique and cool, you just [b]have[/b] to do this path at least once. - Quick PL spoilers and thematic discussion: [spoiler] Songbird literally lives up to her name, she's just a bird that has been caged her whole life that wants to escape, so while Reed has her best intentions, he is so headstrong he can't see he is harming her by putting her back in that cage. So the unveiling of Reed being the 'bad guy' in the Songbird story is extremely well done. The idea to make So Mi a betrayed and cornered animal if you betray her, is insanely compelling given her story and your relationship, and then to make the ultimate level a horror level as retribution is just... perfect. Super unique and unlike anything else in the game period. Great storytelling, great decisions affect the characters and world moment, no notes, just good sh*t. [/spoiler]

There’s something uniquely nostalgic about this game. I don’t know what it is, it feels wrong to play it any other season other than Summer. Maybe it’s the defined and wholesome art style? Maybe it’s the legitimate shenanigans you get up to with friends? It’s that Minecraft syndrome, friends will just randomly get the itch to mainline this game into their bloodstream for two weeks and then it’s gone for another year.

I highly recommend that if you have an interest in this video game, find some friends who are also interested in it as this game is best with a crew of buddies. We call it our favorite interactive chat room as tasks can be as simple or as complicated as you want them to be.

I wouldn’t say there’s any crazy amount of depth here, tasks, missions, world layout all work like a low stakes MMO. Nearly every faction will give you a variant of fetch quest. The Order of Souls will send you out to collect the skulls of undead pirates, the Merchants will have you ferry supplies from one location to another with menial tasks i.e. keep the plants watered, don’t jump with crates, etc. The Gold Hoarders will have you look for treasure to dig up on islands. I think there’s a story? Lol? I have over 100 hours in this game, I have absolutely no clue if there’s a story. Lore, for sure, but story? Couldn’t tell ya.

The fun comes from navigating to these islands, as it’s up to you and your team to manage the sails, make sure you’re supplied, cook food, and defend the ship if necessary. The devs inherently knew there would be downtime so you can sit on the side of the boat and fish, play instruments, interact with pets. None of it is deep, but it’s fun, not so brainless that it’s boring, but not so intense that you have to fully lock in.

But those lock in moments happen more often than you think. Though players are now given the ability to play on “safer seas” and completely avoid PVP, the traditional way to play makes the game that much more dynamic. It’s one thing to be ganked by a megalodon or a ghost ship, npcs. It’s another thing entirely to see a player ship crest the horizon, beelining towards you. There’s of course the chance that it could be a ship of players simply taking the fastest route to an island in the distance behind you, but you’ve been playing for two hours already, you’re at faction level five, there’s a big payout coming your way. Are you going to take that chance?

No, no, no, get into cannon position until they signal you by either flag or by megaphone that they’re just passing through, believe them, but watch your ladders anyway so the filthy bilgerats don’t sneak on board. This extra edge to gameplay makes all the difference, I don’t care about your forts, your mermaid caves, give me your reapers.

The Reapers are my favorite part of the game, both to play as and to be wary of. The Reapers are the strictly PVP faction, players flying the Reaper’s flag will show up on everyone’s map, and once they reach faction level 5, they’ll be able to see the fattened merchant pigs on the map in turn. All of my greatest memories from this game come from either playing as the Reapers, or being hunted by them. Either way, I’m reaping or sowing with my pals.

Here’s a tip. The only deep thing in this game is the ocean, everything else is “number go up”, getting your ship rocked by a pvp player, an npc boss, etc. does nothing other than halt faction progress for a session, which is all just about unlocking cosmetic upgrades anyway. There’s literally nothing to buy other than cosmetics for yourself, your ship, your weapons, pets, etc. There is actually no functional difference between Sea of Thieves and Club Penguin. The treasure is a means to an end, did you have fun playing with your friends for those two hours? Then the game did its job well.

[h3]Today is my last day of playing this game as a F2P account.[/h3]
I spent over 140 hours here, and therefore I’d like to share my experience playing on F2P account, and a general review of the game at large.

Warning - bias.
I will be comparing this game to ESO (Elder Scrolls Online) quite a lot - ESO is my only experience playing MMORPGs before GW2. I’m a solo player not interested in joining guilds or socializing much beyond necessity.

[h2]Character creation[/h2]
In F2P version, only 2 character slots are available, with additional 3 unlocking after buying any DLC. Out of 9 classes (called Professions here) the only one unavailable for F2P is Revenant. Races (of which there are 5) don’t change your gameplay attributes, only affecting animations, backstory, and first chapters of your personal story, plus giving you a few utility skills and elite skill. I must emphasize specifically the sheer visual difference between races - something barely present in ESO mostly due to setting. Here you can comfortably say that you see a charr or asura simply by their size and silhouette. My character is a Charr Thief.

Now I want to wave huge banner: ARENA.NET, PLEASE DO SOMETHING WITH CLARITY AND TUTORIALS.
It’s the biggest and most glaring issue of this game that makes every other positive of the game hidden, poorly explained, or makes you stumble upon it 80 hours later (hello me and defiance bars). I strongly recommend you keeping a tab of GW2 Wiki open to search any odd thing you encounter, and maybe a tab of your search engine in cases where wiki gives you nothing substantial. Ask the local chat wherever it’s appropriate, too - community here is extremely helpful and will happily explain to the newcomers what to do and what is happening (why that happened I will explain later).

Now, with this huge asterisk in mind, back to the game.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
This is something I strongly rate as being better than in ESO. Professions have their distinct identities, playstyles, ways of mitigating or avoiding damage, their own skill and passive trees, and more importantly, limitations - because if everyone can do everything, identity becomes mostly expressed by color of animations. For example, Thief can use daggers, swords (main-hand only), short bow and pistols. That’s it. Elite specializations and other DLC nonsense can unlock usage of some other weapons, but even then you don’t get to use greatsword as a thief (I’m looking at you, meta builds in ESO).
Your character will have access to 5 weapon skills, 3 utility skills, 1 healing skill, and 1 elite skill (aka ultimate). What weapon skills you currently have depends on your profession and what weapons you have equipped in your main and off-hand. These skills are predetermined and cannot be changed or swapped - so for thief, his 2nd ability with dagger equipped in main hand will always be Heartseeker, and nothing else. On the other hand (pun not intended), right-bar abilities (utility skills, healing skill, elite skill) can be freely changed outside of combat. 
GW2 also has another crucial difference compared to ESO. In ESO, most of the time you stand still and spam your rotation buttons ad nausea. In GW2, you also have to keep in mind your positioning, resources, timers, making sure you don’t get killed, etc. Simple example of positioning - Thief’s backstabs deal double damage if you’re behind the enemy. Ways of avoiding your untimely death are numerous, and most important one is your dodge button. Dodge consumes stamina that is only used for dodge, and you can only have it enough for 2 dodges in a row. That forces you to keep attention on what the enemy is actually doing. You can also sidestep attacks, CC interrupt them, use abilities that explicitly say to allow dodge attacks, etc. Once I had a minute-long battle in which I never got hit once, despite being close to the enemy for the entire combat.
Now, gear. Here GW2 is forgiving in one very specific sense - the progression DLCs give is mostly horizontal, so after getting your top-tier gear, it will remain top-tier. You can theoretically come back years later and not change a single piece of your gear. After ESO, where each year pushed DPS further above, and where recently DPS requirements almost DOUBLED overnight, this is a huge relief. Even better, you can practically fully build your character without buying a single DLC.
There is also UNDERWATER COMBAT. There you can use one of specific underwater weapons (again, class-dependent), with their own weapon skills; some class and elite skills are unavailable underwater.
Your build is further refined by Specializations, each of which will give you specific list of passive trees in which you need to choose specific ones to activate. And that’s where the game is slightly less F2P-friendly, because it also has so-called Elite Specializations, all of which are locked behind DLCs and can replace one of basic spec trees. And while playing as base class is viable, elite specs are usually stronger than regular class, changing your gameplay on top of that and often unlocking a weapon to use.
Another system completely barred from F2P accounts is Mastery system. Thankfully, it doesn’t affect your DPS - it’s mostly a list of QoL changes, traversal upgrades, etc.
Now, what to do after reaching lvl 80 (maximum level in the game, whether you have DLCs or not). Honestly? ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ The game is surprisingly reluctant in giving you any concrete goals - ‘find your own entertainment’ moment. You could chase cosmetic unlocks, achievement/titles hunting, refining gear and build, getting legendary equipment (which stat-wise is identical to rarity below it, no FOMO here), play endgame content, etc.

Tiny thing on controls: GW2 has action camera with controls similar to regular action RPGs, but it’s hidden in keybinds settings. Just set a toggle on some easily accessible button.

Now a bit about map and traversal as F2P account. The map is traversable by foot. Doesn’t mean it’s *comfortably traversable* by foot XD. For whatever reason, F2P accounts are not given ANY mount at all, except for 10-hour Raptor trial. Maps are fairly large, so lack of mount will be noticeable. Sometimes extremely annoying. Maps can also be fairly vertical, so, PARKOUR!
On maps, there are hearts (small quests you do yourself), events (usually time-gated and can/should be done by groups of players) and other points of interest. Most of your playtime will be on finishing hearts and doing events either yourself or with other random players that decided to do the same.
Maps also have jump puzzles. Sometimes infuriating. But usually cool.
Maps have waypoints. Unlike ESO, traversing between them always has a cost, except for when you’re in a big city and traversing between waypoints of that city (Black Citadel, Lion’s Arch, etc.).

A bit about inventory management. It takes noticeable time in the game - you will be picking up various loot to then either deconstruct it, identify, sell to merchants as junk, or send to your crafting bag (THANK GODS IT’S FREE, TAKE NOTES ESO). If that sounds miserable for you - you’ve been warned.

2 words on monetization. DLCs expensive. Some QoL stuff sold in premium store, smh. COSMETICS ARE SO EXPENSIVE.


[h2]Community[/h2]
Extremely friendly. Kills are shared, events are also shared, you can revive other players, give/get buffs, food, banners, etc. In overworld, there’s no penalty or toxicity for dealing low damage or dying often - you can still be helpful by doing something, and there can arrive ten other players to help you. There are practically zero reasons to *not* help someone next to you. No wonder PvE community is so amazing <3


[h2]Conclusion?[/h2]
8k characters are really restrictive, smh.
If you want to try it out - go ahead, even without paying. F2P won’t hinder you as much as you think.
If you want a game that explains itself properly, to have mount without DLC tax, to have elite specs - think twice.

[h1]One of the Greatest Games Ever Made[/h1]

Terraria is one of those games that is almost impossible to describe properly.

At first glance, it looks like a simple 2D sandbox game. Then you start playing, and you realize just how absurdly deep and enormous it actually is.

I've spent a huge amount of time in Terraria, and even after all those hours, the game still manages to give me reasons to explore, build and discover something new.

[h2]Exploration[/h2]

Exploration is one of the best parts of Terraria.

Every world feels like an adventure waiting to happen. You can dig underground, explore caves, discover hidden structures, find rare items and eventually reach places that feel completely different from where you started.

There is an incredible sense of discovery, especially when you encounter something for the first time without knowing what is waiting for you.

[h2]Progression & Loot[/h2]

The progression system is fantastic.

There are so many weapons, accessories, armor sets and items that constantly give you something new to work towards.

Getting stronger actually feels meaningful because the game keeps introducing new enemies, bosses and areas that require you to improve your equipment and adapt your playstyle.

And the amount of loot is honestly ridiculous.

In the best possible way.

[h2]Bosses & Combat[/h2]

The bosses are another huge highlight.

There is a great variety of encounters, and many of them feel completely different from one another. Learning their attacks, preparing your equipment and finally defeating a difficult boss is incredibly satisfying.

Combat also offers a ridiculous amount of freedom. Different weapons and builds can completely change how you approach the game, which makes experimenting with different playstyles genuinely rewarding.

[h2]Building & Creativity[/h2]

The building system gives you an enormous amount of freedom, and you can create everything from a simple wooden house to incredibly elaborate bases.

What I love is that building never feels like something you are forced to do. You can play Terraria however you want.

Want to explore?

Go explore.

Want to fight bosses?

Fight bosses.

Want to spend hours building a ridiculous castle?

You can do that too.

[h2]The Amount of Content[/h2]

This is probably what impresses me the most.

Terraria has an absurd amount of content.

There are so many enemies, bosses, biomes, events, weapons, accessories, NPCs and secrets that it feels almost impossible to experience everything in a single playthrough.

Even after hundreds of hours, there can still be something you've never seen before.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Terraria is much more than a sandbox game.

It's an exploration game, an RPG, a survival game, a building game and a boss-rush adventure all at the same time.

The amount of freedom it gives the player is incredible, and the way exploration, progression, combat and creativity all work together is something very few games manage to replicate.

[b]9.8/10[/b]

470 hours, every achievement, Honour Mode included, and I'm still not convinced I've seen everything.

Baldur's Gate 3 is the most reactive game I've ever played. Almost every problem has four solutions, and whatever weird fifth idea you try, the game usually saw it coming. Talk your way out, sneak past, shove them off a ledge, or skip the fight entirely. Your choices stick, and people remember them.

The writing and voice acting carry it. Astarion, Karlach, Shadowheart and Lae'zel are some of the best companions in any RPG, and Dark Urge is worth playing at least once because it's the strongest version of the story. My Durge run was a Lolth-sworn drow necromancer (Death Cleric / Necromancy Wizard / Spores Druid) with a small undead army in tow, and the game rolled with all of it.

Combat is 5e done right. Height, surfaces and positioning all matter, and multiclassing goes deep enough that I was still theorycrafting builds hundreds of hours in. The Patch 8 subclasses only made that worse, in the best way.

Honour Mode is the final exam. One save, no reloads, and bosses with legendary actions that punish lazy play. It forces you to actually learn the systems instead of save-scumming past them, and every dialogue roll gets tense when you can't undo it. Those golden dice were earned.

It's not perfect. Act 3 is massive but can still chug in the Lower City, inventory management is a chore, and a few companion arcs and quest threads wrap up more abruptly than the rest of the game deserves. None of that comes close to outweighing what Larian pulled off.

This is the new bar for RPGs. See you in hour 471.

Dota 2 isn't a bad game — it's just a game that asks for more patience than I have. 😂

After 500+ hours, beating the game on every difficulty, and getting every single achievement, I can easily recommend V Rising.

If you like survival games, vampires, castle building, boss fights, or Diablo-style combat, there’s a really good chance you’ll enjoy this.

One of the things I love most about V Rising is that you can pretty much play it however you want. The progression is easy to understand, the combat feels great, and there are a ton of different weapons and spells you can mix together.

Yeah, some spells are stronger than others and some weapon abilities definitely stand out more, but I never really felt like I HAD to use one specific setup. You can experiment and make a build around what you actually enjoy using.

The boss fights are probably one of the best parts of the game too. There are a ton of them, they unlock new abilities, crafting recipes, and progression, and on the harder difficulties some of the fights can get genuinely difficult. Brutal especially can really punish you if you don’t learn the mechanics.

I also really like how the vampire mechanics actually matter. Blood types give you different bonuses, sunlight is a real threat, and sometimes just travelling during the day turns into you desperately running from tree to tree trying not to burst into flames.

The castle building is another huge part of the game for me. You can make some seriously cool bases and spend way more time decorating than you probably intended. If all you want to do is build a giant gothic vampire castle and make it look amazing, you can honestly spend hours doing just that.

One of the biggest positives though is how customizable the game is.

If you think the resource grind is too much, increase the resource yield.

If crafting takes too long, speed it up.

If the combat is too hard, lower the difficulty or increase your damage.

If you want the game to destroy you, turn everything up and play Brutal.

You really can adjust the game around how YOU want to play, which I appreciate a lot. Not everyone wants to spend hours farming materials or fighting the same boss over and over, and the game gives you enough settings to cut out a lot of the stuff you personally don’t enjoy.

You can also play solo, with friends, or on PvP servers. I’ve personally gotten hundreds of hours out of the PvE side alone, so you definitely don’t need to care about PvP to enjoy the game.

It’s not perfect. Some parts can get grindy, some weapons and spells are clearly better than others, and there are moments where you’ll feel like you’re collecting the same materials for the hundredth time.

But honestly, after 500+ hours, every difficulty, and 100% of the achievements, I still love the game.

There aren’t many games that can keep me interested for that long.

If you enjoy survival games, action combat, vampires, boss hunting, or just building ridiculously over-the-top castles, V Rising is absolutely worth playing.

Highly recommended.

Hunt: Showdown is my favorite FPS, and one of the hardest to recommend to a friend.

Your first hours will go like this: you load into a huge map, walk for a minute, and die. You didn't see who shot you. You don't know where it came from. You just know it was a headshot. The tutorial and the bots for players under level 11 are a nice gesture, but they don't really prepare you for the real thing. The game hands you a map and lets you figure it out the hard way.

The gunplay is a big part of why it feels so different. Mechanics are insanely tight and the hitboxes are tight as shit. Guns are slow to fire, and most of them reload one bullet at a time, so reloading can take forever. Even the ones with bigger internal mags don't spray like a modern shooter. On top of that, nothing is hitscan. When you pull the trigger, an actual bullet leaves your barrel and travels in an arc based on the ammo type and the gun's stats. It has to physically hit a player, a zombie, or an object to count. Shotgun pellets are each modeled individually with their own hitboxes, so birdshot can fly a bit funny. Even the flamethrower's fire has a hitbox.

That means you have to be really mindful of where your gun is actually pointing. Past 100 meters, bullet drop and travel time keep changing with distance, so long range shots take real practice to land consistently. Flick shots are tricky to pull off too. With most guns, I find the best approach is to stop moving for a split second when I fire, so the bullet leaves the barrel exactly where I want it to go. Every shot matters, and missing one usually means you're dead.

Yes, it's slower than most shooters. And yes, you'll sometimes end up in a stalemate. But that's part of the fun. When you're pinned down and you're the fish in the barrel, you have to figure out how to get out of it, knowing that getting hit even once usually means losing the match.

Good headphones are close to mandatory. The sound design isn't perfect, but it's usually good enough to tell how far away someone is, what they're walking on, whether they're indoors or outdoors, and if they're inside, what floor they're on. That information wins fights. Don't play on speakers or in a loud room. You'll miss footsteps, crows, and dogs that would have told you exactly where someone was.

Early on, a lot of deaths will feel unfair. Someone camping in a treeline, someone peeking through a gap in a wall you didn't know existed. But that's the game. Over time you learn the sight lines, which walls you can shoot through, which cracks people peek from, and where you should never stand. Once that knowledge sinks in, the game opens up completely. How long that takes varies a lot. For some people it's a few days, for others it's months.

That's also why it's a tough sell. I've brought in several friends who saw the trailer and wanted to play with my group, and most of them got frustrated and refunded. The playerbase is small but extremely dedicated, and they know this game inside and out, so new players are learning against people with years of map knowledge.

For context, my friends and I usually sit around 4 to 5 stars. Occasionally we get lucky and hit 6 (the top tier), then promptly get our asses handed to us by real sweaty junks. There are still nights where we can't win a single match.

About hackers: they exist, like in any shooter. Maybe I'm just getting lucky on the North America East servers, but in my experience, most of the kills that feel like cheating end up having a real explanation. An angle we weren't watching, a crack we didn't cover, a wallbang we didn't know was possible. With enough game knowledge, you can even start wallbanging people using nothing but audio. A lot of the "this guy is definitely hacking" moments stop looking that way once you understand the game better.

If you're patient and don't mind losing a lot while you learn, Hunt is incredibly rewarding and nothing else plays quite like it. If you want something you can enjoy right away, look elsewhere.

TL;DR: Brutal learning curve, little hand holding, and you'll die constantly at first. Gunplay is slow, punishing, and fully physics based, so every shot counts. Get good headphones. Most "hacks" are just game knowledge you don't have yet. Stick with it and it's one of the most rewarding shooters out there. If you're not patient, refund it before the two hours are up.

Probably the absolute best exploration space sandbox game out there. It took me about 60 hours to find the bottom of the sandbox. Not that I did everything that you can do in the game, but I found the extent of the things that I enjoyed and lost interest. That might not sound like an endorsement but it is. I enjoyed all of those 60 hours. It's well worth the money. The sheer scale of the game is incredibly impressive. There's so much to do (base building, ship building, vehicle building, crafting, pirate hunting, missions, quests, you can even obtain a capital ship (freighter) and create a fleet of ships to complete missions). The only problem is the lack of challenge. I am willing to admit that there might be more challenge to be found if you go to the higher tier star systems, but I didn't really see anything that felt challenging in the first 60 hours. Once I understood the game systems and upgraded my multitool a bit there was no challenge in the Sentinels (corrupted or otherwise) especially if you choose to fight them near a building of some kind. Once I could easily beat them there didn't seem like any reason to grind out the more advanced stuff. I didn't see anything that I needed to power up to take on. I could have gotten into the grind to customize a freighter or base or do fleet missions, or any number of things. But none of it was really calling to me. I'm sure that I will come back at some point and try again. But for now I'm content to put it down. But that's still 60 hours of enjoyment and I think most anyone will find at least that much enjoyment in the game as well.

One of the most overrated games I've ever played and extremely disappointing as an MMO fan who has heard this game constantly praised and called one of the best in the genre.

Fans of this game praise the QOL features and how the game doesn't waste your time; but I find this leads to the edges being sanded off so much that you're not left with much of anything of substance at all. Instant fast travel and basically no sidequests in the base game leads to the world not feeling like it matters or is a world at all. Killing mobs to get XP feels hollow without the context of sidequests giving you a reason to go kill them. I'm aware the heart events give *some* context, but they feel hollow as well with how they're all over the map and how menial the gameplay is; and the context you're given almost never amounts to anything interesting or memorable. 

Playing with a group of friends while leveling isn't fun, either, to the point where it feels like you're not even meant to. My group often would just fast travel to wherever they wanted to be and after 5 minutes our group would be all over the map in different zones doing totally unrelated things. Compare this to WoW where leveling with friends feels like you're ACTUALLY playing a multiplayer RPG. Again, sanding the edges just led to, in my opinion, a weaker experience. 

This isn't even mentioning the complete lack of aura the game has, as the kids say. The world is completely flat and dull, the characters and story included as well. Lion Arch was the only place in my almost 50 hours that felt like a cool memorable location when MMOs are supposed to be FULL of locations like this. 

I came away from this game extremely disappointed and with a feeling of complete whiplash. I genuinely don't understand how this game is constantly praised as one of, if not the, best games in the MMO genre, when it can't even do what MMOs are supposed to do well. The world sucks; it doesn't even feel like a real world because of the lack of context given to what you're doing and the constant instant fast traveling. The story and characters suck. The music sucks and it feels like Jeremy Soule was just phoning it in. The only thing I thought was actually good was the combat and you don't even get to enjoy it as all the mobs die after you do one rotation of your spells.

This is one of those things that just proves you have to experience shit for yourself instead of listening to popular opinion. I have CONSTANTLY heard the GW2 QOL and streamlining praised because "other mmos waste your time"

Turns out, too much QOL makes the game feel like a hollow void of nothingburgers. You need that friction for the world and your goals and accomplishments to feal real and worth your time.

Would I recommend this game? Yes. Have I recommended this game? Yes, countless times.

What's there not to love about a practically infinite universe with endless possibility? This game is in my personal top ten games of all time. But it would be no use to compare NMS to another game because nothing can actually compare. It is as close to an "everything game" as is feasibly possible.

Do you want to be an interstellar truck driver? build castles? hunt space pirates? make new friends? catch and battle alien creatures? be a mayor? shoot things? explore the unknown reaches of the universe? fish?

Myself, I love exploring, finding the most extreme and exotic worlds and documenting them like a xenobiologist. I've played over 50 hours here (and an additional 30 hours on Xbox) and I've loved every moment. Also, Hello Games keeps on releasing major updates even 10 years later! Dota 2 remains one of the most deep and rewarding multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) games on the market, though its steep learning curve isn't for everyone.
Pros
• Unmatched Strategic Depth: With over 120 unique heroes and complex map mechanics like denying creeps, day/night cycles, and high-ground advantages, no two matches ever feel the same.
• True Free-to-Play Model: Unlike competitor titles, every single hero in Dota 2 is completely free from the moment you install the game. Microtransactions are strictly cosmetic.
• Thriving Esports Scene: Supported by a passionate community, its competitive ecosystem offers incredibly high-stakes tournaments and thrilling high-level gameplay to watch.
Cons
• Brutal Learning Curve: The game is notoriously hostile to beginners. New players must memorize thousands of item interactions and mechanics just to understand basic gameplay.
• Toxic Community: Matchmaking can be highly stressful, and player toxicity remains a persistent issue, despite ongoing developer efforts to curb bad behavior.
• Massive Time Commitment: Matches regularly last between 40 to 60 minutes, and leaving early penalties mean you must commit a significant block of time to every single round.

Firstly let me say, I know Terraria is one of the best games to be available on Steam and I know the endgame is extremely rewarding, you become something like a living god. I know Terraria is a very special game that most people like, but I personally just can't get into it for the little things I hate so much.

So... I've tried Terraria numerous times, tried to get into it, but every time I come back to it I honestly find myself losing interest fast because I dislike the game's pacing and how you're at the mercy of RNG for even essential drops. I have wondered why I end up feeling this way about such a beloved game, but I've managed to put the things that put me off it into a list.

1. I really really don't like the early game progression, I feel like it's such a drag and very slow-paced. Enemies feel like they do so much damage and your crude weapons pretty much bounce off them and certain items like the hermes boots or early items you want for single class playthroughs may not appear at all.

2. You cannot make certain essential early items like Hermes boots for some reason, you're completely at the mercy of the game's RNG to find them. If you don't find them some early bosses like slime king and queen bee are nigh-impossible to beat because you can't move fast enough. It just... doesn't make any sense for a game being constantly updated to this day to have hermes boots uncraftable when they're essential for progression and mobility.

3. The game's progression will dump events like old one's army, eye of cthulu and slime rain onto you regardless if you're ready or not. While you are allowed to fight MOST bosses on your own time, the game also dropkicks you with events you have to handle the second you come back to the surface. Heck, one certain boss that most people describe as the hardest in the game can appear from you killing a random sparkly butterfly and the other can be pulled from fishing. I don't get the appeal of that at all.

4. You are pretty much expected to deface your entire world with many boss fighting arenas or else you just won't beat them. You're not allowed to keep certain biomes the way they are or preserve the parts of the world you'd like to appreciate, because you need to do things like building a long highway from one end of hell to the other, and absolutely cover the sky with platforms spanning for miles. 

5. The second half of the game is locked behind you beating a certain boss, and while that does keep harder more dangerous enemies away from you it also means you can never be overly-prepared to take on bosses, because the game's pacing locks you out of the better ores and items until you do the mandatory fights.

6. The game is very mean-spirited with its traps. All these boulders and rolling cactus traps would be easier to deal with when you have proper armour, but you can find these boulder traps that oneshot you at any stage of progression pretty much anywhere underground. And unless you know where to find them you will die to these things so often.

7. The game effectively doesn't care about new players beyond what little knowledge you can glean from the guide, and otherwise expects you to have the wiki to hand at all times for progression or for you to have completed a full world to endgame already. If you're new, just starting out? The game's pacing with its boss/horde events feels manic, and that you need to be speedrunning through it just to keep up with everything going on.

8. The corruption alters your world rather fast and there's no consistent way to stop it other than destroying every last bit of it. Again, an issue with the game's faster pacing regardless of you being on lower difficulties or not. You lose your world so much faster than Minecraft's Skulk can claim it.

I know most people love this game dearly and can handle the pacing, but I personally just can't get into Terraria at all for these small things that drag the experience down. I don't like being at the mercy of the world generation's RNG, I don't like having events dropped into my lap that I didn't activate, I don't like being tied to a world that's going to be turned into one big corruption biome if I'm not fast enough, and I don't like that some items essential for progression just don't seem to consistently appear with every world generation.

Wow. Where do I start?

When this game was first announced for a 2016 launch date, I was stoked. Here it was, a space exploration sim with procedural generation, something I am absolutely fascinated by, something that is right up my alley!

And then... the game came out. A lot of promised features were missing from the game. A lot of features just didn't work properly, or at all. It felt like kind of a let-down... but I played nonetheless. Even in its broken, incomplete state, playing No Man's Sky in 2016 was the most fun I'd had in ages, and the game was absolutely something I could see myself loving if it were just in a better state.

And then, Hello Games began to fix the mess. Then, they started adding in new features. And more new features. And more. And more! AND MORE!

We are being spoiled. Absolutely spoiled. There is SO much to this game, so much more than was even promised back in 2015-16, so much more than any of us could have ever dreamed of. And they're still updating the game!

If you love the solitude of space exploration, resource gathering, crafting, ingredient gathering, cooking, suit/weapon upgrades, and the survival/crafting gameplay loop in general... this game is absolutely for you. If you love multiplayer hubs and the promise of interstellar alliances with other players... this game is also for you.

Follow the main storyline and you will soon be introduced to an ever-expanding universe of galaxies, each with over 18 quintillion planets total (each planet is assigned a 16-digit code using hexadecimal, giving a total of 16^16, or 18.446 quintillion), each with hundreds of thousands of points of interest spread across the surface of planet that are comparable to... actual real-life planets. You'll get access to that star's space station, the hub of each system (well, the systems that have them anyway), and the missions and upgrades available there. You'll get to collect industrial waste for metal that you trade in for advanced modules and items. You'll get to unlock more and more advanced and valuable star types with higher-valued resources. I mean, they even added a new star type with this last update (purple) with NEW elements and resources that they added into the game (helium, quartzite, methane, etc.), as well as gas giants. You'll see an entire periodic table of elements, as small as it is, that comprises an entire crafting system that is so advanced you may never have the time to craft every item, part, and upgrade in the game. And cooking! By my estimates (and by looking briefly through the No Man's Sky wiki, a resource that will be more valuable than anything else out there), there are hundreds of recipes, many of them ingredients that feed into larger recipes. And you'll certainly never even scratch the surface on the number of planets you can land on.

This game is an absolute marvel of programming, algorithm design, procedural generation, and imagination. I could play this game forever. And I plan to.

GTA, but it's in a messed up and punked up version of the future, and it's also an RPG. 

Bought it on release, waited for a few years before playing it. Still has more bugs than I would like, but none of them have been game breaking. Glad I waited, and glad I decided to actually play it and not refund it.

WORLD AND ATMOSPHERE
Incredible world and atmosphere. I have not experienced anything like it. It's best explained by this example: In the middle of a mission, it was raining at night and I was supposed to go inside some store to interrogate a guy. I simply ended up sitting in the car for a while, stepping outside and just taking in the scenery, trying try pretend I was actually there. Never been able to do this so well in any other game. Honestly brilliantly done, it says a lot about how much effort they put into the atmosphere.

Some open world games fail to make the world come alive. Especially the ones that are in big cities. This game manages to make the world come alive and feel interactive on the same level as a GTA game, and that is a huge compliment. It is more buggy, and the vehicle variety isn't as good as GTA, but the game makes up for that in other ways, like with the character customization (build paths and so on). It also has loads of all the "life stuff" that GTA games are famous for, and it does them well.

CHARACTERS AND CHOICES
The characters, the premise and thickening plot are also selling the game hard. Deep and multi-dimensional characters, similar to how they function in The Witcher, but belonging to this world ofc. Over the top, but still believable scenarios where you have make difficult and often very ambiguous choices. It also shows you and forces you to consider what your stance is on a lot of ethical dilemmas linked to a highly technological world where humans, AI and robotic implants mix together in an incredibly corrupt city where the environmental concerns of today where never dealt with. 

Haven't finished the story yet, but at 100 hours, I can safely recommend it. Does require a beast of a PC though, that's also part of why I waited a long time to play it.

TLDR: GTA, but it's in a messed up and punked up version of the future, and it's also an RPG. Bit buggy, and requires a strong PC, otherwise super good.

A huge disappointment, especially given the developer-paid reviewers who hyped NMS as a must-play title.

Calling it a game is quite a stretch — with its bare-bones approach to 'storytelling' (consisting of two written sentences telling you which rock to smash or where to fly every now and then) and gameplay based on bashing rocks and flying around 99% empty orbs masquerading as planets. Suffice to say that in eight hours, I didn't witness a SINGLE EVENT. Let that sink in.


Procedural generation truly reveals its flaws in the modularly assembled lifeforms, which are nothing short of unpleasant-to-look-at abominations, lacking any sense of proportion or aesthetics. Space stations that look good from the outside turn out to have the exact same copy-pasted interior wherever you go. NPCs don't feel alive and come across as poorly animated meshes.

Even the music is an exceptionally bland affair, seemingly aiming to be as unremarkable as possible (and likely procedurally generated, too). The sound effects are flat. There is practically no simulation of physics... in a space game.

Moving on to NMS after finishing Outer Wilds is a depressing experience, but it also serves as a perfect illustration of the difference between procedurally generated "art" and content crafted by hand by people with a genuine artistic touch. 

Honestly, I do not recommend whatever No Man's Sky is.

I don't really write reviews for games unless it's a joke, because I don't really care to. However I feel like I should write one for this game, as it holds an interesting place in my heart. This game is not a masterpiece, not even close, and everyone who tells you it is is lying. This game is unfortunately a shell of what it SHOULD have been, and does not deliver on many fronts. The RPG is shallow, the gunplay is fun but repetitive, and the story is all over the place. So why am I giving it a good review? Because despite all that, I really do love this game, in all of its sloppiness. The atmosphere is awesome and beautiful, it FEELS like a cyberpunk world, the music is great and I listen to some of the tracks regularly. The combat has its moments where I feel like a TRUE edgerunner and can be genuinely fun. The story may not have the best pacing and sometimes just doesn't hit, but when it DOES hit, it hits good. There are so many scenes and story beats that I love and have made me FEEL emotional. I also just love customizing my character and messing around with the awesome photo mode. So is this game a 10/10 masterpiece that should be praised for everything it's done. God no. Not even close. CDPR still screwed us and gave us a game that doesn't even begin to reflect what they promised, but goddammit do I love it. This game is slop, but it's MY slop. I would give it an 8/10 and I still plan to keep playing till I can't anymore. Now the game isn't COMPLETELY bad, and I think some people are FAR too harsh on it, looking at it from a less biased lens, I think it's a fine game, and I think a lot of people can find things to enjoy about it, just maybe get it on sale. And for the people who REALLY love this game, this is not an attack. I LOVE this game, but I'm not going to mindlessly glaze it and praise CDPR for what they have done (though I do really appreciate what they have done with the game and think they made something pretty solid). ALL I ask is that no one EVER forgets how this game was released and how the developers and consumers were treated. Do not forget what CDPR did, hold them accountable. Cyberpunk 2077 is a fine game and does somethings really well. But it is NOT a masterpeice at ALL.

Cyberpunk’s generational comeback needs to be studied. From a horrible launch to a game whose polish allows you to see it for the absolute gem of an experience that it is. Night City is an absolutely gorgeous city. When first beginning my playthrough, I would just get lost in the city. I’d drive, travel by NCART (Night City’s public metro system), or even walk through the streets. There is also a desert area outside Night City called the Badlands that breathes even more life into the game, reminding you that it isn’t just a city you’re exploring, but an entirely different world lush with its own lore and backstory. The only flaw of the open-world setup is that there isn’t much to do in the world (outside of missions) compared to games like GTA. But Cyberpunk has a large number of story-heavy interactive missions that will have you doing a variety of things, and the game gives you the freedom to accomplish many missions in whatever way you like (stealth or guns blazing). The dialogue you pick on these missions can also dictate how the mission ends. I personally found myself repeating the missions over and over because I hated one outcome and wanted to get another one. However, you’ll learn quickly that many missions don’t have a “perfect” outcome, and the outcome YOU like will depend largely on YOUR morals and personal values. The main plot of the base game is pretty good, but if you pick up the DLC, you’ll realize Phantom Liberty’s story is S-tier. The characters themselves are also pretty good (and the PL characters are especially good). The combat of the game is also a big selling point. You can customize your character in a variety of different ways. You can play like a “samurai” with a katana, a regular merc with a gun, etc. You can choose many different abilities according to the cyberware you equip. Equip a sandy? Now you’re moving like the Flash and murdering enemies before they even see you coming. Equip a cyberdeck? You are effectively the closest thing Night City has to a god because you can hack other people’s cyberware and it can go from basic stuff like overheating their cyberware to forcing people to kill each other. If you play Phantom Liberty, you can gain access to a netrunning ability that is so powerful, it's unspeakable in this review. There are many other cool abilities in this game as well, and I’d heavily encourage experimenting. As for the soundtrack, A-tier. The game has many awesome radio songs and battle themes, including one song that you may recognize if you watch the Cyberpunk anime. Overall, this game is absolutely worth checking out as it has so many amazing things going for it - setting, soundtrack, gameplay, characters, and plot. You will find yourself sucked into this huge city of hopes and dreams, and carving your name in history as a legend.

Warframe is a game that does not seem to have much of an idea where it's going and end ups going in a million different directions. From the weird railjack (your spaceship) stuff, to the mini games on your orbiter, to the pvp that nobody plays, it has trouble picking a direction and going somewhere interesting with it. 

[b]Grinding:[/b]  Power progression is spread out horizontally to a ridiculous degree. You get mods to buff your weapons and companions, and then exilus mods to add some quality of life to them, and then arcanes, and dont forget archon shards, then subsuming abilities, ect. Your weapons have a limited amount of capacity to insert mods and so you need to install things called forma in order to more efficiently slot mods in. Unfortunately, you—for some godforsaken reason—need to relevel your weapon back up from unranked every single time you do this, and you need to add multiple forma for many setups. 
You have way too many weekly resets to keep track of, from ETA to EDA to netracell, to archon hunt, to sortie, to duviri circuit/steel path duviri circuit, and descendia/ steel path descendia, Digital Extremes shoves way too much down your throat and because many of the rewards are rotating and may need months to come back, you feel compelled to complete these.  The level of FOMO is I think horrendous in here and it permeates almost every part of Warframe.

[b]Purchasing:[/b] I've no idea why, but in 2026 this game still does not have an acceptable player shop to sell things to others. Instead, people are forced to go off to third-party sites and purchase things using the real money currency (platinum) from there. Digital Extremes also typically does not sell their vaulted warframes/relics/mods directly through their own store, but instead relies on people buying in game in game currency using real cash and then going to these sites. I assume this is done for the optics to be able to say that they do not sell frames/mods/etc. for money and that players have to play to acquire them, but who knows. If you want to sell things in game, you either have to go through the terrible experience of selling through an in-game chatroom moving at a thousand miles per hour, or stand at a bazaar holding up 5 items with no prices listed, no details given.

[b]Design:[/b] Some of the design decisions are quite honestly baffling, from obscure mechanics that can screw over your builds and are not explained anywhere (such as heat inheritance), inconsistencies with how weapons utilize certain mods (multiplicative scaling for condition overload vs additive), needing to wait until enemies in void fissures randomly turn "corrupted" before killing them (why?), to riven dispositions (rivens are unique mods and their disposition determines how much of their benefits apply) being all over the place for different weapons, many of their design choices make no sense to me. For some odd reason, there are also being lips on many edges of the architecture in the game which make it more of a pain to parkour around the map like you're meant to. Random cubes come up out of the ground on certain map tiles and just completely screw up your momentum (again, why?) There are a ton of things in this game that need to be looked at and reevaluated. Side note: some of the quests (looking at you Glast Gambit) are absolutely awful.

[b]Bugs:[/b] Oh my god the amount of bugs, I'm not sure if I've played a session that went longer than 2-3 hours without a bug. Every big update seems to break the game more and more. Personally I would much rather have had time spent fixing bugs and design flaws than bringing in new content, but I am probably in the minority.

[b]Community:[/b] For the most part the community is pretty nice and helpful, but like with all weeb/weeb-adjacent games your get your segment of weirdos that horndog and make things uncomfortable. (Trending more and more in that direction unfortunately.) You have a significant subsection of the community that takes criticism of DE as a personal attack on themselves and go into full cult mode whenever you bring up issues and it gets pretty obnoxious. In my experience there are also people who just AFK for certain lower level and grindy mission types in the hopes that others will carry them. It's understandable considering how many times you need to run certain missions to get what you need, but annoying nonetheless. There has also been a long-running issue with certain mods power tripping and being atrocious to people (if you know you know) which at this point seems like it will never be addressed.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Most of the combat breaks down into ranged (your guns, bows, etc.) and melee. You have a primary ranged weapon and a secondary one, but you really only need one of these. Either one is capable of clearing out whatever mobs are in front of you and although some people use their secondaries to prime enemies for more damage, it's not necessary. Melee is just pressing e and moving forward 90% of the time. The majority of the skill expression in this game is in the form of your builds and crunching numbers. (Not trashing it, it can be pretty fun.) When it comes down to actual combat it plays like a horde shooter where you mow down mob after mob without much mechanical complexity. It also has a pretty severe issue with visual clutter where too many weapons and abilities just clog up your screen with effect after effect and many of the claustrophobic map designs do not help that either. You do have an option to tone down some of the effects in the settings i believe.

There are definitely bright spots in the game, or else nobody would be playing it still. Many of the weapons feel good to use and as far as playing it like a horde shooter, once you get to a certain level of strength it has a satisfying pop to the slaying. The sound design for many of the weapons is also very nice and adds to the experience greatly. You can always find a party to group up with for much of the more popular content even at strange hours of the day which is always nice. The game also ran quite well for me and looks quite nice for a game of this age. All-in-all It has its good elements and it's free, but it comes mired in a massive slew of issues, predatory mechanics to keep you hooked (FOMO, battlepass, takes days to craft warframes/weapons once you acquire the parts unless you pay, etc.) and a massive grind to acquire much in this game.

Despite being an indie game, this is actually reasonably polished for what it is. Nothing gameplay wise feels too broken and it's very well made. Before I bought it I imagined it would be a waste of money but I had just watched an 100 days survival video on Youtube and thought it looked somewhat cool, and I still very much agree with that sentiment today. When it works this game is pretty amazing, there's no shortage of things to do and every mechanic in it feels like it has a purpose, and is integrated well. If you like mechanical realism and don't mind graphical deficiency, then I would say it's a good buy. But notice how I mentioned WHEN it works, because just like anything, this game has it's shortcomings. Those shortcomings fall in the realm of Errors, Corrupted saves, and any other terrible game breaking bug you can think of. These usually are not overly common on the Vanilla game, however they still happen. But with mods it feels like it just never ends. Anything over 20-30 mods is just risking your saves, every day you load up a world is just a gamble it doesn't FUCK your computer or your save. I have spent dozens of hours researching how to fix random unexpected errors or bugs that just happen, you could play normally and not touch anything gameplay wise and then the next day your game just can't update, or won't launch etc. It's a pretty harsh criticism for a positive review but it's only being honest, you just have to be prepared for something to go wrong because it always will. Especially with mods. But even with all of that being said, this game is one of the most well crafted Single Player games of all time, and I will leave no criticism to the gameplay because I've enjoyed every minute of it. Playing multiplayer with my friends was also probably some of the most fun I've ever had in a video game as well, so don't overlook this just because of its odd graphical nature, because it more than makes up for it in gameplay.

I have been playing No Man's Sky since September 2020. After 1,477 hours of playtime and achieving 100% completion, I can honestly say I have enjoyed every single minute.

While the game had its share of early hiccups, those are firmly a thing of the past. Hello Games has crafted something truly miraculous. The Expeditions keep this universe feeling alive and exhilarating, capturing that magical feeling of waking up as a stranger on an undiscovered planet. Sean Murray's commentary in the latest expedition beautifully reminded us veteran players of those formative years, striking a deeply resonant chord. The game's incredible music, gorgeous graphics, and immersive atmospheres pull you in completely.

Why this game is out of this world:
• Freighter Ownership: I love having a massive capital ship where I can park my starships, hoard my loot, and completely customize the layout to my liking.
• The Titan Worms: This remains my absolute favourite update feature! Watching these colossal beasts crash through planet surfaces—and actually being able to ride them—is mind-blowing.
• Incredible Variety & Pets: The sheer diversity of alien races and unique creatures is amazing. Being able to adopt, breed, ride your own pets, and even enter them into pet battles and challenges is fantastic.
• Unique Starships: The endless hunt for rare exotic starships and the incredible bio-mechanical Living Ships keeps the endgame incredibly rewarding.
• Settlement Management: Managing your own planetary villages adds a wonderful layer of community and responsibility to the galaxy.
• A Captivating Narrative: Beneath the sandbox gameplay, there is a genuinely fantastic storyline that ties the universe together.
• Ominous Nostalgia: I absolutely loved the terrifying atmosphere of the infested derelict freighters from the early days. Please bring those scary freighters back, Hello Games!
• Endless Free Updates: With massive, completely free content dropping on a highly regular basis, you never know what breathtaking surprise is waiting around the corner.

A few wishes for the Hello Games team:
• Christmas Expeditions: We veteran players deeply appreciate the chance to replay past expeditions. It would be awesome if the team could rerun them around Christmas again!
• Persistent Base Sharing: Playing with friends is my number one favorite feature. My ultimate dream request would be allowing friends to continue editing shared bases even after the base owner logs off.
Starfleet to the rescue!

I cannot thank the No Man's Sky team enough for their unmatched dedication, passion, and hard work in building this dream of a game.  To the stars!

In conventional usage, boredom, ennui, or tedium is an emotion characterized by uninterest in one's surrounding, often caused by a lack of distractions or occupations. However, boredom is not well defined. It is distinct from depression and apathy. Boredom may damage mental health, but it also seems to have improved creativity in humans.

In Experience Without Qualities: Boredom and Modernity, Elizabeth Goodstein traces the modern discourse on boredom through literary, philosophical, and sociological texts to find that as "a discursively articulated phenomenon...boredom is at once objective and subjective, emotion and intellectualization—not just a response to the modern world, but also a historically constituted strategy for coping with its discontents." In both conceptions, boredom has to do fundamentally with an experience of time—such as experiencing the slowness of time—and problems of meaning.

The expression to be a bore had been used in print in the sense of "to be tiresome or dull" since 1768 at the latest. The expression "boredom" means "state of being bored," 1852, from bore (v.1) + -dom. It also has been employed in a sense "bores as a class" (1883) and "practice of being a bore" (1864, a sense properly belonging to boreism, 1833). The word "bore" as a noun meaning a "thing which causes ennui or annoyance" is attested to since 1778; "of persons by 1812". The noun "bore" comes from the verb "bore", which had the meaning " be tiresome or dull" first attested  1768, a vogue word c. 1780–81 according to Grose (1785); possibly a figurative extension of "to move forward slowly and persistently, as a  boring tool does." A popular misconception is that Charles Dickens coined the term "boredom" in his work Bleak House, published in 1853. The word, however, has been attested since at least 1829 in an issue of the publication The Albion.

The French term for boredom, ennui, is sometimes used in English as well, at least since 1778. The term ennui was first used "as a French word in English;" in the 1660s and it was "nativized by 1758". The term ennui comes "from French ennui, from Old French enui "annoyance" (13c.),  back-formation from enoiier, anuier. "The German word for "boredom" is Langeweile, a compound made of lange "long" and Weile "while", which is in line with the common perception that when one is bored, time passes "torturously" slowly.

Different scholars use different definitions of boredom, which complicates research. Boredom has been defined by Cynthia D. Fisher in terms of its main central psychological processes: "an unpleasant, transient affective state in which the individual feels a pervasive lack of interest and difficulty concentrating on the current activity." Mark Leary et al. describe boredom as "an affective experience associated with cognitive attentional processes." Robert Plutchik characterized boredom as a mild form of disgust. In positive psychology, boredom is described as a response to a moderate challenge for which the subject has more than enough skill.

There are three types of boredom, all of which involve problems of engagement of attention. These include times when humans are prevented from engaging in wanted activity, when humans are forced to engage in unwanted activity, or when people are simply unable for some other reason to maintain engagement in an activity. Boredom proneness is a tendency to experience boredom of all types. This is typically assessed by the Boredom Proneness Scale. Recent research has found that boredom proneness is clearly and consistently associated with failures of attention. Boredom and its proneness are both theoretically and empirically linked to depression and similar symptoms. Nonetheless, boredom proneness has been found to be as strongly correlated with attentional lapses as with depression. Although boredom is often viewed as a trivial and mild irritant, proneness to boredom has been linked to a very diverse range of possible psychological, physical, educational, and social problems.

Absent-mindedness is where a person shows inattentive or forgetful behaviour. Absent-mindedness is a mental condition in which the subject experiences low levels of attention and frequent distraction. Absent-mindedness is not a diagnosed condition, but rather a symptom of boredom and sleepiness which people experience in their daily lives. People who are absent-minded tend to show signs of memory lapse and weak recollection of recently occurring events. This can usually be a result of a variety of other conditions often diagnosed by clinicians such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and depression. In addition to absent-mindedness leading to an array of consequences affecting daily life, it can also have more severe, long-term problems.

Although it has not been widely studied, research on boredom suggests that boredom is a major factor impacting diverse areas of a person's life. People ranked low on a boredom-proneness scale were found to have better performance in a wide variety of aspects of their lives, including career, education, and autonomy. Boredom can be a symptom of clinical depression. Boredom can be a form of learned helplessness, a phenomenon closely related to depression. Some philosophies of parenting propose that if children are raised in an environment devoid of stimuli, and are not allowed or encouraged to interact with their environment, they will fail to develop the mental capacities to do so.

In a learning environment, a common cause of boredom is lack of understanding; for instance, if one is not following or connecting to the material in a class or lecture, it will usually seem boring. However, the opposite can also be true; something that is too easily understood, simple or transparent, can also be boring. Boredom is often inversely related to learning, and in school it may be a sign that a student is not challenged enough, or too challenged. An activity that is predictable to the students is likely to bore them.

A 1989 study indicated that an individual's impression of boredom may be influenced by the individual's degree of attention, as a higher acoustic level of distraction from the environment correlated with higher reportings of boredom. Boredom has been studied as being related to drug abuse among teens. Boredom has been proposed as a cause of pathological gambling behavior. A study found results consistent with the hypothesis that pathological gamblers seek stimulation to avoid states of boredom and depression. It has been suggested that boredom has an evolutionary basis that encourages humans to seek out new challenges. It may influence human learning and ingenuity.

Some recent studies have suggested that boredom may have some positive effects. A low-stimulus environment may lead to increased creativity and may set the stage for a "eureka moment".

Someone in the Anomaly gave me 10 Fusion Ignitors worth roughly 156 million Units, which turned my respectable little space business into a venture-capital-backed logistics empire.
I named my hauler the SS Falcon, my freighter the SS Destroyer, built an S-class Corvette called the USS Avenger, loaded it with cargo space, tractor beams and enough weapons to make “salvage vessel” sound increasingly dishonest, then discovered Creative mode and rebuilt the thing because the first version offended me aesthetically.

For example, the gas giants apparently have a solid surface you can actually walk on and black holes act more like wormholes which teleports you to another corner of the galaxy in no time even though they are called black holes in the game. But honestly, the game fiction wins over realism for the sake of gameplay here and i wont complain. But I really hope the developers make gas giants feel unique and challenging compared to regular planets. They could add atmospheric depth where you have to equip your starship with special reinforcement modules just to fly through the turbulence and harvest rare gases and maybe put a solid plasma core at the center of the planet which could be packed with high value minerals that makes it hard to harvest but worth a lot.
Regardless, I 100% recommend this game for space lovers.

I enjoyed my time with this. It's one of those games where you want to watch a few videos not to learn how to make money super quickly or speed up the grind, but just to learn what activities are available for you to do.

A quick list of things I enjoyed: shopping around for a new ship, creating bases on inhospitable worlds, doing the derelict ship "dungeon crawls", assembling my first custom corvette and naming it "The Dumpster" because it was as ugly as sin.

It suffers a bit from being "wide as an ocean" and "deep as a puddle." There are tons of things to do - some of them are fun, some are just grindy. Some activities are very lucrative but very boring, others are interesting but not very lucrative. It's the sort of game where you need to figure out a goal for yourself and work towards it - allowing yourself to get distracted along the way.

It is a grindy game by its very nature. Farming new upgrade and inventory slots gets pretty annoying. You'll find blueprints for interesting things to install but won't have the space to install them a lot of the time. So you do the shuffle: uninstall stuff, find a storage slot to stick it in, install the new thing you want to try. You realize the new thing isn't that good, so you uninstall it, shuffle it into your inventory, install the old thing again.

I could nitpick flaws all day. I became a space pirate and started shooting up entire fleets of ships... only to realize that there were no meaningful consequences. Nothing came to stop me. So I made tens of millions in a few minutes and earned a bunch of rewards with no real effort spent. I gained the highest outlaw rank in about 15 minutes - something you would expect to take hours or days of dedication.

There's a lot of broken stuff in this game. There's also just a lot of stuff though and a good variety of things to try out. I don't think the game has lasting appeal for me, but I played it obsessively for about 40 hours. This scratched an itch for me.

Best quests: Starfield
Best on-foot combat: Starfield
Best starship combat: X4 Foundations
Best ship design: Elite Dangerous
Best crafting: No Man's Sky
Best base building: No Man's Sky
Most user-friendly: No Man's Sky
Least user-friendly: X4 Foundations
Most variety: No Man's Sky
Most compelling world: X4 Foundations
Best graphics: Starfield
Best controls: No Man's Sky
Most grindy: Elite Dangerous
Least grindy: Starfield

So - none of these games have everything.

For my own personal preferences:

No Man's Sky is a masterclass in modern game evolution, offering a sprawling procedural universe that delivers nearly endless gameplay for solo players and group explorers alike.

Here is a breakdown of how key game features shape the overall experience:

1. Exploration & Planetary Discovery
Unmatched Scale: With quintillions of procedurally generated planets across multiple galaxies, exploration never truly hits a wall.

Biome & Creature Variety: Discover unique flora, fauna, weather phenomena, and ancient ruins on every new world.

Seamless Travel: Moving from a planet's surface into space and warping across solar systems feels smooth and immersive.

2. Base Building & Resource Management
Creative Freedom: Build complex, custom bases anywhere—from sub-zero tundra worlds to underwater chasms or giant freighter starships.

Resource Progression: Mining elements and crafting components creates a satisfying gameplay loop that fuels survival, base upgrades, and gear progression.

3. Starships & Fleet Command
Ship Diversity: Collect, upgrade, and customize an array of starships, including Fighters, Explorers, Haulers, Exotic ships, and Sentinel interceptors.

Freighters & Frigate Fleets: Purchase capital freighters to act as mobile home bases and manage a fleet of frigates on automated outer-space missions.

4. Multiplayer & Solo Flexibility
True Playstyle Choice: Play completely solo in an expansive, quiet universe, or jump into seamless co-op with friends to tackle missions together.

The Anomaly: A central hub where players meet up, trade, show off ships, and embark on community Nexus missions.

Regular Expeditions: Time-limited community events provide shared goals, fresh challenge runs, and unique cosmetics or ships.

Final Verdict
No Man's Sky stands out as a complete, feature-rich sandbox. Whether you prefer quiet solo exploration, building massive sci-fi settlements, or traveling the stars with friends, there is always something new to do—making it virtually impossible to run out of things to experience.

Terraria is easily one of my favorite games of all time. I’ve put nearly 500 hours into it, and somehow it’s still a game I can come back to, start a new world, and get completely invested all over again.
What I love most about Terraria is how much there actually is to do. You can explore, build, fish, collect gear, fight bosses, farm materials, mess around with different classes, hunt for rare items, or spend way too much time making a house look nice when you originally logged on to fight a boss. The game gives you a ridiculous amount of freedom without ever feeling like there’s nothing to work toward.
The progression is probably my favorite part. Starting out with barely anything and slowly becoming strong enough to take on enemies and bosses that would have destroyed you earlier feels genuinely rewarding. Hardmode especially changes so much that it almost feels like the game opens up all over again. There are tons of weapons, accessories, armor sets, builds, and ways to play, so different playthroughs can feel completely different from each other.
Exploration is also one of the biggest reasons I’ve played for so long. Even after hundreds of hours, I still enjoy digging into a new cave, finding structures, searching for loot, or stumbling into something I wasn’t expecting. Terraria constantly gives you that “I’ll just do one more thing” feeling, and then suddenly several hours are gone.
It’s not perfect. The amount of information in the game can be overwhelming for a new player, and there are definitely moments where you’ll probably end up checking the wiki because the game doesn’t explain everything particularly well. RNG can also be absolutely evil when you’re trying to get one specific item. But neither of those things have ever stopped me from wanting to keep playing.
For the amount of content, replayability, creativity, progression, and memories I’ve gotten out of Terraria, it’s honestly hard for me not to recommend it. Very few games have given me this many hours of entertainment while still making me want to come back.
Nearly 500 hours later, and I’d still happily start another world.
Absolutely recommended.
