I bought No Man's Sky at launch, on a PS4, and through playing this game experienced one of the moments defining my current approach to gaming, hobbies, and life in general. 

I had found a planet particularly rich in a certain element / resource, sharing a system with a space station a short jump away that was buying that resource at a premium price. I had been at it a while, mining, loading, flying, selling, a routine constructed of repetitive actions. Go to the same planet, the same place, dig, run the same route, see the same things, talk to the same terminal. I was on autopilot, figuratively speaking. I had a goal in mind: to do this until I had millions upon millions of Units, and then to go fly around and buy a Freighter. I wanted a capital ship -- and this, I'd decided, was how I was going to do it.

A friend came by to visit, to check out the game. The hype around NMS was real, and he was relatively offline, so he was unaware of the negative press circulating at the time of launch. He show up, sat down, we hung out and talked about the game, what was up in general, generally shooting the breeze, as one does. We'd been talking for about an hour, and I'd been sort of absentmindedly playing the game in the background the whole time. It was easy, really. The task didn't take much space in my brain. There was a natural lull in our conversation, and after a couple beats, he said "so... are you... having fun?" 

The immediate laughter, from both of us, opened space for me to explain what I was doing. Suddenly, I was acutely aware he'd come here to see the endless space game with endless planets, and all he'd seen was me, mining the same place, flying to the same station, selling to the same screen. I explained what I was doing and why, and he nodded, but I wasn't able to shake the question. Was I having fun? 

After mulling it over, I realized, no. No I was not having fun. So, maybe I should... play something else for a while? And I did. I left No Man's Sky alone for a bit, and ventured into other places and spaces. It would be years before I returned. 

I build a computer, thought, "hey, I bet No Man's Sky would be rad as hell, it sure does get a lot of positive press and attention these days" 

and brother

No Man's Sky, in it's current iteration, positively whips. I can tell you, without a doubt, I am having fun. 

It's the perfect game to come home to, to play in the late night, to wind down with. It excels at giving you fun and interesting things to look at, explore, and do. [h1]The best shooter in the world.[/h1] in which the guns are just as good as everything else
I’ve finally run out of all the items obtained from lost gear, so now I’m officially old this game.
[h3]generation[/h3]
In all this time, I have yet to find a single game that could show me greater [i]deep[/i] in its mechanics. Overall, the combination of mechanics is so incredibly well-executed that it is hard to grasp without actually playing the game. Procedural generation, coupled with enemy behaviors and types, as well as the nature of the missions, constantly creates a sense of variety thanks to its unpredictability. The maps feature diverse terrain types, each with its own hazards, such as the risk of freezing on an icy map or getting a face full of magma on a volcanic one. At the same time, the constantly shifting size and myriad terrain details can either make it easier for you to escape the bugs or make it easier for them to surround you or attack from positions where you really wouldn't want them to be.
[h3]Guns and classes[/h3]
The game features four classes that are so good when played solo, yet ten times better in a team, that it’s actually startling. They are perfectly balanced and possess traits that fully cover every need. Each class possesses its own unique weapons and mechanics, distinct from one another, that offer advantages in quite specific situations. 
The Driller relies on elemental damage and primarily operates at close range; the Gunner uses suppressive-fire weaponry; the Scout wields highly precise arms; and the Engineer employs crowd-control tools at medium range.
Moreover, each class is capable of handling any swarm of bugs on its own, using its own unique style and methods.
Modules also add even more interest to the game, transforming any weapon into truly unusual devices.
The most striking example is the Gunner's rocket launcher: the rockets can be transformed into laser-guided blades that slice at the enemy in the direction you're looking while circling them; they can be turned into tiny cluster-bomb drones; they can be converted into deployable landmines; or you can simply disable their homing capabilities to unleash an endless barrage of rockets. 
Grenades also have their own specific versions, while they may not boast a huge amount of variety, they still offer very interesting options.
[h3]What's next?[/h3]
I can't imagine a better shooter right now, and I hope that either the game sees further development (though I highly doubt it, I feel its time will run out in a few years) or something similar with an equally original concept comes along. Far Far West, unfortunately, isn't exactly a strong competitor, it won't replace this game for me, simply because the developers decided, for some reason, to make it a roguelike and included very uninteresting weapons. Delta Force? You’d only play that piece of trash if every other shooter in the world ceased to exist, I’ve never seen such boring gunplay. There are plenty of other projects out there, but for some reason, they all chase realism, convinced that it’s what everyone wants... the future doesn't look too bright right now.

Honestly this review is more mixed than negative. Apex used to be such a good game and, to an extent, still is. The basic gameplay loop hasn't changed and the essential systems are all the same its just a different coat of paint, and not a pretty one. None of that is to say its a perfect game, it isn't and there are many problems we can talk about, a couple being over-monetization and too much content but the base game is still there. Apex isn't a corpse being paraded around and there's still fun to be had in the game but it isn't what it used to be and it has numerous problems. If your looking to relive the old battle royale craze then there isn't a better game to do so, but if your looking for a new and exciting game this isn't it either. If you do play it then just keep in mind that its a seven year old live service, and it's not what it used to be. It's more than past time to let Apex rest and bring us Titanfall 3.

Warframe: a game that remains.
You and I have seen it, new kid on the block promises you a cheap to free experience. The honeymoon phase truly is a phase. First comes the willingly support a small or growing developer by purchasing a battlepass or a skin, you know, support the community. All for it, right? Then the first update comes out and you and your friends will not shut up about how awesome an experience is, especially if its pve. Kicking it back, having some good laughs. But then another update comes around maybe... 4 months and you start questioning if the rollout of content is good. Then you question if the game is truly building something great or if its overcomplicating a sandbox of play. After some time, you start to realize, you gear might not fit some oddly perscribed "meta" and that fun you had exploring new content starts to feel like catchup, especially if you go to work, go to school, have a life even beyond that. Then the ugly happens, the breakup. You become so hyperaware that everything behind the seens never really was about you but grooming a community into shelling out dollar after dollar only to be gaslit that they were the problem when something gets reworked, removed, nerfed, or entire storylines became "you had to be there bro", when you stuck to your wallet and patience.

Welcome to Warframe, it... from my knowledge... never did that. Remember when No Man's Sky came out and now it's this bastion of hope in 2020's gaming where even if you don't play it that often, you genuinely wish them well? This is kind of like that, but I argue on a crazier model. I was with Warframe since the start, playing off and on over the years, forgetting account passwords, restarting fresh, but never really "made it far" and I was so scared when free-roam came in that this was just some way to ride the wave of developement.
WOW I was wrong after so many years.
Nothing has changed, in probably the best way to describe it.
New warframe is overpowered? Good, keep it, enjoy it, experiment with it.
New weapons do weird silly numbers? Good, keep it, enjoy it, they DON'T care.
Remember that one story line that happened years ago? From what I can tell, it's STILL here.

I don't see any major number changes, the community CLEARLY still loves this game dearly AND they keep up updates with Soulframe coming out/swinging? Majorly impressed.
This is a game that understands, whales will whale, free-to-play will free-to-play and as long as they keep making things silly and listen to community trends, memes, and feedback in a productive way, then all's good.
PvP is admittedly dead and clan content is mostly just trials and fun runs. But the silly things that made this game fun are arguably a LOT more attractive now that I'm changing my tastes in gaming.

Is it a sensory overload simulator? Yes. But it is also probably one of the chillest games I've seen that rewards clever gameplay with what I'm rolling with and the grind actually encourages you to explore your sandbox, but doesn't make you feel like you're trading anything particularly off.
I don't see any MAJOR fomo and anything that is at the end of the battlepass feels more like a "oh that's cool" versus a "I can't miss that".

Seriously, it's still kicking, I'm still bumping into public groups, and I'm treated fairly for being a truly free-to-play player without the groin kick every five seconds that I need to get the new gacha character because their plot is peak and they have... nice pixels...

Trust me, you'll have that here too. Just you'll need to wait for cosmetics to go on sale or be unvaulted. But beyond that, from a gameplay level, and unlocking things... you are treated VERY fairly.

If you understood the game I'm referring to from the start, you and I went through the Creek and you and I probably aren't looking back.

Two Vietnamese players, Himass and TanVuu, committed a rule violation by interacting with their stream chat during the match. They openly admitted to it and publicly apologized. In return, Krafton immediately dropped the guillotine: a permanent competitive ban and the swift revocation of their Partner status—a hasty, ruthless decision that completely ignored the context and their years of dedication to the game.

But what truly outrages me and the entire community isn't just the disproportionately harsh punishment; it's the publisher's disgusting double standards. A Korean female streamer played the victim, crying and accusing others of cheating, only for the community to expose her with crystal-clear evidence: she had a Chrome tab wide open, actively watching the tournament's live broadcast while playing. That is actual stream sniping and genuine cheating. Yet, what did Krafton do to their "golden child"? Absolutely nothing. Radio silence. No penalty, no explanation. They chose to fully condone her hypocrisy while trampling on the voices of millions of Vietnamese gamers.

It's deeply ironic for a survival game to be unable to maintain the bare minimum boundaries of fairness it set itself. The current wave of top streamers mass-deleting the game and the flood of negative reviews are a heavy but entirely deserved price for their sheer disrespect toward the player base. Krafton may have chosen to cover things up to protect one individual and save face, but they have permanently lost the respect of an entire market. PUBG right now is the textbook example of a publisher killing its own game through blind favoritism.

TL;DR

A truly unique and innovative take on the 4 player co-op hoard genre. Great game to play with friends. The destruction and combat feels awesome and Arrowhead Game Studios makes incredible free content updates adding new enemies and areas to fight in. However, if you want to experience the unique weapons of mass destruction used to eliminate greater threats at higher difficulties, you will have to fork over $ for each warbond (battlepass) that includes them. The prices of these passes are 10$ each, but with there now being a total of 23, it becomes a little ridiculous in my opinion. If you buy one, they do often include the currency to buy another at a discounted price, but the matter still stands. Hopefully this can change in the future with routine additions of premium warbond tokens, but only time will tell. Online discourse has also shown that Arrowhead Game Studio has been known to routinely nerf beloved weapons and other items over the games life cycle, so do with that what you will. If you can ignore these annoying practices, the gunplay and combat loop holds up and you will have a great time blasting aliens with friends–as long as they don't team kill you. 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


While I think it's a great game and truly unique from any other 4-player co-op hoard shooters of the past, It has a glaring issue that leads me to give it a negative review: warbonds. I could understand these being routinely implemented with their prices IF the game was free to play, but it is not. I also largely ignored it for the beginning life cycle of the game as I thought Arrow Head would “throw the community a bone” at some point. It has been almost three years since this game’s initial release, and still nothing. What I am talking about is how are there 23 premium warbonds in the game at this point and not a single one has become free, whether that be through an in-game quest system or something else? It is incredibly frustrating and confusing. You could make the argument of “just don't buy them, the game is still playable” or “You can earn the currency to purchase warbonds for free just through playing”, but those arguments don't hold up in my opinion. 

After playing the game enough, you will want to raise the difficulty to earn more currencies to upgrade your strategems, ship modules, etc. but the enemies will also become harder to kill and there will be more of them. Want to make it easier? Fork over $10 to then work towards better stratagems through a premium warbond. The price is justified and not egregious like monetization practices in triple A titles, but it's the fact that there are now 23, 10$ warbonds without ANY being offered for free, especially after the way the community has routinely supported this game over its life cycle. I mean if you own the Super Citizen Edition of the game, you are granted a Premium Warbond Token that lets you unlock one Premium Warbond of your choice. Why not grant EVERYONE one or two of these tokens once a year with a huge update or if the community completes an extremely hard campaign against one of the alien races? I really don’t think that is asking for too much. 

There have been some difficult updates in the past where I said to myself, “wow this would be 10x easier if I had the stratagems and weapons of _ warbond”. One of these times I actually stopped playing with friends just to “farm” enough credits to purchase a premium warbond for free, but at what cost? Only 10 hours since the spawn rates of the currency and its amounts are so abysmal. Every time I return to the game, I am met with a brief moment of seeing all the cool stratagems and weapons added to the game only to realize I have to pay for it all even though I already paid $40 for the game. That does not feel good.

I wouldn't call Satisfactory a perfect game, although with over 700 hours in it, I obviously like it.

It's weirdly good at supply-chain automation, which apparently is something I really enjoy. Designing factories, balancing production, solving logistics problems, and figuring out how to automate increasingly complicated production chains is entertaining.

Where the game falls short for me is purpose, particularly when it comes to the world itself.

I spent almost the entire game in the starter area. I built a second power plant around the pools, but otherwise, when I found resources somewhere else, I just conveyed them back to my main base. There was rarely a reason to do anything else.

The game doesn't really encourage you to establish yourself in new parts of the map. Conveyors are easy enough to run across terrible terrain that geography doesn't impose much of a restriction. And the different regions aren't distinct or interesting enough mechanically to make me want to move there just because I've discovered them.

A different progression could have solved this. Valheim does this well. Moving into a new area is difficult enough that you naturally establish another home there. You build storage, infrastructure, and production because constantly traveling back to your original base isn't practical. Eventually you get better ways of traveling between locations, but by then the game has already taught you to have multiple homes.

Satisfactory never really did that to me. Instead, the Space Elevator became the anchor. I built around it, and as I expanded across the map, it was almost always easier to bring everything back to that anchor than to build somewhere new.

So eventually the game becomes a loop: unlock something, build another assembly line, optimize it, and repeat. The factory-building itself is excellent, but the larger world doesn't change that loop enough.  oh and the opening of the game says.  build vertically.  so yes.  everthing fit inside a building the size of that pillar thing.  20x20 maybe.  then like 15 stories.  idk.  the they flying shark thing was basically flying through my upper floors.  anyway.

I don't necessarily want more things to build. I want the progression and geography to give me reasons to build differently, in different places, for different reasons.

I cannot believe I am actually writing this review, but apparently I have reached the point where I need to publicly document one of the most baffling design decisions I have ever encountered in a videogame:

You cannot light firecrackers with matches.

That is the review.

Actually, no. Fuck that. This deserves more than one sentence. This deserves an investigation, a committee, and several hours of hearings where one exhausted developer is asked to explain how a videogame containing both MATCHES and FIRECRACKERS somehow decided that these two objects should have absolutely nothing to do with each other.

I have matches.

I have firecrackers.

The firecrackers have a fuse.

The matches create fire.

And yet the game looks directly into my eyes and says:

“No.”

Excuse me?

What exactly is the problem here?

Do the matches and firecrackers need to be formally introduced first? Do they need to build trust? Do I need to take them out for dinner before they are comfortable interacting? Do I need to wait three business days for the firecracker to approve the match as an authorized ignition device?

What the fuck are we doing here?

This is not advanced chemistry. This is not aerospace engineering. This is not nuclear fusion.

It is a match.

You strike it.

It burns.

You put the burning part next to the fuse.

The fuse catches fire.

Humanity has understood this technology for quite some time.

Apparently, however, the universe of this game operates under a completely different set of physical laws.

Here, a lit match can apparently exist five millimeters away from a firecracker fuse while both objects mutually agree to ignore each other. The flame approaches the fuse and the game engine itself presumably intervenes:

“Absolutely not. We do not support that level of technological innovation.”

And I know what somebody is going to say:

“You need a lighter.”

Oh.

Of course.

A lighter.

How foolish of me.

Obviously the fire coming from a lighter is a completely different species of fire from the fire coming from a match.

Lighter flame: approved fire.

Match flame: decorative fire.

My mistake.

Maybe the firecracker scans the ignition source before accepting combustion.

I strike a match.

The fuse says:

“Unsupported peripheral detected.”

I hold up a lighter.

The fuse says:

“Welcome, administrator.”

Brilliant.

Maybe the firecracker requires Bluetooth. Maybe I need to pair it first. Maybe the match firmware is outdated. Maybe I need MatchOS 11.4 or later. Maybe there is a checkbox hidden somewhere in the settings called:

ALLOW LEGACY MATCHSTICK COMPATIBILITY

At this point I would believe anything, because apparently basic combustion is now platform-dependent.

But this does not improve gameplay.

It does not create meaningful strategy.

It does not add depth.

It does not create tension.

It creates exactly one thing:

A human being sitting in front of a monitor saying:

“Wait. Seriously?”

That is the mechanic.

Confusion.

I acquire firecrackers. Great.

I acquire matches. Great.

My primitive monkey brain notices that one object creates fire and another object needs fire.

I experience the dangerous sensation known as “having an idea.”

The game immediately punishes me for this.

Wrong.

Bad player.

You attempted basic causal reasoning.

Please locate the officially sanctioned fire-producing object.

A match has basically one major feature: it creates a small flame. That is why humanity manufactures matches. Nobody buys a box of matches because they like the shape. Nobody looks at twenty little wooden sticks and says:

“Excellent. These will make a fine decoration.”

THEY ARE FOR LIGHTING THINGS.

That is the entire product.

So naturally, in this game, one of the things they cannot light is an object specifically designed to be lit.

Game design has peaked. Pack it up. There is nowhere left for the medium to go.

WHY?

Why can I not take the little flaming stick and place it next to the little flammable string?

What catastrophic event would occur if this interaction were allowed?

Would the simulation collapse? Would the zombies unionize? Would Steam uninstall itself? Would my graphics card explode from the computational complexity of transferring flame from Object A to Object B?

Was there a whiteboard during development that said:

IMPORTANT SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:

- Zombies
- Survival
- Inventory
- Crafting
- Matches
- Firecrackers
- ABSOLUTELY NEVER CONNECT THE LAST TWO

I need to know.

Because somebody had to make this decision.

Someone created the match item. Someone created the firecracker item. Someone implemented ignition. Someone defined which ignition sources work.

And somehow nobody apparently stopped and asked:

“Should matches maybe also work?”

And if somebody DID ask that, somebody else apparently answered:

“No.”

That “no” fascinates me.

I want the design document. I want the meeting transcript. I want archaeological evidence. I want future historians to dig through the source code and identify the exact moment human reason abandoned the project.

Because there must be a line of code somewhere that basically says:

if (item == Firecracker && ignitionSource == Match)
{
    fuckYou();
}

That is what it feels like.

This interaction feels personal.

The game does not merely prevent me from using the match. It feels like the game watches me try, folds its arms, and enjoys it.

“You thought matches could light firecrackers?”

Yes.

“Because matches create fire?”

YES.

“And firecracker fuses require fire?”

YES.

“Interesting.”

Then nothing happens.

This is psychological warfare.

I am being gaslit by inventory items.

I have begun questioning everything I know about combustion.

Maybe matches do not actually create fire. Maybe I hallucinated every birthday candle I have ever seen. Maybe every fireplace ever started with a match was a coincidence. Maybe wood simply ignited itself out of embarrassment.

Forget the zombies. Forget starvation. Forget infection.

The true horror is discovering that causality itself has stopped working.

There is something deeply unsettling about carrying an object whose entire purpose is ignition and discovering that it cannot ignite the most obviously ignitable object in your inventory.

That is cosmic horror.

Ancient gods sleeping beneath the ocean? Whatever.

Impossible geometry? Boring.

A firecracker that rejects matches?

Now THAT is madness.

My survivor is holding the two halves of mankind's greatest technological equation:

THING THAT MAKES FIRE.

THING THAT NEEDS FIRE.

The worst part of this game isn't the player-base nor the undenybly overbearing and overpriced paid cosmetics. It truely is Smurfing.
I won't assume everyone is aware of what a smurf is, so let me briefly explain it. When an experienced player who is (or at least considers themself to be) good at the game creates a new account, they are considered to be using a smurf account. The reason for this is to abuse the matchmaking system to be put into matches with other new accounts so that the better player on the new account can demolish the new players playing on new accounts.
I probably don't need to explain why smurfing is bad. It is players abusing a system to get un-earned and cheap wins off of people learning the game and subsequently putting other new players off the game. Smurfing has been a problem since I started playing this game in season one and to my knowlege there has been no effort to stop or slow the behaviour. As the ever-naive consumer, I can't assume this is a quick and easy fix but since other games don't seem to have as big of a problem with smurfs I wonder why this one does.
You can limit smurfs by playing the ranked mode but then you are playing in games where people's internet reputation is on the line and subsequently tensions can be pretty high (in other words, people get toxic).

Another kicker is the execution of the free-to-play model. Because of the direction of the game in popularity (and this is my assumption) the game seems to be going further away from many players paying smaller amounts (for example, a couple cosmetics or the battlepass) and more towards fewer players paying higher amounts for more exotic cosmetics. Earlier in the game, the highest rarity of cosmetic was Legendary. Most legendary skins were paid for in the premium currency. Nowadays, there is a heavier emphasis on more expensive items such as heirlooms (VERY expensive and/or rare cosmetics) and the extra-premium battlepass. For the average player, this means the average cost is steeper for cosmetics in general.

Understand that while this is mainly a load of complaining, I do enjoy this game heartily when the mood for it strikes. I will always mourn the loss of the story-focused events of course, but I encourage you to NOT BUY ANYTHING until they have sorted out some of these quirks.

*Edit:
I can no longer recommend this game. In my frustration with smurf prevelance in my casual lobbies, I swapped to ranked to at least play fair games. In three sessions, it was exhausting how many teams had suspiciously high success badges, killcounts, and movement (all three) compared to their level (under 50) all while using default skins. The ratio of losing to smurfs vs losing to players my skill level was something like 4:1.
I say this with a clear mind and with a thoughtful conscious: this game is ruined by smurfs.

After more than 127 hours in *No Man’s Sky*, I think I've finally played enough to give the game a fair review.

Hello Games' first venture with *No Man's Sky* was, quite frankly, a disaster at launch. The game arrived with enormous expectations and failed to deliver on many of the promises that had been made. What impresses me most, though, is what happened afterward.

Instead of folding up shop, abandoning the game, and moving on to something else, Hello Games dug in. They seemed determined to turn *No Man's Sky* into the game they had originally promised it would be. Looking back at what they've accomplished over the past ten years, I think they've done an excellent job.

Even more impressive is that they are still developing it.

I hope that continues, especially as Hello Games works on *Light No Fire*. If technology and features developed for one game can benefit the other—such as the improvements they've made to water and oceans—that could give *No Man's Sky* an unusually long life. Ten years after release, the game is still growing rather than simply being maintained.

Personally, I've really enjoyed the quests, collecting and upgrading ships, building bases, and simply exploring the planets. There is always something else that catches my attention and sends me off in another direction.

The game isn't perfect, of course. One thing I would really like to see is more variety within individual planets. Most worlds tend to have one environmental theme spread across the entire planet. It would be great to find worlds with more distinct regions—different climates, terrain, vegetation, or other features depending on where you land. I still enjoy exploring the planets as they are, but mixed environments would make discovering and exploring a new world much more interesting.

Combat could also use a little more depth. Space dogfights are fun at first, but after a while they can become routine. Adding more targetable features to enemy ships—engines, weapons, shields, or other systems—could make battles more tactical and give you more choices than simply wearing down an enemy's shields and hull. That would add some much-needed excitement and variety to space combat.

Even after 127 hours, I still have a surprising amount of the game left to experience. I haven't even gotten seriously into the Expeditions yet, and I'm looking forward to seeing what I've missed there.

Considering where *No Man's Sky* started, where it is today, and just how much enjoyment I've gotten out of it, I think Hello Games deserves a tremendous amount of credit for sticking with it.

**My rating: 9 out of 10.**

This game is one that I genuinely just can't properly explain to someone who's never played it. From the outside, it seems like a really simple 2D game where you mine, build, fight, and follow some kind of linear progression slop system. But that IS NOT what this game is. It's so much more than that, and it has a feeling to it that is genuinely exclusive to Terraria and Terraria only.

I've put thousands of hours into this game, starting out on the Wii U and 3DS, figuring out literally everything for myself with no wiki at the ripe age of like 9 years old when it came out on the 3DS in 2016, I think. So yeah, don't judge me based off my steam time.

I remember sitting there with the big ass Wii U GamePad in my hands playing Terraria with my brother, not knowing that Hardmode even existed, what the class bonuses on armor meant, or that you could actually kill the Wall of Flesh. I don't think I figured that out until like three years after getting the game. I remember one of the main reasons I even played was because I wanted to get the Terra Blade because i saw a random youtube video about it it and thought it was the coolest shit ever. Sadly I never actually got it on the Wii U lol.

Honestly though, I think not knowing what I was doing was part of what made the game so damn magical for me. The genuine vastness of the recipes, items, weapons, armor, enemies, and everything else made it feel like there was never nothing to do. There was always something I didn't know about.

I'd go underground looking for one particular ore—I think it was gold because I had this little Terraria minifigure wearing gold armor—and somehow I'd end up finding something completely different. I specifically remember finding tungsten for the first time, and I don't even know why, but tungsten armor has unironically been my favorite armor in the game ever since.

I remember coming back to my old Wii U world years later and seeing this giant tree-looking house I had built and just being in shock at how much time I must have spent on it. Eventually, all of those little things just turned into memories. But I'm happy to say my parents were wrong when they told me I wouldn't remember all the time I spent playing video games. I'll remember those moments for the rest of my life, and I'll remember this game until I die.

I think the best part is that 10 years later, now that I'm an adult in college with a girlfriend and bills to pay, I still get the same damn excitement creating a new world that I did back then on my Wii U or 3DS.

Maybe that's part of what makes Terraria so special to me. This game has been around and in my life for so long that it's honestly difficult to separate the game itself from my actual memories, if that makes sense. I played Terraria when I was a single-digit age. I played it when I couldn't drive, and I've played it now that I can. I went from playing it on a 3DS and Wii U to playing it on a PC I built myself. It's just always been there.

I've stopped playing for months at a time before, but I ALWAYS come back to this game. And every single time I do, it still just feels like—Terraria.

There are bigger games. There are games with better graphics, bigger budgets, and massive cinematic stories. But for a game that starts you off with a copper sword, an axe, a pickaxe, and some random guy I eventually have to kill to summon a giant wall, it's insane just how far the adventure goes.

Thousands of hours later, I'm still not tired of it.

And honestly, I don't think I ever will be.

338,000 VND.

That is how much I spent on PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS.

At first, I thought I was paying for a serious competitive game — one where skill, reflexes, strategy, and teamwork determine the outcome. I also believed that a major esports ecosystem like PUBG's would put fairness and transparency first.

But after everything that has happened recently, especially the controversy involving Himass and TanVuu, I have lost a lot of that trust.

KRAFTON published the results of its investigation, confirmed the use of outside information during competitive matches, and issued permanent bans from PUBG accounts and official competitions. KRAFTON also acknowledged shortcomings in its own handling and operation of the situation.

I am not defending Himass.
I am not defending TanVuu either.

If competitive rules were violated, disciplinary action is understandable. What disappoints me more is that a professional competitive system was able to let a situation like this happen in the first place.

For a competitive game, fairness is not an extra feature — it is the foundation.

I can accept losing because my opponent has better aim.
I can accept losing because my strategy was worse.
I can accept losing because I simply wasn't good enough.

What I don't want is to question whether the environment I'm playing in is actually fair.

PUBG still has its strengths. The gunplay is good, the audio is solid, and playing with friends can still be genuinely fun. But a game is more than how good the shooting feels. For a competitive title with a major esports scene, the way the developer manages the game and protects competitive integrity is also part of the product.

And that is where I feel disappointed.

I spent 338,000 VND because I believed I was buying an experience worth the money.

PUBG kept the money.

I kept a lesson:

A popular game does not automatically mean everything around it is handled perfectly.

338,000 VND may not be a lot of money to some people.

But to me, it is still money.

And if I could go back to the moment before buying it, I would probably think twice.

Not Recommended.

This game takes you through a complete rollercoaster of emotions. You start from nothing, build your reputation, unlock new jobs, meet people who slowly become important to you, and try to make something out of yourself in a city that constantly tries to break you.

For me, one of the strongest things about Cyberpunk is its message. It shows that even when you hit rock bottom, you can still get back up and try again. Maybe you cannot always change your own life for the better, but you can still change the lives of the people around you.

It also teaches you not to judge a book by its cover. First impressions can be completely wrong, and some of the characters who seem strange, cold or unlikeable at first can become the ones you care about the most.

And then there is Johnny Silverhand. A character who can annoy you, surprise you, make you laugh and sometimes make you think more than you expected. The relationship between V and Johnny is one of the best parts of the whole game.

The graphics with path tracing are absolutely stunning and the optimization is excellent. I honestly did not even want to use fast travel most of the time. I preferred driving through Night City, listening to the radio, watching the streets and just enjoying the atmosphere. Sometimes I caught myself thinking that maybe this is what the world could actually look like in a few decades.

And even if you become one of the best of the best, this game reminds you that it still does not mean you will get everything you want.

V and Johnny Silverhand will stay in my heart forever.

*Cyberpunk 2077* is not merely a video game; it is an extraordinary interactive exploration of technology, identity, capitalism, mortality, and the philosophical complexities of human existence. 🧠🧬⚡ Developed by CD PROJEKT RED, it constructs Night City as a breathtakingly dense sociotechnological ecosystem in which every neon advertisement, towering skyscraper, and rain-soaked street contributes to an atmosphere of unparalleled immersion. 🌆🌧️💡

The game's greatest achievement is arguably its world-building. Night City functions not simply as a setting, but as a living cultural phenomenon. Its juxtaposition of immense technological advancement with social inequality creates a fascinating dystopian paradox: humanity possesses unprecedented technological capabilities while remaining fundamentally flawed. 🤖🏢💰

Narratively, the game demonstrates remarkable thematic ambition. Questions concerning consciousness, identity, mortality, corporate power, and technological determinism are integrated into the experience with surprising sophistication. Where do I even start with Baldur's Gate 3?

I've been playing D&D since I was around 11, so there was absolutely no way I was going to miss this game. I hadn't played the previous Baldur's Gate games, though, so BG3 was actually my introduction to the series. I got it as soon as it became available, and almost 1,000 hours later... apparently I'm still not done with it.

Achievements aren't really the focus for me here. I'm currently at 46/54, but BG3 is one of those games where I'd much rather start another character, try another choice and see where the story takes me than worry about completing a checklist.

The amount of freedom and variation is probably what I love most. Even after so many playthroughs, different interactions, consequences and unexpected outcomes can still appear. You make one seemingly insignificant choice differently and suddenly you're seeing something you've never seen before. It makes every run feel like its own D&D campaign rather than simply replaying the same story.

The modding possibilities make that experience even better. I love that the game can be modded so easily, although I've mostly kept mine to quality-of-life and graphical improvements. For me, it's about polishing and improving the experience without changing what makes the original game so good.

All three acts have something I love, although Act 2 is definitely my favourite. The atmosphere, the story and everything surrounding the Shadow-Cursed Lands just work incredibly well for me.

I love the companions too, although Gale, Astarion and Shadowheart have a special place among them. Gale takes first place when it comes to romance, though. ❤️

As for my own characters, Wizard is easily my favourite class and Drow my favourite race. Character creation gives you plenty to play around with, and combined with all the classes, subclasses, races, backgrounds, dialogue options and different ways of approaching situations, the replayability is enormous.

The story itself is great, but what really makes it special to me is how much it feels like *your* story. My most memorable Tav will probably always be my very first one, whom I played essentially as myself.

That adventure ended in Act 2 because I made a... let's call it a "wrong" decision.

The soundtrack deserves a mention as well. There are some beautiful tracks in there, and naturally, a few of them have found their way onto my Spotify playlists.

My main disappointment is knowing that development was, in some ways, rushed towards the end and that a number of things had to be cut. There are places where you can wonder what BG3 might have looked like if everything originally envisioned had made it into the finished game.

But even with that disappointment, what we got is still far more than excellent.

After 979.5 hours, countless characters, different decisions, romances, successes, catastrophes and apparently the occasional accidental premature ending, I'm still finding reasons to return to Baldur's Gate 3.

And I'm definitely not finished yet.

Some of the core issues remained the same because they are untreated. Other aspects are new and gamebreaking. Let it be said that I solely play fun AbilityDraft and Turbo modes.

This game offers something unique compared to other games, a combination of teamwork, high skill, adrenaline, unique situations and unexpected exciting outcomes. That much has all been said before and it's true, albeit with a high learning curve.

The reason why I do not recommend coming back to this game currently is the reporting system in combination with the state of the servers. Because of the declining player base many people flock to playable servers. Communication is key in teamwork but a common language isn't a thing in this game. None of that has ever been enforced. More than half your games will have people that do not speak your language and have a non existing sense of decorum.

People typically fail to see something wrong with their own gameplay and point the finger of blame to others. Valve/Steam has chosen for a community-driven regulation of behaviour and communication. However, with unlimited reports and all reports valid it is impossible to play as a solo player. Often you get reported by a 3-4 man stack. You get reported for people not liking your gameplay, buying the wrong item (in their mind), due to cultural, racist, and other reaasons. Why is this a problem? The lower your score the less you can do, talking, drawing, notifying allies of their ability (CDs). I've seen the list of on the Dota 2 Development Forums regarding this and it's madness. People will still get reported even without the ability to talk.

Not communicating is a flaw. People that fail to communicate their item timings, overarching plans or movement cause problems for their team. It doesn't make sense at all. There are many better alternatives.

Nevertheless and more importantly, Valve/Steam has been aware of this issue since 2025 and continues to steer their course. There was this beautiful quote I read about this game in one of these reviews "I kept agonising that my game was full of idiots until I realised that there were in fact 10." So if you give me the choice as a solo player between playing with randomised people that hate and report me for speaking English, and playing a myriad of other good games, well then I thank you for the opportunity. I've seen the negative reviews complaining about the boring end-game grind and balance issues in new patches, but honestly, those issues don't bother me because I'm just not playing them and I didn't notice problems with my warframes. This review is coming from a much more relaxed perspective. I’m currently Rank 20 (sitting somewhere between mid and end-game), and since leveling your account means constantly collecting and maxing out new gear, I’ve chosen to just stick to a smaller armory of weapons and characters I genuinely love playing. I spend most of my time just chilling, playing my favorites, and socializing rather than going for 100% completion, still part of the plan tho. That said, if you are a completionist, there is a massive roster of characters to collect, and you will probably really enjoy diving into that grind.

At its core, it's a power fantasy MMO, but the best part is you don't even need to sweat over getting insanely strong to enjoy it. There are just so many wildly fun ways to cause chaos. You can wipe out enemies with music, paint, mushrooms, guns, swords, fire, ice... or you can literally just roll over them as a giant meatball. And when you're tired of all the killing and liberating, you can just go fishing, mine rocks, decorate your room, join or host fashion weekends, or even play a dating sim. Though, if you do like chasing total power, you'll love watching your damage numbers go through the roof and you'll probably get a mini heart attack when they break and go negative.

The only real heads-up I'd give is about the grind, especially if you work a 9-5 or just have a tiring schedule. Some items take a lot of work to get. But honestly, it doesn't hold you back. You won't miss out on the actual game if you don't have everything right away. Just chill, run a mission from time to time, and take it at your own pace.

Plus, the trading system is amazing. In my 1200+ hours, I've only dropped money on cosmetics just because I wanted to. If you have the time to grind, you can find rare items, trade them with other players for Platinum (the premium currency), and play the entire game completely for free. Only a few specific cosmetic bundles actually require real cash. Absolutely nothing important is paywalled.

An absolute masterpiece of competitive strategy that offers thousands of hours of unmatched depth—if your sanity can survive it.

Valve’s flagship MOBA stands as the absolute pinnacle of competitive gaming depth. With over 120 unique heroes, hundreds of items, and complex mechanics like creep denying, high-ground vision, buybacks, and dynamic map objectives, no two matches ever play out the same way. The sheer high-dopamine rush of pulling off a game-winning 5-man Black Hole, executing a clutch Aegis steal, or turning around a 60-minute mega-creep comeback provides a high that virtually no other multiplayer title can replicate. It is a game of pure, unadulterated skill where tactical macro-play, item customization, and split-second reaction times matter vastly more than raw mechanical reflexes.

However, that exact depth creates an absurdly intimidating brick wall for newcomers and casuals. The learning curve is not just steep; it is a vertical cliff that takes hundreds of hours of trial and error just to understand basic positioning and lane matchups. To make matters worse, the ranked matchmaking ecosystem can be notoriously toxic, where a single bad play or missed ability can trigger a wave of angry pinging and mic-screaming teammates. Compounding the learning curve is Valve's habit of constantly shifting the goalposts—massive gameplay overhauls routinely rework hero innate abilities, map layouts, and fundamental mechanics, forcing long-time players to constantly relearn the game from scratch.

Yet, despite the rage-inducing losses and complex updates, Dota 2 remains one of the most generous free-to-play packages on Steam. Unlike competing titles in the genre, every single hero is unlocked completely free from the moment you install the game—no grinding or paywalls required. Monolithic lore events, battle passes, and custom arcade maps keep the meta feeling fresh year after year. It is a volatile, high-stakes digital drug that will make you swear off playing forever, only to have you queueing up for "one last match" twenty minutes later.

9/10 — I spent 2,000 hours learning how to properly stack neutral creeps, got flamed in three different languages during a 70-minute loss, and immediately hit 'Find Match' again. The greatest competitive abusive relationship in gaming history.

I'm one of those that usually doesn't bother to write reviews, only because by the time I get through a game, what needs to said has generally been said, but after completing the latest expedition (23 - The Journey Continues), I'm posting this as both an open letter to Hello Games and a review with the expectation that it'll be read by next to no one and useful to even fewer.

Since the days of Star Wars: X-Wing, Decent: FreeSpace, X: Beyond the Frontier, Allegiance and Freelancer, if the game let me fly, battle and explore in the vastness of space, I was there. So when I first saw Hello Game's E3 preview trailer for NMS, I was floored.

A game that let me seamlessly transition from space to a planet? I could land on said planet and interact with (what I later learned was) procedurally generated terrain and unique fauna, only to then take off and take part in space battles... all without a single loading screen?!?! This game was too good to be true!

Upon release and based on both the news and the reviews... that unfortunately seemed to be the case. So after a few weeks of witnessing public perception of the game implode, I placed this one in the "Star Citizen" bin of empty promises, skipped the purchase, and moved on.

It wasn't until 2021, when I caught a Twitch steam of NMS, that the game appeared on my radar once again. I watched a full year of streams and expeditions go by, until I finally took the plunge during the Leviathan expedition in 2022. I purchased it on sale, and even after seeing the streams, I didn't know what to expect, but since that time I've yet to stop playing.

While I've come to understood why Hello Games has earned the respect of their community, what I didn't appreciate until having played this expedition is the [i] scope [/i] and cadence of content that the devs released. Even in the years that I've been playing, the visual fidelity has increased dramatically and the sheer number of things to do in this game still keeps me occupied for hours.

[list]
    [*]Want to find the perfect planet to call your own? Tally ho!
    [*]Want to build the perfect base on said planet? Ditto.
    [*]Wanna make it a cozy home? Just add a fireplace.
    [*]How about a sprawling industrial complex? Guard rails optional.
    [*]Temple to the glory of Atlas? Amen.
    [*]Spooky underwater abyss hideout? Just don't touch the jellyfish.
    [*]Poop farm? If that's your thing.
    [*]Space battles? Not quite as good as BSG reboot, but yeah.
    [*]Wanna fly a Cylon ship? Just plug yourself in.

    [*]Build your own organic fleet and fly a living ship? Yes. [spoiler] make sure to sanitize after every flight [/spoiler]
    [*]Cook? Oui.
    [*]Fish? You bet'cha.
    [*]Fish on a hellish lava planet? Hot damn, yes!
    [*]Design and fly your own spaceship or corvette? From X-Wing, to Millennium Falcon, to Sponge Bob, yes.
    [*]Go on missions, explore and play through a storyline? Indeed.
    [*]Capture, evolve and compete in pet battles? All while managing to avoid Nintendo's wrath.
    [*]Become a junk hauler? Hey, hey, hey!
    [*]Create your own synthesized track? OMG, they created an in-game MOD tracker!
    [*]And SO much more...
[/list]

I've been playing this game for a bit over 700 hours (900+ on paper, but a lot of that is afk time), and I'm STILL discovering new things. 

A friend of mine reviewed this game in 2021 and at that time, he indicated that while the devs were pushing a lot of content, much of it was relatively shallow, and while I don't necessarily disagree with that sentiment, as NMS strikes me as a jack of all trades, master of none, after having played this expedition and listened to Sean describe this journey, I think that they've mastered being the Swiss army knife of space games, and that's okay.

While you need only look at some of the player creations to realize that there is depth to be found in this game, for me it's a just a fun experience. I love that I can hop on after a long day and spend a few hours either exploring or building without giving it much thought or effort, while doing so in a procedurally generated universe that sometimes tends to surprise (especially the animals).

So, this is probably an unnecessarily long way of saying both "thank you" to Hello Games for deciding not to bail after a painful start, and continuing to push out content for the love of the game.

To those few readers who got this far, if you want a game that scratches the space itch in a casual and expansive way, this is about as good as it gets.

Factorio is not for everyone - I suggest you try the demo first, but if it hooks you, it hooks you hard. There's always something to upgrade, some element to modify that makes the game irresistible to anyone that even remotely thinks like an engineer. You will find yourself spending hours perfecting complex systems that are almost completely incomprehensible once you take a step back.

That's enough for a few hundred hours sure, but why do I keep coming back? One word: MODS.

Factorio is designed to be a modding system first, game second. Even the DLC is a set of mods. The game itself can be modded to become a variety of factory and automation based challenges, and since the addition of Space Age, there are at least a dozen additional planets that you can explore and conquer, each with unique automation challenges and factory rewards. The default Space Age planets are almost perfect to my mind, each delicately crafted towards a specific playstyle, and each created to remove an annoyance of the base game's starting planet, Nauvis.

Play the demo, if it strikes your fancy, I recommend getting both the base game and DLC all at once. The DLC is arguably the faster and more forgiving experience, while the base game lends itself to meticulous efficiency and planning.

Dunno how it was on release, but now this is definitely one of the greatest ARPGs of all times.

-Story. Fucking amazing. Quests, characters, main plot, setting, everything is just perfect. It really surprised me that they created a cyberpunk world that feels unique and fresh. The story of V and Johnny is also amazing. Silverhand really became my friend in the end and I felt really sad to part ways with him. As for other characters... Panam, JACKIE, Judy, hell, even some minor characters felt memorable. We don't see our ripper Vik a lot after the prologue, but hell, is just a really cool guy and nice to be around. As always narrative is CDPR greatest strength.

-Gameplay. To my surprise gunplay is great here. Shooting feels great, killing people(especially with a shotgun) feels great. Grenades are cool, this is one of the few games where I use them, just because seeing enemies torn apart is really fun here. If you want something different, netrunning and smart weapons is actually a pretty interesting playstyle(I did it). Also the world is amazing, Night City is build extremely well and is interesting to explore. Lots of side jobs, beautiful sides to take and just admire the amount of work that went to create it. Vehicles are not the best, but they do their job decently and that is fine by me, this is no the game about cars.

-Music. They really produced their own songs for this, which is already a huge respect, but some of the are certified bangers, which is respect x100.  And not only radio songs, but some of the ambient music is just out of this world. Many thanks to composers, singers and CDPR stuff for creating this, when they easily could just buy some licenses for the radio.

-Graphics. Excellent, don't know what else to say. The game looks beautiful, it really does.

-Technical problems. There were some minor visual and gameplay bugs, but nothing serious. The game is a bit demanding, but my specs aren't really that good and I managed to play it  on high in 60 FPS in QuadHD, so it's not that bad.

10/10. Certainly a must play for any RPG or FPS fans, I am certain that this series will go a long way, so better jump on it at the beginning.

Helldivers 2 is a great game, but ArrowHead are not great developers.
Heres my reasons why:

1: There have been frustrating or even game breaking bugs in the game for YEARS. Despite everyone, including AH knowing about them, it would appear AH is locked out of their own game and are simply powerless to fix them. Bugs such as enemy corpses having huge hit/collision boxes that do not match with the visual corpse that can literally soft lock you, or stratagems bouncing when they are not supposed to, getting ragdolled on random flat surfaces, getting ragdolled back to back to back, or getting stuck on poorly made terrain that can soft lock you unless you're able to kill yourself, or any number of the ways this game finds to crash itself.

2: Crashes. AH, despite probably making millions off this games sales and in game purchases, still cant confidently fix or prevent crashing issues. Multi-million dollar dev team, cant use certain features without crashing. Once again, an issue they are highly aware of, but somehow powerless to fix.

3: Large amounts of menu time. Between the game letting you join a mission that is already finished, getting shown lobbies that are open but are actually full, or joining and getting kicked or losing connection, there is a high likelihood of spending a quality amount of time on your ship, simply trying to get into a match.

4: Give us a problem, we'll sell you a solution. When players complained about the erratic and un-fun quality of the ragdoll mechanic in this game, they simply add an anti-ragdoll armor, and sell it you. There have been numerous times they were presented a problem by the player base, and then packaged the solution in a warbond.

5: Supreme lack of flavor. There is an infinite amount of content that could go into this game, but instead, we're sold a "tank" that is absolute garbage, guns that dont add anything new to the existing armory, or armor meant to address an issue the player base had, but sold in a warbond. The creativity seems to have run out at AH.

I genuinely used to enjoy this game, but now I generally play one match and then hop off, being reminded of all these issues. AH has in the past made a big deal about pausing warbond production to address bugs in the game, but I could not name a single bug that actually effected me that they fixed before jumping right back into cranking the money printing machine. As of now, I wont be giving them any more of my money for these lame-ass excuses of warbonds until they genuinely impress me with bug fixes first. That said, supremely disappointed.

After more than 350 hours in Baldur’s Gate 3, I can confidently say: this game is phenomenal.

What makes it so special is the freedom it gives you. You can talk your way through trouble, sneak past it, fight it head-on, or try something ridiculous and discover that the game actually allows it. Exploring different approaches is part of the fun, and the world’s reactions make your decisions feel meaningful.

The writing and performances deserve enormous praise. Characters have personality, conflicting motivations, and enough depth to make conversations worth paying attention to. Even smaller encounters can turn into memorable stories. There is so much care in the dialogue, environments, and little details that exploration feels rewarding beyond simply finding better equipment.

The combat is another highlight. Positioning, terrain, preparation, and the interaction between abilities give battles plenty of tactical depth. A clever plan can completely change an encounter, while a terrible plan can lead to something hilariously memorable. Experimenting with classes and builds adds another layer of enjoyment—and another reason to start a new character.

The replayability is incredible. Different choices, party compositions, and approaches give you reasons to revisit the adventure. This is a huge game, but its appeal goes beyond its size: it gives you room to make the experience your own.

It does ask for some patience. There are systems to learn, plenty of dialogue, and decisions that can keep you staring at the screen while you consider the possibilities. For me, that is a big part of the appeal. It is a game worth taking your time with.

More than 350 hours is probably the strongest recommendation I can give. Baldur’s Gate 3 combines tactical combat, fantastic storytelling, and an extraordinary amount of player freedom into something truly special.

[h1]TLDR (Full review further down)[/h1]
One of the best games on the market that still gets massive updates constantly even 13 years after it released. Phenomenal looter shooter that some how finds a way to stay feeling fresh

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Overview[/h1]
I firsted played Warframe on the Xbox One years ago and even back then this felt like a full, complete experience. Digital Extremes have somehow found a way to continously improve this game, add massive content updates,  and all the while keeping this game free2play. Somewhere between now and the last year or so, they've added the ability to transfer your progress between platforms / acounts as a way to prepare for a particular update. Because of this, I was able to keep all of the progress I've made a long time ago and returning to Warframe recently was so much more approachable because of it.

[h2]Free2play / Monetization[/h2]
This is a big point of contention when it comes to how a game makes money. Typically when I hear f2p, I automatically assume pay2win mechanics, gacha, gambling, endless ways to spend cash, FOMO, etc. Warframe is NOT like that. They do occasionally tell you about new frames and deals when you log on for the first time in the day, but that's it. You choose to engage with their store. They also don't try to obfuscate the value of a dollar with multiple premium currencies, there's only one premium currency and it's called Platinum. You don't even need to spend a dime to get platimum because you can trade for it for valuable in game items with other players. I've never felt incentivized to spend my own money in Warframe and it's something I appreciate greatly about this game. Don't get me wrong, there is 'pay2skip', cosmetics, etc but it's all optional

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Warframe offers some of the smoothest feeling gameplay on the market, which is crazy to think about considering this is a 13 year old game. You can double jump, glide in the air, wall run, slide, and bunny hop to navigate through the zones. It's confusing at first but once you get the hang of the movement, it is extremely satisfying.

The combat here is just as satisfying because not only do you get a massive aresenal of guns and melee weapons to choose from, but you also get a multidude of 'warframes' that serve as classes. Each warframe has their own set of unique abilities and some how the devs find ways to still add new frames with new abilities. There's also a feature that allows you to transfer abilities between frames, albeit end game level content but it truly allows you to play how you want. The build variety in Warframe is so immense, I still have not explored it at its full potential.

[h2]Story[/h2]
It's been such a long time since I've played as a new player, I cannot really explain what the story is. It's not something I necessarily engage with when it comes to looters. Despite this, there is a core story that you can enjoy if you choose to do so. Over the years, they've added a ton of lore about the Lotus, Warframes, the people that control the warframes, and the multiple factions you'll encounter. On top of the main story there's something called 'Quests' which quite literally have entire storylines embedded within them. Some of these quests have their own unique worlds, gameplay mechanics, and ofcourse story. These are completely free and optional but you do need to engage with them if you're trying to unlock certain things within the game.

[h2]Content[/h2]
The amount of content in Warframe at this point in time is what I can describe as, multiple games within a game. Not in the way that it's a convoluted mess but in the way that you're constantly exploring new things, discovering cool ways to play, finding strategies, etc. You can choose to fish or you can choose to control a giant Railjack in space and have space battles. The best part is, you can choose the content you want to engage with. Like I said in the 'Story' segment, the quests can sometimes contain entire unique worlds. For example there's a quest known as 'Warframe: 1999' that takes you into a retro sci fi inspired world and it gives you such a cool insight on how things were in Warframem before technology got so advanced. The other day I did a quest where I got my own futueristic flying horse. Like how freaking cool is that?

There's one massive elephant in the room when it comes to content and it's inevitable once a game gets as large as Warframe is and that's GAME KNOWLEDGE. As I've explained, there's a lot of content within Warframe and unfortunately there's going to be a lot of times where you'll have to open up Google search and look up something. This is the case for figurering out what quests to do for certain warframes, materials you need and how to farm them, how to obtain mods, how to progress, etc. You'll always have this problem and Warframe could really benefit from a better explanation of how to obtain certain things.

[h2]The Grind[/h2]
If you're a casual player or new, you will most likely not even know that there's some massive grinds within this game. Fortunately, the grind heavy unlocks and farms are reserved for end game but it doesn't negate their existance. The worst grinds in this game have strict time gates, extremely low RNG drop rates, or just not so fun game modes you have to engage with. You want Uriel as a new player? Sucks to be you because you won't even gain access to the farms you have to grind until about 50 to 100 hours in. Uriel is not even the top 5 grind heavy farms for a frame you need to do to obtain. 

[h1]Verdict: S+[/h1]
Top tier game that offers engaging content, consistent updates, and endless ways to immerse yourself in the world of Warframe. There's a home here for both casuals and tryhards. The best part is, this game is entirely free.

I’ve been playing War Thunder since 2020 and have over 2,500 hours in the game, so I think it’s safe to say I’ve experienced just about everything this game has to offer.

At its best, War Thunder is genuinely one of the most enjoyable military vehicle combat games out there. The sheer variety of tanks, aircraft, helicopters, and ships from different nations and eras gives you an insane amount of content to explore. There’s always another vehicle to unlock, another tech tree to grind, or another playstyle to learn.

The gameplay is what has kept me coming back for thousands of hours. Whether it’s landing a long-range tank shot, winning a dogfight, pulling off a ridiculous close-air-support run, or somehow surviving a situation you absolutely shouldn’t have, War Thunder can create some incredible moments. The damage models and attention to detail also make the vehicles feel much more interesting than a traditional health-bar-based combat game.

That being said, after 2,500+ hours, I’m definitely not going to pretend the game is perfect. The grind can be brutal, the economy can be frustrating, balancing isn’t always great, and there will absolutely be matches that make you question why you still play this game.

And then you queue up again.

Despite its problems, there really isn’t another game that scratches the same itch for me. There’s a reason I’ve been playing since 2020 and somehow put more than 2,500 hours into it.

Would I recommend War Thunder?

Yes.

Would I recommend putting 2,500 hours into War Thunder?

**Ask me again after one more match.**

I originally played this right around its release in 2020. It was super buggy and I found the story to be disappointing and boring, so I didn't ever finish it. A few friends recommended that I give it another chance, so lo and behold, 6 years later, I finally gave it another try and completed it. It's still buggy (not as much) and the story is still disappointing and boring. If you're butt-hurt about a stranger's opinion, that's your problem. I may also just be too Corpo. So why do I still recommend this game? I shall tell you.

[u]The Good[/u]
- The world-building is awesome, and is what, in my opinion, the game does best. I loved hearing the different languages, seeing the architecture, the lights, seeing people in different clothing. I especially loved the design of the Corpo environments (again, as a Corpo myself, I'm a little biased.)
>> Love the inclusion of alot of Japanese culture and dialogue.
- I find Takemura to be the most interesting character in the game (and one of the few I liked), his arc, and the [spoiler]guy that's supposed to be the enemy but actually is not trope. Probably my favorite one to be honest.[/spoiler]
- The voice acting is good.
- I like that the dialogue options make it clear which ones proceed with the story and which ones are extra information, like on Mass Effect.
- Having the option of different origin stories.
- Alot of good music.
- The game is straight-up beautiful.

[u]The Eh/Bad[/u]
- To me, alot of the story of the game was just "nuisance simulator" and "but before we can proceed with the story, you gotta help me first" simulator.
- The time you spend in the Corpo area as a Corpo at the beginning of the game feels way too short.
>> It is mentioned later in the game that Arasaka knows how to find people when they want to. Why don't they look for V? They had some pretty vital information given to them at the beginning of the game.
- 6 months to become a merc seems a bit unrealistic. Maybe in the Street-Kid story, but as a Nomad or Corpo, doesn't seem very believable.
- V is just... Not that interesting. He/she is 20-something years old and acts like a really immature teenager. Also is super impulsive, overreacts to literally everything, and doesn't have dialogue options to stop for a minute to be like "wait a minute, maybe this is not what this seems like." You cannot be a calm or pretending-to-be polite V, which was some really missed potential.
>> Alot of times I felt really disconnected from V, like the story was just playing itself and I had no input on their personality.
>> The character motivation isn't interesting. "I just wanna be somebody." Ok... That's... That's it?
- Hot take, but I felt like Johnny was a pretty flat character, but it could have been the choices I was making. He consists of "Arasaka bad." "Let's go to Mikoshi." "Drugs." "Sex." "I hate you at the beginning but I don't now in the next cutscene." "I'm angry again." Insert that with a sprinkle of juvenile dialogue and more "Arasaka bad," and that's him.
- Most of the other characters I just could not connect with. No one really stuck out to me except Takemura and Hanoko.
>> I thought it was funny how we're expected to care about Alt when there is just one cutscene with her, a third of it being a sex scene (that you can't skip by the way).

After the apparent travesty that was this game's launch state, many years later I can confidently say it's good now. Not the best game ever (i.e., I don't like the line the gameplay straddles between RPG and shooter). But you have something with compelling characters and a poignant messages to be found. It is also STRIKINGLY beautiful, particularly on an OLED monitor with HDR enabled. This is essentially the "Crysis" of the current generation (a game that stands heads and shoulders over its contemporaries in both visual fidelity and the processing power it demands). It's impressive that it took ~40 or so hours before I actually started using the fast travel system because the world was just so cool and pretty to oogle.
Something to also commend is that how often there are multiple ways to approach a quest (tip: Tech and Body are the two most important skills with regards to opening new paths, focus on one or both). You can  usually opt to either sneak around or go guns blazing, and they're not mutually exclusive either (there are many build-agnostic paths to quest completion).

It took about 60 hours until fatigue set in and I made a beeline for (an) ending (the one added with the Phantom Liberty DLC). But I ended up leaving a ton of side-quests unfinished, not to mention the game has four other endings from the base game that I could go for. Then there's the prospect of doing an entirely separate playthrough with a different build and different quest responses.

All in all, 8/10. Strong characters and visuals. Decently immersive story. Game-feel is a mixed bag (somewhere between Far Cry and a VATS-less Fallout). Game is also still slightly buggy (mostly just small weird things like cars spawning out of thin air and whatnot).

It feels like time to write a review, mostly because there’s a thought which has repeatedly entered my mind while playing – that being: this game is utterly remarkable (not wanting to overhype, or anything).

That said, I can see 2 ways in which it would really put some people off. Firstly, that it is absolutely brutal. Even on a superb run, you are basically always one momentary slip-up away from ignominious failure, and back to square one. Secondly, that the mysteries buried here, waiting to be picked apart, are almost always highly opaque, besides being vast in number and diverse in scope. They either require a wiki, or a huge amount of exploration and experimentation.

But that is also what has brought me the greatest enjoyment from the game. The exploration is compelling and fun, and learning and progressing through experimentation is such a satisfying gameplay loop. There have been multiple occasions where inspiration hit me of something new I could try, and the resultant discoveries have been little nuggets of deeply gratifying glee. For me, moments like that are some of the best experiences that gaming has to offer, and Noita has succeeded in delivering them again and again.

And, much to my delight, there is clearly still so much more for me to unpack. Over the years there have been a good number of games I’ve played for 70+ hours before, but none where I put this much time in yet felt like I was just scraping the surface. I can’t really compare it to anything else I’ve ever played, though I can see facets from half a dozen of my all-time favourites which it incorporates. As I said – “utterly remarkable” is the most succinct and accurate description I can come up with.

The Good: No Man's Sky is incredibly wide, offering a massive sandbox with tons of stuff to do and a highly addictive building loop. You can craft your own starships, manage freighters, build awesome bases, and check out the latest COSMO patch space station customization. The atmosphere perfectly nails that eerie, beautiful loneliness of space, and the graphics look absolutely stunning if your GPU is beefy enough. Plus, the lore and story are actually super interesting to uncover.

Points to Consider: Just a heads-up that the first few hours can feel pretty slow and tedious while you're stranded on a harsh planet. You really need to be patient here. The exact moment you finally fix your ship and take off past the atmosphere for the very first time—that’s when the game truly clicks, and you'll realize just how massive and special this universe is.

The Bad: The downside of the game being so wide horizontally is that it lacks vertical depth. Most of the core mechanics, from combat to trading, are relatively simple and don't go super deep.

Overall: 8.5/10. An amazing space odyssey. My best advice is to play it slow from the start, don't rush through the content, and just enjoy the journey.

So, at this point in 2026 it's a good game. Not absolutely mind-blowing, but GOOD in the sense of coming from Fallout and Elder Scrolls games. This would be the next logical step from Fallout 4 even thought it's entirely different company and universe. 

The game still has some flaws, bugs and glitches, etc. just like the Bethesda games but they do not detract from the immersion too much.
 
The graphics: For a game with 2015 graphics it runs like crap, at times dropping below 40 fps even on a 4070Ti Super with the ray tracing turned off and DLSS on performance mode. It just reminds me of Fallout 4 and Skyrim all over again. The ray tracing is all a gimmick, it doesn't run well at all. The game engine could have been coded a lot better to handle distant objects, LODs, crowds of people, multiple vehicles and what not. The engine SUCKS. HARD.

If you looked at GTA V and expected this to be better than that, forget it. 

The driving is wonky and feels like a slip'n'slide with the delayed steering and constant drifting around. I hate it, and only use vehicles to get to the next fast travel marker.

Combat is good, very satisfying to watch body parts explode during the more intense scenes, but only with the right weapons/implants. Most Pistols/SMGs/Assault rifles feel like pea shooters and enemies become bullet sponges. Avoid those.

The weapons system is more akin to Borderlands, with different stats, strengths and classes like many other RPGs (Diablo, Divinity, Borderlands, etc.), but also modifiable with some weapons having extra mod slots for scopes, larger capacity clips/mags, less recoil, etc. It gets confusing, so for most of the game I stuck with throwing knives and high damage sniper rifles because they're pretty OP.

Implants, same again - confusing and a burden to keep travelling to-and-from ripperdocs all the time so I just stuck with what worked.

There's a lot to do in the game aside from the main story line. A lot of these are just the usual "steal this vehicle" and "kill this bullet sponge" side quests, which earn you discounts on the vehicles and such. There's no real point in doing them if you hate the driving like I do.

A lot of the side quests are tied to the main story and are actually fun and involving to play. The dialogue and story on these are far superior to the previously mentioned fetch and kill quests and left me feeling satisfied once I completed them.

The endings are all quite depressing. No spoilers, but you will see if you spend as much time in the game as I have.

Buy this game with the Phantom Liberty DLC when its on sale. But only if you like the Fallout and Elder Scrolls games.
