I've owned this game for like 5 years, never really got into it but decided to give it a proper shot with the new build release on stable. Let me tell you, this is one of the best survival games you can ever get into.

1. Hard to learn, easy to master. Your first 50h or so you will probably die a LOT and barely survive more than a week or so. This is the hardest the game will ever be as you learn how to fight, what loot to prioritize, learn the important locations on the map etc. But as you learn, it will be far easier to survive and the game becomes a cozy apocalypse survival sim.
2. Massive, MASSIVE world to explore. Each location has been lovingly handcrafted so there are countless towns you can spawn in to start your survival adventure, hotwire a car and drive to wherever you want. Want to be a rural survival farmer? A Hermit in a log cabin living off foraging and fishing? Be an urban scavenger, fighting off hordes to grab a bagful of food to take back to your hideout?  All possible, you really play however you want.
3. Thriving modding community and robust MP options so you can seamlessly play with your friends on steam. From QOL mods to mods that even change the entire map and add NPC mechanics, if you ever get tired of the vanilla experience, moded Zomboid will keep you busy for a long, long time.

10/10. If you like survival games, if you like Zombie games, just get the game.

If you are reading this, then you probably already know the positives of Baldur’s Gate 3: freedom of choice, great voice acting, strong quest design, memorable companions, and the ridiculous amount of ways you can solve problems. I'm not going to sit here and pretend those things are not impressive, because they are.

But because those parts have already been praised to death, I want to focus on what, in my opinion, makes the game overrated.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is clearly a good game, but I don’t think it is the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. To me, it is also bloated, clunky, awkward, weirdly horny, and surprisingly weak when it comes to the feeling of progression. I will address each of those in the following sections.

[h2]Weak Progression[/h2]

One of my biggest problems with BG3 is progression. For such a huge RPG, I rarely felt genuinely excited about my character becoming stronger.

The story moves forward, the stakes get bigger, and the locations become more dramatic, but my actual character build often felt weirdly static. Gear progression especially felt underwhelming. It is very possible to find strong equipment in Act 1 and keep using it through Act 2 and even into Act 3.

I understand that this is probably good for balance, as it avoids the usual RPG problem where every item becomes useless after two hours. But from a player perspective, it can feel boring. You defeat major enemies, explore dangerous areas, open some impressive-looking chest, and then the reward is something you instantly send to camp because your old gear is still better.

I mean there is clearly something wrong when I'm deep into Act 3 and still wearing gear from Act 1 without feeling much reason to replace it. Loot should be exciting. I should look at a new weapon, armour piece, ring, or cloak and think, "Oh, this changes my build." But too often in BG3, loot just feels like mildly interesting clutter.

[h2]Underwhelming Level-Ups[/h2]

Leveling up has a similar problem. Because BG3 follows Dungeons & Dragons 5e, progression is more restrained. Yeah, I get that it is faithful to the tabletop rules. But as a video game RPG, it can feel really underwhelming. There is no proper skill tree, no big long-term upgrade path, and not many future unlocks that made me excited.

Some classes get fun powers, but plenty of level-ups feel minor. You get one spell, a passive, a feat, or some practical option that feels fine but not exciting. Many of the coolest choices can be taken early, and after that you often just pick whatever is left or whatever seems vaguely fitting.

A skill tree would have helped. Not some bloated mess with 300 meaningless icons, but something that gives a stronger sense of direction. Something that lets you look ahead and think, “Oh wow! I cannot wait to unlock that!” In BG3, I often didn't feel like I was building towards some powerful fantasy version of my character. I felt like I was just selecting from a small menu of practical options.

[h2]Combat: Great Ideas, Clunky Execution[/h2]

Combat is a mixed bag for me. When it works, it can be genuinely great. Positioning matters, height matters, surfaces matter, spells matter, and the environment can completely change a fight. You can push enemies off ledges, block routes, set traps, summon creatures, buff allies, debuff enemies, and turn the battlefield into complete chaos.

But when combat does not work, it becomes slow and clunky. The camera is often terrible, especially in multi-level areas. Trying to click the right enemy, floor tile, ledge, ladder, or doorway can feel harder than the actual fight.

Pathfinding can also be stupid. Characters walk through fire, acid, traps, or other hazards like they are trying to speedrun natural selection. You finish a fight, relax for half a second, and then someone casually strolls through burning ground because why the hell not.

The hit chance system can also feel awful. I know missing high-chance attacks is part of D&D. But that does not mean it always feels good in a video game. Nothing kills the heroic fantasy faster than watching your trained warrior miss a point-blank attack while some goblin with the posture of a wet sock crits you from across the room.

[h2]Inventory Management: Fantasy Warehouse Simulator[/h2]

Then there is the inventory system, and oh boy, it honestly deserves its own prison sentence.

By mid-game, your bags are full of scrolls, potions, arrows, keys, books, notes, quest items, food, rings, amulets, dyes, tools, random bones, and 46 pieces of equipment you are keeping "just in case." Managing all of it becomes a chore.

The game gives you so many items, but sorting through them is tedious. You constantly move things between characters, send things to camp, compare gear, check whether some random note still matters, and try to remember which companion has the potion you need.

Somewhere in your backpack there is probably a useful item. Good luck finding it.

[h2]Act 3: Too Much of Everything[/h2]

The pacing also becomes a problem, especially in Act 3. Act 1 is strong because it has mystery, danger, discovery, and a good balance between freedom and direction. Act 2 has a strong atmosphere and feels more focused. But Act 3 is where the game starts drowning in its own ambition.

The city is impressive, don't get me wrong. There is a lot to do. But sometimes there is just too much. Every building has secrets. Every NPC has a problem. Every street corner threatens to become a side quest. You can’t walk 20 metres without someone asking you to solve a murder, uncover a conspiracy, rescue someone, investigate a basement, enter a portal, or confront a god. 

The amount of content is impressive, sure, but this density hurts the pacing.

[h2]Romance Writing: Too Fast, Too Easy, Too Awkward[/h2]

The romance writing is another big issue for me.

The issue is not just that the companions are bisexual. That alone I can survive. The problem is that nearly every companion feels player-sexual in the same way. Instead of feeling like complex adults with different preferences, boundaries, and emotional pacing, the party often feels like they all joined the same fantasy dating app and instantly matched with the player.

You meet these people, survive a few fights, avoid being completely evil, and suddenly half the camp starts acting like you are the most desirable person in Faerûn. Ridiculous.

The romance feels too easy and too fast. It does not feel like trust is properly earned. It feels like romance unlocks because you picked enough polite dialogue options. I even had scenes that felt weirdly romantic when I was not trying to romance that character at all. I was just choosing normal polite or supportive options, but the game seemed to assume I was interested.

The silent protagonist makes it even more awkward. A companion pours their heart out, becomes vulnerable, or expresses attraction, and your character mostly communicates through silent staring and vague hand gestures. Instead of two people building chemistry, it can feel like one fully acted character falling in love with a mute wax figure.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

That is why I cannot see Baldur’s Gate 3 as the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. It is ambitious, reactive, and impressive, but also bloated, clunky, awkwardly paced, and surprisingly weak as a progression-based RPG.

I respect the game a lot, and I understand why people love it. But for me, the weak progression, messy Act 3 pacing, clunky combat moments, silent protagonist, and weirdly rushed romance writing hold it back too much.

At first, I only played Cyberpunk 2077 for about an hour because I thought the game was a little too dark for my taste. A couple of months later, I decided to give it another chance—and I'm glad I did.

The more I played, the more I realized how much the story, gameplay, and open world kept improving. What surprised me the most was how much some of your decisions and dialogue choices can affect the story and its endings.

My first playthrough was... painful. 😂

I was playing on Hard difficulty with a weak setup and poor equipment, and unfortunately, I wasn't able to save Takemura. I was under a lot of pressure during that mission, ended up fighting the TAC Team, and eventually followed Johnny's suggestion to get out.

I also misunderstood Hanako's relationship with Takemura, so I thought she would somehow make sure he stayed alive. That definitely influenced my decision.

Then came the ending.

I'm naturally a pacifist and someone who tends to deal with problems alone, so when I reached the ending choices, I picked **The Devil**. I thought it was the safest option because I didn't want other people to die because of my own problems.

And then Johnny reacted with:

*"What the fuck was that?"*

That's when I started thinking:

"Oh... I might have made a mistake."

And I was right.

The more I progressed through The Devil ending, the more uncomfortable I became. It felt like I had sacrificed my own principles and conscience just to find a solution. I was basically handing myself over to the corpos—the same people connected to Jackie's death.

The aftermath honestly felt like psychological horror to me.

I eventually chose to return to Earth, and I remember thinking:

"Well... anyways I did'nt sold my soul to the corpos."

I didn't even know the other characters would leave messages during the credits, which made the whole experience hit even harder.

That night, I genuinely couldn't sleep properly because I kept thinking about whether I had made the wrong choice. I started wondering if my real-life personality—being a pacifist and preferring to solve problems alone—had actually influenced my decision.

So I went back and tried the other endings.

The Aldecaldos ending was fantastic. One of the funniest moments was when I gave my speech to the clan and suddenly realized I wasn't wearing pants or shoes.

Don't ask me how that happened. 😂

But the ending I liked the most was **I Don't Fear the Reaper**.

The idea of fighting alone so that nobody else has to die because of my problem fits my personality perfectly. I didn't even know this option existed at first, and if I had known about it, I probably would have chosen it immediately.

The mission itself was incredible. Johnny's dialogue throughout the entire sequence really felt like he was pushing me forward. Playing it on Hard made it even more intense because dying meant the whole attempt was over.

During the final fight, I noticed my HP getting lower and lower and initially didn't understand why. Later I realized it was because of the worsening effects of the Biochip/Relic.

Despite that, this ending felt the most "me."

Ironically, I think Cyberpunk 2077 taught me something outside of the game:

**Sometimes you shouldn't try to solve everything alone.**

Sometimes you need to accept help from other people. You're not alone in the world, and other people can help you carry your problems.

Overall: **4/5**

The game definitely has bugs. I experienced a blocker bug once or twice where a character or vehicle was positioned incorrectly, causing a scene to get stuck and preventing the story from continuing. But those issues didn't ruin the overall experience for me.

My personal ending ranking:

1. I Don't Fear the Reaper
2. Aldecaldos
3. Johnny & Rogue
4. The Devil
5. Jump, Jump

KRAFTON’s handling of the Himass and TanVuu situation is exactly why so many players are losing trust in PUBG.

If KRAFTON has evidence that they violated the rules, investigate it properly and punish them according to a clearly established and consistently applied disciplinary process. But what happened here goes far beyond simply enforcing competitive integrity. KRAFTON itself acknowledged problems with the investigation process, communication, and handling of the situation, yet still imposed permanent bans.

A lifetime ban from PUBG and official esports competition is an extreme punishment. When the company admits that its own process had shortcomings, the community has every right to question whether such a severe punishment was proportionate and whether the investigation was handled fairly.

And this isn’t only about Himass and TanVuu anymore. It’s about the credibility of PUBG’s competitive ecosystem. If players, teams, and fans cannot trust that investigations will be transparent, evidence will be properly presented, and disciplinary decisions will follow a consistent process, then KRAFTON is damaging the very competitive scene it claims to protect.

The cancellation of the final day and the decision to invalidate the tournament results only makes the situation worse. Players and teams who had nothing to do with the controversy were also affected.

KRAFTON cannot demand “competitive integrity” from everyone else while refusing to hold its own procedures to the same standard.

If Himass and TanVuu genuinely broke the rules, show the evidence, explain exactly what rule was violated, explain how the investigation reached its conclusion, and explain why a permanent ban is proportionate. If KRAFTON cannot provide that level of transparency, then a lifetime punishment deserves serious reconsideration.

At this point, I have no reason to keep supporting a company that treats its players, competitors, and community this way. Uninstalling PUBG and walking away is the only response I can give as a player.

This is no longer just Himass and TanVuu versus PUBG. It is a question of whether KRAFTON is willing to be accountable for its own decisions.

## An Anatomy of Disproportion: Why KRAFTON’s Indefinite Bans Harm Rather Than Protect the PUBG Esports Ecosystem

The competitive integrity of professional esports rests upon clear boundaries, unbiased adjudication, and proportionate enforcement. However, KRAFTON’s decision to issue indefinite, global competitive bans against prominent Vietnamese players—notably Himass and TanVuu—following infractions during an exhibition/showmatch event highlights an overreaching, heavy-handed regulatory approach. Rather than reinforcing governance, the publisher's handling of the situation exposes fundamental flaws in tournament operations, a lack of graduated sanctions, and a disregard for regional ecosystem stability.

---

### 1. Disproportionate Penalization and the Absence of Graduated Justice

In established sports jurisprudence and mature esports titles (such as Valve’s CS:GO/CS2 or Riot Games’ League of Legends), lifetime or indefinite bans are traditionally reserved for structural corruption: **match-fixing, illegal betting, or deliberate software-level cheating/hacking**.

* **Conflating Infraction Severity:** Receiving unauthorized outside information or stream sniping during a third-party, online showmatch is unquestionably an infraction that compromises fair play. However, treating such misconduct with the exact same finality as an organized match-fixing ring or an aimbot/wallhack script completely eliminates any sense of proportionality.
* **The Principle of Remediation:** A professional sports regulatory framework should deter misconduct while providing avenues for rehabilitation. A standard penalty structure for first-time information-related offenses ranges from temporary suspensions (e.g., 6 to 12 months) and forfeiture of prize earnings to probation. Jumps straight to indefinite bans eliminate due process, leaving no incentive for reform.

### 2. Deflecting Operational Failures onto Individual Players

A major weakness in the publisher’s ruling is its failure to account for the loose operational standards of the event itself:

* **Inadequate Supervision:** Unlike official Premier circuits (PGS, PGC) that operate with strict refereeing, point-of-view (POV) recording mandates, localized camera feeds, and robust stream delay buffers, third-party exhibition matches frequently run on bare-bones operational protocols.
* **Scapegoating Talent:** When an organizer fails to enforce mandatory delays, secure communication channels, or proper monitoring, they create an environment prone to integrity lapses. By imposing the absolute maximum penalty on individual competitors while avoiding any formal acknowledgment of structural administrative shortcomings, the publisher shifts the burden of organizational negligence entirely onto the players.

### 3. Destruction of Regional Infrastructure and Long-Term Ecosystem Damage

Southeast Asia—and Vietnam in particular—has long served as one of the most passionate and commercially vital hubs for competitive PUBG PC. KRAFTON’s abrupt and unyielding verdict inflicts immediate, collateral damage on this regional foundation:

* **Erosion of Team and Sponsor Confidence:** Esports organizations invest substantial capital into salaries, housing, mental coaching, and branding. When the publisher unilaterally ends the careers of flagship assets over an ambiguous exhibition incident, teams face immediate existential risk. The subsequent withdrawal or scaling back of major organizations illustrates how uncalculated regulatory shocks destroy investor confidence.
* **Stifling Competitive Competence:** Himass and TanVuu represented the highest tier of Vietnamese mechanical skill and international LAN experience. Removing them abruptly from international contention directly degrades the regional competitiveness of the APAC circuit, lowering the quality of regional representation at events like PNC and PGS.

### 4. Lack of Transparency and Independent Arbitration

The ruling highlights an ongoing issue inherent to publisher-dominated esports: the absence of an independent arbitration body.

* **Prosecutor, Judge, and Jury:** KRAFTON acts simultaneously as commercial rights holder, league organizer, and sole judiciary. Without an independent appeals commission or an objective ombudsman, players have no formal recourse to contest findings, present mitigating circumstances, or challenge the proportionality of the punishment.
* **Precedent of Volatility:** A governance model that relies on punitive displays of force rather than transparent, predictable guidelines alienates the professional player base. Competing under a rulebook where penalties can swing arbitrarily to the maximum threshold creates systemic anxiety and drives talent to transition to more professionally governed esports ecosystems.

---

Preserving competitive integrity does not require the immediate destruction of player careers and regional ecosystems. By applying an absolute, irreversible punishment without a graduated framework, transparent mitigating review, or acknowledgment of administrative vulnerabilities, KRAFTON opted for a blunt-force public relations statement rather than sound regulatory leadership. The resulting fallout damages the game's competitive credibility far more than the infraction it attempted to punish.

War Thunder is genuinely a great game. The vehicles are cool, the gameplay can be incredibly fun, and there’s a ridiculous amount of content.

The problem? **Actually getting to that content.**

The grind is absolutely brutal. The further you progress, the more time each vehicle seems to require. Unless you’re willing to put hundreds, if not **1000+ hours**, into this game, getting through a tech tree can feel like a second job.

And before someone says *“just play casually”* — sure, you can. But if you only play casually, you can spend an absurd amount of time grinding just to reach the vehicles you actually want.

Then there are the maps. Some maps heavily favor certain playstyles or vehicle types, which can make matches feel frustrating depending on what you're playing.

**Uptiers** can also be rough. Being put against vehicles that are significantly stronger or more capable than what you're bringing can make some matches feel decided before they really begin.

And then there's the monetization.

Technically, War Thunder is free-to-play. You *can* unlock everything without spending money. But the grind is so long that premium vehicles, premium time, and other paid options start feeling less like optional shortcuts and more like ways to make the progression bearable.

And those shortcuts aren't exactly cheap either.

So yes, it's free to download. **Free to play? Technically. Free to progress at a reasonable pace? That's another question.**

War Thunder is a genuinely fun game buried underneath an extremely long grind, frustrating matchmaking, map balance issues, and an expensive monetization system.

The major highlights of this game are well-advocated by others already.  Allow me to express something few would dare remark upon:  the controller support.

I first played Factorio on the Switch.  The ui and general gameplay screamed "pc game", in that subtle clunkiness that people pretend doesn't exist.  But, unlike most console ports of games developed primarily for pc gamers, this game gave you full controls with controller.  I was very impressed, and I spent a long time just playing the demo there before eventually purchasing on pc.

There are two shift buttons that can combine to a third, a button for a quick menu combined with multi-page radials, and the occasional forced point-and-click moment do not feel..too terrible on a stick since there is a degree of snapping in the parts that matter most (god help you if you want to draw a straight line of landmines in map view though).  Just these alone would suffice for praise, but it does not end here.  The controls are 90% customizable (you cannot create new shift buttons), so if you find yourself not using a particular function much - very likely for any style of play - you can swap the spot in the config with something you actually would use.  We have not reached perfection, of course; perfection would be allowing me to add context features to every command, such as:  commands that swap to green wire mode do something else while a menu is open (I would settle for both, but right now wire mode overrides other assigned commands).

There is a sort of meme that controller = casual, and Factorio is here to quietly shake its head in rebuttal.  These are not casual controls for controller.  My fingers and thumbs are putting in work, and sometimes I actually forget the button sequence for certain commands.  This is no failing; it is laudable.  THIS is the standard all pc games that pursue controller support should strive for.

Someone on the dev team clearly plays, understands and appreciates games with controllers.  Without this, I never would have gotten through the first hour of Factorio.

As a PUBG player since the early days, I am very disappointed with Krafton's decision regarding the recent Asia Star tournament.

This game has the potential to be the best horde shooter (right behind DRG of course) of all time. But it's held back significantly by the developers themselves, who have seemingly lost the grip on what the community wants and the game needs.

As it stands, the game gets progressively worse in terms of performance, bugs and overall quality of life. There are still major bugs in the game, that the devs themselves have introduced and been ignoring for over 2 years now. Balancing is a matter of rolling the dice to see if your favorite new gear gets nerfed into uselessness with the next update. Other than yourself, the devs are also rolling the dice, just in terms of significant changes to the game. There have already been multiple occasions, where something in the game got changed in such an obviously unnecessary, bad and sometimes even game-breaking way (for example a very common, medium-armor-enemy now getting heavy armor), just so that the whole community revolted against it and the change got reverted after a few days. 

Some mechanics in the game seem to simply be there to sell a solution in the form of an armor passive, coming with warbonds, rather than reviewing them in terms of it's contribution to the overall fun of the game. Ragdolling always has been and is still one of the most frustrating aspects, that serves no purpose, other than randomly forcing you in a situation where you cannot do anything and just die, no matter how good you play.
Warbonds are hit or miss most of the times and generally not really worth 10-15€. I really wished the developers would take a step back from churning out warbonds and fix the game's major problems first. I am certain, that this alone would boost both player numbers and retention.

It is unimagineably saddening to me, that such an amazing game gets handled in such a disrespectful way. I really think the game and it's surrounding community deserves better. At it's core, Helldivers 2 is phenomenal, but this core is currently a dim light getting overshadowed by questionable decisions and abysmal community handling.
If you don't own the game, I sadly cannot reccomend a buy. If you do, please don't pay for the warbonds, grab a few friends and farm the credits instead.

To be clear, I do not harbor any ill-will against the developers in any way. Developing and maintaining a game of such scale is a monumental task. And what has been accomplished so far, for better or worse, deserves acknowledgement and respect. But I do question if the devs have the right priorities right now.

Helldivers 2 is, on paper, exactly the kind of game I love. It’s incredibly fun, creative, chaotic, and has a fantastic amount of replayability. Every mission can play out differently, and there’s something genuinely satisfying about dropping in with a group of friends and watching everything descend into glorious chaos.

The graphics are also fantastic. The environments can be absolutely stunning, and there are plenty of moments where you can stop and appreciate just how good the game looks. The developers also deserve credit for consistently updating the game, adding new content, weapons, enemies, missions, and other things to keep the experience evolving. There’s clearly a lot of effort going into keeping the game alive.

Unfortunately, for me, the community has taken almost all of the fun out of it.

What should be a goofy, chaotic co-op shooter has developed a surprisingly sweaty player base that seems to take the game way too seriously. Make a small mistake, bring the "wrong" weapon, accidentally kill someone, don't follow the exact strategy someone wants, or simply play differently than they do, and suddenly you're getting kicked or lectured like you've just ruined a professional tournament.

The whole appeal of Helldivers 2, at least to me, is the ridiculous chaos. You're supposed to make mistakes. You're supposed to accidentally blow up your teammates. You're supposed to have things go horribly wrong and then somehow pull off a victory. That's where a lot of the fun comes from.

Instead, too many players seem obsessed with playing perfectly and enforcing their idea of the "correct" way to play.

I've reached the point where joining random games often feels more stressful than fun because I'm constantly worried that one minor mistake is going to get me kicked or criticized. And when a game that is supposed to be about blowing things up with friends starts feeling like a job where you're afraid of making a mistake, something has gone wrong.

I still think Helldivers 2 is an excellent game. The gameplay, creativity, visuals, replayability, and continued stream of content are all genuinely impressive.

But unfortunately, the player base has completely killed the fun for me.

If you have a group of friends to play with, I can absolutely see this being an amazing experience. Playing with randoms, however, has become an increasingly frustrating experience for me.

[h1]RimWorld: The Ultimate Story Generator and Why It Might Just Be the Greatest Game Ever Made[/h1]

At a glance, RimWorld looks like a modest, top-down indie colony sim with humble graphics and faceless little pawns sliding across a grid. But peel back those simple visuals, and you find a staggering masterpiece of systemic design—not just a survival game, but an unmatched, endlessly unfolding engine for human drama. 

To call it a masterpiece isn't hyperbole; it's an acknowledgment of what happens when mechanics, emergent storytelling, and total player freedom collide.


[h1]The Storyteller, Not the Game[/h1]

What elevates RimWorld into the pantheon of all-time greats is how it frames your experience. Governed by invisible AI "storytellers" (like Cassandra Classic or Randy Random), the game isn't trying to beat you, nor is it just letting you sandbox in peace. It’s actively co-writing a tragedy, a comedy, or an action thriller with you.

One moment you’re peacefully expanding your corn harvest; the next, a heatwave hits, a rabid squirrel bites your best builder, a mechanical dread-cluster drops from the sky, and your resident pyromaniac decides it’s a great time to light the chemfuel storage on fire.

[h1]Emotional Investment Out of Nowhere[/h1]

The true magic of RimWorld is how deeply you care about its inhabitants. Because pawns have distinct traits, flaws, addictions, relationships, and breaking points, they aren't just units—they are characters.

[u]You will remember the pacifist chef who single-handedly held off a raid with a lucky pistol shot.

You will mourn the colonist who caught the plague just days before the rescue transport arrived.

You will laugh, panic, and curse at the sheer absurdity of the situations your people get themselves into. [/u]

[h1]Infinite Replayability and Modding Nirvana[/h1]

No two playthroughs of RimWorld are ever the same. Between the randomized planets, changing scenarios, deep expansion DLCs (like Royalty, Ideology, Biotech, and Anomaly), and one of the most prolific modding communities in PC gaming history, RimWorld can literally transform into whatever game you want it to be. Want a gritty sci-fi survival? Done. A total-conversion fantasy epic with magic and monsters? Easy. 

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

RimWorld is a rare achievement. It challenges your intellect, tests your planning, breaks your heart, and then forces you to immediately hit "New Colony" to try and fix what went wrong. It is a canvas for your darkest choices, your most heroic triumphs, and thousands of hours of unforgettable memories.

If a game is measured by the stories you tell long after you've closed it, RimWorld easily stakes its claim as one of the greatest games ever made.

What kind of colony usually spells your downfall—are you a victim of random Randy chaos, or do your own poorly managed food supplies and pyromaniacs do you in first?

When rules are ambiguous, it is the organizers' responsibility to clarify and apply them fairly, rather than punishing players based on an interpretation that had never been agreed upon. Ultimately, they proved they were willing to sacrifice players—or even an entire region—just to stubbornly enforce a decision that benefited themselves. Yeah, it's a lot better than the embarrassment it was over a decade ago. It has it's charm, but it's also very grindy or requires players to do duplication cheese, so it feels a lot like "MMO stingy" especially once you factor in how silly the very limited number of inventory slots, HORRIBLE inventory management (players have around 30 different inventories of wich they usually can only reach 4 in their "inventory" UI, 10 that require players to be at a specific place (or call a special ship and walk to the right container), call one of a dozen ships or half a dozen ground or water vehicles. On top of that most of the inventories come with a lot of holes that need to be repaired at insane costs.

As soon as you open the inventory it's clear that the world is either a simulation or literal hell, considering how they have to manage items.

Aside from that, it has a zen vibe and a lot of interestiing "I saw something like this, but deeper"-memberberries. All in all mods fix quite a few of the issues and players can always just cheat in more inventory slots, but a lot of the games progression revolves around this god awful mechanic that MMOs used in the past 20 years to milk players for billions. That said it's better than a lot other space survival games, or at least either more varied stuff nicely packaged to do, or is not a completely broken buggy state. 

It reminds me the most of Empyrion, a game that is about as old and also saw a fair bit of expansion and tweaking. Building ships is a lot easier in NMS, but Empyrion has more charm I think. Both only have mostly text ¨read a log" style storytelling. I wish more games would take note of how Abiotic Factor did storytelling in a survival crafter (tjust copying the approach doesn't work for infinite world RNG games, though).

The VR mode is pretty well implemented, a nice surprise.

Overall I guess it's a nice package in 2026, even if every individual part leaves me hoping for a somewhat more narrowly defined game that does it better (and maybe with more handcrafting in a very believable functional world instead of thinly spread infinite world RNG slop)

I was there in the beginning. I pre-ordered No Man’s Sky on PS4, captured by the promise of endless wonders and infinite worlds. I poured hours into it and… well, eventually burned out when I realized there wasn’t as much there as it had promised. I shelved it, not angry or anything, but mildly disappointed. However, even then No Man’s Sky was like nothing else and there was still something there worth enjoying. Then the updates came. Every so often, I’d pick it back up again, willing to see if the rough edges had been sanded off. I even bought a copy for the PC so I could mod it and not have to grind my way through all the element gathering required to play with new toys. I probably stopped checking in around two years ago, but I was pulled in once again with the 10th anniversary expedition. Here was my chance to see all the new stuff in one go, to see if the game matched the potential of those fancy trailers from years ago. I finished the expedition… and now I wish I’d never picked it up 10 years ago. Why? Because I wish I’d started with the game in its present state. It’s so much more user friendly. No hunting fruitlessly for some rare element (hours wasted before!), now I can pin a recipe and it walks me through each part, even helping me scan for it. It’s so much more pretty, blowing the visuals of the release out of the water. And most importantly, it has a stupid amount of variety now. I can build a freaking corvette and walk around in it. I can play alien pet Pokémon. What?!? On the one hand I celebrate the incredible work Hello Games has put into this, but at this point the game has lost its freshness for me. A lot of time put in at the beginning, when it was at its worst, and the little bit here and there I’ve revisited has left me feeling like this last expedition is when I can finally put this game down and say I have seen enough, with a twinge of bittersweetness. You’ve grown up little game. You’ve made it. You’re big now. The lesson I’ve learned? I’ll wait ten years to play Light No Fire.

ESO, for all of it's faults, used to be my gold standard for how MMO progression should work. Turns out, they basically copied everything this game was trying to do, but with their own slight spin to it. And this game, is much, much better.

So, one of my longstanding complaints about another contemporary MMO, FF XIV, is that there's little to no mechanical depth. This game scratched that exact itch, but itself is still pretty accessible and intuitive, for the most part. Gearing is mostly linear but there are still important decisions to make, for some classes more than others.

The only real minor complaint I have about gearing in GW2, is that CD scaling is absolutely bonkers before Lv 80, and that makes it hard to experiment with condition-based builds before then. It's still possible, just the inverse scaling gets out of hand quickly, and means you WILL need to upgrade more often than, say, a Berserker build. While you would think this only affects a few classes, about half the roster is hit by this, with one or more weapon types becoming significantly harder to use during levelling.

However, it's not exactly hard to hit Lv 80, and the vast majority of the game's content is past Lv 80, and this game actually has fully functional level-sync that does not remove skills, unlike a certain other MMO I alluded to earlier. Yes, you can actually use your fully-kitted out Reaper, in Lv 50 events like Triple Trouble, and not only still have a challenge, but also you will actually get rewards according to your level. The level scaling also works upwards as well in the multiplayer modes, automatically upscaling your gear to the appropriate level, although it is probably unwise to level up in PvP, I have heard WvW is not the worst levelling option though.

Now where the game actually truly shines, is the skills system. Every single weapon and class combination has their own unique set of 5 skills for the first 5 of their hotbar. Dual wield setups have different 1-3, or 4-5 skills, based on what the mainhand and offhand are. These are not simply cosmetic swaps either, Mesmer for example, goes from a melee class to a ranged beam-wielding class if you swap from the starting Sword to a Greatsword, and all of your clones will follow suit.

You can swap these skill sets on a cooldown (excluding Engineers and Elementalists), and the next 5 skills are all class specific skills, with 5-ish options for Healing and Elite skills, as well as about 2 dozen different utility skills to populate the remaining 3 slots with. Some of these include "Signet" skills, which are passives that can be temporarily spent for a sometimes entirely different active buff, at the expense of doing nothing during their cooldown.

That's not enough complexity? Well there's also a set of class specific F-Key skills, and also a whole set of 18 equipped passive modifiers that can be anywhere from situational, to build-defining, solely based on how you actually play and use your skills. Some of these go as far as literally altering your stat scaling, and the game just hands you 5 banks, called specs, of 6 passives, three of them choices from three "Major Traits", and 3 "Minor Traits" tied to the spec, and goes "here you go".

When you hit Lv 80, some of the expansions give you extra specs, except this time they are entire subclasses, which are tied to new weapon types and a bunch of new skills, as well as the usual passives and passive choices. Don't be fooled, some of the "Minor" traits on specs, no matter if core game or expansion specs, are extremely powerful and easily can define a build on their own. For example, "Awaken The Pain" makes Spite spec a must-pick for any damage focused Necromancer build, because 10 Power for every single Might stack, that adds up a lot when Reaper can easily fully cap Might stacks just playing the game.

The expansion specializations usually provide passives relating to the new skills you get, but that does not mean they don't provide synergy with more basic skills. Using Necromancer as an example again, I swear I played more than one class, I just like edgy reaper mode, the Reaper spec gives you a bunch of options regarding Chill and Fear. In theory, this also buffs several non-Reaper skills, such as Spectral Grasp, Epidemic, Spectral Ring, Summon Shadow Fiend, or Lich Form, and that's before considering options from weapon skills or the revamped Shroud (F1 transformation) skillset that Reaper comes with.

In this instance, all Fear procs, for a Reaper, will trigger Chill, and Chill lasts longer, lowers enemy attack and defense in addition to speed, and optionally, gives you a might stack every time you hit a chilled enemy, and is now a functional DoT, that also makes enemies explode into chill pulses on crit. Oh and your new weapon type can also pulse Fear/Chill as well.

Are these good options? A mix of yes and no, on weapon skills, it is very powerful, basically giving you free infinite Might scaling and a viral slowing/weakening debuff that constantly reapplies itself, but for utility skills, it wasn't enough to make me want to switch off the tried and true Wells of Darkness and Suffering, and I was already using Spectral Grasp, making it an amazing opening skill only sweetened that deal. I don't think the new Chill sources really shifted my skill choices, but that's fine, what it really did was turn me into a self-sufficient buff machine using my weapon skills.

The new shout skills though, Suffer, You Are All Weaklings, and Chilled To The Bone, those are all winners, mainly as ways to remove debuffs and gain might faster, except that last one, which is basically just purely better than Epidemic as a Chill source. Like it DOES use the Elite slot instead, but also there isn't a better Elite skill for Reaper, so like, it just frees up a Utility slot.

I realize I spent entirely too long ranting about Reaper, but that also illustrates my point, that's one of four subclasses, for one of nine classes, and EVERY SINGLE ONE OF THEM, has this level of complexity, on top of having 2 of 5 of the other specializations available to them. There is a monumental level of depth to this gameplay, and there's also about 7 campaigns worth of story quests alone to experiment with all of this in.

I can't not recommend this game. The free portion of the game alone, you could play that for hundreds of hours, this game is very alt friendly and you have multiple character slots from the start, the game has many different path options to make the base story replayable, and it does work, you won't have the same list of quests twice, unless you go out of your way to make the same choices.

Great Game, Terrible Management....

PUBG is still one of the best battle royale games when it comes to gunplay, movement, and the feeling of winning a fight. Unfortunately, the company behind it seems determined to waste that potential.
Instead of focusing on problems players have complained about for years—cheaters, performance issues, bugs, questionable matchmaking, and inconsistent servers—we constantly get more skins, collaborations, overpriced cosmetics, and monetization.
What frustrates me even more is how some events and decisions are handled when things go wrong. From a player's perspective, it often feels like the company is reluctant to take responsibility for its own failures, while responsibility is pushed onto others instead. Rather than openly acknowledging mistakes and fixing the underlying problems, the response can feel more focused on protecting the company's image and burying negative criticism.
There is also a growing perception of double standards. Certain people or groups seem to receive more favorable treatment, while others are held to a completely different standard. When players feel that insiders or favored individuals are being protected while people from other countries or communities are treated with less respect, it destroys trust in both the company and the competitive integrity of the game.
The most frustrating part is that PUBG itself is genuinely a great game. That's exactly why watching it being managed this way is so disappointing. The core gameplay has kept people playing for years, yet it often feels like short-term revenue, reputation management, and favoritism are prioritized over fairness and the actual player experience.
Updates frequently add things nobody asked for while long-standing problems remain. When the community complains, communication often feels disconnected from what players actually experience in the game.
PUBG doesn't need to be reinvented every few months. It needs better optimization, stronger anti-cheat, stable servers, sensible matchmaking, accountability, transparency, equal treatment of players regardless of nationality, and developers who actually listen to their community.
I don't hate PUBG. I hate watching a great game being wasted by poor management, double standards, favoritism, and a company that seems more interested in protecting its image than admitting when it gets something wrong.
Not recommended—not because PUBG is a bad game, but because I have lost confidence in the way the people behind it manage the game and treat its community.

Um ótimo jogo, mas que exige algo que nem todo mundo tem: tempo

Como um “veterano” de Warframe, posso dizer que é um excelente jogo para quem procura uma experiência de ação, tiro e elementos de RPG. É extremamente divertido, frenético e consegue prender bastante o jogador. Porém, também é um jogo que exige muito tempo, principalmente se você quiser aproveitar tudo sendo F2P.

Warframe não é exatamente Pay to Win. Na minha opinião, ele se aproxima muito mais de “Pay to Go Faster”, e esse é um dos maiores problemas do jogo. Você pode conseguir praticamente tudo sem gastar dinheiro, mas o tempo necessário para conseguir algumas coisas pode ser enorme. E isso fica ainda mais evidente no começo do jogo, quando a progressão é bastante lenta e você demora e um pouco confusa para novos jogadores para liberar novos Warframes, armas e outros conteúdos.

O jogo também possui uma história muito interessante, mas boa parte da experiência acaba ficando presa atrás de grind(e nem estou falando do endgame). Às vezes, você sabe que existe algo novo e interessante para fazer, mas precisa passar por várias horas de farm antes de realmente conseguir chegar lá.

Por outro lado, existe uma coisa que considero excelente em Warframe: é possível conseguir Cash do jogo gratuitamente através do comércio entre jogadores. Isso significa que, com tempo e dedicação, você pode conseguir praticamente tudo o que quiser sem colocar dinheiro no jogo. O problema é justamente o tempo necessário para isso.

E, como um adulto com responsabilidades, trabalho e outras coisas para fazer, o maior inimigo acaba sendo o tempo. Ficar realmente forte e acompanhar todo o conteúdo sem gastar dinheiro pode exigir um investimento de tempo que nem todo mundo consegue fazer.

Mesmo com esses problemas, acho que vale a pena experimentar Warframe pelo menos uma vez e também com os amigos. É aquele tipo de jogo extremamente frenético que você consegue jogar por 10 horas seguidas, parar por meses e, quando voltar, sentir como se nunca tivesse parado.

No final, Warframe é um jogo com muita coisa para oferecer. Ele tem seus problemas, principalmente relacionados ao grind e ao tempo necessário para progredir, mas a quantidade de conteúdo, a liberdade que o jogo oferece e a possibilidade de conseguir praticamente tudo sem pagar fazem dele uma experiência que vale a pena conhecer.

Krafton, this isn’t simply about asking for better treatment in a video game. It’s about respecting a community that has supported your game, helped it grow, and made it part of their culture.

You don’t have to agree with every criticism coming from the Vietnamese community. But you should listen to them, communicate with them, and treat them with the same respect you expect from any other community.

I've played this game with so much love and passion. But recently, the fun and excitement I used to get from it have completely vanished.

First, the good things:

The gunplay is AMAZING. I would always defend this game when talking to other people and tell them that it has some of the best shooter mechanics out there.

The sound design is also absolutely fantastic. You really learn to appreciate how well-crafted it is when using high-end headphones. Being able to hear enemies before they can hear you adds so much to the experience.

If we're talking solely about the game itself, I would always recommend it.

Now comes the bad part.

And I'm saying this from the perspective of a 6-Star MMR player. The lobbies are divided into different MMR ratings from 1 to 6 Stars, with 6 Stars being the highest.

The game has a severe problem with the European servers, where I feel like I'm being matched with Russian and Chinese players most of the time. And when I say most of the time, I mean around 90% of my matches.

The difference between encountering a European team and encountering a high-ping team (usually Russian/Chinese)  is incredibly frustrating.

When I get killed by a European team, I usually don't think twice about it. I know I got outplayed, made a mistake, or simply lost the fight.

But when I get killed in certain situations by players from outside Europe, I often find myself thinking:

"How the hell did I just die there?"

Then I check the player's profile and see where they're from, and it happens far too often. Far too often meaning i feel like i'm only getting killed from High-Ping Teams anymore.

What I'm talking about is the insane difference that high ping can make in gunfights. Whether it's hit registration, peeker's advantage, or simply the way players appear and disappear around corners, the experience can feel completely different.

And honestly, it's becoming so frustrating that it has taken away almost all of the fun and excitement I used to have for this game.

I don't mind losing. I don't mind getting outplayed. That's part of the game.

What I do mind is feeling like the outcome of a gunfight was determined by connection quality rather than by who played the situation better.

It's especially frustrating because I genuinely love this game. The gunplay, the sound design, the atmosphere — all of it is fantastic. I want to enjoy it, but playing at 6 Stars on the European servers has become increasingly exhausting.

And then there's another thing I simply don't understand:

I've encountered players who apparently already have VAC bans on their profiles, yet they're still able to play the game.

How is that even possible?

The lack of communication from Crytek makes this even more frustrating.

The developers have actually acknowledged these problems in the past. Around 1.5 years ago, Crytek talked about potential solutions such as region blocking or preventing players from joining certain servers if their ping exceeds a specific threshold.

At the time, I was genuinely hopeful that something would eventually be done about it.

But since then, there has been very little to no communication about this issue.

1.5 years is a long time when you're dealing with a problem that directly affects the experience of your most dedicated players.

I don't expect the developers to magically fix everything overnight. But I do expect some kind of communication. Tell us what you're working on. Tell us if the proposed solutions aren't technically feasible. Tell us if the problem is more complicated than expected.

Just communicate with the community.

The current lack of communication regarding this particular issue has been really disappointing, at least from my personal perspective.

I really hope the developers take a serious look at the current state of matchmaking and high-ping gameplay.

Because underneath all of this, there is an incredible shooter.

Before anything else, a little context for the playtime shown above. At the time of writing I have just under three hours recorded on this PC version of Stardew Valley, but this isn't my first time on the farm. I originally played on Xbox around the time the game was released and put well over 200 hours into it there.

For some reason that I genuinely can't remember, I never actually finished that original journey.

So, many years later, I'm starting again.

And within minutes of arriving back in Stardew Valley, I remembered exactly why I spent so much time here in the first place.

🌱 What I love most about Stardew Valley is that it lets me play Stardew Valley.

That probably sounds like a ridiculous statement, but it's important to me. I don't feel as though the game is constantly trying to dictate what I should be doing. I can wake up planning to clear part of the farm, become distracted by something in town, decide to do some fishing, wander off exploring and eventually crawl into bed having achieved absolutely none of the things I'd originally intended.

And I've still had a good day.

There are crops to grow, fish to catch, mines to explore, things to craft, people to meet, relationships to build and an initially rather sorry-looking farm waiting to become whatever I decide to make of it.

But I don't need to rush any of it.

🏡 That's perhaps even more important to me returning to Stardew Valley now than it was when I first played it. I have absolutely no interest in creating the most efficient farm possible, following somebody else's perfect route or squeezing maximum profit out of every waking minute.

I'm going to potter.

I'll grow things because I fancy growing them. I'll rearrange something because I don't like where I originally put it. I'll probably spend entire days doing something completely unnecessary simply because it caught my attention.

And Stardew Valley is perfectly happy to let me.

🍂 I'm also returning after years of updates, so there's a lovely mixture of familiarity and discovery. I recognise the world I spent hundreds of hours enjoying, while knowing there's now plenty waiting for me that I've never experienced before.

That's a rather wonderful position to be in.

Stardew Valley doesn't need another review explaining why it became one of the best-known farming life sims ever made. Millions of players have already discovered their own reasons for loving it.

Mine is quite simple.

💜 Stardew Valley gives me a world where I can slow down, make something my own and spend an evening doing whatever happens to make me happy.

My only real complaint is that there aren't enough hours in the day to play games like this for as long as I'd like.

This time I'm also determined to find out where the journey eventually leads.

I'm in absolutely no hurry to get there, though.

After all, the farm will still be there tomorrow. 🌱

After 100 hours of playing this game I just can not get enough. The gameplay and the constant additional add ons are endless.

This game is pretty fun but its kind of absurdly buggy for a game that's been out for as long as it has been. Not even just the newest content they've added is riddled with them, systems and mechanics they've added years ago have glaring issues that either haven't been taken care of or reportedly keep coming back. I am enjoying myself but have had multiple occasions where I've had to just completely reset the game because I get stuck inside of something, my ship doesn't launch from a station, or a quest gets softlocked.

This game is also only multiplayer in technicality; the syncing is absolute dogshite and you will constantly run into issues playing with your friends where they see things you can't and vice versa. A good example of this is that when i made a home base I used the flattening tool to level the ground so that it was easier to build on, and basically every time a new friend came over for the first time to check it out it would completely reset the terrain and bury my house underneath the soil as if I'd never done anything to the ground at all. The missions you can do with your friends are rudimentary and if you join your friend doing an open world event it can just straight up break it for them due to the desyncing, like when I joined my boyfriend who was fighting a dreadnaught ship and not only did it not properly display that he'd already destroyed the ship's shields for me but once he'd completely disabled it he was unable to enter and complete the event because on my end it wasn't complete. Even when I had also destroyed everything it still didn't allow him to finish the event. It just feels like a bit of a half-truth that you can play with your friends in this game, as while you can see your friends and fly around or explore with them you can't really do much else. The missions that you can queue up with your friends are the most basic type of mission that basically either boil down to "kill 8 evil plants" or "scan trees and animals on some rando planet" and don't get any more intricate than that. Even the story missions are pretty boring and basically boil down to "go here and talk to this guy, now craft this thing, now go to this other area and talk to this other guy, now go here and talk to this guy" ad infinium until you're arbitrarily done with the questline as a whole.

It is fun to explore the planets but it does get kind of stale after a while once you realize the way that planets are randomly generated. There are probably hundreds of different prefixes a planet can have but they all boil down to the same type of planet biome: paradise, swamp, hot planet, cold planet, toxic planet, radioactive planet, low atmosphere/dead planet, and anomalous planet. You unlock a few newer kinds like gas giants but you have to complete what is essentially three whole questlines of the aforementioned monotonous quests before you can even see them, and at that point the amount of novelty you can achieve from them becomes a bit neutered. The hazards on each planet basically boil down to "ooooh there's a storm that makes it really hard to see and now the meter on your screen is going down, don't get it get to 0 or you'll take extremely slow damage ooooooooh". Gas giants and some extreme hazard planets have tornadoes that will pick you up and throw you but they are by no means dangerous and by the time you reach said planets you'll barely get any negative consequence for getting caught in one. It would be cool if there was a bit more variety in what things can happen on a planet and if things were a bit more dangerous, but this game doesn't really want to kill you or even punish you too hard for anything at all whatsoever.  

I find the on-the-ground combat to be a bit boring since there are no humanoid enemies to fight; only robots, bugs, living rocks, and the occasional hostile animal which is always feline adjacent. The ship combat is a bit better in my opinion but also gets relatively stale after a short while due to how easy the game kind of is as a whole. Not that I'd want to increase the difficulty, as I'm sure the only thing that would change is how much health the enemies have and how much damage they do. Overall it gets the job done like a lot of the other systems and mechanics this game has, but also feels a bit half baked like those other systems and mechanics tend to feel.

The currency system is a bit confusing in its design, considering that a lot of upgrades require an extremely large amount of currency to acquire but the rate at which you can acquire it by most means awards like 1/100th of the amount you'll need to get the things you want. Units and Nanites are given through so many different avenues but they are in such small increments that you'll likely end up just looking up a youtube video on the fastest farming method for them and sticking to that rather than farming for like 8+ hours just to get one thing, especially if your goal is to get multiple of that one thing such as storage upgrades for your Multi-Tool/Freighter/Starship. I blew through legitimately [b]a BILLION[/b] credits just to get like 10 storage upgrades for a new multitool I got as well as [b]50,000 Nanites[/b] just to upgrade my Multi-Tool from class A to class S. I'm not particularly bothered since I have a relatively quick method of farming for both, but it brings into question what the actual intended route of acquiring that absurd amount of money is when you're basically getting pennies on the dollar in comparison from most of the normal methods.

Overall the game kind of feels like a team of 100 people were split into groups of 10 to make different things for the game and somehow had no communication with each other at all. A lot of the systems don't really coalesce in any meaningful way, and that hinders the enjoyability of it as a whole because it becomes you just hard focusing on one thing until that thing can't be worked on anymore and then moving onto the next thing. I'm just about out of things to do in the game, and it's not like Destiny or something where I can do raids or dungeons or strikes or any other type of missions with my friends that are remotely interesting to do. Overall I have had fun and probably will continue to have fun, but the longevity of said fun really seems to have an expiration date once you've seen all there is to see and done all there is to do. I would recommend still but this is by no means an MMO that you can play and have things to do on indefinitely.

I'm finally writing a review since I started playing this game on and off in 2022.

I'm honestly astonished with how much development continues to happen without even spending since I first got this game. Every time I come back I get sucked in to trying new stuff, collecting things, playing the expeditions because I forget how to play lol.

The current expedition for the 10 Year Anniversary has been my favorite so far. You get to hear the development story and see the showcases of the updates since the very beginning of the game's launch. It makes me excited to return to my main save to try the features I haven't known about or tried.

But this game is COMPLEX. I do have to have my browser up fairly frequently to access the wiki or search questions for answers. One issue NMS seems to consistently have is a lot of bugs, especially for each new update. I remember logging in for the Aquarius update and the water volume kept increasing until it was WAY too loud. LOL. And now for the Cosmos update, some of the objects you try to harvest just don't move! For example, after lack of success with my gravitino coil, I maneuvered my ship's tractor beam to be directly in front of those gross glob things, but they still don't budge. Another bug I kept annoyingly encountering (probably not a new bug) was when I would fight pirates, their ships keep flying into the nearby civilian freighters and getting stuck in little crevices. I think I destroyed a part of that freighter to get to it. Well, I guess encountering bugs is kind of part of the gaming experience! The game still runs well despite them. I can only imagine the technical monstrosity of this game.

But no matter how many bugs and hiccups it has, you cannot deny how extensive, expansive, interesting, and weird this game is! Confusing too, maybe, but how did you all even pull off a game to this scale?

My favorite thing aside from the huge amounts of features to explore, discover, progress, and use are the **expeditions.** Having a trail to follow and a place to start every time I put the game down for a while and come back with a noob brain so I can back up on my feet is fantastic. Outside of expeditions, I can go at my own pace, do what I want, try new things, get creeped out by the weird noises, make and sell a bunch of ice cream, and go mining for ferrite dust for the 1500th time. Love it.

In the PUBG Asia Stars 2026 drama, there's a question the Vietnamese gaming community still hasn't received a satisfactory answer to: why were Himass and TanVuu stripped of their partner status, eliminated from the tournament, and permanently banned within just a few days, while the accusations against streamer Soopi — the person who first raised the whole issue — still haven't been conclusively resolved?

According to KRAFTON's own confirmation, all they could establish was that Himass and TanVuu had read the live chat during the match and picked up some information about how the game was unfolding. Based on that alone, the two players were punished almost immediately. But on the other side, the accusation that Soopi had watched an opponent's livestream to pinpoint their location — the very "stream sniping" she was the first to accuse others of — has never been confirmed or denied by KRAFTON. Even when the community presented evidence such as the streamer having multiple windows open on her screen during the match, the publisher's response stopped at "more time is needed to verify" — a timeframe that appears far longer than what it took them to hand down a penalty to the Vietnamese side.

This is the root of the outrage. No one is demanding that Soopi be convicted without solid evidence — that's the minimum standard of fairness everyone deserves, including Himass and TanVuu. The problem is that this standard seems to apply to only one side. If there isn't enough evidence to conclude Soopi violated the rules, why was there enough evidence to immediately punish the two Vietnamese players — especially when KRAFTON itself admitted that, at the time the decision was made, they didn't even have clear judging criteria or penalty guidelines for this kind of conduct?
The incident at PUBG Asia Stars 2026 wasn't the first straw. Many Vietnamese players have long been frustrated with widespread hacking in PUBG PC, with reports routinely going unanswered, forcing the community to rely on personal experience to cope rather than on the publisher's anti-cheat system. On top of that, the fact that PUBG PC operates in Vietnam without an official local publishing partner has led many to question KRAFTON's legal accountability and level of commitment to this market — when problems arise, Vietnamese players have almost no legitimate support channel to turn to besides submitting a ticket abroad and waiting.

All of this, combined with how this particular incident was handled, has left quite a few in the community feeling that KRAFTON seems to give more priority, more attentiveness, and more caution to regions like Korea, while other regions — Vietnam included — tend to be the ones dealt with quickly, judged first, and heard last. This is a sentiment the community is entitled to express, even if it may not reflect any official policy on the publisher's part.

Stardew Valley is the kind of game where it's easy to get lost in, and the reasons for that show themselves in spades as one begins to play. As a love letter to Harvest Moon and the genre as a whole, it's not difficult to see why it's inspired a lot of other titles in the genre since it's released.

There's not a whole lot I can really say to articulate my affection for this game. It's not something I play too often now (when I do, it's on console, rather than here on Steam). It's a really calming, relaxing game where you can focus on your farm however you want, and there's a variety of ways to complete the primary objective of completing the Community Center. It makes each playthrough unique as you have different farm layouts, different options, and can focus on different ways to grow and run your farm each time. I personally tend to default to the forest farm, though, since I like how it looks.

In my opinion though, Stardew is really best played with friends. I had the most fun recently just building up a farm with a buddy where we each took on a job and shared our resources. By the time we were done we were pretty proud of what we'd built. 

For anyone that's played other farming games that are more recent, it's likely that you will like Stardew. The main thing I'll point out is it has a slow start, and unlike some titles out now that give tutorials over the first week, you're kinda let loose to figure stuff out right away. Take your time to soak up the atmosphere and it can be a real cozy game.

Idk man, a game that lets you build planet-spanning factories having a single end-game objective feels like such wasted potential, you know?

I really hate giving this game a negative review because the amount of free content and developer support we've received over the years is honestly insane. However, the core gameplay loop gets incredibly repetitive. Ultimately, all you do is constantly gather resources, scan fauna, and craft items across planets that quickly start to feel very similar despite being procedurally generated. Even the aliens you meet feel lifeless and static. While you can build bases, the mechanics feel a bit clunky, and the overall building system ends up feeling somewhat pointless.

Compounding these loop issues is the horrible performance. I am running an RTX 4090 paired with an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, and I would expect a locked, stable 120 FPS in a game like this. While space and certain planets run great, most planet surfaces cause my framerate to tank all the way down to 60 FPS, sometimes even dipping into the low 50s due to severe CPU/engine bottlenecks and uneven frametimes. Turning off Low Latency Mode and dropping DLSS to Performance helps slightly, but it makes the game look completely blurry and terrible, which defeats the purpose of having a top-tier rig. 

It's a massive achievement, but between the technical frustration and the underlying gameplay lacking the depth to keep me hooked, I just can't recommend it.

6,000+ hours in PUBG PC, and this controversy is probably the final straw for me.

I've supported this game for years. I've played through the bugs, terrible optimization, cheaters, questionable updates, broken audio, server problems, and countless decisions that made absolutely no sense.

But the way KRAFTON handled the situation involving HIMASS, TANVUU, and SOOPI showed me something much worse than bad game development:

A complete failure of trust.

The issue isn't simply whether stream sniping happened.

The issue is HOW the situation was handled.

Two Vietnamese players were punished almost immediately after an accusation was made. Later, KRAFTON themselves admitted that their initial decision had been rushed and that information had been released before proper verification.

Think about that for a second.

You publicly punish players first.

Then you admit the process was rushed.

Then after the controversy becomes even bigger, the same players receive permanent competitive bans.

How is the community supposed to have confidence in that process?

If a rule was clearly broken, show the exact rule.

Show what evidence was reviewed.

Explain what was permitted during this event and what wasn't.

Explain who communicated the rules to the players.

Explain why the initial punishment happened before the investigation was properly completed.

Instead, what players saw was confusion, inconsistent communication, reversed statements, apologies, and then one of the harshest punishments possible.

This wasn't some random ranked match.

These are people's careers.

A permanent competitive ban should require an extremely clear rulebook, transparent evidence, and a professional investigation process.

Especially when the organizer itself has already admitted mistakes in how the case was initially handled.

And this is exactly why so many Vietnamese players are angry.

It's not simply "Vietnam vs Korea."

It's about whether every player is treated by the same standards regardless of nationality, popularity, organization, or public pressure.

If HIMASS and TANVUU violated a clearly established tournament rule, then punish them according to that rule.

But if the event rules were unclear, if staff communication created confusion, or if permission was given by tournament-related personnel, then those facts should matter when deciding the punishment.

You cannot run an international esports event with unclear communication and then place 100% of the consequences on the players.

KRAFTON should also understand that esports depends on trust.

Players need to trust the rules.

Professional players need to trust tournament organizers.

Viewers need to trust investigations.

And communities need to believe that decisions are based on evidence instead of pressure from whichever side is louder.

After more than 6,000 hours, I've tolerated a lot from PUBG.

Bad optimization? I stayed.

Cheaters? I stayed.

Broken audio? I stayed.

Questionable updates? I stayed.

Aggressive monetization? I stayed.

But watching the company mishandle a controversy involving its own competitive community and then expect everyone to simply accept the final decision without questioning the process is extremely disappointing.

PUBG used to make me frustrated because of the game.

Now I'm frustrated because of the company behind it.

After 6,000+ hours, I never thought the reason I'd consider walking away from PUBG wouldn't be hackers, performance, or gameplay.

It would be losing trust in KRAFTON.

A competitive game without trust in its rules and its organizers has a much bigger problem than any bug they can patch.

It was just a friendly tournament—an event meant for fun and fostering connections among nations in the region—yet it involved a truly minor scandal. Seeing how a billion-dollar company handled the communications surrounding it left me thoroughly dismayed.

They wanted this to be a massive, explosive scandal—something even bigger than the controversies back in their own country. I don't know if there was someone pulling the strings behind the scenes, but seeing how hastily they dismissed all evidence and allegations involving their players—videos, voice recordings, images, and so on—and then handed down a final ruling of a lifetime ban from all tournaments, all while touting the words "FAIR PLAY," made me absolutely furious.

In short, this is truly a fantastic, entertaining battle royale game to play with friends—one you certainly shouldn't overlook. Baldur's Gate 3 is a one of a kind game. It is essentially a turn-based RPG game with open world elements where you can interact with NPCs and complete different quests. It is truly fascinating how well the game is written and how much time and effort the devs put in perfecting all details. It does have many disturbing cutscenes nevertheless I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is curious about the game. 

Story-
You have been captured by an octopus alien and they put a tadpole inside your eye. You break free from that spaceship with the help of few allies and now you need to find a cure or risk turning into the same octopus alien. There are all sorts of plot twists as you progress through the game, some unexpected developments and cool boss fights.

Plot-
It is a dark fantasy RPG with all sorts of creatures. Humans, dwarves, goblins, elfs, orcs etc. live in their teritories. There are evil gods, cults, factions and all sorts of nasty rituals; the game is grotesque and quite disturbing at times. Baldur's Gate is a city where all sorts of merchants, creatures and common people live in harmony.

Gameplay-
The game is an open world RPG where you can interact with the world in all sorts of ways. The combat is classic turn based strategy but the actions are immensly diverse and you can make use of your positioning to gain an advantage. Wizards can cast all sorts of spells, clerics can heal multiple people at the same time and fighters can chop down enemies with ease. You can also diguise yourself to gain access to prohibited areas and persuade an enemy to join your side in case of a battle in future. The gameplay is the reason many people continue to play this game regularly and you will not be disappoited at all.

Music-
The music grows on you slowly, unlike most games the music isn't catchy but you'll find yourself searching for your favorite songs online as soon as you beat the game. Some of the songs have lots of diminished and augmented scales, I believe is inspired from Indian/Asian cultures. If you are into that kind of music, you will enjoy the game even more.

Art-
The art style is fabulous, from detailed armour textures to facial expressions; the devs have done an incredible work. Each new area has a different vibe, making the game even more alive.

Price-
The price may seem a lot at first but the value for money you get is too good to be true. A single playthrough will take around 120-130 hours and you'll probably play more in the future/ or play multiplayer mode regularly which is worth the money in my opinion. The game comes on sale frequently so you might want to wait. I already had the game via family sharing but I bought my own copy as I truly enjoyed the game, it's that good!

Overall, I'd recommend the game to everyone regadless you play turn-based games or not. I'll say however, the game has lot of disturbing content so play at your discresion. Do get it on sale if you are not too keen on playing it right now, you'll be amazed by how good the game is.

Guild Wars 2 reminds me why I fell love in with MMO's in the first place - the sense of wonder I encounter every time I discover something new. Embarking on a grand adventure, never knowing where I'm going to end up by the time I finally log out for the night. A plethora of endless grinds, all of which showcase and actually reward players for the hours they are willing to sink into their respective journeys.

In my humble opinion (and finally having my eyes opened to the possibilities), horizontal progression is definitely the correct way for MMOs to release and manage content. Guild Wars 2 has that in spades. Other relevant MMO's which still use vertical progression ultimately don't end up respecting you or your time, making most achievements and gear seemingly worthless over a game's lifespan.

On a side note, I hope World of Warcraft: Forever continues to take notes from the success of Guild Wars 2, and why this game deserves all of the accolades it receives and more.

With all of the knowledge and experience I have accumulated throughout my years of gaming, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to other players.

Give it a try - you won't be disappointed.
