This incident has seriously damaged my trust in PUBG and the way its competitive scene handles accusations against professional players.

What happened to the two Vietnamese players should not be viewed as merely a dispute involving Vietnam. The bigger issue is the precedent this decision could create for every international player competing in PUBG.

If an accusation can lead to disciplinary action without the evidence and investigation process being made sufficiently clear to the public, then any foreign player could potentially find themselves in the same situation in the future. A streamer makes an accusation, public pressure builds, and the player is punished before the community is given a transparent explanation of the evidence and the investigation.

That is not a healthy competitive environment.

This is also why the issue cannot simply be dismissed as a "Vietnamese community" problem. Today it is two Vietnamese players. Tomorrow it could be players from Thailand, China, Japan, Europe, North America, or any other region outside Korea.

Professional players deserve the same standard of evidence, investigation, and due process regardless of their nationality.

I am not asking PUBG to protect Vietnamese players because they are Vietnamese. I am asking PUBG to apply the same rules to everyone.

If PUBG wants its esports scene to be respected internationally, then accusations should be investigated objectively, evidence should be properly evaluated, and disciplinary decisions should be supported by a transparent and consistent process.

Otherwise, this case risks creating a dangerous precedent: international players may feel that they are not protected by the same standards when accusations come from more influential figures or communities.

PUBG needs to understand that competitive integrity is not only about catching cheaters. It is also about making sure that innocent players are not unfairly punished.

**Today it is Vietnamese players. Tomorrow it could be any international player. The standard must be the same for everyone.**

The Fantasy RPG with MMO features that gives the most Choice, and freedom to innovate.

Other MMO’s lock you into a character who’s role, weapons and fighting style are static, ESO doesn’t. Your character can at any time equip a different weapon and use it, experience with that weapon unlocks skills, a purchased token allows change to any aspect, and for gold or free, you can reset your perks, your attributes, and skill selection. Your equipment interchanges by level, 10 Character slots at start and 15 to unlock.
Story content is designed to be completed solo, with the exception of those group instances such as DLC dungeons and trials, most of this game is solo-able once you have the knowledge, skills and points, all of which is provided for in enough ways to suit anyone willing to put in effort. If you do hit a brick wall, ask for help, it has its faults but once body odour is eliminated :D the ESO player community is one of the most genuine and helpful I’ve encountered, and many of us are just paying forward the help we received when WE were beginning. 

I will likely keep this game in my life now, another temptation to manage- computer gaming is certainly not Virtue, yet not quite Vice by the ancient Greeks standards -  this game is effectively an alternate world to step into with fairly immersive graphics (good for your own mental health to have reality sharper and more beautiful than the games you play) in tales you get to shape, some are funny, some poignant, some are activist, propaganda nonsense you should remember you don’t HAVE to complete. It is now a vast game, see further down for details, and you are gaming for YOUR enjoyment, or you should be. But if you enjoy creativity and the freedom to do “it” differently, fantasy stories, heroic striving, with socialising optional, some maths and puzzles (winning in combat here is effectively who’s done the best math sum, social predictions and maintained discipline in mayhem) this is a reliable outlet. It’s a beautiful world, with many relatable characters, good script options and a depth and breadth of variations, settings and options I’ve rarely seen. Only some recent releases compete, only some of those offer closer than a suspended puppet master view distance, and they are not Tamriel. Whether you want to relax to a story, adventure, furnish your home, blow of steam in a challenge of arms or focus in a deep penetration recce and raid with no “save” option; ESO has you covered. Flight and Sailing are the two activities I want that this game doesn’t offer. Even home decorating can earn you player’s gold and premium store “gifts” in here. See other contributors for ERP guides, I’m too young AND too old for some of those details, suffice it to say that if you do witness an unsought experience, just, back away slowly, port to another zone and TRY to forget what you heard/saw that vampire doing to Shakespeare’s legacy with that werewolf gigolo. 

I began my time in ESO buying the discounted Standard Edition in Dec 2020 ($14 AUD, with no subscription). “Skyrim” was my first RPG in 2008 (High school friends influence after a practical, rural childhood) and after playing it many different ways, I was curious for a Tamriel I could share. From that start, enjoying the challenge of “How far can I stretch that REAL money..?” through the trading game got me Morrowind, Guilds, Summerset, Greymoor, Elsweyr, Blackwood, my summon-able Raven banker and other things. Elite Dangerous: Odyssey was a 2021 release by Frontier Developments. This DLC for Elite Dangerous would allow players to finally get out of their ships and walk across the many planets and moons of their galaxy. It was horribly buggy on release and years later still doesn’t really match the dreams and aspirations of what players wanted.

Star Citizen, a billion-dollar tech demo, was for many years an impressive showcase despite its extreme performance issues and bugs. The ability to seamlessly traverse space stations, ship interiors, planets, cargo holds and asteroid fields was the stuff of dreams. Storing vehicles inside ships inside ships felt like a futuristic Russian doll – no game matched this level of interconnection.

Yet despite its groundbreaking technology, Star Citizen was an unstable mess, often making even basic gameplay loops unreliable. After years of playing it on and off, I found its gameplay consistently held back by bugs and poor performance – enemies unable to react in sub-30 FPS combat, ships randomly self-destructing during cargo runs. Its two solar systems remain largely barren, while repetitive missions provide most of its structured content. It’s fun to imagine what Star Citizen could become, but years of delays and broken promises have left many players frustrated.

Starfield, another poorly delivered space game that had unique and interesting elements that were ultimately undermined by its horrible, undeveloped state. Todd Howard’s baby released to middling reviews, as players complained about a 2023 game utilizing loading screens between all of its sections. You couldn’t manually walk into your ship; it was a loading screen. You couldn’t fly to a planet or moon; it was a loading screen. While Star Citizen was the most interconnected space game I’ve ever played, Starfield felt like looking through a View-Master and swapping to a new reel every few minutes. Yet despite that, anyone who played Starfield would attest to its ship-building system, something that among the most ambitious space games felt fresh and interesting, allowing players to build their dream spaceships while not having to pay the $10,000 Star Citizen premium to own them.

Each of these space games represents a dream that was dampened by software, hardware and developmental limitations. People don’t want the illusion of space, they want space. They want to explore its vastness and the crevices in-between. They want to jump out of a spaceship, EVA toward a planet, enter its atmosphere, and fall toward its surface. Despite this dream, they were met with a continuous chain of waiting rooms, a series of technical messes, and empty planets not worth exploring.

One game that was part of this development race was No Man’s Sky, arguably the worst entry with an endless list of failed promises. Back in 2016, this dream was only starting to be realized, and while No Man’s Sky showed that you could land on a planet and then seamlessly fly out of its atmosphere, it didn’t offer anything to do beyond this simple gameplay loop. 18.6 quintillion ‘unique’ planets sounded amazing on paper, but in reality felt like an infinite procedural generation of barren wastelands that were mimicries of each other.

Then 10 years went by.

It’s hard to even talk about what No Man’s Sky has accomplished in a decade because it feels unreal. If you could make a list of undelivered promises from every space game I’ve talked about, including NMS, the list of expansions and major updates would cover that list and more. Ship building, seamless ship interiors, seamless EVA… The last year alone, NMS has covered a lot of the major features that made people gravitate towards Starfield or Star Citizen. While there are still technical achievements SC has over NMS, it’s hard to think that an indie product managed to implement what took a triple-A multi-studio with hundreds of millions and a custom engine to make.

To put this into perspective, the ability to walk around inside your ship, EVA directly into space, fly the ship, seamlessly enter a planet or moon’s atmosphere, land, explore on foot, return to your ship, take off, fly to another star system or galaxy, all as one continuous journey… I can name three games that have achieved that: Space Engineers, Star Citizen, No Man’s Sky.

Yet, NMS continues to flesh out these experiences. You can customize freighters and frigates, own multiple ships, build a corvette-class ship and its interiors, and have it all sit outside your own space station. Then fly to a planet and manage settlements, walk in any direction and find flora, fauna, pets, bases, salvageable and minable spots, ships, missions, traders, ships flying overhead, underwater caverns, caves, lakes, oceans, rivers, mountains, and sand worms – because why not? Explore other people's creations, learn languages, take on missions from space stations, the list goes on.

What does NMS lack? Sadly, depth.

There is no 6DOF flight system (six degrees of freedom) with forward/back, left/right, up/down movement, in addition to pitch, yaw and roll. You have pitch, yaw, and roll, forward/back, but you cannot strafe horizontally or vertically, nor can you manually land your ship, instead having to rely on an automated landing system. This makes flight feel bad. While it’s fine traversing from location to location, as soon as you try to manually adjust your position in space or atmosphere, and then start shooting at a specific target, it feels like you’re fighting your own ship as it nose dives into an invisible barrier above the planet's surface, every adjustment crashing you into the surrounding cliffs. You’d think that the simplicity would make it more accessible, but it genuinely feels harder to control your ship than almost any other space game I’ve played. Even just trying to come to a complete stop in the smaller ships feels like a battle.

Then there’s combat. Instead of having an awesome series of guns and scopes, you have an arcade-style blaster that feels no different than using your mining laser. The enemies also become repetitive very fast. I’ve hated every combat encounter outside of dogfights. You don’t even have aim assist on controller.

For everything that NMS does right, it feels like the arcade-style approach is limiting its true potential. Now don’t get me wrong, I think NMS’ willingness to streamline elements is what makes the experience feel seamless and unobtrusive, while games like SC make every task and adventure tediously real to an exhausting degree. Despite understanding this, I do think that adding 6DOF and actual guns to the game would improve the experience greatly, and without them it currently feels like wasted potential. This could be THE space game – it has the potential to be everything everyone across all avenues of its genre wants in ONE experience. Even just a list of toggles for 6DOF, manual landing, and removing invisible planetary barriers would improve my experience greatly.

As it stands, NMS is an amazing game that keeps pushing the possibilities of its genre forward. While it lacks depth, you’re bound to get hundreds of hours among its many sandbox hallways. My hope is that Hello Games will overhaul flight and combat and interconnect NMS’ many avenues of play into a more holistic experience. What’s here and what has been achieved is impressive – the greatest redemption story in gaming history... a redemption story that overshadows its most impressive feat: being able to compete with a billion-dollar game on its own turf, and for many, deliver on the empty promises across a decade of failing products.

Thank you, Hello Games, for realizing the dreams of millions of gamers.

**1-STAR REVIEW: PUBG — WHEN “FAIR PLAY” BECOMES NOTHING MORE THAN A SENTENCE IN AN APOLOGY**

I used to think the reasons to criticize PUBG would be obvious: servers, bugs, matchmaking, balance, updates, or poor game design decisions.

After PUBG Asia Stars 2026, I realized that those are not necessarily the most serious problems.

The more serious problem is much harder to repair:

**trust in the system behind the game.**

PUBG Asia Stars 2026 was announced as an Asian regional event involving six regions, with eight participants per region and 48 participants in total. It was originally scheduled across three competition days and carried a total prize pool of USD 70,000.

What was supposed to be an international creator competition quickly became a major controversy surrounding competitive integrity and tournament management.

The dispute began after Day 1 on September 17, 2026, involving Himass and TanVuu. On September 19, PUBG removed the two participants from the remaining matches while an investigation continued. On September 20, PUBG cancelled Day 3 entirely, explaining that the tournament could no longer continue under conditions where all participants could compete with the same level of trust and fairness.

Then came the final investigation.

On September 23, KRAFTON officially stated that it had reviewed **official broadcasts, participant footage, in-game data and replays** and confirmed that Himass and TanVuu had used external information and stream sniping. According to KRAFTON, they obtained information that could not reasonably be known through normal gameplay and used that information in decision-making and tactics. Their PUBG accounts were permanently banned, and they were permanently barred from official esports competitions organized or approved by KRAFTON, including PGC, PGS and PNC.

I am not disputing that finding.

**If a player violates competitive-integrity rules, there must be consequences.**

But this is exactly where my criticism of PUBG begins.

Because KRAFTON itself admitted that **KRAFTON failed in the operation of the tournament.**

KRAFTON acknowledged that it had failed to establish sufficiently clear preventive measures, assessment criteria and sanction levels for the use of external information before the incident happened. It admitted that it did not accurately explain the situation from the beginning, described the Korean participants' boycott as a “withdrawal,” accepted the narrower description of “chat sniping,” and failed to manage Korean- and Vietnamese-language communications consistently. KRAFTON also admitted that it failed to adequately protect participants from personal attacks and secondary harm. It explicitly described this as a failure of its own operations and communications.

That is the part I find difficult to accept.

A tournament organizer can make mistakes.

But when an organizer runs an international event without clearly defining the relevant forms of misconduct, without a sufficiently detailed sanction framework, without mandatory broadcast delay, and without adequately accounting for the risks created by simultaneous personal streams, then later communicates inaccurate information during the crisis, this stops being just a player-conduct issue.

**It becomes an institutional problem.**

KRAFTON's September 20 notice is particularly revealing. PUBG acknowledged that the event had been designed around real-time interaction between streamers and therefore did not mandate broadcast delay. It also acknowledged that the rulebook described fairness and sportsmanship obligations only in broad terms and failed to sufficiently differentiate specific actions such as checking external information through live chat, watching another participant's personal broadcast, or receiving and using outside information.

So here is the question:

**If the operational framework was not specific enough, why should the players be expected to carry all of the consequences of a framework that the organizer itself admits was inadequately prepared?**

KRAFTON now says that it never officially permitted stream sniping at any tournament or event, regardless of prize pool, event format or participant composition.

Then why was the event operated in an environment where participants could stream live, viewers could interact in real time, and no mandatory broadcast delay existed?

That is not an accusation of conspiracy.

It is a criticism of governance.

---

### The third-party software controversy

Another issue that has circulated widely is the allegation that Korean participant Soopi was using third-party software.

The most widely discussed image shows **Input Director** among the programs visible while she switched applications.

But this needs to be handled honestly:

**Input Director is not, by itself, proof of cheating.**

Its own developer describes it as a software KVM that allows one keyboard and mouse to control multiple Windows computers, switch control between systems, and share a clipboard.

Therefore, simply showing that Input Director was running does **not** establish that Soopi used it to obtain prohibited information or gain an unfair advantage.

KRAFTON has not publicly concluded that she used that program to cheat. Instead, KRAFTON later apologized directly to Soopi and said it would support efforts to remove false claims, ridicule and illegally manipulated images targeting her.

I am not going to convert an allegation into a fact.

But this is precisely why the burden should be on KRAFTON to explain its technical standards.

PUBG's general rules are already strict about unauthorized third-party programs and hardware that provide unfair advantages or affect gameplay. KRAFTON states that unauthorized third-party programs can result in penalties, and its Rules of Conduct allow permanent bans for unauthorized programs or devices.

So the meaningful question is not:

**“Was Soopi a cheater?”**

The meaningful questions are:

What software was permitted?

What software was prohibited?

Were KVM applications permitted?

How many computers could participants connect?

Were secondary displays allowed?

Were running processes, peripherals, network connections and screen setups inspected before and after matches?

Were the same technical standards applied to every region?

If the answer is yes, publish the procedure.

**Do not simply ask the community to trust that it was checked.**

---

### The circle controversy

Another issue raised by parts of the community concerns the perception that the safe zone repeatedly favored the Korean side in certain games.

I will not state that KRAFTON manipulated the circle.

**There is not enough publicly available evidence to establish that.**

But I also understand why the question exists.

Because once trust has been damaged, even randomness becomes something people want to verify.

Where are the zone-generation logs?

Where is the underlying match data?

Can the complete circle history for each game be independently checked?

Can the results be audited?

A transparent organizer should not have to say only:

**“It was RNG.”**

Show the data.

If the circle was genuinely random, independent verification should strengthen PUBG's credibility rather than threaten it.

---

The Korean roster boycotted Day 2. The event was ultimately terminated early, and KRAFTON decided not to determine final standings through the unfinished Day 3; instead, prize money was to be distributed under the same standard across the participating regions.

I have been playing this game since 2019, clocking nearly 8,000 hours.

That number carries a lot of weight. It proves I didn’t just pick up the game and drop it; I quit and came back more times than I can count. I endured terrible updates, abysmal optimization, rampant cheating, game-breaking bugs, and even the dry spells when people claimed PUBG was a dead game. Yet right now, I have decided to walk away for a reason I never could have imagined.

To be completely honest, just three days ago, I was still having a blast playing with my friends. Yesterday, I decided to walk away for good. And right now, I am writing these words.

Was PUBG actually good when it first launched? Of course not. Everything back then was unpolished and bare-bones, and I never imagined I would stay attached to it for this long. But somehow, it had this strange, magnetic pull on me.

When player numbers plummeted due to the cheater epidemic and it felt like the game was on the verge of shutting down, I was still queuing up, watching "superheroes" literally flying cars through the sky while spraying down lobbies.

I witnessed the long, grueling process of the developers trying to turn things around. Watching the player base slowly recover genuinely made me happy, because the game I loved was finally coming back to life.

I was there when exceptional players rose to prominence and carved out a professional esports scene. Organizations stepped in, competitive teams were forged, and representatives from my country raised our national flag at the very top of the world championship. Through all of that, I stayed loyal.

When the game transitioned to free-to-play, cheaters surged, performance deteriorated, and the stuttering got worse. PUBG progressively turned into a cash-grab machine: season passes, endless brand collaborations, loot crates, skins, and cosmetic clutter—monetization tactics everywhere you looked. The game found brand-new ways to disappoint its player base time and time again.

Still, I stuck around. In spite of everything, I still found joy in playing with my friends—the simple joy of sticking with a game that defined my youth. A game that gave me memories, and gave me lifelong friendships.

I tolerated and overlooked so much.

Cheaters? Whatever, chalk it up to bad luck. Report them and queue for the next match.

Bugs and frame drops? Annoying, sure, but I got used to it.

Another cash-grab skin or commercial crossover? Hardly a surprise anymore.

I kept making excuses for this game because I just wanted to keep having fun with my friends.

But now, even clicking "Play" doesn't feel worth it anymore.

Do you want to know why?

For those who may not know, at the PUBG Asia Stars 2026 tournament, two Vietnamese pro players—Himass and Tanvuu—received permanent bans from all official PUBG competitive events, alongside permanent account bans in PUBG: Battlegrounds, for allegedly stream sniping during the tournament.

On paper, that might sound straightforward. Cheating in an esports event warrants punishment, right?

Except the reality is far from simple.

Did both players actually stream snipe? Yes.

Did the tournament rules explicitly forbid stream sniping for this event? No.

Did the players double-check and confirm beforehand whether it was allowed? Yes.

Immediately after the backlash erupted, the tournament organizer abruptly canceled the remaining matches of Day 3, shutting down PUBG Asia Stars 2026 prematurely. Within just two days, KRAFTON admitted they had "rushed to publish unverified information" regarding the incident. They subsequently issued an apology for their operational mishandling, yet still proceeded to push through the disciplinary hammer on the two Vietnamese players.

The organizers admit their own systemic failure, yet hand down the maximum possible penalty to the Vietnamese players?
They sweep every allegation regarding the Korean streamers under the rug and exclusively penalize the Vietnamese players?
They issue a direct apology to the affected streamers, completely disregarding the fact that their public accusations against the Vietnamese players were groundless?
They release an apology specifically to the Korean community in Korean, while completely ignoring the Vietnamese community?

Reading this far, anyone with basic common sense can see that something is fundamentally wrong here. There are also toxic behaviors from parts of the Korean community crossing the line to insult my country and our national leaders, among other things, but I will refrain from going further since this review is already long enough.

Speaking as a Vietnamese player, I cannot accept a publisher that treats its player base with such blatant disregard, looks down on our community, and handles conflicts with sheer injustice and disrespect.

PUBG used to be irreplaceable to me. Yet, because of a handful of individuals, an incompetent administration, a sequence of entirely unprofessional decisions, or perhaps some underlying agenda, so many players like myself are forced to walk away with a bitter pill we simply cannot swallow.

I, and many others out there, am not leaving because we lost interest in the game. We are leaving because we cannot tolerate this sheer unfairness and the publisher’s complete lack of respect. We can bear walking away from a familiar game we loved, but we will never accept seeing our entire community treated as second-class, or our country being insulted.

I am quitting because I invested far too much hope, only to be met with the ultimate betrayal and disappointment.

I’m deeply disappointed in KRAFTON and the way this situation has been handled. The changing decisions and lack of clear, consistent communication have left many Vietnamese fans feeling that their concerns—and the Vietnamese PUBG community itself—were not treated with the respect they deserve. Any allegation should be investigated fairly, with transparent reasoning and a chance for everyone involved to respond. KRAFTON’s handling of this case has damaged trust, and the company needs to acknowledge the impact its actions have had on players and fans in Vietnam.

I first knew this game as **PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS**.

It was a long name, but it had history behind it. “PlayerUnknown” was tied to Brendan Greene, the person who helped lay the foundation for PUBG and played a major role in turning the Battle Royale genre into a global phenomenon.

Then PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS became **PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS**.

To me, that was not just a simple rebranding decision. It felt like the moment PUBG started distancing itself from the identity that made the game special in the first place. The creator eventually left the company, while PUBG continued to grow as a massive commercial brand, becoming more and more disconnected from what long-time players originally loved about it.

But the biggest disappointment is no longer the name.

It is the way KRAFTON handled the recent situation involving two Vietnamese professional players.

I fully understand that esports needs rules. If a player breaks the rules, there should be consequences. No professional competition can survive without enforcement.

But rules only have meaning when they are **clear, consistent, transparent, and fairly applied**.

What I find difficult to accept is the feeling that these two players were pushed into a situation where the consequences were extremely severe, while the overall process and interpretation of the rules remained controversial.

When a decision can affect a player's account, reputation, career, and years of effort, the organizer has a responsibility to make sure that the rules, evidence, and enforcement process are clear enough to justify such a serious punishment.

This is no longer just about two Vietnamese players.

It creates a precedent.

If today a professional player can potentially lose almost everything because of a situation where the interpretation and enforcement of the rules are still being debated by the community, then what stops the same thing from happening to another player in the future?

It could be another Vietnamese player.

It could be a Korean, Chinese, Thai, European, or any other professional player.

A serious esports ecosystem cannot expect players to spend thousands of hours practicing, build their entire careers around one game, and then leave their futures vulnerable to rules that may only become fully clear after a punishment has already been handed down.

The most concerning part is not one punishment.

The most concerning part is creating a precedent where the publisher holds enormous power, while players have very little protection when a dispute happens.

PUBG used to be a game that made me willing to spend hundreds or even thousands of hours learning recoil control, reading circles, listening for footsteps, improving positioning, and getting better one match at a time.

But after all these years, I increasingly feel that KRAFTON cares more about maintaining the **PUBG brand** than maintaining the trust of the people who actually built its community.

And then there is another problem that PC players have complained about for years: **hackers and cheaters**.

In a competitive game where a single cheater can ruin 20 or 30 minutes of gameplay for dozens of legitimate players, anti-cheat should be one of the highest priorities.

Normal players do not need polished statements.

They need to enter a match and feel that their skill actually matters. They need to believe that when they die, it happened because another player was better, not because someone was using third-party software.

If a competitive game cannot maintain trust in fair play, then skins, battle passes, collaborations, esports tournaments, and marketing campaigns mean very little.

I still love what PUBG once created.

That is exactly why I am so disappointed by what it has become.

If you are a new player thinking about downloading PUBG PC, I strongly recommend that you first look into the current state of the game, the cheating problem, the way KRAFTON manages its competitive ecosystem, and the recent controversies before deciding to invest your time or money.

PUBG may be free to download.

But your time, trust, and patience are not free.

Once upon a time, there was a young -me- that was looking for new games to play on his tiny little playstation. Low and behold, he came across a game called "Warframe". Opening it up, he was introduced to a magical world of the Tenno ways and magical lands. Fast forward to now, and I have loved it for 6+ Years, and wholly support the developers and Digital Extremes.
   From the very beginning of the story, I was slightly out of the loop. 2 Quests later, and im begging to go through even more of the quest because it, in the most simple way, hooked me like a fish on a line. Storyline mission to side missions, each and every one of them felt like it was made with love. Not for money, no, but for what they had created over the years.
   I stand by my reason that Warframe is a game people should try. If you want a list why and why not, then look no further.
Reasons to play: 1.) It is a free game, with no paywalls. 2) If you are into pay-2-win, then you've got something to look forward to. 3) If you aren't into pay-to-win, don't worry, there is an entire IN-GAME, backed, community market where your simple items could fetch currency worth IRL money. 4) Busy person? Don't worry! Sometimes, you'll have to craft things that may take time. Log on for a few hours, build what ya need, and forget about it until the next time you play! 5) The most important one for last. The developers of this game aint looking to scam you out of your hard earned dollars, but for a free to play game, the dev team made a lot of items able to be purchased with the prem. Currency. However, that being said, I have never seen a team of developers so deeply in tune with their community. Digital Extremes puts, and always has put, the player's enjoyment before their profit. So, if you ever do say "I could probably purchase a bit of Platinum", know that as a long term player, I think your money is going towards the right people in the end. Digital Extremes and the content they produce, for a free game mind you, blows my mind.

Reasons not to:
That being said, Warframe does have it's quirks. If you don't like having to wait the occasional hour, or maybe even 24 for larger builds, then Warframe may not be your best case. Likewise, although the community is extremely, extremely helpful, sometimes other players can overbear on your beginning experience, so I personally suggest running through a few of your beginning missions by yourself. And last but not least, I must cover it. The game is heavily laced with purchases via premium currency. Lots of personalization is locked by Platinum Purchases. Likewise, some frames or weapons may feel impossible to farm on occasion, because believe it or not, you may have to farm for resources, blueprints, or the like. Platinum can fix this of course, which I feel is a flaw, but hey, thats just a picky guy speaking.

No Man's Sky is a fun game, but also a flawed game.
I got this game a couple weeks ago and have had a lot of enjoyment from it, and overall I think it was worth the money I spent on it. But despite the 100+ hours of fun I've had, it's hard to say it is an amazing game.
First I will start with some positives:
-While I have some problems with the story, the philosophical questions it poses more than make up for any issues I have with it. Without spoiling anything, the questions the game makes you confront really make you think about reality in a way that I love.
-The variations in systems, planets, fauna, and flora make exploration extremely fun. It felt like every system I traveled to had something new to show me that I've never seen before, and even though there are a few similarities between worlds they all felt distinct enough for it to be exciting to find new worlds.
-One thing that this game blows out of the water for me is ship design. Every time I went to a space station I would see a ship with a design I had never seen before, and buying new ships not because you need it but because it looks cool is really fun. I have gotten a lot of enjoyment out of just building a collection of interesting ships.
And now, for some negatives:
-While I do think the story was worth doing, it can be really boring at times and sometimes feels like a slog. Often it is just going to one point, talking to a character, going to another point, talking to a character, repeat. And to make this even worse, the story struggles to give me much attachment to many of the characters I do meet. There might be one or two I care about, and that is stretching it a bit.
-Base building. This part of the game just makes me sad because I wanted to actually enjoy it. But when I say that base building in this game is more frustrating than base building in Ark, I am not exaggerating. Buildings you try to place will randomly deform the ground, foundations won't properly connect to the ground sometimes, power generation is a pain in the ass to set up if you don't want to use a bio-furnace that you have to constantly refuel, building on asteroids doesn't work properly, etc.
-The game tries too hard to be both multiplayer and singleplayer, and it makes for a frustrating and annoying experience. For most of the game you will be on your own and never encounter another player. The game even treats the game like singleplayer most of the time because when someone isn't in the same system as you, you can just fully pause the game whenever you want. But then you have the anomaly where you can meet other players and go on missions with them, and many systems like farming, frigate expeditions, and even a certain quest act as if the game is multiplayer by taking several hours to do expecting you to log off from the game and get on later to check on them. It's frustrating because I would enjoy the game so much more if it could decide what type of game it wanted to be, but it tries too hard to be both single and multiplayer.

I do have more positives and negatives I could list, but the things listed are my main points. Overall, I would suggest buying this game if it goes on sale, but for $60 it just isn't worth it imo. The nice part at least is that the devs are still active and putting in new content, and maybe some of the issues I have will be fixed over time. I really do like this game, but unfortunately right now I don't think I can love it.

[h1] I didn't want to, but the game is wasted potential [/h1]

War Thunder provides very good design and sound for vehicles, including tanks, planes, and ships; battles feel realistic and on a large scale when they go well. The aspect of the game surrounding these features, however, is set up to frustrate players until they decide to open their wallet.

The grind

The progress is extremely slow. To get a vehicle you first need to earn research points, then spend lions to buy it, and afterwards carry out more silver and crew training in order to operate it. In each vehicle tree the initial models do a poor job until the various modules have been unlocked. It is frustrating to play a tank with no upgrades against players who have completely researched and trained their crews. The problem gets worse at higher ranks and to reach the top-tier vehicles it takes hundreds of hours. Even when you lose a match time is still taken up and a weak team can leave you with nothing.

Premium vehicles and pay to progress

War Thunder uses two types of currency. One is gained gradually as a result of playing the game, and the other can be bought with actual money. Premium vehicles are promoted as ways of saving time; in practice they often perform just as well as or better than standard vehicles that have the same battle rating. The purpose of premium time and boosters is mainly to make the process of earning silver through normal gameplay seem extremely unpleasant. The prices are very high since a single vehicle costs as much as the full price of the game and bundles cost even more. Players also feel that their progress is connected to how much they spend, because the free method is so slow that many of them feel they have to buy premium vehicles in order to earn silver at a faster rate.

Economy and repair costs

The costs involved in repairing your vehicle and the costs of spawning vehicles penalise you for the way that War Thunder encourages you to play. If you lose a high-tier vehicle the amount of silver you lose in a match will be greater than the amount you earned. Even if you have a premium account or premium vehicles you can still win a match but will end up losing money. It is hard to enjoy trying out different vehicles when each death has a cost.

Balance and matchmaking

Battle ratings are intended to ensure that matches remain fair. The system is generally compressed and inconsistent. You will frequently come across vehicles that are much better than yours, for example ones with armour that you can't penetrate, weapons that have a greater range than yours or aircraft that have obvious advantages. In top-tier matches the contest is often often one of who has the most expensive vehicle. Balance changes can be slow and difficult to predict and problems which spoil matches for months are not corrected.

Gameplay and other issues

The ground combat aspect is hampered by a dependence on air support and a great deal of downtime after a player dies. Although the Realistic and Simulator modes provide a certain level of depth, the number of players is small and games tend to either turn into camping situations or become chaotic. Bugs and problems with hit registration continue to occur from time to time and some of the game's mechanics seem inconsistent. The interface is messy and confusing for players because of the excessive number of currencies, modes, menus, and store prompts. The developers have often given poor communication regarding changes and have not adequately responded to community feedback. Players frequently feel that they are being ignored.

Verdict

Even though War Thunder might be one of the military games ever created, the design decisions always get in the way. The game places a greater emphasis on monetization and slow progression than on respecting the players' time. People who enjoy spending hundreds of hours grinding or who are willing to spend money might well have a good time. However, if you are looking for a rewarding experience, then you should look elsewhere from the beginning.

1. 어설픈 규정과 아마추어 수준의 운영
아시아 규모의 대회임에도 불구하고 운영 프로세스와 규정은 동네 PC방 대회만큼이나 허술했습니다. 주최 측은 처음부터 명확한 경기 규정을 정하지 않아 스트림 딜레이나 채팅 확인과 같은 부분에서 믿기 힘든 허점을 노출했습니다. 이러한 전문성 부족은 친선 경기장을 논란과 비난이 난무하는 아수라장으로 만들었습니다.

2. 토사구팽식 처사와 명백한 차별
대중들의 분노가 극에 달한 시점은 베트남 선수인 Himass와 TanVuu에 대한 성급한 영구 제명 징계였습니다.

억울한 압박: 베트남 측이 사전에 먼저 문의하고 현지 주최측 대표의 동의를 얻었음에도 불구하고, 크래프톤은 입장을 바꾸어 가장 무거운 처벌을 내렸습니다.
내로남불(이중잣대): 한국 스트리머들도 유사한 행위를 했다는 증거가 나왔음에도 주최 측은 이를 묵인했습니다. 이는 명백한 편파 판정이자 중소 지역에 대한 차별을 보여줍니다.

3. 파국으로 치달은 위기 관리 능력
크래프톤은 불과 3일 만에 두 번이나 사과문을 발표해야 했지만, 그들의 행동은 사과와 달랐습니다. 관리 부실에 대한 책임을 인정하면서도 영구 제명 징계를 유지한 것은 오만함과 유저 무시를 보여주는 처사입니다. 마지막 날 경기를 전격 취소하고 상금을 균등 배분한 것은 스캔들로 얼룩진 대회를 황급히 덮으려는 비겁한 책임 회피에 불과합니다.

# **GOODBYE, PUBG. THIS IS NOT WHAT A COMPETITIVE GAME SHOULD BE.**

**Recommendation:** 👎 **Not Recommended**

PUBG was once one of the defining Battle Royale games. Unfortunately, the way the game is managed today has completely destroyed my trust in Krafton.

If you're thinking about buying PUBG or spending money on skins, **think twice.**

### **1. Unprofessional Esports Management**

Krafton's handling of the incident involving Vietnamese players **Himass and TanVuu** was extremely disappointing.

The punishments appeared rushed, the process lacked transparency, and the subsequent apology for being "too hasty" only made things worse.

Punish first. Investigate later. Apologize afterward.

That's not how a professional esports system should work.

What makes this even more frustrating is the perception of a **double standard**: Vietnamese players received severe punishments while issues involving the other side appeared to receive significantly less attention.

### **2. Cheaters Are Still Everywhere**

Krafton seems very quick to take action when a professional player becomes the center of a controversy.

But when it comes to actual cheaters in ranked matches?

Wallhacks. Aimbots. Players moving underground. Suspicious tracking and impossible shots.

The Anti-Cheat system often feels completely ineffective.

And when you report a cheater, you're frequently left with an automated response or a long wait with little meaningful feedback.

**Where is that same urgency when it comes to protecting ordinary players?**

### **3. Poor Optimization & Aggressive Monetization**

After years of updates, PUBG can still suffer from inconsistent FPS, bugs, performance issues, and problems introduced by new patches.

At the same time, the game continues pushing expensive skins and gacha-style monetization.

It's hard to justify spending money on cosmetics when fundamental problems remain unresolved.

---

## **FINAL THOUGHTS**

I used to genuinely enjoy PUBG.

But poor management, questionable competitive decisions, persistent cheating, inconsistent performance, and a lack of transparency have completely destroyed my trust in the game.

**I'm done.**

Uninstalling PUBG and moving on.

Why WoT Remains Uniquely Captivating
Deep Tactical Complexity: You cannot simply rush forward and expect to win. The game requires a solid grasp of armor mechanics, angling, side-scraping, and camo/spotting mechanics. Every map introduces a complex terrain puzzle, and each vehicle class (Light, Medium, Heavy Tanks, Tank Destroyers, and SPGs) serves a distinct, vital role.

Massive Historical Arsenal: Featuring over 600 armored vehicles from numerous nations meticulously modeled after historical blueprints and prototypes, WoT acts as a living military museum. Unlocking and piloting a Tier 10 behemoth delivers an immensely rewarding sense of achievement.

Polished Graphics and Sound Design: Wargaming’s Core engine delivers stunning visuals while remaining exceptionally well-optimized. The roar of engines, the screech of steel tracks biting into mud, and the thunderous boom of artillery combine to create absolute immersion.

                 Debunking the Myth: Is World of Tanks "Pay-to-Win"?
Many new or returning players casually label WoT as "Pay-to-Win" (P2W). However, looking objectively at the modern state of the game, WoT is fundamentally a "Pay-to-Progress" game, not P2W. Here is why:

1. The "Gold Ammo" Misconception

The Myth: You must spend real money (Gold) to buy high-penetration premium ammunition for an unfair advantage.

The Fact: For many years now, all premium rounds have been fully purchasable using Credits—the standard in-game currency earned simply by playing matches. Free-to-play (F2P) players can easily stock and fire these rounds just as much as anyone else.

2. Premium Tanks Don't Equal Automatic Victory

The Fact: A "Wallet Warrior" who buys an expensive Tier 8 premium tank yet lacks map awareness, fails to hide weak spots, and doesn't know how to angle will be sent back to the garage within the first 30 seconds by a skilled F2P player. In WoT, map intelligence and weak-spot knowledge vastly outweigh tank statistics. Furthermore, the absolute kings of Competitive play and Clan Wars are standard, tech-tree Tier 10 tanks (like the S. Conqueror, VZ. 55, Leopard 1, and IS-7) which cannot be bought outright.

3. Paying to "Save Time," Not to Buy "Skill"

Investing in a Premium Account or Premium Tanks simply accelerates your Credit and XP gains. It shortens the journey from Tier 1 to Tier 10 from months down to weeks. It cannot buy you tactical decision-making skills or improve your aim. Talent cannot be store-bought!

4. Wargaming Generosity toward F2P Players

Through regular events like Battle Passes, Marathons, Clan Campaigns, and personal missions, free-to-play gamers can consistently earn top-tier Premium tanks, premium days, and a mountain of resources that used to require real money.

Conclusion
World of Tanks is a challenging game that demands brainpower over button-mashing. If you enjoy deep military strategy, learning complex mechanics, and exercising patience, it is an absolute masterpiece worth diving into. Don't let outdated P2W myths keep you away from one of the most rewarding tactical shooters of the past decade.

Steam Review — Why I Don't Recommend Rust

The game itself is good. The problem is what Rust can do to your time.

Rust is undeniably a well-designed survival game. The building, PvP, raiding, progression, exploration, teamwork, and unpredictable player interactions can create some incredible gaming moments. However, after looking at the experiences repeatedly described by both positive and negative Steam reviewers, I think there is a much bigger issue worth warning new players about: Rust can consume an enormous amount of your time while constantly making you feel like you need to keep playing.

The biggest problem is the repetitive gameplay loop.

You gather resources, build a base, farm more resources, research, craft weapons, collect better loot, defend your base, raid someone else, get raided, lose your progress, rebuild, and repeat the entire process after the next wipe. At first this feels exciting because everything is new. Eventually, however, you can realize that you're repeatedly performing the same tasks just to get back to where you already were.

Rust has no real finish line.

There is always another wipe, another base to build, another resource run, another raid, another weapon to obtain, another enemy to fight, or another reason to log back in. That can make the game extremely difficult to put down. Instead of playing because you genuinely want to, you can eventually find yourself playing because you feel like you need to keep up.

The wipe system makes this even more frustrating.

You can spend countless hours building a base and accumulating resources, only for a raid or server wipe to erase much of that progress. Then you're expected to start over. For some players, that constant reset is the appeal. For others, it eventually becomes exhausting because hundreds of hours can amount to repeatedly rebuilding something that is never permanent.

The time commitment is the biggest hidden cost.

The $40 purchase price isn't necessarily the expensive part. Your time is. If Rust becomes a game you play 20–30 hours a week, that's roughly 1,000–1,500 hours per year. Those are hours that could have gone toward school, work, career development, exercise, family, friends, traveling, learning something new, or simply getting proper sleep.

Gaming is supposed to be entertainment. It becomes a problem when the entertainment starts competing with the rest of your life.

Rust can also create FOMO and an obligation to log in.

You may think, "I'll just take a few days off," but then you start worrying about falling behind, missing progression, getting raided, losing your base, or letting your teammates down. Eventually the thought becomes, "I have to check the base," or "I need to farm tonight." That's when a game can start feeling less like recreation and more like another responsibility.

The community can make the experience considerably worse.

Not every Rust player is toxic, and there are plenty of good people you'll meet. However, the game naturally encourages distrust, competition, raiding, betrayal, trash talking, door camping, griefing and revenge. Someone can spend hours specifically making your experience miserable simply because the game allows it. Losing a legitimate fight is one thing; having somebody repeatedly grief you after you've already lost everything is another.

Cheating is another major concern.

Rust has a long-standing problem with cheaters, and Facepunch has publicly reported hundreds of thousands of bans and millions of cheat reports. Even with anti-cheat measures and bans, encountering a suspected cheater can be especially frustrating in Rust because you're not simply losing one match—you can potentially lose hours or days of accumulated progress.

The high-stakes PvP system can also make ordinary gaming sessions unnecessarily stressful.

When you hear footsteps, see another player, hear gunshots, or notice someone building nearby, you're constantly evaluating whether you're about to lose everything. That tension is part of what makes Rust exciting, but after enough time it can become exhausting. You can spend a large portion of your gaming session worrying about protecting progress rather than actually enjoying yourself.

Then there is the financial side.

The game isn't necessarily limited to the initial purchase. Rust has DLC, cosmetics, skins, marketplace items and other ways to spend additional money. One skin might not seem like much, but $5 here, $10 there, another weapon skin, another building skin, another cosmetic, and eventually the total can become surprisingly large.

Be especially careful if you're someone who enjoys collecting things or feels compelled to have the newest or rarest items. Virtual items can become a very real expense.

The sunk-cost mentality is another trap.

You might eventually think, "I've already played 500 hours, so I can't quit now." Then 1,000 hours becomes 2,000. But the hours you've already spent don't require you to spend even more. If Rust is no longer improving your life or providing enough enjoyment to justify the time you're putting into it, you're allowed to walk away.

Ironically, some of the game's strongest positive qualities are also its biggest problems.

The persistent world, wipes, raiding, progression, competition, social interaction, resource gathering and unpredictability are what make Rust unique. They're also what can make it incredibly time-consuming and difficult to stop playing.

My biggest warning to new players is simple: don't judge Rust only by whether it's fun. Ask whether the amount of time it demands from you is worth it.

A game can be fun and still consume too much of your life.

A game can be well-made and still become unhealthy for you.

A game can have an amazing community experience while also exposing you to cheating, griefing and toxicity.

And a $40 game can eventually cost far more than $40 when you include DLC, skins, marketplace spending and, most importantly, hundreds or thousands of hours of your life.

If you can play Rust casually, set boundaries, avoid unnecessary spending and walk away whenever you want, that's one thing. But if you notice yourself sacrificing sleep, work, school, relationships, finances or real-world goals just to keep up with a virtual wipe cycle, it's probably time to reconsider.

Rust isn't necessarily a bad game. That's exactly why the warning matters. It's good enough to keep you coming back.

Don't let a game designed around endless progression convince you that you have an obligation to keep progressing. Your real life doesn't have a wipe button.

So let me start by saying this and getting it out of the way - I've got a lot of hours in this game.   It's the sort of game you put a lot of hours into.  I've got more than my money's worth and at times I've enjoyed it a lot.  It's not a bad game, the devs seem to genuinely care and I have high hopes for their future projects.

So why the negative review?  Because there is no option.  I can't in good conscience leave a positive review, because of all the things wrong with it.  Do I recommend it?  I guess.  But there are a LOT of caveats.

Slightly Relevant Story Time:

So let me tell you a story.  When I was in my teens, I spent a lot of hours in Frontier: Elite 2.  A LOT of hours.   In Frontier Elite 2 there were two main factions (all human descended) who had spread over a limited area of space, with clear cultural differences between the two.  Beyond that there was a sort of frontier bit and independent worlds, and then.... nothing.  Just planets.  So eventually I tooled up my trusty Tiger 2 with a gas scoop and mining rig and travelled 6 months into the beyond (since you needed to maintain the ship every year lest the engine lunch itself a 6 months journey was pushing my luck) to a pristine earth-like, fighing off a billion bandits to get there... somehow landed the ship on the planet and dropped the mining thingy.   And I felt like a real explorer!  Even though it was just green and the only thing I mined was water.  You see, it wasn't easy to do.  It needed planning, and serious execution.  No matter it was a waste of time in the end and I more or less immediately stopped playing.  Never mind that.  This game was made in 1993, after all.

What is NMS?

No question No Man's Sky is an extraordinary piece of engineering.   And it is awesome when you first scope out new planets and wotnot.   But (extremely grindy storyline aside) there is NO GAME.  It's a cosy base-builder.  Now a cosy ship-builder.   But where's the jeopardy?  Where's the mystery in the universe?

Procedurally Similar:

There are 3 races, who are EVERYWHERE.  There is nothing to distinguish them but their avatars.  They all have the same missions, the same station designs, the same... everything.    If you happen to stumble into a wormhole and end up 167,000 light years away then you'll find the same aliens and the same station design there too!  Wait - 167,000 light years away you say?  No matter, just step into the teleporter and you can go straight back to your base - even if you don't have a teleporter there!  All the above even applies to other galaxies... other dimensions!!!

Even better once you have teleported across inconceivable reaches of space and time, step outside the door and somehow your ship has instantaneously made its way across half the galaxy with its 100ly hyperdrive and no fuel left.   The same goes for your freighter.  In fact, once you have teleports set up you don't really need your ship to get anywhere, unless you're going to explore a bit.  

And as for exploration... there's lots to discover, but at the same time absolutely nothing to discover.   It's too easy.  It's all too easy - making landfall on a new planet should be an exciting adventure but it's so easy to jump / teleport / jump / teleport it becomes routine.  It all means that whilst you can explore in theory endlessly because there is no jeopardy there is no sense of achievement in doing so - which is exactly what exploration should be all about.

The Grind:

Honestly, once the novelty wears off, it's a grindy collecting things game.  Which has no idea what it wants to be.  Stung no doubt by the criticism of the lack of content on launch, they've proceeded to shove in every sci fi trope they can think of.  But it just doesn't hang together.  The main story of the game, with all its dark premonitions, even the character of the races, with the slightly threatening Vykeen or the very logical captain Korvax has the immersion broken completely when the NPCs emote cheerily at you just after threatening to rip your throat out.   I see what it tries to be.  It looks at titles like GTA or The Witcher and thinks hell a Pokemon min-game or a fishing challenge are just the ticket.  But they are jarring in this context.  And besides, what both those games had in the first place was an actual game.

So it's highly forgiving, and I get it, not everyone wants to be punished in a game.  Maybe this disconnect is just a product of how I like to play games.  I love Kenshi, and Rimworld, and Dwarf Fortress, and Star Sector, to name a few.  None of those games hold your hand.  But in a game about exploration should make the exploration bit a rewarding challenge, not routine.  And a lot of this is a product of procedurally generated play.  There's no real room for variation, which is the ultimate irony.  Because it's procedurally generated there is no need to go anywhere either - literally no need to go more than one jump from your home system, in order to see the whole game.  I see why the stations are all identical, so people can find things, but you have teleports, can't you have an explorable randomised station with teleports to get to crucial areas at the entrance? Every freighter, no matter what the freighter, is laid out identically.  

What I'd love to see (at least as an option):

 - If you teleport somewhere, you don't take your ship with you, and you can't instantly call your ship/freighter/whatever from another dimension whenever you want to.  If you want to go to a different system, you have to actually GO there.  No more calling ships or freighters over improbable distances.
- Sparser stations.  There shouldn't be a station in every system, and they shouldn't all have the same services.  Also they shouldn't all be identical.  It just doesn't feel like you're travelling anywhere at the moment.
- Sensible population distribution.  The nearer you get to the centre of the galaxy or whatever, the more stations there are.  Vykeen/Gek/Korvax zones of influence.  Potential border disputes.   I get it's all procedurally generated, but it must be tweakable.  This would all help immersion no end.  There should NOT be an identical districution of the same races 200k light years away.  It's just nonsensical.
- More races.   Where are all the humans?  where are all the races you see travellers being?  Where are they?
- Actually, where do all these Gek/Vykeen/Korvax live?  Do they have home systems, cities, whatever?  I suppose they all live at my settlements.  There you go.
- tougher planet distribution.  It should be HARD to find habitable worlds.  But they are everywhere in this game.  Again I get that people love finding the 3 legged tube creature from hell, but imagine how much more it would mean if you needed to travel through 10 systems to find it.
- Gas giants... WTF?  I know you wanted to do the pretty cloud bands, but seriously, read a science book, guys.  Or read 'The Algabraist'.  I was expecting a whole new game mechanic involving clouds or whatever, it could have given corvettes something else to do, but instead it's just another planet which is a waste really.

Chin Stroking:

I think part of the reason I'm writing the review is because I did put so many hours into this, to discover there is nothing at the end of it.  You think at some point you'll find something, but you never do.  You hope you'll round a corner where you find something new and amazing but it is never there.  The point is, I've wasted a lot of time on it.  Honestly, when I think about it I've spent more time on games I've given negative reviews to than I have on some of my favourites.  I think I am an optimist.  Don't get me wrong, the game is very good at killing hours and hours.  But then most games are.  Maybe I should just get out more instead.  I haven't even seen all the real world has to offer yet.

I’m very late to No Man’s Sky, and I’m genuinely glad I am.

I’d obviously heard all about the launch, the years of updates, and the reputation the game has built since then, but I’d never actually played it. Picking it up now feels like walking into a game that has had a decade to mature into what it always wanted to be.

And I am absolutely loving it.

What surprised me most is just how many different rabbit holes there are. I can start a session intending to progress the story, then suddenly I’m hunting crashed Sentinel ships, salvaging wrecks in deep space, building a Corvette, upgrading a freighter, setting up resource bases, trading between systems, fighting pirates, exploring some completely bizarre planet or just stopping because I saw something and thought “what the hell is that?”

That freedom is probably the thing I enjoy most. There is always progression, but the game rarely feels like it is forcing me down one path. I can optimise things when I feel like it, or completely ignore efficiency and disappear exploring for an hour.

I’m currently playing through the anniversary expedition that takes you through major stages of No Man’s Sky’s development over the years, and it has given me a whole new appreciation for what Hello Games has done with this game. Seeing mechanics, locations and ideas from different eras appear as you progress makes the transformation of NMS feel almost tangible.

There are still quirks. The UI can be obtuse, some mechanics are explained poorly, and occasionally the game decides that the laws of physics are merely a suggestion. But none of that has stopped me wanting to see what’s over the next hill, in the next system, or behind the next completely unnecessary upgrade I’ve decided I suddenly need.

I’ve played a lot of games where exploration is essentially travelling between map markers. No Man’s Sky is one of the few where exploration itself is the game.

If you like sci-fi, spaceships, upgrading gear, base building, exploration, trading, combat and games that are happy to let you wander off and create your own objectives, there is an absurd amount here.

I almost wish I had played it earlier.

Almost.

Because getting into No Man’s Sky now, with everything that has been added over the years, has been fantastic.

Highly recommended.

The best save-scumming simulator since Pathfinder: Kingmaker.

Baldur's Gate 3 looks fantastic and has all the ingredients of a great RPG: an excellent story, incredible voice acting, cinematic scenes, interesting classes, and plenty of quests. Unfortunately, the dice-based gameplay completely kills the experience for me.

So much of what you do comes down to dice rolls that even characters who are supposed to be good at something can constantly fail at it. What's the point of making a decision or building a character around certain strengths when the game can just decide that your character is suddenly incompetent?

Pros:

- Great story, graphics, and cinematic scenes that make you want to keep playing.
Probably the best voice acting I've ever heard in a game.
- Extensive and interesting class and character building.
- Lots of well-designed and memorable quests.
- The game encourages multiple playthroughs if you want to see everything.
- The amount of choices and possible outcomes is genuinely impressive.

Cons:

-The heavy reliance on dice rolls can make your character choices feel meaningless. Even with a high chance of success, you can still fail at something that should be routine.
-The constant failed rolls can turn serious situations into a comedy show. At some point you could put circus music under almost every encounter and it would fit.
-Some characters and dialogue feel more like edgy teenagers than actual adults, which can really hurt the immersion for me.
-The constant save-scumming becomes almost mandatory if you don't want important situations decided by an unlucky roll. This reminds me a lot of Pathfinder: Kingmaker.
-Loading saves repeatedly gets especially annoying when you already know that a failed roll was the only reason something went wrong.

Overall:

I understand why so many people consider Baldur's Gate 3 one of the best RPGs ever made. The production quality, voice acting, visuals, story, and character building are absolutely top-tier.

But personally, the dice system ruins too much of it for me. I prefer RPGs where character progression actually makes you reliably good at something. If my character has the skills for a task, I want that to matter instead of constantly watching him trip over his own feet because the game rolled a 1.

For me, Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age II are still much closer to what I want from an RPG. Baldur's Gate 3 is incredibly well-made, but the core gameplay philosophy simply isn't for me.

I have over 80 short, terrible poems composed by: 
a) Turning procedurally generated star system names into real words, as titles.
b) Picking a rhyme scheme that matches the number of bodies in the system.
c) Composing one line of the poem for each celestial body, trying to nod to its unique characteristics.
d) And being genuinely delighted by how someday, somewhere, somebody might find my Bad Poetry of No Man's Sky systems and be like, "What the actual fuck?"
e) Occasionally making a BaPIT (Bad Poetry Information Terminal) as a monument to the order in which the lines are meant to be read. Complete with free resources as a thank you for paying attention.

NMS gives you a thousand things to do. Then presses each one into your hand, looks you in the eye, and say, "But why? Why would you /do/ any of this?"

I make limericks out of five-body systems because, sometimes, I need to zone out and just *play* something to get through life. Making each system I find into a poem forces me to stay fully engaged in what I'm doing. I find planets, I name planets. But, I name *all* of them along a theme. And, I do it knowing, *knowing* something might happen and erase them all.

There's no achievement built into this game for Best Bad Poem.
The game is simply built in a way that fosters creativity.

It's a glorious thing for any game to achieve.
And, that's before getting into the redemption ark.

Ten years later, 
I finally remembered 
To mention it here.

Take care, and have fun out there. 
Because, if you're not, it's worth thinking about why.

The game used to be amazing. The sunk cost fallacy has kept me in this since 2020, I keep expecting it to get better, but every new update just makes things more frustrating. The Rift (battle pass) used to have a lot more variety in past years, but now it's mostly recolors of previous skins, or just bland, similar outfits. Overall, if I could go back to early DBD, I would in a heartbeat. Every now and then, a video game comes along that pulls me in a little deeper. I first encountered the Baldur’s Gate series in 1999, when I was 15 years old. I still remember meeting Khalid and Jaheira at the Friendly Arm Inn, venturing forth onto the Sword Coast, with places to explore, monsters to fight and a whole fantasy world to lose myself in. I thought it was amazing.

So when I started playing the new Baldur’s Gate III, more than 25 years after I first played the original, I knew I was going to be in for a treat. What I didn’t expect was quite how much of my life it would occupy. And I loved it. Not just playing it, but thinking about it. There were mornings when I woke up already pondering what I was going to do that evening. A quest I hadn’t finished. A conversation I needed to have. A decision I wasn’t sure about. A character whose reaction I was worried about.

That last bit is what really surprised me. Because Baldur’s Gate III is, well, a video game. You create a character, explore a fantasy world, fight monsters, collect magical items, gain experience and complete quests. The combat is based on Dungeons & Dragons, with dice rolls, spells, abilities and turn-based battles. But none of that mattered to me. The “people” did.

Larian Studios, the team who made the game, created an enormous fantasy world, but populated it with characters who feel much less like game mechanics and much more like people you happen to have met. My character was Elaris, an elven ranger. I recruited lots of characters along the way, but my regular party was Shadowheart, Gale and Karlach. I got to know them.

Shadowheart was dealing with faith, memory and identity. Gale was wrestling with ambition, pride and Mystra. Karlach was facing the terrifying possibility that the life she had escaped Hell to enjoy might be painfully short. These aren’t simply backstories that you read in a character menu. Their problems emerge gradually through conversations, quests and choices. You talk to them at camp. They comment on what you have done. They disagree with you. They reveal things. They change. And eventually, you care.

I found myself checking in on them like a good ol’ Tamagotchi. How are they doing? What are they thinking? Do they agree with what I’m about to do? Have I upset them? Should I really be doing this? And then there is romance. Elaris romanced Shadowheart from beginning to end, and this changed the game for me. Suddenly, her opinions carried even more weight. A difficult decision wasn’t simply about what Elaris thought was right. Elaris, or, well, I, was also wondering what Shadowheart would think. That is an extraordinary achievement in game design.

Google tells me that more than 400 people worked on the game for more than six years. There are more than 2,000 characters, around two million words in the script and more than 174 hours of cinematic content. And 248 actors provided not just voices, but motion capture for their characters too. Their gestures, expressions and movements became part of the performances.

Larian built the stage, wrote the script, designed the sets, created the music and lighting, and assembled an extraordinary ensemble of actors. And then they invited me on stage. I wasn’t simply controlling the main character. I was playing the main character. The other actors responded to me. They remembered things. They had their own motivations. Relationships developed. Stories changed. Sometimes I made choices I regretted. Sometimes the dice made them for me.

The result felt strangely close to real life. Not because I confused the game with reality. I didn’t. But because it captured something that most games don’t. The final battle wasn’t particularly interesting to me. The ending I cared about was the closing cinematics and conversations at the party we organised at camp to celebrate our victory and, more importantly, our friendship.

There they all were. The people Elaris had met, helped, argued with, fought alongside and loved. The characters who had started as random encounters and dialogue options had somehow become the company I had kept for nearly 200 hours of gameplay. And then they went their separate ways.

Elaris and Shadowheart got their cottage by the lake. Karlach and Wyll returned to Avernus. Gale made peace with Mystra. Minsc and Boo carried on being Minsc and Boo. Jaheira and Halsin went off to do their groovy druid thing. Astarion continued his blood sucking business. Volo, presumably, continued getting himself into trouble.

Today, I closed the game. For now, at least, I’m done. Maybe I’ll return in a few years as somebody else, making different choices, joining a completely different ensemble and discovering an entirely different outcome to the game. Or maybe not.

What I’ll remember most about Baldur’s Gate III isn’t the battles, the quests or even the enormous world Larian created. It will be the people I spent all those hours with. The strange thing about a game like this is that, for all the technology and craftsmanship involved, what ultimately makes it memorable is something very old fashioned. Spending time with other people and caring about what happens to them. Except, of course, these aren’t real people. They’re people in a video game.

Congratulations, Larian. Legendary stuff.

Apex is an amazing game buried under some incredibly frustrating decisions.

The movement and gunplay are still elite. Sliding, wall-bouncing, climbing, strafing, and combining abilities with gunplay makes Apex feel more mechanically satisfying than most shooters. When you have a good match, there are few FPS games that feel this good.

But then you play for a few hours and remember why the game can be so damn annoying.

The matchmaking can feel miserable. You can have one decent game and suddenly you're fighting players who look like they haven't missed a shot since 2019. Meanwhile, your teammates can range from genuinely good to people who seem to have forgotten they're playing a team game.

Solo queue is especially painful. You can spend 15 minutes looting just for your teammate to launch themselves into a 1v3, die instantly, and leave.

The ranked system can also make the grind feel exhausting. You can play well for multiple games, lose one bad fight, and suddenly feel like all that progress meant nothing.

And honestly, Apex has one of the highest "I should stop playing" to "one more game" ratios I've ever seen.

The game is frustrating, sweaty, sometimes unfair, and occasionally feels like it actively hates you.

But you still queue again.

Final verdict:

Gameplay: 9/10
Movement: 10/10
Gunplay: 9/10
Teamplay: 7/10
Matchmaking: 5/10
Solo queue experience: 4/10
Addiction: 11/10
Overall: 8/10

First thing to note before I start the review, I don't recommend this on lower end PCs. My gpu even on the lowest settings only hits about 30 FPS. Which is not the best but it's tolerable enough for me. It remains steady and constant though, never drops below it.

Alright review time. I already love this game, I literally finished the most recent expedition on my Xbox save. Which that save has like 300 hours on it with tens of millions of units. Almost 100 million. But for the PC, I chose to do a fresh restart. 

Gameplay - Very addictive. I woke up randomly at 1 am and played till 6 am as of writing this review. This game is a sandbox and there's a lot you can do. Go fishing? Yup, you can. Space exploration, though, is the primary focus. You'll end up exploring planet to planet, star system to star system. With a wide variety of planets to explore and various wonders to find. There's a lot of content to this game that it's amazing how different it is today than it was back in 2016. 
If you're not a big fan of survival grinding games though, there is a creative mode option. There is also a settings for difficulty customization if you're interested in that too. No? Well might not be your game then.

Story - For a first playthrough, it left me speechless and curious the whole time. I am an explorer though in most games, so this game was just perfect for me. You spawn in, you got no idea where you are or even who you are. The story follows you finding yourself as well as helping out an alien named Artemis. I won't spoil the rest though, that's for you to discover yourself. The story is said to be around 30 hours long, but it could take longer if you don't know what you're doing. 

Cons - This game requires patience, to which I have, but a lot of players tend to not have nowadays. As stated above too, the framerate on older end PCs is not the best. There is stutters on older PCs. I'm unsure how this game runs on a better gpu, but I did read some reviews online that this game is not optimized well. Frankly, I think it runs better than House Flipper, but that's just me. Also it's very easy to burn yourself out on this game. With the various activities available to you, it could be overwhelming at first. I suggest trying to space out your time (no pun intended). 

Summary - Awesome space game great for players who are curious and love exploring. It's got survival elements, variety of difficulties from normal to a PERMADEATH mode, and you can build ships called Corvettes too. This game gets updated a lot and Hello Games is one of few indie studios that respects their player base.
