[h1][b]Helldivers 2, the game you keep returning to.[/b][/h1]
[hr][/hr]
[h1]The short version[/h1]
[b]Is the gameplay still fun after 200+ hours?[/b] Absolutely.

[b]Is the monetisation fair?[/b] Yes.

[b]Is the game perfect?[/b] No.

[b]Will I keep coming back?[/b] Definitely.

[b]Final score:[/b] 9/10


[h1]The full review[/h1]
Helldivers 2 absolutely blew up shortly after release.

One of the things Helldivers 2 does best is turning complete chaos and destruction into comedy. Accidental team kills are rarely just frustrating. More often than not, everyone ends up laughing about them, especially when they involve an unnecessarily large explosion.

The game is also incredibly cinematic. Between the explosions, desperate last stands and ridiculous ragdoll moments, even an ordinary mission can suddenly turn into something memorable.

[h3]The community is what makes it special[/h3]
There is something about the atmosphere of Helldivers 2 that is difficult to explain.

The community completely embraces the ridiculous Super Earth patriotism, and it makes you feel like part of something much bigger than your own squad.

The entire playerbase almost feels like one giant guild. Everyone contributes towards the same worldwide objectives, even though most players will never directly interact with each other.

That feeling is reinforced every time you drop onto a planet. Somehow, the same music still manages to make the next mission feel important.
After more than 200 hours, that soundtrack still gets me hyped when the hellpods launch.

[h3]Three very different enemies[/h3]
You currently fight three very different factions, and each changes the way you approach the game.

The Terminids give you the classic swarm experience, with large numbers of enemies constantly trying to overwhelm you in melee.

The Automatons mostly engage at range, filling the battlefield with red laser fire and forcing you to make much greater use of cover and positioning.

The Illuminate sit somewhere between the two, mixing swarms of close range enemies with dangerous ranged units.

Each faction encourages different equipment and tactics, and that variety is a big reason the game has remained interesting for me for this long.

[h3]Freedom over perfect balance[/h3]
The balancing is another area that continues to surprise me.

The weapons, stratagems and armour are far from perfectly balanced, but somehow that rarely seems to matter.

There is nothing stopping you from bringing a mech, tank or the same powerful loadout into every mission, yet players still experiment because different equipment is simply fun to use.

Helldivers 2 gives you a huge toybox and mostly lets players create their own chaos.

[h3]Content and monetisation[/h3]
The game has grown massively over the years.

New weapons and equipment are primarily unlocked through Warbonds, which work somewhat like permanent battle passes.

They cost premium currency, but that currency can also be earned naturally while playing. In my experience, by the time I want another Warbond, I have usually earned a large portion of the required currency without deliberately farming for it.

Because of that, the monetisation has never felt particularly restrictive to me.

[h3]Where it falls short[/h3]
The biggest criticism I hear from more active players is the development pace.

Players who spend more time in the game often seem to run out of new content, and major updates have also earned a reputation for bringing plenty of bugs along with them.

I have personally reached the point where every ship upgrade is unlocked, and it has been that way for quite a while. I basically have nothing left to spend samples on, which makes them feel almost meaningless once you reach the end of that progression system.

I have also had missions where players disconnect one by one until I am suddenly left alone. On the higher difficulties, losing your entire squad like that can quickly turn a successful mission into a frustrating experience.

Most of the other bugs I have encountered have been far less serious and often just ended with someone being launched into orbit through ridiculous ragdoll physics.

[h3]Verdict[/h3]
Helldivers 2 is one of those rare games that somehow keeps pulling me back in.

The shooting is satisfying, the three factions feel genuinely different, the amount of equipment encourages experimentation, and the game constantly turns disasters into comedy.

But what really separates it from other co-op shooters is the community. The shared war, the Super Earth roleplay and the feeling that everyone is contributing towards the same ridiculous cause give the game a personality that is difficult to replicate.

It is not perfect. Content can arrive slowly, updates can introduce bugs, and long term players can eventually run out of meaningful progression.

But after more than 200 hours, I still get excited when the hellpods launch.

Balance can be inconsistent, and some Killers, perks, or strategies can feel much stronger than others.
Matchmaking and overall match quality can be pretty inconsistent.

Some matches can feel more frustrating than fun, especially when your team isn’t coordinated.

If all you want is a game where you can drive tanks, fly combat jets, and play a few matches with friends now and then, I’d suggest you pause for three minutes before deciding whether to jump into the rabbit hole called 《War Thunder》.
The wildest thing about this game is that it actually has plenty to offer. From boxy-looking WWII tanks to the steel behemoths of the Cold War, all the way up to modern main battle tanks, fighter jets, helicopters and even coastal naval vessels. You can start out in a beat-up little tank and work your way up until you’re sitting in machines you could never touch in real life. Many vehicles feature meticulously detailed models, weapons, ammunition, cockpits and historical backstories. You might even find yourself studying armor-piercing rounds for the first time just to master a tank, wondering why shells from the same 120mm gun can perform so differently. Before you know it, you’ll be researching aircraft radar, missiles, engines and flight performance. Eventually you realize you only meant to play a game, yet here you are reading military references.
Trouble starts once you get the thought: I need to finish this tech tree. The tech trees in 《War Thunder》 are not designed for casual vehicle testing. They pose a brutally honest question: Do you actually have the time? Without a premium account, research gains can make you feel less like you’re gaming and more like clocking a second shift for the company after work. You finish a good match, check your research points and think you’ve made solid progress. Then you look at the cost for the next vehicle and see that hard-earned XP barely moves the progress bar. You start calculating average research per battle, how much you can grind per hour, how many days it would take playing four hours a day, or eight hours a day. Before long you’ve worked out roughly how many days it will take to complete the whole line.
Then the grim realization hits: it’s not just one tank ahead of you, it’s an entire tech tree. You finally research a new vehicle and feel a flicker of joy, only to see the next one waiting, as if saying, “Congratulations. That was just the warm-up.” A premium account eases the pain somewhat — it just changes the feeling from “this feels like a second job” to “this second job might be manageable.”
And the grind isn’t even the most infuriating part. The real madness is the balance.
You’ll find a vehicle that looks decent on paper, only to spawn into battle and face opponents from a completely different era. Some tanks have armor thick as a safe, while others seem built from cardboard. Sometimes you won’t even understand what killed you before a shell punches straight through your tank from front to rear. Gradually you learn to read battle ratings, ammo types and weak points. But knowing all that doesn’t guarantee victory. Survival sometimes depends less on your skill and more on what match you get placed into.
Worse still, this imbalance shifts constantly between vehicles. A tank you thought was unbeatable can turn into a rolling coffin in the next match, with a new map, enemies or engagement range. That’s when you learn the classic line: “It’s not that this tank is bad; it’s the matchmaking.” Play two more battles, though, and you’ll think: *Damn, the tank really is garbage.
Aircraft have it even rougher. You spend ages learning takeoffs, climbs and target locking, finally feeling confident. Then you lift off and get shot down instantly by a missile you barely saw coming from far away. You dig deeper and figure out the enemy spotted you ten seconds earlier. Next match you study radar. The one after that, missiles. Then aerial maneuvers. This game lures you in one lesson at a time. You think you’re piloting vehicles, but really you’re cramming nonstop.
Let’s not forget server issues. Sometimes you’re in a head-on tank duel, your crosshair locked on the weak spot, mouse clicked — only for lag to make your shot feel like it hit thin air. By the time you register what happened, your barrel is blown off. You’re left wondering whether it was your bad aim, your internet, the server, the game itself, or just a bad day. After the match, you watch the death replay and sink into existential confusion: *How exactly did I die just now?
Even so, the game has a dangerously addictive quality. You can maneuver a tank around a hillside, lie hidden in grass, wait for an enemy to expose their side, and send them straight back to the hangar with one shot. You can dive out of the clouds in a plane, lock onto your target, and shoot them down in a high-speed pass.
You might even hear a nuclear strike alert mid-battle, watch the enemy nuke carrier take off, and react without thinking: climb to intercept. You cripple the enemy bomber’s wing, only to get shot down by its escorts. But the nuke never lands. The post-battle screen pops up:
“Congratulations, Atomic Peace. Only 1.3% of players have earned this medal.”
Staring at your wrecked plane and that badge, all of a sudden your death doesn’t feel like a waste.
This game is strange like that. A terrible match can make you furious enough to uninstall it. But a perfect kill, a miraculous comeback, or a successful nuke interception can make all those hours of grinding feel worthwhile.
So if you ask whether I recommend it? My honest answer: absolutely not. Skip it if you lack free time. Think twice if fairness matters a lot to you. Stay away if you hate repetitive grinding. If watching a research bar creep forward slowly raises your blood pressure, quit while you’re ahead.
The scariest thing about 《War Thunder》 is not that it’s boring. It’s that even with all the things that make you want to scream, after getting blown up, you still click “Join Battle.” You start in a rickety little vehicle, unlock bigger tanks, then jet aircraft, then modern armor, machines you once only saw in military videos. Before you know it, hundreds of hours are gone. You catch yourself calculating: “If I play four hours every day, how much longer until I reach the end?” At that point, you’ve already lost.
True 《War Thunder》 players are not trapped by the game. They keep coming back, tempted by that research bar that is always almost full.
So again, I do not recommend it. Especially not for people who tell themselves they’ll “just play casually.” Once you start playing seriously, your thoughts shift from “What even is this game?” to “Why is this armor-piercing shell so powerful?” to “What’s wrong with this battle rating?” until you’re sitting at your PC at four in the morning, crunching numbers for how many more research points you need.
If you’ve read all the way here, my advice is simple: run. You still have time. But if you’ve already started playing… well, nothing can be done. Good luck reaching the top of your favorite tech tree.

Short review - This game is really good, but there are quite a bit of complaints and concerns. Optimization is so good I could probably play Warframe on an olive garden tablet. 

XL review - This game, if you are able to give it some love and care, is absolutely all about rewarding that love and care. I say this, because Warframe isn't simply a game you can just jump into, and continue to do just that. As you progress through the game, you're going to run into more and more mechanics, game modes, power ups, nuances, side objectives, side grinds, items and resources you need for many things as you play, and that's the amazing aspect of it. The grind. Being to able to achieve all of it, knowing how to do all of it, optimizing doing all of it, it's all very rewarding to know in terms of progression, and how much you feel like a real fan of this game. However... One aspect of this game requires a button combo more powerful than any alt fire, melee attack, character ult... Alt + Tab.

Google, reddit, youtube, the friend who's been playing so long that they've farmed more 75% off premium currency coupons than you've farmed material to craft your first 10 warframes, it's all going to be ESSENTIAL. So essential that I firmly believe nobody is ever going to do a lot of content in this game without needing any of this level of guidance.  anything from finding a crafting material, a certain place I need to be do something so specific, game events, world bosses, game modes, bounties, upgrades for weapons and gear, quest required items, will most likely require you to completely stop in your tracks out of cluelessness and look to the 2nd monitor for guidance due to so many aspects in this game being so non linear, or simply unexplained. You know how in most MMORPG'S or games in general with steps you need to take to to finish something, there are not only steps, and visual guidance, there are sub-steps, tutorials on how to do these things prior to being dropped into the game? Or things simply named after what it is you're looking for, and options to click on something you need and be teleported to where you find it or something? Remember when you were trained for you first fast food/barista job by a manager who can't remember where the ice machine is and you're the one showing them how to properly stock cups a week later? Yeah, figuring things out feels like that at times. 

Thankfully, before you start to encounter this beast of blindness, there are a good amount of hours of playing the game. Fun grinds that lead you into beefing up your frame and weapons, experiencing one of the most fluid and buttery movement system in any video game out there, the absolutely beautiful and engaging narrative found in the main quest line, the amazing, involved and caring dev team, the satisfaction of crafting new frames, learning you can't type 67 in the game chat, relic gambling, and just grand old times to have with a friend or two. But once you leave the beginner realm, you are either going to want to drop the game out of sheer confusion, or full send it to become a true veteran. I've been walking this path after the beginner phase and I have been little brothered by all the powers that be to learn how to do so much like how to do it, when to do it, where to do it, what i do with it, why i do it, knock knock who is it? And I understand as to why there are such dedicated veterans to Warframe. The reward in knowing. Not only to just be able to one day navigate it by yourself, but to be able to one day be the one who teaches it. The beauty in all of this, is how without the help of someone who's been here a long time, there wouldn't exist this special connection to the games community that Warframe conjures up due to the level of guidance everyone hands each other. With this level of complexity in this game it really allows you to appreciate the ones that came before, how knowledge is handed down further and further to the new pipeline of players coming in. The wiki, the youtube guides, the forums, even the guy on Warframe market place who told me he blatantly scammed me out of 30 platinum because I don't know any better. it's all player built, and you become a core part of that index as you play and it is becoming an awesome feeling to jump into things without needing help, or helping someone along the way.
Now you can argue that I'm looking to deep into this. You can easily see that as bad guidance in a game, fair enough. But trust me, play it yourself and find out how you feel. it's worth your time.

During your Warframe journey, this one word will be all you have to describe certain experience's and oh what's that? you think that's just a widely agreed upon opinion of a certain game mode? certain map layout? certain way of doing things? look closer, bub. That's not just something you dislike or can't stand, not just something you think the game could do without, that is a hill. A hill that will be died on to a Digital Extreme. In Warframe there are very common opinions you will come across and the one I have the biggest gripe with is game modes. Game modes nobody likes are in every video game though, you simply avoid them, call it a day, never deal with it until maybe you have an achievement that will require you to play some of it, but then you're done with it forever. Maybe you in a group of friends just don't like the mode but buckle down to play a couple games sometimes. Fair enough right? Well what if I told you there was a game that shoved those unfavorable game modes or repeatable quest down your throat from time to time? put them in the way of mandatory progress? slot them into the weekly resetting grinds for that one thing you really really want that is difference from hitting like a postage stamp to making you the strongest person in the building at your local Dutch Bros? or almost for no reward at all, just as a stepping stone to the big one? Warframe does that exact thing EVERY weekly reset, and with annual events. It's an issue having to deal with the passage of time unfortunately, but also a bit of philosophy that is kind of a double edged sword. There are about 30 game modes in Warframe, and other unique things to do in the open worlds, and of all those game modes in Warframe, to most players, at a time, there are around 3 or 4 modes that when you select them to play it's like "Hell yeaaa run it up" and for the other stuff, there's a sigh, some sighs deeper than others. While you can hear hundreds of thousands of players sigh in unison if you put your ear to the ground, there's the 2 people you can't hear cheering. But they're there. And you know what, that thing 9/10 dentists hate, there's 1 dentists who brushes his teeth with wasabi, therefore Warframe is going to KEEP wasabi. And in this universe, that means YOU will have to dip your soft bristle's into some wasabi and brush because it's all you can do. It sucks to have to play some of these modes to get the last couple of pieces of the puzzle I need, but y'know? it isn't forever I suppose. And this isn't just game modes. This is equipment, crafting, general content, and events. All this being said, Warframe of any free to play rpg, is my standout. I do not play war thunder because I like war thunder. I play it because I like tanks. But this game pushes that tolerance often. If you're looking for tank battles, just know a forced part of the game is having air support bombing you every other match with little counter since often team planes will be off doing the same thing to easy enemy targets (keyword "easy", not "important" targets). There's a multitude of other reasons I couldn't suggest the game other reviews have covered (most being likely right ie, AI slop, pay2win, miserable imbalance, extreme grind, spiteful devs, insufferable community) But this is the biggest one for me to not wanna suggest it to anyone curious about it. I ignored this game for years before caving in, and I feel all my concerns were 100 percent valid despite it seeming like a perfect option for my interest. If I didn't like tanks and planes, this game would have zero appeal to me. I only play because sadly there isn't anything else like it, and perhaps you may end up the same, just know you're gonna need a high tolerance for frustration and outright bitter misfortune. If you want a picture of the future this game has for you, Imagine a bomb stamping on your tank. Forever.

If you have ever wanted to trade your free time for pure, unadulterated engineering bliss, Satisfactory is the game for you. Coffee Stain Studios managed to create an incredibly satisfying blend of open-world exploration, base building, and complex logistics, all wrapped up in a beautiful, vibrant alien world.

What Makes It Special:
Incredible Scale & Freedom: Moving from hand-crafting basic iron plates to building sprawling, multi-story industrial complexes linked by trains, drones, and endless conveyor belts feels incredibly rewarding. The sense of progression is top-tier.

Gorgeous Open World: Planet MASSAGE-2(AB)X isn't randomly generated—it's a handcrafted, stunning map full of lush biomes, hidden caves, unique flora, and dynamic wildlife that makes exploring as fun as building.

Smooth Controls & First-Person Immersion: Unlike top-down factory games, the first-person perspective makes you feel fully grounded in your creation. Building in 3D adds a whole new layer of architectural creativity.

Co-Op Goodness: Running a mega-factory with friends—divvying up tasks like power grid management, exploration, and resource routing—is easily one of the best multiplayer experiences available.

Polished Polish: The performance, quality-of-life features (like smart splitters, blueprints, and zoop building), and humor from FICSIT Inc. make the gameplay loop buttery smooth and endlessly charming.

The Verdict
Whether you're an optimization perfectionist who loves balancing efficiency down to the decimal, or someone who just wants to build cool structures and ride hyper-tubes across mountains, Satisfactory delivers hundreds of hours of high-quality fun.

I installed this game on Steam to leave this review. I was playing this game for years (started around the end of beta) using the WG launcher. I have over 70k battles on my main account, and this is what I have to say:

Avoid this game if you don't want to suffer. This was once one of the best MMO games; now it's just a quick cash grab from the decreasing player base of a dying game. It's still playable (barely), and it will be for the next few years. As long as the player base will pay for premium tanks and loot boxes. 

Players have been super toxic for years now, and after the merge with the RU server, it is much harder to communicate because of all those players from the east using the Cyrillic alphabet, and they play super weird compared to EU veterans. They either push mindlessly or camp on the red line.

In the past the game was more or less balanced, but after years of power creep and hundreds of premium tanks, each one is stronger than the previous ones. This game lost all resemblance of balance a long time ago. There are more premium tanks in this game than normal, F2P machines. 

Every new line of tanks they introduce is stronger than previous ones, and after some time it loses its relevance in one of two ways. Either a new stronger line is introduced or it gets nerfed to the ground.

After all those years WG can't fix basic problems with this game like bad matchmaking, unbalanced tanks, bad map designs, and terrible map rotation.

This game was fun, like, 8-10 years ago; now it's just bad. Matches that take 3-4 minutes and end in 15-0 or 15-1 are super common and most of the time frustrating. Most of the time, one bad player or bad play by a good player turns into a tide that sweeps the whole team in a matter of 2-3 minutes. Sometimes it's not even the player's fault because RNG in this game is a joke. You get +/- 25% to penetration and damage values, so a killing shot can end with the enemy alive on 10 hp when he should be dead. On top of that, there is terrible accuracy RNG that completely ignores accuracy values of tanks that you play with. Very often guns with terrible accuracy hit more often than those with laser like values.

Last year WG introduced tier 11 because they ran out of ideas to milk players only with tier 10 tanks and tier 8 premiums. Most of those tanks (if not all) are created from thin air. Nothing about historical accuracy is there. Sometimes it looks like WG used AI to create them.

Lootboxes situation also got out of control. For years WG offered lootboxes on Christmas / end of the year period and they had a preaty good value for money, but over last few years we get lootboxes every 2 months and their value did go to the ground.

If I can make a short description of WG moves in the last few years, it would be crazy ass monetization, power creep, and an unbalanced game with super unstable servers that lag very often for no reason. The ruleset or whatever it is called in D&D completely runied the experience for me as a wizard during our 4-player co-op playthrough.

It is genuinely not fun to waste all your spell points and/or actions on misses, and deal single digit damage in three turns, just to die to a single strike from one sneaky enemy. During our playthrough the general impression was that the meta is damage, no matter the fact that the game has a wide variety of interesting spells. It's just not worth it to try to stun an enemy for 1 turn and miss, instead of trying to actually damage it. Waste of potential.

The game was also full of technical problems. Bard trying to give us buffs for dialogues, the game confirming it at first, and then not adding the bonus to the final throw value - these sorts of bugs ruined tense moments. 
Constant desyncs and crashes during several phases of the game also ruined the experience. We finished only because of 1 member like the game out of four. Shame.

To be fair, the game looks good and most of the characters have an interesting story. Music also stands out.

It really says a lot about the gaming industry that this could became a GoT. If you are not a fan of the ruleset, I would say you should play Divinity Original Sin 2 instead of this. It was developed by the same studio and it is much more enjoyable.

Rust is one of those games that can be incredibly frustrating and incredibly fun at the same time. The basic idea is simple: you start with almost nothing, gather resources, build a base, craft weapons and tools, and try to survive against both the environment and other players.

The best part of Rust is the unpredictability. You can spend hours building up your base and collecting gear, only to have another player come along and completely ruin your plans. At the same time, you can have some hilarious interactions with strangers, form alliances, raid other bases, or somehow survive situations that seem impossible.

The building and progression systems are satisfying, and there's a huge amount to learn. However, the game definitely has a steep learning curve. New players can get destroyed pretty quickly, and losing hours of progress to a raid can be extremely discouraging. The grind can also become repetitive if you're playing for long periods.

Overall, Rust is a great survival game if you enjoy high-risk gameplay, competition, teamwork, and the feeling that anything can happen. It's definitely not for everyone, but if you can handle losing everything occasionally, the stories and experiences you get out of the game can make it worth it.

I wanted to love Satisfactory. Sincerely.
I like building systems. I like optimization. I like figuring out how things interact. I love games that reward exploration, experimentation, and understanding.
On paper, Satisfactory was the game for me.
Instead, I have rarely played a game that does such a poor job of teaching the player its own basic language.
My problem is not that Satisfactory is complicated. Complicated can be fun. My problem is that it repeatedly hides simple, foundational rules behind trial-and-error, vague feedback, and unintuitive interaction design, then seems to expect the player to treat discovering those rules as gameplay.
That is not meaningful experimentation.
Outer Wilds is built around exploration and discovery. The Witness teaches its rules by letting you observe, hypothesize, test, and understand. In those games, not knowing something is part of the experience. Your confusion creates curiosity.
Satisfactory gives you a deterministic engineering system where A + B = C, then somehow fails to explain what A and B actually do.
Early examples from my playthrough:
The Equipment Workshop was hidden in a menu category I would never intuitively associate with it.
Portable Miners are crafted as equipment, manually equipped, and deployed by hand, while Miner Mk.1s are buildings with conveyor outputs. The game barely establishes the distinction.
Power was especially awful. I naturally assumed that once a machine was connected to a powered network, I could continue the connection through it. Nope. Early machines are electrical endpoints. Power Poles are the distribution nodes. That is a completely reasonable rule — once somebody tells you the rule. The game instead rewarded me with “No empty Power Line connections” and left me to reverse-engineer what that meant.
Production lines and power networks are two completely separate topologies. Again: simple concept. Explain it once and I understand it forever. Instead I spent far too long figuring out something that should have taken one tutorial sentence.
Then I discovered conveyor belts have fixed direction and two sections built toward each other cannot simply connect. The arrows apparently communicate this, but the game never taught me that those arrows represent a hard connection rule. So another completely reasonable action fails until you learn yet another tiny undocumented convention.
Then there are Constructors, Smelters, recipes, manual buffers, inputs, outputs, and automation chains. None of this is intellectually difficult. That is precisely why it is so irritating. I kept hitting walls, asking “what obvious thing am I missing?”, learning the rule, and immediately understanding it.
Over and over.
That tells me the problem is not complexity in the game. The problem is communication.
The early game should teach players how to play the game. Instead I got a tiny tutorial and frustration for hours.
Satisfactory seems content to hand you fifty puzzle pieces with minimal explanation of how they interact and call the resulting confusion “experimentation.”
And that actively damaged my desire to explore.
Once I finally got one production line working, I did not think, “Awesome, let’s go find another iron deposit and expand!”
I thought, “This finally works. I am not touching it.”
That is catastrophic design for a game built around expansion.
The game conditioned me to associate experimentation with the possibility of another obscure interaction rule or another piece of UI nonsense. Expansion started feeling like a bullshit tax instead of a reward.
That is the exact opposite of what a sandbox should accomplish.
I also find the early narrative motivation incredibly weak. Games do not need huge cinematic stories, but they need something that makes me care about progression. The Entropy Centre, Outer Wilds, Inscryption, The Stanley Parable, even something like Road 96 all give me reasons to wonder what happens next.
Satisfactory's early motivation felt like:
Make thing so you can make machine that makes more thing so you can unlock machine that makes next thing.
Apparently, for a lot of people, making the factory bigger is sufficient motivation. That's fine. Clearly this game has an enormous and passionate audience.
But I cannot understand why the onboarding gets such a free pass.
And before somebody says “you just need to play longer,” that is part of the problem.
I should not need 20 or 30 hours before a game begins justifying my time. Superliminal is basically finished in four hours and I would call it an S-tier game because nearly every minute earns its existence.
A long game does not get an interest-free loan on my attention.
The most frustrating part is that I can see the game I thought I was buying underneath all of this. Huge factories. Efficiency problems. Logistics. Optimization. Creative construction. Increasingly ridiculous technology. I can absolutely understand how that could become addictive.
But Satisfactory has done such a poor job of getting me there that I have gone from wanting to love it to actively resenting it.
I even came back for a second attempt months after initially bouncing off it because the reviews were so overwhelmingly positive that I assumed I must have missed something.
I kept giving the game the benefit of the doubt.
Maybe I skipped a tutorial.
Maybe I misunderstood the intended playstyle.
Maybe trial-and-error is supposed to be the point.
Maybe the next unlock is where it clicks.
Eventually the game has to participate in its own defense.
I do not need a game to hold my hand. I need it to teach me its grammar so that I can use that grammar creatively.
Teach me the foundational rules, then leave me alone and let me experiment.
Satisfactory instead repeatedly made me experiment just to discover the foundational rules.
That is tedious, not deep.
Maybe the later factory game is incredible. Maybe people with 500 hours genuinely adore optimizing conveyor networks for their own sake. Good for them.
But at this point I would rather spend my free time playing something that makes me curious, makes me laugh, tells me something interesting, gives me meaningful choices, or simply respects my time.
Satisfactory has mostly made me ask:
“Why the fuck wasn’t that explained?”
Over and over and over again.
FICSIT?
At this point, FUCKIT.
Not recommended.

Hauntingly beautiful, deeply endearing, and above all hard to describe, No Man's Sky is a survival sandbox crafting game set in an expansive multiverse from out of a 70s pulp sci-fi novel. While the game has direction, no doubt, most of the actual enjoyment to be had in No Man's Sky is the result of finding your own fun. The game throws a colossal amount of stuff at the player and all of it is expansive and rich with content, and is no doubt daunting to a newcomer. Before you know it, you'll have a freighter and a stockpile of ships and weapons, you'll have a sprawling fleet of ships to manage and bases and settlements to build, and you'll have craft of all sorts to invest in and upgrade. 

This is not a narrative-heavy experience, but the small glimpses of empathy you can have in this world as you begin to learn more about the creatures who call it home are genuinely wonderful and tragic all at once. An item I crafted became part of a small quest which led me to a megafauna in deep space, who leads a guided meditation with the player character to learn about its role in the fleet it was joining, revealing a deep and earnest love not just for the universe the game is set within, and not just with the highs of the speculative fiction genres it touches upon, but also for the community this game has more than rightfully earned after a decade of continual improvements. 

When No Man's Sky launched in 2016, Sony had dropped the Joe Danger team into a predicament, having been strongarmed into effectively telling everyone that this would be a game that would feel the rain upon your skin for you if you wanted, when what they had made, so long ago, was a pretty albeit simple base building survival game with a lot of area to build in. Since then, they have expanded the game in all directions, making something that at once feels both like the natural conclusion of games like Minecraft, Terraria, and Rust, but also to CRPGs and MMOs of old. 

You can get all the way into the tiniest nuances of so many aspects of the game, build out a T-shaped experience of diving deep into a single aspect such as the creature taming, commanding a fleet, trading goods, fighting enemy craft, or just exploring, or if you want to master the individual aspects, you are more than welcome to with a game that is prepared to be beaten and replayed hundreds of times, and has a truly eye-watering amount of activities to partake in with no additional price tags. 

I cannot recommend No Man's Sky highly enough. Hello Games has produced a truly generational work of procedural game design in a field that felt solved since 2011. It's not a game for people looking to complete an experience or "see the ending", but rather for people who like the design philosophy of an MMO without the snags and burrs and monetization schemes one would expect from the genre, even if the game just barely grazes it at times.

No mans sky seems to be asymptomatically approaching becoming a good game. Hello games continues to add interesting concepts and systems on top of very flawed bones.

I’m just going to list some major issues. The game is never challenging in an interesting way. Difficulty is added exclusively with grinds. Everything feels same-y. Every system will have a set of identical features randomly tossed a bunch of barely distinguishable planets. Every planet must have all the resources available to survive there easily (taking the form of bright glowing plants), so preparation is almost never necessary. All space stations have the same internal structure with a few color changes. The universe teems with spaceships and life, but none of them do anything or matter.

The game wants to be “casual” to a fault. While a few features require some work to reach (autophages, purple stars etc.) the real meat and potatoes are thrusted upon you at the first possible moment. Features like freighters and settlements are given comically easily.

The multi tool sucks. every single thing is done thru this one thing. Why? It just feels shallow. Would it not be cool to look across the galaxy for the best bolt caster or gravitino coil? Would it not be cool to have multiple tools and  weapons strapped to your character?

Combat is shallow and so easy it’s boring, especially in space. There is little tact or skill to it.

However the devs have not sufficiently addressed any of the core problems. Instead they pump out more interesting concepts with often shallow executions.   They have the whole salvaging thing, and the xeno arena, and fossil collecting, but never a survival overhaul or a combat redesign. Hell they hid better worldgen in endgame content most never see

But it’s not over, I have hope for this game still. The cosmos update was legitimately promising tho flawed. If they have the guts to really switch things up they could make this game a masterpiece.

The best way I've ever seen this game put is this: "War Thunder is the best game, ran by the worst company."

I'll start with the pros first, as this game is at its core a groundbreaking and fun experience.
- The sheer selection and representation of military history in this game is its biggest strength, as it has thousands of vehicles for the player to play and an amazing attention to detail for how they are in real life (usually).
- The skill ceiling in this game is phenomenally high, as there are so many ways to get better at the game and so much information to know that you never truly master it all (positions on every map, recognizing vehicles from a passing glance and their exact module performance vs how it compares to yours, weak spots and armor holes, etc...).
- The game is well performing and visually stunning with a massive player base, which help it immensely in terms of making the experience more enjoyable.

Now, that's where the token positives end and the actual gameplay/publisher needs to be dissected.
- Gaijin, the creator and maintainer of War Thunder, is an absolute vile company. Completely ignoring their real life politics, their ties to War Thunder is easily the worst part of the game. They do not care about their players and actively make decisions almost EXCLUSIVELY to spite or harm them. They will ban accounts on the basis of review bombing which is entirely arbitrary and exists to hold a sword over the head of players who want to feel heard. Their support system is also nonexistent, even actively hostile to players. The monetization and laziness of the game are also just gross, and warrant bullet points of their own. 
- This game exists as a cash cow for a company that has no comparable income source. Gaijin monetizes this game so obsessively that user enjoyment is almost contingent on pulling out your credit card. The ever-present grind almost mandates the purchasing of premium vehicles or months of a premium account just to play your beloved Abrams or T90. Keep in mind, these are not some $5 purchase you make flippantly, many of the vehicles in this game cost as much as an ENTIRELY NEW AAA GAME, with an absolutely hilarious $70 price tag (that I am indeed seeing on my screen as I type this review, for Senrai Maiden packs, sigh). On top of that, most truly unique and fun vehicles exist as event vehicles that will never be coming back and often fetch for hundreds of dollars on the marketplace. It is scummy to its core and makes the gap between the f2p and the whale almost insurmountable. In addition to this, they make $70 vehicles utterly unbalanced for months at a time after release so that they can milk the player base eating itself from the inside out for a little while. BMPT-72 on launch made the game unplayable, T58 on launch made the game unplayable, and this only extends backwards in time.
- Gaijin is lazy in how they fix poorly designed mechanics in this game, and it only gets worse. Many mechanics are foundationally broken and directly impact gameplay every single match, yet remain unchanged as Gaijin knows they have the player count and influence to not lift a finger. Volumetric armor making rounds disappear into thin air when it hits a 5mm steel plate? Ship it. Missiles with enough filler in the warhead to turn your tank to rapidly expanding plasma just ricocheting off a steel sheet because it was angled? Ship it. Artillery guns being used as frontline assault vehicles that can either insta-kill any tank in the game or fail to make a dent with 12kg TNT equivalent? Ship it. Every single engagement in this game is a coin flip, and it's tiring knowing your enemy who you played better than wins because the game decides your dart round going 1200 m/s gets eaten by a mudguard. 
- Gaijin also does not care about making the experience unique between tech trees. Count the amount of Leopards in the game and you'll see what I mean. The copy/paste problem is so genuinely infuriating because Gaijin can make a major update for the game and add a new subtree with only one actually new vehicle (Greek subtrees, anyone?). Or, as a matter of fact, just take the entire Israeli tech tree. Five. Hundred. Magachs. The worst part is that Gaijin is NOT running out of vehicles to add from real life, they just don't CARE enough to make the gameplay unique.
- The grind is so overwhelming that without a premium account plus a lineup of premium vehicles it takes months to make even a dent. Modern vehicles at high ranks are so outrageously expensive that it will take weeks for a f2p player to research them, and that's assuming they can even afford the damn thing because at high ranks they probably LOSE silver lions on an average match. I have 600 hours as of making this review, and I'm at ~300/2000 vehicles needed for the collector Steam achievement. 
- With how the damage models work in this game, War Thunder goes from the most to the least realistic military combat sim ever made. You can shoot an artillery shell or ATGM with enough explosive filler to LEVEL. A. FUCKING. BUILDING. at a light tank and you'll get a broken MG/transmission. However, you can also shoot the ground next to a tank and it aimbot ricochets into their ammo at the perfect angle defying physics. Realistically, I want my results to be based on an aggregate of my positioning, skill, and vehicle matchup. What I get is that I'll get 12 kill games because APFSDS rounds will ricochet off my TAM or get 0 kill games because I get the inverse experience. Every battle is a coin flip, and it's exhausting. 
- Map design is abhorrently balanced, and encourages spawn camping on almost every single map. If you play for more than 5 matches you are guaranteed to have a match where your entire team gets spawn camped by minute 3, and that you just have no ability to fight back. Spawn camping is so prevalent that from my experience >85% of matches end in it, and >40% of them experience spawn camping before the match is even half over. Gaijin has no intent to change this either; the newly added Darwin Hill map is just a spawn camper's paradise and abysmal to play (for reference: at one point I got killed by a Merkava near his spawn, I respawned and within 5 seconds killed him back, from over 1.5km away). 
- The community is so genuinely toxic and the moderation is almost non-existent, as to where playing with chat off is nearly a requirement. Every third game you have someone spewing slurs and the vilest hate speech you can imagine in chat either because they're mad or because they were bored. Gameplay is also very toxic as people will camp 24/7 and killing anyone is a dice roll of whether they'll just respawn in a plane, revenge bomb you, and kamikaze into the dirt because I guess you're not allowed to have fun. 
- Some other things that don't warrant bullet points of their own but are worth mentioning: shooting rounds and dying costs you currency that you CAN go net negative on per match, premium currency just does not exist for f2p EVER, the game becomes a repair simulator for 40 second increments, bushes are p2w and just make the f2p grind less fun, Senrai Maidens and goon slop exist just to drive up sales, CAS has severe balancing issues and you WILL die repeatedly from something you had absolutely no control over, non-premium vehicles come stock and are made to be as unusable and unfun as possible (especially top tier)

Nach nun etwa 59 Stunden und dem Gefühl, dass ich nahezu jegliches Interesse daran verloren habe, das Spiel weiterzuspielen, möchte ich meine Eindrücke teilen.


[h1]Mein erster Durchlauf – Balanced[/h1]

Ich bin auf [b]Balanced[/b] gestartet, also mit einem ausgeglichenen Verhältnis zwischen Kampf und Exploration.

Das Spiel führt einen relativ tunnelförmig von Encounter zu Encounter und treibt dabei gleichzeitig die Story voran. Zwar gibt es Abzweigungen und alternative Wege, allerdings vermittelt einem das Spiel sehr schnell, wenn man sich in ein Gebiet begibt, das offenbar „zu schwer“ ist.

Ich bin beispielsweise dazu übergegangen, solche Gebiete zunächst schleichend zu erkunden – nur um erneut vermittelt zu bekommen, dass ich dort offenbar noch nichts zu suchen habe.

Was mich dabei besonders gestört hat: [b]Viele grundlegende Mechaniken werden kaum oder gar nicht erklärt.[/b]

Nach etwa drei Stunden starb meine Gruppe in einem Kampf, den ich im Nachhinein nicht einmal hätte führen müssen. Daraufhin wurde ich wieder an den Strand am Anfang des Spiels gesetzt. Es wurde in all der Zeit einfach nicht gespeichert... >_<


[list]
[*]Wie das Camp funktioniert, musste ich selbst herausfinden.
[*]Dass man regelmäßig Short Rests und Long Rests nutzen sollte, musste ich selbst herausfinden.
[*]Dass man praktisch nach jedem relevanten Schritt speichern sollte, musste ich ebenfalls selbst lernen.
[/list]


Ich habe mich anschließend bei Freunden erkundigt, wie man eigentlich sinnvoll progressen soll, ohne ständig auf Heilung oder Exploits angewiesen zu sein. Wirklich hilfreiche Antworten bekam ich dabei kaum.

Kurz vor Akt 2 kam dann nach einem extrem anstrengenden Kampf gegen die Phase Matriarch Spider der Punkt, an dem ich meinen ersten Charakter endgültig aufgegeben habe. Ich hatte schlicht keine Perspektive mehr für meinen gewählten Schleich-Charakter. Kaum passendes Gear, kaum passende Items und Händler, die für diese Spielweise kaum etwas anbieten.


[h1]Zweiter Durchlauf – Explorer[/h1]

Also neuer Versuch: Zwerg-Barbar auf [b]Explorer[/b].

Und plötzlich ist das komplette Gegenteil der Fall.

Die Kämpfe sind inzwischen so einfach, dass ich teilweise das Gefühl habe, sie auch mit einem einzelnen Charakter gewinnen zu können. Sicherlich helfen mir die inzwischen bekannten Mechaniken, aber auch das Verhalten und die Fähigkeiten der Gegner spielen dabei eine große Rolle.

Mittlerweile bin ich fast durch Akt 2 und habe unter anderem die Githyanki Creche nahezu vollständig ausgelöscht.

Dabei tritt allerdings ein weiterer Punkt auf, der mich mittlerweile massiv nervt:

Mechaniken wie [b]Entwaffnen[/b], die einem Schlichtweg nicht erläutert werden und denen man einfach ausgeliefert ist. Man müsste das Spiel und alle Mechaniken, jeden Schritt kennen, also das Spiel studieren um darauf reagieren zu können. Bedeutet, jeder weitere Kampf, wird ähnlich ablaufen und entweder ich Informiere mich, nutze buggy Interactions oder lade Kämpfe zich dutzende male neu um sie zu überwinden. 

Meine Charaktere werden gefühlt in jedem Kampf ständig entwaffnet. Gleichzeitig kann ich meine Waffen teilweise nicht einmal unmittelbar wieder ausrüsten, geschweige denn aufheben... 

Das Problem ist weniger, dass es diese Mechanik gibt, sondern dass das Spiel einem praktisch nicht erklärt, [b]wie man damit umgehen oder sich davor schützen soll.[/b]

Im Internet findet man dann Hinweise, dass mehr Stärke die Wahrscheinlichkeit reduzieren soll. Drei meiner Charaktere haben bereits 18 Stärke – und soweit ich zu diesem Zeitpunkt weiß, liegt das Maximum bei 20. Viel mehr kann ich also ohnehin nicht dagegen unternehmen.

Und wieder stehe ich vor dem gleichen Problem: Ich muss auf eine Mechanik reagieren, von der mir das Spiel praktisch nichts erklärt.

Und die Belohnungen sind einfach nicht existent. Etwas zu überwinden das extrems schwierig war, droppt in der Regel nichts was auch dementsprechend "WoW" oder "Geil" auslösen würde.  Solche Items sind hinter weirden Interaktionen versteckt. 


[h1]Das eigentliche Problem[/h1]

Und genau hier liegt für mich das grundlegende Problem mit BG3:

[b]Ich verstehe nicht, wo der Spaß entstehen soll, wenn man das Spiel nicht vorher ausgiebig recherchiert.[/b]

Jede Entscheidung fühlt sich potentiell wie ein Fehler an. Man speichert ständig, lädt Kämpfe neu, weil man zu viele Ressourcen verbraucht hat, verliert möglicherweise wichtige Items und erfährt teilweise erst Stunden später, dass man etwas hätte anders machen müssen.

Informiert man sich vorher im Internet, stellt man wiederum fest, dass man bereits vor 10 Stunden Entscheidungen getroffen oder Items verpasst hat, die man jetzt gerne gehabt hätte.

Also lädt man einen alten Spielstand.

Das erzeugt bei mir keinen Entdeckerdrang, sondern eher das Gefühl, das Spiel ständig gegen sich selbst absichern zu müssen.

Natürlich gibt es unglaublich viele Möglichkeiten und Entscheidungen. Aber wenn die Konsequenz daraus ist, dass ich nach jeder größeren Entscheidung überlegen muss, ob ich gerade möglicherweise einen wichtigen Inhalt für die nächsten 10 Stunden zerstört habe, dann nimmt mir das einen großen Teil des Spielspaßes.

Auch die Charaktere tragen für mich bisher nur begrenzt dazu bei. Man kann natürlich seine Begleiter meucheln und auf viele Dinge völlig anders reagieren – aber das bringt mir wenig, wenn ich anschließend nichts davon habe außer Nachteile. 

[b]Karlach ist für mich bisher die einzige Figur, die ich wirklich sympathisch finde.[/b]

Und nur wegen ihrer Geschichte möchte ich mir die restlichen ~100 Stunden ehrlich gesagt nicht antun.


[h1]Fazit[/h1]

BG3 bietet offensichtlich enorme Freiheit, unzählige Möglichkeiten und sehr viel Content.

Für mich fühlt sich diese Freiheit allerdings nicht wie Freiheit an, sondern wie eine Ansammlung potentieller Fehlentscheidungen, deren Konsequenzen ich ohne vorherige Recherche kaum einschätzen kann.

Nach rund 59 Stunden habe ich deshalb schlicht das Interesse verloren, weiterzuspielen.

[b]Für mich persönlich mehr Frust als Spielspaß.[/b]

Factorio can easily be called a perfect game - it's clear the developers poured their hearts into it. It's a game about building and automating a factory, where you gradually unlock new technologies and build increasingly complex production chains. If you have a tendency toward obsessive organization and planning, you'll be in seventh heaven. The game can be fairly challenging for newcomers at first, but the developers did an amazing job with how new things are gradually unlocked through research - you're never overwhelmed right from the start, but instead move through clear milestones: your first research, advanced mining, oil processing, and so on.

The Space Age expansion then adds beautiful and highly varied planets - each one brings something new, so there's always more to do.

This is one of the very few games that truly deserves a 10/10.

If you’ve never played RimWorld vanilla, don’t worry, I haven’t either. At this point I’m convinced the “base game” is just a polite suggestion from Ludeon, because the real RimWorld experience is waiting 20 minutes for your modlist to boot, praying the main menu loads without errors, and then diving into a colony that’s held together with duct tape, ideology overhauls, pony factions, and whatever other madness you installed at 3 AM.

And somehow, it’s incredible.

RimWorld is the only game where the loading screen becomes part of the ritual. You start the game, go make coffee, check your phone, maybe contemplate your life choices — and when you come back, the mod soup has finally finished simmering. Then you hit “New Colony” and lose the next six hours of your life without blinking.

The storytelling is what keeps pulling me back. RimWorld doesn’t hand you a narrative; it hands you a box of matches and says “figure it out.” Every colony becomes a personal saga, especially when mods crank the chaos to eleven.

My favorite example?
One of my colonists, Red, got malaria. Not unusual. What was unusual was when my masterwork‑obsessed builder decided to commemorate the event by engraving the entire ordeal — fever spikes, medical panic, and all — onto a wooden dining chair. Nothing says “family dinner” like sitting on a lovingly carved depiction of Red sweating through a life‑threatening disease.

That’s RimWorld.
Absurd.
Chaotic.
Weirdly heartfelt.
And completely addictive.

If you love modding, worldbuilding, emergent storytelling, or games that let you create your own brand of nonsense, RimWorld is unmatched. I’ve poured a ton of hours into it this past month, and it still keeps dragging me back in with “just one more colony” energy.

Verdict:  
If you’re a modder, RimWorld isn’t just a game — it’s a lifestyle.

[h1]Mechanics MMORPG[/h1]
[hr][/hr][i]Guild Wars 2 had marketed itself from earliest days on its mechanics. They were revolutionary back in its day and even up to this day, game aged very well in that regard. Everything you see in other modern MMORPGs, it started first here. Though, this is where good things about this world end. It's MMO which you play for mechanics and nothing else. Unfortunately, mechanics on its own doesn't make an enjoyable experience and there is precious little else to play this game for.[/i][hr][/hr]
[h1]💖The Good💖[/h1]
Usually, I review game with emphasis of what is bad. In this case, I will focus on positive when reviewing the main game and keep negative points in its expansion. While expansion is not strightly bad, it's difficult to otherwise rate this game. As a MMO it has redeeming qualities for its audience and it's good. However, there is a lot of bad in it also. MMORPG isn't a normal game where you can review it as a finished product for one type of broad gamer archetype. MMORPGs can have many gameplay loops in itself. From how questing and leveling experience is to late game progression and group content. Some play such games for drip, others for minigames. Some as social experiences. Just being a nice place to log in and waste your time might be enough to appease an MMORPG fan. 

[h1]🌈Total Freedom🌈[/h1]
Game back then was marketed on a concept of total freedom. That you can do whatever you wish. While it sounded great back then on paper, in reality I quickly noticed that total freedom means that I didn't felt attached to anything. Lack of character and class identity made me detached from my character. Questing is very arcadey, run into the area and do whatever. It lacks proper context to tie you to the world and what you are doing. Its frequent events and world bosses eventually made feel everythng pointless as world would reset again and again. It does feel good and might be attractive for some people that you can go anywhere, gather all materials. Level up quickly and do questing in whatever way you like.

At a time, it was a revolution upon which Guild Wars 2 marketed itself. Then people tried out and they quickly realized that it isn't as great as everyone thought it to be. At that time those systems were revolutionary and everyone was hyped. Everyone wanted no grind, freedom how to progress. They were tired of traditional MMORPG grindatons and class restrictions. This game had shown everybody that traditional formula isn't that bad. Quickly afterwards game fell hard, but managed to maintain steady playerbase. To this day game feels like a modern MMORPG. Everything what is in most modern such games started right here.

[h1]📋Completionist mindset📋[/h1]
Game has a lot of side activities. Players are free to focus on whatever progression path they choose. Here is a quick list of such activities:
[list]
[*]Jumping challenges for achievements, rewards and talent points.
[*]Vast maps to discover with set achievements.
[*]Massive quantities of content. Hundreds of hours of questing, map exploration, PvP, PvE content. 
[*]Dungeon, Fractal, Karma grinding. Event completion. World bosses.
[/list]
Each of these things represents absolute ton of playtime. Game is mature and has immense quantities of content which all of it is still active and doable. That is impressive as old MMORPGs often are ghost towns. Here however game still feels alive, well, at least until release of Guild Wars 3...

[h1]Progenitor of a new era![/h1]
Game marketed itself on novel ideas. Dodging, targetting, weapons having skills and being able to pick how you want to play. Combat system is a lot more active with a lot of skills needing to be actively targeted and user having a basic dodge in order to avoid skillshots coming to them. Combined with various defensive cooldowns, PvP combat in this game were a lot more dynamic at the time. That dynamism also came when such games were static and people wanted something sleek and modern. This was such a game at the time. Now it just aged gracefully and matured like a fine wine. It speaks to the testament of its ideas that they weren't just gimmicks, they were genuinely innovative enough that they would stand test of time and wouldn't look like quirks or gimmicks found elsewhere.

Game also has very in depth character builds. Class -> Specializations -> Builds. Every class have dozen of specializations which you unlock through leveling and DLCs. Then you combine those classes together. From those classes you pick what you want the most as a talent tree. The end result are incredibly deep build system which allows players to have any flavor they want for their own class. This however is a blessing and a curse. There are no class identity anymore. A necromancer for example can be a summoner or a sustain tank. Every class can play dramatically differently and they are still a necromancer. Game doesn't shift them into sub-classes identity. As a whole, while game gives you a lot of customization, game doesn't have classical archetypes of tank, healer and damager. Everyone can do everything and hence, there isn't a strong class fantasy of what your character can or cannot do. It's amazing for mechanical side of things, absolutely terrible for immersion. World of Warcraft Classic is the opposite. Its strict class system allows players to own their character. Its strengths and weaknesses. You can something which no other class can. Yet, at the same time you only have 3 different flavors of how you can play and game can be very limiting in what gear it can give you to support that playstyle. Not to mention that going into niches is pointless as you won't have any extra skills for the most part. Old Hunters are a perfect example of that. Throughout entire game you lack any viable gear. Then Survival hunter focuses more on melee except you have like 3 skills to use. This game is opposite of that. It's really deep when it comes to finding your own niche, but it loses the soul of what it means to be Ranger/Hunter.

Game visuals at the time looked good, but now had aged and look very underwhelming, but still are serviceable. However, it had set a precedent of focusing a lot of its attention and computational power on making nicest character models it could. As a result, NPC models aged well. It also started that realistic, doll supermodel trend which a lot of other MMORPGs later emphasized, trying to make their women hypersexualized and men hypermasculine.

[hr][/hr][i]Back in a game game was marketed on its looks and mechanics. Well, age made its looks fade away. However, its mechanics proved as exceptionally novel and far sighted. Fast forward time over a decade and now you see every MMO copying its ideas and implementing in their own games. Every game became more like Guild Wars 2. Game was innovative, but it was just that. You wake in a tavern, replenish your ship's supplies, food, wood, cannon balls and customize it's cosmetics.
You talk with an NPC who gives you a quest. You receive a map of an island with red crosses on it.

You unfurl your sails and turn the helm towards the destination.

A few minutes pass. While you're in the middle of the ocean, trying to navigate around a storm, the water suddenly turns black. Combat music kicks in, as a pair of tentacles emerge from the depths.
A wild Kraken appears, and it thinks that your ship is tasty.
You grab a handful of cannonballs from storage and man the cannons.
With a few well placed shots and a couple shredded tentacles, the Kraken leaves you alone.
You repair the damage to your ship, and jump in the water to pick up the Kraken's meat.
Looking at the map, a short detour towards a trading post is possible.
You place the meat on a skillet to cook, while you turn your ship towards the merchants.
After selling the Kraken meat, you set sail towards your quest.
The rest of the voyage is uneventful, and you reach the island and drop the anchor.
With map in one hand and a shovel in another, you set foot on the tropical island before you.
With no minimap, you need to read the map and orient yourself based on landmarks you see.
Eventually you find one of the places where the treasure should be.
Enthusiastically, you swing your shovel in to the sand and hit wood!

You've found a wooden chest, that is one of the treasures on the island.
However, you also found a pack of animated skeletons who would rather you not take the treasure.
You draw your sword and fight the bones.
You notice a lone skeleton carry a big red barrel of gunpowder toward you. Without skipping a beat, you run a few paces away and draw your pistol.

I have a lot of complaints about Satisfactory, but I want to start by saying I think it's a good game which totally rewarded the time and money I invested in it. I came to this as a casual Factorio fan, but this game has one big thing that Factorio doesn't: the feeling of standing on a cliff and looking out over an alien landscape that's been transformed by your work, your factory sprawling so far into the distance you can hardly believe you built it all bit by bit. I love that, and I've never had another experience quite like it in a game. With that said, on to my complaints, which I'm writing here mostly as feedback to the developers:

1. The game has two basic loops. The first loop involves building factories to manufacture product to develop technology to build more factories. That one's great. The second loop involves exploring the environment, getting killed, and then trying to get back to where you died so you can recover your belongings. That one's terrible. I understand why the world needs to have perils: it adds some risk-reward to exploration and expansion. But it's implemented so frustratingly here. For instance, there are moments where the game verges on a first-person shooter. Look, I like first-person shooters, and I'm reasonably good at them. But it isn't where these developers' strengths lie. The combat is awkward and tedious at every stage of the game. And that's when you even get a look at your enemy: half your deaths will be from some kind of gas, projectile, or flying creature that hit you from offscreen. Often you'll realise afterwards you were carrying all of your ammo, jetpack fuel etc. – before you comment, yes, I know it's wiser to leave some reserves at your base, but people don't always play these games optimally – meaning that getting back out there the second time is even harder than it was the first time. It's a shame, because the developers have built this beautiful world, but I found exploring it to be mostly a chore.

2. Progression could be a lot more exciting, and the ending in particular feels deeply anticlimactic. Sure, Factorio doesn't pat you on the back much. Even launching the rocket is just a brief animation that looks like it could be from 1994. But Satisfactory sells itself much more on spectacle – we're in 3D, the only limits here are imagination! – so the lack of it at these moments is more glaring. After hours and hours and hours of labour, you finish a stage of the space elevator, and as a player it feels like an accomplishment; but the game does very little to make it feel like an event. Plus, although it opens up new milestones, it doesn't itself offer any rewards. Why not give us some new powers, even if minor? Why not give us some visual upgrades to the hub? Anything at all???

3. It's unbelievable to me that the game came out in early access seven years ago and after all this time it's still so lacking in usability. If I built a conveyor lift to the wrong height, why is it so many clicks to correct the mistake? Why does troubleshooting problems with your train network first involve "catching" a train before it goes into a station – because, while it's loading or unloading, the game won't let you see anything – hurriedly going into a menu to stop the train, then laboriously inspecting every container? (You can't even rename a train remotely, let alone change its schedule or see what it's carrying.) Why is the fluid system regarded like voodoo by even the most experienced players, when this was never a problem in Factorio?

4. My final point relates to the last one. After you've finished the campaign, you're likely to spend less and less of your time solving problems, and more and more time designing buildings. When a player has thousands of hours in Satisfactory, it's usually because they're playing it as an architecture simulator. The developers must be well aware of this, so it's crazy to me how much that category of player is forced to work *around* the game, instead of working *with* it. Even something as basic as designing a curved road, or a conveyor that goes straight up a ramp, is something you have to watch YouTube tutorials to learn how to do. There are so many simple features that could have been implemented that, across the entire Satisfactory player base, would have saved the equivalent of thousands of lifetimes of fiddling around. (Mods can solve some of them, but not all.) This is a game that's sold nine million copies, where the equivalent of Architectural Digest tours get hundreds of thousands of views on YouTube – and we're still stuck with three types of wall. It feels wilfully stubborn at this point.

After playing a lot more of this after they made it better optimised, I'm starting to realise that it's easily one of the best games ever made. I say that in complete seriousness - it's really just outstanding in so many aspects, but the physics and the way the wand crafting works is just utter genius. 

Everything in Noita ties together so well to deliver an experience that makes almost every other single player game feel really bland. It really feels ahead of its time in many ways, and I think we'll see a lot more games like it once hardware improves and devs cotton on to the fact that physics-based gameplay (meaning gameplay where the physics is a core, fundamental element rather than a tacked-on gimmick) is the surest route to emergent, dynamic gameplay where each play session feels truly unique and exciting. 

It's a shame that all the top reviews seem to blather on about the difficulty, because there's so much going on with this game that is far more interesting than how difficult or not it is. It took me a long time to get anywhere in Noita, but I was never discouraged because the core gameplay is so engaging and unique that I didn't mind playing the first level over and over. 

I will say that the wandcrafting has a steep learning curve, but game mechanics that are this unique and interesting usually do, so it's well worth your time to look at a few tutorials. 

Anyway buy this game it's probably a lot better than your entire steam library combined.

I’m not someone who’s quick to praise a game, but I have to admit: this game raised my standards for RPGs by miles. I played it blindly, avoiding all spoilers for around two years, and finally snatched it up on sale. I honestly didn’t think I’d enjoy it this much.

I was so wrong.

From the first time I opened it, I was completely hooked. My first playthrough-the one I’m writing this after-had me sitting in my chair during summer holidays for around 13 days straight, gaming from morning until evening. No game has EVER made me do this before.

The amount of content is absolutely ridiculous. Every time I thought I was done with an area, I’d come back and find something else. Another quest, another secret, another character, another little detail I had somehow missed. It constantly rewards you for exploring and actually paying attention. This game is what I imagined RPGs were when I was a kid getting into gaming. This game feels exactly like those incredibly detailed drawings of ships, buildings, or cities shown from the side, where you could stare at them for hours, analyzing every single little detail and imagining what was happening inside.

Nowadays, so many games have maps completely filled with pointless fetch quests, repetitive activities, and markers telling you exactly where to go just so you can check something off the map. This game feels completely different. You actually discover things yourself. And almost every character you meet can have some kind of impact on the world or the story. There are so many different outcomes depending on what you do, who you talk to, and the choices you make.

And most importantly, your choices actually matter throughout the entire game. Not just in one quest or one cutscene, but across the whole experience. That alone adds so much replayability.

The turn-based combat also completely surprised me. I never expected it to become my favorite type of combat, but here we are. Every battle feels like a carefully thought-out strategy rather than simply taking turns hitting each other. You have to understand your characters, use their abilities properly, and make them work together. Even random encounters can turn into genuinely fun tactical situations.

And then there are the characters.

I absolutely love how everyone has a distinct personality-not just the main cast, but side characters and even random NPCs. They feel like actual characters rather than objects placed in the world to give you a quest. You can genuinely feel the passion that went into making this game.

There’s so much I could talk about, but I’d rather not spoil anything. Going into this game blindly was one of the best gaming experiences I’ve ever had, and I’m really glad I managed to avoid the spoilers for so long.

I would recommend this game to literally everyone, regardless of what genres they normally play.

Let's start with the pros. The first thing that catches your eye is the huge amount of content. The game has many survivors, killers with diverse abilities, and outfits for them. Besides that, there are many maps, although you won't see some of them very often. For example, I only saw the pizzeria connected to William Afton once, when I was playing on my old account. Now let's move on to the cons. There are quite a few of them, but there are only two main ones. First, the graphics leave much to be desired and, according to rumors, are supposed to be updated in 2027. Second, the game has absolutely no balance. Some killers are so strong that you have virtually no chance of winning in 9 out of 10 cases. At the same time, your skill level as a player doesn't always affect the outcome of the match. You could discuss this problem for a long time, but let's not go into details.

In conclusion, I'd like to say that this game is worth recommending to those who have a regular team to play online or co-op with. ## How to fix Dota 2

* Remove half the jungle camps
* Bring back Unique Attack Modifiers so carries have to choose
* Give more spell-based counterplay while also increasing cooldowns
* Make mana pools something you have to carefully manage again.
* Go back to 6 slots total. No backpack, no scroll slot.
* Rollback the last 8 years of absurd power creep. Only idiots want every patch to be nothing but buffs.
* Remove healing lotuses and wisdom shrines.
* Rework tormentor. If you want it to be a true goal that dictates a team's movements, it should give something more significant than an aghs shard to a random teammate. Give a team a tower they can choose to deploy where one of theirs has died. Make it so the same tower cannot be resurrected more than once.
* Allow players (whose heroes are still alive) to aim tower aggro at enemy heroes, as it is much too easy for experienced players to manipulate tower aggro, while inexperienced players aren't going to have any notion of it. So give the inexperienced players some counterplay.
* Bounty runes are not a bad idea, but they're largely an afterthought. Return them back into the cycle at the main two rune spawn points. There shouldn't be a guarantee of getting a potent combat-oriented rune every time. Make it mean more when someone gets a double damage.
* While we're on the subject, return it to being double damage, and make that double damage extend to spell damage. If PA can get to a point of cleaving a whole team for 4000 damage with a crit without a rune, then high damage ults on heroes like Zeus or Lion should also have the opportunity to put out damage like that if they end up being lucky enough to net the rune that will allow that. It won't break the game, and certainly no more than the currently broken and uninteresting state the game is currently in.
* Add many more trees and make them stay dead longer after a certain point. Leave the tree respawn rate alone during the first 10 minutes, and then make it longer after that. The reason is simple - players should have meaningful counterplay against heroes with a need/usage of trees, but it should be carefully measured so those heroes aren't dumpstered in the laning phase because of this.
* And finally, to add to the tree changes, make more items able to destroy larger amounts of trees. Destructible environments with meaning and purpose to strategic destruction where it matters is more interesting than the tertiary purpose of trees now as mere hindrances for line of sight that have been significantly reduced. Some of the coolest plays in dota are jukes where people used trees and branches to their advantage.

The theme is, of course, COUNTERPLAY. Bludgeoning real counterplay out of the game through arbitrary changes over many years that have caused absurd power creep to just get more and more silly is why the game fails to hold the interest of players for much longer than the time it takes for the new from the last major patch to wear off. Make it mean more to really learn the game again.

Sea of Thieves is possibly one of the worst games that I've played that simultaneously has taken 80 hours of my life up. This game does NOT get updated very well. It has many issues the devs don't fix. The bugs in the game are endless. The game feels very enjoyable when you're by yourself having a fun pirate time, feeling like an actual pirate, but as soon as you get into any sort of pvp situation it turns into the jankiest, shittiest, messiest combat system of any game I've ever played. It's a game about being a pirate, where you expect slow bullet fire with inaccuracy from smoothbore pistols and rifles, sword fighting between cutlasses, and last but not least, intense canon fire that feels heavy hitting and enjoyable. Instead, it is  choose the character with the skinniest body, equip the gun that lets you fly, and then once you're on their ship just buzz around hitting them with the worst feeling sword of any game I've ever played. Once you kill them, you either place a bomb that blows up their whole ship, throw fire bombs that set fire to their ship, or just shoot them with as much bullshit out of a canon as possible before they respawn. In a game with such a huge emphasis and reward system based on PVP, it's insane how shitty the implementation is. It has not once felt enjoyable at all to sink another ship, and I've never gotten sunk and thought "that makes sense I can actually learn from the experience." You may be asking, "but if the PVP sucks so much, then why don't you just play without any other people?" Because the game has such a huge focus on PVP and it removes all threats from the game without PVP. Being on your own little server alone feels so boring because you don't actually have to worry about anything. The PVE is honestly bad as well, but it's passable, but if you have an MMO with emphasis on PVP it better be good quality. I cannot believe that this game still charges 40 dollars, it is a buggy mess full of glitches that could cost you hours, janky and shitty pvp, and the worst feeling sword/gunplay I've ever felt in any game.
