Dota 2 is one of the most popular multiplayer games in the world, but popularity does not automatically make a game fun. For many players, Dota 2 can feel less like entertainment and more like a second job that nobody is paying them to do. Between its incredibly complicated mechanics, frustrating matches, and steep learning curve, there are plenty of reasons someone might argue that Dota 2 sucks.

First, Dota 2 is ridiculously complicated. There are dozens of heroes, hundreds of items, and countless abilities to memorize. A new player can spend hours trying to understand what is happening on the screen while experienced players seem to know every possible interaction. Instead of simply learning how to play, beginners have to learn an enormous amount of information before they can even feel competent. A game should be challenging, but Dota 2 sometimes feels like studying for a final exam.

Another problem is how frustrating matches can become. A single mistake can have consequences for the entire team, and one player's bad decision can make the game miserable for everyone else. Even when a player is doing well, the outcome can depend heavily on teammates. This can turn a game that is supposed to be fun into an argument simulator. Losing is already frustrating, but losing after spending nearly an hour in a match can feel especially painful.

The game can also require an enormous amount of time. Matches can last a long time, and players may spend much of that time trying to recover from mistakes or waiting for the other team to make one. Someone who only has a short amount of free time may not want to commit to a game where they could still be playing an hour later. Sometimes you just want to play a quick game, not accidentally dedicate your entire evening to one match.

Finally, Dota 2 can feel like there is always something else to learn. Even after understanding the basics, players have to keep up with new strategies, patches, heroes, items, and changes to the game. This can be exciting for dedicated fans, but for casual players, it can feel exhausting. Instead of relaxing after school or work, you might find yourself wondering why an imaginary wizard just destroyed your entire team.

In conclusion, Dota 2 has plenty of qualities that its fans enjoy, but it also has major drawbacks. Its complexity, frustrating matches, long games, and constant learning requirements can make it feel more stressful than enjoyable. For players who love extremely competitive and complicated games, Dota 2 might be perfect. For everyone else, however, there is always the comforting option of uninstalling it and playing something that does not require a 40-page instruction manual.

BG3 is basically an old school CRPG but modernized, there's more QOL, there's some great graphics, etc. but it keeps all the imporant stuff that's been lost in more mainstream modern RPGs. your choices have consequences, your companions can die, your stats absolutely matter, and you won't always have everything go your way all the time. it also has a lot of immersive sim elements, like throwing a fire potion on a puddle of water to make steam, then using a lightning arrow to electrify it and block off an area. you're encouraged to think outside the box and actually use at least some of the junk you pick up to solve quests or win fights. someone you're trying to rescue is trapped in a cage, and the villain sets it on fire? don't need to rush before they die, just throw a water bottle at it.

you get like a million scrolls and spells but you can use them pretty creatively to make boss fights and encounters winnable or easier. there's a ton of freedom to what you can do and the same goes for character builds. it's also fairly faithful to DND 5e, but with some changes for balancing purposes so you don't end up as a demigod. even the final act of the game felt challenging, you don't just steamroll through everything by the end (unless you go for a cheesy build i guess).

the writing and characters are very good. they aren't entirely unique, they're kinda the same sorta archetypes you'd expect like the haughty (and hottie) snarky goth elf chick, the angry warrior legally distinct orc woman, but they're well written, well acted, and their stories aren't as straightforward as they initially seem. the narrator is great, very fitting voice acting mixed with some solid wit.

there's a loving amount of attention to detail, btw. the more you get hurt, the more visibly bruised, cut, and muddy your characters get, and it changes depending on the injury. armor doesn't look 100% pristine and has scratches and dents on it that really make it look photorealistic. it's still somewhat stylized and not fully accurate to reality, especially with the environments, which helps it from looking samey. you can unlock more and different dialogue depending on if you can speak to animals, or if you're under a certain condition, or if you did a certain quest, etc.

my only problem is that the setting is very generic fantasy with some minor differences. forgiveable considering DND and the forgotten realms helped popularize a lot of these tropes, but i don't usually like fantasy games so that was a barrier at first. 

also playing this game feels like eating a whole fucking banquet and then having to digest it with how long it is, i'm still waiting to start my second playthrough but i need to gather the willpower and free time to sit through another 130 hours (my actual playtime was off steam)

✅ Massive amount of content
There is an insane amount of stuff to do. Warframes, weapons, quests, open worlds, missions, bosses, crafting, upgrades, syndicates... and then you discover another system you didn't even know existed.

✅ Fast & satisfying combat
Movement is probably one of the best parts of Warframe. Once you get used to bullet jumping, sliding, wall-running and abilities, going back to a normal shooter feels painfully slow.

✅ Almost everything can be earned
You don't need to spend money to enjoy the game. A lot of premium currency can actually be traded between players, and most Warframes/weapons can be obtained through gameplay.

✅ The Warframes are genuinely fun to play
They aren't just different skins. Each one completely changes how you approach missions. Finding a frame that matches your playstyle is extremely satisfying.

✅ Great progression system
There's always something to build, upgrade, farm or unlock. Even when you think you're getting close to "finishing" the game, you discover another layer.

✅ Surprisingly good story
If you go into Warframe expecting only mindless shooting, the story can catch you off guard. Some of the quests are genuinely memorable.

✅ Looks amazing for a free game
The environments, Warframe designs, weapons and effects can look incredible, especially considering how much of the game is available without paying.

✅ The community can be incredibly helpful
Veteran players often know exactly how confusing the beginning is and are willing to help newer players.

🟥 CONS

❌ New-player experience can be overwhelming
This is probably my biggest complaint.

The game throws so many systems, currencies, resources, menus and mechanics at you that you can easily sit there thinking:

"Okay... what am I actually supposed to do?"

The game has improved over time, but there is still a LOT to learn.

❌ The wiki becomes your best friend
And sometimes your second best friend is YouTube.

You'll eventually search something like:

"How do I get this resource?"

Only to discover that you need to complete a mission, which requires a weapon, which requires a blueprint, which requires a resource from another planet.

😂

❌ Farming can take time
Warframe is fundamentally a grind-heavy game. Sometimes that's satisfying. Sometimes you're running the same mission for the 15th time hoping RNG finally decides to be nice.

❌ Inventory/slots can be confusing
Especially early on, understanding Warframe slots, weapon slots, crafting, blueprints and Platinum can be confusing.

❌ The game doesn't explain everything well
There are mechanics I only understood after dozens of hours because the game simply didn't make them obvious.

❌ You will probably get addicted to collecting things
You start with:

"I'll just build one Warframe."

Then suddenly you have 15 blueprints, 30 weapons in your foundry and a spreadsheet in your head.

🆕 MY ADVICE TO NEW PLAYERS

Don't try to understand everything immediately.

Seriously.

Follow the main quests and unlock the Star Chart. Learn the basic movement and combat first. Build weapons and Warframes that look interesting to you.

Don't worry about having the "perfect" build.

Don't worry about having the strongest Warframe.

Don't worry about the meta.

And don't spend your Platinum randomly.

The game becomes much easier to understand once you simply play it for a while.

Also, if something doesn't make sense, ask the community or look it up. Almost every confusing question you have has probably already been answered somewhere.

💰 THE FREE-TO-PLAY PART

This deserves its own mention.

I've played plenty of free-to-play games where "free" basically means "play for 20 hours and then pay us."

Warframe isn't really like that.

You can spend money if you want to support the developers or save yourself some time, but you can also put hundreds of hours into the game without paying anything.

And because Platinum can be traded between players, you can actually earn premium currency through trading.

That's a pretty refreshing system.

⭐ FINAL THOUGHTS

After 118 hours, I can comfortably say that Warframe is one of those games where the hardest part isn't deciding whether to play it.

It's figuring out where to start.

Once you get past that initial wall of confusion, there's an absurd amount of game waiting for you.

It's fast, weird, beautiful, grindy, complicated, sometimes confusing, and occasionally makes you wonder why you're farming the same mission for the 20th time.

And then you finally get the thing you've been farming for...

and immediately start farming for something else.

If you're even slightly interested in Warframe:

Just try it. It's free.

You might bounce off it in the first few hours.

Or you might look at Steam one day and realize you've somehow played 118 hours.

Dead by Daylight (DBD) is a lore rich, thrilling and challenging asymmetrical online horror game, the game has something to offer for all players! 
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WHICH PLAYER ARE YOU?

Casual Player: The game can be played casually and is the only space within the horror genre where you can play as characters from different horror franchises in one space. The game features a vast range of cosmetics for you to change your character's appearance.

Collector - The game features 3 unique perks per character that you can collect to level up your playing and unlock them across your other characters. You can prestige your characters with in game currency!

Achievement Hunter - The game has plenty of achievements, many of which requiring some dedication. (NOTE: If you're a Completionist, that new characters and correlating achievements are introduced regularly so 100% is a chase)

Mechanical Player - The game features many different mechanics across the killers that you will need to master. If you prefer to play with friends (Survivor) then there are a few 'techs' that you can learn to improve your survivability, however they are not absolutely necessary to learn for success.

Competitive Player - The game does not feature an official ranked or unranked mode, however you automatically climb a ranking system based on your performance during a match, with the higher ranks requiring a much better performance in order to progress. Each month your rank will reset and you are rewarded in game currency (amount based on how high of a rank you were).
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NEGATIVES 

If you have seen the games community or other reviews argue about whether the game is killer sided or survivor sided, DONT BE PUT OFF! This is DBD's oldest discussion amongst the community and is very repetitive.

Like any games long standing community this discussion is brought up by players who have been playing for numerous years and thus I believe will not affect your game experience as a new player, or at least it didn't when I first started.

You will be too busy enjoying learning how everything works to be concerned with community heat! Remember the game releases new content often which keeps the game feeling fresh.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CONCLUSION

Overall the game is fun and addictive to play, its a great challenge to begin with, learning how all the Killers operate. Survivor is great with friends. The developers are very active, releasing new content and patchwork regularly. The games community is strong but has opposing views depending on which side they play more, always a fun battle! A strong recommend and a must play with friends!

At first, Warframe can feel a little unusual and complicated, especially because its progression and leveling systems work quite differently from most other games. There is definitely a learning curve, but once everything starts to click, the game becomes incredibly engaging.

For me, Warframe became the kind of game that completely pulls my attention away from everything else. There were times when I forgot about my problems and just focused on playing. Even when I was not playing, I sometimes found myself thinking about what I wanted to farm, build, or do next.

One of the things I really enjoy is the in-game economy. It feels genuinely alive because players have a real opportunity to earn Platinum by grinding for valuable items and trading them with other players. That means even players who do not want to spend much money can eventually afford cosmetics or other things they want through trading and effort.

The Riven system makes the economy even more interesting. Rivens can add another layer to weapon builds while also creating their own trading market, so there is always something interesting happening both in terms of weapon stats and the player economy.

And perhaps the most impressive part is that all of this exists in a free-to-play game.

Warframe has an incredible amount of content, systems, customization, grinding, trading, and things to learn, yet you can experience so much of it without paying anything. I also have a lot of respect for the developers. From my perspective, they genuinely care about the community and have continued supporting and expanding the game for many years.

Amazing game. I hope Warframe continues to grow and is still around for decades to come.

I went into Satisfactory expecting to get bored of it pretty quickly. Factory games aren't normally something I play, and I'd never played one before. Instead, I was surprised by how ridiculously addictive it became. The basic loop of building production lines, figuring out where something is going wrong, improving efficiency, and then inevitably tearing apart my spaghetti and re-kajiggering everything kept me constantly engaged. Hours just disappear because there's always another problem to think through or another part of the factory I want to improve.

It's also a surprisingly chill game. It can get complicated as hell, but most of the time I wasn't stressed, I was just thinking. There's something extremely satisfying about coming up with an idea, building it out, and eventually watching the whole mess actually work. I'm definitely not playing optimally, but figuring things out for myself was a huge part of the fun. I also thought the world looked gorgeous from the beginning. This is honestly one of those games that's much more fun to play than it probably looks to watch because so much of the enjoyment comes from having your own brain occupied by whatever ridiculous system you're trying to build.

There are some annoyances. Certain systems felt less intuitive than others, particularly pipes, and the ladder mechanics are weirdly wonky. I had enough trouble reliably getting onto ladders that they could actually get me hurt or killed, which feels pretty silly for something games figured out a long time ago. I've also had plenty of moments where some part of my factory wasn't behaving how I expected and figuring out why became frustrating. The early juggling of power and fuel had me constantly dealing with blown fuses and running around trying to keep everything operating. None of that came close to outweighing how much I enjoyed the core factory mechanics, though.

This definitely isn't going to be for everybody. If the idea of spending a huge amount of time making resources so you can make other resources, staring at production rates, rebuilding things, and trying to squeeze more efficiency out of an increasingly absurd factory sounds boring, it very well might be. I thought I'd find it boring too. Instead, I've enjoyed it immensely. It's super engaging, extremely addictive, and just a really fun game to sit down with and lose hours to.

I'm at a stage where I feel confident I can write a review for Factorio, so here we go.
 
Factorio is a very thought-based game. Every stage of the process is dominated by thinking about how something can be achieved, and then how it can be achieved more efficiently/en masse. This is an immensely engaging experience, assuming you enjoy maths/logistics/puzzles, etc. It is an immensely customizable game as well, as every feature can be turned on or off at game start. For example, I do not enjoy the bug attacks, so I can disable them. I very much enjoy being forced to build trains to transport iron because my deposits ran dry, so I leave scarcity on. The game offers great depth, as although you can just build the rocket, you can also do many other things, like produce 10 billion blue circuits, or literally make a computer as Factorio offers the systems off of which binary code and rendering can be achieved. Much of this is not even intentional, and is just a byproduct of the immense depth of the game. Baldur’s Gate 3 - Overwhelmingly Tedious and Boring

I genuinely tried. Seven hours in, multiple sessions. Somewhere around the middle I had a tiny moment of “okay, maybe I’m starting to see it”- that lasted about five minutes.
This is one of the most boring games I have ever played.

BG3 feels like taking every slow, fiddly, overcomplicated part of tabletop RPGs and turning it into a video game - then making every single action take three business days. An Indian drama...

The introduction is atrocious. You are dumped into a wall of classes, races, abilities, resources, dice rolls, actions, bonus actions, movement, spell slots, concentration, inventory, companions and unexplained mechanics with barely any useful explanation. Character creation somehow manages to be both absurdly detailed in places and bizarrely restrictive in others. I spent more time fighting the character creator than creating a character. I eventually made a Wood Half-Elf Ranger because “stealth sniper -> get spotted -> RAAAAAGH” is basically my natural playstyle, but the game certainly didn't make understanding my choices easy.

Then there is the actual gameplay.

Combat is an RNG simulator where my greatest enemy is apparently the number 1.
Miss. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Miss. Miss.

Congratulations, you have successfully spent several minutes positioning your character so that a dice roll can tell you to go f*** yourself.

And the damage progression? Incredible.
Hour 1: 1–9 damage
Hour 7: 4-11 damage
Absolutely revolutionary.

The combat is painfully slow. Every movement point matters, every action takes ages, enemies take their turns one by one, animations drag on... Pathfinding is janky and a single misclick can send your character climbing some invisible wall or walking somewhere you absolutely did not intend. I have played games with clunky controls before, but BG3 somehow makes most games' control schemes look like divine intervention.

Exploration isn't any better. You click on a ladder: “You can't go there.”
Click again: suddenly you can. Click beside a doorway: your character attempts to scale the fucking Himalayas. Try to scout around a corner: congratulations, you've been teleported into combat.
I repeatedly felt like I was fighting the interface rather than the enemies.


The world itself has not grabbed me either. I explored the Grove, picked up a pile of vaguely described errands that they call quests, fought some goblins, got annihilated by an owlbear, got blown up by a statue, stumbled into fights I wasn't prepared for. Spent half my time rummaging through containers for mediocre garbage. The game constantly tries to give the impression that there is supposed to be something fascinating around the next corner, only for the reward to be another conversation, box of junk or fight.

The loot is particularly underwhelming. Forget about finding cool gear and becoming noticeably stronger. 
You get another item with slightly different numbers, same ugly piece of armor, pile of useless arrows and another 20 minute inventory-management session.

And yes, I understand that the game is about player choice and role-playing rather than conventional power progression. That doesn't make the gameplay engaging.

The story, after seven hours, is essentially: YOU HAVE A PARASITE. FIX THE PARASITE.

FIX THE PARASITE.
FIX THE PARASITE.

I KNOW. I HAVE BEEN TOLD. PLEASE STOP BEING A BROKEN RECORD.

The characters haven't done anything for me either. The voice acting is generally good but great performances cannot make characters interesting if I don't care about what they're saying.
Shadowheart is probably the closest I've gotten to actually liking a companion. Still not enough.
Astarion is entertaining to listen to but insufferable.
Lae'zel is an aggressive noseless bitch, any line coming out of her makes me physically cringe and want to put my hands on somebody (the writer or smth...).
Gale is a parasitic f*** who has 3 moves, then becomes utterly useless until you go rest.
And the whole party has so far felt more like a collection of personalities I am managing than people I actually want to travel with.

The romance system also feels hilariously prominent for a game that otherwise tries to take itself so seriously.
Apparently everyone is horny enough to jump you after approximately three conversations. Fantastic.
I'm sure this has nothing to do with the soulless gooners that actually LARP sh** like this.

The music is underwhelming at best. It's competent but repetitive and generic compared with games whose soundtracks actually stick in my head.
I ended up wanting to turn it off, replace it with actual good OSTs, like The Witcher's or Lies of P's...

And then there's the technical side.

The graphics look MEDIOCRE for a 2023 game, yet the performance is absurd.
My PC gets hotter running this heap of trash than Cyberpunk 2077 on max settings with Ray Tracing.
It's artificially big and visually inconsistent. Manages to make my hardware work overtime while I stare at two people standing in a room talking about a spermatozoid...

The funniest part is that I can understand why people like the freedom. BG3 clearly allows variying approaches to situations. That's the only place I can really see effort put in.
But for me, that is not enough. I need the actual GAMEPLAY to be fun.
Not "options to potentially make gameplay exist are vast"... Empty theatre room.


This feels less like an adventure and more like administrative work with dice. Pick up item. Miss item. Open door. Miss door. Walk somewhere. Accidentally climb something. Sort inventory. Equip slightly better trousers. Start combat. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Watch six enemies spend an eternity deciding whether to move three meters. Finally get a turn. Use an ability. Miss. Get one-shot. Rest. Repeat.

I have games sitting in my library that give me more entertainment in six hours than BG3 has given me in seven. The Darkness II's entire amazing campaign is shorter than the amount of time I have spent trying to convince myself this game is going to click.

Maybe it gets better.
Maybe Act 2 is secretly the second coming of gaming
Maybe Act 3 gets you a horned girlfriend IRL

I genuinely do not care enough to find out.

Clearly I'm not the target audience. But after seven hours of giving it a completely fair chance, I don't see a masterpiece hiding underneath the geriatric systems. “Overwhelmingly Positive” is absolute insanity.

Pretentous CRPG buried under a mountain of slow combat, RNG, inventory management, awkward controls, weak progression, tedious traversal and endless dialogue.

I didn't ragequit because the game is difficult - it's just tedious.
I rage-quit because I was bored out of my mind, realizing I'm wasting my precious and finite time doing the paperwork/homework equivalent of a "video game".

And when a game makes me look at my backlog and think, “I could be playing literally anything else right now,” that's the end of the road.

I did come across a couple of very minor bugs but it was a smooth experience given the number of hours played. A review from someone who played Noita for 100h with very limital spoilers:

Noita is a game where you create your own spell combinations out of what you can scrape by, while trying to do your best to stay alive and getting as far down as possible. This is what the game presents itself as. It's so much more than that.

There are so many secrets that do not want to be revealed. The game trailer asks "How Deep Can You Go?" and I don't think the creators meant that literally.

There's some things I noticed. Some frustrating design choices in Noita. Meaning, you can die way too easily, if you don't know something. Knowledge is way more important than skill, because at some point, death mainly comes from just trying new things. It's so sad to lose 16h of progress just because you didn't know what would happen in the next few seconds. Completely avoidable, if you had the knowledge. But as I said the secrets do not want to be revealed. [spoiler]"Knowledge through pain"[/spoiler], the game knows what it's doing. Also when trying to figure out some puzzles there's a lot of backtracking and your ability to tinker with wands is locked by rare, or hard to obtain options and this ability is, I'd say, almost essential for "late game" exploration.

The game is hard, no surprise, but not just gameplay, the secrets and overall mechanics that are not explained at all as well. If you want to become insanely powerful and do all achievements you will almost definitely need a guide unless you have a lot of time. Ig it's not a bad thing, I loved learning about some games through wikis and videos, but figuring something out for yourself is much more rewarding. It's just hard and takes time.

That being said, I'm absolutely in love with this game.

Interactability of the world is insane. You can do anything if you're creative enough. Falling Everything Engine is awesome. There's so much things being simulated and my PC is not exploding, honestly a surprise. Also, it may sound weird, but in order to succeed, you have to exploit game mechanics and that is very unique. It feels like it's encouraged even. So, think outside the box.

Wand tinkering, creating your own spell combinations is a complex system, but very clever and super fun. It's like another game in it's own in a way. You really do feel like a proper wizard inventing new weapons of mass destruction. The satisfaction of creating something weird and powerful is crazy. So, experiment, even if it kills you (it often will).

The music style was unexpected, but it fits very well. Good jams, especially in the jungle.

I don't want to spoil anything, so I'll just say - go explore and have a notebook ready. There's a lot of mysteries in Noita. Finding new things is very rewarding and cool.

Even if you don't want to go out from "the intendent way" to solve mysteries and just want to achieve Victory, the game is still worth the price imo. I'm just saying, there's a lot to discover when you become better at the game.

Rust Review: 9/10 — Oy Vey, I Lost Everything Again

Rust is a survival game where you begin with absolutely nothing except a rock, a bare backside, and the confidence of a man who clearly has not consulted his bubbe before leaving the house.

You gather wood, mine stone, build a tiny shack, and eventually acquire enough resources to feel like you've established yourself.

Then another player named something like xX_Moses420_Xx appears, kills you, takes everything you own, and leaves you standing there wondering why you didn't just stay home and eat some challah.

Rust is essentially the digital equivalent of being told, “Come over for dinner, it'll be nice,” and then discovering twelve relatives are already arguing in the kitchen.

The building system is fantastic. You start with a pathetic wooden box and slowly work your way toward a fortified compound. You protect your storage, reinforce your walls, and carefully hide your valuables.

Basically, you're putting more effort into protecting your Rust base than some people put into protecting the last piece of babka at a family gathering.

The survival aspect is brutal. Food is scarce, resources disappear quickly, and absolutely nobody is willing to give you anything for free. You quickly learn that every piece of scrap matters.

And then comes the true Rust experience:

You finally have a good weapon.

You finally have decent armor.

Your base is fully upgraded.

You're feeling confident.

You walk outside.

You hear footsteps.

Five seconds later, you're dead.

Your entire inventory is gone.

Your neighbor is standing over your body saying, “Skill issue.”

At that point, all you can do is stare at the screen and quietly whisper:

“Oy vey.”

The player interactions are where Rust really shines. You can make friends, create alliances, trade, and work together.

You can also experience the most impressive betrayal since a family member said they were “just borrowing” something and then somehow it disappeared for six months.

The game's economy is particularly impressive. You constantly have to decide what to keep, what to trade, and what to stash away.

It's basically Jewish financial planning simulator, except instead of saving for retirement, you're hoarding sulfur because you're convinced you're going to need it later.

And just like a Jewish mother, Rust constantly asks:

“Do you really need that?”

Yes, Rust.

I absolutely need 47 pieces of cloth.

Don't question me.

One of my favorite parts of Rust is how quickly everything can go catastrophically wrong.

You can spend six hours building a beautiful base, carefully organizing your storage, upgrading your doors, and preparing for the night.

Then you forget to close one door.

Now your entire house has been turned into an open floor plan.

Your resources are gone.

Your weapons are gone.

Your dignity is gone.

Some random player has written “Happy Hanukkah” on a sign outside your destroyed base.

And honestly?

You have to respect the commitment.

Despite all the frustration, Rust is incredibly entertaining. Every victory feels meaningful because you've probably suffered through approximately eight minor emotional crises to achieve it.

Successfully defending your base feels incredible.

Pulling off a raid feels incredible.

Finding a massive haul of loot feels incredible.

Even surviving one encounter with a geared player feels like you deserve a little gelt.

Final Verdict: Rust is stressful, chaotic, unforgiving, and occasionally makes me question why I voluntarily do this to myself.

But every ridiculous death, betrayal, raid, and desperate scramble for resources creates a story worth telling.

But after logging so many hours I just wanted to say Satisfactory is, without exaggeration, one of the most addicting and masterfully executed factory-building sandboxes ever made. Coffee Stain Studios took the deep, logistical complexity of automation management and combined it with a beautiful, hand-crafted first-person sci-fi world—and the result is pure digital crack.

What starts as a simple setup of a few miners and belts quickly escalates into vast, multi-floor megafactories. The power curve feels incredibly satisfying—every unlock from basic logistics and coal power to trains, hoverpacks, and nuclear plants fundamentally changes how you expand and navigate the world.  A Hand-Crafted World That Demands Exploration. Unlike many games in the genre that rely on procedurally generated terrain, Satisfactory features a massive, handcrafted map filled with distinct biomes, secrets, slug power-ups, and aggressive local wildlife. Exploration isn't just a side distraction; it's essential for discovering hard-to-reach alternate recipes, rare resources, and scenic spots for your next industrial monument. 

If you enjoy engineering puzzles, resource management, or simply getting lost in a game where "just 10 more minutes" turns into 4:00 AM, Satisfactory is an absolute masterpiece and an essential play.

[h2] So, I have FINALLY 100% this hardcore game, so what can I say [/h2]

I actually cannot believe I have managed to ''finish'' this gem of a game and am writing this review today. It has been 5 YEARS, since I started playing this on and off and honestly, it was one of the most excruciating yet absolutely fcking beautiful experiences I've ever had in gaming. I still have goals within the game I want to reach, but I finally unlocked my last steam achievement, so it's time to talk about it.

Noita, which means ''Witch'' in Finnish, is without a doubt one of the best rogue-likes, if not one of the Best Single Player games of all time. Hands down. I will be the first to point out, that it is one million percent the [b] Hardest [/b] rogue-like I've ever played. Everything and I mean [u] Everything [/u] in the game, wants and will eventually try to kill you. [b] Including Yourself. [/b] Honestly especially yourself. A huge chunk of my runs ended by me saying ''huh what does this do?'' a few seconds before nuking myself and my whole screen and then going ''... what exactly did I expect to happen?'' Like a true alchemist, I played with laws of nature to terrorize this worlds inhabitants with my creations and my personal knowledge of the game, right until I finished the so called ''tutorial'' (killing the ''final boss'') multiple times and achieved my first god run. After that, I unlocked the [i] True Knowledge [/i] of wiki.

Disclaimer: For the Noita elitists coming for me, No I did not finish all achievement pillars yet, but I did finish the Sun Quest without mods on my 4th God Run Attempt and am planning to also finish the 33 orb peaceful ending, so I do have some credence to speak and my golden crown. Now GET OFF MY DCK

This game is a true rogue-like game. You do not unlock perma upgrades (kinda) like more health/dmg/resistances and other stuff featured in games like Hades. Your true perma ''unlocks'', are your [u] Knowledge. [/u] The more you play, the more you know, the more ways you have to bullsht the game that constantly tries to bullsht you.
The game is centered around the historical lore of alchemy and Finnish folklore. I mean, all of the creatures and items are straight up in Finnish. It's a game all about secrets. The only heads up you get is about the controls, but that's it. Everything else? You gotta find out yourself. 99% of the time, the hard way. This game has this beautiful way of giving you a false sense of security, before absolutely obliterating you in the most unexpected way possible. You have 1 million health? Great, you're no longer a coughing baby. You're now A teenager Spartan in a cave filled with 50 wolves. You might just have a slight chance of survival. That's because there is this ''All roads lead to Rome'' mechanic, called [u] Polymorph. [/u] Even if you're an Actual God, with 99% dmg resistance, 6+ stacks of shields, invisible, with all immunities , millions of hp, infinite healing and a wand capable of violating every single human right imaginable, this nightmare of a liquid can whenever turn you into a [i] Harmless sheep [/i] and murder you in a fraction of a second. I have lost runs that were long +10 hours to that thing. Now I am deathly scared of anything pink or purple. [b] Thank you Noita. [/b]

I know this review is all over the place, but like a cracked out alchemist high on mushrooms, I could never make this review properly segmented, so bare with me please.
The story of this game is... interesting. It's cryptic to a point, where the whole community STILL can't figure out all of it's secrets. But it's INSANELY intriguing. I will not spoil anything, because finding out these things is the fun of it, but I can tell you, if I didn't use a wiki, this 100% would take A THOUSAND hours at the least. The game is IMMENSE, packed with content and the fact that [b] Every pixel [/b] reacts and can be destroyed? An absolute curse and a blessing. I have not found any game truly like this, with this depth Ever. For those comparing it to Terraria, as someone who has 1k+ hours in it, shut up. You sound dumb. Not even close. And I love Terraria.

The gameplay tho, that's where it's all at. The game on the surface is simple enough. You spawn, you travel down, game gets harder, you die, until you can travel a bit more further. But the bread and butter of the game, is [i] Wand Crafting. [/i] A lot of the time, you will spend crafting abominable wands, in which you can put an enormous 400+ spells into, their interactions, synergies and ways to kill/quickly traverse/heal/utilize them, to make your dream of finishing the Great Work of alchemists come true. The 250h of play time does not correctly show the Actual time I've spent with this game. I literally STUDIED spells and what they can do, liquid interactions, map memorizing, boss hunt strategizing, making FCKING CHECKLISTS so I don't lose track of my goals... like bruh, if I tallied all of that, the game time would be around 300-350 atleast. The game, is A LOT. Nowadays I can make maybe 50% of runs into a god run. If you need any help with the game, I strongly advise you to check out 2 content creators in specific; DunkOrSlam and FuryForged. Without them, I would not have gotten to where I got, hats off to those gentlemen.
I just want to quickly clear out by what I mean a ''God Run''. Basically when you find out a very crucial piece of knowledge, you'll realize, that you can get an enormous amount of perks, health and immunities and become virtually indestructible to most inhabitants and spells. This DOES NOT mean, you're immortal. You just became a fledgling God, that should be feared. But to Noita, you're still in the ''coughing baby vs a nuke'' situation. There is always a way to die, unless you do a tremendous amounts of work. And even then, a stray polymorph projectile that glitched through your shields can kill you. I've lost extremely long runs to this, TWICE. I accidentally turned myself into gold. Accidentally turned myself into p!ss. I ate too many hallucinogenic mushrooms and exploded. I pet my pet monster too much, it exploded from excitement, killing me.

When it comes to graphical and music design of the game, it's beauty in minimalism paired with complex gameplay, is what [u] keeps making me come back. [/u] It's very beautiful in it's simple pixelated way, as well as absolutely terrifying. It's like a toxic relationship. It breaks my heart constantly, but I keep coming back, because the sex is just too good.

Now, about the 100% journey. Oh boy. I doubt there is a game harder (atleast for me) to complete. This is a Completionist Nightmare. And it only has [b] 14 Achievements. [/b] There is just simply so much to do. Equip all perks, Find and Use all spells and kill Every enemy are obviously the hardest, with the perk one being the easiest of the three. That's because some enemies have a VERY SMALL spawn chance and some are straight up locked to spawn only during certain days of the year in REAL TIME. Aswell as some spells being rare or hidden behind quests you have to complete. Steam doesn't even mirror the True 100%, which is represented by the in game Achievement pillars. I am telling you, it took me 5 years of on and off gaming to achieve a mere Steam Achievements 100%. I have no idea if I'll ever finish all pillars.

All in all, this game is truly one of the greatest gaming experiences I've had in gaming, period. But if you're a casual gamer, it's REALLY hard. I'd advise you to watch some guides, so you're not just suffering constantly, but if you're a hardcore gamer like me, you should really give it a fair shot and go into it blind. Atleast until you beat the ''tutorial'' or get your first God Run. Then use wikis to get an exponential amount of more play time. This might straight up be the closest game to a 10/10 I've ever rated and it's not even my most favorite game.

The community is incredibly friendly. They will teach you new words in several languages, remind you that your parents are disappointed, and offer strategic advice such as:

“Delete the game.”
“Uninstall life.”
“Report mid.”
“Why no gank?”
The matchmaking system is also amazing. You can be a peaceful support player, minding your own business, and somehow get matched with a carry who has played 7,000 hours but still doesn’t know what a ward is.

Every game is an emotional journey. You experience hope, confidence, confusion, rage, acceptance, and finally queue again because surely the next match will be different.

It won’t.

Dota 2 has beautiful graphics, incredible strategy, hundreds of unique heroes, and the ability to turn your closest friends into sworn enemies within 30 seconds.

Warframe is a fascinating setting. The art direction is incredibly cohesive and distinct, the music, sound and voicework is great, and the writing establishes a lot of long term intrigue. And having watched some of the most recent content without really knowing anything about the game, it makes me want to find out why the hell a big title card update quest ends in making your space ninja kids dinner. And why their adult selves are sitting at a table with you in the past, feeding the past version of their sibling. That is a batshit crazy hook and it made me want to try and unravel what on earth gets you to that point.

But Warframe just cannot escape the fact that it is an MMO, and I just don't find Unlocking New Gear being the main pillar of gameplay to be compelling. The combat has great feedback, but its just. Not that interesting to actually play the combat. The quest stories are good, but the missions themselves are indistinguishable from the missions you grind for resources outside of some unique dialogue. And don't get me started on the new player experience. Even after the tutorial revamp, its just terrible. If you don't have a friend who's already heavily invested in Warframe to guide you through how certain systems work or when you should be expecting to get to new content, its a complete mess. Finishing the tutorial would have me think that the next thing to do is start the next quest, which will then progressively lead me through the solar system. But no, as a more experienced friend told me, the idea is actually to go and unlock most of the map, which then grants you access to the next quests. A lot of Warframe is very unintuitive to people who haven't played an MMO before, and its incredibly confusing and offputting.

I know that's just MMO gameplay, but despite how interested I am in getting through to the story and learning more about the setting and its characters, the game itself just isn't fun to me as someone who's primarily motivated by the narrative. This hasn't been my first attempt either, I've had three separate goes of trying to get into Warframe. Its unfortunate that a game that keeps capturing my attention just isn't capable of keeping me engaged. If Digital Extremes ever decide to make a Warframe game in a different format, I'd definitely be interested in trying it out.

[h1] Baldur's Gate 3: An Absolute Masterpiece [/h1]

140 Hours | PC | 54/54 Achievements

Personal Rating: 9/10

[h3] I finally played Baldur's Gate 3.[/h3]

140 hours later, with 54/54 achievements, I can confidently say this is an absolute masterpiece.

And honestly, this isn't even the type of game I usually play.

RTS/CRPG mechanics, click-to-move exploration, D&D systems and heavily choice-driven role playing aren't normally my thing. Yet somehow, Larian Studios made all of it work.

The world is incredibly rich. Every location feels like it has history, purpose and something waiting to be discovered. Exploration constantly rewards curiosity, and the sheer number of ways your decisions can affect the world is impressive.

What impressed me most is how personal the game becomes.

Every party member has their own identity, motivations, flaws, relationships and character arc, but those stories don't simply play out the same way for everyone. Your choices, relationships and decisions genuinely influence how their journeys develop.

The morality system is also exceptionally well handled. The game rarely tells you there is one obviously correct answer. Your decisions have consequences, sometimes immediately and sometimes much later, and there often isn't a clean solution.

Character creation and customisation are equally impressive. There is an enormous amount of freedom in deciding who you want your character to be, how they look, how they fight, what choices they make and ultimately what kind of story they create.

The narrative is another major achievement.

The story constantly gives you reasons to keep going while still providing answers and closure when you need them. Mysteries build naturally, character arcs intertwine with the larger narrative, and your choices continually reshape the experience.

It manages something many games struggle with:

It makes you want to see what happens next without making the journey feel like a checklist.

And the companions?

What a cast.

Thank you, Karlach, for bringing chaos, warmth and an unreasonable amount of enthusiasm.

Thank you, Gale, for somehow turning every conversation into an opportunity to explain something incredibly complicated.

Thank you, Astarion, for being... Astarion.

Thank you, Lae'zel, for reminding everyone that subtlety is apparently optional.

Thank you to Wyll, Halsin, Minthara (1 Women Army)  and everyone else who made the journey memorable.

And of course...

[b] Special thanks to Scratch.[/b]

The best boy.

No further explanation required.

And finally...

[b]Shadowheart.[/b]

Thank you for providing the ideal secluded cottage lifestyle.

Quiet.

Peaceful.

Away from everyone.

Surrounded by animals.

Honestly, that's the dream.

If the game had allowed me to retire to a secluded cottage with Shadowheart, Scratch and an unreasonable number of animals, I probably would have accepted the ending immediately.

Jokes aside, the relationships are one of the biggest reasons this adventure works so well. These characters feel like companions rather than simply party members.

THANK YOU, LARIAN STUDIOS

Thank you to Larian Studios, the developers, writers, artists, designers, voice actors, composers, testers and everyone involved in creating this game.

You didn't just make another RPG.

You created a world that players can genuinely get lost in.

A world where choices matter, characters remember what you do, failure can become part of the story, exploration is rewarded, and ridiculous decisions can somehow become some of the best moments of the entire adventure.

Even if Larian and Hasbro eventually decide to make a Baldur's Gate 4 or decide not to, I'm still incredibly grateful for what you created with BG3.

But...

Let's be honest.

Please make Baldur's Gate 4.
Hint hint.
We need more Shadowheart.

After 140 hours and 54/54 achievements, I can safely say:

Baldur's Gate 3 is a masterpiece.

Personal Rating: 9/10

I came into this expecting a type of game I normally wouldn't spend this much time with.

I left having one of the most memorable gaming adventures I've ever experienced.

Thank you, Larian.

And remember:

More Shadowheart.

[h1]Best MMORPG out there, and still going strong after 2,000+ hours[/h1]

I started playing ESO in 2020 and it's been one of my favorite games ever since. Even now I find myself coming back for long stretches. Most of my time has gone into PvE, whether that's questing or group content, with a little PvP on the side.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Content that doesn't expire[/h2]
2,000 hours in, I'm still finding content I've never touched. [b]Old content stays relevant[/b], and so does the gear you earn from it, so you never feel like you're grinding on a treadmill that resets. I have several characters for different types of content, though you can now swap between multiple builds on a single character instantly, so that's optional.
ESO was my first Elder Scrolls game. It got me hooked on the lore and led me to Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim.

[h2]Great for solo players, even better with people[/h2]
I started out completely solo and only did group content with randoms, and that was a great experience on its own. The community is friendly and dedicated. People are quick to help and genuinely enjoy doing it.

My advice to everyone, no matter how you like to play: [b]talk to people and join at least one guild.[/b] Organized group content has been a blessing for me, and I've made friends I still talk to outside of ESO.

[h2]Addons and performance[/h2]
Addons make a big difference for the UI in group content and add plenty of quality-of-life features. If you're just starting out, I'd recommend [b]Minion[/b]. Console players seem to manage fine without addons, so it's not strictly necessary.

The game also ran well on the laptop I started on.

[h2]Fair monetization[/h2]
Since old content stays relevant, you don't really miss out by skipping ESO Plus. I subscribe for the extra bag and bank space because I run a master crafter, and I love the housing system. But it's a convenience, [i]not[/i] something you need to keep up with the content.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Verdict: Recommended[/h2]

PROBLEM 1: BAD EXPLANATIONS. I had high hopes for this game, but ultimately walked away disappointed because they give you massive tools and don't explain how to set them up. After 30 hours of happily plugging away at goals, it became clear that scaling up was necessary. To avoid dozens of hours of manual production (literally watching small numbers tick away at hand operated crafter, like a cookie clicker), more power is needed than plants can provide. Plants run out and gathering them is a PAIN to begin with. That means coal is necessary, but HOW do coal generators get going? I ended up frustrated, searching the internet for a quick explanation, but NO ONE WHO PLAYS THIS GAME and NO ONE WHO MADE THIS GAME feel like giving a step-by-step setup guide. Water is needed, coal is needed, and then you flip it one, right? WRONG. You need to jumpstart it, but if you do that the breakers pop. Sorry, but this magically constructed machine cannot jumpstart itself and there is no UI element to guide you through. Online, the community stops explaining with "hook it up" or "you need water and coal and power lines". Yeah. No shiz. But why doesn't it work? Your guess is as good as mine. For a massive game with tons of potential, this is a MAJOR oversight in explanation. In the official subreddit, the most common comment about coal generation is that they need better explanation... yet no one supplies that information in the sub. It's like looking at github fior the first time... in game form. Not fun.

PROBLEM 2: CONTROLLER SUPPORT

It's a game. There are plenty of things that DO work on a controller, but not everything can be done with a controller. In its current form, you will need a keyboard and mouse to do the simplest interactions with the most important system: the upgrade module. Let me say that again: You cannot play this game on just a controller. You can't. Simply navigating a menu has not been streamlined for... you know... video game players with video game pads. If it weren't so simple of a need, I wouldn't bring it up here. You can navigate some menus but not others. You can utilize a game pad for everything except that new thing you worked so hard for, and god help you if don't try the mouse out of frustration. You'll be stuck, wondering what button to push to make the damn thing function.

In the end, this game runs great for a lot of people and I applaud them, but the limitations of the dev team begin at making the game accessible. They don't explain things well AT ALL. Truly, this is the worst onboarding I've seen in a professionally developed game and the failure is systemic (not localized to one gap in knowledge but EVERYWHERE in this game). Finally, the controller support is woefully inadequate.

Give this game another five years to cook. Skip it until the community fixes it.

I feel very conflicted on Noita, but I don't think any part of me thinks negatively about the actual game... if that makes any sense. This is a fantastic and brilliant game with both tons of creativity and understanding of what makes a procedurally generated game fun. Building and tinkering with wands is great, there's a ton of spells to choose from, and things feel pretty well balanced in terms of damage values and choices. You can make a lot out of a little, slightly tweaking the base wand you get at the start of the game or concocting some buzzsaw monstrosity that tears through everything including yourself. On the other hand though, the pure chaos of everything going on makes living or dying feel almost truly random at times. You will spend probably 30% of your total game time either on fire or poisoned, and no matter how good your run is going somebody can shoot a light fixture in the next room, have it ricochet and fly into your room, the loose wires from the light shocking the metal you're standing on and stunlocking you which kills you instantly. There's no way to heal unless you complete a level or get a random perk that heals you (of which there are only a handful), so the aforementioned fire and poison damage is pretty horrific when you accidentally step in 0.2cm of acidic blood for a half second and suddenly have to watch yourself take 20 damage. Because of this the game is pretty brutal, although the levels are really short if you speedrun through them. I wouldn't call Noita a "mixed bag" at all, I think this is one of the best roguelites i've played, but it does make me mad a lot and a lot of great runs have ended because of something completely beyond my control. 

One bonus i'll mention that is maybe one of my favourite things about the game is the sheer amount of secrets and hidden mechanics this game has. It's not really something advertised too much but it honestly feels like half of the game is stuff that is completely hidden from the player. For example, I accidentally found out there's an entire alchemy mechanic/system in this game just because I wanted to look up diamond and why I couldn't pick it up like gold. I haven't beaten the game yet but you will likely be finding strange things that I can only assume are objects to get a better ending, and you can traverse biomes that feel entirely optional. You can view this as things to discover and figure out yourself, or use https://noita.wiki.gg/ , I think both approaches could be fun depending on the type of person you are. Noita is a game where you legitimately feel like you learn something every run you do. The copious amount of secrets coupled with the extremely hard difficulty really makes Noita's appearance on the "finnish people are weird and sadistic" meme make a lot of sense.

It is hard for me to get invested in characters. In games, I'm kind of an asshole because if someone does ONE thing that is rude, I hate them and there is no redeeming themselves lol. But I really like meeting new characters in this game. In fact, I think it is the main reason I keep playing. I love the dialogue, how people react, hearing their stories, and just seeing how they interact with you. It's really fun.

The characters aren't cut-and-dry "I am a hero and I am good." There are characters that are like, "I fucking hate you and want to skin you alive, but sure, I'll join your party."

I also find it really cool that characters will comment on things you do. For example (this is very early on, but still, minor spoilers, character names)

[spoiler] Shadowheart often has a comment after you speak to Gale or Lae'zel about how she doesn't trust either of them and asks what you were talking about. [/spoiler]

It just adds something to the experience where usually in games you talk to someone, and then that's it. Here, it feels like the characters are actually paying attention to what you're doing or who you are talking to.

I don't want to lead you to believe this game is perfect, though. There are awkward moments in dialogue where things don't line up and it feels very "video-gamey." The environment looks great in many areas, but there are times where textures are just floating above other objects, or things clip into the floor or the walls.

I am also not a huge fan of how much RNG is in this game. You have ways to manage it, but it can get annoying when you have been strategic in how you approach combat; getting the high ground, grouping enemies, giving them status effects, stunning them. and then when it's time to attack, the strategy meant nothing because you rolled a 3 or simply miss even though it was an 90% chance to hit. Or their saving throw magically works EVERY SINGLE TIME.

Also, for people like myself who feel the need to open every single barrel or box, this game can become kind of a nightmare. I can comfortably say that you do NOT need to loot every single thing you find. It takes everything in me to not think, "Yeah, but what if there is a quest that requires this scratched plate?"

I am progressively getting more okay with skipping past vases, pots, and shelves, but I'd be lying if I said I don't break into a cold sweat and start trembling and foaming at the mouth like a heroin addict waiting for their next fix.

Overall, highly recommend the game, but have realistic expectations. This is not the perfect game. It's a damn good one, but expecting perfection will only lead to disappointment.

Dota 2 has slowly lost its identity.

Over the years, the game has become more and more similar to League of Legends, with increasingly overloaded heroes, ridiculous ability upgrades, and mechanics that feel completely out of place compared to what made Dota unique in the first place.

Aghanim’s Shard and Aghanim’s Scepter are a good example. Instead of simply improving or complementing a hero, they can completely change how abilities work and add layers of complexity that often feel absurd rather than interesting.

The same goes for hero passives. Take Lion, who can permanently stack damage through his abilities, or Slark, who can permanently steal enemy Agility. These mechanics may sound interesting on paper, but they contribute to a game where heroes increasingly feel like they have their own mini-games and endless scaling mechanics.

Dota used to stand out because of its unique, unpredictable and strategic gameplay. Now, more and more heroes have overloaded kits, permanent stat stacking, ability upgrades, multiple sources of scaling, and mechanics that make the game feel closer to League of Legends than the Dota I remember.

The problem isn't that the game has changed. Games have to evolve. The problem is that Dota seems to have evolved in a direction that makes it lose what made it Dota.

At this point, I don't feel like I'm playing the same game I originally loved.

At the time of writing this, I have 481 hours in Baldur's Gate 3. There's a fairly good chance that by the time you're reading it, I'll have more.

You'd think after that amount of time I'd have experienced almost everything the game has to offer. Somehow, I don't think I have—and that might be the greatest compliment I can give it.

Character creation alone is something I've sunk an embarrassing amount of time into. Between appearance, class, stats and proficiencies, the game gets you invested in your character before you've really even started. Across all my playthroughs I've easily spent more than ten hours just creating characters, and somehow I still enjoy doing it.

Coming from more linear games, I probably haven't even taken advantage of the full "you can do almost anything" nature of BG3. What impresses me is how often the developers seem to have anticipated what the player might try. Decisions can have consequences immediately, hours later, or much further into the game, and the amount of work required to accommodate so many possibilities is ridiculous.

I've never actually played as one of the Origin companions because I prefer letting them remain their own characters, although I love that the option exists. Most of my earlier playthroughs were custom characters until I properly discovered Dark Urge. Since then, Durge has basically become my default. Apparently I just really enjoy playing a murderous soul desperately trying to redeem themselves and become an antihero.

Combat was also new territory for me. I was much more accustomed to real-time combat with the option to pause, but BG3 completely sold me on turn-based combat. Positioning, preparation, builds, buffs, the environment and seemingly insignificant abilities can completely change an encounter. Once you realise how much freedom you're actually being given, fights become less about simply beating enemies and more about figuring out exactly how you want to beat them.

The companions are another massive strength, although after enough playthroughs I think everyone eventually finds their favourites and shamelessly neglects everyone else. I certainly have. The romance system deserves praise too. Relationships actually feel like something you build through shared experiences rather than selecting the correct dialogue three times until someone decides they're in love with you. I only wish those relationships had a little more influence on the wider story and ending.

The performances help enormously. The voice cast is excellent—even the narrator became a fan favourite—and there's an impressive amount of personality in tiny animations and expressions. Lae'zel's eye roll deserves it's own shout out.

After 481 hours, obviously the locations have become very familiar and there are still pieces of content I've either skipped or never fully explored. Yet the story has held up remarkably well. The central plot itself is actually quite straightforward; what's extraordinary is the number of different paths the game gives you between its beginning and end.

That's probably why I'm still playing it.

481 hours later, I'm still creating characters, still starting campaigns and still finding different ways through the same enormous adventure.

And I'm definitely going to add another few hours tonight.

The Good: Combat and Castle BuildingAction-Packed Combat: Fast, responsive, and demanding, the combat relies on precise dodges, weapon combos, and active spell casting rather than mindless button-mashing.
Boss Progression: Tracking and defeating over 50 unique V-Blood bosses acts as the ultimate dopamine-fueled reward system, unlocking fresh powers, crafting recipes, and magical abilities.
Immersive Building: Constructing massive multi-story Gothic castles serves as both a functional crafting hub and a satisfying dark fantasy home base.
The Vampire Fantasy: Managing the dynamic day-night cycle—where sunlight burns your flesh and forces you into the shadows—creates constant tension and urgency during exploration.
The Bad: Pacing and GrindLate-Game Slowdown: The early-to-mid game pacing is phenomenal, but the late game can suffer from an increased grind and heavy material farming.
Inventory Management: Hoarding multiple tiers of specialized crafting components can turn late-night base organization into an exhausting chore.
Limited Storytelling: The lore takes a backseat in true "Dark Souls" fashion, relying mostly on item tooltips and brief dialogue rather than an active narrative.

VerdictV Rising offers roughly 50 to 80 hours of highly polished, addictive gameplay. It succeeds brilliantly as a solo or co-op experience, fixing the usually dull combat found in traditional survival crafting titles.

Title: A Masterclass in Isometric Malice, Grinding Incompetence, and Betrayed Devotion: The Absolute Extinction Event of Path of Exile

I used to believe in this game with every fiber of my being. That unwavering, misplaced faith is now my deepest, most agonizing, and most humiliating wound. I didn’t just play Path of Exile; I consumed it, breathed it, and sacrificed thousands of waking and sleeping hours to its dark, fog-choked atlas corridors, treating its punishing skill trees and brutal map grinds as a sacred second home. I spent years defending Grinding Gear Games' glacial patch cycles, actively rationalizing their glaring resistance penalties, and aggressively dismissing the dark warning signs whispering through the community as the mere whining of disgruntled casuals. I was a foot soldier of a cult-like devotion, utterly convinced that this was a world crafted by visionary indie creators who understood the fragile, beautiful bond between an ARPG developer and a passionate player base.

How intensely, unforgivably, and pathetically foolish I was.

What the public sees on the store page is a legendary, deep-as-an-ocean action RPG—a modest isometric masterpiece born from years of dedicated work claiming to channel the ultimate hardcore ARPG experience. But beneath that paper-thin, calculatedly deceptive facade lies a predatory, aggressively hostile ecosystem designed to exploit your time, weaponize your passion, harvest your free community wiki labor, and ultimately punish you for the singular crime of actually engaging deeply with their high-tier endgame loop. The harsh reality of Path of Exile isn't a love letter to the genre; it’s an institutionalized insult, a middle finger to anyone foolish enough to invest hundreds of hours into its structurally hollow and fundamentally broken framework.

Let’s pull back the curtain and talk about the unspoken horror that haunts the upper echelons of this game: the arbitrary, indiscriminate, and utterly cowardly ban hammer and trade restrictions that target the most dedicated players the moment they master currency farming or fast mapping. For weeks, the veteran group chats whispered about it in paralyzing dread. Dedicated players—the exact backbone of the economy, the people organizing multi-stash trading syndicates, keeping multiplayer trade websites alive, and filling the community forums with complex build guides—would vanish overnight, or find their accounts locked behind an impenetrable wall of developer silence. Their names were silently scrubbed from ladders, their stash tabs vaporized, and their accounts flagged for abnormal macro usage. I scoffed at the victims. I arrogantly told myself that I played completely legitimately, that hundreds of hours of honest boss killing, meticulous currency management, and raw survival persistence would serve as my shield.

Then my inevitable turn came.

At level 98, deep inside a high-tier heavily-modded map I had rolled a thousand times for an elusive, mathematically insulting rare drop, the screen seized violently. The dreaded, ominous network disconnection warning flashed across the UI, followed instantly by a forced, unceremonious dump to the login screen. My hands shook uncontrollably as I scrambled to re-enter my credentials, hit enter, and was greeted by the most infuriating, gut-wrenching, soul-crushing message any ARPG veteran can possibly receive: “This account has been banned.”

No warning. No specific rule violation cited. No log data provided. No human review whatsoever. Just an abrupt, summary execution carried out by a completely inept, automated detection algorithm that apparently cannot comprehend the basic reality that a human being might actually want to play an ARPG for more than ten hours a day or use third-party trade macros. I poured my bleeding, broken heart into a meticulously written support ticket—detailing my exact playtime, my absolute adherence to fair play, and my profound, heartbreaking disappointment. No appeal process. No human being willing to look at your case, check your server logs, or grant you basic respect. High-level combat balancing is practically non-existent, featuring lazy one-shot mechanics that demand artificial difficulty rather than tactical engagement. The repetitive grind quickly morphs from an exciting loot hunt into an unrewarding, punishing, soul-crushing chore. Every single system feels half-baked, held together with digital duct tape and the nostalgic goodwill of players who desperately want it to succeed, only to be brutally kicked in the teeth the second they cross the finish line.

My level 98 character—complete with painstakingly optimized passive trees, hard-earned mirror-tier equipment, hundreds of hours of irreplaceable memories, and genuine friendships forged in guild chats—was erased in a single, callous click. All of it gone, vaporized into the ether by developers who couldn’t care less if every single veteran player walked away.

Because if you actually stay, if you actually grind, and if you dare to love this game too much, the only reward waiting for you at the top is a permanent ban screen and a developer who refuses to look.

Path of Exile isn't just another failed live-service experiment; it is a meticulously constructed psychological trap for the devoted and an eternal monument to bad-faith development. Save your time, save your sanity, protect your peace, and stay far, far away from this toxic wasteland. Having played this game for a while, there's plenty of fantastic things for me to say.

For starters, the entire concept is just great. Dwarves in space extracting a fuckton of resources from a planet teeming with life whose only goal is to prevent that. You and 3 other fellas get shitfaced, grab your guns, and mow them down like grass.

The caves use procedural generation, the objectives of each mission swap out every 30 minutes, enemy spawn pools are randomized, and most caves have some sort of bonus objective in them, so no two missions are alike. And while we're on the topic of level design, the different biomes (each packed with their own unique hazards) all look cool as hell. I've been impressed enough by some of these caves to take a few screenshots over the years!

The combat in this game is awesome. If you like horde shooters, this game will certainly be right up your alley. Additionally, the weapons feel VERY satisfying to use, particularly in their sound design (ESPECIALLY the scout's M1000, basically an M1 garand down to the "PING!"). Weapon modification allows you to take any of the weapons, customize them visually, and tune them to your play style, there's not really many "wrong" combinations, and these modifications (outside of overclocks) are very easy to unlock, meaning that newer players don't necessarily have less firepower than more experienced players, which makes multiplayer even with players of wildly different levels still feel very fair.

On the topic of multiplayer, this game has a rather pleasant community! Like all games, you still come across the occasional shithead, but honestly i think that's happened like maybe once or twice in my thousand hours of playing. Older players are always willing to guide the newer ones, and you always get the feeling that everyone's just here to have fun and nothing more. As a woman i should know a thing or two about dealing with toxic players hahaha

As for performance, on my somewhat old laptop (depending on who you ask. I don't think 6 years is too much) i can get between 80-120fps on the space rig and 60-100fps during missions, all with medium settings (which in my opinion still look nice). Stutters are incredibly rare and I'm sure they would be practically nonexistent with someone who has better hardware than mine. The game is also shockingly small, requiring only 3GB of space according to system requirements. On my system, it takes up approximately 5.6GB, and that includes the cached shaders and proton prefix that comes with playing on a Linux system (which while we're on that subject, I've played this game on Windows 10, Linux Mint 23, and CachyOS, and honestly CachyOS has given me noticeably  better performance in this game compared to Windows 10. Linux Mint 23 was roughly in the middle. Keep in mind this is anecdotal).

The price is good too. I'd say this game is well worth it at full price, but of course it goes on sale quite often, usually you can score it for only $9 (which is what I did, and then I went on to buy most of the DLC because honestly the devs have earned my support with the amount of free content they've provided us in the form of updates). Seriously, those free updates are great, the season passes provide a long-term objective to keep you busy even after you complete your assignments, you get hella rewards, and to combat FOMO, you can complete the passes for all previous seasons at any time you like. So do it all at your leisure.

As for the things I dislike about the game, really my only complaint has to be the perks system. I feel like it's such an underbaked feature that has almost no impact on gameplay, save for a couple ones that feel frustrating to play without (such as resupplier or dash). Some of them are just straight up useless too. And you unlock all of them so early on, you just end up collecting perk points that end up doing literally nothing. Oh yeah, the built in mod loader is also weirdly frustrating to use in ways that i cannot articulate but i know that it's far from an unpopular opinion.

Finally, to throw in some extra stuff I like, there's fun character customization options, a banger soundtrack, and all sorts of toys in the space rig. And god is it so satisfying to mine ore and see the glittery chunks go flying!!

To enjoy the game rather than stress over it, I recommend playing on PVE servers, especially for beginners and solo players.
The game offers many features that can only really be used on PVE servers, as they are either useless in PVP or simply impossible to make use of under the constant threat of attack.
Here, you can safely build a base without the risk of losing it to a raid, learn the game mechanics, visit various monuments on the map, where you’ll have to fight some pretty challenging NPCs and solve puzzles. Many PVE servers have PVP zones, houses with NPCs that can be raided, and on some servers you can even call in NPCs to raid your house and play on the defensive.
PVE servers are just an excellent sandbox.

I STRONGLY DO NOT recommend playing on OFFICIAL servers:

All official servers are PVP ONLY and are designed ONLY for clans. This is the developers’ own policy. Read the descriptions of the latest updates (it doesn’t matter when this review was written), and you’ll see that they are useless for solo players because they simply won’t be able to make use of most of the new features.
And if you nevertheless decide to play solo on an official server, you’ll be a punching bag here.
You’ll be killed for fun simply because they can. There will always be more opponents against you, and the enemy will always have better weapons and equipment. Clans will raid your base because they have an excess of explosives and nowhere to use them. They don’t care how well your base is protected, where it is located, or how many resources are inside it (they always have far more resources than you do).

As an exception, you can try UNOFFICIAL (modded) PVP servers where resource gathering has been made easier. This noticeably levels the playing field between solo players and clans — everyone ends up with plenty of resources, regardless of the number of players on their team.

Dota 2 is one of the deepest games in terms of how much players need to assess gameplay over an extended amount of time. While other games like FPS’s and fighting games are always played with a time limit, MOBAs will only finish once a base falls.

Dota 2 sports a bigger map with limited teleporting compared to League of Legends so the game has a painstaking process of resource and economy management. From the gold and experience you get from killing creeps, camps, and opponent heroes, you invest in the best items possible.

By the late game, things start to change drastically for both teams. Dota 2 has an obsession with ascension, giving players trillions of ways to go about besting their opponents.

For essential items, teams can purchase Black King Bar, Lotus Orb, and Linken’s Sphere to deter any incoming debuff. There’s also a long list of tier 5 neutral items that players can pick up from creep camps after the 60-minute mark.

Heroes also get stronger and stronger with talent trees that provide amplified stats on either skills or attributes. Players also have the ability to prolong engagements with the Buyback option, which truly matters in the late game where death timers reach minutes.

Looking at the map, you have bounties, runes, and outposts to capture as well as Roshan who provides the Aegis of the Immortal — an item that resurrects a fallen hero to full health and mana — and some cheese.

Needless to say, Dota 2 doesn’t shy away from giving limitless opportunities to players and teams. With no real time limit to the game, you’ll experience thrilling wombo combos and defiant item builds in every match that you play.

Going seven years strong as a casual Dota 2 player, I’m still dumbfounded at a lot of things that I see. It might even take another seven years for me to nail everything down to a tee.

Satisfactory is basically engineering crack.

You start off placing a miner and a couple of constructors, thinking you’ve got everything under control. A few hours later you’re standing on top of a massive factory staring at 14 conveyor belts, three power grids and a train network wondering where your life went.

The best part is how rewarding it feels to solve problems. Every bottleneck leads to another redesign, every upgrade opens up new possibilities, and every “temporary” setup somehow becomes permanent until you eventually tear the whole thing down and build it properly.

The building system gives you a ridiculous amount of freedom. You can make huge clean megafactories, compact efficient layouts, giant towers, long-distance rail networks or complete conveyor spaghetti. There’s no single correct way to play, which is a huge part of the appeal.

Exploration is surprisingly good too. The map is massive, visually stunning, and full of resources and areas that give you a reason to expand instead of staying in one spot forever.

It’s relaxing, stressful, creative, technical and ridiculously addictive all at the same time.

One of the easiest games to lose hundreds of hours in without even noticing.

Highly recommended.

And yes, you will rebuild the same factory five times because one machine is running at 97% efficiency.
