Guild Wars 2 is one of those games that makes you wonder how something with so much content can feel so completely lifeless.

The world is huge, yet somehow it feels empty. You run around doing events, collecting random objectives, pressing the same abilities, and pretending you're having an adventure. After a while, it starts feeling less like an MMO and more like a very expensive walking simulator with combat attached.

The combat system looks impressive at first, but eventually you realize that most encounters are just visual chaos. There are explosions everywhere, dozens of effects covering the screen, bosses with enormous health bars, and half the time you have no idea what actually killed you.

The progression is another joke. You level up, get your gear, and then... congratulations, you've basically reached the destination. Instead of making progression exciting, GW2 constantly gives you the feeling that you're grinding for cosmetics, currencies, achievements and another collection nobody asked for.

And the UI? Absolutely criminal. Currencies, tabs, menus, inventory clutter, achievements, collections, masteries, crafting materials... You spend almost as much time navigating menus as you do actually playing the game.

The community is friendly, I'll give it that. But even the nicest community in the world can't fix the feeling that you're playing an MMO designed around keeping you busy rather than making you excited.

Guild Wars 2 isn't a terrible game because it lacks content. It's frustrating precisely because it has so much content and somehow manages to make most of it feel like a checklist.

After spending enough time with it, I wasn't asking myself, "What should I do next?"

I was asking myself:

"Why am I still playing this?"

2/10 for the amount of menus, currencies and chores required to pretend this is fun.

they have destabilized society, have made life unfulfilling, have subjected human beings to
indignities, have led to widespread psychological suffering (in the Third World to physical
suffering as well) and have inflicted severe damage on the natural world. The continued
development of technology will worsen the situation. It will certainly subject human beings to
greater indignities and inflict greater damage on the natural world, it will probably lead to greater
social disruption and psychological suffering, and it may lead to increased physical suffering even
in “advanced” countries.

2. The industrial-technological system may survive or it may break down. If it survives, it may
eventually achieve a low level of physical and psychological suffering, but only after passing
through a long and very painful period of adjustment and only at the cost of permanently reducing
human beings and many other living organisms to engineered products and mere cogs in the social
machine. Furthermore, if the system survives, the consequences will be inevitable: There is no
way of reforming or modifying the system so as to prevent it from depriving people of dignity and
autonomy.

3. If the system breaks down the consequences will still be very painful. But the bigger the system
grows the more disastrous the results of its breakdown will be, so if it is to break down it had best
break down sooner rather than later.

4. We therefore advocate a revolution against the industrial system. This revolution may or may
not make use of violence; it may be sudden or it may be a relatively gradual process spanning a
few decades. We can’t predict any of that. But we do outline in a very general way the measures
that those who hate the industrial system should take in order to prepare the way for a revolution
against that form of society. This is not to be a political revolution. Its object will be to overthrow
not governments but the economic and technological basis of the present society.

5. In this article we give attention to only some of the negative developments that have grown out
of the industrial-technological system. Other such developments we mention only briefly or
ignore altogether. This does not mean that we regard these other developments as
unimportant. For practical reasons we have to confine our discussion to areas that have received
insufficient public attention or in which we have something new to say. For example, since there
are well-developed environmental and wilderness movements, we have written very little about
environmental degradation or the destruction of wild nature, even though we consider these to be
highly important.

Hunt: Showdown 1896 – A Masterclass in Tension

There are games that entertain you, and then there are games that make you hold your breath.

Hunt: Showdown 1896 belongs firmly in the latter category.

Crytek’s brutal extraction shooter creates something remarkably rare in modern gaming: an experience where every footstep, every distant gunshot, and every decision feels like it could determine whether you walk away victorious or leave everything behind.

On paper, Hunt: Showdown 1896 is a game about hunting monsters, collecting bounties, and surviving against other players. In practice, it is a game about fear, patience, instinct, and consequences.

And that is precisely where its brilliance lies.

 Atmosphere Is the Real Weapon

The moment you enter the dark and unforgiving wilderness, it becomes clear that this is not simply a setting.

The bayou is alive.

Fog hangs between the trees. Wooden buildings creak in the wind. Distant animals react to movement. Somewhere beyond the darkness, another hunter may be listening to your every move.

Hunt’s sound design is exceptional. A broken branch, a barking dog, a distant gunshot, or footsteps on a wooden floor can be more terrifying than any monster the game throws at you.

Few multiplayer games understand the power of silence quite like Hunt does.

A quiet minute in Hunt can be more intense than an entire action sequence.

Gunplay With Real Consequences

Hunt: Showdown 1896 does not treat combat like a traditional arena shooter.

Weapons are heavy, deliberate, and unforgiving. Ammunition is limited, reloads take time, and every shot carries weight.

Miss your shot, and you may have just given away your position.

Pull the trigger at the wrong moment, and you could lose everything.

That sense of consequence transforms even the simplest gunfight into a high-stakes encounter. Success is not purely about having the fastest reflexes. It is about staying calm when your instincts are screaming at you to panic.

The gunplay feels powerful precisely because it refuses to be effortless.

## The Other Hunters Are the Real Monsters

The creatures roaming the world are dangerous.

But they are rarely the most frightening thing you will encounter.

That honor belongs to the other players.

Once multiple teams begin competing for the same bounty, Hunt becomes something much more than a shooter. It becomes a psychological battle.

Do you attack?

Do you wait?

Do you let another team fight the boss and strike when they are weakened?

Do you risk revealing your position for a better shot?

There is rarely a perfect answer, and that uncertainty is what makes Hunt so compelling.

The greatest victories are not always the ones where you kill the most players.

Sometimes, they are the victories where you never fire a shot at all.

 A World That Encourages Stories

One of Hunt: Showdown 1896’s greatest strengths is that its best moments cannot be scripted.

You might spend several minutes stalking another team through the fog, neither side willing to make the first move.

You might hear footsteps approaching from behind and realize your enemy has been tracking you for minutes.

You might land the final shot with your last round and escape with seconds to spare.

These are the moments that stick with you.

They become stories you remember long after the match is over.

And that, more than anything, is the mark of an exceptional game.

Brutal, Difficult, and Better Because of It

Hunt: Showdown 1896 is not a game designed to make you feel powerful.

It wants you to feel vulnerable.

New players will die. Often. Sometimes without fully understanding how or where the enemy found them. The learning curve can be steep, and the game demands a level of patience that many modern shooters have abandoned.

But when everything finally clicks, the experience becomes incredibly rewarding.

You begin to recognize sounds.

You begin to understand player behavior.

You begin to predict movement instead of simply reacting to it.

At that point, Hunt stops feeling like a conventional shooter and starts feeling like a game of chess played with rifles.

A Shooter That Refuses to Follow the Crowd

In an industry constantly pushing for faster movement, bigger maps, more explosions, and increasingly chaotic firefights, Hunt: Showdown 1896 takes a completely different approach.

It slows down.

It creates tension instead of spectacle.

It lets silence breathe.

And most importantly, it trusts the player to create the excitement.

That is a bold design philosophy, but it pays off spectacularly.

 Verdict

Hunt: Showdown 1896 is one of the most atmospheric and uncompromising multiplayer shooters available.

It demands patience. It punishes mistakes. It can be frustrating, unforgiving, and brutally unfair.

But when it works, it delivers a level of tension that few games can replicate.

This is not simply a shooter.

It is a game about uncertainty.

About listening to the darkness and wondering whether the next sound you hear will be your salvation—or your death.

And when you finally escape with the bounty, battered and exhausted, knowing that one wrong decision could have cost you everything, the victory feels earned in a way that few games can match.

Hunt: Showdown 1896 doesn’t just ask you to survive. It asks whether you have the nerve to keep going when everything is on the line.

Greetings, Guardians. 

My name is Reisender—some of you might know me from Trials, LFG raids, or weekly GM Nightfalls. Destiny has been, and always will be, a part of my life story. 
The memories made in this game are likely just as sacred to others as they are to me. Those evening raids with friends, earning that first Title, and foremost, of course reaching the Lighthouse for the first time. 
Early attempts at solo dungeons, finally nailing that Flawless run these are the moments that made this game so special. 
The wonderful early days of Destiny 1 on Venus, followed by Destiny 2’s Spire of Stars, Saturn, and the interconnected story spanning both games. 
However, ever since the Forsaken DLC, when we sadly lost Cayde (Rest in Peace) some of us noticed how Bungie let the game deteriorate.
Not because of the developers themselves, but because of upper management. 
A franchise slowly killed off and fed a diet of increasingly recycled content until most players were fed up with it. 
Seriously, who thought it was a brilliant idea to remove the Red War as the introduction to D2? That was and remains the best possible story introduction D2 could have had. 
But anyway, I don’t want to badmouth anyone else's gaming experience. 

Now, after nearly 14,000 hours, my journey is coming to an end. 
I want to thank my clan for the wonderful moments and fun memories. 
We were a loyal team for the past eight years. 
Thanks to all the Guardians out there who continue to protect and cherish the Tower. 
Say hello to Ikora, Banshee, and Zavala for me. 
And let’s not forget Ada and those beautiful armor ornaments, of course. 
I wish all new and continuing Guardians great success and fun in the worlds of Destiny.
Enjoy the game to the fullest and hold tight to those beautiful moments. 
Signing off Reisender.

[h2]The Factory Must Grow.[/h2]

[b]Current playtime: 461.4 hours – and rising rapidly.[/b]

I bought Factorio because I thought I was getting a game about automation.

What I actually got was an unpaid full-time job as a [b]factory planner, logistics manager, railway engineer, and professional train accident victim.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h3]It all starts so peacefully...[/h3]

A few miners.
A few furnaces.
A few belts.

[i]“This time, I’m going to build everything properly.”[/i]

Remember that sentence.

It’s probably the last time you’ll ever believe yourself.

Less than two hours later, there’s a yellow belt carrying copper halfway across the factory, three underground belts desperately trying to save the design, and somewhere there’s a single inserter that nobody remembers the purpose of.

But it works.

[b]So we don’t touch it.[/b]

[b]Spaghetti successfully established.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

Eventually, you discover main buses, trains, bots, and circuit networks and start thinking you finally understand Factorio.

[b]You don’t.[/b]

You build more iron production.

Now you’re short on copper.

You build more copper.

Now you’re short on green circuits.

You build more green circuits.

Now you’re short on iron.

...

Okay.

[b]More iron.[/b]

[h2]THE FACTORY MUST GROW.[/h2]

[hr][/hr]

[h3]And then Space Age comes along.[/h3]

Now you’re no longer limited to admiring your terrible organization on Nauvis.

You can spread it across [b]multiple planets and even into space.[/b]

[i]Progress![/i]

Eventually, you’ll spend 45 minutes making a production line 3% more efficient while the machine right next to it has been sitting idle for six hours because you forgot to place an inserter.

But that can wait.

[b]The 3% was important.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Of course, there are enemies too.[/h3]

Biters, for example.

But they’re harmless compared to the natural predator of every experienced Factorio player:

[h2]THE TRAIN.[/h2]

461 hours of experience mean absolutely nothing when you cross the tracks without looking.

[i]*BONK*[/i]

[b]Problem solved.[/b]

Unfortunately, you were the problem.

[hr][/hr]

And eventually, you reach the point where you ask yourself:

[quote]Why do I even need more science?[/quote]

The answer is:

[h2]YES.[/h2]

Why produce 1,000 SPM when you could produce 2,000?

Why 2,000 when you could produce 5,000?

Why have I spent the last two days doing nothing else?

[h1]GREAT SHOOTER - RIDICULOUS SKILL GAP[/h1]

Apex Legends is actually a really good shooter.

The gunplay feels great, the Legends are interesting and the movement can be incredibly satisfying.

But the movement is also one of the reasons I eventually lost interest.

[h1]>>> THE MOVEMENT SKILL GAP IS INSANE <<<[/h1]

There are players doing:

* Tap strafes
* Superglides
* Wall bounces
* Movement combinations I don't even know the name of

Meanwhile I'm just trying to shoot the guy.

[b]I never properly learned most of these techniques.[/b]

And yes, I understand:

They require skill.

They require practice.

And if someone spends hundreds of hours mastering them, they deserve to be better at them than me.

But at some point it becomes ridiculous.

I don't want to spend dozens of hours in a training area practicing extremely specific inputs just so I can move like the people I am fighting.

[h1]HIGH SKILL CEILING = GOOD

NEEDING A MOVEMENT DEGREE TO COMPETE = NOT SO GOOD[/h1]

For experienced players, this depth is probably one of the best parts of Apex.

Being able to master movement that most players cannot do must feel amazing.

But for newer or more casual players, the difference can be brutal.

Sometimes you are not fighting someone who is simply better at aiming.

[b]You are fighting someone who appears to have unlocked a different physics engine.[/b]

And that is where Apex can become frustrating.

[h2]THE GOOD:[/h2]

* Excellent gunplay
* Very satisfying movement
* Interesting Legends
* Great team fights
* Extremely high skill ceiling
* Mastering the game can probably feel incredible

[h2]THE BAD:[/h2]

* Massive difference between casual and experienced players
* Advanced movement requires ridiculous amounts of practice
* New players can feel completely outclassed
* Some mechanics feel like something you have to specifically study instead of naturally learning by playing

I still think Apex Legends is a good game.

[b]I just don't want to enroll in Apex University to learn how to walk properly.[/b]

Maybe one day I will come back.

But if I see someone bounce off three walls, change direction in mid-air and delete me before I even understand what happened...

I'm going back to the lobby.

Rating: 8/10 — I hate this game. I also can't stop playing it.

Dota 2 is one of the greatest games ever made.

It is also one of the most mentally exhausting, rage-inducing, time-consuming pieces of shit you can voluntarily install on your computer.

And somehow, both things are true.

The first thing you need to understand about Dota 2 is that this isn't a game you casually play.

You don't "play one game."

You play one game, lose because your mid died three times before minute 10, tell yourself "okay, last game."

Then you queue again.

You lose again.

Now you're angry.

So naturally, you queue for another game because apparently the solution to losing Dota is more Dota.

The Good

When Dota 2 works, it's fucking beautiful.

There is an absurd amount of depth in this game. Hundreds of heroes, ridiculous item combinations, positioning, timings, map control, farming patterns, vision, counter-picks, spell interactions and team coordination.

A single decision can completely change a game.

You can be getting destroyed for 30 minutes and suddenly find one perfect team fight.

One Ravage.

One Chronosphere.

One Black Hole.

One perfectly timed save.

One buyback.

Suddenly the enemy's entire advantage disappears.

That feeling is fucking incredible.

Few multiplayer games can give you that kind of satisfaction.

And the best part?

There isn't always one correct way to win.

You can split push.

You can team fight.

You can rat.

You can snowball.

You can turtle high ground for 40 minutes and somehow turn the game around.

You can completely change your hero's role depending on the situation.

That's what makes Dota special.

The Bad

Now let's talk about the bullshit.

The community.

Holy shit.

Dota players can turn a perfectly normal game into a psychological warfare simulator.

Someone dies once:

"MID DIFF."

Someone misses one spell:

"REPORT SUPPORT."

Your carry doesn't like your item choice:

"NOOB."

Someone disconnects:

"GG."

And somehow, after 15 minutes of everyone flaming each other, the team still has to coordinate a five-man smoke.

It's fucking ridiculous.

And let's not pretend we're innocent.

We've all been that guy.

We've all typed something we immediately regretted.

We've all blamed someone else for a loss.

We've all said:

"If my team wasn't garbage, we would've won."

Would I recommend it?

Yes.

Would I recommend it to my worst enemy?

Absolutely.

The amount of quality content you get instantly for free when playing this game makes it an instant recommendation. I mean, DE put an insane amount of passion into this completely free 2 play game. And I mean actually free 2 play, without any predatory tactics. It's crazy how much this game respects its players.

That being said, it isn't immune to criticism, and it very much deserves some. Despite having really solid mechanics, this game really struggles to make fights challenging. This results in an endgame that lacks much to do in terms of going all out with your broken builds. Even worse, the early game feels sluggish, forcing you to go through repetitive content until you start engaging with the deeper mechanics.

While engaging with the building mechanics and gathering new frames is pretty fun, I wish that, for once, I could have the same amount of fun with the actual combat outside of the power fantasy and fun frame abilities. Warframe even added a complex melee system with its Duviri update, but for some reason, it has seemingly abandoned it and decided to never ever use it again. Which is unfortunately a pretty common scenario when it comes to some of Warframe's earlier content. I really enjoy the gameplay, which is why I wish the updates would find a way to take it to a more interesting level, especially with the newer endgame updates.

There's also the topic of the cinematic single-player content, which has grown massively in scale as the game has evolved. Despite having some really cool surprises, it ultimately suffers from a pretty misguided approach to writing. Even though the game takes its time building up its world, it really struggles to introduce characters who are likeable enough to carry you through the story and It ends up making me not really care for it. They've been improving on this a bit with the 1999 update, but there's still a long way to go before the story becomes truly engaging.

Overall tho this is definitely an impressive game that gives you so much for so little and respects the time you put into it. Despite seeing the potential for something much better, I still can't deny how great this game is.

340 hours later, and I’m still optimizing things that already work perfectly well.

Satisfactory is one of those games where you tell yourself you’re just going to rebuild one small production line.

Three hours later, you’re standing next to a conveyor belt in the middle of the night wondering why your aluminium production is running 4.7% below target.

And that’s exactly why I love this game.

The basic idea sounds simple: gather resources, build production chains, automate them and keep scaling up. But at some point, you’re no longer building a factory.

You’re building a system.

Conveyor belts turn into logistics networks. Power generation becomes infrastructure planning. Trains connect entire industrial regions. Production rates get calculated, bottlenecks get hunted down, and perfectly functional factories get demolished because you suddenly thought of a cleaner or more efficient way to build them.

Satisfactory scratches a very specific itch because it rewards both creativity and technical thinking.

You can build glorious spaghetti and still make progress. Or you can spend hours balancing production ratios, aligning buildings and turning your factory into something that starts looking suspiciously like actual engineering.

The world also feels like more than just a backdrop. Exploration, finding new resources and building remote outposts regularly pull you away from the industrial rabbit hole you’ve created for yourself.

It’s not perfect, though. The larger your industrial empire becomes, the more the game can start feeling like actual work. Rebuilding becomes a massive undertaking, small mistakes can propagate through entire production chains, and eventually you spend a disturbing amount of time fixing problems you created yourself.

So basically IT, but with better scenery.

But that complexity is also exactly what makes it so satisfying.

Very few games can make me look at a factory after hundreds of hours and still think:

“I can build this better.”

And then start rebuilding it all over again.

340 hours. Absolutely recommended. One of the best factory-building and automation games I’ve ever played.

[b]My score: 10/10[/b]
⭐ [b]TL;DR:[/b] The gold standard of cozy and farming games. Unmatched in variety, depth and sheer amount of content, with enough freedom to make the game whatever you want it to be.

🟦 [b]NOTE:[/b] Although I only had around 30 hours on Steam at the time of writing, I've played hundreds of hours on other platforms over the years.

[h2]Overview[/h2]
The best game in its genre, hands down. There's really very little to say: [i]Stardew Valley[/i] is the modern benchmark for cozy and farming games, and I don't think there's anything else on the market that matches its variety, mechanical depth and sheer amount of content.

And, much like [i]No Man's Sky[/i] (read my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/averagemage/recommended/275850/]🔗here[/url]), this is a game that has received constant free updates for ten years, with more still to come. That's an absurd amount of value for a game that already had plenty to offer at launch.

[h2]One Thing I Liked / One Thing I Didn't[/h2]
✔️ [b]Liked:[/b] The sheer flexibility. You can take your time, plan a speedrun to wealth, become a farmer, a rancher, a fisherman, an explorer, or even treat the whole thing like a dating sim. The game rarely tells you how you're supposed to play it.
✖️ [b]Didn't:[/b] The late game can get a little too grindy for my taste.

[h2]Key Points[/h2]
[list]
[*][h3]DIFFICULTY:[/h3] Highly customizable. There is combat and there are time-based challenges, but there are virtually no penalties for ignoring them or coming back when you're better equipped. You can set your own pace and choose how much challenge you want.
[*][h3]PRESENTATION:[/h3] Don't let the almost amateurish-looking sprites and environments fool you: that naïve charm is an integral part of the game's visual identity and remains remarkably consistent. The soundtrack is beautifully composed, with several tracks already considered classics, while the sound effects have been copied by countless other games in the genre.
[*][h3]STORY:[/h3] A classic farming game/cozy game with an ongoing narrative and a touch of magic. The real strength of its story and relationships is that every player gets to experience them differently.
[*][h3]GAMEPLAY:[/h3] You can genuinely do almost anything. If you like fighting, you can fight. If you like fishing, you can fish. If you like exploring, there's plenty to explore. If you like challenges, you have plenty to tackle. If you just want to take it easy, nobody is stopping you.
[*][h3]TECHNICAL POLISH:[/h3] Aside from a few glitches that can occasionally be useful, the game is surprisingly clean and elegant under the hood. Controls and collisions are consistently reliable, and the systems work together with an impressive level of polish, especially considering [b]the game was developed primarily by one person[/b].
[*][h3]MONEYxCONTENT VALUE:[/h3] Absolutely worth it. At €14, it's practically a steal, and there's no real reason to wait for a sale. There's simply too much game here for the price.
[/list]

🟪 [b]NOTE:[/b] If you're into mods, it's worth knowing that ConcernedApe has always been very active in keeping updates compatible with the modding scene. There are countless mods available to refresh or expand the experience, and many of them remain compatible even after major updates. That's a big plus for a developer who clearly understands the needs of PC players.

I’ve played 1,000+ hours of Satisfactory, and I can honestly say I deeply enjoyed every minute of it.

What I love most is that the game never feels like a race. I took my time with each milestone, decorating my factories, optimizing production, and making everything look as good as possible before moving on to the next stage. Eventually, I ended up laying roads and railways all across the map, connecting everything into one massive industrial network.

And then you unlock drones… that’s when the game starts getting even more exciting. The feeling of finally having your entire production network connected and watching everything run smoothly is incredibly satisfying.

That said, after spending so many hours in the game, I definitely find myself wanting more milestones, more types of ores, and greater variation in parts and production chains. I’d love to see:

- More milestones and late-game progression
- More types of ores and unique resource deposits
- Greater variation in parts, components, and production recipes
- More maps or larger areas to explore
- Water transportation and boats
- Underground areas to build in
- Underwater exploration and production
- More reasons to keep expanding after reaching the endgame

There’s something special about Satisfactory where you can spend hours just improving one small section of your factory because you want to, not because the game forces you to.

Overall, be careful. Once you get hooked on this game, time works differently. You’ll think you’ve only been playing for 30 minutes, look at the clock, and somehow 5 hours have disappeared.

Ok, so let me start. I actually enjoy this game, I am saying this as someone who unfortunately enjoys this game. The only reason I have to not like it is  that my play group needs to sleep. as an insomniac I am often left awake later than everyone else. All my friends are asleep by around 12am. I really actually love the gameplay loop to the contrary of what I have to say about it. tbh if you are actually playing with friends or even randos its an amazing and enjoyable experience. But however the moment you decide to click the solo option when everyone else is asleep, be extremely careful what missions you choose to play. I played an extremely low level mission and thanks to both there not being multiple players, and the randomly generated environments make for a completely unenjoyable gameplay experience. 

A mission, fairly early in the game that with a group of three took around fifteen to twenty minutes, took me over an hour and a half just because the recourse I needed refused to spawn anywhere. I literally played this mission with a group not five minutes before and we had no issues. 

Obviously the game doesn't balance difficulty for one player vs. three or four, and tbh its not actually any more difficult solo. The only difference is its a completely unenjoyable slog that almost feels like it is actually punishing you from selecting the solo option. To the developer's credit I actually was able to finish the mission I selected, I just wish I had more time or interest in doing others after the time I spent doing so.

In the time I played solo i finished two missions. That took me around two hours to accomplish!!! Seriously I have played solo rounds of Helldivers 2 with less complications, and that game is legitimately challenging to run solo missions. Overall this game does in fact require some amount of strategic planning solo, but not nearly as much as  Helldivers 2, and this game still has the nerve to be as annoying as it was in solo mode.

In truth I do feel a sense of accomplishment surviving a mission solo, but no matter how high the reward it isn't worth it, especially since the game doesn't provide any incentive what so ever to play solo. There are no bonuses and no benefits to running a mission in solo, so if you either want to run missions alone or just to warm up before playing with your group I can't in good conscience recommend this game. 

The drone is next to useless and a detriment at best. To its credit your drone can in fact heal you when you go down, I know it happened when I dug too deep with a pit underneath me lol. The only actual drawback in this area is that the drone doesn't actually feel like clearing the area or even securing it like an actual player would before it resurrects you, so you end up in the poop as soon as your back.

The game performs very well, and I experienced no crashes at all. All things you attempt to do in game respond well and controls are fluid. 

Literally the only issue I have with this title is the experience solo. When it boils down to it, I'm not going to quit this game because of my issues, I just wish they weren't there and want to give people a heads up.

**Recommended — 576+ hours**

Path of Exile is a wonderful game about killing monsters, collecting loot, and slowly realizing you've accidentally enrolled in an unpaid university course.

I started playing thinking, "Oh cool, Diablo but free."

576 hours later I'm staring at six different resistance numbers, moving gems around like a crackhead doing electrical work, and getting genuinely excited because a chest has the correct combination of coloured holes in it.

10/10.

I mostly play Necromancer, because why fight my own battles when I can bring an entire unemployment line of skeletons, spectres, golems and other assorted dead people with me?

Sometimes my army deletes half the map.

Sometimes a boss looks vaguely in my direction and I immediately become a historical event.

That's Path of Exile.

The amount of content in this game is fucking absurd. Every time I think I understand it, another mechanic crawls out from underneath a rock carrying seventeen currencies and a crafting system that apparently requires a minor in economics.

And somehow I love it.

The developers and support staff deserve genuine credit too. My experiences with them have been great. I've had reward/drop issues sorted out by actual humans, and I've always gotten the impression that the people behind this ridiculous monster genuinely give a shit about it and its community.

Is it beginner friendly?

Absolutely fucking not.

The passive tree looks like someone dropped a plate of spaghetti onto a motherboard and called it character progression.

But once it gets its claws into you, there really isn't anything else quite like it.

It's complicated. It's occasionally infuriating. It will happily murder you because you forgot that 41% chaos resistance is apparently the defensive equivalent of wearing a promising hat.

Then you'll get one beautiful drop and forgive everything.

Free game, by the way.

I've paid considerably more money for games I've played considerably less.

See you in maps.

Found this little indie game while looking for something to play with friends and honestly I'm surprised more people don't know about it.

You pick one of these cute little characters and then you and 9 other players spend some quality time together on a small map. The art is pretty charming and there's a surprising amount of attention to detail for such a tiny studio.

The gameplay is very simple. You just walk around, click on things and occasionally fight some of the local wildlife. There's also a little economy system where you collect gold and buy funny items for your character. Very cozy.

My favorite part is the community. Since this is such a small indie title, everyone seems to know each other. Every match feels like I'm sitting down with a few close friends for a relaxed evening. Sometimes we have disagreements about which direction to walk in, but that's just part of the wholesome co-op experience.

There are also hundreds of characters, which is honestly insane for a game this small. I've been playing for a while and still haven't seen everything. Some of them have really cute names like "Pudge" and "Techies."

The developer is clearly very passionate too. They keep releasing updates and adding new content despite the game being made by what I assume is like three people.

If you have 40 minutes to spare, definitely give this hidden gem a chance.

Sea of Thieves is a first-person multiplayer action-adventure game developed by Rare that embraces the ultimate pirate sandbox experience. Players navigate open waters, search for buried treasure, engage in naval ship battles, and fight skeleton crews either solo or with up to a 4-player crew. Here’s a quick breakdown of its advantages and drawbacks.


+ Unmatched Pirate Atmosphere & Water Physics – Features stunning ocean physics, sailing mechanics, dynamic weather, and immersive hand-drawn maps.

+ Pure Co-op Teamwork – Sailing, adjusting sails, firing cannons, and repairing the hull requires fluid communication and coordination with your crew.

+ Fair Horizon Mechanics – All progression is strictly cosmetic, ensuring veteran players have no statistical advantage over brand-new players.

+ Safer Seas Option – Offers a dedicated peaceful game mode allowing players to enjoy voyages and story missions without the threat of hostile crews.

- Open-World PvP Threat – In standard High Seas servers, aggressive enemy crews can attack at any time and steal hours of gathered loot.

- High Time Commitment – Completing longer voyages, world events, or Tall Tales stories requires substantial, uninterrupted play sessions.

- Repetitive Voyages – Beyond cosmetic rewards, the core gameplay loop of gathering and delivering chests can feel grindy over time.

I think I finally found the game I needed.

After **185 hours in The Elder Scrolls Online**, I can honestly say that this game has become much more than just another MMO for me. Somewhere along the way, Tamriel stopped feeling like a world I was playing in and started feeling like a place I could come home to.

There’s something incredibly special about being able to explore, discover new places, build your character, complete quests at your own pace, and simply get lost in the world for hours. ESO gives you so much freedom that you can play it the way you want without constantly feeling like you’re being pushed toward one specific goal.

And honestly, that freedom is probably what made me stay.

I love the feeling of logging in without necessarily having a plan and somehow ending up spending hours exploring, doing quests, improving my character, or discovering something completely unexpected.

**185 hours later, I still feel like there’s so much left to see.**

ESO became the kind of game where I don't just play it to finish something. Sometimes I log in simply because I want to *be there*.

It’s not perfect, but it gave me something I didn’t realize I was looking for in a game: **a world that feels like home.** 🖤

 — Tamriel, I’m not leaving anytime soon.**

Best mmorpg I've played, and I play a lot of these. The lore is immaculate, the NPCs are likable and funny, the quests are enjoyable, and it's just a fun time. The exploration is probably my favorite thing. Going around and finding skyshards and completing zones is a great way to just chill out. The progression is also quite nice. It isn't like WoW where you keep grinding to get marginally better stats on gear, but it isn't like Guild Wars 2 where it's horizontal gear progression. To get new gear, you go find it wherever it's dropped, That could be a dungeon, a delve, world boss, whatever. You then learn to craft and upgrade your gear. The crafting and combat skills are what level the gear's effectiveness, unless you buy a max upgraded gear piece from a guild trader. I cannot stress enough how important crafting is. Not only can a player finish writs every day to earn around 1k-5k gold daily, but they also get materials and coffers of goodies every day. Crafting involves reading motifs of certain styles, so of which can be found pretty much anywhere. 

Time for the lack-luster stuff. I would recommend staying away from PVP. Broken. Always has been. Cyrodiil, the massive multiplayer real-time war mode, is fun, though. If you get together with a band of your countrymen and go fight, it's an enjoyable experience. FOR THE PACT OOHRAHH! Another thing that isn't so great for newbies is that the game doesn't really emphasize the important factors of a good ESO experience. For example, the game doesn't even mention how important crafting is to progressing a character. Most of the important details regarding crafting, gear locations, etc. has to be google'd. The third thing is the multi-classing system. It is a cool concept, but it makes more broken classes just that much more broken. For new players who do not have access to multi-classing, it isn't a fun experience. It turns PvP into a reaction time battle instead of a battle of strategy. Whoever can shmeat their opponent with a kagillion damage first wins.

By moving away from the long standing elder scrolls musical motif, the new season trailer perfectly summarizes the new content.  Like the game or don't like the game, but it doesn't feel much like elder scrolls.  The development team just started refreshing the skill lines, but at the current development pace it could take years.  Fortunately, there do seem to be some fresh ideas percolating under the surface, but for now the game is a bit of a mess.

As far as the new season PvE content goes, it's mostly rewarming older content, and feels like it was rushed out the door. The quests are a bunch of "messenger" missions, (go here, get something, come back), with a very minimal story that seems aimed at sending players to older content (I keep getting sent on quests where I am immediately told "oh, you already did that").  The new Night Watch zone was basically a remix of existing bosses and similar content.

Given the new direction, it's possible the developers will save PvP, but the current PvP balance is hopelessly bad, and has had a huge drop in population (there use to be several high population campaigns, now there are two small campaigns.  

The "ability balanced" campaign (Vengeance) can potentially be huge (almost 1000 simultaneous players), but it usually has a small population on one faction, and almost nothing on the other two. When the population is high enough, it's brilliant, with huge chaotic battles the ebb and flow. The game play is reactive, and skill based, but the skill floor and ceiling are close enough together so even new players aren't "stomped" (skill matters, but it's still a fight).  Unfortunately, Vengeance needs a lot of players in each of three factions or the play is very unbalanced and when the population is unbalanced (as it normally is), the game play becomes one sided and campaign collapses.  

The free form campaign (Grey Host)  has had the population cap lowered to silly levels because it can't support all of the complicated armor mechanics (and it often isn't full).  It's been reduced to a a boring "your armor plays the game for you" meta. Plus, with most of the necessary armor is locked behind pay walls, so Grey Host has become pay to win. (I played it for years, but have lost interest since I can watch players from a distance and know what's going to happen based on how their armor behaves).

(There is a third "BlackReach" campaign, but I've never seen it anything other than dead).

After more than 2,300 hours, I can no longer recommend Hunt.

This game has been in development for over eight years, yet Crytek would rather pump out endless events, Battle Passes, and cosmetic DLCs than fix its rotten foundations.

You fall through the ground near certain ledges, move around like you have fucking bars of soap strapped to your boots, perfectly placed shots simply fail to register, trades are ridiculous, audio sometimes becomes unreliable, and high-ping players are still allowed to ruin servers in other regions.

Once you reach a certain skill level, these “minor issues” are no longer simple annoyances: they completely invalidate matches. All the time spent mastering the game, reading situations, and making the right decisions? You can shove it up your ass—your match just got ruined by some tiny detail completely unrelated to your skill.

It also took eight years to receive compensation when a cheater is finally caught—and even that comes with caveats. Not to mention the supposedly fixed bugs that magically return with the next update.

The art team is the only team that deserves any praise. They continue to create outstanding designs for a game that is technically inexcusable for its age.

Crytek has a gem on its hands and would rather cover it in paid costumes than make it work properly. Hunt is only surviving because it has no real competitor.

The day another studio takes this concept and setting and builds it on solid technical foundations, you are completely fucked.

I've been playing MMOs for 20 years (mainly WoW), and I'd never really given Guild Wars a shot. When the expansions and such were on sale, I picked up the game to see if I'd like it. I was burnt out on WoW and wanted to try something new. I ended up leveling several classes to level 80, but I ultimately decided that the game isn't for me. Here are my thoughts:

+ Amazing combat system that's super different from all of the MMOs I've played. The action combat style is really engaging to me, with the dodges and everything.

+ GW2 nails exploration. If you're the kind of player who likes getting lost and immersed in the world, it's a great game for you.

+ WvW is a really interesting spin on traditional MMO PvP.

+ No sub fee and horizontal progression means you can get into the game after a long break and not have really missed anything.

- Despite the cool combat concepts, GW2 combat feels super floaty to me. Abilities don't feel very punchy compared to WoW.

- The weapon swap stuff. GOD I hate the weapon swap stuff. It feels so clunky and awkward to suddenly change your entire kit mid-combat, but some people enjoy it, so to each his own.

- The difficulty ramps up drastically from the base game into the expansions. I gave up in Heart of Thorns because I wasn't having fun with how hard I was getting hit and how much I needed to lock in. Felt really bad.

- The biggest downside for me, the PvE meta is for everyone to stack in a little ball so all of your boons and buffs can be applied to everyone at the same time, so ranged builds aren't really ranged at all. Completely destroys the dungeon/raid fantasy for me.

- The gem store feels very predatory to me. I know people say you can farm gems, but I still think it's really gross to sell things like extra bag slots for real money, and the rotating cosmetic items feel like major FOMO capitalization.

All in all, if you're someone who doesn't care about the downsides I listed, give GW2 a spin. I'm glad I tried it, and maybe I'll give it a go again sometime, but the game is not for me.

People think Sea of Thieves is a swashbuckling pirate adventure. It is not. It is a high-stakes, ocean-bound casino where you gamble your sanity, and the house always wins.

Eight hours in. You are either sitting on a mountain of digital gold, or you have absolutely nothing to show for your existence except a hull you’ve had to patch for the twenty-seventh time. Your ship looks like Swiss cheese held together by splinters, frantic bucket-tossing, and pure, unadulterated stress.

“I can profit,” you whisper to the empty ocean. “Just one more run.”

But you said that fifty deaths ago. You said that before the ocean turned ink-black and a Kraken snapped your mast like a dry twig. You said that before a Megalodon decided your sloop was a chew toy. You said that before the paranoia of a tucked pirate made you slash at shadows, terrified someone was waiting to detonate a gunpowder barrel in your lower deck and vaporize your progress in a blinding flash of green fire.

Yet, you push through. You clear the vaults. You slay the skeleton lords. Your deck is now practically vibrating with the cursed glow of villainous skulls and ancient chests. The wind suddenly feels malicious. Every crashing wave sounds like a cannon firing. It dawns on you: I need to sell. Now.

You drop the sails, catch the wind, and make a desperate, white-knuckled dash toward Port Merrick. Freedom is so close you can smell the tavern grog.

Then, you see it.

A silhouette cutting through the waves on the horizon. The dreaded red emissary flag. A Grade 5 Reaper sloop, moving with the terrifying, silent efficiency of an apex predator that has already smelled your fear.

Sweat boils on your forehead. Your heart rate spikes. You frantically angle the sails, but the wind immediately shifts against you. The chainshots fly, spinning through the air in agonizing slow motion. Your mast falls. Fire engulfs the deck. In a matter of seconds, eight hours of meticulous, grinding survival are violently redistributed to a crew who are currently playing a hurdy-gurdy over your sinking corpse.

The screen fades to black, and the rage doesn’t come. There is no screaming. No thrown controllers. Instead, there is just a sudden, deafening silence in your own head. You stare into the dark reflection of your monitor, looking at a stranger with dead, hollow eyes. The adrenaline drains out of you, leaving behind a cold, crushing weight in your chest. You realize you haven't blinked in three minutes. You listen to the hum of your PC cooling fans and calculate the real-world sunlight you just traded for absolutely nothing.

You feel a profound disconnect from reality. You sit paralyzed, bargaining with a god that doesn't exist to rewind the server clock by just five minutes. Your soul practically detaches from your body, hovering somewhere above your gaming chair, begging you to uninstall the game, shut down the computer, and go look at a tree. You accept that nothing matters. The gold is an illusion. The pirate life is a lie.

But then, the ethereal doors on the Ferry of the Damned swing open.

You spawn on a fresh, empty ship. You look at the map table. The wood is pristine. The cannons are loaded.

“I can make it back,” your broken brain rationalizes. “Just one more run.”

Dota 2 is a good game on paper, but it actively punishes experimentation and respects none of your time. The fundamental flaw lies in an automated report system that treats having a bad game as an intentional crime. If you struggle on a core hero like Phantom Assassin or try to test an off-meta build, teammates will immediately weaponize griefing reports against you without any verification. This causes your behavior score to rapidly decay, sending you into lower-tier lobbies(where I obv play)  where report abuse is even more rampant.

Compounding this issue is the total refusal to implement a forfeit option in solo queue. Instead of being able to concede an obvious defeat, players are routinely held hostage in 45 minute slow loss scenarios where the outcome was already sealed at minute twenty. Adding a forfeit option would actually accelerate player skill development exponentially by allowing players to experience and learn from dozens of varied macro scenarios, rather than forcing everyone to sit through unwinnable states where no meaningful skill can be improved.

Dota 2 is one of those games that makes you want to uninstall it, close Steam, and never play again… only to launch 
it again 10 minutes later.

Let’s start with the good.

In terms of gameplay depth, Dota 2 is genuinely one of the most impressive competitive games out there. The huge number of heroes, items, abilities, strategies, combinations, and possible builds makes every match potentially different. There is always something new to learn. Even after hundreds or thousands of hours, you can discover a new mechanic, a new strategy, an unusual build, or realize that you have been playing a hero completely wrong.

And that is exactly why the problems with the game can be so frustrating.

Dota 2 itself is incredibly good.

The problem is everything surrounding that gameplay.

The biggest issue is that one player can completely ruin a match for nine other people.

Someone dies twice in the first few minutes and immediately decides the game is over. Someone starts insulting the entire team. Someone refuses to cooperate. Someone spends 40 minutes farming the jungle while the rest of the team is desperately trying to defend the base. Someone makes one mistake and then spends the rest of the match explaining why everyone else is responsible for losing.

And somehow, the player with 5,000+ hours who is screaming at everyone about how terrible they are will usually make an even bigger mistake five minutes later.

Matchmaking can be another adventure by itself.

Sometimes you get an amazing match where both teams are evenly matched. Every fight matters, every tower matters, and one good decision can completely change the game. You get comebacks, smart rotations, team fights, Roshan contests, clutch saves and genuinely memorable moments.

Those are the games that remind you why Dota 2 is so addictive.

Then you get the opposite.

A completely one-sided match where the outcome is basically decided after 15 minutes, but somehow you still have to spend another 30 minutes watching your Ancient slowly disappear.

At that point you are sitting in front of your monitor thinking:

“Why am I still playing this?”

The match ends.

You click “Play Again.”

And that is probably the most accurate description of Dota 2.

It is a game that can make you angrier than almost anything else, yet somehow convinces you that the next match will be different.

Toxicity deserves its own section.

Dota 2 toxicity has become almost a fundamental part of the experience. Insults, spam pings, sarcastic voice lines, blaming supports for everything, blaming the carry, blaming the mid player, blaming the offlaner, blaming the draft, blaming the matchmaking…

Sometimes it feels like people don't actually queue to win.

They queue to find someone to blame when they lose.

The funniest part is that everyone thinks they are the main character.

Your carry thinks the support is useless.

The support thinks the carry is useless.

The mid player thinks both supports are useless.

The offlaner thinks the mid player ruined the game.

And the enemy team is somehow cheating.

Perfect teamwork.

There is also the problem of smurfs, boosters and unfair matches. Valve has taken measures against smurfing and has banned large numbers of accounts for this kind of behavior, which shows how serious the problem has been. But the fact that these issues have been such a major topic in the community says a lot about how important matchmaking integrity is for a competitive game like Dota 2.

Then there is the learning curve.

Dota 2 is not a game you simply install and understand.

For a new player, it can feel like being thrown into a university exam without ever attending the classes.

There are dozens of heroes to learn, hundreds of items, different roles, abilities, counters, timings, farming patterns, map movements, ward locations, objectives, Roshan timings and countless small mechanics that experienced players take for granted.

A new player can spend hours learning the basics and then meet someone who understands the game far better and gets destroyed in seconds.

The experienced player thinks:

“Easy.”

The new player thinks:

“What the hell just happened?”

But once you finally understand the basics, something changes.

You start seeing the game differently.

You stop simply reacting to things and start predicting them.

You understand why the enemy is moving somewhere. You recognize a potential gank. You know when to fight and when to retreat. You start thinking about item timings, map control, objectives and positioning.

And that is when Dota 2 becomes truly amazing.

Few things feel better than winning a difficult match because your team actually worked together.

A perfectly executed team fight.

A last-second save.

A successful smoke gank.

Stealing Roshan.

Defending your high ground for 20 minutes.

Turning a completely lost game into a comeback.

Those moments are incredible.

And those moments are exactly why people keep coming back.

Dota 2 is not a bad game.

Actually, the opposite is true.

It is an incredibly good game surrounded by an incredible amount of frustration.

Gameplay: 10/10.

Depth: 10/10.

Variety: 10/10.

Teamwork: 10/10 — when your team actually works together.

Learning curve: Pain.

Matchmaking: Sometimes a lottery.

Toxicity: Basically its own game mode.

Amount of time you can lose: Unlimited.

Dota 2 is one of those games where you completely understand why people love it while also completely understanding why they hate it.

You can have the best match of your life and immediately follow it with the worst match imaginable.

You can spend an hour playing perfectly, lose because of one stupid decision, stare at the defeat screen for a few seconds and say:

“That's it. I'm done with Dota.”

Then five minutes later:

“Okay, one more.”

And that's the Dota 2 experience.

I recommend it to anyone who enjoys extremely deep competitive games and is willing to spend hundreds of hours learning, losing, improving, getting tilted, recovering, and occasionally experiencing one of the most satisfying victories a multiplayer game can offer.

For everyone else…

Stay away.

I have no idea how this game feels in multiplayer. But in solo... it's kind of fun. Combat will take a while to become interesting, same as base building. But about 10 hours in - and the game actually starts feeling interesting.

[h3]Story - 6.5/10[/h3]
They tried. That's as far as I can go with this. The setting is there, the lore is there, most of it relies on indirect narrative. Some bosses have kind of interesting stories and locations also tell a bit about what happened in this world before, and what perils it's facing now. But the main story is essentially you just waking up from the grave and choosing to challenge Dracula himself, to climb at the top of the food chain. And in order to do so, you're just going through a number of lesser bosses, each one located in farther and farther biomes, and each one providing you with either major upgrades to your character, or recipes for crafting new structures and/or gear.
Kind of like Valheim, but without procedurally generated world and way, way more bosses.

[h3]Gameplay - 7.5/10[/h3]
It takes some time to pick up. At first, it's painfully simple. Just slowly move around, dodge every once in a while, and button mash your attacks to both fight and harvest resources. Base building is pretty limited at first, too. If you, however, manage to go approximately to the middle of Act 2, you'll unlock enough skills for combat to actually start feeling interesting. Three skills on weapons, multiple weapons to choose from with each feeling pretty distinct, and three spells from different schools to complement them. By then, you'll also have access to different armor versions, trinkets, gems to upgrade your skills, etc - in other words, you'll start forming an actual build. And the game starts feeling less like mindless button mashing, and more akin to just a decent, top-down slasher.
Bosses are where the combat shines the most, naturally. And credit where credit is due - the devs really tried their best to make bosses feel fresh, distinct, and have few tricks up their sleeves to make them stand out. But, again, only on late act 2 and onward. Don't let the first several hours of the game bore you out of your mind.
In terms of the survival elements, the grind is a bit tedious, and made even worse by the fact that you're a goddamn vampire lord, who can even have servants and human cattle. But for some reason, still forced to regularly go to chop wood or mine ore. Building your lair, on the other hand, is quite enjoyable. You're rewarded for planning your base, creating designated rooms for different purposes (workshop to get better timber yields from sawmills, forge to get better yields from furnaces, etc.), and you get quite a lot of potential for decorating and creating a truly beautiful castle, worthy to be called a lair of a vampire lord.

[h3]Graphics - 7.5/10[/h3]
The style is nice, the locations are diverse and beautiful, boss design is also pretty cool. The armor and weapon design, all the effects from your skills and spells - all of it is very edgy, which... works really well for the game about vampires XD

[h3]Sound - 6.5/10[/h3]
Nothing noteworthy here, I'm afraid. It's not off-putting, but I really can't even remember anything noteworthy about this game's voice acting or sound design, or even soundtrack.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
7/10. It takes a while to pick up the pace. If you enjoy base building just for the heck of it - it's nice. If you enjoy vampire thematic in particular, with a lot of different aesthetic of weapons (swords, whips, scythes, pistols, etc.) and witchcraft (all elemental, necromancy, blood themed or purple void themed) to choose from - you might enjoy it, too. I have no idea how it plays in PvP or even in coop. But for a slow paced, relaxed evening with a bit of farming, some boss fight and some base building - it will hit the spot just fine.

Ich bin kein Neuling in dieser Welt. Schon als vor Jahren die ersten Schritte in Guild Wars gesetzt habe, war ich von Stunde an gefesselt. Als dann Guild Wars 2 angekündigt wurde, war klar: Dieses MMO würde ich nicht verpassen. Und es hat mich nicht enttäuscht.

Was Guild Wars 2 für mich auszeichnet, ist die atmosphärische Welt. Tyria fühlt sich lebendig an, nicht wie eine Ansammlung von Quest-Hubs. Die dynamischen Events machen das Erkunden sinnvoll – man stolpert ständig über etwas, das gerade passiert, statt stumpf von Aufgabe zu Aufgabe zu rennen. Das Kampfsystem ist actionlastig und flüssig, mit dem aktiven Ausweichen und der Waffenwahl fühlt sich jede Klasse anders an.

Die Geschichte hat Höhen und Tiefen. Die ursprüngliche Kampagne und Heart of Thorns haben mich emotional mitgenommen, spätere Kapitel manchmal weniger. Dennoch schätzt ich den Fokus auf den eigenen Charakter und die langfristige Entwicklung der Welt. Das Geschäftsmodell ist fair: Nach dem einmaligen Kauf des Grundspiels und der Erweiterungen kann man sehr viel kostenlos spielen, ohne unter Druck zu geraten.

Kritisch sehe ich, dass manche Systeme für Einsteiger überladen wirken können – Traits, Ausrüstungsboni, Crafting. Auch der Endgame-Loop ist nicht jedermanns Sache, wenn man klassischen Raid-Progress sucht. Aber für mich, der vor allem die Welt, die Erkundung und das gemeinsame Abenteuer liebt, ist Guild Wars 2 nach wie vor eines der besten MMOs am Markt.

Fazit: Wer eine MMO-Welt sucht, die man auf eigene Faust erleben kann, ohne monatlich zu zahlen, ist hier richtig. Für mich als GW1-Veteran ist Guild Wars 2 nicht nur ein Nachfolger – es ist die Heimkehr in eine Welt, die ich nie wirklich verlassen habe.

This world is hostile. It will kill you for looking at it the wrong way, and your own incompetence is just as capable of killing you. So let death be your teacher. Every time you return from it, return stronger, not because the world has granted you anything, but because you have learned how this plane functions.

So die. Learn. Understand this world more deeply than it understands itself. Strip it down to its barest components and study the machinery beneath. Then take that knowledge like an axe and carve the world open with it.

Subdue what was once thought invincible. Break what was thought unbreakable. Become something the world no longer knows how to kill.

[hr][/hr]

But seriously, this is the perfect game for anyone technically minded, with a willingness to learn from their mistakes. It slowly builds a toolbox of knowledge in your head, until eventually you find yourself wielding it with the same confidence as any conventional arsenal.

The wand crafting is absurdly deep, less like a conventional crafting system and more akin to a tape and instruction-based programming language. Its physics sandbox draws from the classic Powder Toy-style simulators, giving you a vast world of interacting systems to prod and break. Add on top the alchemy, which somehow manages to tie everything together, interacting with practically every other system in a beautiful mix of predictable and unpredictable ways.

It is the sort of game you can play for thousands of hours and still discover something new every day.

Not because it is endlessly adding things for you to consume, but because there is always another interaction to understand, another system to pull apart, another piece of the machinery beneath the world that you have not yet quite figured out.

Best FPS game out there, but...

...holy shit, Respawn, what happened?

Apex has some of the best gunplay, movement, legends, and overall gameplay ever put into an FPS. That’s what makes the current state of the game so damn frustrating. You’ve built an incredible game and then seemingly made it your personal mission to let everything surrounding that game rot.

Every season, we hear about how you’re “working on” the cheating problem. Every season, somehow, it gets worse.

Cheaters are everywhere. Boosters are everywhere. People openly manipulating ranked games, farming badges, boosting accounts and abusing whatever exploit they can find. And the most insulting part? It feels like some of these people have been doing it for so long that they’ve basically become part of the ecosystem.

And let’s talk about boosters.

Boosting has become so normalized that it’s hard not to wonder whether Respawn actually has any incentive to kill it off. Boosters mean more accounts, more purchases, more battle passes, more cosmetics, and more money flowing through the game. Meanwhile, legitimate players get to spend their evenings fighting people who somehow have Predator-level aim while playing like they have a second set of hands.

You tell us you’re banning cheaters.

We hear it every season.

“Anti-cheat improvements.”
“Enforcement waves.”
“We’re addressing the issue.”
“We’re taking cheating seriously.”

And then you queue into ranked and discover that apparently the “enforcement wave” was a gentle breeze.

The community isn't asking for perfection. Nobody expects you to magically eliminate every cheater on Earth. But when the same problems keep coming back season after season, eventually “we’re working on it” stops sounding like an explanation and starts sounding like a loading-screen tip.

The worst part is that Apex itself is still fucking incredible. That’s why people are so angry. If the game were bad, people would just leave. Instead, we keep coming back because when Apex works, there genuinely isn't much else like it.

The movement feels incredible.
The gunplay feels incredible.
The legends are unique.
The fights can be some of the most intense moments in any FPS.

And then you lose a ranked game to someone blatantly cheating and you're left wondering why you just voluntarily subjected yourself to that experience.

Apex doesn't need another shiny cosmetic, another overpriced heirloom event, or another “we're aware of the issue” statement.

It needs its fucking house cleaned.

Fix the cheating.
Fix boosting.
Actually punish repeat offenders.
Stop letting ranked integrity become a joke.
And most importantly, make players believe that the people ruining the game are actually being dealt with.

Because right now, Apex feels like the best FPS game ever created being held hostage by the worst parts of its own community.

That was gutted and turned into a cheap rip off of League of Legends at some late point in its development.  Which likely happened when the Chinese government owned Tencent bought out StunLock right as LoL was at the height of its popularity.  Because this games combat mechanics are a copy-paste of LoL.

If you are playing PvE 2 spells, Chaos Volley, and Corrupted Skull will carry though though the entire game, all other spells and abilities are trash because they take the place of those two spells. Warframe is a great example of what happens when you are given a power fantasy without an actual claim to the power. It offers all the trappings of the indulgent form of gaming, where the systems are there to ensure the player has to engage as little as possible with the gameplay itself. 

The game happens in two very distinct states, the first of which is the one where you are met with a wall of numbers greater than the ones you possess, and the second in which your numbers surpass the wall. The issue arises when there is no real power to be gained. It is all illusionary, as the solution is always to stay in the second phase of play, up until you are granted the resources necessary to up your numbers enough to turn your character into a whirlwind of destruction - thus granting you access to the second part. You are not assumed to learn the character or weapons, but the game expects you to instead learn how to make the character grow in statistical power. You do not have to engage with the systems of combat - which are plenty and are in fact quite interesting - as you are either killing things faster than you can blink, or are so overwhelmed with their statistical advantage that no amount of prowess piloting the character can give you great enough edge to overcome the stacked odds.

I picked the game up again because I thought the Valkyrie and a few other characters looked interesting. Turns out, it does not matter much which vignette you choose as your avatar, as the skills and weapons are mostly an aesthetic choice and not a gameplay one. Your job as the player is to find the rotation of button presses that kills the enemies the fastest, after which you grind for the necessary resources that enable the button presses in the first place. It is sad to see the myriad of different builds the game enables you to create, when all of them boil down to the screen being filled with an explosion of gore. In that sense, the game is more akin to something like a bullet heaven with a few extra steps, than the character action game skin it wears on its bones. It is all flair and no substance. The power part of the fantasy is then relegated to an invisible overlord, whose job it is to gradually drip feed the player progress, after they have spent enough time making things explode into tiny chunks of meat. Except even this amount of engagement is not true for the most part. The overlord actively pushes the player to disengage from the core combat systems, with the treadmill rewarding those who can do the most iterations on a mission, in the least amount of time. To be granted power, you must then learn how to glide through levels as fast as possible, in order to get to the chest of loot at the end. This skipping of the gameplay is repeated enough times, until the overlord graciously gifts the player with the next increment of the fantasy. The player did not necessarily learn anything about the game, other than the fact that progression means engaging as little as possible with anything outside the meta-systems governing the power scales.

Imagine fighting against someone in full plate armour. Now, you’d assume to overcome this foe, you’d have to learn footwork and likely how to grapple to pin them down for the coup de grâce. Perhaps you’d need to learn how to half-sword or at least know where the gaps in the armour are to then sink your dagger into. Well, if it was up to the previously mentioned overlord governing your power levels, you’d instead resolve the gap in fighting proficiency by going out to the countryside and by beating up peasants to the death. After piling enough corpses onto the fields, the god from the machine would descend to grant you an assault rifle to shoot the knight dead with.
You gained nothing more than a razed village and a magical gimmick that can shoot bullets with enough velocity to pierce armour. The whole exercise was meaningless and utterly devoid of any true power. It was but a juvenile fantasy with arbitrary rules set to help jerk off the ego of the person drooling over their own greatness. In the same vein, playing Warframe is like playing with dolls to keep your ego sated with constant self-aggrandizement, without ever having to face any real work to warrant such validation. Whatever power you assume to claim is not yours but a manifestation of a mind too entrenched in fantasy to mistake holding a sword for knowing how to wield it.

Before i start the actual review I want to point out that Hunt Showdown is an EXTRACTION SHOOTER. These games are very often defined by slow gameplay, high stakes, permadeath and most importantly dying often. If these concepts seem annoying to you and ruin the experience for you, then Hunt will most probably not be your game and dropping a bad review about it being the game that it is doesn’t help that fact.
If you do like those concepts, then the game is in my opinion one of the best Titles in the genre and there are many dopamine hits to be chased.

Now to the more detailed stuff:
I have played around 1100 hours. A few years ago the game was maybe more grounded than before, which in my opinion has pros and cons. I find the event mechanics interesting and they definitely impact the gameplay more than before, but sometimes maybe a bit too much. I did enjoy the older „event“ system more, because grinding a battle pass is always a commitment and the event skins felt a bit more „thought out“ (some battle pass skins are still solid and the new one looks quite good, but some skins maybe feel slightly lazy, as they just repeat the same design with a few weapons)
The gunplay is still nice, you can still play every gun in the game and at least in my opinion you don’t have to cuckhold yourself with meta gear. Other loadouts are fun too, and every gun (even the deringer) has enough kill potential to be able to do something. The new guns often tend to be stronger at launch, but never unrepairably broken.
My biggest criticism of the game would be the long term progression. While prestigeing does serve that purpose it doesn’t feel too impactful or rewarding, as it is just a number going up. The hunter tier progression was IMO pretty nice, though that system removed some of the cooler looking tier 3 hunter variants, so it would be cool if those could be added back as some form of progression reward or variant too. Other long term goals, that go side by side with the prestige system would be very cool, as that would make the long term incentive to play more stable.
If you‘ve read this far and you have decided to buy the game, maybe we’ll see in the bayou. Have Fun!

Why do I have to purchase the same cosmetics for every single class if I want them? Why can enemies hit you through the floor or ceiling?  Why does there need to be 50 different matrix cores per class when most of them are worthless? Not enough to make me stop playing, but issues that tarnish what is an otherwise great game.

[h3]Satisfactory 1.2
[/h3]

I´ve always loved building things in games like 7 Days to Die, Empyrion, or No Man´s Sky, so I had a feeling Satisfactory might be a game for me.

What I wasn´t sure about was whether a game that is “just” about building factories could really keep me entertained for very long.

[b]Holy macaroni, was I wrong.[/b]

It has been a long time since a game has hooked me as much as Satisfactory has. Of course, the main focus is planning and building production facilities - to Save the Day.

And building in this game feels incredibly smooth. The one thing I really missed at the beginning was a proper free-build camera like you find in some other building games. But once you finally unlock the Hoverpack after roughly 80 hours, you barely touch the ground anymore anyway, so it becomes something close to having a free-build camera.

Satisfactory should come with one big warning, though:

[b]If you enjoy games where you can build things, there is a very good chance you will become addicted.[/b]

This game is a digital drug. It is an incredibly polished gem with very few genuine flaws.

[b]There is almost no grinding, either.[/b] Only during the first few hours will you regularly have to collect leaves and wood to keep your first generators running. Once you unlock coal power, even that is over. Resources are infinite, and when you dismantle something you have built, you get 100% of the materials back.

That makes experimentation painless. Built something wrong? Tear it all down and start again. Nothing lost.

As for the objective: You are a Pioneer on an alien planet. Your job is to exploit its resources and manufacture a wide variety of products, which you then send to a space station using a Space Elevator.

At first, these are simple products requiring only a few resources. Towards the end, however, you are producing increasingly complicated high-tech components that require entire factory complexes to manufacture.

And that is part of what makes the game so satisfying: You actually have to use your brain a little.

Nothing too complicated - you won´t need to write a PhD thesis. Most of the time it comes down to questions like: How many machines or resources of type A do I need to keep X machines of type B running?

And once the production chains become really complicated, there are calculation tools available on the web to help you out.

At first, the varied map feels absolutely enormous. Important collectibles are scattered all over the world, unlocking new technologies and components and giving you a good reason to go exploring.

There are several hostile species on the planet as well. If you eventually get tired of being attacked all the time, you can simply change creature behavior to passive.

There is even an Arachnophobia Mode that replaces the genuinely nasty spider-like monsters with something considerably less terrifying. It´s a small but very welcome accessibility feature. Thank you, Coffee Stain Studios.

So there really isn´t much to complain about. Perhaps the excellent, chilled-out, almost hypnotic background music repeats itself a little too often and could use a few more tracks.

Another criticism is that the game does not officially support modding out of the box. There is an active modding community and a huge number of mods available, but you need a community-developed mod manager to use them. Not everyone is comfortable installing third-party software.

Why, Coffee Stain? Why so half-hearted here?

Did I mention that you can build entire railway networks, either for your own transportation or to move products automatically?

Or Hypertubes for personal transportation, basically like something out of Futurama?

Or - unfortunately unlocked much too late - even teleporters?

As a casual gamer, you´ll probably see the credits after around 300 to 350 hours.....

.....and immediately start a second playthrough to build even better, bigger, and more efficient factories.

[i]All so you can win the Golden Nut.[/i]

So join in, Save the Day, and save all the puppies and kittens on Earth.
The Factory must grow!
