Intro:
It's a MOBA, if you never played MOBA, take your time learning the game and watch some videos for newbies (ideally play in between, you will better understand what they are on about). Don't worry if you get completely destroyed vs players early on, it will take some time to understand how things work and you will often get matched up against players with thousands of games played. Which is like adult gorilla vs 6yo human in a fist fight, except here you get to continue living and learn from them.


Gameplay:
Compared to LoL for example, dota has much more depth. It is more tactical/strategical game, if you can plan ahead just a few minutes temporarily changing your strategy you can impact the outcome of the game. It feels like even when you are at 5:30 kill disadvantage you still can turn things around. While in LoL it would just be another 25minute stomp.

Heroes can be played differently (in different lanes with different builds), and generally people don't complain until you fail miserably. Game feels a lot more dynamic, there are so many more factors to consider - Night/Day, Trees are 10x more interesting than brushes, Gateways, Curriers for your equip, Runes, TP, neutral items, shop items have much more depth and impact etc. etc. 

There is no dedicated jungler (normally). Not many people like that role, and even if they do, they end up having these bipolar games where you are either praised or hated. But at the same time, jungle has much more complexity to it. it can even be cleverly used by supports to assist your lane for example!

You can deny friendly creeps(minions) to reduce enemy exp gain and farm. You have much more early game build options than just doran and tear and maybe few more niche items. Some heroes like invoker have like 20 different abilities.... The list of depth just goes on and on...


$$$ Paywall:
NONE. You can play all heroes, no restrictions. Pay strictly for cosmetics or Dota plus if you are lazy to google things it can provide some nice statistics and a shop helper, although I generally play with player made guides.


Cons:
PINGS, one thing I still didn't get used to.. Pings are just not very intuitive and even after customising still feel clunkier and not so well made. Missing sometimes has voice sometimes it doesn't, 'get back' is written in chat with no warning sound :D, who reads chat when you are in middle of a teamfight? there are similar pings for important things though, so with some customisation it can be just fine.

I suppose a steep learning curve, but honestly it's not that bad. Once you understand most basics you are golden and it feels more like finding little Easter eggs when you realize you could have been doing this and that as well.


To wrap up:
There is loads of good things that I didn't mention in this wall of text. So go and explore, in worst case you will decide it's not for you and maybe come back to enjoy it 6years later like I did :D.

So, let me preface this with my current mixed feelings. I'm a Old school Hunt player but I wasn't here from the start, Just like being a Millennial stuck between an dying era and a new era, that's were I sat with hunt for a very long time.

TL;DR: If you never played Hunt and you like large sandboxy experiences in a PvPvE Extraction environment, This is the game for you. If you're an Old head that took a long break from the game, Embrace the changes or stay away as you'll be more heartbroken than anything. Also it's live-service so enjoy it while you can.

Let me lay out the facts before any opinions of mine. Hunt is indeed a Co-op/Solo experience where you interact with other players on a map with objectives. This may be Doing the main objective of Claiming and extracting with any bounty tokens you pick up in a match, or any personal goals a user might set, such as getting their weekly/dailies fulfilled or finding equipment and gear on the map to take back for later deployments. It's a Sandbox experience as Crytek puts it, as you can leave whenever you want, you just need to find the extracts and you can go. 

The Perma death aspect of the game is very minor, if you cannot extract for whatever reason (You died, ran out of time on a map) that hunter is lost, you get a portion of your exp and anything you unlocked during the mission but that's it. It's not a very hardcore experience in that regard as with the way equipment works you'll be back on your feet like nothing happened rather quickly, along with the fact that most of the weapons and tools in the game are very viable to use to kill other players, you just need to be open to using them in a few interesting ways.

The microtransactions have picked up quite a lot but they have done away with the old systems that used to use blood bonds. The only things you can purchase with blood bonds is the current battle pass, bloodline quests, and any skins/hunters/animations off the store you like. You'll always have them so there's no repurchase, you may have to unlock said weapon or item again if you prestige but it will still be yours. Besides that you can still purchase DLC packs if you do not want to purchase the currency if you rather that. Fair warning, you will see hunters/items you don't own or that aren't even available on the store, as it was a limited time event thing before hunt had it's engine upgrade. They are making efforts to bring that content back but it will not be in it's original form entirely, so if that's a pet peeve for you then make a pass on this.

The gameplay is very simple. There's no Shield, No Blue juice or any of that crap. You have 150 HP as a hunter, if you loose it all you get downed and loose one of your big or small bars. If you get headshoted by anything (So long as you take 1 damage to the head excluding pellet based projectiles, melee that's unable to do 150 Damage to the head, and non-weapon tools) you also go down. If you're a solo the only way you can get back up is if you have necromancer, and you lose it once you revive yourself but you get full 150 back no matter what happened.(Unless you already burned your last bar while alive, tough luck.) While if you're in a team, a teammate can pick you back up but you won't recover that bar. Once you're on your last bar if you go down again you're dead for good unless a teammate has a bounty token and gives up some of their bar to pick you up, then you're back on your last one again.

With that all outta the way, let me move on to more opinion based takes.

THE GOOD

Hunt is a great game if you enjoy audio importance, if you love to listen to sounds as each one has important morsels of information to digest to help you win encounters and fights more, or just keep yourself alive from making a foolish choice. Each class of gun has unique sounds, and exotic choices also have another audio cue when close enough so you can already know what kind of fight you're getting into. This does mean it's harder to enjoy the game with noisy company unless you basically silence them but it's very rewarding to make some rather impressive displays of game knowledge just from a few audio cues.

The weapons are very well balanced nowadays, With nothing being an outright winner in all categories. There's no Rifle beats Shotgun, Shotgun beats Pistol kinda archetype here. I can and have won against Snipers or Long rifles with only a Shotgun and melee in tow, but you're pushed to figure out how can you best play with your surroundings and tools to make the best of a bad situation. Everyone is going to have some weaknesses of their loadouts, But playing to their strengths is key to finding yourself walking out with more than you started with.

There are many tools in the game you can use that seemingly have a main purpose but with the interactions in the game world, you'll find out that they can be used in many ways to get the upper hand or cover up a mistake you might have made. I'm not gonna go over all of them but I'll go over the classic Choke bomb in the game. It's a tool you prime and throw like a explosive, but instead of an explosion you get a large blurry choke cloud that will consume any fire within it, and prevent any more fires in it's AoE. If you walk through one, your character will begin to uncontrollably cough, which acts like the aim punch when you take damage. Just with those two facts alone you can create some interesting situations that either buys you some time, or control how your enemies approach you.

THE BAD

You are going to lose, and maybe at best tie with some situations in the game. Doesn't matter if you're solo, duo, or in a trio, sometimes you get into situations where it's practically unwinnable, or you just didn't have enough information to make the right calls in the moment. Because Audio is so key in the game, players will make use of it to draw your attention or avoid it entirely to get the drop on someone, and there's not much you could have done about it but been even more careful.

The kinds of people you'll be encountering in the game is a mixed bag, you'll get a lot of good ones but there's always bad apples in any group. It makes matching up with randoms a bit problematic as you don't know what you're in for if you join up with two other folks that have entirely different goals than you do going into that match. You can always leave if you want if you match with people that you don't mesh well with but just keep in mind you loose your hunter if you quit while you're downed.

They have been pretty good at patching bugs lately but there's always going to be room for something to ruin your day, learning all the "Quirks" of the engine as you play can be a little frustrating when it costs you a fight or even the match if that's the last team. Besides that the AI in the PvE portion can be very finnicky, you cannot trust them to do or commit to attacking any player they see as they're also drawn to audio, so as I would put that portion in good, it's quite annoying to get attacked for something an ally has done inside while you're outside.

I have not had this much fun with an FPS since Killzone.
Gameplay loop revolves around doing missions with varied objectives where you fight bugs/robots and gather a wide array of minerals for ammo/health replenishment and reward currency.
The missions are always procedurally generated so each one feels different and fresh.

Positives:
- Very replayable missions with big enemy, layout and objective variety
- Good gunplay and mostly well balanced
- Fantastic weapon customisation systems, especially with overclocks that can completely change how a weapon functions
- Strong class identity, great for us RPG lovers
- Space dwarf vibes are done really well, with each biome and enemy having its flavour
- Excellent sound design
- Many visual customisation options and rewards to earn
- Very generous pricing and no microtransactions (only several dev supporter packs), entirety of post-launch content was added for free
- Plethora of difficulty options and modifiers that allow you to have fun regardless of your skill/experience with FPS games
- Although it's namely a co-op game it can still be enjoyed solo with a helper bot that assists you in various ways

Negatives:
- There is jank (especially with player collision and some achievements) but nothing too annoying
- Bad reconnect feature that does not work most of the time
- Perk system is poorly designed; many are useless, Dash should have been a baseline ability and Iron Will is so much better than everything else
- Some bosses are pretty meh/annoying
- Cosmetics should be unlocked for every class at the same time, no reason for having to unlock the same reward four times

Overall strong recommend. It's also often on sale and for that price a real steal.

TLDR: If you like Battle Royales and don't really care for the Titanfall universe, you'll probably enjoy this game, but otherwise it's just a disappointment. 

I do fundamentally think I could never truly appreciate this game. I've already thought that the Battle Royale sub-genre of shooters is just inherently flawed, and Apex Legends unique character abilities isn't enough to get me to change my mind on that, since it doesn't do enough that's unique or creative outside of that. If you already don't like Battle Royales, this game just won't change your mind.
Additionally, I'm a massive Titanfall fan, and to think that this is the spiritual successor to that series hurts me deeply. While I feel there is potential for this game to explore the lore and world-building of the Titanfall universe in a different manner than the previous Titanfall games, this game mostly just feels like it's just wearing the skin of Titanfall and not much else. Titanfall absolutely mastered the interweaving of elite on the grounds soldiers and behemoth super weapons into a gameplay flow that you don't really get to see all that often, and even though they would be much harder to implement properly in a Battle Royale (maybe the successor to Titanfall shouldn't have been a Battle Royale :P), it's still a disappointment to have them nowhere. As well as this, the movement in this game is an absolute sham. To think that the excellent freeform movement of the game that essentially created Movement Shooters has been reduced to something so simple is just heartbreaking. Where the hell is wallrunning? Not even Ash can do that? Not a single legend can Wallrun, and everyone is slow when it comes to combat movement. Titanfall gunfights were a lot more about how you move and constant repositioning in order to gain the upper hand, and the movement in AL just doesn't let you do nearly the same. 
All in all, if you already enjoy Battle Royales, this game will probably be up your alley. At this point though, I'd take a 3rd Titanfall game with microtransactions as bad as this game has them so long as it feels like Titanfall.

Hunt: Showdown has a pretty solid gameplay loop that lets you play for 30 minutes or 3 hours depending on your mood. Matches are short enough to not be long in the tooth, but long enough to let you get stuck in and actually experience the game. Of course, your raid can be cut short by someone shooting you from 100 meters out, but getting back in is so quick you don't lose much time. 

The old timey guns also gives people who aren't shooter savants a snowball's chance in hell at winning a fight. Positioning is key, and head to head fights aren't as common as you think. Often you'll be shooting at someone who doesn't know you're there, or is otherwise engage with someone else. People will be shooting at you in the same way. The game gives you great feedback about what's going on around you though, so you're never completely clueless. Sounds cues for footsteps, equipment jostling, and gunshots are well defined, and help  quite a bit when deciding tactics in the moment. 

That being said, this game is HARD. You're going to run into a lot of people more experienced than you, and you WILL die more often than not. This game is not for the easily discouraged, and especially not for those who can't find joy in the little victories. 

But if you can swallow your pride and go into this with a student's mindset, there's quite a bit of entertainment to be had.

It's pretty much a 10/10 and more importantly a game that respects your time / appreciates you playing. "3 day wait times for crafting, grinding for materials, you have to pay to rush crafting and buy SLOTS!!!" Yup. All true. 
-Crafting times help me pace rather than blowing through everything in a few months
-Material grind in many cases is only necessary if there's something you desperately want. If you're in no rush to get something, you'll inevitably get it as the game sends you all over doing different missions
-The premium currency in the game can be obtained by trading with other players. You can VERY EASILY play this game start to finish without paying a cent and more importantly without feeling like you had to grind like crazy / miss out on fun stuff to do it (I'm looking at you, Helldivers 2). 

I pay $10 for premium currency almost every time I reinstall not because I need the plat but to pay for what I get out of the game. Every 100 hours or so you'll remember the game is f2p and feel compelled to buy some currency as your way of contributing to the game's continued success.

Some advice for new players:
-Set your matchmaking to solo for the first few missions in the game or get a friend to install it with you. You'll sour on this fast if you get matched with some bozo with a maxed out frame/weapon joins and melts everything just by existing. Once you're stronger, understand the movement and have gotten the hang of things start joining lobbies
-Spend your free plat on slots no matter how tempting those pretty cosmetics are
-Don't feel dumb looking up plot summaries of missions after you beat them. The plot of this is insane and hard to follow but people much smarter than you and I have mapped it out and explained it very well
-Pace yourself. Don't try to juggle grinding everything all at once.

V Rising is a smooth fusion of top-down action RPG combat and survival crafting that nails the vampire power fantasy well for the genre.

Then there’s Fashion Frame. You think you’re farming to get stronger. You’re actually farming because your shoulder armour doesn’t match your emotional support cape.

Some grinds will test your patience. The new player experience occasionally feels like being handed the keys to a nuclear submarine and told to check the wiki. But the combat, customisation and sheer amount of stuff to do keep pulling me back.

Played the entire free version to completion before touching a single expansion: level 80, full Personal Story, zero mounts, zero elite specs. This is not a demo. It's a genuinely complete game.

The free tier gets you all 9 professions, max level, the full story, PvP, dungeons, fractals, and hundreds of zones. In 48 hours I finished the story and still had only touched about half the map: 123/303 tasks, 218/486 waypoints, 72/226 vistas. There's an absurd amount to do before you'd ever need to pay.

What works:
Combat feels fluid and current for a 2012 game, with 10 skills, weapon swapping, dodging, and no forced rotation
Dynamic events make the world feel alive instead of quest-marker soup
XP for exploring, not just killing; climbing to a vista actually matters
Horizontal progression means your gear stays relevant, so you're not chasing a treadmill
Community is unusually helpful, cooperative by design rather than competitive
Personal Story is fully voiced with real cinematic weight

What's rough (in the free version):
Only 2 character slots
Tight bag space and trading post restrictions
Core classes feel "fine"; elite specs (paywalled) are where the real class identity lives
Story ends on a clear "now go buy the expansions" note

None of that feels like manipulation though, it feels like an honest first chapter. The expansions go on sale constantly, so if you wait, catching up is cheap.

Bottom line: Play the free version first. All the way through. Then decide. You'll already know the answer.

As a disabled gamer who primarily plays solo, I cannot recommend Sea of Thieves. While Rare has partnerships with disability charities for positive public relations, the core architecture of this game remains fundamentally exclusionary and ableist.

1. Rare falsely advertises Safer Seas as an "extended tutorial", stripping away 70% of gold and capping progression at level 40. This excuse makes zero logical sense. The mode provides absolutely no guidance, tips, or tutorials on how to deal with massive emergent threats like Megalodons, Krakens, or Skeleton Ships. Furthermore, it does nothing to teach a player the ropes of PvP combat (ladder climbing, different canon balls, throwables, ect.) which is highly chaotic and completely unpredictable. It is not a tutorial; it's a refuge that Rare intentionally crippled to make disabled and lower skilled players feel like second-class.

2.Accessibility Doesn't Ruin PvP as other major online games prove that implementing robust accessibility features does not compromise competitive integrity or ruin gameplay. For example, Apex Legends and Fortnite feature excellent visual sound indicators, highly customizable colorblind settings, and advanced menu-to-speech options that seamlessly bridge sensory gaps. World of Warcraft features built-in click-casting, automated targeting options, and extensive user-interface scaling to accommodate physical limitations. These features exist in highly competitive environments without breaking the game's balance or drawing complaints from the player base. Rare’s refusal to modernize their settings is a choice, not a mechanical necessity. A simple feature like a crosshair is considered cheating despite that there is still a chance to miss and despite that some disabilities can affect spacecial judgement. There are third party software's you can add but it is risky as Rare's Anti Cheat system can flag it which may result in an account ban just to make the game physically playable. 

3.  Whenever a player leaves constructive feedback or suggestions on how to improve Safer Seas or add accessibility features, even when offering balanced compromises that wouldn't devalue the PvP player experience, they are met with extreme hostility and complaints. The vocal player base treats Rare's rigid "shared world" philosophy as infallible law, weaponizing toxic "get good" remarks or hiding behind the phrase "It's a pirate game." They treat basic requests for human accessibility as if they are demands for an unfair competitive advantage, creating an aggressive echo chamber that drowns out marginalized voices and shields the developers from accountability. Even the moderators will lock any post on Safer Seas even if its about the concerns of accessibility.

So, if you are a gamer that needs accessibility to play I highly recommend to avoid this game.

A Convoluted UX Nightmare Burying Deep Potential  •  As someone who has only spent about two hours in RimWorld, please take this perspective for what it is—a raw first impression of the user experience, and I enjoy the discovery of a game, and don't use tutorials. Simply put: the user interface is an absolute mess. It genuinely feels as though the developer went out of their way to overly complicate every single interaction. I spent my entire initial playtime just trying to reverse-engineer the designer's thought process and figure out why things were structured in such a counter-intuitive, fragmented way. It leaves me seriously questioning how this game maintains an "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating. Are these reviews authentic, or is this a case of collective Stockholm Syndrome? My theory is that players who stick around simply develop a high tolerance for these flawed systems. Once you invest dozens of hours learning how the developer’s mind works, you build the muscle memory required to look past the terrible UI. At that point, the sheer mechanical depth and emergent gameplay probably take over, making the experience enjoyable despite the interface, not because of it. While it is incredibly tempting to completely tear this game apart based on how frustratingly unfunctional it feels upfront, I am trying to remain open-minded. There is clearly a massive amount of depth hidden under the hood. However, forcing players to fight a convoluted spreadsheet-management simulator just to execute basic tasks is a massive barrier to entry. The depth of a game should be found in its strategy, not in its menus.

As much as I have a want to play this game, I can't in my heart recommend it to anyone. Playing a tank combat game is fun, in concept.

When you look at the game mechanics: Different classes of tanks with different strengths and weaknesses. Different ammo types to assist in dealing with said tanks, it seems in depth and fun and it is.

The feeling of progressing up a line of tanks, getting better and better as you go along (in theory. Some tank lines follow this and some others are weird.)

The issue comes with subtle things that you might not notice at first. Of course as with all games, there are skill issues which can severely hamper your experience when there are people who have been playing this for over a decade and you as a new player do not have the map, tank and mechanic knowledge that they do. Learning these things can take quite a long amount of time to get used to.

The first major issue is the way that the game economy works. You are heavily incentivised to take a mixture of ammo types, but long story short, each tank has a "standard" round which can sometimes be good...... If you are being matched up against tanks that are the same tier as you. Unfortunately you are at the mercy of a matchmaker which can pit you against tanks up to 2 tiers higher than you, which feels awful a lot of the time. This will force you to use the "premium" round, which requires you to pay a lot more credits for each one you fire. Even then you may not be able to dent those higher tanks because of the variance between each tank's armour penetration stat. Having this happen a lot will make the gameplay feel horrible, all while draining your credits, which is the currency you earn for playing the game and need to use to supply your vehicles, upgrade them and purchase new ones. You can also be matched against tanks 2 tiers lower than you, which makes you feel godly, but just rebounds the same issue to other players. Overall a terrible design choice.

The second major issue is that, while its not been confirmed as a problem, you will start to notice that you have a better time while playing solo rather than in a platoon with friends. While this is an unspoken thing, a...... theory if you will among players, the same patterns can come up in many testimonials, which all but proves it. This effectively turns the game into a single player game, which if you are like me and wanting to play with friends....... is kind of a no go. I don't want to sit in a chat with 3 friends while we all queue solo just to have some fun.

Unfortunately these things take a little while to gain experience with, where you get gripped by the good pieces of the game that drew you to it in the first place, leaving you between a rock and hard place later in your journey.

The game is egregiously monetised, often selling "premium" tanks that have all the bells and whistles compared to the tech tree tanks you work your way through, becoming a pain to face in the field, A good player can work around this, but not every player will be good and if you are just starting out, this will be even more frustrating.

Having your team get consistently scraped along the floor in most games wouldn't be as bad if you had a load of fun doing some damage in a game, but unfortunately the progression in the game is linked to you doing well in the match AND winning. You hit a great game where you did record damage, got 5 kills and blocked loads of damage? well if your team torpedoed into the enemies and got killed quickly, then sorry to say that you'll get minimal xp and credits, making the progression through the higher tiers a slog without paid xp boost missions or a serious amount of time to devote to just playing this game.

Its a shame, because there is a lot to like about the immersion of a gigantic tank battle across varied environments, but honestly........ the novelty will wear off soon and you will get more frustrated as you get better only to be hampered by many of the points I've listed.

You would be better spent with your time and money elsewhere. Don't be like me and take 1000 hours to come to that conclusion (I have played for a large amount of hours on consoles or the WoT PC dedicated client before playing on steam) or worse.......... like some of the veterans who are way further down the rabbit hole

Rimworld is my first colony management game, and likely my last one, as I never cared for the genre. That being said, by no means is it a bad game, at all, it's actually one of my favorite games and considering that this game attracted me should put into perspective how cool it is. I still haven't gotten any DLC, and yet I'm still plenty satisfied with what I have gotten out of the game thus far, and of course mods are a wonderful, wonderful addition. 

I went into Rimworld completely blind (I thought guns had limited ammo, no idea mechs even existed until a fair while etc...), with the help of the in-game tutorials which helped me a lot, and despite not having played a game like this before, I found my way pretty smoothly. What really got me into the game was the dynamics between your pawns that you, yourself craft in your mind. The struggle of learning the game, and the unknown really got me hooked because it's rare when I experience I game that's totally different from what I know to heart which is almost always racing games. 

Being hailed a "story teller" frequently, I think Rimworld does a decent job at doing so, but as I briefly mentioned before, you make it yourself based on what happens in your colony. The simplicity of the game with almost entirely still images making up the world, actually does wonders for the game, to me at least. It really lets your imagination do the work without even trying, and you really start to care for your colony. I found myself to be pretty min-max-y over time, and while I overwhelmingly prefer the story telling aspect of the game, how the game functions and encourages you to do things like making killboxes starts to almost force you to min-max. I never play on crazy difficulties because that doesn't interest me and I've never even beaten the game (I never felt the need to, I love just growing a colony), but those critiques still top my list of complaints for the game. 

In terms of story though: great stories are made with Rimworld. My favorite playthrough is still my first one, which I played around 50 hours on, and yet I only made it 2-3 years into the game. Having things like your main cook being incredibly depressed because his wife was kidnapped and killed, and then his fellow colonists throw him in jail so he stops going on food binges, is amazing. Making good stories, good or bad, unsurprisingly is the best part of this game, and it has you hoping to encounter another great series events like these. My playthroughs seem to have been very tame compared to others', so keep that in mind, anything, and I mean truly anything can happen. 

Rimworld in my opinion has near infinite replayability, and mods add to that, whatever it is you decide to add, and I still haven't tried any of the DLCs yet, but I definitely will at some point, which can completely change various aspects of the game. 

To wrap up though, I have 500+ hours on Rimworld, and I still haven't seen everything there is to see, and I can assure you that I'll be back for more, a lot more, and Rimworld is definitely worth your attention coming from someone who first had zero interest in this kind of game.

I was gonna write a whole spiel about how this is a really shallow game designed to optimize the most theoretical playtime via grinding and "progression" in a way that would make Ubisoft envious, but the truth of the matter is that's why people play it.

Those people are wrong. Their idea of fun is wrong. And all of my group's hours (across however many platforms and services we tried it, probably like 350) in this game was for the sole satisfaction of knocking down their sandcastle as they built it. We would sail around and sink sloops laden with loot for no other reason than to rob them of hours of mindless drudgery. We'd pretend to be friendly just to see if someone bought it then blast them to oblivion. We'd stay hidden on an outpost to wait for somebody to stop by before logging off, then shanghai them, sink their sloop, and sell all their loot not because we planned on doing anything with it, but because it meant they lost everything. They would cry and bemoan not having anything, and still we would hound them to the ends of the map to sink them. They would say they just wanted to do Tall Tales, and still we would pursue them again and again to deprive them of progress. Once, a particularly unlucky soul had arrayed some 80% of his loot on the shore as if safe to do so, flaunting his wealth in the slums of Chicago, as it were. Before he had finished unloading he was sunk, and on each return trip he watched bit by bit as his progress was undone. The game allowed him to respawn and try and save his efforts, only to die and see a bit more gone to us. Try after try he sailed back to crash into the island, desperately clawing at us only to get a birds-eye view as his pirate soul left his body of how little we hadn't sold. It very well could have never put him up with the vain hope of grasping that loot back, but it didn't. It wanted him to see and feel each and every thing we did. He got notifications of his loot being "donated". And none of that ever was for our own gain. We did not put a single dime of it towards a super expensive cosmetic we would use. It is still out there as some digits in a file on Rare's servers. 

Understand now that we were not the  psychopaths to be blamed: the game is the true sadist. It let people like us clock out and exact imagined revenge. It let that poor man suffer. It created the illusion of a happy little goofy pirate game and then let us hide behind the curtains. Never did Rare take any action against us, our piratical escapades of terror only stopped because one of us was banned for calling a victim a "LIL' BITCH" in a thick accent via megaphone.

To be honest, I wouldn't bother with this game. While the leveling is fine, it is certainly no better than World of Warcraft. The classes don't feel unique since they are all purely focused on dealing damage. Navigating the zones is incredibly frustrating; enemies are packed far too close together, there are too many of them, and they take way too long to kill. 

Questing essentially amounts to helping conveniently placed NPCs with time-consuming tasks, and that is what you will repeat every 10 levels until you reach level 80. Most of the time, these quests do a poor job of explaining what to do, leaving you expected to just figure it out on your own. 

The monetization somehow feels even greedier and more predatory than Blizzard's model with WoW. Sure, you can play the base game for free up to level 80, but the entire experience is designed to intentionally create inventory and convenience frustrations that practically force you into the cash shop. Transmogging your gear costs a specific resource that is incredibly tedious to acquire for free. Furthermore, basic quality-of-life necessities, such as material storage, bag slots, and unbreakable gathering tools, are locked behind microtransactions. It frequently feels like the game purposefully designs annoying systems just to sell you the solution, which feels highly manipulative for an MMO. 

On a positive note, the expansions are actually pretty well-written, feature a more classic quest design, and offer decent gameplay. Unfortunately, unlocking endgame elite specializations for your character isn't tied to a dedicated class questline. Instead, you just run around map-completing and collecting Hero Points, which is tedious, and the areas you have to navigate to get them are extremely annoying to deal with. 

Progression in the expansions is also deeply frustrating because of the Mastery system. Once you hit level 80, your normal leveling stops, and you are forced to grind Mastery points and experience to unlock basic navigation abilities, like gliding or bouncing mushrooms, just to get around the maps. The game does a terrible job of explaining how this system works, how to effectively gain experience for it, or where to find the points you need, leaving you feeling completely stuck and lost. Obtaining mounts is also a major, time-consuming chore. People often claim this game respects your time more than World of Warcraft, but I wouldn't say it does that at all. 

The endgame is also exceptionally boring. Dungeons are overly complicated, Fractals are simply not worth your time, and I haven't touched PvP, so I cannot comment on it. I get why people start playing this game, it does look really cool, but honestly I couldn't give you a single good reason to try it.

++The Good++

World & Lore: The story was great (honestly better than Star Wars), and the atmosphere and environments are beautiful.

Gameplay: The gunplay feels amazing, there are tons of Easter eggs to discover, and there is enough content to keep you busy for hundreds of hours. It's incredibly fun with friends.

--The Bad--

New Player Experience: The UI and direction are confusing at first. I found myself glued to Google just to figure out what to do next.

Campaign Quality: The Edge of Fate campaign was dookie cheeks! Easily the worst campaign I've played in my life. Most of the other campaigns were decent to awesome, though I accidentally played them backwards since the game is so confusing to navigate.

The Raiding Barrier: While most content is solo-friendly, entering raids as a new player is tough. Groups often want to farm as fast as possible, and the tricky mechanics make it intimidating to jump in.

Verdict: Despite the bad it is a generational game if you give it a solid try where there is nothing quite like it. Highly recommend!

I am horrible at writing reviews, but here we go.

[h1] Summary [/h1]

 I started playing Guild Wars 2 in Feb of 2023, shortly after I got tired of playing RuneScape for the past 2 decades. I fell in love with it and bought the first two expacs shortly after. So far, I only have about 1300 or so hours in it and I am still having a blast playing the game, whether it's on my main character or on my alts, there is always something to do. Given the dynamic events that pop up constantly, it makes the world feel more active and engaging, no matter what area you're in. The community has been really great and even met some new friends after joining a guild a few years ago. I would highly recommend giving this game a shot for anyone looking for another MMO to try out. 

[h2] Favorite Detail [/h2]

The other thing that I love about GW2 is the fact it's not a subscription based game. Yes, it has a MTX shop, but the game does have to support itself somehow given that you just need to buy any DLC's once for your account and you'll have access to them all the time, rather than needing to worry about a sub. 

[h2] Quick overview [/h2]

There are 5 unique races and 9 classes to try out, each class having its own difficulty and playstyle. Each Class does have its bounds for what gear and weapons you can equip, but I personally think its well balanced. Once you've played enough to venture and acquire legendary gear, the legendary gear can be accessed by any character on your account once they hit level 80 which is amazing!. 

[h2] Performance [/h2]

The engine itself is a bit dated, and only runs on DX11 so there is a CPU limitation when it comes to larger battles and open-areas, but it's not too horrible. I have enabled Nvidia Smooth Motion and it does help out a bit, even though its really fake frames being generated. Overall, I'd say give it a try and see how it goes for you. Even with GW3 being announced, I'll still play GW2 as its been one of my favorite MMO's to date.

[h1]In a nutshell[/h1]
One of the best, if not the best, base-building and RTS games of all time. Yes, it's not just "story generator" like Ludeon calls it, it is a strategy, real-time one more precisely. In this game, you must survive and plan your further survival firstly, to then later enjoy impenetrable fortress you have built with sweat and tears, and finally either escape this awful planet, destroy its biggest threats, [spoiler]or even merge with planet's hidden supercomputer, local archotech.[/spoiler] Or just stay and enjoy your local utopia! Or just get overwhelmed by the threats and lose. Losing is normal, it is part of game too! RimWorld adopted its inspiration's, Dwarf Fortress, motto: "Losing is fun!"
[hr][/hr]
[b]Gameplay: 10/10
Graphics: 8/10
Audio: 9/10
Value: 10/10
Replayability: 10/10
Perfomance: 7/10 (perfect in early, painful in the late game)
Stability: 9/10 (no game-breaking bugs, only "honest exploits")
Overall: 9/10[/b]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
In short: choose scenario, customize it, start, gather first resources, survive first threats, get more workforce, build a little town, do the quests, explore the world, survive against even bigger threats, research key technologies, modernize your settlement and optionally choose which ending to finish to then try to complete it (or lose). It is a general progression of the game though, and each step in each playthrough is unique. Beware: this game is not for the faint of heart most of the time, especially on regular or higher difficulties. And you will quickly get affectionate to your colonists!

The core problem is managing your colonists, which are in this game called "pawns", more precisely managing their mood and needs. Sleep, food, recreation are examples of those needs. If needs are unfulfilled, pawns may go into mental breaks, or even die if this need is medical care and nutrition. You may have heard lots of stories and memes of losing the game because critically important pawns die or simultaneously go into mental break during serious threat, and yeah, that's how usually it ends! I mentioned that this game is a strategy. Why? Because managing needs is its own kind of art! And remember, it isn't game that is so cruel to your pawns, those were your own mistakes that silently murdered your settlement!  Unless you play "Losing is fun" on naked brutality in sea ice with Randy Random as storyteller. Oh, forgot about storytellers. Don't worry much about them: they are difficulty settings themselves, or "styles" of gameplay. Cassandra Classic is persistent, Phoebe Chillax is like Cassandra, but "lazier", though more "explosive" in terms of threats, and Randy Random is just random, he is icon of this game (he is the one with purple shirt)! Randy can be either too harsh for you or too peaceful, you never may know ahead what can happen.

About pawns themselves: in RimWorld, technically everything that is not static is called so, but in particular it means your own human colonists. They are EVERYTHING for you. Only they can be controlled directly. They have their names, traits, passions, skills, preferences, and even backstories! For a pawn to be as effective as possible, you must respect its personality. And about threats: those are such events guaranteed to happen that can damage or even destroy your settlement, so you must act depending on the threat. For example, raids. Mindless hordes of human zombies that belong to agressive factions ("civilizations"), or non-human ones, even robotic, that want to either just damage your settlement, kill your pawns, kidnap them, or outright destroy everything. There are several ways to deal with raids: defense, preemptive strikes and more, including just abandoning your tile. But don't underestimate the threat if it clearly is too big! Pride and overconfidence is what ends the game. There are so much more types of threats, there are even unnatural (in Anomaly DLC) and cosmic (in Odyssey DLC) ones, not just raids. Rule of thumb is to be ready to deal with anything! Even at cost of giving away valuables ("wealth management"), because it is these valuables that determine size of raids.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Composition[/h2]
I know that description above can be little too abstract, but I've written so to give the general idea of how the game [i]feels[/i], not just to list every nothing that everyone already have read or knows. If you wonder whether should you buy all DLCs or not, I recommend to buy all of them. But if you want the distinct ones, start with Biotech, then Ideology, Odyssey and the rest. OST is awesome, artstyle is awesome too. Don't get fooled by "minimalism", just like in Dwarf Fortress, mechanical wonders are hidden behind minimalist artstyle. Also, RimWorld has almost infinite replayability, considering how much things you can customize. Some playstyles even have distinct, unique mechanics, for example, "vampires" (sanguophages) with their special abilities and blood (hemogen) need; "robots" (mechanoids) with their gestation, repair, charging; "magic" which is there called psycasts that can teleport stuff around the map, get invisible, summon thunderstorm, or even cause the love and so on. And if there is something you lack, you can find mods in Workshop page! "Vanilla expanded" mod series is the most popular choice at the moment of writing this review.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]My experience[/h2]
I've personally played lots of fun scenarios, including mountain base, plains base, nomadic playthrough, but mostly tropical playthroughs with focus on high-tech. It was disappointing at times because of lack of depth for some mechanics (transhumanism particularly), but it is just me being petty. Overall experience is extremely positive and fun. You may wonder why this long review was written by someone who has just 5 hours total, and it is because I've been playing "unofficially" 2000+ hours and decided to finally buy the game to support the creator, and potentially make my own mods. Who knows, maybe I will actually create the high quality mods, or will it stay empty words.
[hr][/hr]
[b]Thanks for reading this review, enjoy RimWorld![/b]

I really wanted to love ESO because the Elder Scrolls universe is great, but the monetization makes it incredibly hard for me to enjoy.

You already buy the game and expansions, and then there's an optional subscription on top of that if you want the experience to feel more convenient. Then you have the Crown Store, cosmetics, DLC, loot-style items and all the other things being sold separately.

I understand that MMOs need a steady source of income, but ESO sometimes feels like it's designed to constantly remind you that there's another thing you could pay for.

The game itself has a lot of content and the world is fun to explore, but the whole business model just takes away from it for me. I don't want to feel like I'm managing a subscription and a virtual wallet while I'm trying to enjoy an RPG.

3/10 — I wanted to explore Tamriel, not explore the Crown Store.

I started playing Hunt: Showdown right when it left its beta phase, convincing myself to buy it after a friend’s relentless recommendation. I will never forget those first 20-30 matches or the unmatched atmosphere: the "heavy silence" surrounding you, forcing you to listen to every single twig snapping; the pitch-black nights; and the constantly pulsing danger of players and monsters lurking in every shadow. It created an unforgettable, truly unique experience that set it apart from every other FPS on the market. 

Visually, what Crytek created with the CryEngine is nothing short of phenomenal. You get a truly cinematic experience, complemented by a minimal HUD and surprisingly solid performance. Sure, there are occasionally laggier periods especially right after major patches or new map releases but these issues usually get ironed out over time.

Unfortunately, a few persistent bugs have plagued the game for a long time. I consider myself one of the lucky ones with over 500 hours, I’ve only encountered one maybe every 100 hours or so. But when they do happen, they really hurt. In a high-intensity match filled with adrenaline and action, it stings when the game essentially gives you the middle finger and leaves you completely helpless.

It was never an easy game. Even back then, long ammo dominated, and players would gladly rat in bushes for hours. Yet, all of that was easily forgiven because everyone agreed that despite its flaws Hunt was a stroke of genius. A fundamentally fresh concept (I mean, cowboys and zombies? Sounds like a B category film premise, but Hunt made it work flawlessly).

Fast forward a few years, and the game has drifted into a very different direction. Tarot cards, fast-firing weapons, "drone beetles"... Don’t get me wrong, I actually like some of these additions. For example magic was always subtly present, so things like tarot cards fit the lore and can be interesting mechanic. But somewhere along the way, the core soul felt a bit lost. Matches feel increasingly rushed and shifted away from hunting bosses or engaging in meaningful PvP to grinding through Battle Passes and getting rare skins.

At its core, Hunt is still a brilliant, pioneering diamond in the rough. However, sometimes less is more IMO. Many of the mechanics and additions bloat the experience rather than genuinely improve it. I deeply miss the simplicity that once defined it (WHICH already came with a CRAZY steep learning curve).

I don't necessarily blame the developers... it's a live-service game, and they have to sustain a business model. And it remains a deeply enjoyable game, BUT I think, it has been heading in the wrong direction for quite a while now.
If you thinking of getting the game, at least do so on a sale, see if it clicks with you. Happy Hunting!!

Never has a game made me feel so productive while accomplishing absolutely nothing with my life.

Gonna start by saying Factorio looks simple at first: mine some rocks, build some machines, and eventually make a cute little factory.

Give it about three hours, and suddenly you're calculating the iron requirements for seventeen different machines while questioning why you haven't eaten.

You start with a tiny furnace and somehow end up constructing an industrial complex that could probably supply electricity to a small country.

Up goes the factory, the production lines, the conveyor belts, and most importantly, your sleep schedule.

Never have I seen a game turn the phrase "I'll play for five minutes" into waking up at 4 AM surrounded by belts and inserters.

Gonna be honest, the bugs are probably the only thing preventing me from covering the entire planet in pollution and machinery.

Let one biter attack your factory, and suddenly you're spending the next two hours building a defensive wall like you're preparing for World War III.

You think you've finally stabilized everything, until one belt backs up and your entire factory enters an economic depression.

Down goes your productivity, your sanity, and your concept of time.

Never the less, Factorio is ridiculously satisfying because every problem can eventually be solved by building something even more complicated.

Gonna need more iron? Build another mining operation.

Give me more electricity? Build more power.

You need more resources? Build trains.

Upgrading the factory somehow makes you need even MORE resources, which means MORE trains, MORE belts, and MORE machines.

Never have I been so happy to watch little robots carry tiny boxes around.

Gonna rate Factorio a solid 9/10, because it's one of those games where you sit down thinking you'll play for an hour and suddenly the sun is rising.

Let me know if you're planning on playing Factorio, because once you start, there's a very real possibility that you may never escape.

You have been warned.

Issue 1 - The combining tree : I was not really a fan of the resource tree and how it functions. Resources require other resources that require other resources. Some need to go through the processor 5 times, some just once, some are manufactured in 5 seconds, some in 30, some are made in single item batches, some are made in bulk. Half of your factory will be working their ass off while the other half will do nothing waiting for components. You will be hearing the assemblers and drills start and stop and start and stop constantly- and no amount of tweaking or over/underclocking will make the process smooth and actually satisfying.

Issue 2 - Unmovable terrain : When building any kind of building you are at the mercy of the map- even terrain is exceptionally rare so you will either have grass and rock clipping through your floors or have your entire building floating above ground.

Issue 3 - Tedious cupon unlocks : I get that unlocking stuff from the shop is a good idea but the fact that the cupons get exponentially more difficult to obtain makes unlocking stuff a real chore. Issue 4 - Clip n Snap : They did try to implement some sort of grid system however most if not all machinery and stuff has odd dimentions. Instead of stuff being in clean grid intervals objects are like 1.05 foundation wide and 1.40 foundation long. In short : Nothing quite clicks together nicely- despite being grid based everything appears habhazardly thrown everywhere. Unless you are not using foundations and just placing everything on the terrain... then yes- they ARE habhazardly thrown everywhere. Worst part : to accomodate for that developers made everything clip through everything- conveyors through rock, players through rock, pipes through machinery, conveyors through conveyors - everything clips through everything.

Things that i liked : Animations are nice
Character movement and items are excelent-

Unlocking new tiers and components isn't a reward - instead of thinking "oh great now i can make new components" i'm thinking "oh great... ill need to add more splitters and assemblers to my incomprehensable, ugly cluster of clipping conveyors to make some new trash that i'll use to pile on the trash"

⭐ Hunt: Showdown — A Brutal, Beautiful, Beginner‑Friendly Extraction Shooter
Hunt: Showdown is one of those rare extraction shooters that feels intimidating at first glance but becomes incredibly rewarding once you step inside its world. What makes it stand out is how welcoming it actually is for beginners. The game teaches you to slow down, listen, and think — and once you get the rhythm, Hunt becomes one of the most addictive shooters out there.

A Diverse Cast That Actually Feels Meaningful
One thing I’ve always loved about Hunt is how diverse its roster of Hunters is. Crytek doesn’t just throw in random characters — they build personalities, backgrounds, and visual identities that make the world feel alive. You see representation across different ethnicities, genders, and styles, and it never feels forced. It feels like a world full of real people who ended up in the bayou fighting monsters.

Beginner-Friendly Despite Its Reputation
People love to say Hunt is “hard,” but honestly, it’s one of the easiest extraction shooters to get into once you understand the basics. Unlike other extraction games that drown you in loot systems, armor tiers, and endless menus, Hunt keeps it simple:

You pick a Hunter

You pick your weapons

You go into the bayou

You survive

The clarity of the design makes it way easier for new players to learn positioning, sound awareness, and pacing. And once you get your first few kills, the game hooks you forever.

DLC That Gives Real Variety
Hunt’s DLC packs are some of the best in the genre because they actually give you variety, not just recolors. New Hunters come with unique vibes, new weapon skins feel fresh, and the cosmetics help you express your identity in-game. Whether you want something gritty, stylish, creepy, or heroic, Hunt’s DLC lineup has something for every playstyle and personality.

Giggle the Clown — One of My Favorites
Giggle the Clown is easily one of the most iconic Hunters in the entire game. The design is creepy, funny, and stylish all at once — and running around the bayou as Giggle feels like you’re starring in your own horror movie. The in‑game store makes it easy to grab characters like Giggle without any grind or nonsense, and it’s one of the reasons I love Hunt’s cosmetic system.

Necromancer — A Solo Player’s Best Friend
If you play solo, Necromancer is one of the strongest abilities in the game. Being able to revive yourself changes everything:

You can take more risks

You can clutch fights you “should’ve lost”

You can outplay duos and trios

You stay in the match longer instead of instantly dying

Necromancer gives solo players a fighting chance, and it’s one of the reasons Hunt feels fair even when you’re outnumbered.

Final Thoughts
Hunt: Showdown is a masterpiece of atmosphere, tension, and tactical gunplay. It’s diverse, beginner‑friendly, and full of personality thanks to its DLC lineup and unforgettable Hunters like Giggle the Clown. And if you’re a solo player, Necromancer turns the game into a whole new experience.

It’s one of the most unique shooters ever made — and it deserves way more players.

In the spirit of my Factorio review, this is one for the people who are how I used to be - for the bleeding-hearts who shudders at the mention of the dreaded "STEM." First, a quick comparison if you have played neither this or Factorio:

Factorio: Far deeper on a mechanical level, especially with an extensive and rabid modding community. A much more flexible skeleton, designed for folks who want to solve more complex engineering issues with harsher penalties for failure. Ore nodes deplete, pollution attracts retaliation, and you can't solve spatial restrictions by building vertically. There's a ton that the game does better than Satisfactory, too, but this is a Satisfactory review. Factorio's a great game. If you're a logic game pervert, go play that one first.

Satisfactory: This one is for base builders and explorers. It is an overflowing eye candy buffet. It's also far more forgiving—your core resources, deep within the earth and mineable at fixed nodes, are infinite. In a 3D plane, your building space is also more-or-less infinite. You can spend a grotesque amount of time painting floors, walls, ceilings, lights, elevators, and more, or you can slap your machines on bare earth and make the world your factory floor. It's freeing, fun, and gorgeous.

You don't need to be an engineer to start playing Satisfactory. You just need to want to build something, and the engineering know-how will fall into place. The heart of the game is the bespoke puzzles and logistical challenges that emerge from your own series of decisions, and its systems guide you effortlessly along the track. You'll be amazed at the compounding results of your incremental progression as you go from burning mulch to oil to uranium, spreading your sprawling cityscape of a factory across a gorgeous, hand-crafted world. Shout-out to the ability to randomize the resource placements within it, though, for freaks like me who can't engage with something like this if it's the exact same puzzle everyone else is playing.

If you're curious, give it a shot. It's a gem.

TL;DR is that the game has a lot of visual charm, fun combat and builds, interesting world, and engaging building, but falls shorter when those initial pros get expanded in the later game to becoming meta-reliant builds, relying on bosses to not do certain moves at the right time and the right place to win, and the world hindering your efforts just for the nerve of being there to begin with.

The Good:
- Visual Style. The unique visual style is honestly gorgeous. From the design of some of the enemies, the castles you can make, some of the cosmetics you can get, it's honestly all very good looking
- The combat. At times (more about this later) the combat can be really enjoyable, especially when you find weapons you like and feel natural with. There's lot of options so finding a weapon you enjoy or spells you like the synergy of is almost impossible not to find. 
- The building. Building in this game feels fun and well crafted. Granted, I'm not the best builder and my layouts are something out of nightmares for better players, but I never felt like it was too hard to understand.
- The world. Some of the biomes and ways how to navigate around the world feels interesting. Each area has unique hazards you have to learn your way around that I actually find enjoyable.

The Bad:
- The bosses. I am probably gonna get strung up and hung for this, but some of these bosses are unbearable. While in most games with bosses and their difficulty being a centerpiece like in a souls game for example, usually you can step away from the fight when you beat them with a sense of accomplishment and adoration for the boss. This game does not give me that after a certain while. Once you start getting to around Act 4 or maybe even 3, the boss difficulty scales from them having movesets that test your cooldowns, positioning, and managing your timings for your attacks to an artificial difficulty through gimmicks that feel almost impossible to deal with. If you fight them in their lair area, it's a place that if you walk even a single step out of line and that's it, fight is done, you died. Some of which is unpredictable and requires cooldowns that the boss already had you burn, making it a roll of the dice if you win or not. Or if they are a wandering boss, they only wander in a path that forces you to fight them in a 1x1 block with impassible terrain on either side with enemies potentially showing up that you can do nothing about. It's a constant cckblock that makes getting the later bosses unfun.
- The builds. In a game where you're allowed and even encouraged to experiment with all sorts of weapons and spells and counterplay, it eventually boils down to the meta being the only viable option in the late game. If you enjoyed a certain playstyle and found it fun, well unless that style is the meta, too bad, you don't get to play the fun game anymore. Before anyone goes, "technically you can play the game with anything and win," yes, you can, but I also enjoy being able to play my favorite version of the game without feeling like I'm being sounded with a spiked rod just because I'm not playing the meta and playing the game in the way I have fun with.

The Ugly (Personal Gripes):
- Building can be fun, but with how you're expanding new buildings almost constantly, it gets really annoying to have to reconstruct whole rooms or wait forever to get materials to make whole new ones just because you can't get rid of the older unlocks. If they were to make it so that the new building is an upgraded version of the old ones you needed where you can make the things the old one did with the new one and save yourself some room and space, that'd solve this easily. This gets a lot more noticeable when it comes to forging. 
- While most biomes are fun, there's a few exceptions. For example, the Cursed Forest intentionally nerfs your character since you have to settle with a weaker cloak that allows you to see through the woods rather than one that actually would allow you to get to a closer gear level to fight the things in it, especially it's late-game wandering boss. I've never enjoyed an area in a game all about gear levels that forces you to take a weaker alternative just to be in it, against enemies that easily stomp you because of it.
- Multiplayer can be a blast assuming you play it with friends. I've had experiences in other server-based base-raiding games before where someone who's been grinding since the servers conception still sticks around waiting for new players to feel a glimpse of enjoyment before running them off the server and complaining no one is coming in to give them something to do. While V Rising is better at this issue than those games have been, it's still a problem with how steep the grind can be at times for new players to stand a chance in anything other than PvE or playing with friends.

Rimworld is like a more accessible, futuristic version of Dwarf Fortress with heightened modding possibilities.

The content of the base game alone is enough for plenty of play time with tons of fun to be had from running a cannibal cult, to being invaded by an army of rabid tortoises. The UI is easy to understand, the premise is fun and freeing, the gameplay itself is a simple yet engaging loop that makes you never want to put it down, and the music is some of the most relaxing and fitting pieces I've heard in my years of gaming. What really puts this game over the top though are its DLCs and the modding community. Each DLC provides a unique, useful, and worthwhile expansion to the vanilla game that gives you a plethora of new possible situations to play out in an equally expansive amount of different ways, and the modding only further serves to enhance that. The workshop is full of a lot of questionable low effort content, but also plenty of gems - full conversions (KOTOR, ESCP, FCP, Rim Effect), DLC sized expansions (Vanilla Expanded, Biomes!, Landforms, Multiplayer), and an endless selection of smaller individual mods to craft your own personal experience. I for one enjoy creating collections to convert Rimworld into other franchises I wish had a similar game like Star Wars, Tarkov, Elder Scrolls, Baldurs Gate, etc.

Basically what I'm saying is, Rimworld is more than one game, it's quite literally whatever you want it to be. It's so modular that there isn't really an end-all-be-all to what a reviewer could say playing it is like other than "settlement management".

It's a good game, give it a shot - it rarely ever goes on sale, and when it does it isn't a big difference so don't bother waiting. If you're tight on cash the DLC isn't necessary although I would say Ideology, Royalty, and Biotech are absolutely worth the extra money (in that order).

It has come to the point where unfortunately I feel more negative about this game than I do positive, and I wanted to write a review about why that is for anyone interested in the game. There's a several frustrating things which interfere with enjoyment in playing this game, increasingly so as more time passes.

First, we need to talk about logistics. A key part of the game, and enjoyable...as long as you don't try to interact with vehicles. The most recent 250 hours you see of my playtime were spent attempting to work with tractors and trucks in a working logistic system, no mods or anything; 3 different playthroughs with around 70-80 hours each. The problem is, once your pathing becomes complicated enough around stage 4-5 with the recipes you gain at that point, you will have tractors/trucks freezing in place for no reason at all, forcing you to come and manually push them or move them even if you are across the map and doing something else. I tried three different save files to create working logistics systems with vehicles, even following video tutorials at one point to make sure I followed *working* directions, and still your whole system will become locked up and unplayable. This isn't even mentioning the fact that there are NO CURVED ROAD pieces to turn your car, so you have to follow another online tutorial to learn how to build curves yourself in the blueprint maker. So just avoid vehicles then, right?

Here's the second problem. Conveyor belts are going to be your only solution all the way until the point you've unlocked trains, and they work flawlessly as long as you're following basic design principles. But the problem isn't conveyors, it is what they're attached to; splitters/mergers and the manufacturing facilities you will use throughout the game. Satisfactory's buildings are large, very very large. You will need to practice your slide jumps and agonizingly careful movement techniques in order to traverse the pieces of your factory to do maintenance, because everything is so large in scale that it's horrible to move through without blade runners and still difficult with them. You will find yourself constantly moving just to get different angles to connect power to things, adjust your belts, and change products in your manufacturers as you continue to upgarde. This is barely alleviated by the jetpack which you'll have to tap hover to see things from above unless you want to hop from object to object, and only somewhat solved by the hoverpack, which takes a lot of work to get to and you're already worn out by that point. If there was better movement options like variable speed for the blade runners or at least omni-directional sprinting so you don't catapult forward accidentally while using them and fall off your 307th object, then that would be an improvement.

We're finally at the last point of this review, and it ties everything together into the final big problem you'll deal with in this game; you are actively punished for trying to build with the environment at all, half because everything is so large and half because 80% of the world isn't flat enough to build on without frustration. I mentioned trains earlier when talking about your options for logistics, and they have their faults too. They take an unbelievable amount of space, and are the single most tedious thing to try and place in the environment with their rails and stop points. So you'll need to do what I end up having to do every time if you don't want to break your back working on miniscule adjustments, or apparently as I found out, what most youtubers suggest. Build in the air way above everything, so you don't have to interact with the bumpy uneven world you cannot terraform, and live with how ugly it is so you can fit your absurdly large buildings. I know the devs said it was too late into the game's development for them to add terraforming into the plans, but they did not need to craft a world that's okay at best for exploration and TERRIBLE for building on.

Bonus pain point: Trying to use the parachute at all locks you into an incredibly nauseating animation every time you use it as well as hand mining resources, and no sliders/checkboxes in the settings disable it.

TL:DR: Vehicles are still terrible and have AI that breaks when you actually try to rely on it, there are no curved road pieces this many years into the game, movement options are frustrating and limited, building scale is an annoyance to deal with at any real scale, the environment punishes you for trying to use it and there is no terraforming, trains push the scale annoyance dial to 11, and drone AI will break if you try to use it at any real logistical scale too besides minor deliveries. There are enough factory games releasing now that will substitute this and you won't miss anything.

[h3] I was told I couldn't do it. [/h3]

I was trapped: stuck inside a randomly spawned treasure vault that I had managed to glitch myself into with a teleport bolt. The wall enclosing me was made entirely of steel; my chainsaw wand was of no use to me here. In order to breach this wall, I needed one of the following: (a) a concentrated mana potion to melt the steel into steam, (b) an acid potion/spells to eat through the metal, or (c) a luminous drill wand to cut through the steel. 

I had none of these things. But, I did have one thing: a dream. A stubborn, stupid dream to make use of my fire immunity buff and fire potions to light up a blazing hellfire and do the one thing that I was told that I could not do: melt through the steel walls.

My fire potions did their work, my water potion was cooked into a steam potion, and all of the remaining objects in the room had melted down into molten metal. The prospect of this thin veneer of molten metal encapsulating the steel frame, pushing the chemistry engine of the game to its absolute limit, gave me hope that I could do the impossible: melt the steel frame that had become my tomb.

I kept firing my teleportation wand haphazardly, banging my chainsaw wand hopelessly against all edges of the frame, hoping in vain that I could breach the hull. Briefly, I managed to get stuck in the ceiling from a wanton teleport bolt, getting stuck and losing oxygen in a pocket of molten metal that had somehow managed to become enwedged [i] above [/i] me in the ceiling. And was growing. This gave me hope that the environment was changing and that salvation might yet be near.

I began to kick at the molten metal, causing it to shift around in little pixel chunks. I brought my focus to the bottom left corner: this is where I would make my stand. I kicked and kicked, hoping to somehow, someway breach the steel metal that could not be breached with the tools that I had at hand. Until, finally, a sign of hope: a kick, a spark of molten metal flying out of the side of the steel vault: a breach. [u] An exit. [/u]

I loaded up my teleport want, aimed, said a quick prayer, and fired. And I came out on the other side of the wall. I did it. I was freed. And what of the steel wall of the treasure vault that I could not possibly break out? A definite, real breach.

Even after this many hours and with the flow of new content having weakened a bit i still return for a couple missions every now and then, because the game is just plain good. great, even.

The different classes work together to cover all of a team's needs quite handily. The scout has superior mobility for gathering resources and helping with certain hard to reach mission objectives, and of course he is also important as the main light source in the caves, but the average scout will most likely struggle with large swarms of enemies as his weapons are more equipped to handle a fewer quantity of high priority targets rather than a flood of cannon fodder. So he needs some adult supervision from a REAL man with a REAL portable swarm missile rack or the rough equivalent, which is the gunner. The gunner is conveniently also equipped with an OH SHIT button, that being the shield bubble projector that scares enemies away just enough for them to not want to be inside of it, while also blocking projectile attacks and quickly restoring shields for anyone inside. The gunner may be a veritable walking fortress in his own right, but he is one man with one set of eyes, luckily the humble engineer has his own eye that (mostly) never sleeps, his sentry turret, although most engineers carry a pair of them. They do provide a respectable amount of firepower, but another often overlooked advantage is the fact that they'll automatically start spraying whatever threat enters their monitoring area, and thanks to their distinct firing sound your teammates will know for sure that it's time to stop digging in their butts and start digging into the crowd of bugs that may want to take a bite out of their butts. Your engineer may even have a Weapon of Mass Destruction hidden under his cap if he didn't go through his entire ammunition stockpile in the first 5 minutes of the assignment. And the driller is also there. The driller has no thoughts in his head as his weapons require approximately zero finesse and they solve the problem of impending enemy swarms by making the entire cave generally inhospitable to non-humanoid lifeforms. One of his weapons is a septic tank with a nozzle. His hatred for arthropods is only matched by his hatred for the non-precious varieties of rock and stone (he's the driller he has drills and they drill). He may struggle with distant threats but that's where the scout shines thanks to his armaments having better than average precision. It's the perfect circle of camraderie.

The enemy designs are honestly quite incredible as every non-fodder foe either has a very distinct look or makes a very distinct sound or even both at the same time, so dying or failing a mission only feels unfair in exceedingly rare cases, since at any given moment you have detailed information about what enemies are present and where, so with a solid plan even the largest waves can be weathered by experienced enough players.

The playerbase can be a bit overbearing to some (larping! he's talking about larping!) but underneath that it's actually shockingly good. The number of times where I got kicked for seemingly no reason or where the host simply ragequit due to dying too many times etc. in all of my games was like in the single digits, maybe, MAYBE it ventured a bit into the double digit territory, but generally when I boot up the game I don't find myself considering whether I should go at it solo or try my luck in the public lobbies and hope I can properly finish at least one mission. I think people just like this game so much that they don't mind a bit of hardship occasionally. We shall dub this phenomenon "having fun". Perhaps more similarly good games are in order to help further our understanding of "having fun".
Honestly in my top 10 of all time, and that is a stacked list. For the right kind of brain this game is unlimited dopamine.

Factorio is one of those rare games where you sit down intending to play for an hour, then suddenly realise it's 2am and you've spent the last three hours redesigning a production line because one belt wasn't quite efficient enough.

What makes it so good is the constant progression. Every problem you solve creates a new problem to solve. You start out manually feeding a few machines, then you're building automated factories, trains, logistics networks, circuit-controlled systems and eventually entire production chains in space. There's always something that can be expanded, improved or completely rebuilt.

The automation is incredibly satisfying because the game rarely tells you exactly how you should solve something. You understand what needs to happen, then design your own solution, and when you finally stand back and watch a complicated factory running automatically, there's a genuine sense of achievement.

Space Age takes that formula even further. Just when you think you've mastered your factory, you're suddenly dealing with space platforms, asteroid processing, new planets and completely different logistical problems.

It's complicated without being complicated for the sake of it, ridiculously addictive, and has an enormous amount of replayability.
