[h1]95.6 Hours of Responsible Planetary Development[/h1]

When I first bought Satisfactory, I became completely obsessed.

I played for almost [b]24 hours straight[/b]. At one point I left my PC running just so my friend could join later and we could keep the factory going.

And somehow, the fun never stopped.

[h2]Our Contribution to the Planet[/h2]

We landed on a beautiful alien planet and immediately decided to:

[list]
[*]Destroy the ecosystem
[*]Build factories everywhere
[*]Cover the landscape in conveyor belts
[*]Build walkways so our factories looked nice
[*]Build a road around the entire planet
[*]Automate absolutely everything
[/list]

You know, standard environmental practices.

[h2]The Best Part: Making It Look Good[/h2]

I love that Satisfactory isn't just about making the numbers go up.

You can actually spend hours designing your factories and making everything look good. Roads, walkways, buildings, production lines, lighting...

Did something need to look nice?

No.

Did I spend 45 minutes making it look nice anyway?

[b]Obviously.[/b]

We even built a road around the planet for our car.

Was this necessary?

[b]No.[/b]

Was it useful?

[b]Not really.[/b]

Did we build it anyway?

[b]Yes.[/b]

And then we discovered the pipes.

[b]...The road suddenly seemed considerably less important.[/b]

[h2]We Basically Invented Uber[/h2]

Eventually our factory became so automated that we had trucks driving around collecting resources for us.

At one point we had effectively created [b]Uber, but for oil.[/b]

Instead of picking up some guy outside a nightclub at 2 AM, our trucks were driving across an alien planet to pick up petroleum.

This is what gaming has become.

[h2]The Building Bug[/h2]

I originally played Satisfactory back in Early Access, and I've recently started coming back to it.

Big mistake.

The building bug is still strong.

I keep telling myself:

[i]"I'll just build this one thing."[/i]

Three hours later I'm standing on top of a factory wondering why I need another 47 conveyor belts and whether this particular walkway really needs to be symmetrical.

[b]It does.[/b]

[h2]10/10[/h2]

Started with a factory.

Ended up industrialising an entire planet.

Would absolutely do it again.

I really wish there were more options to experience the game in a PvE environment. It wouldn’t even need to offer the same rewards or progression as PvP. I’d be perfectly happy with significantly reduced rewards—10% of the normal XP or rewards, for example—or even a mode with no meaningful rewards at all. I’d just like the option to enjoy the gameplay, explore the mechanics, fight AI enemies, and spend more time in the game without always having to participate in PvP.

I’m not asking for PvP to be removed or changed for the people who enjoy it. I’d simply love to see an additional PvE option for players like me. The core game is something I genuinely enjoy, and having a way to play more of it in a PvE-focused environment would make a huge difference for me.

Shockingly accessible considering how high the skill ceiling is- i am not ordinarily the type of person that enjoys automation games, and held off on starting for a long time because I was intimidated by Factorio's astronomical skill ceiling. When I started, it eased me in with very simple logistical problems that grew very gradually until eventually it clicked that I was now working with problems I never thought I'd even be able to understand, much less attempt to solve. It also gives you an enormous amount of control over the exact kind of experience you want, both through in game options and mods. The most beautiful part of the game to me is that you don't need to go in with an intense minnmaxxing mindset- the game's issues have a way of flowing into each other such that it only ever feels like you are solving a couple issues at a time. This means that even though you have to build massive, complex factories, it never really feels overwhelming. I strongly recommend giving this a shot if you have any interest at all.

This is a polarizing game. Some love it, some hate it (but play it anyway, go figure); and some who loved it before hate it now. My personal journey - I really loved it at first, quit when I felt the quality going down, picked it back up when a friend wanted to play, and I'm now loving it again.

tl;dr - If you're an older gamer who loves the Elder Scrolls franchise, is okay with playing a dumbed down version, wants to play it with friends, and doesn't mind paying for an MMO subscription, this is worth checking out. Some deeper points:

1. If you don't like games with a semi-freemium payment model, this game probably isn't for you. To get the most out of the game, you need an MMO subscription.

2. It takes a very special person to like playing this game without a subscription, and most people aren't this special. You have to not be a hoarder, have excellent inventory management skills, have zero interest in crafting, be immune to FOMO, not care about cosmetics, have excellent planning skills (ie, I need to go to these towns at this cadence to do these things...), and enjoy organic character progression (ie, have patience with leveling, acquiring gear through social interactions, not wanting to rush to end game).

3. The golden age is over. Keep in mind that this is an old MMO. When it first came out, the graphics were beautiful, NPC interactions were fully voice acted, and questing was deep (ie, not just fetch quests, messenger quests, or bounty quests). Now, the graphics are comparatively mediocre with clunky animation, better game voice acting exists, other games have pushed the boundaries with questing depth (so this now feels just average), and slop updates introduced fetch quests/bounty quests/messenger quests.

4. You have to be okay with children complaining. The kids complain that PvP is unbalanced, then they complain again when the meta changes and their OP characters are nerfed. Meta changes happen to rebalance the game. Also, you need skill to be good at PvP. I lost all the time in the beginning, but now I win consistently with off-meta mid-tier gear because I now have skill. And I still lose to top-tier players with top tier gear. That's a me problem because I chose not to grind for top-tier gear and they have better skill, not a problem with balance. The children don't seem to know the difference.

5. Werewolves are OP. I hate them. They need to be nerfed. PvP is so unbalanced.

6. Be aware of the difficulty curve. The game starts medium, then gets hard in the middle levels, then gets easy at the higher levels; then at end game, it is as hard as you want it to be (giggity), ranging from stupid easy to very challenging.

7. I really like how a character of any level can go to any zone with party members of any level, and the content can still fun for everyone.

8. I really like the combat system. You have to know frame rates and button lockout periods like a fighting game, find gear and ability synergies like a puzzle game, develop a rotation like a traditional MMO, and have creative reactions when things go sideways. It is a full brain experience that is both cerebral and kinesthetic.

A little prologue: I have been following Stunlock Studios since Bloodline Champions. The battle system they have build there is the bread and butter of the studio. It is to this day great and they needed time to find their niche, because MOBAs are a bit of a devisive topic, as I have learned over the years. 

I have bought this game on its EA release and was pretty hyped. The vampire theme felt fresh for me, the fights felt rough in the beginning, but I persevered, beat some mobs, forged weapons, built a castle, farmed ressources.. Fight, Loot, Repeat! 
Since the game was not finished yet, I put it aside and bided my time. A friend, who is quite apprehensive of MOBAs but loves Vampires had the idea, to play the game with me. We wanted to grind out each achievement. So we did, for the last month. 2 hours a day at minimum. 

In the beginning everything was new, we built ourselves up, upgraded our castle. We choose brutal difficulty to play this game once and get through all achievements. This was a smart idea, but we did not know the remifications yet! 

We were in awe with the graphics, learned certain mechanics and tried to wing the game as we went. My friend who dispises MOBAs did not like the fighting very much, but he learned, he grew, he shut up about it, as long as it worked. The game was fun for him, to a degree. I had the time of my life on the other hand and was caught between Stunlock nostalgia and a challenge I signed up for. 

Then we faced the first acts boss and he took a while. This brutal boss was our first reality check and a warning of what was to come! We struggled, I explained what I understood of the boss and we tried again and again and again. 

(On normal difficulty we would have breezed through the game, as we understand it, since the brutal difficulty only adds health and one or two mechanics.)
So we went through the game: Two german vampires hiring servants and commanding inmates, putting fear in those so called big shot bosses. 

We had to grind in certain areas at times, since some ressources were scarce and our equipment needed repairs for sure or our servants could not handle their farming tasks anymore.

But Simon Belmont! This son of a gun was a nemesis of ours. We had to cheese him once into fighting another boss. The second time around we had to abuse the fact, that enemies AIs are not the best, to slay him, because we both did not manage to drink his blood the first time. 

Solarus and Adam were an even greater chore. Dracula became nearly impossible, hadn't we discovered a video explaining the fight in excruciating details going as far as putting a special emphisis on phase 4, where you needed two specific spells to stand a chance.

We 100%ed the game! My friend did not like it. I loved it, although some bosses tested my patience. 

Would I recommend the game to you? HECK YES! But be prepared it is not about the roleplay at times, it is more about battling bosses, gathering resources and upgrading your gear. So if you dislike challenging bossfights this game might have a slightly bad taste for you. 

Would I recommend brutal difficulty and 100%ing? Only if you played the game once casually. We did it blind and it was feeling too hard at times. Don't get me wrong. Most of the time it felt fair to loose against a boss.

The game is fun, graphics are consistent and great, bosses are pretty unique to fight against. The battling system to this day is one of the best IMO. Money spent on the game is money spent well!

I don't want to say this game is bad, but it's genuinely just not for me. I bought the base game + DLC at full price without hesitation, so I definitely didn't want it to just gather dust in my library. But I simply cannot get through the early game. Here are the main points that made me quit:

1) Forced Refactoring vs. Linear Progression
I believe a game can be hard, but it should allow players to achieve linear progression through their effort. This game, however, constantly forces you to backtrack, tear down your past work, and rebuild. In the eyes of a perfectionist player like me, this is exactly like software development: I've written a pile of "spaghetti code," and leaving it there is disgusting to look at, but refactoring it is exhaustingly painful.

2) The Micro-Friction of Inventory Management
Even if I gather the courage to bite the bullet and refactor, having to clear my inventory every time before tearing down and rebuilding is the kind of micro-friction that completely turns me off. It's 2026 now, and there are so many good games out there. To play Factorio, I'd have to pass up on several other interesting games.
But right when I want to sit down, plan things out, and get into a flow state, the game suddenly pops up and says: "Hold on, your inventory is full. Go find a wooden chest to dump these 2,000 iron ores and 500 broken belts before you continue."
It’s exactly like having a burst of inspiration to write a masterpiece, only for the system to prompt, "C drive is full. Please clear junk files to open Word." This forced downgrade from "high-level macro design" to "low-level micro management" completely destroys the gaming experience and flow. Anyone would find this incredibly frustrating.


Let's be honest, folks: the underlying framework of this game was designed in 2013, and 13 years later in 2026, it feels outdated—at least in the early game. I know the mechanics improve later on (with logistics bots). My question is: it's 2026, why do the designers still think players must serve a "20-hour prison sentence" before they are worthy of enjoying a smooth experience?

The list of Rare software's sins is long and extensive:

-The filesize of this game is ridiculous - 134GB on my PC. This game does not have nearly enough content to justify such a filesize. Such a filesize is a product of Rare's horrible optimisation. The excuse that the PC version needs 4K textures is tragic and absurd.

I won't even dive in detail in the server issues from a few years ago when the servers were so bad there was a community made calendar to mark server outages and at one point 20 out of 30 days in a month were marked.

You can not call yourself a professional gamedev studio and then not fix a bug for years, unacceptable.

-The game does not run well consistently. The framerate seems stable but then boom, a stutter and a drop to 0 fps while selling loot for example. This happens to both me (decent PC) and my friend who has a beast of a PC. It happened to him in combat aswell almost losing us a fight. Unacceptable in 2026.

-Rare insists on still providing support for older consoles which is holding the entire game back. It's time to kiss the old gen consoles goodbye and upgrade to the newer version of the unreal engine.

-Rare also insists on time limited events so they can fully utilize FOMO. Simply said that's a scummy business tactic. Even after being called out by the community Rare has doubled down and continued to spam out time limited stuff. So much for listening to the community.

-The content in general has been BAD recently and coming out slow as hell. This is the type of game that you can ENDLESSLY pump out new content for and it won't feel overwhelming, it's every dev studio's wet dream. Some of the recent seasons have been awful with season 14 being the worst example, having boring content and half of it not working on release. I suppose this is a case of "this game is not for me", but I honestly don't get what's so good about it.

Yes, the gunplay is good, that's great, but it's not enough of a reason why a game is "good".
There is too much bureaucracy in this game. Too many menus, too many different places to access menus, too much things in general. The UI is cramped, for reasons that make no practical sense.

I will never understand the reason why a game would want to add so much friction for what, at the end of the day, is simply a utility to buy/sell/retrieve/dismantle/fuse items. Why the need to talk to different people in different places or click in different menus to do the exact same thing, just with slightly different items?

But hey, if you're into that, good for you.

Another thing is the level design, it sucks. I'm sorry, but I don't get what's so fun about spending 70 minutes doing the "trickster" mission to jump between mirrors in search of a bonfire to lit, to open a random door the size of a phone charger hidden on a wall that you need to jump into the void to reach. Why? To waste my time? For what reason?

The game has a system that points you to things, it signals "go there" and you go there. Unfortunately, the devs decided that this is only useful when there is only one path: forward. When you get a labyrinth of a map you just get the "explore" goal and that's it, your problem.
And it's not like you're fighting through enemies, doing puzzles in front of you or exploring obvious paths, this ain't resident evil nor castlevania, or dark souls... you're looking for an out of sight hole in which you can insert yourself to "press forward", this is bad game design.

I don't want to watch a video tutorial about how to clear a mission and I don't want to play it twice for a time bonus, the times bonus should be about how quickly I kill the enemies, not about how quickly I find a random path in a shitty map.

Finally the grind. It's that type of game. Grind, grind, grind. Do farming missions to get better gear to get higher power to do higher missions to get better gear... you get the idea. The end goal? Dunno, being strong? Not sure. The lights gets (or used to get) reset anyway.

I play it to spend time with my friends, but goddamn do I find this shit boring. Would not recommend.
Even if you like this type of game, the "unlimited grind, bureaucratic" kind, there are better ones out there than this.

I wanted to like Noita because its core gameplay is great. Exploration is tense yet exciting. Customizing wands is immensely fun, and experimenting with spell combos is satisfying once you find one that clicks. Heck, even seeing how different materials interact with each other is also satisfying in its own way. It also has mods!

However, Noita is relentlessly difficult, and it doesn't encourage you to keep playing no matter how many times you will inevitably fail. The devs want players to experiment, but the game punishes experimentation. It doesn't explain much about its mechanics either, which is both intriguing and annoying. I might return to it someday, but that day is not today.

Overall, Noita has a lot going for it, which is why I wanted to like it, but its difficulty hinders the experience. If you like the idea of testing your patience, experimenting, and failing repeatedly, give this game a go. If not, I can't recommend it.

PoE used to be mostly just another Diablo 2 clone, but it adapted and expanded that sort of end-game style of gameplay to such an extreme that it has become its own unique experience.

It's hard to actually describe that sort of experience in text, you are better off watching some build showcases to see what i mean, but it is the reason why i played this for so long, more than any other game of this genre, and why i recommend it despite the many flaws that it has. And it's free to play so you can always just give it a try yourself.

As an example, in most other arpgs, a ranged build that reliably shoots something like 10 projectiles with every press, with extra explosions and effects would be considered to be around the endgame point of that build. In PoE i am covering the screen with 100+ arrows per second, and thats not even close to the endgame, that's just a build ive quickly thrown together just to get through the campaign a bit faster. Creating a slam so large it covers the entire screen and more, projectiles and lightning chaining through an entire horde of enemies in a single cast, teleporting and slicing everything across half the map in merely a few seconds with flicker strike, having all the monsters explode by just standing near them. PoE took various old skills and concepts to an extreme that i have not seen before and this is what i love about it.

Technically the gameplay itself is nothing complicated, in fact the goal of most builds is automating and simplifying as many of their skills, buffs and effects as possible, so it often ends up being kind of braindead. The real complexity lies within the process of building up to that point, balancing all the different scaling vectors, all the possible interactions, conversions, etc to maximise damage, clear potential, speed and defenses, and there are a lot of ways to go about it.
To support all that, there is a ludicrous number of skills, supports, item bases, mods and mod types, a giant passive skill tree, customisable passives in the form of jewels and many other things, this game goes all out on quantity over quality, but without completely dropping quality either.

As for the bad parts:

-Crafting 
Technically the crafting system is almost as complex as the builds themselves, there a lot of ways to go about it too. However, realistically, it is an incredibly frustrating system driven almost entirely by RNG.  There are a myriad of generally pointless mods, especially the many uselessly low tier mods that can always appear regardless of item levels and almost every crafting session involves at least one case of spamming whatever currency you need by the hundreds until you finally get the right mod. The chances of getting something good is always low and usually accompanied by a chance to undo some steps or completely brick the item and having to start over, if even possible, and that applies to nearly every single goddamn step in the crafting process.
Even after learning how to optimise it and even crafting for profit, i have to say this is by far the worst crafting system of all rpgs that i have ever played. And i am counting those that don't even have item crafting, it is THAT frustrating and i am neither a masochist nor a gambling addict to enjoy this.

-Visual clarity
Non-existent, with the kind of crazy builds you can get in the endgame. (and they still somehow managed to make this even worse in poe2)

-Player trade / economy
The player market isn't exactly a bad thing by itself, it allows players to trade for various items while focusing on the content they prefer and helps ease out the issues with random loot systems. That's the theory at least, in practice the PoE economy is focused entirely on the market, with the loot being balanced around it instead. Which results in the next part:

-Loot
Extremely random, too scarce, the vast majority of drops are nothing but trash. This is caused both by balancing around the marked and the ludicrous item mod pool that doesn't properly reward or account higher level itemisation. Only in very recent leagues has this been improved and even so, it doesn't feel like it's anywhere near enough still.
This also leads to the worst SSF experience of all games in the genre that i have played.

-Overall balancing
I have mentioned the variety of skills and items already and while most are viable, there are still a lot that do not work outside of extremely specific niche setups, or with prohibitively expensive gear, or some that simply aren't viable at all. All due to bad balancing and power creep

-Lack of QoL in certain aspects 
No inventory sorting, no automatic pick ups, no automatic tranfers, a billion clicks to do anything through your stash even after all the hotkeys they added, always spawn in town when logging in instead of your hideout, not enough inventory filters.

-Others
No way of disabling cosmetics on your end. Lots of players going around with loud, flashy and obnoxious cosmetics so all the town areas end up feeling awful because of it.
Adding poe2 enemies to existing poe1 systems without always properly rebalancing them
Servers aren't always stable and this is an always online game.
No offline game mode.

Regarding the price of the game, on paper it is free but if you do get into it you will eventually need to buy some stash tabs. I have managed to touch the endgame the first time i played without any of the fancy tabs and it was fine, but you will definitely need at least the basic stuff like a currency and trade tab should you go any further than that. Consider the "free to play" aspect to be more of an unlimited trial version.

This is a great game, it's crack for engineers. The factory must grow! Then it has to become more efficient! Optimize for size, for reproducibility, automate everything... you end up thinking like a programmer. The only minor downside is that as you get deeper into the game, it starts to feel more like an engineering job than a game.

I have around 600 hours in Satisfactory and finished Phase 5.
That probably tells you most of what you need to know.
**Graphics: 8/10**
Very good for a factory-building game. The world is beautiful, huge and visually distinct enough that exploration remains enjoyable even after hundreds of hours.
More importantly, your factories actually look impressive. Watching a gigantic production system that you designed operate across the landscape is part of the reward.
**Characters: 7/10**
There are barely any characters in the traditional sense, and that is completely fine.
ADA works extremely well, and the strange voices connected to the Mercer Spheres add just enough mystery and humor without getting in the way of the game.
"Sing us a song."
Somehow that fits Satisfactory perfectly.
**Story: 7/10**
There isn't much conventional story, but there doesn't need to be.
The light metaphysical background, FICSIT, ADA and the Mercer Sphere mystery give the world personality without forcing a narrative onto a game that is fundamentally about building systems.
I actually prefer this to a mediocre story constantly interrupting me.
**Combat: 5/10**
It exists.
It works.
That's enough.
Satisfactory understands that fighting is not the point of Satisfactory.
**Build System: 10/10**
This is the game.
At first you build machines.
Then you build production lines.
Then you build factories.
Eventually you realize that you are not really building factories at all.
You are designing a graph.
Resources are inputs. Products are outputs. Every machine is a transformation. Belts, tractors, trucks, trains and drones are edges connecting parts of the graph.
You can put walls around parts of it and call them separate factories.
But nobody escapes the graph.
The progression is excellent because old production never really becomes obsolete. Items from earlier phases remain relevant later, so your system grows instead of simply being replaced.
And if your architecture is bad, eventually the game exposes it.
**Game Design: 10/10**
Brilliant.
The developers understood that optimization itself can be gameplay.
There is no single correct factory. You constantly make engineering decisions: centralized or distributed production, belt capacity, transportation methods, resource allocation, redundancy, scalability and physical layout.
The game rarely tells you that your design is wrong.
It simply lets you discover the consequences 50 hours later.
That is much more interesting.
The progression also forces increasingly complex dependencies without completely invalidating what you built before. By the later phases, you are no longer solving individual production problems. You are managing an architecture.
Only a small percentage of players ever finish Phase 5.
I understand why.
Without some kind of design philosophy, the complexity eventually eats you alive.
**Gameplay: 10/10**
One of the very few games where I can spend hours doing something that sounds completely ridiculous when described:
"I redesigned the transport system for aluminum."
And somehow it is fascinating.
There is always another bottleneck to remove, another production chain to optimize, another transportation problem to solve or another factory to rebuild because you suddenly understood a better architecture.
And sometimes the best gameplay is doing nothing.
Build the system correctly, let it run overnight, come back and see whether your assumptions were right.
That is deeply satisfying.
**Overall: 10/10**
I have rebuilt almost everything multiple times.
Not because the game forced me to.
Because every time I understood the system better, I wanted to build it again properly.
After hundreds of hours, Satisfactory stopped being a factory-building game for me.
It became a game about architecture, graphs, optimization and emergence.
Machines are just the visual language.
Nobody escapes the graph.
**10/10. Masterpiece.**

Ahh RimWorld!! It is one of those games where you sit down intending to play for an hour, look at the clock again and somehow an entire evening has disappeared.

It is an absolutely brilliant colony simulator, but calling it that almost undersells it. RimWorld is really a story generator. You give your colonists somewhere to live, try to keep them fed, safe and reasonably sane, and then watch as the game creates stories around them that you could never have planned yourself.

Sometimes those stories are heroic. Sometimes they're tragic. Sometimes they're completely ridiculous. And sometimes you find yourself committing acts that would probably get you brought before The Hague because one of your colonists really needed a new kidney.

That's the beauty of RimWorld.

The simple art style suits it perfectly, the soundtrack is fantastic, the modding community gives it almost endless replayability, and every colony feels different from the last.

It can be peaceful, brutal, hilarious, heartbreaking and utterly unhinged, often within the space of about twenty minutes.

I remember playing this game when it first came out.
The first [i]Destiny[/i] was a bit of a bust - at least to me - it was interesting, but the hype train was way too strong and nobody was ready for the ships to be loading screens. After a hundred or so hours I had my customized sparrow with a purple void engine and end game armor - and I’d log in every now and again to take my whip out for a spin.
When [b]Destiny 2[/b] dropped, it was bombastic, it was focused, it had toppled every issue that the original had and multiplied its best aspects. I enjoyed [i]The Red War[/i], which was the base game when it first came out - and I felt that it was a wonderful introduction to the experience on so many levels. About a hundred hours later I was grinding [b]Gambit[/b] matches while traveling the surface of Mars during the [i]Warmind[/i] campaign and loving the title. 
You have to understand, this entire experience was based off of a grind that looks like a massive mountain from the outside, but once you get into a groove the cycle becomes addictive. You’re always a deployment or two away from the next bounty being complete and by the time you’re ready to log off for the night, there’s that one challenge that you could complete with just [i]one more[/i] match.
Exploration tasks, world bounties, event hunting, nightfall missions, vanguard deployments, the crucible, raids, gambit - there was always [b]something[/b] to do!
I put more and more effort into the core experience until I unlocked my personal favorite weapon: [i]Breakneck[/i] - a legendary gambit drop with a unique rampage that increased the autorifle fire rate and damage per kill. It was a beast in PVE and saved my caboose in PVP many times. It wasn’t the most broken, OP, or best - but it was mine and I had earned it over nearly 200 hours of grinding.
And then I placed the game back on the shelf and moved forward for a time.

Years later, I returned - and I wasn’t alone.

There was a wide eyed and lovely woman at my side and I was teeming with excitement to show her this experience that effortlessly stole my time away. I got her a copy and booted it up with her and - 

[i]There is no Red War…[/i]

What?

The priceless, emotional, and intense opening that set the stage for your [i]guardian[/i] to reclaim their light, learn their abilities, and grow into this vibrant world is all completely gone. It is replaced with an incredibly boring and criminally tedious opening. That pretty girl never got through the tutorial after hours of suffering through veritable fetch quests. I felt heartbroken for her, heartbroken for the experience - but chose to hop on and enjoy the game myself.

[i]Curse Of Osiris[/i] was gone… [b]Warmind[/b] was gone. I had quests open to go to Mars - and it was [b]vaulted[/b] forever! My gear, the weapons and armor I worked so hard to earn, upgrade, spec, and build around have either been deleted from my storage (as with everyone else's) or their power levels have been capped to ensure these things could [i]never[/i] be wielded in any serious manner.

The experience that I loved, the story and enemies I fought, the worlds that I explored, the adventures that I enjoyed - deleted. They didn’t fade to time, they were not casualties to circumstance, they were not shut down for lack of players - they were heartlessly deleted and callously overwritten. The game was once a premium experience with an upfront cost and some cosmetic in-game whaling, but now it is a free-to-play gacha title. Dime a dozen and full of predatory behavior - worst of all being a kernel level anti-cheat that ostensibly writes away the ownership of your computer to the corporate overlords in charge of [b]Bungie[/b].

This, in and of itself, is all the review that you’ll need.
[b]Destiny 2[/b] was - [i]WAS[/i] a [b]wonderful[/b] game that I could have easily recommended. It was addictive, it was satisfying, it was interesting, and there was a world of opportunity full of satisfying combat and well written factions.
Do you know how much I love [b]Destiny 2[/b]? I have a baby [i]Fallen[/i] plushy and 5 of the physical [i]Grimoire[/i] books. I love them. I love[b]d[/b] [i]the game[/i]

I came by to play the game just a bit more and pay my final respects - as it is now a live service game with no more live service… a “[i]dead service[/i]” game some call it.
It asking to install kernel level anti-cheat with paperwork reserving the right to strap a bomb to my motherboard - hard pass. I can’t reminisce - but I can tell you something.
This is a game all about grinding to earn quality loot, empower your character, and explore the world.
It routinely destroys the loot you’ve earned, nerfs the progress of your character, and deletes the world that you come to love and grow familiar with.

Games are more than just photos, movies, music - they are a multi-faceted artform that can be [i]experienced[/i]. When the greedy suits in charge of [b]Destiny 2[/b] order vast swaths of the game to be deleted from existence, they are destroying those things - they are destroying music, visuals, the [i]experience[/i]. They are destroying [b]Destiny 2[/b]

There is an insidious darkness that is not content with manipulating customers or “enshittifying” goods/services to achieve a better bottom line; there is an evil that is more than happy to erase beauty and human experiences from the world. It takes the strength of a [i]Guardian[/i] to stand up and defy it.

~

Want to make  space marine cyborgs that razes tribal villages ? A drug empire ? Harvest organs from anyones that decides it's a good idea to attack you ? Despite the minimal graphics, this game really shines in its complexity. You have to manage the ressource of your base, the defenses, the mood of your colonists, their health, the food they eat, etc. The game itself is built like a system.

Rimworld is not an easy game. You're gonna get thrown in that planet and it's gonna be up to you to figure out how to survive. You will make mistakes on your first colonies, and only after hundreds of hours you will really be able to understand deeply its mechanics, and at this point, the game really feels rewarding.

You are not obligated to do warcrimes and unhinged stuff in the game if you do not want to, but the option exists and the game doesn't punish you or reward you for your morality, except some colonists may be unhappy, like any normal human being that would be forced to eat human flesh... Yeah... Any 'normal' human being that isn't a cannibal or a psychopath.

A playthrough takes a lot of long game sessions, you will grow attached to your characters and everything you built, and this, and the randomness of events, is why the developper markets the game as a 'story generator'.


The DLC are also fair considering the number of hours you will play in this game, and are worth their price, though only buy them once you have played the base game.

Once you hit max level, which I recommend doing by just leveling up normally and exploring while doing the heart quests to learn the basics of the game. The strikes which are used mostly as an intro to raids, not all of them are available to the base game as some are in EoD and SotO. In the expansions (HoT, PoF, EoD, and VoE) you get these things called specializations which are like sub-classes in TTRPGs that give you whole new ways of playing your class and new weapons to use. Things like raids and of course the story and more generally speaking the open world have many in game achievements related to them. Ranging from a collection of reading books scattered around one map, to for raids speedrunning all of the raids in insanely short periods of time with all of the challenge modes active. 
PvP in this game has two different game modes, one called WvW with 3 teams that fight over multple maps per week as they claim small bases here and there. The game certainly has solid foundations and intriguing depth, but I will focus strictly on its fundamental flaws—plenty of people are already singing its praises.
    • Misleading Core Premise: The game is advertised as a colony simulator and story generator, but by default, it functions strictly as a brutal Tower Defense game disguised under sim mechanics.
    • Punished for Progress: You cannot freely build a grand, beautiful base. Wealth-scaling raid mechanics actively punish prosperity, turning city-building into guaranteed annihilation unless you rely on killboxes.
    • Forced Poverty Optimization: The optimal way to play forces you to keep colonists in artificial squalor and micromanage misery, rather than building a thriving, high-standard society.
    • Flawed Quest Scaling: Quest difficulty relies on the same broken wealth formulas, offering absurd suicide missions to small settlements and penalizing you for taking good rewards.
    • Exploiting Dumb AI Over Real Tactics: Instead of encouraging realistic defense and strategic thinking, the game forces players to build cheesy killboxes to abuse the enemies' flawed pathfinding AI.
    • Anti-Economic Logic: The mechanics contradict fundamental economic, strategic, and logistical laws. Real-world power and security rely on capital, surplus, and stockpiles; here, productivity is an existential threat that forces deliberate self-sabotage and asset dumping. Managing labor around penalizing wealth rather than rewarding growth directly mirrors the bureaucratic stagnation and decline of the European Union.
    • Reality Check for Potential Buyers: This review is for rational players deciding if the game is worth buying, not for blind fanatics pissing their pants in euphoria over mastering the developer's arbitrary rulebook—rules that have long lost any connection to logic or the real world.
    • The Illusion of Depth (The ONI Trap): Much like Oxygen Not Included, the game hooks you early with engaging survival mechanics, but the moment you try applying real-world engineering, logic, or economic principles, you realize the underlying systems are fundamentally degenerate.
    • Vanilla Means Vanilla: I refuse to fix broken design with endless mods or cheat through custom sliders just to make a game bearable. This critique applies strictly to the unmodded, default game as intended by the developer—this is the way.

Hunt: Showdown 1896 is one of the most intense and unique shooters I’ve ever played. What makes it stand out is the way it combines PvP, PvE, survival, and extraction into one experience. Every match feels dangerous because you’re not only fighting monsters—you’re also listening for other Hunters who could be waiting around the next corner. The sound design is especially incredible; a single gunshot, broken window, or set of footsteps can completely change the way you approach a fight

The gunplay is slower and more deliberate than in most modern shooters, which makes every shot feel important. You have to think about your positioning, ammunition, noise, and when it’s actually worth taking a fight. The bounty system makes things even more exciting because once you claim the bounty, you become a target for everyone else, turning the trip to extraction into one of the most stressful parts of the match.

The atmosphere is another huge strength. The dark western setting, creepy monsters, abandoned locations, weather, and incredible audio create an atmosphere that very few multiplayer games can match. The game can be terrifying even when nothing is happening, because you never know when another Hunter is going to appear.

Overall, I’d give Hunt: Showdown 1896 a 9/10. It can be frustrating, unforgiving, and difficult to learn, but that’s also what makes winning feel so rewarding. When you survive a fight, grab the bounty, and successfully extract while knowing another team was hunting you, there’s genuinely nothing quite like it.

[h1]One of the best games ever[/h1]

Hunt: Showdown has one of the steepest learning curves I have ever experienced in a video game.

The good thing is: [b]you start making progress surprisingly soon.[/b]

The better thing is: [b]you never really stop learning.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]You will lose. A lot.[/h2]

You will lose hunters, equipment, money, and sometimes fights where you still have no idea what just happened.

Modern games often try very hard to keep players comfortable and make sure you never really lose anything important.

[b]Hunt is different.[/b]

It can be hard. It can be frustrating. Sometimes you will have a terrible day and lose hunter after hunter.

But that's exactly why every victory feels so damn good.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The atmosphere. The sound. The details.[/h2]

The atmosphere is among the best I have ever experienced in a video game.

[i]Maybe the best.[/i]

And the sound? [b]Absolutely incredible.[/b]

I highly recommend playing with good stereo headphones. With Crytek's own sound engine, sound is not just there to make the game feel immersive — it is an essential part of how you understand and play the game.

Every match feels special.

I still remember great plays and intense moments from [b]2024[/b]. How many games can you say that about?

The attention to detail is insane.

The weapons. The reload mechanics. The different animations.

And the weapon sounds...

[b]Oh my god, the weapon sounds.[/b]

I don't even care about weapons in real life. But in Hunt?

[i]That's something completely different.[/i]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]And then everything comes together.[/h2]

The most rewarding moments are when everything you have learned suddenly pays off.

You hear something.

You notice a clue.

You understand what is happening somewhere on the map.

You make a prediction.

And then...

[b]You are right.[/b]

You make the right decision because you understood the situation — and that decision wins you the match.

[quote]Yeah. That's Hunt.[/quote]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]But some days, Hunt is also just losing.[/h2]

[b]A lot.[/b]

And honestly?

A Sandbox of 13 Years of Content: Nearly every mechanic introduced over a decade of development (Delve, Heist, Expedition, Harvest) is woven into the endgame Atlas. The level of content variety is staggeringly vast compared to any competitor.

The Definitive ARPG Economy: The economy—driven by trading functional currency items like Chaos and Divine Orbs—remains the gold standard for multiplayer ARPGs, creating a thrilling market dynamic every single season.

Thriving Parallel Support: Grinding Gear Games did not abandon the game; it still receives regular, massive four-month seasonal content drops and dedicated balance cycles.

How About The Disadvantages & Outdated Elements?

Cruel Onboarding for New Players: Trying to learn PoE 1 in 2026 without an extensive video guide, a build planner, and a spreadsheet is a recipe for a breakdown. The game severely lacks native onboarding tools.

Outdated Click-to-Move Controls: Going back to click-to-move and strict armor socket-linking after experiencing the fluid WASD movement and separated gem systems of PoE 2 feels like stepping backward in time.

The Infamous "Campaign Tax": Having to trudge through the mandatory 10-act campaign to reach the endgame for every single new character you make remains a tedious chore.

Conclusion. If you can push past the brutal learning curve and the archaic inventory requirements, Path of Exile 1 is a magnificent monolith. It provides a deeper, more customizable experience than almost any other game on the market.

There is something beautiful about the randomness in Rimworld. It can create wild stories where nearly anything can happen. 

Every new colony feels like an entirely new experience despite the how basic the game may look to someone who has never played it. 

    One of my favorites games was of a crash landed colony of 4; a pyromaniac middle age man addicted to weed, an ugly teenager that had creepy breathing but was kind, a grandma with dementia that only knew how to cook, and a Labrador retriever.
    The start was smooth sailing with some hints of luck and fortune. A small hut was built along with a farm. Despite their disadvantages the colonies base slowly grew a large compound. One day the teenager got insulted by the drug addict because he was ugly and snapped, destroying the entire weed stockpile. Because of this the drug addict went into withdraw and started a fire inside. With the grandma away picking berries the teenager ran in alone to beat out the fire and try to save the colonies hard work. In the heat of the blaze he passed out. As this was happening the addict snapped out of his trance, realized what he did and, ran back in to save the teenager. By the time the grandma returned with her berries everything was ash and she was alone. 
    The grandma was able to get by on her own for the most part. Sleeping on the ground in a small cave. She would mainly eat berries and cook occasional meals from her small garden. Due to her bad back she couldn't work very hard and was slowly starving. To survive she slaughtered the dog for food and one less mouth to worry about feeding. After she butchered it, she had a dementia episode wandering aimlessly... 
    call it karma but she wandered straight into a colony of massive highly aggressive insects. Poor soul didn't even know what hit her. After the insects knocked her unconscious a man in black wandering by saw the situation and tried saving her. Running in with a revolver he was determined! He spotted an insect, aimed, fired, and killed one the size of his leg, but this only angered the colony... before he could react he was surrounded by a swarm overwhelmed and eventually turned into insect jelly along with the grandma.

All because of 1 insult...

I could've save scummed to keep the colony healthy and alive, but the point of Rimworld isn't to beat the game. Rimworld is not a game... Its a story generator and for the best experience roll with the punches and enjoy wild unpredictable stories to come.

RimWorld is one of those games that looks simple at first, but the longer you play it, the more you realize how deep it actually is. It is not just a colony builder. It is a story generator where every colonist, every bad decision, every raid, every mental break, and every disaster can turn into something you remember.

What makes RimWorld so good is how much freedom it gives you. You can build a peaceful farming colony, a high-tech fortress, a trading settlement, a brutal survival camp, or something completely unhinged. The game gives you the tools, then lets everything go wrong in the best way possible.

The colonists are what make the game stand out. They are not just workers. They have traits, relationships, skills, moods, addictions, injuries, breakdowns, fights, love stories, and grudges. Sometimes your best doctor gets food poisoning during a raid. Sometimes your strongest fighter has a mental break and punches a stack of artillery shells. Sometimes one terrible choice turns into a chain reaction that destroys your whole colony, and somehow it is still fun.

The replay value is insane. Different biomes, different starts, different storytellers, different playstyles, and a massive modding community make it feel like you can always come back and try something new. Even after losing a colony, it usually makes you want to start another one right away.

It can be a little overwhelming at first, and the game definitely has a learning curve, but once it clicks, it becomes one of the most addicting colony sims out there. Every run feels different, and every colony ends up with its own story.

If you like survival, management, base building, strategy, dark humor, and games where chaos creates the best memories, RimWorld is absolutely worth playing.

It is weird, brutal, funny, stressful, and somehow one of the best storytelling games ever made.

My First RimWorld Colony, or: How I Spent Full Price to Watch Three Idiots Die
I bought RimWorld at full price.
Not just the base game, either. I bought all the DLCs too. No sale. No bundle discount worth mentioning. I looked at the total for several seconds, thought, “That seems like a lot,” and then paid anyway.
Then, before even properly learning how doors worked, I downloaded 150 mods.
This was my first mistake.
My second mistake was looking at those 150 mods and thinking, “Yeah, this should be stable.”
I started a new colony with Cassandra Classic on Strive to Survive. I had been warned that Cassandra was the “normal” storyteller, which I interpreted as “reasonable.”
I would later discover that Cassandra’s idea of reasonable was giving you twenty minutes to become emotionally attached to someone before dropping a refrigerator on them.
My three colonists were named Hannah, Derek, and Paul.
Hannah was a decent doctor and cook. She was also incapable of violence, which I didn’t notice until after landing.
Derek could shoot, build things, and had a burning passion for mining. Unfortunately, he was also a pyromaniac.
Paul was our researcher. He had terrible shooting, terrible melee, terrible construction, and a bad back.
I liked Paul immediately.
The colony began surprisingly well.
We landed in a temperate forest beside a river. There was fertile soil nearby. There were berries. There were deer. There was even an old ruined structure that looked like it could be converted into a house.
“This is easy,” I thought.
For the first two days, everyone slept on the floor because I forgot beds existed.
On day three, I finally built bedrooms.
Technically, it was one large wooden room with three beds separated by flower pots, but I considered this major progress.
Paul spent most of his time researching batteries while sitting at a research bench outside because I forgot to put the bench indoors. Every time it rained, his research speed dropped and he became slightly more miserable.
I kept wondering why.
Derek built walls.
Hannah cooked.
Everything was going suspiciously well.
Then I remembered the zombie mod.
I had installed it because I thought zombies would be “a fun little extra threat.”
At first, there were only two of them wandering near the edge of the map.
I zoomed in.
One was missing an arm. The other was wearing what appeared to be a cowboy hat.
“They don’t look that dangerous.”
I ordered Derek to shoot them.
Derek fired six times.
He missed six times.
One bullet hit a muffalo about forty meters behind the zombies.
The muffalo became angry.
I learned what “manhunter” meant.
Derek immediately ran toward the colony with an enraged muffalo behind him and two zombies slowly following both of them.
Paul was still researching batteries.
Hannah was making simple meals.
Nobody seemed particularly concerned.
I drafted everyone and discovered, for the first time, that Hannah was incapable of violence.
She stood there.
I clicked the attack button again.
Nothing.
I checked her bio.
“Incapable of: Violent.”
“Oh.”
The muffalo reached Derek.
It hit him once and cracked two ribs.
Derek fired his revolver at point-blank range.
He missed.
I genuinely didn’t know that was possible.
Paul came outside carrying a knife.
I don’t remember giving Paul a knife.
Paul stabbed the muffalo twice, got kicked in the chest, and collapsed.
Derek finally shot the muffalo.
It died.
I celebrated for approximately three seconds.
Then the cowboy zombie bit Derek.
Hannah dragged Paul into the hospital, which was actually just his bedroom with the bed set to “medical.”
Derek killed the zombies and stumbled inside.
At this point, I was feeling pretty confident again.
Sure, Derek was bitten. Sure, Paul had been kicked by an animal approximately six times his weight. But Hannah was a good doctor.
She could fix this.
Then a notification appeared.
Solar flare.
The batteries I had spent three days researching stopped mattering immediately.
Not that I had built any batteries yet.
So technically, the solar flare did absolutely nothing.
But it made me nervous.
Hannah treated Paul first.
Paul survived.
Then she treated Derek.
The bite became infected.
I wasn’t sure whether this was a normal infection or a zombie infection because I had installed so many mods that the health tab now looked like the dashboard of an aircraft.
I clicked around.
There were percentages.
There were timers.
There was something called “viral progression.”
That sounded bad.
Derek got out of bed that evening anyway because his recreation was low.
He walked outside and played horseshoes.
He had a zombie infection.
And he decided this was a good time for horseshoes.
Paul joined him.
For a little while, it was actually peaceful.
The sun was going down. Hannah was cooking dinner. Paul threw horseshoes badly. Derek was slowly turning into the undead.
I remember watching them and thinking, “You know what? We might actually be okay.”
Then Derek had a mental break.
Derek has begun a fire-starting spree.
I stared at the message.
“No.”
Derek walked into the wooden storage room.
“No, Derek.”
He lit the medicine on fire.
“DEREK.”
Then he lit the food on fire.
I paused the game.
The entire colony was made of wood.
I unpaused.
Hannah ran in to fight the fire.
Paul ran in to fight the fire.
Derek walked into the bedroom and set his own bed on fire.
At this point I was laughing so hard that I stopped making good decisions.
The storage room became completely engulfed.
Hannah got burned.
Paul got burned.
If you enjoy being on some wild cowboy shit, this game may be for you.

This game is fun but has very annoying problems that make me want to play it less and less.

The good:

You can interact with anything. Blow it up, kill it, shoot it, etc. Very cool
Lots of cool weapons
Challenging game
You can fly
Cool powerups
Some very useful mods for QOL and gameplay

The bad

1. Sharply rising difficulty - its fun to play a game that is challenging, but not when level 1 is braindead simple, level 2 is meh, and level 3 you are underpowered against huge waves of enemies. I seriously don't understand what they were thinking here. 

2. Bad weapon drops - yes there are cool weapons.. if you get lucky enough to get them. Sometimes you get a spell in your wand that kills enemies in 1 hit and has infinite bullets. Sometimes you get one that takes 10 hits to kill the same enemy. Oh and it also kills you. 

3. Bad wand system - The way the game works is that you have wands, these wands have slots for spells, and you can theoretically have cool builds. The problem is that 1) you can only change spells in between levels, 2) if you don't get good weapons, you have a shit build and the game will be 100x harder for basically no reason. There are some cool ideas but the reality is that you will die on level 3 from being underpowered. Summoning a rain cloud or using a teleport gun is not going to get you past them. And even if it does, you will be progressively more and more fucked because you can pretty much only upgrade spells/wands through buying them, and you only get gold from enemies.

4. Slow movement - this is a minor thing but damn does your guy move slow. There are perks that you can get that make you move faster or fly faster, and they make the game more fun.

5. Crappy wands - there are basically 2 things that make your wand unique: the spells it comes with and its firing speed. If you find a wand that has useless spells (75% of them are useless) and bad rate of fire, what exactly are you going to use it for? Nothing. And even if you do find a wand with cool spells, you can't remove spells from existing wands unless you are between levels. 

6. No tool tips for spells unless they're in your inventory - There are a lot of spells, but good luck trying to figure out what they are from their icon alone. You can't read anything about them unless they are in your inv. And even then its a sentence and doesn't explain much. Doesn't tell you if the spell will also do damage to you

7. Friendly fire - you will kill yourself a lot in this game. It makes the gameplay tense, which is cool in a way, but what's not cool is how many wands will come pre-built with shit that will kill you if you use it wrong. This wouldn't be so bad if the first 2 levels weren't a boring grind, but when dying means you have to play through a boring 10 minutes over and over you start to avoid weapons that can do damage to you. But guess what, that means you need to get lucky if you dn't want to be stuck with weak weapons.

Mods 

Thank god this game has mods as it makes the game way more fun. Or at least less annoying. I haven't explored them all, but the ones I like are:

Gold comes to you (otherwise you have to go touch it to pick it up + it expires) which is helpful when u kill  1 guy but he's still around his friends. 
Health packs - dead enemies sometimes drop health packs
Random builds - you get something more interesting to start with

Anyway, I think this game would actually be really cool for PVP as well. Maybe speed up the guys a little bit and make it 5x5 or something, or even a free for all. So much potential here to have a really fun experience, but I guess its an old game and the devs have moved on. Or they just like making the game hard and annoying, maybe they are French.

Rimworld is quite enjoyable, the caveat is that without the DLCs or Mods the game feels a little shallow in terms of content. The game is filled with questionable design decisions which will often need to be metagamed or modded to fix. I vehemently disagree with the notion that this is a "story generator" and that it should be exempt from criticism on a "design" level because "duuuh you're supposed to let the story happen!". This game requires you to learn, strategize, optimize, and design with active intent in order to get anywhere and not die to a giant raid because you have too much corn sitting in the corner. This game HAS endings. If it were purely a story generator then you wouldn't need to have so much input for it to "generate" your story and if losing really were fun, then why would anyone bother winning in games? Because it isn't "fun". The stories YOU can make about them are "fun". The "story generator" part of the game is 90% from your own imagination because the game itself is actually pretty light on character interactions and development, and faction relations affect very little. All that said, you can mod the fug out of the game, and while that isn't credit I can give to the developers for what modders have done, you can still get a lot of hours of fun from Rimworld, despite its flaws. I do think the DLCs are quite pricey considering some of them don't actually add a ton to the game, (Royalty and Biotech), and they never go on very big sales. Try looking on key resellers for better deals.

Just realised that despite playing an ungodly number of hours of this game, I never gave it a review. So yes, it's very good! (And it can turn into a real time sink). 

Broadly it's a colony simulator with light RTS elements when there are raids, roughly once every 10 in-game days. It's small scale, typically growing from three to around a dozen or more pawns. So much of the fun is keeping track of individual pawns with their different stats and quirks and their struggles to secure food and build a comfortable, safe base. I get more out of the game taking a role-playing approach with imperfect colonists (using imagination to fill in some blanks) rather than a more min-maxy playstyle.

There's lots of scope to tweak difficulty-related settings and even more mods (which I mostly skip) to shift the game style to more "realistic" combat, different aesthetics, turning your colony into more of a resort etc. For relatively unmodded gameplay, check out YouTube videos from Quill18. The DLC is good but best left until after you're familiar with the base game mechanics.

A couple of downsides: the community wiki is pretty essential, as the game itself doesn't do a good job of making clear the difference between types of weapons, armour, farm animals etc or some mechanics. 

Mid-late game, the colony can tend to plateau. You're basically secure, but have a lot of grindy resource collection if you want to build the official end-game space ship and prepare for the end-game sequence of raids. 

And on normal to higher difficulty (unmodded) the game effectively makes a walled, compact base mandatory to deal with raids and pawns' slow walk speed - sprawling, unwalled villages are too inefficient and hard to defend (at least without a lot of micromanagement in combat).

As the OG factory management game that jumpstarted the genre, Factorio is one of those games that is difficult to put down once you pick it up. It keeps your brain active, helps you train your ability to stay alert, and helps you push your comfort levels as you focus on expanding your factory in the face of overwhelming odds from hostile fauna on an alien planet. With the Space Age DLC, the game expands beyond the starting planet and into the surrounding solar system. And with an active modding community, procedurally generated resource nodes, and a wealth of different settings, no two playthroughs are guaranteed to be the same.

Pros:

- Incredibly stable

- Very well optimized

- Active Modding Community

- Plenty of blueprints available

- Active Development Post-Release

- Intuitive mechanics and progression

- Helpful at teaching players the importance of proactive solutions

Cons:

- The learning curve is nothing to sneeze at, especially with resource management and distribution. Take some ideas from let's plays on YouTube if you find yourself struggling or stuck.

- Lots of mathematics and planning involved

- Resource availability and distance from spawn is dependent on world spawn settings and RNG.

- Overwhelming number of calculations slow down sim speed when scaling production massively. Known issue that affects megabase and speedrun playthroughs.

Neutral:

- Retro sprite-based isometric graphics that aren't to everyone's tastes

- Better with friends. Solo playthroughs can be quite tedious in the early game, but not atrociously so, and can be quite fun.

Sea of Thieves is a fantastic pirate adventure game where you can sail across a huge open world, search for treasure, fight skeletons, battle other crews, and live out your dream of becoming a pirate.

The best part is the freedom. You can explore islands, complete voyages, fight world events, customize your ship, fish, collect treasure, or simply sail around with your friends while absolutely nothing goes according to plan.

The naval combat is especially fun. Managing your sails, repairing your ship, firing cannons, and boarding enemy ships makes every battle feel chaotic and exciting. And of course, there's always that one teammate who accidentally drops the anchor during combat.

Playing with friends makes the experience even better. You can work together as a crew, communicate during battles, and celebrate when you successfully sell a massive haul of treasure. Or watch everything disappear because another crew sank you five minutes before reaching the outpost.

The game has beautiful visuals, great music, tons of customization, and plenty of content. However, progression can sometimes feel repetitive, and getting destroyed by a much more experienced crew can be pretty painful.

Overall, Sea of Thieves is one of the best multiplayer pirate games, especially if you enjoy exploration, teamwork, adventure, and completely unpredictable situations.

The Scout lights the way and immediately spots something valuable in the worst possible place. Engineer gives him a platform, Gunner keeps the bugs busy, and Driller starts removing half the cave because apparently walls are optional.

At some point someone finds compressed gold, so naturally the entire operation stops for a very important scientific procedure:

[b]WE’RE RICH![/b]

Mission Control complains. Everyone ignores him.

Then the swarm arrives, the cave turns into chaos, somebody shouts [b]ROCK AND STONE![/b], and the Scout starts flying around the room doing the only sensible thing: not standing anywhere near the Driller.

Because sooner or later, [b]the C4 comes out[/b].

And somehow the Scout is the one who needs reviving...again...

That is basically DRG: excellent co-op, strong class synergy, destructible caves, procedural missions and a community that turned random voice lines into traditions.

This being said, the game does pick up because, obviously, that is one of the biggest points of an RPG while being, as said, beginner friendly. It for sure can be on the challenging side if you are into that kind of thing.

One really important thing to note is that you have the tutorial, which is forced unfortunately, but it isn't that much of an annoyance and takes more or less a few minutes. There are quite a few beginning choices the game puts you through for immersion, each one mostly affecting your story. The only real non-cosmetic choice is your profession.

Races are honestly, pretty diverse or maybe basic. I am not sure, because I have only really played those really shitty peaked in the early 2000s MMOs. you have Sylvari, which is kind of just your typical elf, tree people that connect with nature and like an idiot, I wasted my first slot on them. You have asura, who are in lore, highly intelligent magic tech users. I have no clue they're pretty cool, and they have the best design choices. One of the hairstyles is literally Mickey Mouse. Humans are actually somehow not at the back end of this game. They're a very popular choice but not a bad one. Norn are almost like giants. They're very tall, and their design is honestly pretty cool. They are basically just independent warriors in lore. I actually have no comment on the furry class other than it is just adorable but also goofy at times. the necromancer straight up looks like a leopard and a cow fused together.

Your story completely changes depending on your race. I really dislike how many of the beginning choices are cosmetic. It confused me a little because I had thought it was going to be the type of game that changes stats depending on what you do at the start. After the tutorial, the game gives you full control over the quests and exploration you do.
i found the map to be, while big, semi digestable and shouldn't be super overwhelming. It explains level differences, which should also tell you (if you have common sense) where you should and shouldn't go at your current progression. 

There are 9 professions you are able to choose at the start. It's mostly standard. I chose necromancer for two reasons: one being pure cheese and two. I really enjoy being able to look edgy and summon undead companions. This game adds an exclusive called messmer, a mage that relies on illusion magic. Each of these professions have sub specs so technically if we count those it brings us to 27 professions unfortunately some are locked behind a paywall so that was a bit disappointing to me when I found out.

The in game Codex and menus helped me understand everything in the moment. The milestones and phases helped separate complex systems so nothing felt like it was too overwhelming, you also can move at your own pace which helped immensely.

-Addicting gameplay, who would think building a factory would be so fun? The intrinsic gameplay and goals helps you plot and plan your next steps until the end of the game. I am not joking, I often would play for 4-6 hours straight. I would dream of rocket fuel system loops, my nuclear power chain, or my next steel factory in my sleep when I wasn't play. This is the first time I had a game impact my dreams at this level, it was WILD.

-The gameplay was never too challenging in where I found the wildlife too hard stopping me from progressing, and there is a bonus that the wildlife never attacks your base, or factory components.

-The research and ticket systems both worked really well to not only break up certain periods of waiting in this game, but it also helped in establishing a good system to gather resources you're not able to just yet, or further expand with alternate recipes.

-The alternate recipe system was such a great idea. I loved having options as you find more and more hard drives. Making copper ore with a smelter? Or make more copper ingots per ore with water, but requires more buildings. It was a min/max dream come true.

-Hand crafted map makes the game feel more believable and fun to explore. I love procedural generated games, but I am glad Coffee Stain chose to make a hand crafted map. The different cave systems, or landmarks make this feel like a fun land to explore and build on. It also helps with the variety of creatures and environments. There is a choice in the beginning to pick a starting biome/location, and I found that while I chose Rocky Desert, all four locations seem to have their own pros and cons. 

-Replayability is absolutely there. I may look at making the game harder in my next run, but unlocking alternate recipes from the start, or changing ALL of the ore locations on the map and randomizing them. The options to customize are endless. I really enjoy that option.

What I didn't like:
- Some production outputs felt very chore intensive, such as the fused modular frames, or the nuclear pasta. Those were the bane of my existence. Nuclear Pasta I just made more buildings to produce them, but jesus the fused modular frames took a whole night of planning (and paper) just to make around 3 of them a minute. It was rough.

- Literally nothing else, perfection.

Pros:
Vibe: Has its own flavor of open world survival craft which melts in Victorian-Dracula era style vibes and art; flipping the standard script of the traditional "good guys hunting bad things" into "what if maybe the 'monsters' of the night are actually the antihero and humanity is the enemy?" The day-night system keeps me thinking about when I'm going to what and where all the while playing into the theme of the game. 

Building/crafting: I absolutely love the castle building and look forward to spending my free time progressing and designing my base. Devs found a way to make progression/combat/biomes seamless and more deep than expected without over-burdening the player - even when I hit a place of "omg I need so much of this thing to make this" I ended up with what I needed and I didn't have to mindlessly dump all of my free time into that. 

Boss fights/combat: They nailed it. Its one of the core components of the games design and it works. I'm only about 20 hours in at the time of this review but so far they have felt like a consistent crawl to run progress, and am excited to see the mid-late game combat and weapons style. With an almost pleasantly overwhelming amount of weapon styles and spells (most of which I haven't even unlocked yet) I found myself spending time in between efforts to explore what's-what and a player should have no shortage of what can make their playstyle stand out and define how they play through the game.

Survival: Super fun thing that took me a while to notice is the game actually does have a traditional energy/hunger/mana system in a very untraditional way. It snuck up on me, in fact, in the way of the blood/feeding system, which once I realized what was going on there, I smiled and thought it was very clever and cool. Consumables increase stats and bonuses and of course, the flip flop into build/survive by day and hunt/progress by night is a cool mechanic. 

Cons: 
Honestly? There's really not much I can say but to be as fair and impartial as possible I gotta try. Maybe the soundtrack? It could be that maybe I haven't figured it out or its me thing but the game could benefit from some raw Victorian style classical bangers that would pair well with your castle building or other aspects of the game. You would expect to be hearing some organ and string orchestra while cutting through the fog and building your eerily beautiful delve on the mountainside but its not there - doesn't make or break the game by any means but its something to consider. 
Also, one thing for me was the controls. I play keyboard and mouse, so learning to navigate and control my character effectively using the devs system took some adjustments but it absolutely works once you're used to it. I wouldn't suggest any change there, just a heads up to anyone who might by it that you'll be learning a new kind of live control system. 

Worth it? Hands down. I'll be playing this for quite a while.

I played through the base game as a veteran of this type of game.  That's your factorios and captain of industries.  In terms of play style, I think captain of industry is the very best version of this kind of game if you're only ever going to buy and play 1.  This is because it lets you focus on the macro with the ability to focus on the micro without the micro completely dominating play when 'the belt going the wrong way' constantly causes your factory to stop, etc.   It is difficult in satisfactory to keep track of what is happening.  The codex doesn't by default show you the actual ratios/burn rates of inputs/outputs and many things are 2-4 step processes or more and it is not reasonable within the game or even a simple notepad to keep track of your needed inputs and outputs.  I'd reckon there's a mod that puts a better calculator in game, but the in-game codex is really hard to follow for a really critical function you need.

There aren't easy tools to setup a bunch of assemblers/set a bunch to make the same thing at once/copy a handful of things on the ground and paste them.  I simply don't enjoy needing to build 100s of the same thing being locked out of blueprinting and having clunky UI.  Yet, every single game that's similar in style seems to have this problem--except captain of industry.
Now you can avoid this if you do not enjoy the repetition/CPS - use mods.  I wanted to experience Satisfactory vanilla.  So it's something to be aware of if you don't enjoy the tedium.  Smart blueprinting will help save a lot of clicks.

So if you enjoy a Palworld/3d factory builder, I think you'll be at home and fine.  The game is done well with some specific exceptions that I will notice that a regular player may not.
Fluids don't work correctly.  There are rounding errors that cause pipes if you're trying to do ratio math to not work and have pipes stop as they didn't include any way to burn off or just dump excess liquid.  That's 'fine' but there's no reasonable way without serious trial and error and you just hope the pipes don't stop.

The game lacks any kind of alarms, so there's no way for you to know something has stopped on the other side of your base until there's an actual stoppage.

Train signaling can bug and if it does, it will not fix itself, it requires you to physically operate each train that bugged to make it reconsider signals.

The enemy AI is a bit simple however there are many ways to 'solve' dealing with them despite this and players that like to push what they're doing and try stuff I think will enjoy this more than some Halo level enemy AI.  

I don't feel exploring -- which is a major cool aspect of the game.  Similar to subnautica exploring gives unique rewards and it's a sculpted map (not random) so it's fun to see what the world has.  Unfortunately I don't feel I was compensated much for my efforts.  One of the key items you find unlocks new recipes to use.  Unfortunately due to the UI and difficulty or simply cost of using alternative goods nearly all the found recipes are not useful and you're simply burning them off to get the ones you want.


It's a game trying to do many things and I feel it generally does that well.  I feel if you're not having fun -- go get some mods to alleviate the pain points if you feel them.

The game also has no circuitry and really nothing at all to control factory flow.  Those with a big mind for this will still make really cool things, but I found the lack of logical controllers and even just more basic finite train controls such as waiting for a specific amount of ore across all cars before leaving instead of all or nothing rather limiting to me. 

My play was starting in the 'hardest' biome, with random ores with the hope the game was more difficult.  I felt pretty satisfied with that.

I think this game has a lot of charm and there's a lot of things that will always be difficult taking the factory game to a 3d world and this is the best example I'm aware of this type. I really enjoyed Satisfactory and spent over 70 hours playing it. I loved exploring the world, gathering resources and, most of all, building increasingly complicated production lines. There is something genuinely satisfying about watching everything come together and seeing your factory slowly grow.
However, after a while I started asking myself one simple question:
Why am I actually doing all of this?

Apart from building the Space Elevator and progressing through the different tiers, there doesn't seem to be much of an actual goal or purpose behind everything you build. You keep creating more and more complicated production chains, but eventually it can start to feel like you're building just for the sake of building.

And even if you really enjoy this type of game, I think the lack of a stronger long-term objective can eventually make the gameplay repetitive.

That said, I would still recommend the game — but with one important warning:

Plan your factory properly from the beginning.

You will almost certainly come back to your starting area later and look at the mess you created when you had no idea what you were doing. At first, you might think, "I'll just put this machine here and connect it somehow." Later, you'll discover that you need to fully optimise your production capacity to create one extremely complicated component, and suddenly your entire early factory becomes a nightmare.

Satisfactory is a game where order, balance and harmony really matter. Everything needs to work together, and production needs to be carefully planned.

Also, be careful with overproduction. Producing way more of something than you actually need can create unnecessary bottlenecks and make your whole production chain more complicated than it needs to be.

My advice: before you start building seriously, read a few guides and understand how production chains, resource rates and factory planning work. Going in completely blind is fun at first, but you may regret it later when you're forced to rebuild half of your factory.

Overall, a very enjoyable factory-building game with a lot of depth, and I definitely recommend it if you enjoy automation and optimisation.

Just don't forget to ask yourself: "What am I actually building this for?"
