It handles progression, exploration, and combat in ways that feel genuinely innovative, even if a few aging systems keep it just short of absolute perfection.

The Pros
Horizontal Progression & Time Respect: Unlike games that invalidate your gear every few months, Guild Wars 2 utilizes horizontal progression. High-tier gear locked in years ago is still relevant today. You can take a six-month break, log back in, and jump straight into content without feeling penalized.

Dynamic Open-World & Community: The world of Tyria feels alive. Dynamic events and massive zone-wide "meta events" naturally draw players together without needing a formal party, creating one of the most welcoming and non-toxic communities in the genre.

Fluid Combat & Best-in-Class Mounts: Combat is active and responsive, emphasizing dodging, positioning, and skill combination rather than standing still and executing a rigid rotation. Additionally, its mount system (unlocked in expansions) sets the gold standard for gaming—mounts feel like distinct vehicles with weight, momentum, and unique traversal utility.

No Subscription Fee: The base game is free to play, and expansions are buy-to-play. There is zero mandatory monthly cost, making it extremely easy to pick up and play at your own pace.

The Cons
Visual Clutter in Group Content: In massive open-world boss fights or large-scale World vs. World (WvW) battles, spell effects and particle animations turn the screen into a blinding light show, making it hard to see what’s actually happening.

Overwhelming UI & Inventory Management: The menus, wallet currencies, and inventory bags can easily overwhelm new or returning players. You will spend a fair amount of time clearing out inventory clutter or consulting external wikis to understand what specific items do.

Mixed Story Quality: While the world lore is rich, the narrative delivery in the core base game and early campaigns can feel dated and uneven compared to story-heavy MMOs like Final Fantasy XIV.

The Verdict:Guild Wars 2 is an absolute gem for casual gamers, explorers, and anyone seeking a high-quality MMO that respects both your time and wallet. If you can look past some interface quirks and visual noise, it offers hundreds of hours of fantastic content.

Most progression is permanent and account-wide. While you can create Alts if you want to play a different class, the game is designed so that you effectively can complete 100% of all content in the game on a single character. While you must be a minimum level for some quests, there is no maximum-level for any quests or content; attempting any content below your level will scale to you and grant you EXP equivalent to your level. The game utilizes a system similar to Diablo 3's Paragon points - once you are at max level, you then continue to "level up" permanently, but instead gaining "Mastery", which you spend to gain permanent account-wide buffs that will then apply to any existing or future alts you will play on. If you have multiple max-level characters, they will all effectively share progress.

Although it takes an insane grind to get each new different mount(there are like 6 total) beside the initial one you get for buying any expansion, all of the mounts and their respective EXP/skills are permanent and immediately accessible between all of your characters. Speaking of mounts though, while everyone you see in-game will be rocking their epic-skin flying mounts, don't expect to be flying anytime soon. As someone who came from WoW and FFXIV, I was expecting maybe a week of some google-found gold grind to get in the air; No. You must own the "Mount expansion" 'Path of Fire', then either level a char to 80 or use the character level boost, and then proceed to grind for what seems to be well over 150 hours to acquire the flying mount. As I said before,  its then permanently and immediately useable on all characters even at level 1, so I'm not necessarily complaining- but I was quite surprised that was the case. I guess I'll be on my Lizard for a while.

As for the story, each of the playable races has a unique start of the story up to level 40. When you create any character of any race, you answer some multiple-choice questions that further change your characters story within the same race. At level 40, there are still 3 different branches of the story, as you align with your chosen military group(soldiers, nerds, sneaky illuminati).

This is a really good game. Good game design in many aspects. But starting with any potential cons, there are some minor problems with not teaching players good habits. You can box yourself in a corner so to speak if you make mistakes early on. If you don't research military packs and make it a focus to push back biters and get the edge up on them, you could lose your save to them (albeit very easy to avoid this if you're paying attention.) If you don't plan ahead and limit your spaghetti and give yourself enough space to expand, you will spend dozens of hours rebuilding. The gameplay loop is fun, and unlocking robots helps with any rebuilding you may have to do, but I think it could respect your time a little better because this game is a huge time sink. That's ok for some but you should know what you're getting into, especially on your first playthrough. It took me about 70 hours to beat the game, but I could've done it under 50 had I not made mistakes early on.

All that being said, the game is paced well, the hotkeys once you learn them feel great and efficient. The progression is satisfying but is very open ended and non-linear, meaning you will need to make your own plans/goals for each session you play to progress and stay motivated. However, this is nothing new for the genre, and I think the way that the research tree works specifically with the science packs is genius and provides more structure to your gameplay than other similar games. The tutorials are great and the in-game manual is perfect and has lots of gifs and explanations and even hands on tutorials when needed to make sure you learn something. Trains are TOUGH to learn though, even after beating the game I'm only 85% sure I understand them. Learning AE2 w/ Channels in modded minecraft is a piece of cake compared to learning train signals in this game. But everything you need to know about the game and how to play it is all available inside the actual game and I highly applaud the devs for that.

Other minor nitpicks: I wish the production menu had some sort of note explaining how to view electricity production as it not being in the same place as everything else makes it a little unintuitive. Also wish that there were more hotkey hints in the train menus so that players know that they can, for example, press Ctrl to view train paths in order to diagnose pathing problems.

To wrap everything up, if you're willing to commit to a 50-100 hour playthrough and lots of learning and possibly rebuilding sections of your base as you go then I highly recommend this game. Calculating ratios themselves can be tedious and kirk's calculator will help greatly with that, but whichever way you choose to play the game I'm sure you will find great enjoyment if you are a fan of factory/automation games and stick with it. 9.5/10.

[h1]¿En esta economía? ¿De verdad?[/h1]

I’m assuming if you’re looking into an MMO over a decade old, you already know the deal: lots of content, lots of overlapping features, diehard community, far past its peak. That’s the broad strokes for anything that meets the criteria, and if you haven’t already tried this, you’re probably familiar enough with MMOs that you’ve seen it before. The real question is: what sets ESO apart in terms of monetization and gameplay experience that makes it worth (or not worth) playing?

I thought long and hard about whether this is something I’d recommend or not, and I’m settling with a highly conditional “not recommend” because I’m assuming you are the average person with an average budget. This is what I’d call a solid 5/10 not because it’s particularly inaccessible, low budget, obtuse, or badly written, but because at the price point you can be enjoying the game you can instead buy several other singleplayer RPGs or subscribe to a different MMO of similar nature for a better deal. That’s the short version. If you are one of the following:[list]
[*] A fan of The Elder Scrolls as a franchise
[*] The person in your friend group who repeatedly lore dumps on their unwitting compatriots
[*] Not particularly limited on budget and want a voiced fantasy story in a popular IP[/list]
I would recommend this game to you with enthusiasm. Why you in particular?

[h1]For Elder Scrolls Fans[/h1]
Where to begin? At the price point of the base game, you could feasibly buy in when it’s on sale for just Vvardenfell, never craft or gather a day in your life, sell your whole inventory every time you come to town, clear the whole zone almost entirely solo, and drop the game for a grand total of ~$5 USD. What you’d get would be a solid story experience that hints at Morrowind and lets you meet all the big names with high stakes in cool places. You may even get enough gold to get your own guar or nix-hound. It’s all canon (as canon as something can be in TES anyways), it’s all official, it features well-known voice actors that frequently work with Bethesda, you’ll get plenty of hours out of it, and you may even wrangle a friend in to cooperatively clear the zone. I’d say it’s nothing but positive, even if you just liked Skyrim’s gameplay.

[h1]For Lore Nerds[/h1]
TES has plenty to sink your teeth into, and you’ll be drip fed enough fun facts about the setting that you’ll have enough anecdotes to fill your part of an entire back-and-forth tidbit-trade conversation. I’d recommend the subscription for this subset of players, and suggest joining the UESP in-game guild and becoming a wiki editor there. You’ll learn about all the Dark Brotherhood splinters, see what Khajiit and Argonian territory really look like, and read every lore book you come across (which does offer progression for the Mages Guild). However, I’d also recommend considering [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/standardheadache/recommended/212500]other MMOs[/url] to make sure you have the right match for your interests.

[h1]In This Economy?[/h1]
If you just want TES 6 and don’t care what you’re paying to get it, here you go. Slightly deeper combat, expansive story, lots of ways to flex that bag. The real TES 6 is never coming out.

[h1]Why Not Others?[/h1]
Despite recent QOL changes, the game-changing one is the crafting ingredients bag. That bag is still gated behind a subscription. Inventory management is nightmarish without it. I’m not going to liquidate all the goodies I get out of a dungeon every dungeon and not regret it a little. The new battlepass has a premium version that doesn’t come with the subscription either, which is odd. The subscription is steep for what it gets you, and the game doesn’t promote prosocial behavior very well for an MMO. The art style is pretty, but the graphics are dated, and without a buy-in with the franchise, I’d just say pick up TES games and mod them until they break.

[h1]Parting Advice For Newbies[/h1][list]
[*] Always get carrying capacity at the stablemaster.
[*] Bag upgrades are a priority.
[*] Try before you subscribe.
[*] If the game is giving something away for free*, get it if it is at all reasonable to do so.
[*] Always fill your research slots.[/list]

A unique experience in ways that exalt and crucify it and also you in more or less equal measure - gun to my head, I'd lean towards a rec over a rec against, but with a bunch of caveats.  
 
First off, you've gotta bear in mind that this isn't exactly *a* game, but three or four of them Human Centipede'd together by a supergroup of Finnish sadists. It's Spelunky with Liero characteristics married to Powder Toy with out-of-bounds content that is genuinely more of an ARG than anything else - it doesn't really matter how smart you are, you simply do not have the time to figure all that stuff out unless you're looking to make Noita your actual job for a while. I wouldn't recommend it, as the job's 99 percent done, anyways. Leave the two holdouts of Iwo Jima to tinker with the Cauldron of Nothing for another five years and binge the wiki whenever you get too mad at whatever it is that voided your 6 to 50-hour run of a game you can generally "beat" within the hour.  
 
And void your run it will - if the simple attrition of bad RNG and getting poisoned/set aflame by stray pixels and eating potshots out from the fog of war doesn't get you, then getting frozen or electrocuted or turned into a sheep or eradicated by a rare gimmick will probably do the trick. 

If *that* doesn't,  then *you* probably will when you go to the wrong place, trigger the wrong boss, drink the wrong thing, tinker with spells in the wrong way, tinker properly but without the required secondary abilities, head out of bounds, shoot the wrong thing at the wrong guy, put on Depeche Mode's Wrong, or stand between fish and a Death Cross and get a faceful of undisclosed interaction. Look, it's alchemy, and the sociopaths at Nolla are pleased as cheese to provide you with the authentic Nigredo experience. Seriously, just read the wiki when you start to crack - "spoiler" and "cause of death" are synonymous in this thing, and devoting an entire afternoon to learning one thing and that one thing being another pioneering discovery in being BTFO is only all that fun if you're really cleared your schedule. 

Now, if none of that scares you off, the good news is everything else. The game's more freeform than it lets on and losing is closer to winning than you might think. The engine is built from the ground up to render Hardcore Powder Toy, and Hardcore Powder Toy is really what this is at the heart of it - the rest of the game is there to issue prompts and force you to think outside the box and interact with the world in ways that similar idiot-goes-down roguelikes can scarcely comprehend. 

Case in point: the wand building is probably the star of the show, though a portion of the wands you naturally find are deliberately cursed to forbid it. Get past that, and you've got carte blanche to assemble novel healing spells, evil clouds of whiskey that detonate alcoholics, heat-seeking boulders, sawblade vortices, and room-clearing superweapons. Unless you read a bit too much of the wiki, that's all on you, and you have every cause to be proud of your latest psychotic creation when it clears half the game and then you as well. Treat every run like one big experiment, chiefly because that's exactly what they are.

In short, a stupendous slog, a rare pain in the ass, technically unwinnable sadomasochism, and a unique experience with maybe one other thing out there remotely like it after half a decade - I don't think you'll regret feeding it a week of your life.

When Path of Exile launched on Steam in 2013, I played through the campaign's three acts with a friend, took down Dominus and thought, "that was alright", and didn't touch it again for 13 years. After sinking 700+ hours into the sequel and completing everything from 0.5's seasonal content, I was craving more Path of Exile and decided to check it out again. While it's definitely showing its age in some areas, Path of Exile is still an incredibly deep and addictive experience that is somehow free to play.

Playing the original after sinking so much time into the sequel feels like replaying a favorite game in another language with a randomizer mod installed. A lot of the crafting currency is named the same but has different effects, player movement and traversal skills are simultaneously faster and clunkier, crafting is more deterministic but way more complex and fragmented, and old Expedition is still here. Both games are unique enough that POE2 isn't a strict upgrade and both target specific audiences: POE1 is built off of the DNA of Diablo, while POE2 is built off of the DNA of Elden Ring. 

However, the biggest problem with this game is competition from its younger brother, POE2. Last season brought a massive rework and upgrades to that game's endgame, and all of the leagues ported from this game are significantly better in 2 in every way. The only POE1-specific endgame that I really enjoyed was Blight, but that required really specific juicing just to get decent drops from it. Blight also requires a fixed amount of time to complete, so even without optimizing the fun out of the game it feels like your time is better spent just running maps in the long run.

In fact, loot across the board is pretty bad this season, resulting in a "poverty league". Coming from POE2 0.5's buffed endgame loot to this game's un-buffed (from the last league) loot is a huge step down, and the poor player retention shows the playerbase's stance on this. Zizaran, one of the top POE streamers/YouTubers, interviewed the devs about this situation for an hour and a half and their response was basically, "don't worry guys, we'll fix it next season"... two weeks into this season. According to various forums, it seems to be a running theme of unnecessarily nerfing rewards from old content to push people into new content, and it's hard to ignore that when you see clips of streamers getting dozens of Divine Orbs from juicing Voyages (the new league's mechanic) in a very specific manner.

Voyages are fun and all, but they highlight a reoccurring issue with endgame content: single portal instances. Every few years I'd check the reviews for this game and the negatives frequently had the same complaints about connection stability issues. This is still an issue in 2026 and is exacerbated by GGG's obsession with one-shot runs. All endgame content that doesn't take place on the Atlas counts as failed if you leave the instance. It's easy to say, "get gud noob lol just don't die", but this also includes crashes and disconnects, whether its your internet dying or the servers hiccuping and dropping your connection. This season I failed two Voyages near the start due to no fault of my own: one because of a "deadlock detected" crash, and one because the servers lost connection even though my internet was working fine (and on a wired connection too). This is extra frustrating over something like losing a Delve run because you have to first farm Allflame map drops, run the small map to chart the area, chart at least nine maps so you can connect a larger Voyage map together (all hallways have to connect and maps have different shapes), and then run the actual Voyage.

Outside of loot and stability issues though it's an amazing game. If you're looking for a spiritual successor to Diablo 2 that has 14 years of updates and tons of content, this is the game for you. The campaign is a slog, endgame is obtuse, and you'll have to take a college course or two if you want to create your own successful builds, but it's still an incredibly rewarding experience with an unbelievable amount of build diversity. Highly recommended if you're trying to stay sober, since you won't have time for drugs when you could be playing Path of Exile (or Path of Building) instead.

I’ve put 181 hours into V Rising, which is honestly something I normally don’t do. I usually get bored with games long before I put anywhere near that many hours into them, so that probably says a lot about how much I enjoyed this one.
V Rising is a nice mix of a survival game, ARPG, and base-building game. You play as a vampire, explore the world, collect resources, build and upgrade your castle, craft better gear, and take on bosses to unlock new abilities and progression. The combat feels a lot like an action RPG, with different weapons and vampire abilities that let you build your character in different ways.
What I really like is that there’s always something to work toward. You’re constantly unlocking new abilities, better equipment, castle upgrades, or another boss you want to take down. The castle building is also surprisingly addictive – although you do need to like world building for this. 
There’s some grinding involved, and traveling around the map can get a little repetitive, but it never bothered me enough to stop playing. 
If you like games like Diablo, Valheim, or other survival/building games, I’d definitely recommend giving V Rising a shot

Factorio saved my life.

Factorio is one of those rare games that takes a relatively simple concept and develops it into an incredibly deep, satisfying, and addictive experience. Developed by Wube Software, Factorio is primarily a factory-building and automation game where players gather resources, research new technologies, construct increasingly complicated production systems, and defend their creations from hostile creatures. While this description may make the game sound straightforward, Factorio quickly reveals itself to be one of the most creative and rewarding strategy and simulation games available.

The main strength of Factorio is its outstanding automation system. At the beginning of the game, almost everything must be done manually. Players mine basic materials such as iron, copper, coal, and stone before crafting the machinery required to begin automating these processes. However, what begins as a few simple mining drills and furnaces can eventually become an enormous automated industrial complex involving transport belts, assembling machines, trains, robotic systems, electrical networks, and many other interconnected technologies.

Watching a factory gradually develop is extremely satisfying. Every improvement feels meaningful because it is usually the result of a problem the player has personally identified and solved. For example, a production line may initially provide enough iron plates to support a small factory, but as the factory expands, demand increases. The player must then decide whether to add more furnaces, improve transportation, increase mining production, or redesign the entire system. These problems constantly encourage experimentation and make progression feel rewarding rather than repetitive.

One of the best aspects of Factorio is that there is rarely only one correct way to solve a problem. Players have enormous freedom when designing their factories. One person might build an extremely organised base with carefully planned production lines, while another might create a chaotic network of conveyor belts that somehow manages to function perfectly. Both approaches can be successful.

This freedom gives Factorio an impressive level of creativity. Although it is primarily based around logic, efficiency, and resource management, it often feels similar to a sandbox game. Players can spend hours improving sections of their factory even when those improvements are not technically necessary. There is something extremely enjoyable about looking at an inefficient production line and thinking, “I can make this better.”

The progression system is another major strength. Researching technologies continuously introduces new possibilities and prevents the gameplay from becoming stagnant. Early production systems that once seemed complicated eventually become relatively basic as technologies such as oil processing, advanced electronics, robotics, trains, and more sophisticated manufacturing systems are introduced.

Factorio handles this increasing complexity particularly well. Instead of immediately overwhelming the player with every mechanic, new systems become available progressively. This means the player's knowledge develops alongside the factory. By the time advanced production systems are required, the player has usually developed enough understanding of the basic mechanics to begin experimenting with them.

This progression creates an excellent sense of accomplishment. Looking back at the small factory created during the beginning of a playthrough after developing a huge industrial network demonstrates just how far the player has progressed. Few games provide such a strong visual representation of the player's increasing knowledge and capabilities.

Factorio is also extremely effective at encouraging problem-solving. Almost every stage of the game introduces some form of logistical challenge. Resources must be transported efficiently, electricity production must keep up with increasing demand, production ratios must be managed, and different materials must reach the correct machines. Instead of these challenges feeling frustrating, solving them is usually the most enjoyable part of the game.

A particularly impressive feature is how naturally the scale of these problems increases. A player may initially worry about transporting iron across a short conveyor belt. Several hours later, they may be designing railway networks capable of transporting huge quantities of resources between distant locations. Eventually, players can manage extremely complicated automated systems where hundreds or even thousands of machines operate simultaneously.

Despite this complexity, Factorio provides excellent visual feedback. Conveyor belts visibly transport materials, machines display their activity, and production lines can generally be understood simply by watching them operate. Seeing thousands of individual resources moving throughout an enormous factory can be strangely relaxing and highly satisfying.

Combat also provides an interesting additional challenge. Industrial expansion creates pollution, which can contribute to conflict with hostile creatures surrounding the player's factory. Players therefore cannot always concentrate exclusively on production and must sometimes invest resources into weapons, ammunition, walls, turrets, and other defensive systems. This gives expansion an additional strategic dimension because players must balance industrial growth with survival and security.

Another major advantage is replayability. Because factories can be designed in so many different ways, beginning a new game rarely feels identical to the previous one. Players may attempt more efficient layouts, experiment with different transportation methods, increase the difficulty, play alongside friends, or explore modifications created by the community.

Factorio's multiplayer mode is particularly enjoyable because multiple players can collaborate on the same factory. One player might concentrate on resource production while another builds railway systems or develops defences. Building a huge automated factory alongside friends can transform an already engaging single-player game into an excellent cooperative experience.

The game's modding community adds even more longevity. Factorio has extensive modification support, with community-created mods capable of adding new mechanics, technologies, resources, challenges, and quality-of-life improvements. This means players who have already spent hundreds of hours mastering the standard game can significantly change their experience.

Factorio's graphical style also suits the gameplay exceptionally well. It does not rely on realistic graphics or flashy visual effects. Instead, the industrial artwork clearly communicates what each machine is doing. Large factories packed with moving conveyor belts, robotic arms, trains, machines, and resources have a distinctive appearance that becomes more impressive as the factory grows.

Most importantly, Factorio consistently rewards the player's intelligence and creativity. When a complicated factory system works successfully, it feels like a genuine achievement because the player designed it. The game does not simply provide rewards for completing repetitive tasks; it rewards understanding, experimentation, optimisation, and planning.

Overall, Factorio is an outstanding example of how excellent game design can transform a simple idea into something incredibly deep. Its combination of automation, construction, resource management, research, combat, and problem-solving creates an experience that can remain entertaining for hundreds of hours. The satisfaction of transforming a small collection of manually operated machines into a massive automated industrial system is difficult to match.

[h1]A survival RPG with its own characteristics and a true understanding of vampires[/h1]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]★ 8.5/10 — The vampire gameplay is well done, and the survival process is indeed time-consuming[/h2]

[b]⊕ BEST FOR:[/b] Players who like vampire themes, castle construction, top-down combat, cooperative survival, fixed maps, open-world PvP, and custom Private Games.

[b]⊖ NOT FOR:[/b] Players who are unwilling to collect repeatedly, prefer random maps and story-driven RPGs, want to freely advance the process, permanently retain the progress of the Official Servers, or are ready to play single-player with the default settings.

[b]▣ Media Benchmarks:[/b] Metacritic PC 83/100 · OpenCritic 83/100 · IGN 9/10 · PC Gamer 89/100.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]◆ Opening[/h2]

As of Update 1.1: Invaders of Oakveil, new areas, bosses, weapons, and main features have been added through free updates, and paid DLC only involves cosmetic packs and soundtrack content.

[h2]◆ Strengths[/h2]

[b]⊕ The identity of a vampire does affect how you play[/b]
The sun will burn in a few seconds, and you have to find shadows on the way during the day, but the shadows will move over time. The blood pool has been consumed, and the bonuses provided by different Blood Types are also different. Shapeshifting can help rush, sneak, and explore, and some special areas must also be entered by it. Silver, garlic, and human settlements have their own places to pay attention to.

You will choose to hunt at night and go back before dawn. You will also detour because of the sun, the enemies on the road, or the blood type you are looking for.

Production, research, production of equipment, arrangement of Servants, and detention of Prisoners reserved as blood sources are all carried out in their own Gothic castles. At first it was just a place to stay, but slowly a decent vampire palace could be built. The Advanced Game Settings of Private Games can also adjust resource output, crafting time, enemy strength, blood drain, sunlight, and death penalties.

[b]⊕ The combat is excellent in the survival game, and the fixed map also makes value[/b]
The combat uses a top-down angle, WASD movement, mouse aiming, and movement abilities (Veils), weapon skills, and spells. With another weapon, the basic attack, skill, and attack range will all change; the spell school and equipment also support different builds such as melee, ranged, summoning, control, and damage over time.

It is not as complicated as a dedicated action game, but the movement, combat feedback, and build options are already better than most survival games. Many V Bloods have their own moves, arena mechanics, and phase changes, and they need to be familiar with them before they can deal with them. Brutal will increase skills and change combat behavior, not just increase health and damage.

The factions, resources, enemies and patrol routes in each area are different, and different factions can be encountered in the wild to fight each other. You can take the opportunity to pick up a bargain, or you may bump into a patrol that can't be beaten at all when you are on your way. After you are familiar with the map, the fun of exploring comes more from your understanding of the environment: where is it dangerous, which way to transport materials, and where to find suitable prey. These experiences are useful in collecting, castle site selection, and PvP.

[h2]◆ Weaknesses[/h2]

[b]⊖ The upgrading of the production chain makes the upgrade feel fulfilling, and it is really abrasive[/b]
The problem is that the later, the more steps will be taken to collect, refine, transport, and make a string. Many early materials have to continue to be collected in the later stage, because they still have to be used for advanced materials.

Version 1.1 reduces some chores in the castle. The Treasury allows the crafting and construction to directly use the territory inventory, and the Redistribution Engine can transfer items between production facilities, but it is relatively late to get it.

Private Games can increase resource output and shorten crafting time, but the steps to take are still those. To play alone, you have to fight monsters, collect, ship goods, arrange production, and maintain the castle by yourself. Two or more people divide the labor, and the rhythm will be much better.

Room and flooring bonuses will also affect the layout. If you want to build a castle beautifully, you have to consider production efficiency.

[b]⊖ Although the growth route is very clear, there is less freshness when replaying[/b]
Following the Journal, you basically know what to do next: defeat the V Blood boss, get the unlocked content (V Blood Unlocks), get new equipment, Spell Points and recipes, and then go to the back area until the final boss. Weapons and skills can be selected, and some bosses can also be played in a different order, but many tools necessary to advance the process still have to defeat the designated boss to get them.

If you start another game, it will still be those areas, roads and resource points, and the growth route will be much the same. Compared with survival games with randomly generated maps, after the first round is played, the next round can bring a lot less freshness of exploration.

[b]⊖ The castle needs to be reopened for large-scale updates, and the built castle will inevitably make people reluctant[/b]
As of version 1.1, large-scale content updates have made changes to maps, units, and systems, and players have been asked to reopen the save. The old local saves, Private Games, and self-hosted servers can be left in the corresponding old version to continue playing, but they cannot be brought into the updated world. The Official Servers will be reset during large-scale updates, or they may be cleared in a fixed cycle, and the characters, resources, and castles cannot be left forever.

If you can save the blueprint or building layout, at least you don't have to build it from scratch every time. Of course, map changes and server balance must also be considered, and it will not be as simple as directly importing the old save.

[b]⊖ Even if you have to fight for PvP, you have to fight for who has time[/b]
If players want to fight for territory and find each other's castle, they must also consider whether their layout is convenient for production or more resistant to Castle Raiding.

However, in a server that opens castle raids and wipes regularly, the amount of resources, clan size, online time, progression speed, and raid hours will all affect the results. Organized clans can collect, produce, and guard their homes separately, and it is much harder for small teams and people who enter the service late.

It's really exciting when the competition is fierce, but if you can't follow the server's schedule and want to stay competitive, you may have to invest more time than expected.

[h2]◆ Conclusion[/h2]

From the first time I played it in 2024 to the present, what I admire most is that "V Rising" has added so many things and still retains its original characteristics.

If you can accept fixed maps, linear growth, and are willing to spend time collecting and operating, the vampire survival experience it provides is indeed worth a try.

I'm generally not into base building and crafting, yet this game still hooked me.  One of the top 10 games ever for me.

The combat is the highlight, a wide variety of enemies and bosses, with different abilities, tactics and themes.  Your own abilities are also quite customisable.

The sunlight and shade mechanics are clever and thematic.

The base building is straightforward and if you like beautifying your base, you can certainly do that.  Gear crafting is fairly railroaded although there are a lot of different weapon types that give you a different fighting style.  There is some grinding for materials, but if you get the right servants, buildings and flooring this becomes faster, and the amount of grinding never became annoying.

Definitely more fun multiplayer.

Criticisms?  Stylistically, I think the game would have felt more "vampirey" if turning into a bat and flying everywhere was an earlier part of the game, possibly replacing the teleporters.  There are enough vampire themed mechanisms to remind you you're a vampire and not a superpowered frontier castle builder, but the line occasionally felt blurred as I knocked down my nth stone boulder.

Overall, a great game.

The core of World of Tanks is fun

15 vs 15 is a cool idea that gives fight a sense of scale and epicness. It also gives a chance of newer players to learn how to play by sticking to a safe place and learn from it, but it usually ends up punishing any type of misplay so hard that it teaches the player to not even try, in turn, making them camp or not take advantage of a good situation

The tier system was an interesting concept from the pre-matchmaking/MMO origins this game has to keep the new players to certain playstyles on lower tiers, while people who already knew more about their tanks could skip this and go straight to higher tiers. So many economies to handle, the credits to do any kind of tank management, experience to tamper any kind or change of playstyle any player wants to do, crew experience to make the long time players even better (even if, in theory, the abilities sound cool), experience for experience, free experience, etc. In turn, these systems create the bigger problem of grinding, so much grinding for so many things JUST to play a single game. I already said how players don't have any incentive to try anything; these systems make it worse because you can even go negative in some matches. 

Of course there is paid gold and premium time to make all of these easier.
The game is not ashamed of it, since at the end of the day, that's the end goal, not making a fun game (that was just a happy accident).

This game cant change, it only looks as beautiful as it does and sounds as amazing as it does because it asks for so much money or time to keep players in it.

I would advise any player looking at this game to turn back and look at other options, strategy games for the ones who want the slow paced gameplay or free-to-play shooters for the ones who want in some action (really, its easier to get in a real game there than in here).

And even if they don't, even if they charge 500 dollars for skins in their game, or sell limited time stuff for exorbitant prices, or sell that single player game at 100 dollars, they wont be as greedy as Wargaming has been with this game and every single one of their titles.

Noita is an amazing game marred with some bad design decisions. How you manage these decisions will determine whether you quit early, keep going only to get frustrated well into it, or experience it fully. Judging from global achievement completion, a vast majority of players will fall within the first two categories.

One of the most obvious of these decisions is the cryptic nature of the game. It won't take long to realize that nothing is really explained that well. This applies to not just the secrets, but also basic mechanics and wand building that are essential to beat the base game - something Noita experts colloquially refer to as "beating the tutorial". There is an irony to this because how can one beat the tutorial when there was no tutorial in the first place?

As a result, this produces artificial layers of difficulty for the game which would've been easily solved provided the player has a certain skill floor, but we'll get to the purpose of skill in a moment. In any case, any review of the game under 20 or so hours will likely have this issue, where players adopt the opinion that the game is naturally difficult.

Some of these players that keep going might get surprised that what they thought was a glaring skill gap was actually a knowledge gap pertaining mainly to insufficient wand building, and partly to certain potion interactions and secrets that are difficult to find or figure out.

In fact, the knowledge gap is so significant, that in some cases it can completely fill any skill gaps, assuming the player knows how to utilize it. This can trivialize skill to such an extent that it is no longer required to play well, rather - the wands will do all the work for you. Getting there, however, is a question of how much time are you willing to spend before you inevitably look for information on the wiki.

That brings us to dying. People comment how easy it is to get “Noita’d” all the time. And yes, it’s easy to die. But no, you don’t have to. This might be a hot take but if you have a history of roguelites, or have played 2D action games like Soldat way back, you will rack up experience quickly and a base run will be possible in almost all cases - provided you put in some effort to bridge the knowledge gap.

This is because there is a certain quality to a methodical approach to combat even with just basic wand building, and as long as you learn how to evade certain enemies and play the game with proper focus, you should be able to reach the base level boss vast majority of the time. Deaths usually come in the form of, well – trying anything new.

And this is the conundrum at the heart of Noita. You're expected to experiment with wands, yet this will often kill you. You can only carry four and tinkering with them everywhere is locked behind rare or hard to get options. You're expected to explore outside the usual boundaries, but this will often kill you too. You're expected to solve secrets, yet the important ones are so well hidden, that consulting the wiki is basically a necessity.

None of it would be a problem if it didn't take such a long time. Experimenting, exploring, backtracking, researching - this is tens of hours of gameplay, hundreds for some people. To lose progress because you did not know what would happen in the next 5 seconds is a completely solvable issue. And once you start an ambitious run again, you will often have to do the very same, long-winded checklist from scratch.

This is why I said the game had bad design decisions. Gameplay is otherwise good. Wand building is actually really clever. Falling Everything engine is a technical marvel. In fact, I'd recommend it just on the merits of the engine alone. I love many parts of it and there is nothing like it, it’s just the sum of its parts I have issues with.

But, for some people it could very much turn out to be exactly the experience they wanted.

I think ESO is genuinely in a stable spot right now; the game has lots of DLC and zones available to strike your fancy for questing and activities, and there's always the ability to integrate and try to enjoy sociability and find your niche. The community is relatively welcoming and you can choose just how much to integrate yourself, should you so choose, as you could rely on companions and find ways to solo a lot of content on your own, besides trials and few other endgame activities. The group finder is easy to use and robust with toggles and preferences to engage in group content without the true reliance on social integration, you could literally group up for one activity and never interact with those people again... or it can also be a good way to find some new friends. 

The only "complaint" is how integral the subscription service of ESO+ feels to enjoy the game; the craft bag alone is invaluable to keep yourself from having a min-max inventory management throughout your gaming experience. Sure, you could optimize things yourself and really try to find a way to do it, but the game just feels more enjoyable (and accessible) relying on the subscription service as not only do you get the craft bag, but you get all access to previously released content and a stipend of crowns each month which you can choose to rollover and save for larger purchases. Which, in all honestly, feels pretty worth it to me as I am actively playing the game and I don't feel a need to add crowns to my account beyond the stipend... there are some things you might be hit with FOMO over, and there's always other currencies you could use for most things, but really you don't NEED anything, they have some tantalizing offers of assistants (which, I have collected over time) but really you can always port back to a home base and take a few minutes to clear out your inventory yourself, it's not a need. Just about prioritization and what kind of gamer you are; if you like to whale money you can definitely do that here, or you can play conservatively and find ways around most things to save your IRL coin. 

I genuinely do recommend it if you're looking for a more casual MMORPG that lets you jump in as frequently as you'd like without penalty, especially as they've pivoted towards seasonal content with tomes instead of incentivizing daily logins, you get more flexibility with your free time than you'd have in other games. Limited time events are very forgiving with their requirements of completion, in my opinion, so you never feel like it's predatory. 

All in all, after 1000+ hours on PC (and a few hundred on XBOX back in the day), I give ESO a tentative approval so long as things maintain their relaxed feel and the devs continue to listen and implement changes to benefit the community to keep it alive.

As of August 2026, Guild Wars 2 may reign at the top for me in terms of "best MMORPG on Steam".  I've put thousands upon thousands of hours into MMORPG's, all the way back to to the old school games like DAOC, WoW, EQ2, Rift, etc.  These days it really feels like you either have to grind your face off (or spend all your money) in the Eastern style MMORPG's like Lost Ark, BDO, etc., or play an older MMORPG that was built back when companies created games to have fun! 

The progression system and incredible depth of content are what makes GW2 the "best" IMO right now.  There is just an insane amount of content to play with in GW2.  It spans the original game, 4 mini-expansions (Living Worlds), and 6 full expansions.  Every expansion unlocks more ways to play the game, more game systems like mounts, housing, etc.  I've only played through about 1/3 of the available content on this time around.  I have four lvl 80 characters, and a group of other characters that I created but just haven't played enough. While I have several lvl 80 boosters available on my account, I prefer to level up the characters by just playing the game.  Even the open world PvP system (World vs World) is still super active, which is a rarity in comparison to other older MMO's.

One of the best things about this game is the account-level progression system.  As characters hit lvl 80 in PvE levels, they can contribute to the "Mastery Point" levels for your account.  There are separate MP pools for each expansion and the base game, and every one of those improves some aspect of your account.  It could be unlocking content, improving travel powers or mount abilities, or making your character more effective for things like PvP, WvW, or PvE dungeons / raiding.  A variety of things like Mounts, Minis, weapon / armor skins, etc. are all unlocked for your entire account, so every improvement you unlock is available for every character on your account.

Elder Scrolls Online is probably the most similar game these days to GW2.  ESO is also a great game, but whenever I played it I admit that I felt like it was a MMORPG that you played solo 95% of the time.  You may occasionally see other players in the world, but they can largely be ignored.  Many parts of the game feel like ghost towns because if there are players around, you just don't see them much outside of towns.  That is not the case at all in GW2.  I constantly find myself grouping up with other players for events and other game content. Between special calendar events and the world events that run 24/7, there is always something to do with other players. You don't even have to join a guild, though I do recommend doing so.  I've seen groups of players get together for special events like Triple Trouble, where they are coordinating three separate raid groups to take down massive bosses in the world.  Players actually spend time helping each other out in GW2, which is something that I didn't see nearly as often in ESO.

If I had to recommend any MMORPG these days, it would be GW2 first.  Especially if you are tired of the East-Asian styled grind-fest MMORPG's, this one would be right up your alley.  Plus it's free to play through the base game, so why not give it a shot?

With the amount of time I've put into ESO, it's pretty hard for me to give it anything other than a positive review. That said, the game definitely feels like it's moved into a different stage compared to when I first started playing.

There's still an absolutely ridiculous amount of content to get through, but the focus seems to have shifted more towards maintaining and improving the existing game rather than constantly expanding the world with massive new areas. It's a little disappointing to see that change, but there's still more than enough content here to keep you busy for a very long time.

One thing I'd definitely warn new players about is the amount of monetisation. There are subscriptions, different currencies, cosmetics, crates and plenty of other things to spend money on. None of it is necessarily required to enjoy the game, but it's surprisingly easy to spend more than you originally planned, so it's worth keeping an eye on.

What I really like about ESO is how easy it is to play however you want. You can spend hundreds of hours completely solo if that's your thing, or jump into groups whenever you feel like being more social. Companions and group-finding systems make this even easier, and when you do interact with other players, I've generally found the community to be pretty friendly and helpful.

Despite what you might hear, ESO certainly isn't dead. There's still a huge amount of content, plenty of players and loads of things to work towards.

Overall, ESO is still an easy game to recommend. Whether you're completely new or returning after a long break, there's an enormous amount to explore and plenty of ways to play.

I bought this on a deep sale and it sat in the pile for a long time.   Much like the plot of V Rising itself, the game was resurrected from the depths of my backlog to rise as.. this game I played a lot of.

I've played many games over many decades.  I also knocked about with Vampire LARPers in the 90s (it was cool, they LARPed all over downtown) and learned a surprisingly large amount of White Wolf vamp knowledge from those kids back then.  I also enjoyed the hell out of games like Neverwinter Nights and other isometric combat games like that.  So, given that V Rising has done a fantastic job of covering so many aspects of Vamp 'gameplay' it's no surprise I stuck around for as long as I did with this one.

When I started the game I had little expectations.  What actually transpires (and V Rising does a very good job of it) is the player will grow their little powerless rat-munching vamp into one more powerful than Dracula itself, and you'll experience every step of power creep along the way.  Overall, this translates to the overarching and empirical objective: Grow in Power Rating.  It's a number comprised primarily of your attack and defensive stats, which is comprised of your weapons, armor and spell power ratings. You'll start at power level 1 or so, and in order to beat Dracula you're going to have to get that up to over 90.

Getting from that start to that endpoint involves a lot of combat, crafting, base building, and exploration.  I'll touch on each point briefly here, otherwise this'll get too wordy. 

1) Combat: V Rising (VR) appears, to me, to have an isometric style combat that has learned a lot from, and plays similarly to, many other action games of its kind.  Everything scales in VR, including the themes around combat and attack offerings, weapons, and spells.  Each of those individual components come with their own sort of skill tree, which means that each will grow in power as the game progresses.  A huge part of this game is beating bosses, and upon beating those bosses, drinking their blood and acquiring their powers.  So combat is not just inflicting terror on citizens and monsters to get their stuff, but also, and more importantly, finding and beating the bosses of each subarea so that you can improve various aspects of your power.

2) Crafting: As mentioned, in order to grow in power in VR, you're going to require increasingly better armor, weapons, spells, and more.  In order to achieve those improvements the player will need to find the items required for assembly, the 'blueprints' to make the thing, and the tool required to do so.  

3) Base Building: A fun and essential component to VR.  You'll need this base to improve everything, and it's also the place to house your thralls that you capture. It's not perfect, but it's pretty damn close to a Sims 4 experience with a Vampire tileset. 

4) Exploration: The map is quite large, feels large, and transportation will vary as VR progresses.  Each section of difficulty presents itself and plays like a biome in any other game, so you'll have a clear distinction when you're 'not in Kansas anymore'.  Oftentimes a change of biome means a complete change in combat tactics and considerations, so it's not just about 'tougher enemies' but also a slow, creeping introduction of more complex challenges to overcome, both strategically and tactically.

So it's a good game. But as I said up front, it was a tortured experience - which I felt thematically acceptable. 

It's like, I'm always striving for more power.  It's never enough.  Every successful harvest of souls leaves me yearning for more power, the next kill, and that feels extremely on-brand for a vampire.

There's a ton of other things worth mentioning here - like the capturing of prisoners, the power of varying blood qualities and using them to your advantage, building up your horse, transforming in to different creatures so as to improve travel time and access previously unattainable areas, and more. 

It's absolutely worth mentioning that I played this exclusively on controller.  I have been K&M almost exclusively since the early 90s, but nowadays I just like to chill with controllers for some reason.  So everything I've done here I've done from a relaxed gaming position, playing with a controller.  

I haven't played this in a few weeks but I've mastered the game well enough for my liking.  I have to go back and beat Dracula but that's just a matter of red tape; I have the tools, I just can't be asked with the challenge of 'ol Drac right now. 

The game is over 24 months past V.1 release at this point and it's got a lot of DLC on offer.  It looks to me like the DLC is just for aesthetics.  Which is cool.

Before I go, here's some things.  
1.  No, I didn't play multiplayer.  No comments there.  
2. No technical issues at all. 
3. Generally, if I have played something for 100 hours it means it's good in my books.  I don't have much interest or time these days in playing games that suck. 

V Rising is a good one for vamp champs and old dorks like me. Grab it on sale, because it will be eventually, and then play it when you want to.

I want to say that Noita is the best designed game I've ever played but that wouldn't be quite right. It was in early access/pre-release for a long time, evolving, iterating and growing and the result is a game that was as much grown as it was designed.

However it came to be, Noita IS the best single player game ever created.

It doesn't just have depth but a recursive quality where even seemingly simple game mechanics have layers to them and those layers interweave with other mechanics. The world is large and unforgiving. Except actually, the world is colossal and brutal. It is also fair in the same way life is fair - sometimes bad things happen and sometimes there is nothing you can do about it, but there is always a reason why and there is always a lesson to be learned.

If you are going to play it, you will need to be patient and you will need to learn. Not just facts - though there are plenty of those - but through hard-earned experience. You will need to get good technically and be fast enough to apply that huge amount of knowledge and experience gained over countless deaths to get the point of mastery.

Except you never really master Noita. Like life, you can only ever get to a good place, not as a destination but as a staging point from which you can respond to life's difficulties with strength.

Of course like life, you never really win at Noita either. You just have stories you can tell.

And maybe some nice jewellery to wear at the end of it.

Je to moje takřka srdcovka. Hraju vlastně od vydání a hraju dodnes, což ji vzhledem k jejímu věku řadí do takové té kategorie nesmrtelných klasik.

Bez toho, abych to nějak zbytečně vyzdvihoval... v téhle hře si nový domov najde snad každý, koho baví MMORPG.

[b]Open World[/b]

Chceš open world exploraci? V tomhle směru je GW2 i po těch letech podle mě bezkonkurenční. Jsi completionista, co rád hledá, sbírá kolekce, achievementy a různé kraviny, o kterých jsi ještě včera ani nevěděl, že existují? Tohle přesně je open world explorace zde. 

V jednu chvíli kácíš stromy nebo zjišťuješ, jak můžeš pomoct v nějaké usedlosti, a za moment ti nad hlavou prolétne obří drak a hned pod ním běží stádo hráčů, kteří ho jdou zmasit. I takový je open world v GW2. 

[b]Group Content[/b]

Zajímá tě spíš instancovaný content pro partu? Je ho tu hromada, původní dungeony jsou sice už staré, ale "Fraktály" stále frčí, plus tu jsou "Dragon Response mise" které slouží jako obdoba původních dungeonů.

Máš rád raidy a těžší endgame, kde tě hra ztrestá za každou chybu a po třetím wipu už začínáš přemýšlet, jestli není čas jít spát? Určitě si tu najdeš své. 

Jak u group contentu pro partu tak u raidů je možnost si daný content jak ulehčit tak samozřejmě ztížit, což znamená že si tu najdeš své i jako nováček tak jako ostřílený veterán.

[b]PVP[/b]

A pokud nejsi vůbec PvE hráč, ale baví tě PvP, ani tady tě hra nenechá na holičkách. Ranked 5v5, občasné 2v2 nebo 3v3, případně prostě jen bezhlavá mlátička pro zábavu v unranked/custom arénách.

Navíc jsou v PvP staty normalizované, takže je úplně jedno, jestli máš nahráno tisíce hodin a gear za miliony, nebo sis postavu založil před pěti minutami. V PvP jste si všichni rovni. Teda alespoň co se statů týče. Skill si bohužel koupit nejde :o)

A pokud máš rád PvP, ale raději větší organizované bitky ala castle siege, ani tady GW2 nezklame. Máš tu WvW, kde se na obrovských mapách mlátí tři strany o kempy, tvrze a hrady, staví se obléhací stroje a občas se proti sobě postaví tolik lidí, že už vlastně ani nevíš, co se děje, ale je to zatraceně zábavné.

[b]Ostatní[/b]

V neposlední řadě, hra má silný důraz i na ekonomiku, takže pokud tě baví třeba sběr surovin, crafting a následný prodej, nebo si chceš rovnou zkusit flipování na aukci, i v tomhle směru si tu dokážeš najít svoje.

A jestli je ti tohle všechno tak nějak ukradené a hledáš jen nové místo, kde můžeš vychillovat a třeba poznat nové lidi, i tady si svoje najdeš. Rybaření, závody, housing, minihry a spousta dalších aktivit, u kterých můžeš prostě jen tak existovat.

[b]Komunita <3[/b]

Právě komunita je jedna z věcí, která mě na téhle hře baví možná nejvíc. Lidi jsou na dnešní poměry online her až podezřele přátelští. Když někde nevíš, co dělat, většinou se stačí zeptat a někdo ti poradí. Hra má podle mě jednu z nejpřátelštějších a nejvíc pomáhajících MMO komunit vůbec. Rovnat se jí může snad jen Animal Crossing nebo babiččin kurz vyšívání.

[b]Horizontální Progress[/b]

Tohle všechno je zabalené do relativně kompaktního balíčku s horizontálním progressem, kdetý zní to možná nudně a na internetu na to najdeš hromadu negativ... 
Ve skutečnosti to ale znamená hlavně to, že si od hry můžeš kdykoliv odfrknout. Klidně na rok. Klidně na pět let. A když se vrátíš, nezačneš od nuly a nemusíš několik měsíců dohánět gear, protože všichni ostatní už mezitím utekli o tři tier­y dál. Prostě pokračuješ tam, kde jsi skončil.

A rozhodně se nemusíš bát, že kvůli tomu nebudeš mít co dělat. Spíš naopak.

GW2 je podle mě jedna z mála MMO, která respektuje tvůj čas.

[b]Žádné P2W, battlepassy, subscription nebo VIP statusy[/b]

A ještě jedna věc, kterou bych měl zmínit: žádné P2W. Nic, co si můžeš koupit za reálné peníze, ti nedá přímou výhodu nad ostatními hráči. Maximálně si můžeš nakoupit herní měnu a tím si zkrátit některé části progresu. Ale pořád se bavíme spíš o desítkách hodin, které si můžeš ušetřit, než o něčem, co by bylo potřeba.

Potřebovat to rozhodně nebudeš. Když budeš mít trochu povědomí o tom, co děláš, nebo se prostě ve hře zeptáš někoho zkušenějšího, tak máš podle mě do nějakých 200 hodin jeden build vytažený na velmi slušnou, endgame použitelnou úroveň.

A pak už je to jen na tobě.

Můžeš hrát dalších 5 000 hodin, dělat achievementy, grindit skiny, chodit raidy, PvP, WvW, prozkoumávat mapy, nebo klidně tři hodiny stát někde v Lion's Arch a kecat s náhodnými lidmi.

A všechno z toho je vlastně validní způsob, jak hrát Guild Wars 2.

Za mě jedna z těch MMO, které tu budou ještě hodně dlouho po tom, co většina dnešních „nových MMO killerů“ dávno zdechne.

This game is awesome but can there please be a rework to safer seas. I know there's huge discourse over  safer seas being a crutch on the "true experience" of sot, but it's very evident that different people want different things. There will always be an audience for PVP similarly to how there will always be an audience for those who want to play without the risk of running into other players. I don't understand why so many companies want to police how their player-base chooses to play their games. Why even put safer seas into the game if you're going to leave it as nothing more than a glorified tutorial.  

I really enjoy playing high seas with friends, but I'm often on sot alone, so playing safer seas just allows me to grind out everything in a less stressful manner. I just don't understand why it's so punishing. Why can't I have my own captained ship, what purpose does that serve. How would me having my own ship in safer seas somehow be unfair to those playing in high seas. I can't even decorate the ship I'm given in safer seas. What truly makes a pirate, a pirate, if they don't even have a ship to call their own. Not having a ship means I'm unworthy to be titled a captain, which also means I am forbidden from selling to the sovereigns. Aren't the sovereigns just meant to be a quality of life feature. Why would that be stripped from players just because they choose to play a less risky game mode. I also don't understand why reputation would be capped as low as level 25. I don't think it should be capped at all, because once again, reputation is a part of sot that doesn't necessarily impact other players in high seas. I understand certain reputation gain being excluded as its PvP oriented, but for general faction reputation to be capped just to force people into eventually playing high seas is dumb. At least cap it to level 45 instead of something as low as level 25.

All this is going to do is eventually lead players into dropping the game because it doesn't fit their play style. Catering to both parties cannot be that detrimental to high seas servers as there will always be demand for PvP. Improving safer seas will never cause players to dwindle in numbers, but forcing your players out of a gamemode that serves nothing but a couple, worthwhile hours of stress-free grinding, will. [b] Why offer to cater to the parts of your player-base that crave an experience outside of the main gamemode, when you don't truly believe they should enjoy the game just as much. [/b]

DRG really is a great game. It blends several insanely good mechanics. My favorite being that you have to collect resources to buy upgrades, overclocks and more. It also adds a ton of diverse biomes that create a unique cave each time you load in for a match. It has a ton of events, random occurrences, missions, overclocks, and more. 
It also creates a near perfect multiplayer experience with there being 4 classes and infinite builds to choose from. The community is super friendly and helpful. Even when solo the game still has great playability. When I first started playing the game it was honestly so exciting to learn new things and buy new upgrades and guns.
But as i achieved more and more hours in the game, started getting almost all the overclocks, getting most achievements, and all there really is to do, DRG suddenly lost its shine. It feels like there's nothing to do. Obviously there are the Summer, Oktoberfest and Halloween events but they just do the exact same thing each year. The game doesn't update nearly often enough and when it does I learn all the new bugs, biomes and events in a few hours. 
Perhaps its because i spent too much time on the game, and its time to put it on the shelf for the last time. Its still fun to occasionally play it with friends, but at the end of the day It feels like i already achieved everything there was to do in my first 200 hours of the game. 
I thank DRG and its community for all the fun I had in it, maybe I will comes back for more, but I feel like it was about time to leave a honest review about the game.

There is just SO much content in Guild Wars 2. There’s always something to do, and even when you’re just walking around because you don’t have a mount yet (if I remember correctly), you’ll randomly run into events and somehow end up joining them. I also really loved the story, which surprised me because I’m usually the type of person who skips MMORPG stories. It’s been a while since I played, so I honestly don’t remember everything anymore. I probably forgot half of what I was doing, what my build was, or even where I was supposed to go.  But I still remember how much I enjoyed playing it.

I also remember that we were planning to buy all the DLCs because there was a huge sale going on. It was supposed to be my birthday gift, but I refused. lmao the whole argument was “if we ever run out of games to play or get burned out, we can always come back to this game years later” 

Funny enough, I’m kind of glad we didn’t buy it.
Because that person isn’t here anymore.

And now, thinking about it, I guess it’s a little bittersweet. There are games that you miss because they were fun, and then there are games you miss because of the memories attached to them. This one is definitely both.

But I think I’ll come back someday. Maybe I’ll play completely solo, start a new character, and experience everything all over again. I’ll probably be completely lost at first, but honestly, that might make it even more fun.

Nothing beats wiping another team, stealing the bounty, and somehow making it to extraction while your entire team is one hit away from death. It's definitely not an easy game. The learning curve is steep, and sometimes you'll spend 20 minutes setting everything up just to get headshot by someone hiding in a bush. But honestly, those frustrating moments make the victories even better. The setting is also a huge part of the experience. The dark Wild West atmosphere mixed with monsters and PvP gives Hunt an identity that most shooters simply don't have. Not perfect, but if you like tactical shooters, extraction games, or games that actually make you nervous, give it a try.

One of the best games I've played. Do NOT let the 2D aspect turn you away. I was initially offput by having a factory game in 2D (especially after Satisfactory was my introductory game to factory games) and I wasn't the biggest fan of the graphics, but this game ended up being one of the best games out there.

If you have no experience in automation games, this one can be pretty brutal to start with. I would probably recommend starting with Satisfactory. I tried this game first, got lost even in the tutorial, and put it down for a long time. After understanding the concept of the game better from Satisfactory, the tutorial felt much more approachable because I then understood the flow of the game and the purpose of everything.

There are ways to get around the 2D aspect with things like railways that are lifted higher off the ground or belts that go underground. These help a lot. The game is highly optimized so extremely large factories are possible without performance issues.

Mods are built into the client and very easy to download and update.

Resource patches are of limited quantity. Personally, that gives me a lot of anxiety, especially with the enemies. I'm really not a big fan of having to ration everything in an automation game. I just want to build large systems and fight bugs. Thankfully, there's a mod for that! If you're like me, get an infinite resource mod to make the game a little more chill. If you like the challenge of rationing resources, you can do that too! Resource patches are plentiful, don't get me wrong. You can get a ton of resources from one patch, but it's really just the fact that it's limited that gets me anxious.

This game also never goes on sale. The devs have made a stand against that. But the game is well worth the full price. The DLC also adds at least 4-5x playtime per run. Highly recommend Space Age.

Map size is incomprehensible. I believe a video I saw said that the fastest mode of transportation (train) would take you 3.5 real life hours to travel from one side of a world to another. It's virtually endless. This let's you spend thousands of hours in one save (if you want to) making the absolute largest factory you can comprehend.

Can't recommend this game enough. If you like building cities or factories, automation, base defense, this game is #1. Don't let graphics or 2D turn you away.

What more can I say really? Guild Wars 2 is truly special to me. People who know me know that I have played a ridiculous number of hours in this game over the last 15+ years. It is one of my "forever games" and because of this I'll probably still be playing it until I'm 90 (or at least until they stop making content I guess). 

Guild Wars 2 truly redefined the MMORPG genre when it was released, and in my opinion to this day it easily remains one of the best ever made. And of course, on top of everything, [b]**THERE IS NO MONTHLY SUBSCRIPTION.**[/b]

The world is massive and full of content, events, rich lore, and story that continues through each expansion. Whether, on the one hand, you just enjoy casual-friendly content like playing through the story, participating in events in the open-world, and (eventually) collecting legendary weapons, or, on the other hand, you're a mega-hardcore sweatlord who enjoys challenging raids, fractals and competitive PvP/WvW battles, there is always something to do.
The game also does something that a lot of other MMOs don't, and that is respect your time. There is no endless treadmill to catch up to everyone else. You can play whatever you feel like doing, whenever you feel like doing it, and if you take a few months (or even years) off, you're not going to come back feeling behind or left unable to participate in newer content, something that can easily happen in other games.

In terms of actual gameplay, movement and combat is so fluid and freeing when compared to games like WoW and FF14. Things feel weighty and fun to play, which only continues as you unlock more ways to traverse through the world, such as gliding or using mounts to navigate through maps in different ways.
Factoring in the different classes, weapons, skills and, specialisations, unlockable armor/skins, there must be an almost infinite amount of different ways you can customise the way a character plays. Yet even if you pick a terrible combination you still feel like you have an impact and are contributing well during event. Expansions also add 'elite specialisations' that are almost new classes of their own, completely changing your character further and giving you access to even more weapons and abilities.

If want a rich online world full of things to do, while still having the possibility of a real life, I really recommend you give this game a try. Even if you have played it before and it's been a few years why not give it another go. The base game is free, so you literally have nothing to lose.

As someone who's been playing this game since 2014, I can confidently say it's dead. It's dead because the six-figure sums pouring into its accounts obscure the obvious problems. These are problems that have existed in the game all this time, problems that could have been solved, problems that were being solved, but something went wrong, perhaps in 2018 or when wheeled vehicles were added (I have no complaints about them; they're well-balanced, and you need to know how to play them). It's not that World of Tanks was ever incredibly diverse, balanced, or fair to the player—there were attempts to fix the situation (now I think the developers didn't fix anything back then; the scale of the accumulated problems simply wasn't that great).
And what about the problems?
I've spoken to a lot of people who have been playing this game for quite a while (10 years or more). 
1. Lack of playability for some vehicle classes on some maps.

1.1 Well, I think you understand, playing a heavy tank in open space when there are three SPGs in the battle feels abnormal, especially when you're trying to show initiative and do something.

1.2 Or the opposite situation – light tanks on urban maps. I don't know how this is supposed to work in theory. The game assumes that light tanks are used as medium tanks, despite the fact that light tanks usually have the weakest firepower. And the question is, what should a tank do on such a map, whose main task is to spot the enemy? If my firepower is only enough to fire into the enemy's rear.

1.3 I won't write much about this situation with SPGs, because anyone who decides to go down this slippery slope is bound to suffer.

2. The huge amount of vegetation on the maps and firing positions.

2.1 The developers, realizing that battles in the game end in 4-5 minutes with a score of 15-0 or 0-15, instead of increasing the health of all tanks by the same percentage or decreasing damage per minute by the same percentage, decided to simply provide numerous firing positions for less active players. Of course, this will force everyone to hide in the bushes; there's no other way. Now it turns out that even the slightest ingenuity is severely punished by health loss and your ass. Adding such firing positions to team spawn points was a big step. Have you ever had a Tier 10 heavy tank just standing in the base, firing from the bushes instead of doing what it's supposed to? And a minute later, you discover there's nothing left of it because the enemy team just happened to have guys with at least some, but not zero, gray matter in their heads?

Yes, I'm specifically addressing you, the IS-7 player on Murovanka, who decided to hide in the bushes when he could have been more useful than a damage-absorbing sponge.

3. Community.

3.1 The previous point flows smoothly into this one. You see, perhaps we would have a different game, also not perfect, but still different. But it turns out that the main target audience of this project turns a blind eye to all the problems. I don't know why, but they're happy with everything. They're willing to sacrifice half their salary, and not just their own, to buy a tank. So that later, that tank gets nerfed, and then they'll buy another one. 

3.2 It often happens that your team faces guys like that IS-7 I mentioned above, and not just one or two, but usually five to nine. You seem to be doing everything right, effectively eliminating opponents and taking key positions on maps from which to engage and win, while several other players are doing the same. However, this game works differently than others. What do I mean by that?

4. Game Mechanics

4.1 In most online games I've played, you can win even if your allies is outnumbered or even if you're alone. In such cases, accuracy, understanding the gameplay, mechanics, and taking advantage of your weapons and character's strengths are key. In World of Tanks, it's different. It's still crucial to know the map and its features, vehicle characteristics, and understand the core gameplay mechanics (the 15-meter bush distance, the three-caliber rule, and the 50-meter range aren't even included in the basic tutorial, as far as I remember; I learned this from third-party content creators). But this is where shot spread comes into play; you can add +-25% to damage and penetration. That's it. Nothing more. I remember countless battles I could have won, and in some, even earned the Kolobanov Medal, BUT I was just unlucky. The shell missed its target, and it didn't penetrate. That's all.

Someone will inevitably say, "You're a bad player," and so on. Maybe you, my little tank enthusiast, are right, but do I need to prove anything to you, or vice versa? I guess i'm just tired of World of Tanks. But it was fun. I still remember those races on Chaffee and the game mode where everyone drove armored Rolls-Royces, T-18s in his best time and even tank soccer.
Well, this is the end and perhaps it's for the best. peace to all.

At first, V Rising promises a lot by rekindling a nostalgic itch for old-school MMORPGs, but over time its major flaws become impossible to ignore. Progression is strictly gated behind boss fights, and figuring out how to obtain the materials needed for better gear just to survive those fights often becomes a tedious chore.

The core mechanics fall flat in several key areas:

The game advertises a class-free system, but in reality, it is completely build-free. It is virtually impossible to create a meaningful or specialized setup. Weapon differences are minimal, and the passive bonuses provided by blood types are laughable and utterly unimpactful.

Combat suffers from a severe lack of options. Having a basic dodge locked behind a long cooldown does not feel tactical; it just makes your character feel sluggish and disabled. Fighting boils down to basic kiting mechanics. To make matters worse, almost all bosses look aesthetically similar and share visually repetitive abilities.

The world design fails to reward the player. The map is far too vast compared to your movement speed, making traversal feel slow and boring because environments all look identical.

Castle building is fun and straightforward at first, but it quickly gets bloated by a wave of redundant crafting stations. Simply adding higher-tier versions of the exact same benches is an artificial solution that clutter your base and adds unnecessary confusion.

What hurts most is that progress feels punishing rather than rewarding. Defeating a boss often unlocks items or crafting benches that are completely useless until you defeat a completely different boss in a higher tier, a bizarre design choice that turns every milestone into a dead end instead of a payoff.

It pains me to leave a negative review because the game truly hits a sweet spot for nostalgia early on. But ultimately, it degrades into a repetitive grind and a rigid checklist of boss encounters. With zero character customization, overly simplified combat, and flawed progression, V Rising falls short. 

It is a massive shame, because with a few key tweaks, this could have been an absolute masterpiece.
