Overall after 350 hours I can definitely recommend it, althought there are a few aspects where I believe Factorio didn't reach it's full potential or developers couldn't find enough time to add more depth.

Generally - it's a spreadsheet game like EVE Online and similar to it. The main appeal of the game (at least for me) is not the fight with biters, not planet exploration, but optimization. How well can you structure the base. How well can you solve ratio problems, belt configurations, train system (honestly, figuring out how train signals work in this game without any guides or tips feels like discovering who Zodiac killer is on your own), mini-extraction colonies defense, etc. It's basically a giant puzzle-optimization game.
After you finish the main game and would like more - play Space Exploration. You won't regret it.

The good: 
- Game is massive. As in there is a lot to do and find what exactly to your taste (deathworld or peaceful settings, or no biters at all; being a spaghetti belter or ADHD-optimization fiend;) and it is further pushed by some achievements (finish game under X hours, building no more than X items by hand, not using drones, etc.).
It took me around 55-60 hours to finish the game for the first time. And it wasn't a chore, it was a race with myself and it felt really incredible to see that rocket go off to space for the first time.
- The whole automation and verticle-horizontal scaling just tickles that specific engineer itch in my brain, same way my work does. There is no hand-holding how to do things. There is also no "correct" way to do things. Pretty much any approach has it's right and scenario to exist. Just watching how other people solve same issues, how they structure their bases, what they focus on, etc. - is incredibly interesting on it's own.
- Mods. My god, this community is one of the most amazing ones in terms of mods. Almost anything that you can think of - you can find in mods. Things that trick you, make progression easier or harder, bring QoL changes or completely restructure the early and late progression, as well as providing absolutely mindblowing late-game on par or even above the official DLC (Space Exploration, I'm looking at you). Mods alone can double or triple your time spent in Factorio.

The neutral:
- Developers announced that there will be no more major updates after 2.1, because they want to move onto other projects. It's completely fair and the level of polish and depth that Factorio has rarely achieved by other games, even (or especially) AAA/AAAA ones.

The bad:
- Some resources feel heavily underutilized. Mostly that issue is regarding stone and water. It feels like developers had plans in future for those things, but never got to it. Stone is utilized as primary requirement in 2 recipies in the whole game (might be additional recipe in DLC that I am blanking on). Maybe that's just me, but in every single playthrough I had only single offshore pump (that provides 1200m/s) and that was enough to launch all things needed to space.
- There is almost no utilization to brick/concrete except 2 recipies and purely aesthetics. Having buildings suffer productivity penalties or have less stability/hp if built on exposed ground would've given it at least some usage. As well as nicking the idea from Space Exploration that it absorbs pollution (which in turn made me cover the base in stone/brick/concrete almost completely).
- Cliff destruction is locked behind DLC planet (if you own DLC, if you own only basegame - it's available in basegame tech-tree). Like... WHY? I guess thanks that we have elevated rails, but it's still weird.
- Early game (burner-based stuff) goes by way too quickly. You move on to steam energy quite fast that it doesn't make sense to invest into burner stuff. Which once again feels like an underutilized part of the game and once again was saved by Space Exploration.
- The difficulty jump that goes from sustaining your Nauvis (starting) base to maintaining space platforms and bases on other planets in DLC - I honestly wasn't prepared for that. It took me maybe 8 or 9 iterations of attempting to permanently shifting focus to other planet only later to find out that some stuff is broken on platform or Nauvis and I had to revert to my savefile before leaving the planet. Your first base and space platforms must be fully selfsufficient well oiled machines that do not need your intervention at all. Then you can focus on new planets.

And that's it. That's the biggest downsides I could find for Factorio, to be honest. Very specific things that definitely don't ruin your experience for at least 100 hours, which is an incredible feat.

Congrats and thank you to Wube team for creating truly an amazing experience and propelling the genre to wider audiences where we now get more and more automation games with each month that take inspiration from Factorio.

And remember - THE FACTORY. MUST. GROW.

Noita is hands down an incredible game. That said, it's not a game for everybody... and I came very close to leaving it a bad review in my first twenty hours or so of playing. I'll do my best to review the game fairly so you can see whether the game is for you:
Above all, Noita is a game about creativity and leveraging knowledge to succeed. You can't expect to win a run on the first attempt, nor the second, nor the third (yes, it has been done, but that's beside the point). As effectively none of the game's systems are spelled out to you - short of the controls - the only way to learn is through experimentation.
That gives rise to one of the biggest points of contention for the game. If you don't know that the spell to cast an explosion will hurt you, the way you'll learn is invariably that you'll get hit by yourself casting it. Given the small starting health pool and admirable output on some spells, it often will result in death and a new run. The speed at which a good run can be taken away from you after hours of labour can feel brutal. If you learn to enjoy the absurd ways in which you end up dying, and be willing to accept the inevitable deaths, Noita can in these early stages feel very fun.
Once you get you first victory, it will feel earnt over the ridiculous odds the game seems to throw at you. But more than that, when you play more you'll realise just how easy winning can become when you learn the ways to exploit every opportunity.
Difficulty and progression aside, I can only call Noita an incredible game because of its phenomenal depth. Being able to drag and drop spells of all sorts (projectiles and modifiers, through to logic gates (which I've honestly never used)) allows you to feel as if you are genuinely creating your own magic, rather than the mage classes in many other games which prescribe you very specific options, even if varied. Wands act as vessels, constraining your choice of spells so you have to be situationally opportunistic, whilst holding onto resources to build with better wands later in a run. Editing is restricted, meaning that you have to be decisive about what choices you make between segments of a game, and choosing between your well-crafted wands and those in the wild which may boast better spells/stats, but sacrifices something important you're holding.
I could go on about wandcrafting, but it is (in my opinion at least) one of the best systems in a game, for both being creative and allowing the user to be just as creative. And Noita offers many more complex systems, from alchemy to a world where every pixel is simulated.
It's also pretty funny when a creature with the world's longest Finnish name appears in your death messages.

**SPOILERS**
More on this - a brief but very significant set of spoilers:
[spoiler]This is a game where you can legitimately own an infinite health pool, and yet without the proper protection you could lose a run in a matter of seconds. It's a game where you need exponents to represent some enemy health, where you can at the end of a massive run struggle to find ways to find the firepower to die when the rest of the world has failed.[/spoiler]

There's so much more I could offer with draws to the game, but the main point is that it's easy to become annoyed if you're expecting to win. The fun of Noita - for me - is learning, and being able to exploit the knowledge you gain to get yet more knowledge, and slowly bend the world to your will.
I'll just finish by quoting the game - "The sacrifice of oneself to the pursuit of knowledge is the highest tribute to the gods."
P.S. love to From Grotto for composing the soundtrack

I feel by reading other reviews, you know how this game plays. You know the mechanics they applaud, and You know what you could be getting into.
However, none of that says anything about what playing this game feels like.

In Noita, you are simultaneously invincible and paper delicate, and Noita never lets you forget how delicate you are. 

You've all seen it, you've all imagined it. A wizard harnessing the power of nature, through study and breadth, the ideal archwizard becomes that of a demigod. Someone who looks so deeply into natures wrath that they end up embodying its wrath. 
It's a romantic image, a pleasing one, one could even call the wizard lucky for existing in the way they do. The path of a wizard, from this perspective, seems the most appealing thing in the world.
They do not tell you about the bodies, they do not tell you about the hubris. 
Noita is an accurate simulation of being a fool. A very, very powerful fool, maybe even a knowledgeable one, but a fool nonetheless.
You hold wands in your hand, a hubristic stand against the forces of nature itself. You think that you can control nature, that using the right combination of spells, you can harness the same wrath the world gives, and give it back tenfold, hundredfold, a thousandfold. 
but the forces of the universe, what a horrible thing to behold! If you wish to grasp it's most devoted strength, then you must be willing to die to get it, and you will die.
You will die, over, and over, and over.  No matter how competent you are, no matter how strong you think you've gotten with both your knowledge and your careful usage of what the world gave you.
 Noita will teach you to be scared. 
You are the apex predator of a deep, deep ocean, but the ocean is not scared of you. It knows that you can bleed, it knows that you are simply a more fortunate corpse waiting to be brought down by the horrors of the deep.
In this game, you hold and shoot hellfire of your own design, but never forget, you are far from fireproof.
and if you're not always vigilant, if your instincts fail you, if you forget your power holds just the same amount of threat to yourself than the enemies you point it at. You will die. 

The profession of a wizard is lined with corpses all the way down, and this game does not fret at turning you into one at the slightest whim.
You respawn, and as a holy fool, you feel that you will succeed this time.
This time you wont die, this time, you will best nature, misfortune, and your own hubris all at once.
You have no proof, no skills nor vested knowledge that put you above the corpses that came before you, but you know you won't die, because that's just the way it is.
There need not be any further justification.

The best automation/industrial game bar none. It is extremely optimized and runs on my mid-spec (low-end GPU) laptop. I recommend doing the first playthrough without the dlc nor guides, and a second run with the dlc. Amazing mod support and integration, without requiring external programs.
Additionally, I recommend 2 websites that help with [url=factoriocheatsheet.com/#space-age] basic ratios and designs [/url] and [url=factoriolab.github.io] a calculator for dedicated designs. [/url]

I don't need to praise Factorio's excellent game design decisions or how satisfying growing the factory is. Wube knew what they wanted to create and made pretty much only good decisions when developing it further. What isn't praised enough is the excellent optimisation and the best controller control scheme I've ever seen in a game like this, making playing it on the Steam Deck a pleasure, both on the go and on the TV from the couch whenever I prefer that over sitting at my desk.

So, you've seen the overwhelmingly positive reviews, and you're still on the fence. Maybe it's the art style, or maybe you aren't sure this is the kind of game you're looking for.

I'm here to tell you to take a leap of faith. 

This is the kind of game that takes a minute to click, but once it does, you can't put it down. The other reviews and jokes about how addicting this game is are not exaggerated. It takes problem solving, an inherently dopamine-inducing task, and gamifies it, turning it into short repeatable loops almost. If you're a programmer, it takes what you love about programming and makes it into a game. If you aren't a programmer, this game will make you wonder why you aren't one (AI crisis not withstanding).

The art will grow on you if it hasn't already. The soundtrack is impeccable. The quality of life this game provides is the gold standard, I've never seen another game do better QoL than this one. The modding is done with ease through the Steam Workshop, integrated directly into the game, and is one of the best modding scenes I've seen (amongst Minecraft and Project Zomboid). The DLC, while priced the same as the game, actually feels like an extension of the game, and offers tons of hours of content. 

All in all, buy it. You will not regret it. The only regret I can confidently say I have about this game is that I wish I had more time to play it.

An exraordinarily intricate powder sandbox with a healthbar and perk system hapazardly slapped on to the side that frustratingly claims to focus on experimentation yet refuses to give you even a scrap of actionable information to actually experiment with in game. The only possible way that "death is a learning experience" here is if you immidiately google the name of whatever killed you (provided it even was an enemy, otherwise you may as well chalk it up to spontaneus cardiac arrest..) to find out what absurdly niche mechanic or ridiculous damage resistance this 1 innocuous creature you've never interacted with across 50 hours and 300 runs used to break the """game""" in its favour (Seriously though why the actual fuck are frogs of all things able to hit you for every frame???).

For a real rougelike this wouldnt be an issue but Noita insists that game knowledge and spell unlocks be the only measure of progression between your utterly ardous, multi hour runs, a perfectly fine concept that is completely and totally butchered by the fact that you will not learn or unlock a single goddamn thing from 99.9% of your actual runs and deaths. The general mechanics and unlock requirements are so utterly obtuse and inexplicable that any actually usefull information about them is EXCLUSIVELY found in irl wiki pages and community content creators, which imo is a bit of a turnoff for people who play play videgames for the whole "videogame" part...

The real kick in the nads is that every genuinely good aspect of Noita feels completely at odds with itself, its like two different games that have been conjoined at the hip and are each trying to tear themselves apart from the other and killing themselves in the process.

If it werent trying so hard to be a grueling gamey game for gamers you'd have a perfect powder puzzle sandbox with actual freedom to experiment and genuinely interesting secrets to work through, this is borderline impossible though because you've gotta metagame the absolute shit out of the game for hours on end in order to get powerfull enough to even think about approaching any of the games puzzles and secrets without getting instantly obliterated by every enemy the second you step off of the critical path.

And if it werent trying to be a chaotic physics sandbox you'd have an almost fair rougelike that encourages creative spell combonations and environmental kills with a "final" boss that actually feels slightly rewarding to beat, as it is the game is so unabashedly reliant on RNG and cheesy game breaking bullshit that (even without looking anything up) finally winning a run still feels absolutely joyless and unearned even after hundreds of failed attempts.

TLDR. Noita is an outragously fun particle sandbox that i utterly adore trapped inside of an abysmally dogshit videogame that i utterly fucking loathe.

HOW?

Hunt: Showdown is one of those rare games that pulls you deeper the more you play, until you realize you can’t quite let it go.

At first, it can feel slow, brutal, and pretty unforgiving. But once you get past that, you start to realize there’s a lot more to Hunt than just shooting people. Every step, every sound, and every decision matters. The game makes you slow down, pay attention, and actually think about what you’re doing. That’s when Hunt really starts to click.

The sound design is easily one of my favorite things about the game. A distant gunshot, a branch snapping, footsteps, or a flock of crows suddenly taking off can tell you that someone is nearby without you ever seeing them. You’re constantly listening for clues and trying to figure out what’s happening around you. That feeling of never being completely safe is a huge part of what makes Hunt so addictive.

The gunfights feel incredibly satisfying because every shot matters. You can’t just run around spraying bullets and expect to win. Positioning, timing, patience, and knowing when to push or back off can completely change the outcome of a fight. Even when you think you’re screwed, there’s usually still a chance to turn things around.

What I love most is how unpredictable every match is. You can load into a game expecting a quiet run, and a few minutes later you’re in the middle of a massive fight with multiple teams. Things can go from completely calm to absolute chaos in seconds. You never really know how a match is going to play out, and those unexpected moments are what make Hunt so memorable.

Of course, the game can be frustrating as hell sometimes. You’ll get killed in the dumbest way imaginable and just sit there thinking, “What the hell just happened?” One bad decision, one missed shot, or one moment of overconfidence can cost you everything.

And then, five minutes later, you’re already queuing for another match.
That’s Hunt.

It’s not just another shooter. It’s a game that rewards you for paying attention, thinking ahead, and learning from your mistakes. You start recognizing sounds, reading situations better, and making decisions you wouldn’t have thought about when you first started playing. Even losing can turn into a story you end up laughing about later.
If you’re looking for a fast, casual shooter where you can turn your brain off and just run around shooting things, Hunt probably isn’t for you.
But if you want something tense, unpredictable, rewarding, and genuinely different from most shooters out there, Hunt: Showdown is absolutely worth trying.
It’s one of those games I can keep coming back to, no matter how many times it kicks my ass.

I want to like this game. I want so very, very badly to like this game. But I can't. This is easily the most complex ARPG I've ever played, and I've played a lot, and as a consequence of that and certain design decisions, this game is outrageously hostile to casual blind playthroughs. To clarify what I mean by this, I mean playthroughs where you pick up the game knowing little to nothing about it and do a quick playthrough of the campaign and maybe a little endgame. That's usually what I want out of ARPGs, as I usually find endgame content in ARPGs to be mind-numbingly boring and I'm not super fond of replaying ARPGs to try different classes. So I'm not here to judge POE's endgame, not that I've reached it anyway.

What I am here to judge is the campaign playthrough. The actual campaign, from what I've played, is honestly pretty solid. The issue is the mechanical density of actually playing the game. Everyone knows about the skill tree. The thing is ridiculous, far too large to truly be able to parse and craft a decent build out of without many, many hours of playtime fiddling with it. I would be okay with this, except respeccing without already having a good build to farm currency is sufficiently expensive to be basically impossible. Compare this with, say, Grim Dawn, where unless you're undoing every single skill point, it's viable to respec. Or, Diablo 3 and 4, where respeccing your skills is completely free and can be done at any time outside of combat. This gives a high level of flexibility to try out builds, and if they don't work, you can change them immediately. That just isn't really possible in POE.

Add on to that the relatively high level of difficulty, especially if you don't know about the need to stack resistances, and you can very easily build yourself into a corner where your only viable option to fix things is to start a new character. I hate starting new characters. There's no reason why the game has to make respeccing expensive, or even limited at all. Just let me fix my build without having to play the entire game again.

And this is just the passive skill tree. There are so many mechanics that you straight up are not going to be able to deal with if you don't spend half of your playtime in the wiki. League mechanics that have been added to the main game, item crafting (good luck figuring that out blind), etc etc etc. What it comes down to, again, is that POE is only suited for folks who are willing to play only with build guides or those who are willing to sink dozens upon dozens of hours replaying characters, even if you try to do research to plan out your build beforehand. And frankly, that's just a miserable experience from my perspective. If that sounds like fun to you, then yes, absolutely play POE. If not, avoid it like the plague.

ETA: Okay, so after I posted this, I found out about the change to sockets (gems no longer needing to match socket colors) that had been made, and decided to give the game one more try, with the thought that if GGG is willing to make a big change to make the early game easier, I can at least give them one more chance. What I ended up doing is taking an established build as a baseline, but tweaking it to match my preferred playstyle more.

Over 40-45 hours, I completed the campaign and poked at the atlas a bit. My original review is still valid, the only reason I was able to get through the campaign without exactly following a build guide is because I had about 20 horus of previous experience on failed runs, plus I've watched a ton of playthroughs of the game, and even then, I still had to use a build guide as a base. This game is still completely unapproachable to a casual player who wants to just do a blind playthrough of the campaign. You simply will not succeed.

However, I can at least say now that the campaign is pretty fun. I do think POE is a good game, it just doesn't provide the experience I actually want from a Diablo-style action RPG. That's okay, but I'm still leaving my review as a thumbs down, primarily as a warning for anyone else who also wants the sort of experience I want. I enjoyed my time with the game, but it was largely in spite of the experience it offers, not because of it. Still, I do plan on trying out POE2 when it comes out of early access in December, so we'll see how that goes.

1. Some people get overwhelmed by the sheer amount of stuff in this game. Just take your time and enjoy the ride.
2. If a particular new phase (such as blue science) has you stumped, walk away and do some math and/or draw it out. Coming back with fresh eyes and a plan can make it less stressful.
3. Build out your blueprint and export/import it between games to build out your library of designs.
4. While you can use other people's blueprints (and they can be instructive), solving problems is one of the primary points of pleasure for the game. Use your noodle before you seek out a solution.
5. You can beat the game with incredibly inefficient factories, so don't sweat whether your setup is the most optimal. Address what you need to and bring your learnings to the next factory!

If you're tired of MMOs where last year's content becomes a ghost town the moment a new expansion drops, GW2 is the antidote. This is a game that respects your time in a way almost nothing else in the genre does. There's no vertical gear treadmill forcing you to abandon everything you've built, just a massive, growing library of content you can tackle at your own pace, as grindy or as chill as you want it to be. You'll never be locked out of succeeding anywhere in the game due to gear.

The open world is where GW2 truly separates itself for me. Every single zone stays alive and relevant thanks to meta events and world bosses. There's no old content here, just content. Log in years after a zone released and you'll still find full squads zerging a world boss or coordinating a meta chain. No other MMO keeps its world breathing like this.

And then there's the combat. It looks simple on the surface, but master a hard encounter and you'll realize how deep it actually is. Every class has multiple elite specializations that completely reshape how it plays. Same profession, entirely different playstyle. Trying them all is half the fun, and every one of them is genuinely viable. 

Years in, still going strong, still worth your time. 10/10.

I tried several MMOs before giving this one a shot because the idea of an MMORPG has always fascinated me. I played the WoW free trial for a bit, TERA (arguably not the greatest MMO), Albion Online, and a few others. None of them managed to hook me for more than about 10 hours. They always felt somewhat daunting, and I could never really get invested, even after giving them multiple attempts. I think one of the biggest reasons is that most of those games never truly felt like MMOs to me. Sure, I could see other players running alongside me, but it often still felt quite lonely. Everyone was focused on their own tasks, and there seemed to be very little actual cooperation. Guild Wars 2 managed not only to hook me, but to genuinely fascinate me as a game. The world of Tyria is beautiful, and although it might not be everyone's cup of tea, the horizontal progression allows me to slow down and actually appreciate the world, the characters, and all the little details that went into making Tyria feel like its own living place.

The most impressive part for me so far has been the world bosses. Most of the time, I struggle to understand what exactly is happening on my screen because of the absurd number of visual effects going off all at once. Nevertheless, it looks absolutely epic. More importantly, it makes the game feel alive. You see huge groups of players gathering together for a common goal, which sometimes leads to funny and unexpected interactions along the way. The mounts also feel amazing in this game. Admittedly, I've only gotten to try the Raptor so far, but I can already say that the way it moves and handles feels like a breath of fresh air compared to mounts in other similar games. When it comes to actually feeling like an MMO, Guild Wars 2 absolutely nails it. The world genuinely feels alive, and I haven't even gotten into Fractals or WvW yet. Overall, this is definitely a game worth trying, and I genuinely feel that it's unfairly overshadowed by bigger titles like WoW and FFXIV. I'm looking forward to spending, hopefully, many more hours in this wonderful game!

THE TRAGICALL COMEDIE OF THE DWARVES OF HOXXES
Or, Rocke and Stone, a Cautionarie Tale in Five Actes

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

SCOUT, a nimble youth with grappling hook, who dieth alone in darkness, oft.
GUNNER, a stout fellow of shield and zipline, whose beard hath seen much.
ENGINEER, a builder of platforms and turrets, exceeding smug.
DRILLER, who solveth all riddles with fire and a hole.
MOLLY, a mule of metal, patient beyond all mortal reason.
MANAGEMENT, unseen, ungrateful, undying.
ONE KNAVE, who hath the cheats, and shame hath none.

PROLOGUE

Enter CHORUS, holding a pickaxe and a pint.

Two hundred hours, both alike in dignity,
In fair Hoxxes, where we lay our scene,
From ancient grudge 'gainst arachnid enmity,
Doth dwarven blood make civil hands unclean.
Beneath the crust, where light hath never crept,
Four little men with beards go forth to mine —
And there, good sir, is where mine own life slept,
For I sat down at eight, and rose at nine.
Not nine at night, I pray thee mark me well.
Nine in the morn. The sun did mock my face.
So hear my tale of heaven wrapp'd in hell,
Of joy, of dread, of one most cursèd case.
　Give ear, and I shall speak both praise and blame:
　The game is great. The game hath ate my frame.

ACT I — WHEREIN THE MINE IS DESCRIB'D

Behold a rock! A planet made of spite,
Where every stone doth harbour something ill.
Descend, ye lads, in pods of dreadful height,
And dig — for MANAGEMENT demandeth still.

But mark the wonder: here the earth is soft.
No corridor is writ by author's hand.
Art thou beneath? Then dig thyself aloft.
Art thou above? Then sink into the sand.
Art thou beset, encircled, sore afraid?
Then dig a hole and hide within it, friend —
A coward's grave, yet one thine own hands made,
Which is, methinks, a noble sort of end.

Then falleth dark. The lights are snuff'd. And lo —
A thousand chittering things do rise below.

ACT II — THE PRAISE, LOUDLY SUNG

O rare! O excellent! O free of charge!
Six seasons hath the company bestow'd
And ask'd no coin, nor battle-pass, nor barge
Of shining tat upon the buyer load'd.

(CHORUS aside:) In this our age of purses picked at dawn,
Where every joy is rented, never own'd —
Here standeth one who gave, and then gave on,
And for such virtue should be justly thron'd.

And more! The fellowship! Ye gentle folk
Who greet the novice not with jeer nor curse,
But dig him out and share the healing yoke
And cry "ROCK AND STONE!" till lungs be worse.

There is no game where strangers are so kind.
'Tis PvE — there is no foe to find
Save bugs. And so we love. And so we drink
At yon Space Rig, and dance, and fail to think.

ACT III — THE FAULTS, SPOKEN PLAIN

Yet stay. No jewel is without its flaw.

FIRST, at two hundred hours, thou shalt see
The selfsame missions wearing selfsame straw;
The cave is new, the shape of it is not.

SECOND, the grind! O tyrant Overclock!
Thou random cruelty in a shining box —
I open twenty. Twenty times I mock
Mine own poor fortune. Fie upon thy locks!

THIRD, that the Scout in skilful hands doth fly,
But in the fool's, doth simply hang and die.

FOURTH — and here I speak with feeling — should
The Host's connexion falter, break, or bend,
The mission dieth where the mission stood,
And thirty minutes perish at the end.
(This wound doth smart the sharper in Baghdad,
Where routers keep their humours, and go mad.)

ACT IV — THE SICKNESS OF THE SOUL

Now hear the graver charge. This game doth eat.

Not gold, nor coin — it asketh none of those.
It eateth thee. Thy Tuesday. Thy retreat.
Thy sleep, thy dawn, thy dignified repose.

For see how cunning is the trap it lays:
The mission runneth twenty minutes' span,
And at its end — reward! — the number sways
Upward, and lo, another doth began.
There is no wall. There is no natural close.
There is no chapter's end whereat to bow.
Only that whispering serpent, well-compos'd:

　　"One more. But one. And thou shalt sleep. But now —
　　observe: the Deep Dive endeth in a day,
　　and thy good friends are waiting. Wouldst thou stray?"

And so at three o'clock the mine doth glow
Upon a face that hath forgotten day.

Remedy: Count missions, not the hours.
"Three runs and out" hath edges. "Two more hours"
Is water in the palm — it hath no shore,
And thou wilt find thyself at four. Then more.

ACT V — WHEREIN THE KNAVE IS UNMASK'D

But softest now. Here lieth my chief complaint,
And 'tis a wound the makers will not tend.

I enter'd honest. I had no mod nor paint,
No trickery, no toggle, no pretend.
And yet — thrice over! — did I find me set
Beside a knave whose numbers were untrue:
Whose foes did perish ere the swarm was met,
Whose ore did multiply from empty blue.

How cometh this? Attend, and I shall teach:

Item, this game hath no Anti-Cheat at all.
No EAC, no BattlEye stand in the breach.
"'Tis PvE," saith they, "who takes the fall?"
— I do, good sirs. I take it. It is I
Whose evening curdles, and whose runs are lies.

Item, the flag that marketh "MODDED" true
Dependeth on the mod's own honesty.
The gentle mod declareth what 'twill do;
The cheat injecteth, and declareth ye nothing.
And so the filter catcheth honest men
Who wish'd their helmet green, and lets pass then
The very villain that it sought to bar.
O bitter irony! O crooked star!

Item, the Host is God within that stone.
The client asketh not; it merely nods.
Whate'er he claimeth, is. Thou hast no throne,
No proof, no plea, no court, no better odds.

Remedy, such as it is:
　Set "Prevent modded lobbies" — 'twill help some.
　But better: HOST THINE OWN. Be thou the sun.
　Or gather friends in Discord's warmer hall.
　And if thou seest ore from nothing come —
　Depart at once. Take not that tainted crumb,
　For cheated progress cleaveth to thy name
　And rotteth quietly the honest game.

EPILOGUE — THE RECKONING

Enter CHORUS, visibly unslept.

The Judgement of the World	The Verdict
Steam, the great mob	97% approving — "Overwhelmingly Positive"
Steam, this past month	94%
OpenCritic, the learnèd bench	85 — "Mighty." Top 5 in the hundred
The purse	some nine dollars, at 70% off

And thus I end. What manner beast is this?

A game that knoweth what it is, and does
That single thing with such unhurried bliss
That eight long years have not undone its buzz.

Its virtues: honest coin, and honest folk,
And earth that yieldeth to the eager stroke.

Its vices: two, and both from one strange root —
It trusteth. Trusteth thee to know thine hour;
It trusteth him who hosteth to be mute
And truthful. Sweet assumption. Costly flower.

NINE OF TEN, if thou hast friends to call.
SEVEN AND A HALF, if thou must trust the wild —
And all that difference groweth from one gall:
The knave, unbarr'd, who entereth undefil'd.

Now go. Thy pickaxe waits. Thy bed does too.
　　Rock and Stone, good sir. Rock and Stone. Adieu.

Exeunt, pursued by a Glyphid.

I'd love to recommend this game to my friends, but every other year it becomes a more expensive product, and I just... can't.

People will use arguments like, "The base game is perfectly fine, just play it and if you want more, get the DLCs later." This ignores the fact that game developers commonly leave out features that feel like they belong in the base game so they can sell them later. I'm not claiming that's what happened here, but it easily could be, and nobody would be the wiser for it.

Fact is, you could probably ignore Royalty and Anomaly, but Biotech and Ideology fit so naturally into Rimworld's futuristic colony setting they feel like they should have been present from the start. They could have been released as free updates. But no. They effectively raise the price of the game from $35 to $80.

It certainly doesn't help that Rimworld and its DLCs have never gone on sale for more than 20% off. What is this? Nintendo? "Our games are timeless and don't depreciate in value"? I understand a developer not wanting to play the sale game, but when you're refusing to meaningfully discount anything AND offering DLC that rival the base game's price, you have to realize what you're doing.

If you want to buy Rimworld, and all its DLCs, at base price, you will pay $150. In another year or two that'll probably be $175.

The question I have is: where will people choose to draw the line, and why?

The gameplay itself is enjoyable. Combat is fun, Fractals and raids are well designed, and the graphics are surprisingly well compared to some other MMOs. I genuinely enjoyed optimising my character and working towards ascended gear.

However, as a new player, the progression model eventually became too frustrating and limited.

I bought the core expansions (spent about $80 AUD for 3 expansions) expecting to have access to most of the game, only to discover that many of the guides, farming methods and progression systems point you toward content locked behind additional expansions or Living World episodes.

For example:

-Want some of the most useful mounts? Additional content required.
-Want access to some of the most efficient gold farms? Additional content required.
-Want certain maps, currencies and vendors recommended for ascended gear progression? Additional content required.
-Want many of the current endgame systems? Additional content required.

None of these things are obvious when you first start playing. You only discover them after investing dozens of hours into your character and looking up how to progress efficiently.

Can you play with only a few expansions? Absolutely.

Can you reach level 80 and enjoy the game? Yes.

But you'll repeatedly find yourself reading guides or receiving advice that ends with, "You need another expansion or Living World episode."

That eventually killed my motivation.

For veteran players who already own everything, this probably isn't an issue. For a new player, though, it feels like the complete experience is spread across more than a decade of paid content.

If you're happy buying the full collection, you'll likely have a great time ($150 AUD+).

If you're expecting that buying a few expansions gives you access to most of the game's progression, you may be disappointed, as I was.

All in all, Hunt is a great game for those looking for an EXTRAORDINARILY Hardcore Extraction Shooter experience. One wrong or panicked peek can end a run very quickly. It accomplishes the intense feeling of survival like no other shooter in the genre manages to create. However, with this, I have three minor gripes

The game feels more like a battle royale with extraction shooter mechanics than it does a full extraction shooter experience. Very rarely do you manage to extract as a new player and you will almost never be able to avoid players in a match. I don't think this is a bad thing, and it is definitely a skill issue on my part, but it feels weird having to rebuy a loadout every single time when I most likely won't have that hunter live long enough for it to make a difference. I could be doing this very wrong though and may just need some free hunter runs to fully understand how to live.

It feels like whoever gets the objective first is at a disadvantage. You now have the whole map rapidly converging on your location piling explosives, flaming beetles, and gas in whatever structure you decide to bunker down in. Fights are often decided before they even begin, and a 3rd party can ruin your run instantly due to the incredibly fast TTK and audio signals fights give off. Even if you're using silent weapons, people will hear the other party fighting back unless they are ALSO using silent weapons.

When I say this game has high TTK, I mean you can jiggle peek once and be back in the lobby. There are so many one-shot mechanics I don't live long enough to learn how to take fights differently. There is no safe way to peek, showing yourself for even a second can be a fatal mistake.

Despite all this though, I still found myself having a lot of fun at times with the game. If I could describe it with one sentence, it would be "There are rare EXTREMELY high highs, and common EXTREMELY low lows". This game makes you want to quit it, but for some reason, that draws me back into it. It accomplishes a very unique feeling in an admittedly at times frustrating, but fun way.
Peak if you like MMO games. Don't buy it if you're buying it for the Elder scrolls theme because you played skyrim, because you'll just leave a negative review.

After spending a lot of time in Sea of Thieves, I can confidently say it's one of the most memorable multiplayer games I've played. Every voyage feels different. You might set out to dig up treasure, only to end up in a naval battle, fighting a Kraken, or making an unexpected alliance with another crew.

The sailing mechanics are fantastic and reward teamwork. Whether you're adjusting sails, patching holes, or firing cannons, everyone has a role to play. The world is also gorgeous, with stunning oceans, dynamic weather, and islands that are genuinely fun to explore.

One thing to keep in mind is that the game can be unforgiving. You can lose hours of treasure to another crew if you're not careful, but that's also what makes every successful haul so satisfying. The progression is mostly cosmetic, so the focus stays on improving your skills rather than grinding for better gear.

This game is at its best with friends, but even solo players can have incredible adventures if they're willing to learn. If you enjoy open-world sandbox games where every session creates its own story, Sea of Thieves is absolutely worth playing.

This game is a testament to my willpower to conquer some of the worst pain I've ever endured. Gleba. Don't go there.

The Good:

-It looks quite nice and runs at a decent frame rate on modern hardware.
-The aesthetic is extremely nice.
-The sound is very detailed and clear, and a large part of the gameplay.
-There's a lot of variety to weapons and tools.
-The gameplay requires strategy, mechanical aim alone isn't sufficient.
-Rounds feel varied, there's so much randomness fights are always unique.
-No substantial pay2win.

The Bad:

-Running long distances becomes dreadfully boring.
-Made worse with PvE and sound trap fatigue.
-The game is buggy, bug fixes are slow, they fix one thing, and break others.
-Some bugs are literally multiple years old and go unfixed, they have become an inside joke.
-There is no QA. It's obvious new things simply aren't tested before released.
-The UI is truly atrocious. They force the same UI for console and PC. "Netflix" is not an appropriate UI for a game.
-Low technical competence in general. Things like "updates" which re-download all 90Gb of the game. Instead of the few Gb difference.

The Ugly: These things aren't merely bad, they're game breaking.

-Matchmaking. The MMR system they have only has 6 ranks. lol
-You're frequently matched against players 2-3 ranks higher than you.
-New players aren't protected from this, as a new player you can face prestige 100 players with 2000+ hours.
-Most new players leave, the game has a massive player retention issue.
-The game is riddled with performance issues.
-With my specs I play at 180fps but there's constant micro stutter and freezing. They can't fix this.
-There is no AFK protection, AFK team mates throw entire rounds.
-There is no ping protection, EU server is full Chinese players abusing high pings
-There is no region lock, so on EU servers we have obnoxious people screaming at us in Russian.
-Server quality is very low. 30 tick is embarrassing in 2026, and there's constant spikes in packet loss and lag.
-Most good players agree that things like weapon balance through the cost to buy them is bad, yet Crytek ignore this and keep doing it.

Conclusion:

Overall the game (the look, the feel, the combat) is very good. You can have fun rounds, but they are rare. Because balanced and fair rounds are rare. This is made worse by an aged an established community who have become insanely good at the game (1000's of hours of play is common) and through bad matchmaking can punch down, That problem is amplified because new players rightfully don't like this and leave, which drains the matchmaking pool of players at the low end, reinforcing the problem.

The promise from the community is "git gud" and spend 100+ hours to learn the game and after all that you can have fun games. But this is not the case, at 300 hours I can say for certain that it doesn't get better. At its core, Noita is nothing but RNG garbage. Luck becomes such a fundamental factor in every stage and mechanic of the game that the gameplay loop ends up feeling like pulling the crank on a slot machine. Despite its promises of infinite replayability and choice, attempting to minimize the frustrating luck factor will make the game boring and repetitive.

I enjoyed the exploration, the experimenting, and even the deaths and restarts, but I am fucking tired of everything now. Once you learn most of what there is to the game, it just feels empty. 
Sure, the process of learning itself was fun, but once you exhaust it the game's replayability feels extremely shallow. Even with mods. It is just deceptively masked as deep and complex.



At first, you will be learning how to identify every enemy behaviour, synergies and every little interaction that can get you killed instantly. This will take deaths upon deaths, but it will be fun because it does feel as if you were an alchemist learning the rules of this world. 
However, the game becomes stale after you learn 90% of everything there is to learn. Not to mention memorizing every random heart spawn location and praying they spawn. It stops being "LOL now I learned X situation kills you, that was fun" and becomes "I will probably be dead soon, I could have survived if I had X perk/spell/wand"

You will spend most runs begging that your seed gets a decent perk lineup. Half of the perks are either so useless you'd rather teleport past the trigger and come back with more gold to reroll (more RNG), or so hyperspecific that by the time you are capable of building your wands around and utilize them, you will probably be dead. Assuming of course you get dropped the spells needed for it, of fucking course. 
You could have dozens of ideas based on your past knowledge. You could have hundreds of theories you want to try and test with this rare perk in a creative way. None of it will matter because if you don't get dropped those specific spells to make it work, you are fucked. You probably were anyways since you didn't pick the broken perks, or straight-up missed them due to bad luck.

You will also especially beg that the wands you find aren't complete dogshit either, alongside their spells. The spell system looks elaborate and deep at first, but at its core it is nothing but bloated junk. Most wand builds you can make won't deviate much from each other. There are around 10 types of wand builds you can make early game, until Kolmisilmä. Sure, you can vary some spells here and there, but the idea behind the build will still be the same. These builds will consist of the same fucking broken spells you will pray you get in the next wand spawn, before you inevitably fail to do so and get your ass handed in a steel platter by some off-screen bullshit, Hiisi Base, or any of the following biomes.
And of course, good luck if you tried being creative and making a specific build outside of these broken 10, because you will need that RNG in your favor much more. You could have found the perfect combination of spells, a new build you had in the back of your mind for the past twenty runs that suddenly became achievable. Yet nothing will matter because the wands are also RNG, if your wand and any wands you find are shit and do not allow for your build to happen, you will eat the ground the next biome. 

So, you are met with two options:
Trying to go for specific creative off-meta builds, which is the most RNG dependant garbage that will probably get you killed.
Or:
Picking up the most versatile and broken spells, perks and wands each run so that you can stop dying (still not guaranteed, just less RNG bullshit), thus making all of your runs feel the same boring and repetitive adventures.



Of course, the community is also very receptive about any criticism of their game. If you say anything bad you will be screamed at by monkeys yelling "skill issue" over and over again. This will completely destroy and invalidate any of your arguments. 
But I got to give it to them, it takes mental skill and fortitude to keep gambling on this piece of shit. Ask them about their win/death ratio and see for yourself the [strike]luck[/strike] skill needed. When they start sperging about how their first 1000 deaths do not count because they were still learning, and how "real pros and speedrunners can consistently beat it" while sweating and stuttering all over their words, you will understand.

The game throws you into an interesting world, it encourages you to investigate, explore and learn from it. Then, it invites you to experiment with new spells, wands and perks just to spit on your face and force you to go back to the same broken shit run after run. The only lesson you learn is to not deviate from the path. I guess it is learning, after all. I learned to stop playing this garbage.

Noita is a roguelite with a pixel based world about wand building, alchemy, and secrets. Every grain of sand, every drop of acid, can be interacted with or kill you. This is a game that will expect you to know things you could not possibly know without either having an expertise in cryptography, puzzle solving, and ARGs, or a wiki you can tab in and out of. If you go in blind it'll probably take you 80 - 100 runs just to beat the main boss, but there's so much more to this game.

Wand building is integral to your success, and it will kill you even hundreds of hours into your playthrough. Polymorph is another concern for instant death. It transforms you into a weaker creature, who does NOT have your extra life perks, inventory of healing spells, or health pool, for the terrifying seconds until it wears off. It's fair to warn you now, that if you give this game a chance you will be better off looking up the more hidden unlocks after you get comfortable playing, if you respect your own sanity and time.

That being said, when this game is good you get to feel godly. Wands that delete everything. Perks that make you feel untouchable. Actual message toasts of the gods fearing you. Feats that feel special compared to most games. But this all comes at a cost. It has to be gained through knowledge, experience, time, and probably an external guide.

If you haven't been scared off here's some advice from someone with a little experience. Get experimental, don't be afraid to die early on, don't be afraid to go off the beaten path and explore, learn some basic alchemy, value your health more than your wealth, and be patient.

I recommend playing with a few mods to help new players ease into the game's many mechanics.

1) Edit Wands Always - Normally, you can only tinker with your wands in holy mountains (checkpoints at the end of every zone) which crumble and become unusable once you leave them normally. This mod will allow you to tinker anywhere and let you get creative and discover new spells while still allowing the game to be challenging.

2) Items work in inventory - There are a few stones in the game, a fire stone and a lightning stone, which allow the wielder to be immune to each element, among other things. This mod will let them work without you needing to actively wield them, essentially making you immune to those elements at the trade-off of 1 inventory slot.

3) Spell Lab - This is the sandbox mode where you can experiment and create any wand you want. 

Play with these, get a few wins in, turn them off when you feel ready to take on the game how it's meant to be played.

This game has two major problems:
1. There is absolutely no way that any human being could reasonably play this game in a fulfilling way without using a wiki. Pair that with how strictly unfair the game can be and that makes for an experience that’s not very fun after the first hour.
2. People preach that the true "meta-progression" of this game is experience and wisdom but that is simply not true.
At the time of this review I have around 7 hours of experience. In most Roguelikes a person with that much time would be considered to have the fundamentals of the game understood. In Noita, however, a person with 100 hours is considered a "noob". For most players, it will take them over 150 hours to complete the tutorial. I have been saying this for as long as I’ve been playing games, but being hard for the sake of a challenge and being hard just to be hard are not the same thing, and hard for the sake of hard is not fun. Your time is better spent playing Rogue Legacy 2 or Magicka 2 if you want to play a fun roguelike or magic-casting game.
150 hours should not be a barrier to entry for any game.
This also has a third but less relevant problem: The "no hand-holding" philosophy also extends to the Steam page and marketing. Nowhere does it tell you truly how much time and grief you will have to sink into the game to even have a basic grasp of what you’re doing.
If you insist on playing it, however, I would recommend you do ten or fifteen runs and then looking at some mods that can potentially lighten your burden.

Elder Scrolls Online is a job using the mantle of The Elder Scrolls universe to pass itself as playable. There's no challenge in combat, progression is filled with incredibly repetitive and menial tasks, there's an absurd amount of backtracking and running around during questing and inventory management... It's just boring.

Every game mechanic feels like it was engineered to be as boring and repetitive as possible. And what are the rewards for your job done? scraps. Scraps of currencies, of materials, cosmetics,  drab dyes... the only slightly interesting group of rewards that you can find is in the convoluted 3-layered microtransaction shop with an included unfriendly lootbox system added on top.

But what if you don't care about cosmetics, and still want to play an RPG adventure game? You'll find the most meaningless exploration combat experience in the market. The combat is not shallow, surprisingly, there are some nuances that can be interesting, but if not even the bosses can deal 1% of damage to your health, none of it matters. you can never upgrade your health, use the first skill and still probably complete most, if not all, questlines in the game.

The only redeeming factor ESO has is its story, which not even sometimes is. Some stories are deep, meticulous and genuinely interesting, but the other half simply brings powerful or famous in-universe characters out of nowhere with piss-poor explanation, saying to the player about the 50th world ending event the player is destined to stop. Even then, there's poorly any motive of playing the good stories if the combat is meaningless and the rewards are shallow.

Maybe this isn't the game for me, as I tend to dislike MMOs and their gameplay, but the way Elder Scrolls Online treats the player feels like a genuine offense of my time and will. But hey, if you don't mind a game having zero gameplay, the most grinding-engineered progression systems and hunting for scraps, 1 currency at a day for a reward costing 1000 currencies, and solely focusing on upgrading your character's appearance, this might be the game for you. Otherwise, stay away from this mess.

I have over 20,000 hours in Path of Exile. I don't say that to appeal to authority, but to make it clear where I'm coming from. I've played through countless leagues, watched the game evolve, adapted to almost every major system overhaul, and defended GGG through plenty of controversial changes over the years because I believed they were ultimately making the game better.

This is the first time I genuinely feel like Path of Exile has lost sight of what made it special.

I'm not going to speculate about conspiracy theories like the PoE 1 developers intentionally trying to push players toward PoE 2. I have no evidence of that, and I don't think it's a productive discussion.

What I do think is undeniable is that ground loot has been getting worse and worse with all the nerfs and system changes, and Allflame is easily the worst it's been.

The frustrating part is that GGG knows players aren't happy with it.

During the Mirage League Q&A, the developers acknowledged the overwhelming feedback regarding poor ground loot. They specifically said they were increasing loot for Mirage and that they intended to do even more in the following league.

Naturally, many players—including myself—expected Allflame to be the league where those promises would finally materialize.

Instead, the opposite happened.

The primary ground-loot strategy was again nerfed, and nothing meaningful replaced it.

That leaves only a few possibilities:

1. GGG doesn't want Path of Exile to be centered around ground loot.
2. They believe the current state of ground loot is acceptable.
3. They somehow forgot what they had publicly discussed.

The third option seems extremely unlikely, which means we're left with the first two.

And both of those create a much bigger problem than simply "less loot."

---

Right now there are essentially four ways to acquire valuable items:

* Kill monsters and rely on ground drops.
* Do mechanics with predetermined rewards, such as Ritual windows or similar systems.
* Kill bosses for their specific drop tables.
* Gamble through mechanics like Stacked Decks and other RNG-heavy systems.

On paper, that sounds like healthy variety.

In practice, it creates a serious progression problem because only one of those reward types naturally scales with character power: killing increasingly difficult monsters.

Here's where everything falls apart.

The primary way players increase map difficulty is through map modifiers, but those modifiers mostly just scale ground loot quantity and rarity.

This creates a major problem: if ground loot itself isn’t valuable enough, then making maps harder stops being meaningful. You’re simply taking on more dangerous content for rewards that don’t scale in a satisfying way.

That breaks one of the core ARPG loops Path of Exile is built on.

In a healthy system, difficulty and reward should scale together: you improve your character, you take on harder content, and that harder content gives meaningfully better rewards. That loop is what makes progression feel rewarding.

But when the best currency comes from running easier maps quickly rather than engaging with harder, more dangerous content, that loop collapses. At that point, there’s little incentive to push your build further once you can comfortably clear basic endgame maps.

Instead of asking “how strong can I become?”, players are pushed toward “what’s the fastest, easiest content I can spam for profit?”

That shift fundamentally undermines the ARPG experience, where investing into a stronger character should always translate into being able to tackle harder content for better rewards.

---

So here we are 20k hours later, and I'm finally seeing the game I love so much be taken out back for some unknown reason. They were fully bought by Tencent in 2024, so maybe that has something to do with it?

During the Allflame Q&A, Mark emphasized that if player numbers aren't growing, then there's only one direction they can go. This was concerning to me because it felt like the devs' focus was centered around player metrics and business growth rather than what dedicated players found fun and what kept them playing.

It's almost as if they are saying that, at this point, players with 10k+ hours who play 6+ hours a day are becoming less of a priority because they're likely to move on anyway, so the focus shifts toward making the game more accessible for new players.

Historically, GGG built its reputation by making a game for passionate ARPG fans, trusting that if the game was exceptional, the players would come.

Lately, that philosophy feels less visible.

Whether that's actually changed internally or not, it's certainly the impression many veteran players are walking away with.

For the first time since I started playing, I struggle to recommend it to friends.

As much as it pains me to say it, if someone asked me today which game to start, I'd probably recommend Path of Exile 2 instead.

I never thought I'd say those words.

GG, GGG.

100 hours in and I still learn fun and exciting bs that will instantly end your run despite how well and long you've been going. In my last run I learned the game will just crash and corrupt your data, and apparently your save can even get wiped, how wonderful.

Finally, I can't recommend this game! Yes, even after playing it for over 800 hours. But lately, the servers have become so unstable that you lose more hunters to disconnects than to the enemy. The game has a problem with cheaters and a graphics engine problem, and ultimately it's 99% luck and 1% skill. You could start right at the boss, or he could be on the other side of the map. You could start without adjacent teams, or you could go into a fight after 30 seconds. You can spend 20 minutes in the game, or you can die almost instantly from some random solo stalker. Your teammates can disconnect, leave, or try to kill you right away. You might meet some cheaters, or even better, have them in your random crew and watch them clear the map. You can meet people with a ping of 100+ who are never where you see them. You can't do anything about any of these things other than endure them and think it can't get any worse. The gunplay is mediocre at best, and the physics are strange.  You can jump and change direction in midair. It's fun, but it kills the immersion for me. The only constant in this game is that you will repeatedly equip one hunter after another and spend more time in the menus than playing the game. The matchmaking is broken, and people with a handful of hours will meet people with thousands of hours. If you're lucky, none of this will happen, but hunt won't be hunt if you're really lucky. In 1% of all matches where nothing of the above happens, the game shines: it's fun and rewarding. In all other cases, it doesn't. It has a good atmosphere and a nice setting, but ultimately it's a big waste of time (and money).

## จุดเริ่มต้นที่เรียบง่าย

ตอนเริ่มเกม คุณมีเพียงเตาเผาหิน เครื่องขุด และสายพานไม่กี่เส้น

ทุกอย่างต้องทำเอง

* ขุดแร่
* หลอมเหล็ก
* ผลิตเฟือง
* วางสายพาน
* เติมเชื้อเพลิง

ช่วงแรกเหมือนเกมเอาตัวรอดธรรมดา

แต่ประมาณชั่วโมงที่ 2–3 เกมจะเริ่มเผยตัวตนที่แท้จริง

คุณเริ่มคิดว่า

> "ถ้าเครื่องนี้ป้อนของให้กันเองได้ก็คงดี"

แล้วจากเครื่องจักรสองสามตัว โรงงานก็เริ่มเติบโตจนกลายเป็นเมืองอุตสาหกรรมขนาดมหึมา

---

## เกมนี้สอนให้คิดแบบวิศวกร

Factorio ไม่ได้ให้คำตอบสำเร็จรูป

มันโยนปัญหามาให้คุณ

* ทำไมสายพานตัน?
* ทำไมเตาหลอมผลิตไม่ทัน?
* ทำไมรถไฟติด?
* ทำไมไฟฟ้าดับ?
* ทำไมหุ่นยนต์ไม่ยอมสร้าง?
* ทำไมผลิต Science ไม่ทัน?

ทุกปัญหามีคำตอบได้หลายแบบ

ไม่มีคำว่า "วิธีที่ถูกต้อง"

มีแต่ "วิธีที่เหมาะกับโรงงานของคุณ"

นี่คือเหตุผลที่ผู้เล่นสองคนสามารถสร้างฐานที่แตกต่างกันอย่างสิ้นเชิง ทั้งที่มีเป้าหมายเดียวกัน

## ความสุขที่เกมอื่นให้ไม่ได้

สิ่งที่ทำให้ Factorio แตกต่างจากเกมสร้างเมืองหรือเกมบริหารทั่วไป คือ "ระบบทุกอย่างเชื่อมโยงกัน"

เมื่อคุณเพิ่มกำลังผลิตชิป

คุณอาจต้องเพิ่ม

* เหล็ก
* ทองแดง
* พลาสติก
* น้ำมัน
* ไฟฟ้า
* รถไฟ
* เหมืองใหม่

การแก้ปัญหาหนึ่งอย่าง มักสร้างโจทย์ใหม่อีกหลายอย่าง

แต่แทนที่จะรู้สึกน่ารำคาญ มันกลับทำให้รู้สึกเหมือนกำลังแก้ปริศนาขนาดยักษ์

ทุกครั้งที่เห็นสายพานไหลลื่น รถไฟวิ่งเป็นจังหวะ และโรงงานทำงานได้อย่างสมบูรณ์ ความรู้สึกนั้นอธิบายได้ยาก

มันคือความพึงพอใจที่เกิดจากการสร้าง "ระบบ" ที่ทำงานได้จริง

If you love the world of Elder Scrolls, this is for you, if you love the rich lore and stories of this world, this is for you. For me this was my first MMO ever back when it first released in 2014 on console before moving to PC 4 years later so ESO has a special place in my heart,

 With that being said I think I've finally burned out on this game after so many years and it's taken me 2 years too late to realize it. After last years announcement about the change from paid content to new content via Updates and adding quarterly Seasons, this confirmed that my enjoyment for the game has decreased every year. Going so far as to put the game on hiatus for 2-3 years and coming back to play catch-up, not feel any sense of urgency of missing out on anything "Special" in terms of story content. 

After having played both of the new Storylines for this Season or rather for the year, I can safely say I wasn't satisfied. The storylines were fine enough (roughly 10hrs worth of content in total) but with the new Seasons structure with each one having a different theme/focus in terms of content that releases (Story, PvP, Limited Co-op events, Dungeons), they leave a lot to be desired to have to wait a year or year and and a half for new content that may or may not be more my cup of tea. I like the idea of not having to pay for content anymore, but the frequency and quality in content (Specifically story content in my case) just isn't up to par with what I come to expect.

Pros:
-Plenty of years worth of Storylines to immersive yourself in from over the years since release.
-Beautiful and immersive world to get lost in and explore and call home.
-Music is some of the best I've listened to in any series
-Voice Acting cast is top notch and adds a huge level of immersion 

Cons:
-Delivery of story content is lacking heavily, it could use cutscenes or other in-game story tools to tell it's story instead of having standoff's with NPC's with stiff animations that just give you details and what your next task is, which can be unimmersive after a while.

-Storylines can be played in any order by players, which is fine except for the fact that none of the storylines have any sense of urgency or forward progression to the overall worlds story or character developments. Some storylines (like the last 3) act as sequels to storylines previously established but even those feel standalone enough to not need to play previous content.


Overall: I've enjoyed my time with ESO over the last 12 years but I've come to the conclusion that what is here, isn't enough for me or what I'm looking for anymore. Especially in terms of it's story content and the way it's presented and delivered. I think now is the time I step away and try other things, give the developers time to cook and figure out what the future of ESO is going to be. As it stands right now, I'm done with ESO.

V Rising is sort of a finished game. As in, there is sort of progression with sort of endgame with sort of gameplay loop. Up to Gear Level 85ish the game is very solid but then transforms into an utter slog of farming Rifts, rolling secondary bonuses on gems, rolling secondary attributes on legendary weapons. Rift farming feels genuinely soulless, like farming in MMO but without all the things making it fun. Luckily, there are means to modify droprates/vendor prices within in-game settings, but as a game creator, your line of defense should never be "there is a button to skip the part that isn't fun".

And mentioning soulless mechanics – servants. They provide no meaningful value to the experience. You catch them, give them gear, and then send them on literal mobile game expeditions. You can’t assign them any meaningful activity. They can’t patrol regions. You can’t take them as your combat companions. You can’t even encounter them in places where you send them to. Half of Vampire appeal is being able to mind control people and create thralls, yet the mechanic is basically non-existent outside of underbaked resource generator. 

Speaking of dominating people, the other use is keeping prisoners in cages to extract blood from them. For as essential to endgame as “100% Bloods” are, getting them is pain in the back. You either encounter them naturally or play Corrupted Fish minigame where you throw anywhere from one to a few dozens of fish at your prison and see it roll random outcomes until eventually you get 100% Blood. Yet another needless grindy part. Once again, "you can just turn off the part that isn't fun" shouldn't be a line of defense for game designers.

The game itself is made with being PVP experience in mind. All the skills, cooldowns, and movement are balanced around players duking it out. Those of you who are familiar with isometric action games may get a heart attack hearing that the base cooldown of dash is 8 seconds. The game tries to compensate for terrible mobility by providing the player with abilities that block/reflect attacks. However, this introduces a design trap in which bosses are balanced around these abilities. If you don’t run Frost Barrier and/or Ward of the Damned, you are at significant disadvantage against most encounters. And in the game where you get 2 non-Ultimate spells total, sacrificing 1 or 2 of your slots for survivability just doesn’t feel exciting or fun. In some encounters, the game effectively taxes you and takes away your ability to play around with its other toys. 

As far as encounters go - on brutal for the most part, they are fun, with Simon Belmont being the clear peak. However, after him it feels like the game goes downhill fast. The final gauntlet of 5 bosses is homogenic and features very similar dynamics of: avoid bullet hell, spend half the time waiting for your turn, groan when enemy does his mechanic blocking damage or teleports to the other end of arena. Out of these, Adam is probably the most engaging to fight, as his speed is actually matched with the player really well, and the flow of combat feels rather healthy. Either way, after some time, the final bosses don’t even make you angry, they make you numb. They are very flashy, but the more you break them down, the more boring and tiring they become. This game feels really unique in offering an interesting 'power fantasy' style of a vampire game. The castle building is is good enough to have fun with, and I will say the boss design is addictive and fun. If you want to feel like a vampire, and like the sort of albion online, diablo style kind of combat, its great.

BUT, this is not a practical game for an adult with responsibilities to play in my opinion, at least on default settings. Everything takes too much time. You need more resources? You teleport there and then, you can't teleport back. You have to walk it all the way back to your base for the vast majority of the game. Yes this can be turned off in settings, but it's odd to me that the default is to have items prevent teleportation on by default. 

The whole game is balanced around PVP. And if that's your thing, power to you. For me, I played solo PVE for the whole game (I did play on a server with other folks around, but I fought each boss independently). Once you get to late game, every resource takes quite a long time to craft. Armor takes literal minutes to craft. Combined with the walking back and forth to get resources, any time you are trying to improve your gear, or your castle ends up feeling like a perpetual fetch quest where you spend more time waiting than playing.

The in game solution for this are the servants. You can capture certain enemies and turn them into your servants to go to the resource camps and get them for you. Sound great right? Well, here's where this games obsession with waiting comes back: The minimum time you can send a servant out on a mission is 2 hours. The maximum length of these missions, is 16 hours. Luckily, these are real life hours so you don't have to be in game for the whole time. 

But there's more of this real life time mechanic. If you play on a server ( the community that plays this game is really nice, so I would recommend playing on a PVE server), you have to keep filling up your castle's heart with essence or you could lose it. In the first couple tiers of play, completely filling up the heart with essence keeps it protected for 2ish days. I am very lucky that I was able to log on frequently enough early on that I never lost my castle, but it was something that was on my mind while I wasn't playing the game.

 But this is where this gameplay loop started to break down for me. As an adult with a job and other real life responsibilities, I really only have an hour a couple times a week and maybe a few hours on a Saturday to indulge myself in a little bit of gaming. These mechanics created a sort of addiction stress loop for me, similar to a mobile game, where if I didn't log on that day, I'd loose something. If I didn't optimize the servants I was sending out, I feared that the next time I would log in, I'd have to spend my 1 hour walking to and from the iron mine just so I could get better gear.

Other than that though, this was quite a fun time. If you are a student on a summer break, I can envision this being a great time. The boss design is solid, and I enjoyed the mostly linear progression of the game where you always have someone to fight next. It just really is a bummer that all the mechanics, like bat form and the machine that allows you to do some basic crafting automation aren't available until the last 10-15 hours of gameplay. I ended up giving up on the servants at that point because I couldn't get them better gear without spending even more hours gathering resources to automate making them armor, to send them out to get me more resources. I ended up just having them collect fish until I beat Dracula.

In summary, only play this game if you can play really consistently for 80-100 hours, or mess with the settings to allow you to teleport with all items and increase basic resource drop rates.

Sea of Thieves – A Pirate Adventure Like No Other

Sea of Thieves is one of the most unique multiplayer games I have ever played. It is much more than just a pirate game; it is an open world where every voyage becomes a new story. Whether you are sailing alone or with a crew of friends, every session is full of surprises, challenges, and unforgettable moments.

The first thing that stands out is the beautiful art style. The ocean looks alive, the sunsets are breathtaking, and storms create an atmosphere that makes every journey feel like a real pirate adventure. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself stopping for a moment just to admire the scenery.

What makes Sea of Thieves truly special is that there is no single way to play. You can search for buried treasure, hunt dangerous skeleton captains, fight ghost fleets, explore mysterious islands, solve ancient riddles, or simply sail across the sea looking for adventure. Every voyage is different because the world is shared with other players, and you never know what will happen next.

Player interactions are the heart of the game. Sometimes another crew will become your greatest ally, helping you defeat powerful enemies and sharing the rewards. Other times they may attack without warning, leading to intense naval battles where strategy, teamwork, and quick decision-making determine who sails away victorious. These unpredictable encounters create stories that no scripted game could ever match.

The sailing mechanics are simple to understand but rewarding to master. Managing the sails, steering through storms, repairing damage, and coordinating with your crew during combat creates an experience that feels both challenging and satisfying. Every member of the crew has an important role, making teamwork essential for success.

One of my favorite parts of Sea of Thieves is the sense of freedom. There are no strict paths forcing you to play in a certain way. You create your own goals, your own adventures, and your own memories. Some days you might spend hours collecting valuable treasure, while on other days you may lose everything in an epic battle. Surprisingly, even those defeats often become the most memorable stories.

The game has continued to grow over the years with new voyages, enemies, mechanics, cosmetics, and seasonal content. Developers have consistently expanded the world, giving both new and veteran players fresh reasons to return. There is always another mystery to uncover, another island to explore, or another legendary pirate waiting to challenge you.

Sea of Thieves is not just about collecting gold or becoming rich. It is about the journey itself. It is about laughing with friends after a hilarious mistake, surviving impossible situations, escaping enemy ships with only a few planks left, or celebrating after finally selling a ship full of treasure. These moments are what make the game unforgettable.

If you enjoy exploration, teamwork, naval combat, and creating your own adventures instead of following a fixed story, then Sea of Thieves is absolutely worth playing. It rewards creativity, communication, and curiosity more than almost any other multiplayer game I have experienced.

Every time I set sail, I know that I am about to create another unique story. That is the true magic of Sea of Thieves. No two adventures are ever the same, and that is exactly why I keep coming back.

Fair winds, calm seas, and may your treasure always reach the outpost safely. See you on the Sea of Thieves!

I have used the standalone client for the last 13.6 years, but only recently started using the Steam app to launch the standalone client. I use the `-portal Provider` launch option to use the standalone client with my existing account. I have never purchased any Guild Wars 2 (GW2) content via Steam. [u]This is an important note for newbies: you can't mix and match game clients[/u]. If your account started on the Steam client, any purchased content is only available through Steam. If your account started on the standalone client (even when launching via the Steam app using the launch options like I do) any purchased content is only available via the standalone client.

Now with that said, I love this game a lot. I've played off and on since the original launch. I paid the full box price before it became a free-to-play game. I love the combat, the music, the art direction, the story and the characters are also pretty good. What I love most of all is that this game respects my time. Not a single other MMORPG has done that in the last 25 years.

There is no gear treadmill in GW2. You pick your pace and you pick your objectives. You could take a multi-year break (of which I have taken many) and GW2 will be right where you left it, waiting for you. There's no rush. There's no FOMO!

You can join several guilds, whether they are PVE or PVP-focused, and find people to complete open-world and instanced events with. There's always someone around willing to jump in and lend a hand. Which gets to the other really big selling point for me: the community.

The majority, say 95% of players, are very generous and understanding of newcomers. Of course, there's always the 5% that are going to be sweaty try-hards. It's night and day when compared to games like World of Warcraft, which was pretty toxic back in the day.

Anyway, you should give this game a shot. You might bounce off, but don't feel bad about that. There's a lot to do, and there's no rush! GLHF :)
