Headline: 1600+ hours in. The slow decline of a giant, and what it desperately needs to survive.With over 1,655 hours registered on Steam (and many more outside of it), I have invested serious time and money into ESO. However, we have to face reality: the game is slowly but surely dying. The first major blow will come with the release of GTA 6, and the final nail in the coffin might be Guild Wars 3.
As someone who loves this universe, I want to share what this game is missing and what could have saved its outdated combat and PvP systems. 
1. Combat Synergy: Moving from "One-Button Spams" to Combo Chains (Inspired by Conqueror’s Blade)The current combat feels rigid. Instead of abilities simply triggering a one-time effect with a cooldown, ESO desperately needs a dynamic combo and chain system bound to a single key. Inspired by the Glaive mechanics in Conqueror's Blade, abilities should flow as continuous animations based on timing:
1st Press: Triggers a wide, sweeping weapon animation.
2nd Press (Perfect Timing Window): Transitions smoothly into a heavy follow-up strike.
3rd Press: Executes a powerful finisher that breaks blocks or knocks enemies down.

Note: Players should still be able to animation-cancel out of this using a dodge roll.

In ESO, this would look like combining Critical Charge -> Uppercut -> Reverse Slash into a single, evolving skill slot with its respective morphs. 
The same should apply to buffs. Imagine combining Dragon Blood -> Wing Buffet -> Earthspike Mantle into a 32-second sequence. To maintain all three effects at maximum efficiency, you would need to re-cast the ability within a strict 28–30 second window. Missing the window reduces the buff's effectiveness by a percentage, which you can only restore in the next cycle. This would add actual skill expression to buff management.

2. PvP Arena Evolution: A MOBA-style SystemESO’s massive library of item sets makes it perfect for a MOBA-inspired PvP mode. Before entering the map, you lock in three of your owned sets. You don't start with them equipped. Instead, you hold lanes, capture objectives, and earn points during the match to gradually "buy" and assemble your build depending on how the match progresses.To add more depth, racial passives should synergize with RNG maps. For example, Nord passives could receive a slight bonus on winter/snow maps, making team composition and map variance matter.After thousands of hours, I want this game to thrive, but without a fundamental rework of its core mechanics, it will not survive the next generation of MMOs.

So this game is billed as a real "hardcore" shooter with a short TTK, married with compelling fantasy elements, by many on the Youtube and elsewhere. But the first half of this statement reflects an absolutely false impression of the game. It will 1,000% disappoint and disgust someone looking for even vaguely realistic/grounded shootouts with "cowboy guns" and/or other late 19th century firearms. 

Credit where due, the graphics, the game premise and lore, and it goes without saying the sound design are all amazing. It is the dev's apparent ignorance/bizarre ideas about how humans actually move and the performance of bullets fired from guns, including 19th century guns, where actual gameplay falls apart and deep into a bottomless pit of stupid.

The character movement is inertia-less, as time from full speed pressing D to full speed pressing A is on the order of .05 seconds. Games seeking to model actual human movement use roughly .25 of second as the minimum time it takes for an athletic human to arrest inertia in one direction and begin moving in the opposite. You simply cannot have good gunfighting in a game if you give characters movement qualities more appropriate to squirrels on cocaine than humans. That's starting with a broken foundation.
TL;DR-Gameplay footage reveals jigglepeak squirrel-on-crack nonsense that is neither physically realistic at all nor cinematic, and this is mostly down to the inertialess deceleration and acceleration. Frankly the "good" players frequently look like something is broken in their keyboard and mouse, or like an unseen hand has grabbed the character's perspective camera and is shaking it hard as possible.

The ballistics and lethality are also asinine. You'd think with them getting right down to listing meters-per-second on every single projectile it would be quite accurately modeled in most respects. But nope, sheer damn foolishness again. The lethality is bizarre-Even a "buffalo rifle" round to the heart takes two shots to said pump-house to kill. And centerfire projectiles travel no more than 40 meters, and frequently no more than 20 meters, before losing very substantial lethality, inexplicably. That's just not how any bullet, ever, actually works. They don't have drag chutes to suddenly reduce velocity at some set distance between 20-40 meters. The only gun type in the game which actually kills to the torso with one shot is the various shotguns.

 Which presents an obvious game balance problem when every other gun in the game, even high-powered rifles, are artificially forced to use at least two shots to the torso to kill a healthy opponent. So what do they do? OF COURSE they shorten the lethal range of buckshot to something absurd like 10 meters or so. Truly the silly penny has dropped in the stupid machine with this hare-brained "balance" scheme. Imagine nerfing shotgun range *because you nerfed the lethality of everything else for no good reason*, instead of just using a more grounded approach to firearm terminal performance.

The game devs then compound the dumbassery further by having a mechanic to penetrate walls and other light material with shots, but then have the material penetration performance bear no resemblance to reality. "No resemblance to the reality in the modeling" is a running theme for Hunt.

 Even a 44-40 solid lead round loaded with blackpowder, in my direct shooting experience, easily penetrates through 2'' of sawn pine boards at 20 paces. By comparison, even their best penning ammo, so-called "full metal jacket" (too many historical and basic physics mistakes to get into with the different ammo types in this game btw) has FAR less penetration than anyone who has done any shooting will expect, and again inexplicably loses tons of lethality by going through the thin wooden boards. Hell, corrugated metal siding *stops* the rounds from many large bore handguns in Hunt, as absurd as that sounds. If you don't want to model material penetration even close to correctly in your game, then just have any solid object stop bullets. One or the other. This "neither fish nor fowl" penetration mechanic is inane.

Some other odds and ends of Hunt failings I didn't get to above: Despite the fact that the characters have inhuman lack of inertia in their movement/change of direction, their rate of fire with lever action+pump action weapons is dreadfully slow from the shoulder, as is their aimed ROF with single-action revolvers. *I'm* significantly faster with firearms of those types in my collection than the supposed hardened gunmen of Hunt, and any cowboy action shooting competitor is LIGHT YEARS faster at getting lead down range than the "gunslingers" of Hunt. Also, the devs apparently think keeping the stock on your shoulder and cheek welded to the stock when working a lever/bolt/pump action long gun is some kind of "magickal" high skill "trait", instead of an absolute basic of shooting that even new and inexperienced shooters learn quickly and easily. There's no good reason for abysmal shooting habits and performance to be the "defacto" for the characters in a game of this kind, but that's what we got. I have to think it can only come down to some sort of extreme subject matter ignorance on the part of whoever was in charge of designing that aspect of the game.

Conclusion: Sadly the public must continue to wait for a multiplayer shooter which even begins to do justice to gunfighting with "Old West" firearms. It says something about what a rut multiplayer FPS games are stuck in that seemingly every FPS is either some arcade nonsense, or if it is even vaguely grounded and physically realistic then it is inevitably a simulation of 20th/21st century military battles. Of gun battles before 1900 and/or gun encounters NOT being fought by soldiers on historic battlefields there is precious little, basically nothing. And that's weird when you think about it, given the popularity of Western movies, novels, the sport of cowboy action shooting, etc. A huge gaping niche and opportunity in the market exists for the first developer who does a good job of an "Old West" pvp FPS .

I've supported Grinding Gear Games for years because I believed in what this company was building. I've spent around €5,000 on supporter packs and MTX because I wanted to support the developers. Looking back, I honestly regret it.

Path of Exile 1 and Path of Exile 2 have become some of the most frustrating games I've ever played, not because they're difficult, but because they're so unstable.

Path of Exile 2 is full of crashes, freezes, random client closures, and bugs that completely ruin entire play sessions. When I got tired of that, I went back to Path of Exile 1, expecting the more established game to be reliable. Instead, I experienced the same problems.

I finally had a great Voyage, found valuable loot, sent it to the surface, and then the client crashed 3 minutes later, just before I completed the Voyage. When I logged back in, the loot was gone. Hours of gameplay wasted because the client couldn't stay open. Losing rewards because the game crashes is unacceptable.

In the most recent Path of Exile 2 league, I dropped an Algur's Legacy only to lose it because an Expedition monster spawned outside the map and couldn't be killed. Then the game crashed, my portal closed, and the item was gone. G-fing-G. 500 DIV gone!

The game is advertised as free-to-play, and technically that's true. You can download it and finish the campaign without spending anything. In my opinion, though, that's where the "free" experience ends. Once you reach the real endgame and start mapping seriously, premium stash tabs become practically essential. Currency tabs, map tabs, fragment tabs, premium tabs for trading, and other specialized tabs aren't luxury purchases anymore. They're quality-of-life features that become requirements if you want to engage with the endgame efficiently. I don't believe the average player can realistically experience the full endgame without spending a significant amount of money. (Around 200 USD)

What frustrates me even more is the communication. Grinding Gear Games constantly talks about transparency, listening to feedback, and improving the game. There are developer videos and statements acknowledging issues, but from my perspective as a long-time supporter, the same problems continue to come back. The messaging is excellent. The execution rarely lives up to it.

The MTX compatibility between Path of Exile 1 and Path of Exile 2 was one of the biggest promises made to the community years ago. That promise still isn't even nearly delivered. It's difficult to keep believing new promises when old ones remain unfulfilled.

I understand that no game is perfect. Bugs happen. Server issues happen. But after years of support, I expected stability, accountability, and for the company to follow through on what it tells its players. Instead, I've experienced crashes that delete my rewards, years of repeated technical issues, and promises that remain unfinished.

After spending roughly €5,000 supporting this company, I can no longer recommend giving them your money. If you're considering buying supporter packs or MTX, I'd wait until the games are stable and the company starts consistently delivering on the commitments it makes to its community. Which by the way won't happen.

- There is no other game that can induce this much rage and bliss in me at the same time. Playing PoE means constantly alternating between praising the developers as geniuses and wondering whether a monkey, homeschooled by a pigeon and armed with a crayon, could design better systems and leagues. GGG can release a genuinely excellent league, then follow it with something as bad as Keepers or Allflame and somehow still appear proud of the result. I have no idea whether their QA team blindly approves everything, whether their playtesters are ignored, or whether everyone occasionally loses the ability to recognize obvious problems. This cannot always be defended with "We take risks, because otherwise every league would be boring". My sweet summer child, veteran players knew within the first 150 hours that your league was terrible. Then you buffed it, and it was still terrible.

- PoE1 no longer feels like a game being developed entirely for the people who actually enjoy PoE1. More PoE2 mechanics, ideas, pacing decisions, visual clutter, friction, and experimental systems keep bleeding into it. Instead of preserving the identity of the game that built their audience, GGG increasingly seems to use PoE1 as a convenient testing ground for PoE2. Stop trying to fix what made the game successful just because it does not match the philosophy of your newer project. If I will want to play PoE2, which I like too, I will play PoE2. Not a reskinned version with worse graphics and rewards in PoE.

- There is also no truly challenging, structured endgame in PoE. If you cannot create your own goals and find enjoyment in optimization for its own sake, you will eventually become bored. The entire endgame is a repetition loop. You juice maps, kill Ubers, farm currency, upgrade your build, and then repeat the same content with larger numbers and often mediocre rewards. 
You need to be a very particular kind of autistic, natural-born tinkerer, theorycrafter, and min-maxer, to keep enjoying it for thousands of hours. Personally, I can spend entire evenings crafting items, planning builds, calculating modifiers, and optimizing systems. The game itself is often boring. Understanding and breaking the game is the fun part.

That leads to another problem. Once your character becomes powerful and you finally understand how to juice maps properly, the game stops looking like an action RPG and starts resembling a graphics-card stress test.

Ten thousand monsters spawn at once. Fifty glowing orbs chase you across the map. A hundred overlapping ground effects cover every surface. Millions of visual and sound effects go off simultaneously, most of them contributing nothing except noise, confusion, and irritation.

Would you like to see your character? Understand what killed you? React to an enemy attack? Play Solitaire.

The PvE aspect is also very good. The monsters and enemies throughout the map make every trip dangerous, even before you encounter another player. Most importantly, watch out for those damn dogs...

The game definitely has some bugs. Sometimes your teammates’ names will appear as “Unknown,” and occasionally your settings may reset and need to be adjusted again. These problems can be frustrating, but regardless of all that, the game is still extremely fun.

Hunt offers an experience that very few other games can match. Every match feels unpredictable, stressful, exciting, and rewarding. Even after taking breaks, I continue to come back, and that says a lot about how enjoyable the game really is.

Here's your full-length ghoulish rundown for Elder Scrolls Online, grounded in where the game actually sits in 2026:

Elder Scrolls Online — RECOMMENDED

Eleven years in the ground and this MMO refuses to stay buried — in fact, in 2026 it clawed its way back into being genuinely worth your time. If you bounced off ESO years ago and wrote it off as a hollow Skyrim knockoff, it's time to dig up the corpse again, because ZeniMax finally stopped bleeding players and started listening to them.

The big one: they tore out the annual paid-chapter model and replaced it with a seasonal system where future content lands free as part of the base game. Imperial City, Orsinium, Thieves Guild, Dark Brotherhood — all the old DLC coffins got rolled into the base game. That alone kills the single biggest reason people avoided this game: the endless nickel-and-diming. Now instead of one bloated expansion a year, you get a steady drip of seasonal events, new systems, and experimental activities that keep the world feeling alive instead of embalmed.

Under the hood, the quality-of-life work is where it really shines. Hero's Return smooths the terror of coming back after years away. The new Challenge Difficulty system finally answers the veteran solo crowd who wanted their world to actually fight back. Class Mastery makes pure-class builds viable again for the buildcrafting obsessives, respecs happen right in the UI now, and they've even started a visual overhaul of combat abilities — Dragonknight first — to drag the old animations into the modern age.

What still haunts it: it's an MMO, and it wears all the genre's baggage. The shared world can shatter immersion when forty other players are stampeding through your solemn story moment, and the combat, while improved, still won't satisfy anyone chasing the tight feel of a proper action game. Newcomers can also drown in the sheer volume of content with no clear thread telling them where to start.

But here's the ghoulish truth: for an eleven-year-old game, the pace of real, meaningful change in 2026 is legitimately impressive — most MMOs this age are decaying husks going through the motions. ESO is doing the opposite. If you love open-world RPGs, deep buildcrafting, and can stomach an MMO's crowded-graveyard quirks, there's a genuinely massive world here to lose yourself in. Wander into Tamriel. Just don't expect to crawl back out anytime soon.

Sea of Thieves is the most controversial game I've ever seen gameplay-wise. You can absolutely have fun in it, but expect it to cost you your sanity. There is a lot of content for new players to engage with, just be prepared for your fun to get ruined by literally anything, not necessarily other players. If you do want to buy this game, make sure to have a friend in your crew to share the highs and lows with - solo slooping can be a challenge even for veteran pirates. Treat the following wall of text as a warning a la "abandon hope all ye who enter here" - don't expect to always be able to have your cake and eat it too, especially as a new player. PvP may be in a weird spot right now, but it's still a core part of the game - just remember that you can often choose whether to interact with it and how. Awareness will be your best defense, but you'll have to get used to sticking your head up and out to the horizon like a paranoid meerkat.

Now onto the breakdown. I'll start with the easy stuff and get the good points out of the way. The visuals are great if you're able to max out the settings and certainly add to the atmosphere of the game. Unfortunately the devs had chosen to stay on an ancient version of UE4 because reasons. Whatever "2026 edition" is supposed to mean, it's got absolutely nothing to do with the technical aspects of the game - no modern graphical features are available; I guess the only thing it has in common with modern AAA titles in that sense is the install size.
But back to the good: the character design is a masterpiece of comedy if you nail the right pirate appearance. The faces they can have, the way they can walk or crouch, the expressions they make in emotes is a big part of why I still enjoy SoT. IMO you're better off looking and dressing like some stupid mental asylum reject than going for a more serious or grounded look - it's guaranteed to get at least a chuckle from most of the people you meet.
The audio aspect is more straightforward. The music is fantastic, the sound effects are nicely made. In fact, here's a bonus - if you enable text to speech in the game's settings (might also have to dig around in xbox settings as well) and pick some wacky TTS voice, you can have a lot of fun with whatever gibberish it says from what you type in chat. You can't hear your own, so have a friend in your crew stream their game back to you (they probably need to have TTS enabled too).
At the end of the day, the game is founded on player interactions and the situations that come out of it. It's not called Sea of Thieves for nothing - be mischievous, take risks, have a bit of a laugh at someone else's expense. It's these kinds of situations that end up becoming memorable feats.

Unfortunately this is where my platitudes end. Time to get to the real reasons for the negative review. There are two sides of this coin - the state of the game and the development process.

Your first clue for the technical state should be the aforementioned install size. Over the years it had gotten bloated from ~30 gigs all the way to 140. This is thanks to the ridiculous amount of cosmetics, plus the tall tale assets (the game's campaign mode), coupled with a lack of effort on Rare's part to optimise the install size actively or retroactively. As such, if you're not interested in said tall tales or owning dozens of wardrobes worth of dresses, the game will happily waste your disk space whilst you only really interact with 20-30% of its size.
The gameplay itself is riddled with bugs, inconsistencies and oversights. The servers are sluggish and unstable, with high overhead and lag spikes on a regular basis. This alone creates a whole spectrum of gameplay issues, including SoT's infamous "9/10" hit registration (it's more like a 50/50 dice roll), backspawning, long loading times, broken captaincy books, bugged inventories, unharpoonable loot, occasional disconnects and more. How they function in general is still a mystery to me because, for example, even though the game has servers in both Europe and North America, it's still entirely possible to encounter an American whilst playing from Europe or vice versa. If you dive to a quest, the game will try to put you in a different instance with other people, and if it succeeds, you might just find yourself in a server full of hourglass players. This is a PvP mode where participants dive directly to each other to fight. Since the game doesn't create dedicated hourglass instances and just mixes the participants with the rest of the people, you might find yourself surrounded by sweaty or at least PvP-interested players, some of which might stay on the instance after their fights are finished.
The existence of hourglass itself is a symptom of how Rare have been treating the concept of PvP in the game. In its early years, a good balance was struck in its design - PvP was less of an activity and more of an intrinsic risk involved in doing just about anything, but especially world events. A massive glowing beacon in the sky is an invitation not just for you, but for everyone else on the server. Most importantly, you'd always have the opportunity to choose whether to engage with it, based on your circumstances. Do I already have a lot of treasure onboard? Are there any players near the event or actively doing it? Are they new or experienced? Should I sneak onboard, roll in guns blazing or just leave? Questions like this are what is supposed to shape your choices and your adventure, driven by risk, reward and uncertainty created by the activity of other crews. But apparently it's not something new or highly casual people could handle, so Rare in their infinite wisdom have sought to throw this balance off completely by introducing a gamemode with PvP only (hourglass), a gamemode with no PvP whatsoever (safer seas), events with forced PvP (such as the skull of siren song), and as the cherry on top, diving anywhere at anytime with effectively no cost.
Diving itself is a very problematic mechanic. It was introduced in line with Rare's misguided philosophy of trying to cater to new players as much as possible. On paper the idea appears good - a smoother learning curve and a faster way to start off your adventure. But as with many other features, it was implemented carelessly, its costs never considered. The game's core design encourages and thrives on player interactions which need time to happen, but since diving lets you change servers the moment things start to feel boring or inconvenient, it effectively has every server reset itself continuously, which paradoxically makes them feel even more empty and boring. People who stay and commit are not rewarded, and people who disengage are not punished.

I could go on for a while like this listing the bugs and mistakes alone, but let's move on to the development process. Today's Rare has nothing in common with the Rare that once released legendary titles like Battletoads or GoldenEye 007. Any sort of competency has gone out the window. The inability to properly schedule and distribute workloads has given rise to technical debt, missed deadlines, failed events, a sharp drop in content amount [b] and [/b] quality, meaningless FOMO slop, dramas within the community and an all-time low player trust in general. A number of incidents such as the recent bruno thing or the doubloon reset reveal the utter lack of respect the devs have for their players, both the new ones they apparently were trying to please so hard, and the old ones that had been supporting them and playing their game ever since its release. This has gotten so bad that their admitting to "missing the mark" with almost every dev update for the last several years has solidified itself as [i] the meme [/i] within the community. 
Leave it to Rare to hit a new bottom every single time they try to deliver content or even just open their mouths.

You should consider buying this game if you enjoy challenging survival games with a heavy emphasis on action and where you can play an ambitious vampire in a quest to drink basically everyone tasty enough in the lands, up until the final boss: Dracula himself.

The gameplay's loop is fairly standard for the genre: you gather resources, you build yourself a nice castle (where you can craft/upgrade), you equip yourself with your flashy new weapons, you hunt down some bosses to unlock new recipes. Repeat.

Pros:
- The graphics are fine and the game's aesthetic has its charm.
- If you enjoy a challenge, the game will give you one, especially if you play blind directly on Brutal difficulty.
- There are tons of bosses. I got tired of hunting them down way before reaching the last 5 ones.
- You don't need to grind that much compared to other survival games (it is relative tho, and depends on your previous experiences with this genre, ofc).
- You can build a good-looking castle/garden with ease. It won't require that many resources.
- Tons of magical powers to unlock (you get them by killing bosses). They will help you adapt to the wide variety of bosses you will face (they can be swapped, even mid combat :P).
- A wide variety of weapon types.
- Quite a few travel forms and means of transportation (I won't spoil them).
- The servant system, to help you gather resources.

Cons:
- Meh musics. There aren't that many of them (and boss battles all share the same theme...).
- Blood drinking. At first, it won't bother you, as you will just drink whatever mob crosses your path. But when you discover how potent 90-100%quality blood types are... you will want to drink it exclusively for boss fights. The problem is that your blood pool diminishes when you cast/transform/regenerate (so basically all of your main actions aside from attacking with weapons and crafting lol). In practice, you will be drinking quite often from the highest blood types available to you, which means going back to your castle to drink the blood from your captured victims. It's not fun: it's a chore, especially after a full playthrough (THE GAME IS LONG).
- The sun. I know, "we are vampires in a survival game, ofc the sun should have a great impact". I agree, this mechanic (if you stay 20+ seconds exposed to the sun, you will take massive damage) is interesting and forces you to either fight during the night or to jump from shadow to shadow. The problem is that many tough bosses are not in-door --> they are exposed to the sun during daytime! It means that you have to wait irl minutes for nighttime to come. So not only do you have to backtrack to where you died, but you also need to wait for the night before attempting that outdoor boss again! It doesn't sound like much but, trust me, in a game with so many challenging bosses, you will start being annoyed by how many "daytime alt tab breaks at the teleporting gateway" you need to take.
- If you have played mmos like WoW, or played the SoulsBorne series (including Sekiroh and ER), you won't be impressed by the bosses' design. Some are fun challenges (like Simon Belmont), but others are quite literally chores. Take the old man in the cursed forest for example: he flees from you while aggroing the annoying mobs of the annoyingly thick forest.
- Adds. While Elden Ring became infamous for its sometimes ridiculous boss attack delays, this here game has bosses summoning adds/making clones of themselves way too often. When the hardest part of a boss is its add phase (multiple of them sometimes, if you don't kill the boss fast enough), and when you have add phases on so many bosses, it starts to get annoying.
- AoE clutter. It keeps you on your toes and forces you to better position yourself, but sometimes it can become quite ridiculous when the attack indicators pile up onto each others WHILE SOME ADD IS CHARGING AT YOU.

That's it. Despite my complaints, I recommend that game.

TL;DR: a challenging experience that I didn't find particularly enjoyable. Some might greatly enjoy that game for its many qualities tho, so don't be afraid to give it a go.

I'm a veteran of the WoW, Guild Wars, and Destiny communities and this is still my favorite MMO of all time.  
Some of my favorite things are:
1) Unlike GW2, ESO's megaservers ensure every map feels so alive and populated, I love constantly seeing other players on their adventures, especially in the cities and so forth. 
2) The voice acting is always phenomenal and immersive. Engaging from the first moment you enter the universe.
3) Queueing for group content feels easy and low pressure, even in early-game stages. Unlike the LFG systems in other games where I often felt like too much of a noob to try, the ESO dungeon finder system tends to foster an attitude of "anyone can give it a go"
4) On the other hand, group activities are truly optional. If I want to focus on single-player experience, I love playing ESO like I'm playing Skyrim. Spending time exploring the environment, reading lore books, and talking to NPCs. 
5) The amount of content is just mind boggling. At 1000 hours, there are still zones I have never completed the main storyline for.
6) The housing system and decorating is next level. It truly is like a completely second game within this game.

I highly recommend V Rising to anyone who enjoys crafting survival games combined with the vampire fantasy theme. This game is filled with unique items, upgrades, powers, locations, and challenges along your vampiric journey. I enjoyed playing V rising with a friend on brutal difficulty. 90% of the game was amazing and designed very well. However, it's not a perfect game. I'll share more below so you know what to expect. 

VAMPIRISM
Excellent. They nailed the vampire fantasy in many ways, in addition to many other creative ways I wasn't expecting. There's the typical dependence on consuming blood to survive, transforming into creatures, and using all kinds of super cool powers. The character creator is also pretty good. It's not as extensive as some other ones where you can adjust every muscle, but there's enough preset body features to make your vampire character your own. 

WORLD-BUILDING
This is an immersive world filled with many points of interest, NPC's roam along roads, NPC's react to your presence in different ways depending on your form, unique monsters and interesting enemies lurk within every zone, and the world in general looks and feels like a dark vampire fantasy.

PROGRESSION
This game will keep your attention the entire way through. I didn't get bored once. V Rising does a great job giving you a reason to always be doing something fun, whether that's building your base, upgrading your base, crafting a new weapon, upgrading your weapon, fighting a new boss, unlocking new items, increasing your gear level, uncovering a new part of the map, and much more that I won't spoil. I was always pleasantly surprised by how much more content there was to experience. 

COMBAT
In my opinion, this was the part of the game that was hit or miss, and contributed entirely to the 10% that made me want to stop playing several times through. First, there are many weapons and vampiric powers with unique abilities that really let you choose your own combat style. Loved the customization. Second, I played on Brutal difficulty all the way to the final boss, so if you play on a different difficulty, your experience may be very different than mine. Here's what I absolutely hated about combat in this game: melee builds make this game FAR much harder compared to ranged options, counter abilities don't work against many boss attacks, getting hit by abilities that I dodged or moved out of, attacks that track your movement this intensely making dodging or moving out of the way literally impossible, bosses being immune to crowd control effects causing many powers to be irrelevant, inconsistency between which enemy attacks have area of effect indicators and which don't, inconsistency between which timed enemy attacks have visual countdown indicators and which don't, and inaccurate hitboxes. For a game with bosses this difficult and this important to the core gameplay loop, I expected a better experience here, and for these issues to be nonexistent. I absolutely love games with challenging boss fights, but these were big enough issues to slowly erode my enjoyment for the game over time. 

CRAFTING
V Rising has many of the same elements you would find in your typical survival crafting game, and implements those elements well. Collecting materials doesn't abuse your time, you get enough materials for the farming run to be worth it (except fishing--its abysmally tedious), crafting items and building your base is satisfying, you can customize your base in many ways and really make it your own style, and constructing/moving/changing/rearranging your base is very easy. Too many crafting survival games fail this core aspect of their game, but V Rising is not one of them.

Customizable procedural world/planet generation lends variety and flexible difficulty, the crafting system builds on itself and continuously challenges the player to build and refine their factory layout, throughput, and energy consumption, and the need to repel alien bug attacks with personal weapons or defensive bulwarks adds tension and the need to monitor your factory's pollution. All this for at least 83 hours until you launch a rocket (or 131 hours when you fly out of the solar system in [i]Space Age[/i]).

Having jumped in in 2024 (11 years after its crowdfunding) I can appreciate the obvious influence Factorio has had on other developers -- notably those behind [i]Satisfactory[/i], [i]Shapez[/i], and [i]Palworld[/i] -- but I find the influences on Factorio more interesting. [url=https://youtu.be/CtALqDo9rX8?t=629]Per[/url] Michal "Kovarex" Kovařík, the creator of [i]Factorio[/i] and Wube studio director, The [i]Industrial Craft[/i] Minecraft Mod was a big inspiration in its broadened crafting tree and production line construction tools presented as a collection of machines to orchestrate. He also cites the [i]Civilization[/i] games for their expanding tech trees, and [i]Transport Tycoon[/i] as inspiration for [i]Factorio[/i]'s logistical systems. 

The challenge of mastering these crafting, logistical, strategic, and efficiency tools is a potent combination for anyone with an interest in problem-solving. Needing to continuously shift your engineer's attention to immediate concerns can be combatted by knowing to build more than you immediately need and to leave yourself space to make modifications later. While pre-optimizing is a useful approach once you understand the systems in play,  improvising new ways to build your production chains has also been a source of satisfaction in my later playthroughs. This flexibility in how one can approach constructing a factory is definitely a strength of the game in that it affirms the player's ability to both learn the mechanics and to imagine new and possibly better approaches to reaching that tantalizing rocket launch.

My parallel enjoyment of [i]Zachtronics[/i] games definitely biased me towards enjoying [i]Factorio[/i], but the pull to master systems that heavily intertwine, the tension of building steadily but sustainably, and the intrinsic and extrinsic desire to optimize your creations all got me hooked.

[i]Factorio[/i] is easy to recommend, with or without the expansion, just take warning that it is possible to lose an amount of play time on Nauvis equivalent to scores of shorter experiences.

The design respects the player by offering no hand-holding or forgiving safety nets; its steep skill ceiling demands genuine mastery, disciplined squad coordination, and adaptive execution. Victory is never guaranteed. It emerges from navigating stochastic chaos, calculating risks under pressure, and executing flawless tactical maneuvers when the variables align.
The atmosphere is immersive and uncompromising, offering a paradoxical sanctuary: a game whose unyielding brutality temporarily relieves you of the mundane weight of reality by forcing absolute presence. Ignore the superficial detractors who lack the patience for depth. Experience it firsthand, master its mechanics, and embrace the friction.

I love ESO, but I can not in good faith recommend this game to anyone. I noticed a lot of other reviews mentioning that "you have to sub and then buy DLCs on top of that" which is just misleading. The subscription gives you access to the DLC areas. I am fully aware that the only way to access the crafting bag is via subscription and it is annoying that ends up being the case, but I don't think it's that bad.

While yes, the game does have loot boxes; they are mostly cosmetic. The only things that are pay for convenience in the loot boxes are research scrolls; the books for mount speed, stamina, and carrying capacity which you can just buy from the crown store by themselves anyways if you don't want to wait for the stablemaster in game; and other miscellaneous consumable foods, potions, and poisons which you can either make better food in game and the tri-potions can be bought in-game as well.

I will admit that PVP is at it's worst state it's ever been since the dragon knight and werewolf reworks. It is absolutely unplayable whether it be battlegrounds or cyrodill or imperial city. There is literally nothing positive I can say about PVP.

When it comes to PVE however, I understand that the bar to entry seems inexplicably difficult at first, and that isn't due to how hard the content is but rather due to how hard it is to find reliable players. Most ESO content is able to be accomplished if you're willing to learn. However I will admit there is a large amount of players that will either actively sabotage other player's content or just refuse to learn the content and expect to be carried.

The most disappointing thing about ESO is how technically fickle the game is. It will repeatedly crash if it's not running under "just the right conditions" and it will crash OVER AND OVER again. ESO support will be of absolutely no help because they are incapable of being honest with their playerbase. They will ask you to go through a very basic battery of support steps that are already listed on their support site before even attempting to assign a real person to your support ticket. After that they will ask you to "narrow down" what programs are causing the issue and if you give them that ammunition, they will tell you to not run that program anymore if you want ESO to work. In my case that was discord. However that will not fix the issue. You'll be asked to re-install your operating system, and that might temporarily allow ESO to work for 1 night, only to crash the next morning.

Now you're left with a game that crashes every 5 minutes and still no solution.

TL;DR : Most negative reviews misrepresent the actual problems with ESO; Crown store mostly doesn't effect gameplay, PVP is in the worst state it's ever been, PVE is more of a community issue than a gameplay issue, ESO has tons of technical difficulties, ESO Support is mostly unhelpful and always tries to shift blame onto unrelated programs when possible.

Starting with context for this review:
These are somewhat first impressions, as I've been playing the game over the weekend, am currently in act 3, and played Path of Exile 2 first. I wanted to try this game out because a new league just started and I was curious how the series got itself going.

The game features a fairly simple to pick up gameplay style in that of Diablo or other Looter Dungeon Crawlers of choice, with a fairly flexible system for building your characters, with characters all sharing the same level up grid but starting at different locations. There are specializations unique to each class though, so that may also determine who you pick to play. Now the fun part are the skills, naturally. In this game you gain skills from gems you find at random around the world, and from quests the game gives out from time to time. There are also gems that don't give skills themselves, but rather add powerful effects to other skills. But the caveat to all this is the way you equip these skills are slots on your weapons and armor. This quickly becomes an issue because it cripples your builds when you don't have sufficient slots on a weapon, or perhaps even the slots not being linked to each other which is required to use those supporting gems. Sure, you can use items to *gamble* for more slots and/or links, but then you have to move all those gems from one piece of armor to another and it gets a bit on the nerves after a while, especially considering how unintuitive the controls are. At least, on controller that is. And no, I will not use KBnM because of a physical disability that cripples my right hand. Digressing aside, this game is rather clunky compared to its successor. There are a lot of Quality of Life features not in this game that are in its sequel that I'm a bit baffled on as to why they're not in this game considering it, being live service, is getting entire content updates still and thus you'd think that little things could be used to spruce up how things go. Maybe they have and I just haven't been around long enough to witness the horror of the earlier builds.

I think what makes this game a "Do Not Recommend" from me, though, has to be the complete and utter lack of enemy variety and the extraordinarily boring bosses. Each of the three acts so far have featured most of the same exact enemies, just recolored and copy/pasted. At least in Act 3 the crabs have been model swapped with beetles. But the most egregious examples are the groups of necromancers with skellymen. And as much as I like a good necromancer and skellyman, it's a bit dull when every dungeon features them, it's just green in act 1, black in act 2, and red in act 3. And it's the same song and dance each time, take out the necromancer so he stops rezzing the skellies and then swat the skellies down. Second most example would be the Golem enemies. They're just the same rockmen, just made of different colored rocks each time. They're not even interesting, they just hobble towards you and bonk you when they're close enough. And as for the bosses, they're rather pathetic. They all follow the same song and dance, you smack them a tiny bit more than a regular mook then they poof and summon a wave of mooks, then they poof back in. Rinse and repeat for as many "phases" the boss has and you're done. Though some lesser bosses at least have the dignity of just going down without summoning ads, but that's just more pathetic. To compare it to the sequel, the bosses don't really ever reach a point where you're just one-shotting until you're at end game when your builds finally kick off and obliterate things, where as I'm not really even optimized and I feel dang near immortal and unstoppable here. 

I dunno, maybe some people are into it, but I am not.

This all said, it's not a bad game. It's got its charms and such, as they say. But I think I'm going to stick with PoE2. Y'all have fun now!

After 414 hours in the Bayou, I can confidently say this isn't just the best extraction shooter on the market. It is quite possibly the best game I have ever played. It is a pure dopamine machine.

Here is why Hunt: Showdown stands in a league of its own:

--Brains Over Aim--
In 2026, let's be honest: everyone has decent aim. While raw mechanical skill and flick shots might carry you in other shooters like Counter Strike 2, here, they won't save you if you get outsmarted. Hunt is a high IQ game that heavily rewards positioning, patience, and strategy over mindless running and gunning.

--Near Perfect Balance--
The game is 95% perfectly balanced. Literally every single weapon is viable and deadly if you understand its strengths and use it in the right context. There is no absolute "meta" that you are forced to play.

--The Best Sound Design in Gaming History--
This is the true game changer and what separates Hunt from every other game ever made. The audio is an absolute 10/10. You could almost play this game blindfolded. The spatial audio is insanely realistic. A gunshot echoes exactly how it should whether it’s 25, 200, or 800 meters away. Because it’s a PvPvE environment, every snapped twig, heavy footstep, or aggravated monster serves as a critical sound cue. You have to play attentively. The audio doesn't just immerse you, It decides on what choices your gonna be making next. I've never seen another game utilize sound like this.

--A Solid Community--
The community is surprisingly fantastic (about 80% perfect, which is rare for competitive shooters). If you don't want to roll the dice with randoms, the official Discord is packed with chill people ready to squad up and communicate.

--Respect for the Player (Zero Pay to Win)--
The developers respect your wallet. The graphics are a gorgeous 10/10 (especially with the recent engine updates), and while the DLCs and skins are incredibly well designed, they are 100% cosmetic. There are absolutely ZERO pay to win mechanics, and you can unlock plenty of great skins just by playing the game.

--The Verdict--
100% recommended in 2026 and for years to come. This is well on its way to becoming my most played game of all time. If you want a tactical, high stakes shooter that respects your intelligence and rewards your patience, buy it.

This is practically a rage game. I've played challenging games before, the problem is that for this game the challenge works directly against the appeal of the game. As the game is presented, there are two main appeals of it. One is making your own spell combinations, and one is that every pixel in the environment is simulated separately. This theoretically gives a lot of freedom in the spells you can use and how you manipulate the environment, and with lots of different spells and modifiers available, I'm sure there are a lot of possibilities.

The problem is, you will die before you get anything good going, almost every time. You only start with a small set of basic spells and have to gather more, but there isn't actually that much available per stage and you can only modify anything after the stage. This means that for the first few stages, your resources are very limited and for me it tended to be more about finding a lucky predesigned wand than experimenting my own spells. I simply didn't have enough resources to try making something good myself. And if you don't have any interesting spells, you won't be able to mess with the environment much either.

So you get through the first few stages and you can finally start experimenting, right? Wrong. Why? Because you're dead by then. I never made it past what felt like the beginning, after many attempts. I'm sure that over time it gets easier, but it's not fun to constantly die before you can get started with anything. With other roguelikes you get a taste of the gameplay even before you get good, but here it felt like the whole appeal of the game was beyond how far I got. I didn't get to experience any of the fun parts, and I value my time more than to keep playing something that just isn't fun.

Another problem is the way of dying. It almost always felt like something impossible to counter, and something that wasn't interesting. It was always something like an enemy that came out of nowhere, a sudden boss fight that I had no chance of beating, an unexpected effect of a spell I was trying if I had the luck to try anything experimental at all. And every time after dying, I'd have to start from the same boring section with the same boring basic spells again. I couldn't rush through the beginning either, because I'd have to gather resources all over again in the hope that I could get anything interesting.

I had high hopes for this game, all the spell combinations and the simulated pixels seemed really interesting. But the unforgiving difficulty really works against it, you never get to actually try anything interesting. If you even get lucky enough to get something interesting going, the game will kill you before you get to properly try it out and send you back to the same boring beginning without anything. It seems like it would be a good and interesting game if it wasn't as unforgiving.

Looking at the positive reviews, I'm not the only one with this experience either. They seem to have similar struggles. I don't know if they enjoy losing over and over again or they think it's somehow worth it, but for me I'd rather play a game where I'm actually having fun most of the time.

I originally picked up V Rising because the idea of combining survival mechanics with Hack and Slash combat sounded interesting, and it turned out to be one of the biggest positive surprises I've had in the genre. I played most of it solo, but I also spent a good amount of time in co-op with a friend. Both ways of playing are enjoyable, although the experience feels slightly different depending on whether you're building your vampire empire alone or with someone else.

The combat is easily one of the game's strongest aspects. It has a fast pace, responsive controls, and a wide variety of weapons, spells, and abilities that encourage experimenting with different playstyles. Boss fights are particularly enjoyable. Every V Blood boss introduces unique mechanics and rewards you with new powers, recipes, or crafting stations, making progression feel meaningful instead of simply increasing your numbers.

The survival mechanics never felt overwhelming to me. You still need to gather resources, refine materials, and manage your equipment, but the game keeps introducing new tools and upgrades that make the grind feel rewarding. Rather than surviving just for the sake of surviving, you're constantly working toward expanding your vampire castle and unlocking new technologies.

Castle building deserves special praise. It's surprisingly deep and gives you a lot of freedom to create a home that not only looks good but also serves practical purposes. Organizing crafting stations, decorating rooms, and gradually transforming a small fortress into a massive vampire castle became one of my favorite parts of the game.

Exploration is also handled very well. Every new region introduces stronger enemies, different resources, and increasingly difficult bosses. Because progression is tied to defeating specific enemies, exploring the world always has a purpose. I rarely felt like I was wandering around without a goal.

Another thing I really appreciated was the value for money. I bought the game for very little compared to how many hours I ended up playing. It's one of those rare games where I constantly felt I was getting far more content than I paid for.

If I had one criticism, it's that the later stages can become somewhat grindy, especially when farming resources for higher-tier equipment. Depending on your server settings or whether you're playing solo, some crafting timers and material requirements may also start to feel a bit repetitive. Fortunately, the gameplay loop remained enjoyable enough that it never became a dealbreaker for me.

Pros:

+ Excellent blend of survival and action RPG mechanics
+ Fast, responsive, and satisfying combat
+ Great variety of weapons, spells, and builds
+ Rewarding V Blood boss progression
+ Deep and addictive castle-building system

Cons:

- Endgame can become grindy
- Resource farming occasionally slows the pacing
- Some crafting timers can feel unnecessary when playing solo

Probably the best designed game I've ever played. The developers know what makes the game fun, and stayed true to that. There are some minor nitpicks I'll mention below, but for the most part, every moment spent in the game will be enjoyable, with only rare cases of grind or frustration.

[h2]Awesome Design[/h2]
The game wants you to have fun. The classes are clear roles you can fill and you just know how to be effective because that's what those classes are good at. The engineer is good at single target and taking out stragglers, the driller is insane at crowd control, the scout is fast and good at taking out high value targets, and the gunner can singlehandedly bring the team back to life or prevent them going down, as well as having high sustained single target damage and even some burst damage. You know what role of the team to fill because your tools work well for that thing. You don't need to even communicate. I mean, probably 70% of my games, the only communication we've had is "look at this" and "rock and stone" and "ready". That's how good the teamwork is, and it's all automatic. You don't need to be someone who is good at teamwork. It's so well designed, that someone who played nothing but sniper in battlefield and camped would be a good teammate in this game.

[h2]Genius Design Choices[/h2]
If you die, you still get some of the rewards you got through the mission, and can be revived in most cases. There is no punishing the player like in many games. You just about never think "that was unfair" even when 3 bulk detonators show up while in uplink. Plus, difficulty is optional, you can just choose a lower difficulty and it only marginally affects rewards. Each weapon feels good (apart from the minigun and smart gun which are garbage) and satisfying to use. The world immerses you with atmosphere and giving you a near-sandbox level of freedom to do random stuff. You could for example just dig straight through the wall instead of going through the normal passages, or draw the enemy back into a more open area or a chokepoint. You could stay together, or have people split for some objectives like finding resonance crystals, and the game doesn't punish you for it. Overall, the game's design is not "opinionated". There is no "correct" way to have fun. They give you the field and the toys to play with, they don't say "nuh uh you're not allowed to do that". It's a breath of fresh air from all the "hey you failed so I'm going to take all the things you like about the game and everything you find enjoyable about it and destroy it" that you see in e.g. games that add "roguelike" mechanics despite having no damn clue what makes them work.

[h2]Criticisms[/h2]
There is a ton of RNG and grind you have to do if you want specific (or all) weapon overclocks. It took me around 450 hours to unlock every weapon overclock I wanted to use, and that's working somewhat "efficiently" and minmaxing. In fact, the last one I considered "good" was one of the last 5 or so I got, so I really did have to unlock absolutely everything in order to get the ones I wanted. This doesn't [i]feel[/i] like that much of a grind because the game itself is fun and you don't absolutely need it, but bear in mind that if you want to experience everything, it will take ~400 hours.

It's somewhat fun singleplayer, but really it's a multiplayer game. The community and cooperaction is about 70% of the game. That's not the fault of the game really so much as just "it's that type of game", much like Insurgency is just that type of game.

It does have a bit of that disease of "you're going to play every day... right? Right..?" in that there are weekly mission objectives (mostly for cores for overclocks) and limits to what you can achieve daily. Along with that, it has some time locked things. For example, I'd love to get the horse mask, but can't until a specific time of year, and I'm not even sure if I can then. This is good and bad. It gives a reason to keep playing aside from just the fun of playing, but why do you need that? And it's also just kind of FOMO.

The amount of actually useful weapon builds is low. For the most part people won't care if you use non-meta builds, but it's pretty obvious there's like, one, maybe two builds per class that are actually "canon" and the rest are just for the sake of variety. For example, no one is going to use flamer + face melter with wave cooker + gamma contamination. That's just not a viable build. Basically, there are good builds, and only a few of them, and then there are tons of useless things no one has a reason to use. Those builds are still really fun, but it is obvious the other overclocks and perks are just to pad it out.

They call it Cracktorio for a reason - this game really is addictive. But unlike a lot of other "addicting" games, I think Factorio does it quite well. The game keeps you hooked because there's always something to do and every task leads into another. You might think that the goal of an automation game is to set up everything and then just sit back and wait for stuff to finish, but that's Satisfactory. In Factorio, you always have something to build or redesign or expand. You want to automate the next science pack, but you're low on green circuits so you expand that first, but now you're low on iron plates so you expand that, but now you're low on ore so you expa-- oh, no free ore patches? Go take some more territory from the biters... but you want a tank to do that more efficiently, so you work on that research, but your military science is a bit slow because... And now you understand the feedback loop. You are [i]always[/i] busy. And that's great.

One of the major successes of the game is that it manages to keep your todo list full without feeling overwhelming. With your factory humming in the background, you can take your time to grapple with a new problem and work on things one step at a time. For example, a lot of new players stumble at oil processing because there's a whole new fluid system to figure out. But you can break it up and work through it piece by piece; the factory will handle itself (it's automated!) while you work out the details of refineries and chemical plants.

The biters act as an antagonist to your growing factory. I'm going to tell you to leave them enabled. They're a great outside pressure that gives meaning to your factory expansion (military science is almost useless without them), and more importantly they provide pushback to prevent you from expanding freely. Too much freedom can make a game dull, so having biters constrain you makes designing the factory a lot more interesting. If you're worried about difficulty, don't be. The game provides plenty of options to turn them down if you really need to, and it's not too hard to set up a few turrets and a wall to keep them out. The biters' strength is modulated by your factory's production, so it scales perfectly for both new players and veterans. Just one bit of advice: restart if you spawn in a desert for your first game.

Factorio is also very good at establishing long term goals with meaningful results along that path. The end goal of the base game is to launch a rocket, and you are a [i]long[/i] way from accomplishing that at the start of the game. But it's not all MacGuffins as you work towards it - the science packs you automate are legitimately useful on their own. For instance, the second science pack forces you to automate belts and inserters as ingredients, two core parts of your factory. Later, utility science forces you to automate the ingredients for construction bots, which are very useful for ...construction. That's not to mention the great tech unlocks along the way like trains or modules, which redefine how you build the factory.

And if you're the kind of person to really get into the technical side, there's a ton of toys to play with. Trains aren't hard to dip into (there's a short 3-minute tutorial by DoshDoshington if you need help with signals), and they can get very in depth with dynamic routes serving dynamic items, or even fancier if you're so inclined. Absolutely the best train logistics system I've seen in any game. But the real technical draw is the circuit network system. Logic and arithmetic operations on signals coming from items that can be used to control logic in your factory... how about a nuclear reactor that manages fuel insertion for optimal efficiency? Or a computer? Don't worry if you aren't into doing that stuff by the way; the game is perfectly playable without bringing out the spreadsheets.

I'd be remiss not to mention Factorio's incredible quality of life. The only bugs in the game are the enemy biters, and everything Just Works when you want it to. Need to find where you produce something? Ctrl F on the map. Need to check some production stats for a machine? Mouse over it and it's in a panel on the right. Installed too many speed boost legs and you're struggling to move accurately? One click to toggle them. I could fill the review's text limit with just QoL features. It's fantastic stuff.

I’ve played a lot of co‑op games, but Deep Rock Galactic is one of the few that genuinely feels like a memory every time I boot it up. I used to play this with my best friend back in middle school, and somehow the game still carries that same magic — the kind that makes you laugh even when everything is going horribly wrong.

If you’re thinking about getting DRG, just do it. This game has a soul. It’s loud, it’s chaotic, it’s ridiculous, and it’s perfect.

There’s something special about dropping into a cave and instantly knowing things are about to get messy. You hear that first distant screech, someone yells “Swarm incoming,” and suddenly everyone’s scrambling like it’s a school fire drill. And when you finally make it to the drop pod with 2 HP, no ammo, and a bag full of minerals you barely survived collecting… that’s the kind of moment you remember.

The game has this rhythm to it — the kind you only understand after a few missions. The quiet mining, the sudden panic, the clutch saves, the last‑second escapes. The kind of chaos where someone falls into a hole they swear wasn’t there five seconds ago, and everyone else has to figure out how to rescue them without dying themselves.

And the Space Rig? It’s honestly one of the best parts. Dancing, drinking, kicking barrels, yelling “ROCK AND STONE” for absolutely no reason — it’s the kind of hub that feels alive even when you’re not doing anything.

Deep Rock Galactic is more than a co‑op game. It’s a vibe. It’s a memory. It’s a tradition. It’s the kind of game where you and your friends become a little squad of idiots who somehow pull off miracles.

I absolutely recommend this game 100%. Whether you’re mining solo or diving deep with your best friend, DRG delivers some of the most unforgettable co‑op moments you’ll ever have. Iv'e played this game for years on Xbox and every moment was amazing.

Well, giving negative review to this game seems almost unfair since there is a lot of quality and charm in this epic vampire power fantasy. ARPG-style gameplay is fun, tons of weapons and different combos/skills, environments and monsters are unique and varied, vampire castles can be designed to your heart's content. Combat is tight with some boss fights really well designed requiring to learn enemy movesets, gimmicks or counters.

However ultimately this game does not respect your time with annoying, limiting mechanics - fighting and traveling during the day is often impossible (good luck when sun comes up during a boss fight in an open field), teleporting with majority of items is forbidden (making a teleporter a one-way really because as soon as you loot anything you cannot teleport back), traversal through enormous map takes forever (even though running as a wolf is fun first few hours). In that respect, game is similar to vanilla Valheim. If that is something that does not turn you off - you will probably like V Rising.

Extraction shooters typically breed a specific kind of anxiety: the hoarding complex. Games like The Cycle (rest in peace, though it was never quite my cuppa) and Arc Raiders often turn me into a digital pack rat, leaving me more concerned with stockpiling gear than actually using it. Hunt: Showdown 1896 operates on a distinctly different wavelength, sitting somewhere between a battle royale and a Tarkov-lite to forge a subgenre entirely its own. You don’t scavenge for your kit; you curate it beforehand. You bring exactly what you want to use, provided you can afford the in-game currency to buy it.

That economy is a fascinating engine. For veterans sitting on years of playtime who refuse to prestige, the currency has long lost its meaning. But I am someone who resets the loop. I prestige, and because of that, the economic treadmill remains genuinely engaging. It forces you to interact with the sheer variety of weaponry and the distinct tactics they demand. Yes, there are undeniable meta choices, especially with the game's new loadout system, but Hunt remains remarkably balanced by the great equalizer of a well-placed bullet. Gear does not guarantee survival. There is a specific thrill in taking a "free" hunter into the mud and—through pure skill, positioning, and patience—wiping a trio of players who just spent a small fortune on their loadouts.

Visually, it is gorgeous for a multiplayer title, but the true gem here is the texture of the sound design. I find the audio to be nothing short of phenomenal. It is incredibly rare to play a shooter where you can rely on acoustic cues with unwavering faith. You can sit in the brush and count three distinct sets of footsteps rushing past a compound. From a quarter of the map away, you can listen to a distant firefight, identify the exact firearms the other teams brought in, and make a decision on whether you have the tools to outgun them. The audio isn't just window dressing; it is radar, intelligence, and atmosphere all rolled into one.

It is a game I play in distinct, obsessive streaks—a month of heavy rotation followed by a few months away to breathe. The consistent updates ensure the game is always shifting (sometimes to its detriment, but usually in a positive direction). And it is undeniably frustrating at times. But here is the highest praise I can give it: in nearly 600 hours of playtime, I can count on a single hand the number of times my frustration was actually directed at the game. When you die, it is almost always your own fault—a missed shot, a poor rotation, or a heavy footstep.

It is a brutal crafted ecosystem that rewards patience and punishes hubris, an atmospheric loop that I will inevitably keep returning to.

Hi. This post is mainly for new players or people considering buying the game who think it's full of fun moments and great times with friends, just like the videos online.

For my first 30 hours, the game felt amazing. Like any other online game, but with one big difference: everyone interacted with each other. I met a lot of kind players, completed activities together, got help, and learned a lot about the game from them. But I have to say this: the number of genuinely good people is tiny compared to the number of toxic, annoying players.

I'll keep playing until I finish the Pirate quests because I enjoy them, and I paid for the game after all. But now that I've reached 48 hours, I can honestly say choosing this as the online game I'd move to after Battlefield and Fortnite was a huge mistake.

I'm not saying the game is bad. It's actually beautiful, relaxing, entertaining, and unique. I enjoyed it so much that I thought, "This is my game. I'm done with everything else. I'll grind this until I become a Pirate Legend."

Then suddenly two players show up who somehow don't die no matter how many bullets you put into them. Even after three sniper headshots while they're standing still, they're still there making fart noises, laughing, emoting, and climbing onto your ship. Meanwhile you've spent an hour doing a boss event, another 15 minutes defeating it, and 5 more minutes painfully carrying every piece of loot onto your ship one by one because of the slow movement speed... and then they kill you, laugh at you, and take everything.

Sure, every online game has toxic players. Some people are just like that because of whatever they've gone through in life or .................. .

But what really amazes me is this game's respawn system. You die, respawn on your ship, get killed again, respawn again, get killed again, over and over while they're throwing every insult imaginable at you and laughing for absolutely no reason. They don't even know you, and you've done nothing to them.

The reason I'm writing this review is because this literally happened to me a few minutes ago.

I found two players whose ship had gotten stuck. I boarded their ship, repaired all the holes, and warned them that they'd hit some rocks. I was doing an event on that island, and when they came back I even told them through the speaking trumpet that there was plenty of loot and I was too lazy to carry it all to my ship. They sailed away, so I continued my event where you have to use the lantern to make the skeletons vulnerable before killing them. I died a few times during the event, respawned, then suddenly heard a noise on my ship. I couldn't see anyone. I went to check the rowboat behind my ship... and instantly got sniped.

That's where everything started...

It's honestly hard to explain everything that happened afterward, but situations like this happen constantly. Then you run into players firing strange purple and green cannonballs that disable both your anchor and sails at the same time, while their ship somehow moves faster than Sonic or the Road Runner.

This game is not beginner-friendly. I seriously mean that.

If you have a friend who's already a Pirate Legend, play with them. Or at least someone experienced. Otherwise, don't start solo. Play with friends your first time. At that point you'd probably have a more relaxing experience playing Dota 2 instead of squeezing your $200 controller in frustration and wondering why, in 2026, you didn't buy ARC Raiders instead.

Putting all that aside, I know I'm a noob. I just started. Almost every time I finally collect loot, something like this happens. After more than 40 hours, I still haven't managed to buy my own ship or even a decent cosmetic set.

Now here's my question for the developers and this community:

Why is everyone so used to the cheaters?

Seriously, why does nobody seem to talk about them?

Combine that with everything I mentioned above, and the game becomes miserable. It feels like poison. Maybe that's not the best comparison, but that's exactly how it feels. The game is full of cheaters and players whose only source of enjoyment is killing random people and stealing a chest worth only 200 gold.

And on top of all that, the progression and money-making systems are painfully slow. Even if none of the problems above existed—which they absolutely do—that would still be an issue.

Honestly, it feels like Rare intentionally doesn't do enough about cheaters. It's suspicious, and it's becoming more and more obvious.

Very underrated game in its genre. Here are my pros and cons for V Rising:


POSITIVE:

- The combat is fluid, responsive, and skill-based, quite similar to League of Legends abilities. You have skillshots, aoe spells, ultimates, summons, effects, etc. You have a weapon which grants you a basic attack + 2 weapon abilities, and 3 spells that you can chose from various schools (2 base spells and 1 ultimate). While quite simple, you can mix and match a lot and obtain different builds.

- The open world feels alive. There are different factions that have towns, settlements, and are roaming around. Of course (almost) everyone is hostile to you, however factions may fight between them. It is also possible for roaming bosses of different factions to fight each other, leading to some funny cheese moments.

- The whole vampire/blood/shapeshifting mechanics are great. The blood system is super interesting and allows for different strengths. You can also turn into wolf/bear/rat/bat/etc, unlocked by bosses and each form having its own utility (mainly outside of combat).

- The base building is nice, being very simple but allowing for some nice designs.


NEGATIVE:

- The grind is a bit tedious at some parts, however the game has the option to modify this by reducing craft times, increasing loot, etc.

- Brutal difficulty is very hard when playing solo, however not impossible. A lot of bosses can be beaten by cheesing them, however without cheesing some have BS abilities that one shot you or summon annoying minions that distract your fight. However this is also a skill issue...

- The camera rotating management needs some time to get used to

"I bought a PvPvE shooter. Instead, I enrolled in an advanced course called 'How to Have a Heart Attack Every 15 Minutes.'"

Hunt: Showdown 1896 doesn't hold your hand. It quietly waits for you to make one tiny mistake, then enthusiastically introduces your fully geared hunter to someone who has been sitting in a bush since the Industrial Revolution.

The sound design is criminally good. Every twig, chain, broken glass, horse, dog, crow, duck, chicken, and apparently every living creature in Louisiana has signed a legally binding agreement to reveal your exact location. By the end of a match you'll instinctively apologize to birds for existing.

This game isn't won by the player with the best aim—it's won by the player who can identify the difference between footsteps on mud, wood, metal, water, and "that guy is definitely flanking us." If your headphones cost less than your keyboard, my condolences.

It requires accurate shooting, map knowledge, quick decision-making, and above all... listening. Sometimes the best strategy isn't pulling the trigger—it's standing perfectly still for two minutes because a duck looked at you suspiciously.

My biggest complaint? You still can't look down while climbing down ladders. Apparently my hunter can banish ancient abominations, survive gunfights, stitch bullet wounds together with dirty hands... but checking whether the bottom of a ladder is clear is simply beyond human capability. Peak realism.

Losing a hunter doesn't hurt anymore. It's just a recurring tax you pay to the Bayou. Every expensive loadout is merely a generous donation to another player's collection. You're not buying gear—you're sponsoring strangers.

And yet... despite the camping, the panic, the betrayals, the jump scares, the mosquitoes that probably hit harder than some weapons, and the occasional player who can hear you inhale from 80 meters away...

...you press "Play Again."

Because no other game rewards patience, awareness, teamwork, and controlled paranoia quite like Hunt: Showdown 1896.

[h1]V Rising: A Gothic Masterpiece of Survival and Action Combat[/h1]

[i]V Rising is a phenomenal achievement in the survival genre, masterfully blending top-down action-RPG combat with deep base building and vampire lore. Developed by Stunlock Studios, this game successfully avoids the typical survival pitfalls by making you feel like a powerful predator reclaiming your empire, rather than just another weakling trying to stay alive. With its fluid mechanics, rich atmosphere, and highly rewarding progression, it stands as an absolute must-play for fans of both survival games and action RPGs alike.[/i]

[h2]🧛 The Vampire Power Fantasy and Atmosphere[/h2]
The atmosphere in V Rising is brilliantly dark and gothic. From the sun-dappled forests to the grim, foggy farmlands and cursed woods, the world feels incredibly alive and dangerous. What makes the game truly stand out is how it forces you to adapt to being a vampire: the sun is your absolute enemy, and navigating the shadows during the daytime turns simple travel into a tense, thrilling puzzle. The visual style is crisp and stylized, perfectly capturing the moody, blood-soaked aesthetic of a dark fantasy realm.

[h2]⚔️ Combat and Blood Types[/h2]
Combat is heavily inspired by Stunlock's previous arena-shooter pedigree, meaning it is fast, fluid, and completely skill-based. Utilizing a mix of directional skill-shots, dashes, and weapon abilities, every encounter feels incredibly engaging. The "Blood Type" system is a stroke of pure genius. Feeding on different targets—like a rogue, a brute, or a worker—grants you unique, dynamic buffs based on the quality of their blood. This turns hunting into a strategic choice, as you actively scout for the perfect prey to boost your specific playstyle.

[h2]🏰 Castle Building and Raiding[/h2]
The base-building mechanic is exceptionally rewarding. Instead of just throwing together a simple wooden shack, you erect a massive, multi-floor gothic castle complete with grand pillars, blood fountains, and production workshops. Watching your domain grow from a small coffin in the woods into a sprawling fortress is intensely satisfying. Managing your territory, defending it from rival players (on PvP servers), and commanding your own vampire servants to gather resources gives you the genuine feeling of being a dark lord ruling over the land.

[h2]⚠️ Drawbacks[/h2]
While the game is incredibly polished, the resource grind can become quite intensive, especially in the late-game stages where crafting top-tier gear requires massive amounts of rare materials. For solo players on public servers, progression can feel significantly slower and punishing if caught in the crosshairs of larger clans. Additionally, the progression relies heavily on defeating specific V Blood bosses, which can occasionally feel like a rigid checklist rather than organic exploration. However, these factors take very little away from the stellar core loop.

[h2]🏆 Conclusion[/h2]
V Rising is a shining example of how to perfectly execute an early-access-to-full-release journey. It successfully combines the tactical depth of an ARPG with the addictive loop of a survival builder, wrapped in an unforgettable vampire fantasy.

Whether you are dodging sunbeams, hunting powerful bosses for their magical abilities, or expanding the walls of your majestic castle, the game offers hundreds of hours of high-quality entertainment. It is an incredibly rewarding indie titan that deserves a permanent spot in your collection.
