This game used to genuinely be my favorite and was so for years. I remember how chaotic it was when the game had just first came out. The community was trying to figure out which voyages were the funnest, the best ways to beat skeleton forts, and how to PvP properly. While it was pretty boring up until about the first anniversary update when new food types were added, tall tales became a thing, arena (rip) was added which all made the game super multifaceted, I still really enjoyed the first year. I remember when we first got the megalodon in the first ever major update and you had to summon it but only by cooperating with other pirate crews. I remember when cursed sails added new npc ships you could fight in the world. I remember when the rare did what seemed like the impossible and added a whole new region with the devil's roar, a volcano-themed region that was more unforgiving but had much better and unique loot that then original three regions.

I talk about the first year of the game because sot had a rough launch. People would play, find it boring, and leave. Only some players stayed around outside of the major updates before the anniversary update came out. But SoT survived because the beating heart of this game is its dedicated community. This feels relevant now because here we are 8 years later and it feels dead again, but now not even the updates feel like they bring life back into the game. Back in 2018, it felt like the game was ambitious and loved by its developers, and I still somewhat believe rare still cares, but it also feels like back then they actually knew their community but now they feel out of touch. Year 1 and most of the years following, it felt like rare really understood that there was a symbiotic relationship between those who mained PvE and PvP. In other words, you had people who primarily preferred doing voyages and just kind of doing their own thing on the seas (like me) and people who preferred to play the game mostly by fighting others or focusing on world events (events where rather than just one crew being able to participate like regular voyages, all crews can hone in on the specific event and fight together or against one another for relatively good loot). Rare was really good at balancing rewarding both communities with good updates while not isolating one from the other to maintain a good community balance. I mean sure, you had the Arena which was a PvP-exclusive gamemode, but unlike modern PvP updates it still prioritzed team work (originally only galleons were allowed in the Arena, which meant you and to cooperate with 3 other crew members to win against the other ships in the match) and also the Anniversary Update as previously mentioned still had plenty of goodies for the main open world gamemode, like fishing, cooking, and the tall tales which were more PvE oriented. Another example was the emissary update, an overhaul to the trading companies (the people who you get and do voyages for) which added more incentives like earnable experience and gold multipliers that made the grind for Pirate Legend (the game's "end game" reward) easier to help boost the PvE side, but also added the Reaper's Bones, a PvP-oriented (but not exclusive) faction that was incentivized to hunt down and plunder the PvE crowd. It overall was an organic way of keeping both groups in contact. Rare has done this plenty of times over, making updates that reward both crowds to both do their own thing and to organically interact with each other.

All of this made the community bustling for years. Sure, you had some toxic folk, but generally both sides lived in an effective harmony. PvE players would grind the game by doing voyages. Voyages created loot like chests which would circulate in the game. Loot incentivized PvP players to strategically attack PvE players for their loot so they instead could profit, or to form an alliance with and protect PvE players so they could get a share of the money earned. If the PvE player lost their things, then they would go back and fight the PvP players after respawning, or vice versa if the PvE player won and was able to cash their loot in. In either case, it made a healthy ecosystem where there existed opportunities for both groups to have fun in their respective way, but also in one which meant both groups were still interacting, making for one big and cohesive community. This created fun, awesome stories that make up the back bone of SoT.

That was until updates started isolating the two groups. Sea of Thieves would start adding more Tall Tales without any incentive for PvP to happen organically, which meant part of the PvE community would stop interacting with the PvP community. On the flip side, updates created more world events that exclusively focused on the PvP aspect of the game, meaning that most PvE players would stop doing world events, leading to less interaction. Ultimately, SoT added both diving and replaced Arena mode with hourglass, which were like gamemodes within the main open seas world where the former allowed you teleport to voyages automatically if your were a PvE player and the later would automatically teleport you to someone who wanted PvP if thats what you desired. Not to mention, both teleported you to new servers rather than keeping you on the same one the whole time. What this created were exclusive missions of sorts that all but ensured that you would no longer organically interact with the other community except for in isolated cases. Now I'm not necessarily saying that both updates killed the game, after all they certainly are time savers which means you can get more missions/fights into a single play session than before, but the reality is that the time cut out was the time where either community could organically interact since you're teleporting to events, not sailing to them.

Don't get me wrong, as a PvE main I love being able to dive. Means I can get more money and reputation (experience) an hour than ever before, but it means that I almost never get into PvP interactions anymore unless I go out of my way to do so, which defeats the purpose of emergent encounters with other players that make those awesome stories.

The final nail in the coffin for me is that the game does get updated still, but unlike maybe four years ago when each update was fun and refreshing, recent updates (so like the past 2 or 3 years) have been nothing short of underwhelming. The developer team keeps running into problems which means that updates get pushed back ridiculously far, content is cut, or otherwise regular content updates get replaced with bug fixes. What this has created is a community expectation of underperformance. In other words, I don't look forward to updates anymore because I always assume they'll flop in some way. This has outright killed the community.

TL;DR, sorry for the rant. I've had years to think about this and I finally wanted to leave a review. Stunning graphics, potential for a fun time, but the community feels dead and the new content feels lackluster. Plenty of content in the game for those who want to try it out, but the lack of a community will make it boring fast. I have hopes that this game can get back on track, but I right now I can't in good faith recommend playing it, especially for the price it's at right now. Maybe get it on sale, but even then I don't recommend. Come back and see if the game is alive again in like a year or so. Thanks for reading.

To start: ESO Has an amazing world, solid voice acting, and one of the most casual-friendly MMO combat setups I've played.

The problem is that almost every system is built around friction:

-Inventory management is absolutely miserable without ESO+.

-The UI is so lacking that addons are essentially mandatory. I considered a minimap addon essential within my first week.

-The game constantly buries information behind unintuitive awkward menus. I spent a solid 10 minutes trying to figure out how to leave a dungeon group.

-Questing is often incoherent. Major characters can appear alive, dead, or meeting you for the "first time" depending on which storyline you happen to be playing. It is very jarring and breaks immersion.

-Progression becomes increasingly about grinding currencies, collections, achievements and champion points (CP). Notice the absence of "gear" on that list. More on that later.

-Endgame optimization effectively expects constant weapon/bar swapping to maintain buffs and access your full toolkit.

-The "solution" is spending dozens of hours grinding Antiquities for Oakensoul, a ring that removes bar swapping by limiting you to a single six-button action bar. I'll be honest, I had choice words for ESO over both the swapping and the "fix".

-Gear progression eventually becomes shockingly horizontal for the average MMO player used to continued vertical gear progression. Once you've assembled a competent endgame build, future upgrades often feel like minor percentage increases rather than exciting power spikes, and these are very few and far between.

I reached 500+ CP, completed all 3 alliance storylines as well as several DLC stories, acquired Oakensoul, capped all tradeskills and have most of my tradeskill trait research done, fully geared my character in build appropriate legendary sets, and was soloing dungeons and world bosses without difficulty. 

Then I realized there wasn't much left except making numbers slightly bigger via CP grinding or collecting things for no apparent reason.

If you love housing, achievements, collectibles, and grungy medieval fashion with a bunch of neon lighting tacked on, ESO can easily provide thousands of hours of content.

I don't. 

After about 3 months, I felt like I'd seen everything the game actually wanted me to do. Instead of looking forward to logging in, I was working through a checklist of daily tasks and long grinds with very small rewards at the end.

I cancelled ESO+ and have moved on.

I am deeply disappointed about the current gun meta and the gunfight situation. For me, the game has never gotten to that degree of anti-fun. I have been playing since 2020, here and there. Almost played every event, and I almost got every battle pass just for the sake of supporting the game. I am tired. So close to leaving. I believe that I am included in a considerable number of silent players who feel like this. Let me explain:

I am generally okay with balloon, event stronghold, and general macro changes. Moreover, I do not go with the general phasing and immersion criticism against the event and event compound. I am generally okay with world changes. But those are the only things I am okay with... Gunfights are the all-time worst.

Close-quarters fight standard:

- Everybody has a gear or some joke weapon in their possession with an instant death guarantee, like a lance, a bow, and a crossbow with custom ammo, or a katana with a perk.

- Everybody has shorty shotguns with infinite ammo or slugs.

- Everybody has dual-pistols with custom ammo or a Lemat with a slug.

Those standards resulted in the instant ending of gambling fights, and they are remarkably boring. Everybody dies within seconds. Who shoots whom first with their joke weapon or some bullshit gear determines the end result of the fight. I have not seen a Nagant pistol in maybe six months. I do not claim that old hunt was perfect; But, you used to fight with pistols, you used to miss shots, and you used to pay for your mistakes. I clearly remember that. Fights have no climax. No mistakes. The only strategy is limited to corner peak timing and one-shotting your opponent.

What about keeping your distance and initiating rifle fights? Yeah...

-Try finding and chasing the Maynard guy in the bushes 120 meters away

-Try initiating the fight against the waiting joke weapon, slug squad, in the bushes

-Try initiating the fight against the waiting joke weapon, slug, and trap squad in the stronghold

-Try initiating the fight against the waiting joke weapon, slug, and trap squad in the stronghold, while Maynard guy 120 meters away shoots you constantly, and 20 minute waiting enjoyer shorty shotgun rusher squad thirds the fight

-Try to evade a headshot from ##### or 1234567891324325's shorty centennial

Everything is anticlimactic. Every single cool aspect or story-creating gunfight is getting bypassed. Whether you win or not, it is instant, includes one tap, a headshot, a joke weapon, and it is anticlimactic. I am tired. There is a disgusting predictability about player behavior, not about the end result but about how it will occur.

Shorty shotguns should be removed. Not a nerf, not an arrangement, they should be removed. Dual pistols should be extremely limited, maybe one option per ammo type, and should require a costly perk. Bow should have a stamina debuff while aiming. Bomb lance should be scarce or situational. Slug should be removed. Weird joke ammo, like turning your crossbow into a shotgun, should be removed. There should be no silencer snipers. Game needs a cheater tracing system, and we should have access to it too, like Valve's Overwatch. I can sense the distinction between a good-luck player and a suspicious wall-hack user. Please search "hunt showdown cheats", and you will see for yourself.

I am suggesting and complaining in terms of gameplay. For example, is Maynard sniper's strongest weapon in the game? No, not the slightest. Should it be removed? Absolutely yes.

Whether the community or developers acknowledge that or not, I do not know, but I strongly believe that the game rings alarm bells. If it continues like that, there will be a seemingly sudden collapse in its player base; However, the collapse will be rooted in long-term problems of the game.

Thanks for reading.

[b]The developers don't want their players to enjoy the product. They want players to suffer and to pay for every drop of positive emotion, and by doing so to build up the player's dependence on spending money.[/b]
 I have been playing this game since 2010 (I am from the beta test) and I have finally moved my account over to Steam in order to leave a review here, so that other people don't waste their time.
[u]Cons :[/u]
- The server list is forever loading, a playable ping is a rare sight, and playing from Canada is hard because of the ping.
- The technical side never gets fixed, yet the economy has been cranked up to the point of absurdity.
- At high tiers there is no point in playing without premium: the grind takes 2-4 times longer, your credits go negative, and you can't consistently play the tank you actually want.
- They added tier 11. On a fair number of tier 10s you can barely scratch their armour, you are just a punching bag.
- Artillery waits 2-3+ minutes for a battle, tanks from tier 7 and up wait 1-2 minutes regardless of the server population, and it rarely drops you in within a couple of seconds.
- There is no balance in team matchmaking, no matter what the developers write. Even battles are rare, usually one of the teams simply falls apart in the first 2-3 minutes.
- In practice the game itself decides when you win or not. You will only get a fair battle after a string of blowouts. It is not you who decides when you win, the game decides it for you by selecting dishonest teams.
- The grind, combined with such poor matchmaking, turns into torture, and at tiers 9-10 the game punishes you with a credit loss even for a win with premium and squeezes you back down to tiers 7-8.
- There are plenty of maps, only a few of them are interesting, and you can't pick them, most maps are built as though the developer had never played the game himself.
- A pile of new maps has been added to the old ones, and on most of them you can't play properly: sit in the bushes for the whole battle. Play actively, and you fly straight back to the lobby.
- You will always be sent to the lobby by projectiles from players flying at you from the void and you will never see them.
[u]Pros :[/u]
- It used to be pure masochism, now grinding vehicles is sometimes even engaging, but with the bad balance even that small pleasure gets lost.
- Lots of tanks with different mechanics. It used to be boxes with a gun that penetrate every other shot, and an autoloader felt like a revelation.
- Fifteen days of premium is enough to grind out a up to tier 9-10 tank. It used to be that a month of round-the-clock play wasn't enough.
- Missions hand out a lot of credits, farming has become easier, but it is pitiful pennies next to what the top tanks cost and next to the negative credits after a battle on tier 9 and 10 tanks.
- The community has become mixed, players now occasionally prefer team play over driving out alone to self-destruct, but a great many toxic players have appeared as well, don't believe me? - Take a look at the comments.
- The overall graphics of the game have become stunningly beautiful.
Conclusion :
- The technical side and team balance have gone unfixed for 10+ years.
- Without premium there is no point in playing, with premium at tier 10 you still end up negative.
- [i]The longer you play, the less enjoyment you get.[/i]
- You will often be thrown onto a team of weak players, you often won't have a chance at winning.

World of Tanks is a game I have thousands of hours in, and that makes this review even harder to write...

Because the truth is: I used to love this game. The core concept is still fantastic — tactical tank battles, armor management, positioning, map knowledge, and the satisfaction of mastering a vehicle. Few games have managed to capture the feeling of commanding historical tanks in such an accessible way.

Unfortunately, over the years, many design choices have pushed the game in a direction I can no longer recommend.

The biggest issue is the growing gap between new and experienced players. A newcomer entering the game today has to face years of accumulated content, highly specialized veterans, complex mechanics, and a huge number of powerful premium vehicles. The learning curve has become extremely steep, and the game does very little to make this first experience enjoyable.

The balance has also suffered from years of power creep. Newer tanks, especially premium vehicles, often feel stronger and more forgiving than older ones, making many tech tree vehicles frustrating to play. The increasing importance of premium ammunition also changes the way many engagements play out. What was once a situational tool has become a standard part of high-level gameplay, creating situations where armor and positioning can sometimes feel less meaningful.

The monetization has also become increasingly aggressive. Premium tanks, battle passes, subscriptions, boosters, special events, and various paid systems constantly encourage players to spend money. None of these features are necessarily bad individually, but together they contribute to a feeling that the game is becoming more focused on monetization than on improving the overall experience.

The 2.0 update did bring a welcome breath of fresh air. New content, changes to progression, and some quality-of-life improvements showed that the developers were still trying to evolve the game. For a short time, it felt like World of Tanks was moving in a better direction. However, these changes were not enough to fix the deeper issues that have accumulated over the years: balance problems, accessibility for newcomers, and an increasingly complicated ecosystem.

After thousands of hours, I reached the point where I simply cannot recommend World of Tanks anymore. The foundation is still excellent, and there is a great game somewhere underneath all these decisions, but the current direction makes it harder and harder to enjoy.

Like many former players, I eventually moved to War Thunder, which has its own problems but offers a different approach to armored combat and progression that feels more refreshing today.

I will always appreciate the countless hours I spent in World of Tanks. But for new players looking for a tank game today, I would think twice before starting this journey.

Going in, you should know that this game is extremely hardcore.

There are almost no second chances, suboptimal gameplay gets shut down extremely fast, and the entire map is designed to rat out your position.

That said, the gameplay itself is wonderful. The world is immersive, the sounds are implemented well, and the graphics are awesome. The guns are balanced - whenever by the damage, velocity, accuracy or price. There is no unfair weapon in this game.
Even the cheapest 25 bucks revolver can one-shot to the head, which makes this game more skill dependent than money dependent. That characteristic is really attractive, since domination through wealth is something that most other extraction shooters struggle with.

I would recommend this game to people that already have a lot of experience with various PVP shooters, or to those that have the grit to push through irritating, unforgiving and unfair matches at the start.

TLDR - The Absolute Best ARPG Ever Made

Pros: Unlimited build depth, incredibly rewarding. (10,000+ builds. 9,876 of which will fail in yellow maps.)
Cons: My wife left me, and I can still see the passive tree when I close my eyes.


Since I made a review about POE2, I feel obligated to review POE1.

I see a lot of players saying how good POE2 is (I still think it's pretty rough in its current state). But if you've played POE2, enjoyed it, and haven't played POE1, you're doing yourself a disservice—and honestly, the entire ARPG genre.

Allow me to explain what you're missing.

---
##1. The Very Small Passive Skill Tree
---

Most games give you a skill tree with a few meaningful choices. POE1 politely hands you a constellation containing 1,300+ passive nodes that resembles a neurosurgeon's MRI after twelve cans of Monster Energy.

Peak game design.

Do you want +10 Intelligence?

Or would you rather spend seventeen passive points hiking across the galaxy to reach a keystone that permanently sets your Life to 1?

Don't worry—you're immune to Chaos damage now, so clearly this was worth it.

People say the passive tree is intimidating.

Wrong.

It's actually very straightforward.

If you don't spend your first 40 hours staring at Path of Building while Zizaran calmly explains that your character is mathematically unsalvageable because you allocated "10% increased Maximum Life" instead of the nearby "+16 to Maximum Life," that's really on you.

It's not a game.

It's a religious pilgrimage.

---
##2. A Flawless "Zero Third-Party Tools Required" Experience
---

One of POE1's greatest strengths is how self-contained everything is.

To comfortably play the game, you only need a few lightweight companion apps:

*Path of Building (Community Fork)* - To simulate playing the game so you don't have to actually open the game.
*Awakened PoE Trade* - To price-check the 400 pieces of garbage you pick up every map.
*FilterBlade* - Because without a custom loot filter, your screen will be covered in so much text that your graphics card will melt.
*Craft of Exile* - To calculate the 0.0003% chance of crafting the item you'll definitely brick.
*PoE Ninja* - To discover that Divine Orbs are somehow worth even more than they were yesterday.
*PoE Regex* - Because naturally you'll be writing regular expressions just to identify map modifiers that instantly delete your character.
**A Twitch stream** - Preferably someone spending 14 Mirrors crafting an item you'll never afford while casually saying, "This is actually pretty budget - league starter."

Who doesn't love needing seventeen browser tabs, three overlays, a spreadsheet, two Discord servers, and a youtube tutorial just to decide whether a pair of boots is vendor trash?

The best part is that every veteran calls these "optional."

It's immersive.

---
##3. The Most "Socially Enriching" Trade System Ever Created
---

While lesser ARPGs lazily let you click Buy, POE1 believes commerce should build character.

To purchase that underpriced item for a single Alchemy Orb, you'll experience the following unforgettable journey:

* Copy-paste the same whisper to 47 players.
* Get ignored by 44.
* Discover two are permanently AFK.
* Finally receive an invite from xX_Shadow69Slayer_Xx.
* Enter a hideout decorated with highly questionable anime pixel art.
  (   .   Y   .   )
* Stand perfectly still.
* Exchange exactly zero words.
* Type "ty".
* Leave immediately.

It is, without question, the deepest multiplayer interaction ever designed.

Forget Wall Street.

The POE economy is powered entirely by Chaos Orbs, sleep deprivation, and people who listed an item eight days ago.

Nothing teaches emotional resilience quite like spending 45 minutes buying one map before someone declines the trade because they sold it twenty minutes ago and forgot to delist it.

---
##4. Visual Clarity? That's a Skill Issue.
---

Other games make sure players can actually see what's happening.

POE1 considers that cheating.

By the endgame, your character moves at Mach 4 while simultaneously exploding three screens of monsters into a seizure-inducing light show consisting of approximately six million particle effects.

Then...

You instantly die.

What killed you?

* Corpse explosion?
* Reflect?
* Volatile?
* Ground effect?
* A white crab?
* A microscopic green pixel hidden beneath seventeen overlapping spell effects?

Nobody knows.

Not even the game.

You respawn in town and receive the valuable life lesson that awareness is temporary, but suffering is forever.

If you can consistently see your own character, your graphics settings are too low.

Or your build isn't dealing enough damage.

Probably both.

---
##5 The Endgame
---

Congratulations!

You beat the campaign.

Now you can finally start playing the game.

Welcome to the Atlas, where every mechanic GGG has ever invented over the last decade has been carefully preserved inside a single map because deleting content would hurt someone's feelings.

Would you like to:
- Delve?
- Heist?
- Expedition?
- Harvest?
- Blight?
- Legion?
- Breach?
- Ritual?
- Ultimatum?
- Betrayal?
- Sanctum?
- Delirium?
- Essence?
- Strongboxes?
- Shrines?
- Incursion?
- Bestiary?
- Harbinger?
- Abyss?
- Synthesis?
- Necropolis?
- Beyond?
- Torment?
- Conquerors?
- T17?
- Uber Elder?
- Uber Shaper?
- Uber Eater?
- Uber Searing?
- Uber Maven?
- Uber Sirus?
- Uber Cortex?
- Valdos? (You wanted to delete your character anyway...)

The correct answer is "yes."

Unfortunately, your Atlas Passive Tree says "no."

Don't worry though.

Once you've invested another 300 hours you'll discover you've been farming the wrong mechanic the entire league.

After 4,200 hours, I have finally finished the tutorial.

I can confidently say POE1 is one of the greatest ARPGs ever made.

It has absurd depth, nearly unlimited replayability, and enough content to consume your free time for the next decade.

I would never recommend it to anyone I care about.

My wife came back.

She saw the Atlas Passive Tree on my second monitor.

She left again.

The game is free.

The cost is everything else.

See you next league.

[h1]The Gameplay: [/h1]
Build a bunch of stuff, but with a solid gathering and combat mechanics. Your strength is entirely determined by your gear and there is no experience or skill tree that muddies that, instead you kill bosses to make progress on your character. So killing 2000 enemies only gets 2000 enemies worth of material, no strength or anything like that. But killing a boss will allow you to now craft better armor or refineries etc. It's an odd, but still very enjoyable gameplay loop. 

[h1]The Story:[/h1]
It isn't really prominent, most of it is environmental story telling which does a good job here. It's not completely bare-bones and the bosses/enemies etc have a very thoughtful placement that tells a story of it's own. There is also your self-made story on how you go about this which is open ended. This is not my favorite style but again it got the job done and it hit the parts that mattered to make it enjoyable for me.

[h1]The Visuals:[/h1]
This game has a lot of confidence and charisma in their art. They know how to give you and your castle good drip. The attacks, the gestures, the style of the environment and enemies all are a delight for the eyes in a well done cartoonish style. Each area has it's own look and feel, and they look and feel great.

[h1]The Sound:[/h1]
This game had a big sound budget, and you can tell. It gets carries it hard, from the sound effects of combat to the music. which are all powerful in their own right. However the voice acting of each an every boss, or your character trumps all that. It really makes fighting each boss unique and anything you do that involves your character talking that much better.

[h1]The Experience:[/h1]
This game reminds me of Tribes of Midgard at first, which also had mechanics were just as weird. However, this game set itself apart with the theme and attention to detail on the small things. I found myself really loving this game whereas I couldn't wait to get off of Tribes. There was love and hella craft put into this game and then you add in the castlvania cross over too... oomf, so good. It's an easy recommend in my book and I can see myself playing it long after I already 100%ed it.

Season 19 was meant to be a game changer, new world additions, PVP updates of course, but also a fully *NEW* reworked Kraken fight/event, and in case you guys don't know, we have wanted this for YEARS now, but instead of following through with this, they cut the content that would add to the overall Adventure mode experience and kept ALL THE PVP instead, adding all of their resources into that instead of what the community has been begging for, FOR YEARS. First of all, the matchmaking is a joke. When you're a 3★ player getting matched against 6★ players, the game becomes absolutely unplayable. Since the player base isn't large enough, this happens far too often.
Another major problem is the weapon balancing. A bow can one-shot you from like 20 meters away, while a shotgun can't even kill someone from 10 meters? That's ridiculous. The last thing I'll mention is the progression and reward system. It's simply broken. There is virtually no reason to prestige unless you really care about a handful of weapon skins. There's also almost no incentive to fight over the game's main objective—the bounty. It rewards so little that most players only go for it because they want the PvP fights. If your goal is to progress and earn Hunt Dollars, you're actually better off avoiding other players and just running around the map collecting loot.
Lastly, the new Hunt Dollar crates are a joke. You drag one across half the map to an extraction point only to receive a measly 100 Hunt Dollars. It's an awful reward. Final verdict: I had some fun playing, but most of the time I was frustrated and simply didn't enjoy the game. Save yourself the frustration and avoid this game.

I'm just now realising I have never left a review for what is one of my favourite games of all time. Noita is hard, often unfair, brutally punishing and painfully esoteric. Health is scarce, death is quick and frequent, if the enemies don't kill you the environment will, if that doesn't do the trick oftentimes you'll wind up inadvertently killing yourself. The tutorial is non existent, comprising of just basic directions, how to kick, how to throw, now off you trot and figure it out. It took me over 50 hours and around 200 deaths just to beat the first boss and get my first "win". I thought I had seen everything...I had barely seen 10%. 

The level of depth and complexity in Noita is frightening, it's a roguelike where the only thing you retain between runs is knowledge, you carry your learning with you and *that* is how you grow your strength for future runs. The gameplay is essentially a deckbuilder, spells being cards and wands being your hands, the limit is legitimately your imagination and understanding of the spells, mechanics and interactions. No matter how powerful you get, how many immunities, how much health, something can nearly ALWAYS kill you. But the feeling you get when a run goes from a struggle to an abundance is addictive as hell and that is the thing that keeps me coming back.

If you get easily frustrated and don't want a challenge, look elsewhere. If complex systems put you off and a single mistake you didn't see coming until the millisecond before it killed you and ended a 6 hour run would make you blind with rage, play something else. But, if you can laugh that off and if you enjoy something that pays off your hard work and rewards exploration, digging, thinking and planning, you will find a lot of joy in Noita.

V Rising looks like another survival crafting game, but Stunlock Studios managed to create something much more unique: a vampire action RPG where every system perfectly supports the fantasy of becoming a powerful creature of the night.

The gameplay loop is incredibly addictive: explore Vardoran, hunt powerful enemies, absorb their blood to unlock new abilities, improve your gear, and build your own gothic castle. Every upgrade feels meaningful, and progression constantly gives you a new reason to venture further into the world.

The combat is where the game truly shines. Fast, responsive, and skill-based, it feels closer to an action RPG or even a competitive arena game than a traditional survival title. Boss fights are varied, satisfying, and require you to actually learn patterns, dodge attacks, and adapt your build.

The castle building is also a fantastic addition. Creating your own vampire fortress, decorating it, and slowly transforming a ruined hideout into a true dark kingdom is incredibly rewarding.

And while the game is already great solo, V Rising is definitely better in co-op. Playing with friends completely enhances the experience: you can share resources, build your castle together, specialize your characters, and take down powerful bosses as a vampire clan. This is where the fantasy really comes alive.

After its early access period and its 1.0 release, V Rising feels like a game made with a clear vision and a lot of passion.

If you enjoy survival games, action RPGs, or simply want to live your best vampire life, this one is absolutely worth your time.

That's when the game starts playing you.
Suddenly every torch blinks in Morse code. The terrain starts whispering your Steam password. Mushrooms are no longer mushrooms—they're unpaid therapists trying to convince your bloodstream that gravity is optional. You stop mining because you need resources. You mine because the wall blinked first. The music isn't background ambience anymore. It's evidence. Every Holy Mountain feels like an interrogation room where the bricks already know what you did three runs ago. The gods aren't angry because you broke the temple. They're angry because they accidentally overheard your internal monologue through six kilometers of solid rock.
You finally build the perfect wand. Twelve modifiers. Infinite mana. Greek letters that look like legal documents. A black hole, a healing bolt, three sawblades, something called "???", and a spell whose only purpose appears to be violating the Geneva Convention across multiple dimensions simultaneously. You fire one test shot.
Reality crashes to desktop.
The explosion isn't an explosion. It's an argument between mathematics and religion. Half the biome evaporates, the other half becomes sentient, a sheep achieves nuclear fission, the sun briefly exists underground, and somewhere in Finland a developer smiles without knowing why.
Fifty hours later you don't ask, "What killed me?" You ask, "Which law of physics reported me?" Two hundred hours later you instinctively avoid suspicious-looking puddles in real life. Three hundred hours later you hesitate before turning on a microwave because it might contain polymorphine. Four hundred hours later you catch yourself staring at gravel, waiting for it to cast Chain Bolt.
The tutorial never ends. Reality never begins.
10/10. Would willingly drink glowing cave sludge because the voices promised "better wand synergy," only to discover the voices were the tutorial all along.

World of Tanks remains one of the most recognizable online military combat games thanks to its successful blend of strategic gameplay, authentic armored vehicles, and competitive multiplayer action. Developed and published by Wargaming Group Limited, this free-to-play title places players behind the controls of a massive selection of tanks inspired by real historical machines. Rather than focusing on nonstop shooting, the game emphasizes battlefield awareness, careful positioning, and coordinated teamwork. Every engagement rewards patience and tactical thinking, making each victory feel earned through planning instead of simply relying on quick reflexes. Whether commanding a heavily armored giant or a nimble scout, every decision on the battlefield can significantly influence the outcome of a match.

The game's greatest strength lies in its enormous collection of more than 800 armored vehicles representing 11 different nations. Every tank class offers its own distinct role, ensuring that no two playstyles feel exactly alike. Light tanks excel at scouting enemy positions with their speed, medium tanks offer flexibility in both offense and defense, heavy tanks dominate the front lines with powerful armor, tank destroyers specialize in devastating long-range attacks, and self-propelled artillery supports allies from a distance. Each vehicle has its own strengths, weaknesses, armor profile, mobility, and firepower, encouraging players to experiment with different technologies and discover which combat style suits them best. Unlocking new vehicles and improving existing ones creates a satisfying sense of progression that keeps players invested over the long term.

Combat is designed around tactical decision-making instead of reckless aggression. Maps feature varied terrain, urban environments, open fields, hills, and defensive positions that constantly influence the flow of battle. Understanding sightlines, hull positioning, camouflage mechanics, and enemy armor weak points becomes just as important as having accurate aim. Players who communicate effectively with teammates and coordinate attacks are often rewarded far more than those attempting to fight alone. This strategic foundation gives every battle its own unique rhythm, with matches frequently shifting momentum as both teams adapt to changing battlefield conditions.

Beyond its standard random battles, World of Tanks provides numerous activities that extend its longevity. Players can participate in ranked competitions, clan warfare, cooperative PvE missions, and rotating seasonal events that introduce fresh objectives and exclusive rewards. Daily missions, progression systems, customization options, and collectible content provide additional incentives to continue playing. Frequent updates also introduce new vehicles, balance improvements, and gameplay adjustments that help keep the experience evolving. This steady flow of new content prevents the game from feeling stagnant and gives veteran players plenty of reasons to return while offering newcomers a constantly expanding battlefield to explore.

Presentation is another area where the game continues to impress. The tanks are recreated with remarkable attention to detail, from their exterior designs to their animations and battle damage. Explosions carry satisfying impact, shell ricochets sound convincing, and environmental effects help create immersive firefights across a variety of locations. The maps balance visual quality with functional gameplay, allowing terrain and cover to become meaningful tactical elements instead of simple scenery. While the game is accessible enough for casual players, it still captures enough historical inspiration to appeal to military enthusiasts who appreciate authentic vehicle designs.

Like many long-running free-to-play games, World of Tanks is not without drawbacks. Progressing toward higher-tier vehicles can require a considerable time investment, and premium options offer faster advancement for players willing to spend money. The steep learning curve may also discourage newcomers, as understanding armor mechanics, spotting systems, ammunition types, and vehicle roles takes practice. Nevertheless, players who invest the time to master these mechanics are rewarded with a deep and highly satisfying multiplayer experience that continues to evolve through ongoing developer support.

World of Tanks stands out because it successfully transforms armored warfare into a thoughtful, team-oriented competition where strategy consistently outweighs brute force. Its impressive selection of tanks, diverse game modes, polished presentation, and long-term progression systems provide exceptional replay value for fans of tactical multiplayer games. Although its progression model may occasionally test players' patience, the depth of gameplay and consistent updates make it one of the strongest and most enduring online vehicle combat titles available today.

I love this game. I love, love, love this game

This game is like learning a language. At first it feels impossible, there are so many things to keep track of, so much to do, so much going on that you don't know what you're supposed to do or what is expected from you

But, as you learn how everything works, concepts start fitting into place. Suddenly things that felt crazy become familiar

I would say this most difficult concept to learn about this game is that everything is slow, like pulling yourself through mud. Except at any point, the mud can turn into a raging river that whips you off your feet.

For the people that love this game, that swap from slow to fast is amazing. For the people that hate this game, that swap is the worst.

Guns are slooooow, reloads are sloooow, animations and running speed are slooooow... except any bullet from any range can 1 shot headshot you (fast). Melee can one shot you (fast). Explosives will  one shot you (fast)

The constant flip from agonizingly slow to suddenly lighting fast is often too much for a new player, or for people expecting consistent play speed

Characters are vanity items - no hero shooter mechanics here.

Guns are available to everyone regardless of time played.

Game mechanics are available from the first match. 

The game asks you to do one thing - get a bounty token out. How you do that is up to you. For some that freedom of choice might be a bit overwhelming at first, but later understanding that freedom lets you do so much more

Onto the actual critiques of the game:

The menus and UI are a pain. No matter what they try to do to sort, or organize the menus it's just always a pain to do things at scale. Applying multiple charms or animations to items or guns is at least 3 menus

There isn't much in the way of onboarding new players. There isn't a reduced size map, or new player modes, you get into the same game that I would get into. Granted, there is some level of matchmaking, but I don't think the levels make any sense

Matchmaking. It feels like its not been considered well. From my understanding its an individuals rank vs the level of the opposing players rank. If I at 6 stars die to a 2 star, my level will drop, and their level will rise. However, if I kill a lower rank player, nothing really happens. The issues with this system, as many reviews have pointed out, is that I can run solo in a team game mode (there by getting placed in lower skill lobbies to give me a handicap), get killed by lower levels to drag my rank down relatively quickly, self revive and win a game by killing the last guy alive with the token.

You may think that sounds pretty boring, but in most games, I'm balls to the walls fighting, killing 2-3 teams before being downed. As most of the players are lower rank than me, nothing happens while I'm getting kills. But I'm getting de-ranked only when I die. For newer players, I can understand this must be very frustrating (check the reviews that call out hackers, and their play time and you can see this viewpoint in real time)

Weapon balancing feels arbitrary. Every weapon in the game is viable (one shot headshot) - but some require insanity to be used. Some guns get forgotten about, while others are left untouched due to the fear of upsetting the community. That or the person who is deciding which changes to allow is using an excel spreadsheet to make their decisions.

Onto the Good!

The events are amazing, holy smokes I love them. Cool mechanics added each time, new things to see and do, often new weapons added (that aren't DLC!!!! :D!)

The VIBES! Game ooooooooozzzzees vibes all day every day. It has its identity down - Eldritch horror cowboys and cowgirls! Yeeeeeehaaaw! Did I mention the art?! And the music!? Ahhhhh - so good

Core Issues, Time Sinks, and Missing Features
While classified as an MMORPG featuring PvE and PvP, Guild Wars 2 feels more like an unbalanced PvE sandbox heavily focused on cosmetic collecting ("Fashion Wars"). Below is an honest breakdown of what new players should expect.

💰 Buyers' Advice for Steam
Do not buy individual expansions one by one. You will be forced to purchase living story chapters separately—either for real money or substantial amounts of in-game gold. If you plan to stick around for more than a few weeks, wait for a sale and grab the Complete Edition.

Key Systemic Flaws
1. Inventory Management & UI Friction
Resource management is overly tedious. Players are constantly interrupted to manually deposit materials into storage or clear cramped bag spaces. During events like WvW Rush, new players spend more time sifting through loot clutter than participating in gameplay. While monetization of bag slots is expected, forcing manual UI interactions every few minutes is an outdated design choice that bloats playtime.

2. WvW & PvP Balance
WvW (World vs. World): The monthly team reshuffling and guild matchup systems create severe balance issues. Large alliance guilds dominate maps, creating massive queue times during peak hours and leaving casual players with no room to participate. The mode lacks dynamic formats like Battle Royale or Extraction mechanics that could revitalize random encounters.

Structured PvP: Heavily impacted by balance power creeps during new release cycles, automated scripts/bots, and frequent AFK players. Match lengths are drawn out with minimal reward yield, even in mid-tier ranks (Gold II).

3. Progression, Story, and Alt Accessibility
Third-Party Dependency: The game relies heavily on external tools. New players will spend their first 100+ hours referencing YouTube and the Wiki just to understand item utility, as native search integration is lacking.

Unskippable Dialogue: Story progression involves lengthy, unskippable dialogue sequences that require knowledge of prior lore. The lack of a story skip feature makes playing alt characters an arduous chore.

4. QoL, Support, and Alt-Friendliness
Support Responsiveness: Customer support experience is subpar, with low resolution rates on tickets.

Lack of Built-In Addon Integration: Essential features like DPS meters (ArcDPS), item trackers, or fast loading mods are absent natively. Furthermore, account-wide quality-of-life mechanics (like gathering tools, legendary items, and infusions) require tedious manual swapping across characters.

A game that respects neither your money nor your time.

You can call this an MMORPG with PvE and PvP, but honestly? It’s an unbalanced mess of PvE and Fashion Wars. Here is the harsh truth before you press "Buy":

⚠️ CRITICAL WARNING FOR STEAM BUYERS
If you decide to buy the expansions separately, STOP. You will end up paying way more because you’ll have to buy Living World story chapters separately (or farm crazy gold for them). Unless you plan to drop the game after a month, buy the Complete Edition on sale!

The Good, The Bad, and The Timewasters:
1. Inventory Nightmare & Artificial Time-Wasting 🎒
From minute one, your inventory, bank, and Material Storage will be choked. Every few seconds while questing, you’re forced to open the UI and spam "Deposit All Materials" like a monkey. It’s 2026—why is this even a thing?! Buying bag slots is a blatant cash grab, but forcing us to manually click deposit every two minutes is straight-up stealing our time. Jump into WvW during a Rush event as a new player, and you’ll spend 80% of your time stressing over what junk to destroy to free up space.

2. The WvW Disaster ⚔️
WvW in its current state is completely brain-dead. Matchups shift once a month, stacking 999-player mega-guilds together. Want to farm with your guild? Good luck! A massive guild is running 24/7, leaving zero room for you. Want to chill in the evening? Enjoy sitting in an endless queue. The monthly reset makes zero sense when scores refresh constantly—it turns into a boring, endless slog. ArenaNet needs to drop a Battle Royale or Extraction mode here to save this dead content!

3. PvP is Broken 🎯
Zero balance whenever new specs drop. Half your games have AFKers or script bots. Battles drag on forever, and the rewards/profit are laughable—even sitting in Gold 2 with useless teammates.

4. "Wiki & YouTube Simulator" 📖
This is the only MMO where I spent my first 100–200 hours watching guides and reading the wiki just so I wouldn’t accidentally delete crucial items. And guess what? There’s no native button to open the wiki without mods.

5. Unskippable Boring Story & Alt-Unfriendly Mechanics 📜
Sure, there's "a lot of content," but it's a nightmare if you hate endless, dry dialogue. You often need to know deep lore just to follow along. The worst part? NO STORY SKIP BUTTON. Want to play an alt? Suffer through the same slow cutscenes ALL OVER AGAIN.

6. Useless Customer Support 🎧
My brother and I sent 10 support tickets combined; they actually helped with one—and that felt like a miracle. Fire the support team and put those resources into fixing dead game modes so we don't feel like flies trapped in syrup waiting in queues.

7. Zero Native Addon Support & QoL ⚙️
No built-in support for basic QoL tools like FastLoad, ArcDPS, or Item Search? That’s BASE GAME stuff. Unlimited gathering tools are locked to a single character unless you manually swap them, and tracking down legendaries or infusions across alts forces you onto third-party sites. It’s all designed to drain your wallet and your precious time.

Path of Exile has become an industry leader and a true cornerstone of ARPGs over the past 14 years and anyone that has any interest in ARPGs should play it to at least get a sense of what a true build makers paradise is like. Don't expect a simple game though. PoE is anything but simple, even if you end up playing a 'simple' build, which is part of what makes it great.

I've still got my beta acceptance letter from 2012 in my account email, and I still enjoy the game today even after playing it for years on the standalone launcher, PS4, and now here. The number of times I've gone through Act1 may be bordering on some sort of condition.  I remember someone watching me play the early beta and how they reacted to seeing the passive tree, it was instant nope. I love the flexibility it allows, but I love making my own builds, which this game is perfect for. If you typically need a build guide, this game may be a little much for you, try 2 first as it's generally a lot simpler to wrap your head around. 

So yes, Path of Exile 2 exists, and I like that game a lot too. I'd even go so far as to say that PoE2 may be a better overall game, but there is something truly special about the original that the second still lacks. Hearing the *ting* of a special drop still excites me. Finding the right slots and links on an incredible item still gives a thrill. Figuring out how to slot your gems so you become so powerful you're wiping the whole screen with a single skill is what it's all about and it's still as gloriously confusing to try and figure out as ever and ultimately satisfying in a way that most games never hit when it all works.

And then there is the speed, Zooming around a map in PoE once you got your run speed up always feels great. Slogging around in PoE2 maps generally does not, even if the combat feels more fluid in general. That said, the UI in 1 is pretty godawful and is completely outdone and mostly fixed by 2, especially the controller binds. 

Both games explain their mechanics in the same way, extremely poorly. You'll have to fumble your way through whatever league mechanics never got explained properly in game (which is most of them) until you understand whats happening or what you need to do, but most of them aren't too difficult to figure out.

As someone that has been a huge fan of ARPGs basically since they were born with the original Diablo, I think this may actually be my choice for the best ARPG ever made. D2 obviously has a lot of history behind it and nobody would question the gameplay, but I'd say D2 has not aged well and the resurrected release just kinda highlighted to me how much PoE has pushed the ARPG genre forward.

Go play it and dont be scared about the passive tree. Dive in and make a build that could be awesome but likely sucks then try again with something else or go play something else until next league, thats PoE in a nutshell and I love it.

It's got a lot of good gameplay, but then they follow it up with some really dumb design choices that make the game super frustrating to play.

As an example, there is NO WAY to turn off "Medium core", aka drop items on death. Now by default you don't drop your gear, so that's good, but by dropping the rest of your items on death, it means that if you die on a boss with anything on you (like consumable health potions to heal before re-engaging the boss) you're screwed. Now you have to pull the boss while on low health, then try and loot your shit, then reset the fight.
This gets made all the worse if you decide to use the late-game amulets, which also drop on death. And because Item Level is everything, now you're 25 item levels lower than anything on the run back to the boss and will die in one or two hits. 

Speaking of Item Level, I think it's a really questionable system. I get the idea, it's a way to scale enemies while allowing for flexibility in gear. 
But in practice what it means is that later on in the game you settle on one weapon, because it becomes super expensive to have separate weapons, and if you ever switch off of that weapon, it'll lower your item level and you'll now take a lot more damage.

There's more, like the game being impossible to play with anything higher than 60 ping. I played with a friend on 120ms, and I had so many times where I was dodging abilities on my end, and then the game saying "no fuck you, you got hit".


Anyway, if you're looking to play solo or with low latency, look at changing some server settings. Otherwise you're gonna be in for a bit of a rough time.

This game is a must-play. Let me break down why:
Firstly, it sharpens several vital human qualities. Vigilance is paramount; at any second, a galleon might rise from the abyss, seeking to annihilate you and your entire crew since your kindergarten days. Then there is Reliability and Trust. Few games test your faith like this: you’ll find yourself wondering if your comrade is only drunk in-game, or if he’s actually started chanting in Latin in real life. You are forced to believe that when he detonates a gunpowder keg, it wasn't a drunken blunder, but a simple misclick.
The game also hones your Communication skills. You must clearly alert your partner to a hull breach even as thirty skeletons charge at you on a Megalodon. Stress resistance is equally critical; events unfold with such suddenness that you must remain composed, even when you realize you aren't playing as a duo, but as a solo survivor—because your blackout-drunk friend just launched himself into the depths via cannon to scout Poseidon’s realm.
But most of all, this game is the ultimate test of Multitasking. You will master the art of: plugging eight leaks simultaneously, kneeling in prayer for your buddy to sober up, hurling spears into a Megalodon's maw, and dodging enemy fire—all while your "dear" friend at the helm "tends" to your well-being by throwing buckets of his own vomit at your face, turning your screen into something straight out of Plants vs. Zombies. Yet, it also grants you the glory of becoming Jason Statham, harpooning a colossal Megalodon to ride it into battle.

The Elder Scrolls Online proves that you don't need to play a single-player Elder Scrolls game to get lost in Tamriel for hundreds of hours.

The world is massive, and the best part is that almost every location feels worth exploring. From ancient ruins and mysterious caves to beautiful cities and dangerous landscapes, ESO captures the feeling of adventure that made the series famous. 🗺️✨

The freedom is incredible. You can become a warrior, mage, assassin, healer, crafter, treasure hunter, or something completely different. The class system, skill lines, crafting, housing, and countless quests give you endless ways to customize your character. 🛡️🧙

The storytelling is surprisingly strong for an MMO. Many quests feel personal, with memorable characters and fully voiced dialogue that makes the world feel alive. The ability to explore almost all of Tamriel with friends is a huge bonus. 🤝

The amount of content can be overwhelming, the combat may feel simple compared with traditional action RPGs, and some of the best features are locked behind expansions or subscriptions. Still, the sheer amount of things to do makes it one of the most complete MMORPG experiences available. ⭐

I started with a simple quest. 200 hours later I was decorating a house, crafting gear, stealing from NPCs, and still finding new places on the map. 😂🏰

Deep Rock Galactic is one of the best co-op games I've ever played. Every mission throws you and your team into procedurally generated caves filled with bugs, valuable minerals, and plenty of opportunities for complete chaos. 🪲💥

Each class has a unique role, and they complement each other perfectly. The Scout lights up the caves, the Engineer builds platforms, the Gunner keeps everyone alive with heavy firepower, and the Driller solves problems by making new tunnels. Teamwork isn't optional—it's what makes the game so satisfying. 🤝

The progression system is excellent, with weapon upgrades, overclocks, cosmetics, and seasonal content giving you plenty of reasons to keep coming back. Even after hundreds of missions, every cave feels different thanks to the random generation. 💎🔫

The grind for certain upgrades can take time, and higher Hazard levels become brutally difficult without good communication. Still, the amazing community, fantastic soundtrack, hilarious moments, and endless replayability make those minor complaints easy to overlook. 🚀

I wanted a game with genuine player interaction, but when I tried to ask questions and seek help in the world, I was met with sarcastic, unhelpful answers. You are pretty much left completely alone, forced to constantly search Google or read a massive wiki just to figure out how to progress. The mechanics are incredibly overcomplicated for a newcomer—the inventory is a bloated nightmare of junk, the build systems are total option-overload, and the solo story mode features cruel, frustrating difficulty spikes.

I am out £150 between expansions and gems, and I am leaving the game feeling completely lonely, exhausted, and forcefully isolated. I didn't want to rush or min-max, I just wanted a kind home where I could make friends and play at a 'go slow' pace. Sadly, this game has just left me feeling heartbroken and left behind.

Hunt: Showdown is just phenomenal. In terms of atmosphere, sound design, and pure tension in the bayou, this game simply has no equal. The gunplay feels fantastic, every single shot carries weight, and the adrenaline during firefights is off the charts. The core gameplay loop hooks you completely.

But there are a few things that are absolutely infuriating:

The UI changes. It’s an absolute disaster. Why turn the menu into an unreadable mess? By the time you gear up your hunter and find the traits you need, you’ll develop a nervous tic. Usability just flew right out the window.

The keybind display bug. This makes my blood boil! If your game is set to English but your Windows keyboard layout happens to be on anything else when you launch it, the UI completely breaks the tooltips. Instead of telling you to "Press F", it just shows "Press |||"—and it does this for literally every single keybind on the screen. The worst part? It stays like that until you completely restart the game with the English layout selected. It's incredibly annoying to look at.

Yet, despite this technical sadism from the devs, I still find myself hitting that "Matchmaking" button over and over again. The gameplay itself completely overshadows the flaws.

After spending a good amount of time in Guild Wars 2, I finally understand why so many people call it one of the most underrated MMORPGs ever made.

Coming from World of Warcraft, the biggest adjustment wasn’t the combat or the classes—it was the philosophy of the game itself. GW2 doesn’t push you into an endless gear treadmill. Instead, it embraces horizontal progression, encouraging you to explore, experiment, and simply enjoy the world. It felt confusing at first, but once it clicked, I found it incredibly refreshing.

What I loved

* Extremely casual-friendly. Whether you have an hour after work or an entire weekend, the game respects your time.
* A massive world spread across many expansions. At first it looks intimidating, but I actually like how each expansion feels like its own adventure.
* Buy once, own it forever. No mandatory subscription constantly reminding you to “get your money’s worth.”
* Questing feels natural. Dynamic events, exploration, and world interactions make the game feel alive instead of sending you from one NPC with an exclamation mark to the next.
* Dialogue, quest stories and NPC interactions have much more personality than I expected from an MMO.
* The community is genuinely welcoming. Veteran players often go out of their way to help newcomers.
* Most importantly, this feels like a game made with passion. There are countless small details that show the developers cared about creating a world rather than just another live-service product.

Things to keep in mind

* If you’re coming from a traditional MMORPG like WoW, expect a learning curve. The game’s systems and progression work very differently, and it took me a while to understand what I should actually be doing.
* Fourteen years of content is both a blessing and a challenge. As a new player, I often had to look up lore videos just to connect the story. It’s not really a flaw—it’s simply an enormous amount of content. My advice is to take it slow and enjoy one chapter at a time instead of trying to catch up all at once.

Final thoughts

Guild Wars 2 is a truly unique MMORPG that deserves far more attention than it gets. If you’re looking for a fantasy world where you can explore, relax, follow great stories, and progress entirely at your own pace without feeling pressured, I can wholeheartedly recommend it.

Noita is the third most fun Roguelite game I have ever played. Let that be known. Being third does not mean it is weak — it just means the two games above it have not been blown up by me yet.
The difficulty of this game is basically high-level gameplay inside another high-level gameplay. You think you are a wizard, but in reality, you are just a fragile office worker. You think you are exploring an underground world, but the underground world is actually giving you a performance review. Fire burns me, poison drowns me, electricity stuns me, acid gives me a little kiss — the whole experience is basically: “Life as an adult is already exhausting enough, and now I am getting brutally educated by a tiny pixel of liquid.”
But honestly, this game is unbelievably addictive. Every death feels like a failed situationship: it starts with great chemistry, slowly goes completely out of control, and then somehow everything explodes. One second I am carefully studying wand builds, and the next second I have become a full-time researcher investigating my own cause of death.
The Steam Workshop is even more insane. It turns Noita from “a pixel wizard suffering simulator” into “a public exhibition of modders’ mental states.” Some of the custom maps and content are so rich that they do not even feel like mods. They feel like love letters written to the world by creators who lost their minds at 3 a.m. Some of them are even crazier, bigger, and more creative than the base game itself.
If you like pixel art, Roguelite games, magic, explosions, and the abstract joy of saying, “I literally did nothing, so why am I dead again?”, then this game is absolutely worth trying.
The only requirement is patience. If you do not have any, do not worry — this game will train you. And if it cannot train you, it will at least beat you into becoming humble.

You can explore maps, complete events, fight world bosses, do story missions, PvP, WvW, fractals, raids, strikes, mounts, crafting, achievements, fashion, whatever. The game does not constantly force you into one path, and I really like that. You can leave for months, come back, and not feel completely useless because your gear is outdated.

The world itself is probably the strongest part. Tyria is colorful, full of different zones, and the open-world events make the maps feel more alive than in many other MMOs. You are not just collecting ten wolf skins forever. Sometimes you randomly join a group of players fighting a huge boss, defending an area, escorting NPCs, or doing a big meta event across the whole map. Those moments are still great.

Combat is also fun. It feels more active than the classic “stand still and press skills” MMO style. Dodging, moving, weapon swapping, positioning, and timing actually matter. Some classes feel really satisfying once they click, and the game gives you a lot of freedom to experiment with builds.

Another thing I respect is the mount system. Mounts are not just faster horses. They actually feel different and useful in different situations. The raptor, springer, skimmer, griffon, roller beetle, skyscale — each one changes how you move through the world, and getting them feels genuinely rewarding.

That said, the game definitely becomes repetitive after some point. Once the initial excitement wears off, a lot of the loop becomes map completion, farming events, doing dailies, grinding achievements, collecting currencies, unlocking cosmetics, and repeating similar content for rewards. It is not always bad, because the gameplay is enjoyable, but you do start to feel the pattern after a while.

The story is also a bit mixed. Some parts are genuinely good, and there are characters and moments that are memorable, but it is not always consistent. Sometimes it feels epic, sometimes it feels a little cheesy or rushed. I would not say the story is the main reason to play, but it adds enough context to keep things moving.

Guild Wars 2 is not a perfect MMO, and if you need a game with endless fresh content every single day, you may eventually burn out. But it respects your time more than most MMOs, has a great open world, fun combat, amazing mounts, and a lot of things to do.

It does get repetitive later, but honestly, most MMOs do. The difference is that Guild Wars 2 is still enjoyable enough that coming back after a break feels easy.

Definitely worth trying, especially if you want an MMO that does not punish you for having a life.

I bought this game a couple of days after it released in early access in 2018 and have revisited it on and off over the years.

I really wanted Hunt to succeed, but every time I come back, I remember why I didn't continue playing, and things haven't gotten better over the years. 

Let's start with the GOOD: on paper, the core gameplay loop is actually great. Give me an objective-based extraction shooter over a loot-based one any day!

BUT (and here's the BAD): this quickly gets overshadowed by a plethora of issues the devs have failed to address:
- Negative and unsportsmanlike behaviour is 'meta'. You may want to say "git gud," but there's something deeply wrong when the dominant strategy revolves around cheesy tactics, bush camping, and other borderline exploitative practices. This seems to be even more the case in higher MMR.
- There is no real balance. The latest attempt at balancing loadouts feels like an overcomplicated solution. - it's patchwork thinking instead of addressing the root cause.
- I do have to give credit where it's due: the engine upgrade made the game feel much smoother. Unfortunately, that improvement has been overshadowed by persistent server issues...
- The content has become stale. I'd even go so far as to say some of the recent additions are harmful to the core experience. The latest update (Road to Hell) completely undermine the game's core loop of tracking monsters and gathering clues... And the optimal strategy is rushing the balloon, fortifying that position, and farming kills. If I wanted to play king of the hill, there are much better games for that.

As for the UGLY: the monetization feels completely out of balance and unworthy of a premium game that also sells battle passes. I bought several skins, but honestly, the coolest ones are the default hunters with hunter progression. I don't understand why the developers don't make those the premium offering. I don't want another dark, borderline pay-to-win skin. I'd happily pay for the opportunity to unlock a skin I can lvl up through skill - that would actually feel rewarding. The current monetization just feels lazy and predatory.

The frustrating part isn't that the game has flaws (all live services do!); it's that, after years of updates, many remain unsolved. It's like putting a patch on a festering wound. It may look OK, but under that, the meat is rotting. At this point, I no longer believe that crytek is interested in fixing the issues that matter most.

In the end, the game feels like an empty shell of what it could have been. I really wanted to love this game, but after eight years, I don't think I'll be coming back.

On the bright side: it's not too long now until Hunger comes out, something fresh to sink our teeth in!

Final note and to echo a friend's review: credit your goddamn devs who worked on the game, crytek!

If you like sandbox games and atmospheric, pirate sailing open world games, then try it.
If you want story-rich, handholding, railroaded games, then avoid it. It does have missions, but they are all dynamic and sandbox, and you will still need to find your bearing in the open sea using a compass and a map. No arrows or markers or pointers in this game, you need to actually use your head to get to places.
If you like some PvP in the open world and don't mind cosmetic-only progression, then try it. There is a PvE game mode for those that don't like PvP. You can do all of the story content and get as much gold as you want there.
If you want or need RPG progression, then avoid it. There is progression, it just won't make your character stronger. It will unlock more cosmetics and more missions (Voyages) to do.
Simple as that.

If you ever wanted a sandbox open world pirate experience with infinitely replayable PvE, PvP, and some great hand-crafted story content to complement (but not the focus), this one fits the description well.

Play this game for the atmosphere of being a pirate in a great open world.
Don't play it if you need to see your character's level increase. Your character does not get stronger, everyone is equal in the open world in this game to make PvP fair and everyone have a chance. PvP in this game is entirely skill-based, not grind-based. 1000h-player and 10h-player are equally strong (mechanically), being differentiated only by their knowledge of the game. And PvP can be avoided by playing in Safer Seas.

If the idea of being a sailor in a ship, or the captain of a ship, and sailing in the open world and living a pirate's life then you'll like enjoy it. If you require constant levelling and RPG progression and becoming stronger through "grind" then you won't like it because the game doesn't have these. Everyone is equal in Sea of Thieves, except for cosmetics (obtained by playing).

It's a game entirely focused on emergent gameplay. Finding emergent treasures, fighting emergent game enemies,  hunting sea monsters, fighting other players, teaming up with other players. Looting others and others looting you, going on adventures on the ocean and then going back to the tavern to sing a song. This is what this game is about.

It has PvE mode (Safer Seas) and it has story content. It's just that those are not the focus of the game. If you want to experience 100% of the content, then you 100% will play on open world PvEvP mode (High Seas).  It has great story content (Tall Tales) but most of the people with 500h+ hours are the ones who enjoy the open world sandbox gameplay. The story contnet is great, awesome even, it's just that it will probably not last you 100h+ hours, only the sandbox open world will.

It's also very playable as a solo player, contrary to popular belief. Half of my gameplay time is playing solo, the other half is playing with friends (or randoms). Playing solo is viable but you need to learn the game and have patience and persevere as you will possibly get sunken early on. If that's a problem for you then either play PvE mode or play with friends. If you don't have friends, playing in Open Crew is a thing, just matchmake and the game will put you on a crew in seconds.

It's well-known but somewhat "underrated" game considering it does not always get a mention in great pirate games. Contrary to popular belief, there is a lot of PvE content and PvP does not happen all the time. In my first 30h of the game, maybe 1h to 2h of those have been in PvP engagements at most. That's less than 10% of my playtime, and I only, exclusively play on the open world PvP mode. So PvP is not what everyone says it is, as long as you do not mind the occasional PvP (this is an open world pirate game, PvP is expected, to say the least). If you really hate PvP and want to be completely sure it never happens then play in Safer Seas or look for a different game, and that's fine.

If those points interest you, give the game a chance, it's much better than some people think.

For what it is, and within the extraction shooter space, Hunt Showdown sports itself to be one of the more stable games within its gameplay loop, and its ability to keep its players interested. 

Being someone who has been burned by the Edge of Darkness edition and played at a minimum 3 wipes of Escape From Tarkov, Hunt Showdown is the OG having been out since 2017/2018. 

Hunt is not trying to jump on a bandwagon and I don’t think it ever has, the large base of the community caters towards players in their late 20’s and early 30’s as working professionals who can play a couple of semi-casual games in a week, and its simplistic loot system overhauls the clunkiness of many other looter shooters that try to embody the tetris nightmare inventory of other extraction shooters.

To me at least, this is a game that has a medium floor with a high ceiling in that your mastery of this game is designated by your ability to understand sound cues and your ability to navigate the mechanics which I find new players coming from Siege or Apex or other fast paced shooters to consider alien, matched with the extremely wide FOV. 

The other idea that makes Hunt alien is its usage of double action firearms and the slower fire-rate of its weapons that makes it less of a laser beam tracking game that many other games are often guilty of. The fact that your ability to use your cunning to win specific fights, and that because you’re not constrained by the round based timing of games like CS:GO where the pressure of an interval commits to risky plays, your ability to showcase somewhat slower or more methodical based aggression within engagements is one of the reasons I like this game so much. 

One of the greatest challenges that I’ve found and understood was that Hunt for new players can be hard to pin down due to the consistent events that churn out every quarter similar to how leagues are introduced in Path of Exile. Meaning that many players are unfortunately met with a lot of catch-up for previous patches to understand things like wild targets, loadout changes and what sort of new enemy types are on the bayou and how you’re supposed to deal with them. 

As a veteran player, the consistent roll-outs of battlepasses being recycled in its weekly missions with free-skins in tandem with its quarterly events makes the game consistently fresh and exciting. To the rest of the community, it commits very much to a pub-styled drop-in and drop out style of play for those already familiar with its mechanics. 

While there are some instances of server instability, its matchmaking queue and its ability to get people into games is really a big upside that I think many games within this space have yet to figure out. 

Overall speaking the game is able to healthily bridge the gap and overcome its adversities to stay relevant from the many years this game has persisted, and I happily enjoy it. While I think this game fits a niche that not everyone may like, I’ve spent many hours trying to get better at it.
