# World of Tanks — History Nerd Heaven With a Health Bar 🎖️

I love history. Especially WW1, WW2, military technology and basically anything where someone looked at a giant piece of steel and thought:

**"You know what this needs? A bigger gun."** 😂

And this is probably one of the biggest reasons why I enjoy World of Tanks so much.

## 🪖 The Historical Side

For me, unlocking a new tank isn't just:

*"Nice, +20 penetration."*

Sometimes it's literally:

*"Oh shit, that's a Tiger II."* 😃

I genuinely enjoy looking through the tech trees, recognizing tanks I've read about, comparing different versions and then actually being able to drive them.

Tiger, Panther, T-34, IS, Sherman, Churchill...

For someone interested in the World Wars and military history, this game is basically **Pokémon but for people who collect armored war crimes.** 😂

And surprisingly, Wargaming actually puts quite a lot of effort into this part.

Many tanks are recreated using historical documents, blueprints, surviving vehicles and museum references. Of course, not everything in WoT actually rolled onto a battlefield — some tanks were prototypes and others existed basically only as drawings on some engineer's desk.

But honestly... I like that too.

It's interesting seeing not only what countries built, but also the absolute madness they **wanted** to build. 😂

## 🔧 Authenticity vs Gameplay

Now, let's be clear.

World of Tanks is NOT a simulator.

Historical accuracy stops very quickly when a 60-ton tank starts repairing its destroyed tracks in 6 seconds while being shot by an artillery shell from another postcode. 💀

Gun performance, armor, mobility, reloads etc. are obviously changed for balance.

And that's fine.

Because underneath all the historical stuff, WoT is still an arcade competitive game.

The important part for me is that the tanks still **feel like those machines**.

They look right, sound good, have recognizable strengths and weaknesses and there is enough historical detail that someone interested in tanks can genuinely appreciate it.

## 💥 The Gameplay

And then you press Battle...

Sometimes you have an amazing match where positioning, armor angling and knowledge of weakspots actually matter.

Other times your entire team discovers a previously unknown migration route to one corner of the map and dies there in approximately 90 seconds. 😂

That's World of Tanks.

You can understand armor layouts, penetration values, spotting mechanics, positioning and every tank on the enemy team...

...and still get deleted because somebody in a bush 450 meters away decided your existence was unnecessary.

## 🧠 Knowledge Actually Matters

This is probably another reason I keep playing.

WoT rewards knowing things.

Knowing tanks.

Knowing armor.

Knowing guns.

Knowing maps.

Knowing where someone will probably go before he even gets there.

You slowly stop seeing:

**"IS-3"**

and instead your brain sees:

**"Lower plate, cupola, don't shoot the turret you idiot."**

Which is either game knowledge or the beginning of mental illness. Hard to tell. 😂

## 🎖️ Final Thoughts

World of Tanks definitely has its problems.

Balance can be questionable, matchmaking can make you reconsider your life decisions and sometimes RNG apparently receives direct instructions to personally fuck with you.

But underneath all that is still a game about something I genuinely love:

**Tanks, military engineering and history.**

Being able to go from famous mass-produced machines to obscure prototypes and completely insane blueprint projects is something very few games offer on this scale.

For somebody who loves history — especially the World Wars — simply exploring all these vehicles is already half the fun.

Then you add the battles.

And suddenly it's 3 AM and you're researching the suspension of a Soviet prototype because you need **4% better traverse speed.**

Finished a normal run and I would highly recommend against buying this game, even for hardcore roguelike lovers. There are several critical flaws in the game design, that might not be obvious at start, but eventually will cut your fun from the game considerably.

1. First of all, there is no accessable healing. Outside from killing some minibosses, you have exactly 8 full heals for the whole run (7 temples + 1 in the dark cave). There are couple healing spells, but good luck getting them, and anyway those have limited charges, which can be recharged only ~7 times. There is a Vampirism perk, but good luck getting it, when there is a huge pool of perks and you get to choose only 1 out of 3 random.
As result, while the world is big and has a lot to explore, you simply can't. Without any form of selfsustain, even if you play very carefully - you will lose all of your hp due to chip damage you receive here and there. Eventually you will be forced to enter the next temple and keep pushing for the final boss instead of world exploration.

2. Perk system is flawed b/c of complete randomness. In most roguelikes perk/skill system is the one of deterministic parts of the game - you pick up exactly what you want/need, which allows you tone down randomness of your run with a specific build. In Noita there are over 100 perks, at least half of them are meh, several (like Vampirism or Fire/Toxic Immunity) are a must have, and some are completely useless.
For the normal run you get to choose a new perk exactly 7 times, each time 1 out of 3 random, and some perks can be stacked, so even if you pick them once - they still stay in the pool and can appear again. Also there is a reroll option, but it costs gold, and the cost ramps up very quickly and never resets between temples.
Funny enough, if players could pick their perks manually - I am pretty sure 99% of people would pick Vampirism as a first one, simple b/c of how overpowered this perk is without any other selfsustain.

3. Spell system is... weird? Or more like the spell pool. There are over 100 spells, and even a lot more of different spell modifiers. But many spells are not really different - just copies of each other with slightly different stats. Some spells are not really 'spells' like Bomb, Disc Projectile, Holy Bomb or Nuke. Many spells have charges and are very limited in usage, b/c those can be recharged only once per temple.
Another huge flaw is that you can't edit wands outside temples (need a perk for that). As result you can edit wands only 7 times, and if you found some wand with spells/modifiers you want - you have to pick it up and bring to the temple. But your inventory is very limited - you can carry only 4 wands, and once you entered temple - you can't backtrack and bring some other wand to the same temple, b/c wand editing no longer will work, you have to go to the next temple.
Overall, while the spell system might be fun from time to time, depending on what you managed to get, in the end it feel too bloated and doesn't work well with random loot. It could be much better, if instead of many similar spells, the game would only provide a set of basic spells like magic missile, that could be upgraded with different modifiers making it a fire missile, an exploding bolt or a custer bomb.

To sum it up roughly, Noita is basically an incomplete clone of Terraria with a flawed spell builder.

This game is awesome. There is no subscription fee and its made to be easy to return to, so you can just kinda play it when you feel like it and you're always progressing in some way. They don't increase gear item levels so the gear you get now can be used in end game content pretty much forever. The community is pretty wholesome given how chill the game is and there is a TON of LGBTQ+ representation which is nice to see, along with the main cast having several gay characters. 

Instead of running around doing fetch quests you just kinda run around the maps and engage in whatever is happening, and the more helpful you are the quicker you gain experience. And they get really creative with it. The last thing I did to gain more points to level up my class was to swallow a toxic piece of bacon and trying to stay alive for a minute straight while it tries to kill me. I also got turned into a bunny and had to sneak around healing NPCs to fight for me. You never really know what to expect and it makes it more interesting.

It has a very smart design, where everything you do progresses you in some way across all of your alts. The world feels dense and alive, and literally everything you do gives you little loot boxes that you can open (not the kind that needs you to pay real money), so its exciting. The endgame content is challenging without being anxiety inducing, and everything is added with purpose. All the zones have so much depth and content to do, and it never really gets boring or repetitive. I've also never played an MMO before where you could unlock pretty much everything you need through PvP. So you could play it as a PvP game if you wanted to as well. The game makes it easy to jump between different types of content, which makes it very ADHD friendly. 

The combat actually feels impactful, and even in large scale battles you feel like you're doing something rather than just pressing buttons and watching a health bar slowly trickling away. I usally feel really disconnected from the combat system in other MMOs, but here it feels more like playing an ARPG like diablo or PoE, and it goes for quality over quantity when it comes to the abilities, so you don't get overloaded. At the same time there is a lot of self expression to be done with the builds. Your play style is based not only on the class you pick, but the specialization you pick for that class (each class has 4), the abilities you pick and the weapon you use (each weapon comes with a different ability set for every class). So there is a lot of variety and you feel like you're actually forming your own style rather than having the same abilities as everyone else and having one optimal play style you gotta master. It feels like you are expressing yourself through the combat system rather than being a clone of everyone else playing that class. On top of that there is a dodging mechanic while makes it a bit more engaging, on top of the normal telegraphed stuff you see in other MMOs.

Sea of Thieves is one of the best pirate games made. The water, weather, and overall atmosphere are incredible, and sailing with friends creates some of the funniest and most memorable moments. The sound design is excellent, the music fits perfectly, and discovering islands, fighting skeletons, hunting treasure, and taking on world events always feels like a real adventure.

There are Tall Tales (Stories/Missions), PvP, PvE, fishing, sea forts, ghost fleets, and plenty of cosmetics to work toward. Every voyage can turn into a completely different story, just you can get side tracked really easily.

The biggest downside is the PvP. While it's a core part of the game, it can be frustrating when you've spent hours collecting treasure only to lose everything to another crew out of the blue. The game can be a bit jank at times, but i guess it,s the games own charm, If you're playing solo, you're at an even bigger disadvantage against organized groups, unless you enjoy playing safer seas.

The progression is almost entirely cosmetic, so if you're looking for stronger weapons or better ships, you won't find that here. Server issues and hit registration can also be annoying at times, and some players can be toxic, especially during PvP encounters.

Sea of Thieves is a fantastic game if you enjoy creating your own adventures rather than following a strict story. It's at its best with friends, where every session can become an unforgettable tale of victory, or complete chaos. It isn't perfect, and the PvP won't be for everyone, but when everything comes together, there are very few games that capture the feeling of being a pirate this well.

If you are new to the MMO genre, The Elder Scrolls Online can feel overwhelming at first. You are dropped into a massive world with complex systems, countless stats, and a level of freedom that makes it hard to know where to begin. However, once you get past that initial learning curve, it quickly becomes clear why this game stands out from the rest.

​Streamlined Combat
Unlike many traditional MMOs that clutter your screen with dozens of hotkeys and a daunting list of ability bars, ESO keeps your interface clean and intuitive. You primarily focus on a streamlined combat bar—using five active abilities plus one Ultimate—which makes the action feel much more immersive, skill-based, and manageable. It is a system that emphasizes active combat mechanics like dodging and blocking over simply memorizing long rotations.

​Unmatched Customization
One of the best parts of the experience is how much control you have over your character. From choosing your race and alliance to fine-tuning your appearance down to the smallest detail with intricate sliders, the character creation is incredibly deep. You can truly build the hero you want to be, and with the variety of classes available, you can experiment with completely different playstyles without being locked into a rigid path.

​A World That Adapts to You
I also appreciate that the game continues to evolve to meet players where they are. With the introduction of systems like challenge difficulty, you can tailor the level of danger to your personal skill level, whether you are looking for a relaxing narrative journey or a tougher tactical fight. Whether you are a fan of the Elder Scrolls lore or just love being lost in endless hours of high-quality storytelling, ESO offers a persistent world that feels genuinely alive. It is a rewarding experience that respects your time and lets you progress at your own pace.

PS.. I also have to mention the housing system. While many MMOs treat player homes as an afterthought or a simple menu, ESO treats them as a core part of the experience. The amount of freedom you have to decorate, renovate, and truly make a space your own is incredible. Whether you are a casual decorator or someone looking to build a massive, complex estate, the player homes here are on an entirely different level compared to other games, making them one of the most rewarding long-term projects in the game.

The game has sort of moved on from when I last played, and with POE2 now the hot-ticket item, POE1 is something of a relic of its time. But I played this game from closed beta until the 5th league consistently, then on and off a little since then. 

There is boundless, unlimited fun to be had in POE. By the time you're 20 characters deep and you've tried a ton of different builds-- base classes, ascendancies, gimmicky gem combinations, or funky uniques you came across-- the game is patched and all of that functions or is balanced entirely differently. You come to know the language, the shortcuts, the special combinations that are tried & true and you learn the method to the madness to try new things each patch. It becomes something of a language to you; like all MMOs or intense ARPGs in their own right. But POE is something of a bottomless well of inspiration; the story is interesting, the monsters horrific, the zones exciting & varied. Even when you're 100 times looped through the campaign, there is still some fun to be had in going through with new skills or ideas in play; new challenges when the gear doesn't fall when you need it, or the crafting messes up at that pivotal point of growth. 

POE is a landscape that is always in flux and exploring it has been one of lifes great pleasures for me.

This game has a lot going for it—an expansive map, rich lore, and a grab bag of genuinely smart features. But it’s all buried under layers of bloat and time sinks that sap the joy out of the experience.
The level-scaling keeps you feeling oddly powerless. No matter how much you invest in your build, the game drags you back down to whatever the current zone demands. Combat mobility is another drag: get brushed by an enemy and you’re slowed to a crawl, which makes every encounter feel stickier than it should.
Mission design leans heavily on padding. Objectives are stretched to the far corners of each instance, and mounts are mysteriously disabled inside them, forcing long, empty runs between bite-sized tasks. Encounters don’t help either: trash mobs can take ages, while some elite-looking enemies melt faster than a shirtless, barefoot zombie. The tuning is inconsistent, and the time-to-kill rarely matches the threat telegraphed on screen.
Strip away the busywork—the backtracking, the sluggish debuffs, the marathon treks—and you’d have a tight, compelling adventure. As it stands, the game’s best qualities are smothered by design choices that seem aimed at padding playtime rather than elevating it. There’s a great game in here; it just needs to be freed from its own grind.

500 hours is not a milestone that I reach with very many games. Sitting here about a year and a half after I first started playing Deep Rock Galactic though, I can confidently say that this game is a personal all-timer, as well as one of the most well designed video games I've ever played.

Ghost Ship Games are one of seemingly very few dev studios in this current gaming landscape who really seem to "get it"; They aren't here to sell you lootboxes, FOMO skins in a battle pass, or make you download 15 external launchers so you can play some bloated, unoptimized AAA piece of crap- they're here to make a kickass video game that delivers on all its promises and still [i]continues[/i] to get better to this day. Every piece of gameplay relevant content in Deep Rock is unlockable for free by simply playing the game, and 99% of cosmetics are also unlockable in the same manner. The game does feature a battle pass system, but it's completely free and you can switch between current and previous seasons whenever you want to work through them at your own pace.

In an industry plagued by greed, apathy and deceitful marketing, DRG is a much needed breath of fresh air and reminder of how far a little integrity, passion, and respect for your playerbase can take you. It's one of few games released in recent years that I can say I'm truly proud to be a fan of, and has most certainly earned its "Overwhelmingly Positive" review score. Simply put, this is gaming done the *right* way, and if you should take anything away from this review, it's that Deep Rock is an incredible game made by a team who really cares about their product, and they will most certainly treat you right as a player.

---------------------------------------
Right then, now that I'm done glazing GSG, let's actually talk about the game itself: Deep Rock Galactic is a co-op, class-based horde shooter that, if I had to summarize, would say is sort of like a combination of Team Fortress 2 and Left 4 Dead. You have 4 classes to choose from and a mission objective to fulfill, which can range from mining precious minerals to escorting heavy machinery through the fully procedurally generated cave systems, all while fighting off hordes of alien bugs. 

The pacing of missions in this game is really well done. Depending on the mission length and skill of everyone on the team, missions will usually take about 15-45 minutes in total, with big "swarms" of enemies happening every 5-10 minutes. This results in brief periods of intense action, followed by comparatively calmer periods of ambient waves where you have time to mine materials and work on the objective. It creates an engaging flow where you never feel too overwhelmed or completely bored out of your mind either.

The difficulty in DRG is modular, catering to players of any desired level of engagement. If you want an adrenaline pumping, balls to the wall action shooter where you're constantly fighting for your life, it can do that, or it can be a chilled out mining sim where you occasionally fight things- and anything in between. It's one of those brilliant types of games that can be as easy or as hard as you want it to be, and your rewards for taking on harder missions are adjusted accordingly (but not to an extent where it feels like you're "punished" for not playing on high difficulties). It's very casual friendly, but offers a lot of depth and difficulty options for players seeking more of a challenge.

DRG does class balance remarkably well, with each class having a strong sense of identity in terms of how they traverse the caves and what they excel at in combat:
-Gunner is an all around beast in combat, but is somewhat lacking in mobility 
-Scout has excellent on demand mobility with his grappling hook and excels at picking off priority targets, but struggles against large groups of enemies
-Driller excels at crowd control, and can use his drills to manipulate the terrain to he and his team's advantage
-Engineer is a generalist in and out of combat, equipped with decent mobility via the platform gun, as well as sentry guns that are great at locking down an area 

Every playable class feels like they bring something of value to the team, with none ever fully outshining the others. I find it particularly cool how their mobility tools are designed to be useful to the whole team- not just the person using them. You don't even have to be consciously trying to help your teammates, but because anyone can use a gunner's zipline, an engineer's platforms, or the tunnels and shortcuts created by a driller, you often end up helping your team as a byproduct of simply helping yourself. It's a really genius way of handling co-op game design, and is just one of many reasons why I think DRG is such a masterclass in this genre.

The game was clearly designed with co-op as its main focus, but in my experience, it's still fully enjoyable as a singleplayer game as well. In solo missions, you're joined by an autonomous drone named Bosco (we love him very much) who is able to fulfill a lot of the functions that you'd otherwise have to rely on your team for to complete missions in a timely manner. Unlike many other co-op games, it doesn't feel like you're not getting "full experience" if you choose to play Deep Rock by yourself. It's really just a matter of preference, and I find myself having a pretty good time either way. 

It's worth mentioning that the community for this game is exceptionally nice and welcoming towards players of all skill levels. Even after 500 hours, I can count on one hand the number of times I've ever actually had a bad experience with people in a public match. Players regularly coordinate with their team in chat and make sure everyone is ready before starting objectives, and post-mission dance parties in the space rig are a frequent occurrence. I don't know what it is about space dwarfs that seems to really bring out the best in people, but you'd be hard pressed to find a less toxic gaming community out there, and for a co-op game like this, I think that's a pretty major selling point.

---------------------------------------
Overall this game is an incredible experience, and while there are many more praises I could continue to sing about it (and had planned to before I realized how close I was to already hitting the character limit lol), you should really just do yourself a favor and experience what it has to offer for yourself. Regardless of which angle I approach it from, Deep Rock Galactic stands out as an industry leader in just about every front imaginable, and for the evident amount of love in care that has been poured into it throughout the years, I think it is well worth the modest asking price.

[h1]One of my favorite games ever[/h1]

Extraction shooters are one of my favorite types of shooters. I like the risk of losing more than just a single match. It feels similar to playing an ARPG on Hardcore, giving items more value as the chance of losing the gear you have gives you a reason to aquire more than one of them. Hunt however is kinda [i]casual[/i] with it's risk vs. reward scaling which I find surprisingly nice here as it just means we spend more time fighting than managing inventory and storage. Some other games in the genre have you sifting through endless storages playing Tetris with items but in Hunt we just hire a new hunter, slap on a loadout with like 700-1500 hunt dollars depending on how you like to play, pick a couple perks for the Hunter and go. A minute of prep, usually max 5 min in a queue, game on.

The game looks and sounds great, runs very well and the gunplay is very, very good. The bigger guns will absolutely deafen you and even the smaller pistols feel weighty enough and the fights are intense. Soooo intense. Most fights aren't won by just who shoots better but with who read the situation the best. Are there monsters around you? Are they a hindrance to you or a possible shield preventing a free push? Do you have the high ground? Do you have a way out? Can you rotate and flank or should you place down some traps and hold the fort? Did you recognize their gunshots earlier? Are they carrying shotguns or rifles? Do they even know I'm here?

Questions and answers will start flying in your head like the meme where Zach Galifianakis is overthinking equations. It will become second nature for you to avoid certain things and ignore others when know you don't need to worry about it right now. Above all Hunt is a game of knowledge and that makes getting better very satisfying because it's not the headshots that taste the sweetest, it's the outplays.

Ridiculously immersive. Seriously, the lightning is fantastic, the sound design is impeccable (in both clarity and quality), the dark aesthetic is consistent across the board, the Hunter designs are all very good (and awesome if I may), the quality and attention to detail in every single PoI on all maps... It looks, feels and sounds fantastic.

Gameplay wise it's addictive. Only extraction shooter I've personally tried that didn't feel kind of miserable. That signature extraction shooter dread is very much present though, it's just not disgustingly punishing. Gunfights are brutal, good number of PVE monsters to fight, decent handful of bosses. 

Plenty of weapons to try (for me it's the Vetterli rifle, you will most likely fall in love with specific guns thanks to skins and sound design alone, it's all well balanced imo. You should pay attention to their stats and how they handle but it's not like there's a consistent meta, most players at least from my experience run what they like more or less). Perk system to build characters. Lots of variety. Also a lot of different gadgets (drone-like bugs you can control remotely to scout an area, remotely detonated TNT, a jar of bees you can toss, dynamite, flashbang, grenades, it's all there and more!)

Only things I don't like are certain perks.

- The Serpent is one, it lets players steal Bounty Tokens, aka, THE item you want to extract with at a distance. Sure, they need to be close (25m I believe?) and it takes a few seconds, but if they're being sneaky and know the layout of whatever place the token is in, and depending on the spot where the bossfight took place, there's an alright chance they can make a run for it without really engaging in the fight if they do it properly. - Hundred Hands. Again getting killed with one shot anywhere on your center of mass at a decent distance is not very good. It takes practice from the Bow user to do consistently but like, to me, the main draw from the Bow and similar weapons should come from the fact they're very quiet and obviously don't produce muzzle flash. Predicting with it is not hard to do and unless the Bow user is far away, compensating for the arrow's drop off is not necessary, just aim anywhere on the chest area at up to 30-ish meters and there, insta kill from what may be the quietest weapon in the whole game.

I really wanted to enjoy V Rising because the game itself has a lot going for it. The visuals, combat, progression, and survival mechanics are all excellent. Unfortunately, the controller implementation completely overshadowed those strengths for me.

My biggest issue is the camera controls. The default controller scheme requires continuously holding L2 to freely rotate the camera. I don't mind isometric games at all, I actually enjoy them, but this is one of the most uncomfortable controller schemes I've experienced. Constantly holding a trigger while moving, fighting, dodging, and managing abilities quickly became frustrating and unnecessarily fatiguing.

Before deciding to leave this review, I spent a good amount of time trying to solve the problem with Steam Input. I tested custom configurations and community layouts, expecting to remap the controls into something that felt more natural. None of them achieved the result I was looking for. From my experience, the game's controller implementation limits what Steam Input can do with the camera controls, leaving the default behavior essentially unchanged.

This isn't a complaint from someone who gave up after a few minutes. I genuinely wanted to make the game work on controller and invested the time trying to fix what I considered its biggest flaw. Unfortunately, after exhausting every solution I could find, I came to the conclusion that this is simply how the controller support is designed.

For me, the camera controls were a major drawback that prevented me from enjoying an otherwise excellent game. If the developers ever add native options for more conventional camera controls or allow greater customization, I'd gladly revisit my recommendation.

Until then, I can't recommend V Rising based on my experience as a controller first player.

V Rising is an outstanding survival crafting experience.

The combat feels fantastic from beginning to end. It's responsive, satisfying, and offers a huge amount of build variety through different weapons, spells, passives, and jewel modifications. Every V Blood boss feels unique and requires a different approach, making each victory rewarding. We played on Brutal difficulty, which was challenging without ever feeling unfair. Learning boss mechanics and improving over time made every encounter satisfying. It's also fun when roaming bosses unexpectedly run into each other and start fighting.

Castle building is another standout feature. The building system is intuitive and easy to use, and I really enjoyed designing, decorating, and continuously expanding my castle. New crafting stations, decorations, and upgrades keep unlocking throughout the game, giving you plenty of reasons to keep improving your base.

Exploration is consistently rewarding. Every region has its own distinct atmosphere, enemies, resources, and bosses, so there's always something new to discover.

Progression is excellent. Unlocking new abilities, crafting stations, and recipes through boss kills and research always feels meaningful. I expected the game to be much grindier than it actually was. Gathering resources can occasionally become a little repetitive, but it never felt excessive.

I had previously played the game solo and never finished it, but this time I experienced it with two friends in PvE, which made the game even more enjoyable. We skipped PvP entirely, and for us that was the right choice.

Visually, the game looks great. The gothic art style, music, and sound design all work together to create a fantastic vampire atmosphere. The gameplay is clearly the main focus rather than the story, and that's exactly where the game excels.

The game is quite long but never overstays its welcome because there's always another meaningful goal to work towards.

Performance was flawless during my playthrough. I didn't experience any bugs or technical issues.

Overall, V Rising is an outstanding survival game with excellent combat, rewarding progression, satisfying base building, and a world that's genuinely fun to explore. Highly recommended.

If you’re looking for an MMO with a massive world, deep lore, and hundreds of hours of content, The Elder Scrolls Online is one of the best options on Steam. Whether you enjoy questing, PvP, dungeon runs, crafting, or simply exploring, ESO offers something for almost every type of player.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its storytelling. Unlike many MMOs where quests feel repetitive, ESO delivers fully voiced characters, interesting side stories, and zones that feel alive. Fans of The Elder Scrolls series will especially appreciate the lore and freedom to explore iconic regions across Tamriel.

The combat can feel a little unusual at first compared to traditional MMOs, but once you get used to it, it becomes fast-paced and rewarding. Character customization is also excellent, allowing players to experiment with different classes, builds, weapons, and playstyles without feeling locked into one role.

Visually, the game still looks impressive, and the soundtrack creates an immersive fantasy atmosphere. The community is generally welcoming, especially for new players joining guilds or group activities.

That said, ESO does have a few downsides. Some content is locked behind DLC or the optional ESO Plus subscription, and inventory management can become frustrating without it. The combat animations may also feel clunky to some players, especially in the beginning.

Overall, The Elder Scrolls Online is a fantastic MMO that continues to improve with regular updates and expansions. It’s easy to recommend for both Elder Scrolls fans and MMO players looking for a huge world to get lost in.

My S.O. and I like to spend time together later in the day playing whatever multiplayer game we can get our hands on. We typically play through a game (or at least a good portion of one) before moving on to the next or getting distracted by something else. It's usually the second. One day he mentioned trying V Rising. At first I wasn't sure, but over time the idea grew on me, especially since it looked fun and fit with my recent aesthetic interests.

V Rising is a survival RPG where you play as a vampire, roaming the world, drinking blood, climbing the ladder of bosses, and eventually facing Dracula himself... and that's really all it is! Somehow, though, I fell in love with it. It even became my own cozy game. It definitely isn't a cozy game by design, but it became one for me.

You can build your own castle and gardens, transform into different animals, explore a variety of biomes, and place your castle almost anywhere you want. You can play in your own private world, open it up to the public, or simply share it with a friend.

Interested?
~~~~

• Art/Graphics

The art is pretty good. It reminds me of many modern games with a similarly smooth, stylized look, such as Fortnite. However, V Rising uses that style in a way that perfectly suits its darker theme. The world is filled with rich, realistic color palettes that give everything a gothic atmosphere.

The textures especially shine when you're building your castle, and oh my... the castles are gorgeous. You can create almost anything you can imagine, and the building system lets you achieve an incredibly high level of gothic elegance.

The animal forms are always fun, and the wolf form is surprisingly adorable despite the simple art style. If the visuals aren't what you expected at first, trust me, they grow on you. The game manages to feel sleek, clean, and fast-paced while also being detailed and atmospheric, which works wonderfully with its top-down perspective.

It's a beautiful game, and the lighting is absolutely top-tier for me.

• Music

Originally, the music didn't stand out much to me. I wasn't expecting anything on the level of Castlevania, but it initially felt fairly simple.

Over time, though just like the art, it really grew on me. The soundtrack feels mysterious, subtle, and ambient. There were plenty of moments where I'd simply wander through a forest biome, listening to the quiet strings alongside the sounds of nature.

It feels dark and haunting while also being oddly comforting. It really captures the feeling of being a vampire, making me think about both how powerful and how lonely they can be. (It reminded me a lot of Alucard from Castlevania.)

• Gameplay/Mechanics

The gameplay flows beautifully.

As mentioned before, this is a survival RPG, but it also plays from a top-down perspective. When you're venturing outside your castle to hunt, gather resources, or defeat bosses, it almost feels like a Diablo-style game. You're constantly collecting materials to bring home and craft into new equipment and structures.

Combat is where the game really shines. It's fast-paced, responsive, and incredibly satisfying. Unlike Diablo, however, movement is done entirely with WASD while aiming and attacking with your mouse. At first this feels a little unusual, but it quickly becomes second nature.

Your main abilities are mapped to Spacebar, Q, and R, and boss fights can become incredibly intense. There are plenty of moments where your adrenaline spikes because you're constantly dodging attacks and making split-second decisions.

There are also many different weapons to suit your preferred playstyle. The Sword, Axe, Mace, and Spear each serve different combat purposes while also excelling at gathering specific resources. Axes chop trees efficiently, Maces are best for mining, and Spears deal extra damage to creatures. As you progress, you'll eventually unlock bows and even dual pistols, giving combat even more variety.

• Magic

Alongside the weapon system is an excellent magic system.

Every boss you defeat unlocks new crafting recipes, equipment, and magical abilities. There are schools of Blood, Fire, Frost, Necromancy, Illusion, and Storm magic (along with passive abilities). They're called different names in-game, but that's essentially what they represent.

You can only equip four abilities at once, so you'll need to think about how you want to build your character. Whether you prefer charging headfirst into combat, chaining together fast combos, or staying at a distance while supporting yourself with ranged spells, there's plenty of freedom to experiment.

• UI/HUD

The UI takes a little getting used to. There are a lot of menus assigned to different keys, and remembering what each one does can be confusing at first. K opens the V Blood menu, J opens your spellbook, B enters building mode, Tab opens your character menu, and so on.

Once you get used to it, though, it all feels very intuitive.

The HUD itself is clean and unobtrusive. Your current objectives stay tucked away in the top-left corner instead of constantly demanding your attention. Aside from your minimap, the day/night clock, your abilities, and your blood meter, very little clutters the screen.

• Overall

This game has grown on me so much, and I absolutely love it.

It took a little while, but the combination of the art, music, and gameplay creates an atmosphere that genuinely feels like living as a vampire. If you enjoy top-down action RPGs or Diablo-style gameplay, I think you'll really enjoy V Rising.

It has an atmosphere that I haven't really found in another game. Even compared to something like Vampire: The Masquerade, V Rising feels unique. Playing it has also made me even more excited for Dawn of the Bloodwalker.

For me, it's become a relaxing comfort game. It's incredibly easy to boot up, spend a few hours building a castle, gather resources, defeat a boss or two, and log off feeling satisfied. Unlike many survival games, it never feels overly stressful. Aside from managing your blood supply, most of your time is spent building your castle and progressing through the game's excellent boss system.

Overall, I give V Rising a **9.2/10**.

Deep Rock Galactic is a delightful take on the cooperative horde shooter. Each dwarf has both unique weapons for dealing with hordes of giant alien arthropods and unique team traversal/utility tools to get around the dark and sprawling caves generated for all the different random mission types. The progression curve is very enjoyable, with leveling up your dwarves as the initial goal and unlocking weird weapon modifications as the endgame.

The game is less opinionated than most horde shooters about how quickly you'll progress through its different difficulty levels; you still have to traverse the caves to find and mine minerals regardless of the difficulty, so there's still lots to do even if there aren't constant enemies.

Since its release, the game has had so many incremental free releases that the amount of content to explore here is staggering. Thankfully, there's a pretty good in-game guide to the basics of all the missions and events.

Because the game's caves are labyrinthine and light is a limited resource, this game has a steeper learning curve than usual with regard to situational awareness. Expect to get horribly turned around and need help from your teammates until you've gotten the hang of using the in-game tools for keeping track of the map, the cardinal directions, the objectives, and your fellow dwarves.

TL:DR; A fun roguelike where your personal creativity with combining and using spells is rewarded by a very reactive environment. Has some odd gameplay omissions and additions that I don't quite understand the reason for. Feel's not quite finished, and is more frustrating than fun a lot of the time.

Noita's 2 top features are its custom spells and its fully simulated environments, and they both react with each other well- pun intended. coal and oil burn, water extinguishes, acid melts, etc. You can put together some pretty powerful or highly unadvised spell combos as the game goes on or if luck permits on a run. This is the games highlight, and why most people would want to play it.

The player fragility and often unclear directions or mechanics conveyance make most runs a mixture of high tension exploring, entertaining experimentation and frustrating lack of room for error. You are not given an objective for the first mine, just... get in there champ, I guess. I didn't know I was supposed to be looking for a purple teleporter to get my level ups and new spells. Why am I here at all? I dunno, something to do with eggs based on the intro.

Also, you can eat things on the floor. I only know about this because the key map on the pause menu says so, the tutorial at the start of each run doesn't mention it. I've yet to find anything worth eating, or not actively harmful. Is this a joke? I know there's at least one perk related to it, but other than that I'm stumped.

Why is there no run button? you can fly a pretty decent distance and height by default, but you're stuck at a kind of half jog speed without spell assistance. If you're going to make us replay the intro mine every time you die- and you will die a lot -why can't I dash through if I'm quick and reflexive enough? Or just for fun?

Running through would be inadvisable most of the time anyway unless you're very familiar with the levels, as most things in this game are quite deadly- but I think that should be a choice the player makes. Player fragility is not uncommon in roguelikes but most things here kill you in 1-3 hits if its not a continual status effect like burning. You would think this fragility would be twinned with high dexterity and dodging- but the best way of playing seems to be blasting things at max range slowly.

I think ultimately I enjoyed the elements of Noita that it sells itself on, but everything else either feels unfinished or frustrating. It felt like 2/3's of a game, and a decent 2/3's at that, but what's there can be as annoying as its entertaining and what's not there feels like an aching absence of narrative context or mechanical encouragement.

It really just comes down to RNG and having a prisoner that is preferably already at 99% blood quality.

Other than that most achievements are fairly straightforward where if you simply play the game you will unlock most of them, however as I said you need to complete the game on Brutal. This is the sole reason as to why the difficulty rating is hard as especially Dracula is a tough boss. The gameplay is very unforgiving, mechanics poorly explained, and you can't use logic to extrapolate on how your upgrades interact with the world. You have to learn through trial and error in a roguelike game that will kill you in 1-2 hits from explosions starting off-screen and send you back to the start. I also managed to get myself soft-locked early on from a polymorph potion turning me into an uncontrollable, wall-clipping worm that ran out when I was stuck in a wall.

There's mods that allow respawning, which I'd recommend if you're giving the game a try - but beware that damage immunities will not make you immune to damage you'd expect. Being immune to damage from electric shocks for example does not mean you can fire a lightning bolt in water and be fine, because against all reason - a lightning bolt does explosion damage instead of shock damage. 

A friend who plays this game also informed me that fire immunity does not even grant you damage reduction from lava - even though you'd assume both are heat damage. 

I really wanted to like this game, but because it feels like it's trying to cheat the player at every turn. There's definitely difficulty you can learn to handle, but with seemingly random explosions everywhere - self-damaging spells, and unclear mechanics - I find there's not a proper learning curve to get you into the game without looking up guides to prepare you in advance for all the unfair nonsense the game will throw at you.

Deep Rock Galactic is a game I ended up loving way more than I expected. It has such a strong gameplay loop, and everything about it feels like it was built by people who actually understand what makes a game fun to keep coming back to.

The mining is probably one of my favorite parts because it is not just something added on the side. It is built into the whole experience. You are digging through caves, making your own paths, searching for resources, finishing objectives, fighting off swarms, and trying to make it back out alive. It gives every mission its own personality because the caves feel different, the situations change, and things can go sideways pretty quickly.

I also really like the mission structure and progression. There is always something to work toward, whether it is leveling up, unlocking new gear, upgrading your character, or changing how your dwarf looks. The customization is a big part of what keeps the game interesting. It gives you enough freedom to make your character feel more personal without making everything feel overly complicated.

The game also has a lot of charm, but what I appreciate is that it still has enough action and chaos to keep it from feeling too simple. Personally, I would like to see them continue leaning a little more toward an older teen or adult audience. There are already plenty of games out there that feel like they are trying to appeal to everyone, especially younger players. Deep Rock Galactic has enough personality, grit, humor, and attitude that I think it could keep growing in a slightly more mature direction and still feel completely natural.

I also played the other game that came from this universe all the way to the end, and I really enjoyed that too. I think it says a lot that this world and style can work in more than one type of game. Whether it is the main co-op experience or the other third-person style game, they seem to know what makes Deep Rock feel fun and recognizable.

Overall, I think Deep Rock Galactic is heading in a great direction. The mechanics are strong, the missions are fun, the progression feels rewarding, and the customization gives you a reason to stay invested. I really hope they keep building on it because this is one of those games that already has a great foundation and still feels like it has a lot of room to grow.

Guild Wars 2 is, in all seriousness, possibly the best MMO ever made.

Ignore the 16 hours, my actual time is over 850 hours.

I've played Final Fantasy XIV, I've played World of Warcraft, I've played Old School Runescape, and I've played the worst Korean grind fests in existence. But nothing, and I mean NOTHING else in the MMO space has ever caught and kept my attention like Guild Wars 2 has.

The sheer amount of content that this game has is absolutely astronomical. Heck, 850 hours in and I still have barely touched a significant amount of different elements of the game like PvP and World vs World. The base free game has a good amount of content, but even just getting the combo expansion pack of Heart of Thorns and Path of Fire, will give you hundreds of hours of things to do. The depth that exists within Guild Wars 2 is phenomenal and even a single expansion pack can give hundreds of hours of gameplay. Level 1-79 is just the tutorial, the real game begins at 80. EVERY expansion is designed for level 80 (max level) in mind. 

A notable reason for the depth is because of how combat works overall. It's a mix of classic tab-targeting with a kind of simplified action combat. It was fairly new for the time the game was released in 2012. Every class of 9 has tons of usable weapons, and all of them play quite differently. Combine that with the massive amount of skill and feature combinations, and there's so many different ways to play any one class. And then when you start getting into prestige classes from the expansions? Over 600 of my hours in the game have been spent on a single class, and I've barely even delved into some of the prestige classes for it. There's so many different ways to play and so many different things to try out.

To top that off, there's three primary game modes, each that scratch a different itch for what you might want. PvE, PvP, and WvW (World vs World). Each fills a different role in the game, but each of them can progress without too much influence form the other. PvE is exactly what you think it is, running around questing (although quests don't work the same in GW2 as most other MMOs). PvP can be pretty intense. And WvW is a kind of in-between with massive scale contests between three different teams. It would take too long to describe each, but suffice to say, one of them will almost certainly speak to you.

But the most important and special feature of GW2 is its horizontal progression. If you started the game in 2012 and got ascended or legendary weapons or armor, that very same equipment is still perfectly usable to this day. There's no constant treadmill of loot. Once you've got it, you've got it. The "end-game" is mostly about convenience than anything. Yeah, things take a while, but you never feel that you're underpowered, because it's not hard to get to a perfectly viable point. Legendary weapons have the exact same stats as ascended, it's just that you can freely change their stat at will instead of having to spend gold to do so. You can use ascended weapons items for the entire game and never bat an eye, because they're just as good. You can take a break from the game for a month, come back, and be right where you were. No catching up. No feeling of FOMO (except for the daily/weekly quests, which isn't honestly a huge deal). It's a game that respects your time. Not because it is fast, but because it honors the amount of time you put into it.

Also, the game can run on pretty much any computer from the past 15 years. The devs have made sure to keep the low settings of the game usable for even the lowest-tier of potato-PCs. So don't worry about your specs, you can play this game and it'll run fine.

GW2 has its flaws, bugs, and various problems, sure, like anything. It can be a bit confusing at first, some of the bag restrictions are annoying, and some of the systems are a bit dated. But the community is mostly very nice (maaaaaaybe not PVP sometimes) and people are happy to help when you ask questions for the most part.
I've never played an MMO that has kept me on this long and where I'm always happy to play it. It's worth your time and a lot of fun.

P.S. You can access the wiki from the in-game chat by typing "/wiki (insert thing to look up here)". Don't be afraid to use it, because you absolutely will.

[b] I have been playing this game f2p for 1000hrs+. Here are my 5 top tips for other f2p players. [/b]

[h3] 1. Don't focus on winrate, focus on damage [/h3]
If you are f2p, you can be sure matchmaking is biased against you most of the time. So don't rely on winning the match, just focus on getting as much damage as possible even if you draw or lose. Accumulating damage often increases your chances of winning as a secondary effect. Having low winrate but high WNX rating is totally fine.
Another big thing - accept that your tank may be simply inferior to an enemy's tank (especially against paid premium tanks) - pick your fights accordingly.

[h3] 2. Buy premium days using battle pass chips from the store [/h3]
Game isn't worth your time unless you have a premium account. For f2p players, this is the most OP strat to getting premium time completely free. +50% xp and credits, as well as daily 5 x3 multipliers (easily the best thing about premium). Will accelerate tech tree progression HUGELY.

[h3] 3. Get MASSIVE credits using tier VIII premium tanks [/h3]
Completely free as well - once you have enough bonds (you can get them for free in many ways), go to the store and buy any tier VIII premium tank. I most highly recommend T-34-3, 122-TM and SU-130PM (but it's totally up to your preferred playstyle). Join a clan which runs credit boosters regularly (many youtubers/streamers have these kinds of clans open to all skill levels), pair it with personal credit booster and WOT premium and play these tanks to print 500k-1M credits per hour.

[h3] 4. Prioritise equipment rather than buying loads of new tanks [/h3]
From about tier VI onwards, you should try to put 2, ideally 3, pieces of equipment on all your tanks. These seem to cost a lot, but the price is definitely worth it if you select the right equipment and you can cover the cost with a few tier VIII credit grinder matches (see point above). You can be sure paying players already have their tanks fully equipped, so doing the same evens your odds against them.

[h3] 5. Save up millions of credits for big 50% discount sales [/h3]
Every few months, there will be a huge 50% credits discounts on consumables and all tech tree tanks & equipment will also have a purchase discount. Use this opportunity to stock up on consumables (buy hundreds at a time), buy new tanks and 2 or 3 pieces of equipment for each.

[h3] 6. Miscellaneous advice [/h3]
- Use small repair kit & small first aid kit & NO FOOD - saves huge amounts of credits for wealth-building
- Don't spend gold! You can't really earn gold f2p other than a couple painfully slow ways.
- Use automatic fire extinguisher - although more expensive per unit, you only pay when it's used in battle. Normal fire extinguisher is bought every match.
- Use tanks.gg to look at armour models and learn from your mistakes. Accept that certain (often pay-to-win) tanks are simply superior to yours.
- Don't hesitate to use premium ("gold") shells - you will lose few credits compared to what you can make back with tier VIII credit grinders
- Learn how the camo system works - not being seen by the enemy is far more effective defence than hard cover. It's heavily mathematical and will take some time to get used to.
- If you're playing a light tank, ignore the chat - 90% of players aren't smart enough to play one well but love to play armchair general (me included, probably)

Deep Rock Galactic is my absolute favorite space racism shooter. I remember watching gameplay videos and thinking that mining rocks looked super tedious. I never expected that once I bought it, I wouldn’t be able to put it down. It's got one of the most immersive worlds I've ever experienced in a game.

The game features four distinct classes, each with its own unique personality. These characters have sparked tons of memes and fan art over the years. The voice lines are iconic and super catchy. Fan-favorite robotic companions like Bosco, Molly, and Dotty (Doretta) are absolutely adorable, though Molly can be a bit annoying sometimes. Because "leave no dwarf behind" is a religion to me, I always bring Dotty’s head back home. After all, dwarfs mine rock and stone, and so does Dotty. That makes her one of us.

With a wide variety of weapons, builds, biomes, enemies, mission types, and modifiers, the gameplay stays fresh and diverse. For casual fun, there are also cosmetics and arcade machines, offering a glimpse into the limited entertainment available to a dwarf. That said, beginners might feel a bit lost at first, you often won’t know where you are or where the objectives are, and a moment of distraction can leave you separated from your team. The 3D map, rather than a flat 2D layout, can take some time to get used to. Because of this, I highly recommend greenbeards jump into multiplayer right away. Having a greybeard around to guide you makes a huge difference, helping you learn the basics and preventing small mistakes from turning into mission failures.

The game nails the balance between power fantasy and real challenge. An optimized build lets you dominate hordes, but Haz 5+ and Elite deep dives quickly remind you how important teamwork and resource management are. In clutch situations, a single resupply slot can decide the entire team's fate, making skill, strategy, and experience absolutely critical.

I used to play exclusively with my friends in private lobbies, but once I started joining public lobbies, I found that most players are incredibly friendly and helpful. It’s honestly one of the most wholesome communities I’ve ever come across. If I weren’t currently hooked on Helldivers 2 and playing all the other stuff I grabbed during the summer sale, I’d jump back in a heartbeat, this game just holds a very special place in my heart.

I had been wanting to scratch a vampire itch for awhile now and have always been on the fence about this game. The appeal of facing tons of bosses, building my own castle, and slowly but surely becoming the number 1 vampire was so alluring.

[b]PVE, PVP, or SOLO?[/b] - I played on a PVE sever, so no fighting other players. Which, if all you want to focus on is the bosses and castle building, then this is the way to play. So you dont have to worry about others destroying your castle that you spent hours on. Because once its gone, you gotta start from scratch. The community of players I saw, out in the wild, are super friendly and helpful. At this point in the games life, they are mostly people who have already completed the game several times and are just helping others with bosses. So if you need help, especially late game, they will help.

I hear PVP servers can be super sweaty, and very difficult for new players. So play at your own discretion.

[b]Castle Building[/b] - was awesome! Keeping in mind, you wont have the coolest things at first, but certain bosses you defeat allow you to craft cooler and cooler things for your castle as the game progresses. From, different lighting options(with several colors), to wallpaper to change up your castles look, flooring, decorations etc...,,you can literally make your ideal castle. Designing each room with different lighting and decorations really made the place feel alive, especially with your servants walking around. I spent so many hours building my castle the way i wanted.

[b]Progression[/b] - can feel a little slow. On normal, your usually on an even playing field with the enemies, but on brutal they are typically like 3 lvls above you. So for combat on brutal, its alot of trial and error. Constantly running back to finish the job or pick up your gear. Gathering enough materials can take a bit too, but luckly if your playing in your own server, you can tweak those setting and get material faster.

[b]Boss Fights[/b] - good depending on who you ask. Each boss has their own cool design, attack, or gimmick. Like diablo or PoE. They can certainly have a learning curve to them. So optimizing your spells and weapons are a must on brutal. Towards the end game, i did have some help, from other players on the server, for the final boss. It was awesome, their was like 6 or 7 of us all fighting [spoiler]Dracula.[/spoiler] It wasn't easy, we failed dozens of times, due to his scailling with more players. But in the end, we got it done and it felt like i was raiding in an MMO, it was a highlight of this game for me.

[b]My only gripes are small nitpicks:[/b]
- Your walking speed in crazy slow. A chunk of gameplay is the dreaded walk back to your gear or boss, once youv'e been killed.
- Needed more character customization options. The character creation is rather lacking. Wish it was more fleshed out to build my ideal vampire.
- If you play on a PVP or PVE server, expect not many plots of land to build your castle. The ideal/bigger plots of land are likely already taken. You wont have to worry about this if your playing on your on solo server.
- TRISTAN THE VAMPIRE HUNTER....F YOU. WHY ARE YOU A FREE ROAMING BOSS IN THE STARTING ZONE AHHHHHHHHHHHHH.

[b]Biggest Positive:[/b]
Shout out to that one castle who had a loaded flower garden for anyone to gather (to use for crafting gear/potions). So helpful. You are the real MVP of this game.

[b]Overall 9/10 game.[/b] If i had more time,  i would have stretched this game out longer because of how fun it is. But i paid $7 for this, and i got MORE than my moneys worth of it. [b]Highly Recommend.[/b]

On that last part, I must say, the game's quite intuitive, for the most part. As is the basebuilding system.
The only complaint I've found myself to have are some things I find to be oddities and a bit nonsensical, primarily about controls (keybinds, options, etc.) but you get used to it. 

Overall, great game if you love OWSC + Vampires + Action combat

V Rising is part ARPG, part survival crafting game that balances on a tight rope between the two effectively. The combat system never felt dull or like I was playing it on auto-pilot. I was constantly changing my build to meet both the challenging boss fights and other players. This game begs to be played with friends, especially in a competitive environment. It was very fun having one group of friends ambush another while they were farming resources or trying to defeat a particular boss. The base building and castle siege mechanics were very fun to play around with, and I remember fondly as I conquered an enemy castle like a medieval king coming to claim his rightful place against the plebeians who dare reach above their station. Some of the later boss fights, but especially the last 4, felt like high level raid bosses in an MMO, with a lot of dodging, bobbing and weaving, as well as perfect timing necessary to survive the encounter. The endgame systems, when not directly related to pvp, felt more like a vehicle to facilitate the pvp than anything else, and I could definitely feel my friend's patience wearing thin as we got more involved in the end game gameplay loop.

This is one of those things that I regret having to say, as it is a beautiful game with a solid set of mechanics. The maps aren't horrible to look at, nor explore, nor play. Despite this you wonder: Why the no?
There are numerous points where players with the knowledge of the history of the game and just real world history can point to several vehicle choices that are outright confusing. They underperform for their tier while others tend to over perform in the same tiers. All of these due to configurations that just...didn't really exist. I can understand the desire to make things fun to draw in new players, but telling players to hit up the main three because that's what the game is balanced around and thusly will be the only way to have fun while learning the game reeks of shoddy craftsmanship.
Collector tanks: Too many early tanks have been moved into the "collector" area of the store in the desire to simplify the tech tree, but even back in the day these early tanks tended to perform incredibly poorly. Really, their poor performance should have designated them for permanent removal from the game rather than putting them in a hidden store section.
Premium tanks: I wouldn't have a problem if there were no fomo or gatcha mechanics in a lot of these, because they're usually not awful nor good. Yet their advertising and sale method leaves a slimy taste.
The early game: Say you're new, you've just made a new account, you're not a well known twitch streamer, but rather an average Joe. The game is incredibly, overtly hostile to you as a person. With accessibility features reaching the bare legal minimum to avoid a lawsuit, story and training modes that train you the wrong way to play a map with the philosophy of: "We trained him wrong, because it was funny." and a player base that generally doesn't want to interact with a new player. This builds into newbie bullying crews who seek out and actively try to make new players have a bad time. Attempting to contact them with a request for help learning the game leading to a slew of insults, and then a block. All of this is not at all helped by the social media presence that this game has. With only the best being promoted and highlighted over the average player you won't see how the game will actually treat you. A few of them actively call new players fecal matter, though in much less a polite term, and encourage the idea of elitism within the game. Others simply tend to pull up the ladder behind them and leave a string for the best to climb if they're interested in trying. With zero moderation features that matter, no active moderators, and zero intent to course correct, what we get is simply a game that is hard to experience despite its beauty, difficult to learn despite the numerous excellent players, and hostile to the individual despite it being team based PvP. How could anyone knowingly tell others to try the game with that in mind? When the UI and systems within the game itself is designed to be confusing, convoluted, and hard to look at you don't want people to be introduced to that. You just don't want people to suffer like that. I do hope in the future that the rare unicorn player I encountered who did bother to help becomes the norm rather than the exception.

I played this game for the past 5-or-so years. For me it started off when i was a small kid, watching my grandpa play a cool tank game and occasionally tried my own hand at it. During the covid lockdown i decided to give this game another shot and have been playing ever since. After 2.0's release i can say that the game is in a better state than it was before.

Pros:
1. Visuals/Effects/Sounds - The game looks phenomenal and runs surprisingly well. Wargaming's in-house game engine truly does wonders. I think I've never enjoyed looking at my screen more than while playing the mirny-13 event. The lighting, VFX and the maps look absolutely gorgeous. And the OST for this game is beautiful. All that, mixed with pleasant sound effects for every vehicle in the game makes it a really enjoyable experience. Every time I play the FV4005 I can't help to set the sound effect volume to max because of how juicy the firing and reloading sounds.
2. Stability - I honestly don't remember the last time wargaming's servers were down/had issues. That, mixed with good optimization allows for anyone to play the game even with below-average system requirements.
3. Events/Campaigns - There is always something to do in this game. Limited time events are enjoyable and bring good rewards for old and new players. And the new mission campaigns mixed with battlepasses, where even the free version can get you a lot of useful resources (equipment, credits, boosters, etc.) makes the grind more enjoyable.

Cons:
1. File size - This is more of a personal gripe, as I play on a laptop with quite limited memory and the fact that basically a quarter of my storage is taken up by WoT is not too good. I won't go into more detail, but I think lowering the filesize would be really appreciated by everyone.
2. Heavy monetization - I personally don't care about this *too* much. Most tanks with the exception of only a few are balanced (ahem ahem the lefh). A good chunk of premiums can be gotten with enough time on your hands and premium time is basically free at this point. And I think the addition of tier 11s and countless buffs of tech tree tanks made them more than viable in current day meta.
3. Lack of communication - I miss the days when wargaming were typing out every single change that they make/are planning to make to the game. I wish there would be more transparency between the players and developers. I think it would definitely help avoid future issues and drama related to paid content and balancing.
4. New player experience - This game is hard to get into without external sources. This game does not teach you about important mechanics, such as side scraping, camo, spotting, etc. I feel like there should be tutorial campaigns for each class of vehicles to allow newer players to grasp their tank's and game's mechanics easier. Also the fact that tiers 1-4 are riddled with bots is not a good thing. One thing i miss about old WoT was how each tier was equally playable. There was a lot of variation for tanks of lower tiers that made them interesting to play. Now the game truly begins only when you get to tiers 5-6. Anything before that is just one game to get the next tank in best case scenario and using free exp in worst.
5. Maps - The maps are miserable to play. You can't choose which maps you play and you can't ban more than 3 maps. That is genuinely not enough to actually enjoy this game. And each map being three corridors where heavies sit for the entire game and snipe each other's weakspots is simply not fun. I think random events did help fix that issue but that doesn't stop bad maps from being bad. I wish wargaming would experiment more with maps and their design to see what works and what doesn't.

I think this game has huge potential and after 2.0's release I can say that with 100% certainty. It has a lot of good going for it but the bad simply overshadows it. Wargaming needs to focus on fixing known issues that people have spoken against to bring back older players and give them the WoT they've dreamt of.

I never thought I would be writing a negative review for ESO. It was one of my favourite games, and for years I recommended it to other people.

Unfortunately, my experience with customer support completely changed my opinion.

My account was permanently banned for "Cheating/Exploiting". The only evidence presented to me was a copy of private chat messages where I discussed an external script related to Tamriel Trade Centre, a community trading website.

That script never interacted with the ESO client, never modified the game, never automated gameplay and never communicated with ZeniMax's servers. It simply processed information from a third-party website.

From my perspective, support appears to have concluded that words such as "script", "developer mode" and "codes" automatically meant cheating, without first understanding what was actually being discussed.

A permanent ban is the most severe penalty an online game can issue. I expected a proper technical investigation and a clear explanation of what rule I had actually violated. Instead, I received a generic response quoting the Code of Conduct and my chat messages.

Whether you agree with my project or not is irrelevant. The important question is whether it actually violated the rules. I am still waiting for an explanation of what my software supposedly did to the game itself.

I lost several months of gameplay, an account that's been around for years, and money invested, only to be completely wronged out of nowhere.
They have no proof of anything because it doesn't exist, they didn't want to know, and they ignore messages when confronted with requests for evidence that I cheated in any way.

There is no quality of ESO's support investigations.

The game deserves praise.
The support, in my experience, does not.

I'm having a lot of fun playing casually as a new player. I'm only 30 hours or so in but there's a bunch of really stand out things in GW2 I wanted to mention from the top of my head.

Questing is super chill and done so well in this game. It gives me a lot of freedom to enjoy my session how I want whilst making meaningful progress each time. I don't feel the need to be rushing levels, I would actually argue I'm levelling a bit too quick for my liking but the way the game scales you down I don't think it matters too much.

Exploration and my curiosity are almost always rewarded which is great as a new player. In a huge world with lot's of content, it makes me excited to keep playing. I really like the scouts, you can go to a new area whenever you want, talk to a scout and they give you a run down of what is happening in those areas, this is such a great way to deliver lore easily without needing to read walls of text. Honestly it has really helped me get invested in this world.

Events too feel great and a lot of the time the way they happen give the world so much life. I overheard some NPC's talking about hunting a boar once, I thought that sounded cool so I looked for them in a building, spoke to the hunter and essentially offered help and began an event. That's just a really basic example there have been a good amount of cool event moments and I have only done 2 areas. There is just so much life in this games world because of these moments. The animations are also amazing and give the game so much life and character. Then there is the music which just glues it all together to honestly create one of the most beautiful game worlds I've spent time in for a long time.

I can't say much about the story yet as I'm super early but there are a lot of voice acted cutscenes which I really enjoy. I love that my character has a voice, a backstory and place in Tyria.

As an artist in games that does handpainted work, I have to say a lot of the art in this game is beautiful, the painted world map is actually the best world map I've ever seen. Deep Rock Galactic is a cooperative first-person shooter developed by Ghost Ship Games. The game focuses on teamwork, mining, and survival in procedurally generated cave systems filled with dangerous alien creatures.

Players take on the role of space dwarves working for a mining corporation. Each mission sends them deep into alien planets to gather valuable resources while fighting off waves of hostile insects known as Glyphids. The combination of mining and combat creates a unique gameplay loop that blends action with exploration.

One of the strongest aspects of the game is its class system. Each dwarf class has a specific role: combat, support, mobility, or engineering. Teamwork is essential, as different abilities complement each other and help the team survive and complete objectives.

The procedurally generated caves are another highlight. No two missions feel the same, as environments change in layout, size, and danger. This keeps the gameplay fresh and encourages players to adapt their strategies.

The combat is fast-paced and satisfying, with a wide variety of weapons and upgrades. Enemies come in different forms, from small swarms to massive, dangerous creatures that require coordination to defeat.

Visually, the game has a distinctive style with dark caves contrasted by glowing minerals and lighting effects. While not realistic, the art direction is effective and supports the atmosphere perfectly.

The game also shines in its cooperative design. Communication and teamwork are strongly encouraged, especially in higher difficulty missions where coordination is the key to survival. Playing with friends often leads to chaotic and memorable moments.

However, the game can feel repetitive over long sessions, as the core mission structure remains similar. Some players may also find solo play less engaging compared to co-op.

Overall, Deep Rock Galactic is an outstanding cooperative shooter that combines humor, teamwork, and exploration. Its replayability and strong design make it one of the best modern co-op games.

You find gems, which you can equip into your armor and jewels and weapons and those gems are your skills. You do have a skill tree, but from what I saw, they are all passive buffs. Your active skills are the gems. I liked it, because this way you can use mage or archer skills with your barbarian. I liked it a lot. But unfortunately for me, ultimately this system makes me want to play less and less. Don't get me wrong, it works, it's not bad. It just makes it incredibly difficult to upgrade you armor and weapons. Stats alone aren't enough, you need the correct number, color and link of the sockets. You get modifiers among your regular drops from enemies and I believe crafting your stuff is the way to go, instead of waiting for drops. To me, this made it harder to enjoy the game fully. I felt becoming weaker and weaker and instead of playing the game more to get better stuff, I needed to stop what I was doing and craft or trade for better stuff.

It also resembles D2 a lot in my opinion, though I played that game for like 5 hours during my life. It sometimes made me want to give that game another chance too.

Other than that, I don't know what to say, it's a great hack and slash game. I didn't pay attention to the story and I am at the earlier stages of Act 4.

That being said, I'd rather play this game, than Diablo 4, honestly. I wouldn't say it's objectively superior or anything, I just didn't like D4 at all.

Since then, a friend of mine showed me POE2, the successor of this game, which is in early access now, this gem situation is completely different over there, so I'm sure I'll give that game a chance, when it reaches a more full status. Honestly, I highly recommend World of Tanks if you love strategy. 

The combat is super tactical and rewarding, though matches can start a bit slow sometimes because everyone is waiting for someone else to make the first move and push.

Visually, the game looks great. The tank models are really realistic and detailed. 
The sound design is also pretty good—it sets the right atmosphere for tank warfare.
One of the biggest highlights for me is the map design. Every single map feels unique and forces you to use different strategies. Plus, the Dynamic Events are incredibly cool and add a lot of realism to the matches.

The optimization is also absolutely insane. I used to play on Intel integrated graphics and still got 150 FPS on medium settings (and 80 on high). When I upgraded to a 2080 Super, I was getting 80 FPS on 1440p Ultra, and now on my RTX 3060, it runs beautifully at around 120 FPS. Anyone can run this game.

Now for the downsides: the premium tanks. The tech tree tanks are balanced and fun, but some of the pay-to-win premiums are straight-up broken and can really ruin the experience. Matchmaking tries its best to balance things by player skill, but those P2W tanks still mess things up. The good news is that if you're skilled enough, you can still outplay and destroy them. (And honestly, artillery needs a buff!).

As for the community, teamwork actually happens naturally most of the time. You do get the occasional selfish teammates who throw their lives away instantly and start typing a storm in chat.
