I've been playing Guild Wars 2 on and off since launch in 2012 after discovering it through Angry Joe's review. Most of my playtime was before it came to Steam, so my hours there don't tell the whole story  I've easily put around 4,000 hours into the game over the years.

One of the biggest reasons I keep coming back is that there's no monthly subscription. I can take a break for months and jump right back in without feeling like I'm wasting money. ArenaNet has also done a great job creating a beautiful world with unique art direction, memorable maps, and some of the best mount systems in any MMO.

The combat is still one of my favorite MMO combat systems. It's fast, active, and feels different from most tab-target MMOs. Questing and open-world exploration are easy to get into, while endgame content can be surprisingly challenging. Dungeons are definitely dated and a bit rough compared to modern content, but they still have their charm if you go in with friends.

The expansions add a ton of content, and I love how each one introduced new maps, elite specializations, mounts, weapons, and gameplay systems. The recent addition of housing is something I've been waiting for for years, and I'm excited to see where they take it next.

That said, I do think the game has changed over the years due to community feedback, sometimes for better and sometimes for worse. The annual festivals and events are fun, but after over a decade they can feel repetitive since they're mostly the same every year. I also noticed the community changed quite a bit after the Steam release, which isn't necessarily bad, just different from the older GW2 community I grew up with.

I've played plenty of MMOs, including World of Warcraft. There are definitely things I miss from WoW, but after all these years Guild Wars 2 still feels like home. WoW has changed so much that I barely recognize it anymore, while GW2 has managed to keep the core identity that made me fall in love with it in the first place.

It's not a perfect MMO, but after more than a decade and thousands of hours, it's still one of my favorites and one I'll probably keep returning to for years to come.

[h1]PATH OF EXILE : THE PASSIVE TREE WAS ONLY THE BEGINNING[/h1]

[hr][/hr]
[h2]OVERVIEW:[/h2]
Path of Exile is one of those games that feels overwhelming at first, then somehow turns into something you can't stop thinking about. Between the gigantic passive tree, countless skills and enough loot to fill an entire warehouse, it throws a lot at you right from the start. Yet beneath all that complexity lies one of the most rewarding ARPGs ever made.

I played through the game as a Templar alongside friends who picked Witch and Ranger, and what started as a casual co-op adventure quickly became nightly sessions of comparing builds, celebrating lucky drops and wondering where the last six hours went. We went from clueless exiles barely understanding support gems to discussing resistances and arguing over who deserved the next unique item.

I ended up enjoying the experience so much that I immediately bought Path of Exile 2. Few games have managed to pull me into their world quite like this one.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]GAMEPLAY — ★★★★★[/h3]
Deep, satisfying and endlessly customizable. Every build feels like its own journey.

[h3]CO-OP EXPERIENCE — ★★★★★[/h3]
Experimenting with friends and watching different builds evolve is incredibly fun.

[h3]BUILD VARIETY — ★★★★★[/h3]
The possibilities are almost overwhelming, and that's part of the charm.

[h3]ATMOSPHERE — ★★★★★[/h3]
Wraeclast is dark, brutal and packed with personality.

[h3]ENDGAME — ★★★★★[/h3]
Just when you think you're finished, the game opens up even further.

[h3]LEARNING CURVE — ★★★★☆[/h3]
Confusing at first, but deeply rewarding once things start to click.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]THE BREAKDOWN:[/h2]


[h3]THREE EXILES, THREE COMPLETELY DIFFERENT JOURNEYS:[/h3]

One of the best parts of playing Path of Exile was experiencing it with friends. I played Templar while my friends chose Witch and Ranger, and despite traveling through the same world, we all ended up feeling completely different. The Witch was blowing up entire screens with spells, the Ranger was picking enemies off before they even got close and I was busy smashing everything that survived. Seeing our builds slowly evolve and complement each other made every session feel special.

[h3]THE PASSIVE TREE IS TERRIFYING... UNTIL IT ISN'T:[/h3]

Looking at the passive skill tree for the first time felt like staring into another dimension. It looked absurdly complicated, and I honestly thought I'd never understand half of it. But after a while, things started making sense. Suddenly I was planning paths, looking for synergies and realizing just how much freedom the game offers. What seemed intimidating at first eventually became one of my favorite aspects of the game.

[h3]LOOT NEVER STOPS BEING EXCITING:[/h3]

There is something magical about hearing a valuable item drop. Every boss fight, every strongbox and every random enemy had the potential to give us something amazing. We constantly linked items in chat, celebrated upgrades and occasionally argued over who deserved that shiny new piece of gear. The game does a fantastic job of making loot feel meaningful.

[h3]THERE IS ALWAYS SOMETHING MORE TO LEARN:[/h3]

Even after dozens of hours, Path of Exile always felt like it had another layer waiting underneath. New mechanics, crafting systems, maps and league content constantly kept us curious. The deeper we went, the more we realized just how massive the game actually was. Instead of feeling repetitive, it kept rewarding curiosity.

[h3]THE GAME THAT SOLD ME ON ITS SEQUEL:[/h3]

I originally jumped into Path of Exile expecting a fun ARPG to play with friends. I didn't expect to become completely invested in it. Somewhere between experimenting with builds, laughing at ridiculous deaths and chasing better gear, I realized I genuinely loved the game. By the time our adventure was over, buying Path of Exile 2 wasn't even a question anymore.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]FINAL THOUGHTS:[/h2]
Path of Exile is complex, rewarding and dangerously addictive. Whether you're theorycrafting your next build, hunting for loot or simply exploring Wraeclast with friends, it constantly gives you reasons to keep playing.

[b] Somewhere along the way, Wraeclast stopped feeling like a game and started feeling like home.

Firstly, I had thought the game was pay to win because you could buy gold but... the thing is, the game does not have vertical progression. There are raids to do, and cool stuff at endgame, but gear itself? you just need one set and you're golden (there's legendary sets and stuff, important too but at first you can just go exotic).

Because of that, being able to buy gold is not ever necessary. Instead, the currency conversion system functions as a way for you to convert the gold you earn and grind for into premium currency so you can get cool stuff without having to pay cash. That means that, unlike XIV where if it's in the mogstation it's staying there unless you fork over the moneys, you can reasonably grind for anything in the premium shop in GW2.

I have End of Dragons, Path of Fire, and Heart of Thorns iirc... that unlocks a great deal of features, and the expansion content doesn't just die because it's old like in XIV or other MMOs. I do think that's a nice feature, though one downside is that unlike XIV buying one expansion does not net you every other expansion automatically. I have been playing Guild Wars 2 for several years now, ever since my father recommended it to me after returning to the game himself, and during that time it has become my favorite game of all time.

One of the things I love most about Guild Wars 2 is that the core game is completely free. It allows new players to experience the main mechanics, world, and story without having to spend any money upfront. I also appreciate the fact that there is no monthly subscription fee. I can take a break for several months and return whenever I want without feeling pressured to keep playing just to justify a subscription.

Another feature I love is the game's horizontal progression system. Unlike many MMORPGs, older content remains relevant years after its release. Top-tier gear stays useful instead of becoming obsolete whenever a new expansion launches.

I originally started playing Guild Wars 2 because my father recommended it to me after returning to the game himself. He had been playing again for a while before convincing me to give it a try. What impressed me was that despite his account being nearly a decade old, he didn't need to spend weeks grinding for new gear just to become relevant again. We were able to jump into content together almost immediately, which is something I rarely see in other MMORPGs.

My biggest complaint involves account management between ArenaNet's launcher and Steam. I originally started playing through ArenaNet's launcher and progressed quite far into the main story. Later, when I decided to purchase the expansions through Steam, I discovered that Steam accounts and ArenaNet accounts are separate. Instead of linking to my existing account, Steam created a new Guild Wars 2 account tied to my Steam profile, meaning I had to start over from the beginning.

Fortunately, this wasn't a dealbreaker for me because I genuinely enjoy the story, and the Personal Story offers a surprising amount of replayability. The choices you make early on can lead to different experiences and outcomes, making a second playthrough enjoyable rather than tedious.

My other complaint concerns the Living World seasons. At least when I purchased my expansions, it wasn't possible to buy the individual Living World seasons directly through Steam without purchasing the Elder Dragon Saga Complete Collection. Since I had already bought Heart of Thorns, Path of Fire, and later End of Dragons separately, buying the collection would have included expansions I already owned. As a result, I had to purchase the Living World seasons through the in-game store instead. This may have changed since then, but it was frustrating at the time.

Overall, I have completely fallen in love with Guild Wars 2. Even if you're unsure whether the game is for you, I can easily recommend giving it a try. The core game is free, and the amount of content available without spending a single cent is already massive. If you enjoy MMORPGs, there is a very good chance you'll find something to love here.

If you're looking for a vampire themed survival game, V Rising delivers a very good multiplayer experience. I highly recommend playing it with other people, as the game is primarily focused on the PvP aspect. That said, you can also enjoy it as a pure PvE game on your own private server. Solo play is viable too, it's just more grindy, and you'll be missing out on the main aspect of the game.
The soundtrack is pleasantly chill, setting a relaxed atmosphere that fits the gothic aesthetic well. One of the game's strongest features is the wide range of settings available. You can customize the game completely to your liking. If you're the type of player who likes to relax and doesn't want to deal with stressful boss fights, you can go down that road. On the flip side, if you enjoy a serious challenge and heavy grinding, you can adjust the settings accordingly and feel right at home.
The ability system seems fairly simple and it is. If you're someone who loves spending dozens of hours experimenting and creating crazy, nonsensical builds, this won't be your thing. The game follows the philosophy that simplicity is beauty. The system is clear, easy to understand, and very straightforward in its progression. Even players with no RPG experience will feel right at home. 
The level design is nicely varied, with distinct biomes like dark forests, snowy peaks, and cursed swamps. Each area has its own feel and enemy types, which keeps exploration engaging.
The progression system might rub some people the wrong way. Personally, it's not my cup of tea, but I can endure it. I can understand that the "go here, kill this, and this unlocks for you" style can feel clunky and even annoying to some players.
Building your castle is intuitive and fun. The grid system keeps everything tidy, and there are plenty of cosmetic options to make your lair look great. Overall, it's a solid and satisfying system that adds a lot to the game. Optimization is solid overall. The game runs smoothly and I didn't run into any serious bugs or crashes.
Now, about the boss fights and overall difficulty. We played on the hardest difficulty, and I have to say that the boss fights themselves are well balanced, at least on paper. Enemy abilities are straightforward and well telegraphed, so you can immediately see where the main danger lies. All the bosses have their own unique design, so it never feels like a copy-paste template. However, there's something I personally hate in games and I'm becoming allergic to, "pseudo power" determined by your gear level(item level). It's perfectly fine to have numerical displays so players can tell at a glance whether something is better or not. But the monster scaling? When a monster is just "X" gear levels above you, it suddenly becomes a bullet sponge. The monster has "X" times more health. I'm not a fan of that. It just turns monsters into bigger bullet sponges, and it gets annoying.
TLDR; Great with friends, okay solo. Fine building system, simple builds, good customization, but ruined by gear scaling and repetitive progression. Monsters become bullet sponges, grind gets old fast. Play on private servers with adjusted settings for the best experience.

[h2] Pros: [/h2]
- Chill, atmospheric soundtrack
- Wide range of customization settings
- Simple, clear, and beginner friendly ability system
- Straightforward progression 
- Solid optimization
- Enemy abilities are well telegraphed
- Unique boss fights
- Map diversity

[h2] Cons: [/h2]
- Designed primarily for groups, solo play feels like an afterthought
- Progression is a linear boss checklist style can be annoying for some players
- Poorly designed gear scaling
- Repetitive grind gets old fast
- Limited replayability - the world is static

[h1] Overall rating: 8/10 [/h1]

From a gameplay perspective, the fantasy of playing as a vampire is incredibly well realised in V-Rising. 

I love the way the screen gradually becomes brighter and more exposed when in the sun while a harsh, angry beam of light shines down on the character from the direction of the light, culminating in this awesome, blinding high contrast effect. It turns what would otherwise be a pretty standard lighting system into a high stakes game of figuring out where it is safe to stand. The lighting system is dynamic and moves as the day goes by, which not only has a verisimilitudious quality but also accurately update and checks when the character is exposed. It's an incredibly robust system and one of my favourite mechanics in the game. It goes without saying, but the team that put it together did an incredible job.

The character needs to feed on blood to survive, and the team have built this system in a very clever way. Each living creature has a blood type and a blood quality. The blood type determines what benefits it bestows to the character, while the blood quality determines the quantity and effectiveness of those benefits. This is not something I really payed much mind when I first started out, but as I started to become aware of blood quality and how better quality blood gives better buffs, I started to "get a taste" for it as it were. I became more selective about the blood types I was consuming and going out of my way to find my favourites, like I was a vampire looking for a good feed. 

The game features a buildcrafting system where you can claim territory build your own castle which you can live in and develop technology to improve yourself and furnish your castle. You get to brood around, take prisoners and order minions to do your bidding. It's great and I'm a sucker for this, but I do have a few issues with it, notably when it comes to making castles with multiple levels. If I build a second floor to my castle, but decide I want to move the stairs or swap out the stairs for another version of them, there's no easy way to correct that. I have to remove the entire upper floor, including all of the walls and furniture, and then all of the walls and pillars sorrounding the stairs. This is frustratingly tedious, and means spending minutes removing and replacing pieces just to change one thing.

Path of Exile is widely regarded as one of the best action RPGs ever created, offering an incredible amount of depth, content, and replayability without requiring players to purchase the game. Since its launch, it has continuously evolved through regular expansions, leagues, and updates that have kept the experience fresh for both new and veteran players.

One of the game's greatest strengths is its character customization. The massive passive skill tree and diverse skill gem system allow players to create endless build combinations. Whether you enjoy summoning armies of minions, casting devastating spells, or slicing through enemies with powerful melee attacks, Path of Exile provides the tools to craft a playstyle that feels uniquely your own.

The world of Wraeclast is dark, atmospheric, and rich with lore. Each area is carefully designed, featuring memorable environments, challenging enemies, and rewarding exploration. The game's story gradually unfolds through quests, dialogue, and environmental storytelling, creating an immersive fantasy experience.

Path of Exile also shines in its endgame content. The Atlas system, challenging bosses, seasonal leagues, and extensive itemization provide hundreds or even thousands of hours of gameplay. Few games offer the same level of long-term progression and meaningful goals for dedicated players.

What truly sets Path of Exile apart is the passion of its developers, Grinding Gear Games. The studio has consistently expanded and improved the game over the years, listening to community feedback and delivering substantial free content updates that rival the scope of paid expansions in other games.

Overall, Path of Exile remains a benchmark for the action RPG genre. Its deep customization, rewarding progression, rich endgame, and generous free-to-play model make it a must-play for anyone who loves loot-driven adventures and character-building systems. Even years after its release, it continues to stand among the very best ARPGs available.

I have a lot of thoughts about Noita. 

First of all, it's a beautifully made game with an amazing look and feel. "Every pixel is simulated" sounds like a gimmick at first, but it's so much more than that. It's more than just a mechanic, it just means that Noita is literally *made of* simulated pixels - it's a part of everything you see and do. The unforgiving, high-stakes nature of the exploration, the lifelike movement of the enemies, and the opaque mystery of its huge world all combine to create an unbelievable atmosphere reminiscent of Rain World. 

Presentation aside, the gameplay itself is essentially a "roguelike" (used loosely) in which you can become unbelievably powerful provided you have the knowledge to do so. The magic of this game is that it is designed around that, and the difficulty scales as your knowledge does. It doesn't expect you to know how to become powerful, but if you do, there will always be a genuinely threatening challenge for you. 

The "wand-building" can sound offputting, as many games have tried and failed with systems that allow you to create your own spells, but that's not what Noita does. It's very difficult to explain until you try it, but it's not designed around predesigned combinations of spells; it's an entirely modular system that you can eventually harness, like a programming language for blowing stuff up. Despite this, it's incredibly simple to use from the beginning.

If you are a fan of games that reward exploration, roguelikes that encourage you to break them with endless powerscaling, incredible dynamic soundtracks, mythological and psychedelic themes, and games that are punishing in the sense that they *just don't care about you*, you might love Noita.

[b]Introduction :[/b]
V Rising, développé par les Suédois de Stunlock Studios, est sorti officiellement en 1.0 en mai 2024 après deux ans d'accès anticipé qui ont fait du jeu un véritable phénomène. C'est un mélange étonnamment réussi entre action-RPG en vue isométrique, survie multijoueur et base building, le tout enrobé d'une thématique vampirique assumée jusque dans les moindres détails. On y incarne un vampire qui se réveille affaibli après des siècles de sommeil et qui doit reconstruire son château, traquer le sang des mortels les plus puissants pour absorber leurs pouvoirs, et survivre à la lumière du jour qui te désintègre littéralement si tu te fais surprendre. Le jeu se joue en solo, en coop privé ou sur serveurs PvP jusqu'à 40 joueurs, et il s'est trouvé une niche absolument méritée entre Diablo et Valheim.

[b]Ce que j'ai aimé :[/b]
[list]
[*]🩸 Le concept vampirique est exploité à fond : soleil mortel, aversion pour l'argent et l'ail, miroirs, transformations en loup ou en chauve-souris, c'est l'essence même du mythe respectée jusqu'au bout
[*]⚔️ Les combats en vue iso sont nerveux, exigeants, et chaque boss a un moveset clair à apprendre, on est très proche d'un Diablo couplé à un souls-like
[*]🏰 Le château est un vrai bonheur à construire, les pièces ont des effets concrets sur le craft et la production, on customise son repaire avec passion
[*]🌒 Le cycle jour/nuit a un vrai sens gameplay, on planifie ses sorties en suivant les arbres et les ombres pour ne pas griller au soleil, c'est génial
[*]👥 Le coop en clan transforme l'expérience : on partage le château, on assigne les rôles, on planifie les raids ensemble, c'est extrêmement satisfaisant
[*]🩹 La progression par absorption de sang (chaque type de sang humain ou animal donne des stats différentes) est une mécanique originale qui pousse à varier les victimes
[*]🎨 La direction artistique gothique avec ses tons sombres et ses effets de lumière est vraiment classe, le jeu a un style affirmé qui le distingue immédiatement
[*]🆕 Les mises à jour post-launch sont énormes, Stunlock continue de pousser du contenu gratuit deux ans après et la 1.1 a redéfini la partie survie
[/list]

[b]Ce que j'ai moins aimé :[/b]
[list]
[*]📖 La narration est quasi inexistante, on comprend qu'on est un vampire qui se réveille et basta, l'ambiance fait beaucoup mais on aurait aimé un fil rouge plus marqué
[*]🎮 La caméra fixe en iso peut gêner sur certains combats, notamment quand des éléments du décor masquent l'action, c'est parfois imprécis
[*]🌐 En PvP serveur public, l'expérience peut être brutale, perdre son château à un raid nocturne en pleine déco c'est rude pour les nerfs
[*]⚙️ La courbe d'apprentissage est costaud au début, le jeu te lâche sur la map sans tutoriel détaillé et il faut bouquiner ou regarder des guides
[*]🔄 Le grind de certaines ressources tardives peut s'étirer, surtout en solo où il faut tout faire soi-même
[/list]

[b]Conclusion :[/b]
V Rising est une vraie pépite et probablement l'une des meilleures sorties du studio Stunlock à ce jour. Le mariage action-RPG/survie/base building fonctionne à merveille et la thématique vampirique est traitée avec un sérieux et un respect du mythe qu'on voit rarement. Les combats sont nerveux, le château est un plaisir à monter et à défendre, et le coop en clan offre des dizaines d'heures de fun garanti. Quelques bémols sur la narration absente et une caméra parfois capricieuse, mais à 35h au compteur je n'ai pas tout vu et je suis sûr d'y revenir pour explorer le contenu de la 1.1. Si t'aimes Diablo, Valheim, ou simplement les vampires faits avec amour, c'est un achat les yeux fermés en promo. Et même au prix fort, vu la durée de vie offerte, le ratio est imbattable.

Sometimes, certain games just click for me. They consume my waking thoughts, my dreams and I obsessively play them when fancy takes me. And it doesn't have to be made in the latest Unreal Engine XD engine either. V Rising is one of those games for me. I played the demo recently and I was instantly hooked.

Many spells from different schools to unlock, gems with massive modifiers to those spells, multiple gear sets and options to fit your playstyle, things to build, things to upgrade, easy way to move base to the new biomes and multiple bosses that are fun to fight (some not so fun though).

If I had few minor gripes it would be that you cannot afford to throw things away in this game because it might come up wayyy later in the game as an crafting requirement. But hoarding is standard in any survival-crafting so there's that. Another one would be rescource hunting times but so much of the options can be changed to fit your needs WITHOUT STARTING OVER a la Valheim. You're at that stage where you simply want to focus on killing bosses and progress? Increase resource yield rate to 3x times. You are a massive hoarder but the stack size is too small? Set it to max! The game getting a bit easy and you want to have a challenge? Increase enemy numbers, damage and health and go to town! But make no mistake Brutal difficulty option exists and that changes up bosses to a whole new level. They hit harder, larger health pool and have new moves.

In sum, V Rising is a highly customizable fun survival-crafting game that has so many features that it will keep you busy and engaged for a very long time to come.

I bought V Rising about a month ago, and it has completely exceeded all my expectations.

First of all, I want to point out that all DLCs are purely cosmetic. This was actually one of the reasons why I didn’t buy the game earlier. I thought I would be forced into endlessly buying DLCs and that purchasing the base game alone wouldn’t be enough. I’ve always wanted a game where rewards feel thoughtfully planned rather than completely random. I don’t want to kill a boss and receive an upgrade for a class I’m not even playing. V Rising reminds me of older classics where progression was designed with care.

The building system is great, and I especially like how new features and mechanics are introduced gradually. The game keeps expanding naturally without becoming overwhelming. I really dislike games where you’re expected to learn a thousand new mechanics within the first hour. Fortunately, V Rising is not like that at all.

I don’t want to exaggerate, but I’m genuinely enjoying this game a lot, and I’m very happy that I decided to buy it. (An AI actually explained the DLC system to me, which helped me finally make the decision.)

Deep Rock Galactic stands as a masterpiece of cooperative game design, primarily because it strikes a flawless balance between chaotic, high-stakes action and essential teamwork. Dropping players into the treacherous, fully destructible subterranean depths of Hoxxes IV, the game assigns you one of four distinct dwarven classes: the Gunner, the Engineer, the Scout, or the Driller. Unlike many multiplayer games where class roles overlap or feel cosmetic, Deep Rock Galactic ensures that every single class is vital to the team's survival and navigation. The Driller blasts shortcuts through solid rock, the Engineer places platforms to bridge massive gaps, the Scout illuminates pitch-black caverns and reaches high-up mineral veins, and the Gunner deploys shields and heavy firepower to hold back overwhelming alien swarms. This tight mechanical synergy transforms every mission into a rewarding puzzle where success relies entirely on genuine coordination and mutual support.

Beyond its brilliant gameplay loop, the game thrives on a legendary community culture that is almost entirely devoid of the toxicity plaguing modern multiplayer gaming. Developer Ghost Ship Games brilliantly weaponized positive reinforcement through simple in-game mechanics, most famously the dedicated "Salute" button. Pressing it causes your dwarf to hoist their pickaxe and shout "Rock and Stone!", an infectious rallying cry that instantly diffuses tension, celebrates a hard-fought victory, or seals a pact of teamwork. This minor design choice, combined with a progression system that rewards cooperation rather than individual competition, has fostered a uniquely welcoming environment. Whether you are playing with lifelong friends or dropping into a lobby of random strangers, there is an immediate, unspoken bond of camaraderie that makes every session feel like an shared adventure among trusted crewmates.

Finally, the game excels due to its masterful execution of procedural generation and environmental design, which keeps the experience infinitely replayable. Every dive into the caves feels genuinely dangerous and unpredictable, as players are forced to navigate complex, multi-layered vertical labyrinths where threats can emerge from any angle. The dark, atmospheric lighting requires strategic management of flares, turning basic exploration into a tense, immersive survival experience. Supported by a consumer-friendly development model that eschews predatory microtransactions in favor of free seasonal battle passes and immense developer transparency, Deep Rock Galactic doesn't just respect its players' money—it respects their time. It is a rare gem in the gaming industry that perfectly pairs addictive, satisfying gunplay and mining mechanics with a heart of pure, unadulterated fun.

World of Tanks was one of the games that introduced me to armored warfare. I started playing it back in 2010 on the North American servers and spent years playing across multiple accounts before eventually moving to Europe. Like many long-running online games, it changed considerably over time. The problem is not that it changed, but the direction those changes took.

The original version of World of Tanks was far from perfect. Progression was painfully slow, especially for free-to-play players. Reaching higher tiers could take months of grinding, earning credits was difficult and premium accounts provided advantages that many players simply could not afford. Looking back, there are many things about the old progression system that deserved criticism. However, despite those flaws, the game itself felt far more straightforward than it does today.

Most of the knowledge that mattered was directly related to tanks. You learned armor layouts, weak spots, map positions, angling techniques and vehicle matchups because those were the things that decided battles. Knowing where to shoot a KV-1, how to deal with a Hetzer or how to position a Tiger often mattered more than anything else. The game certainly had mechanics that experienced players understood better than newcomers, but most of those mechanics were connected directly to the vehicles themselves rather than a growing collection of systems surrounding them.

Over the years the developers solved many of the game's original problems. Progression became significantly faster, new players gained access to more rewards, higher-tier vehicles became easier to reach and quality-of-life improvements were introduced across the board. On paper these changes sound entirely positive, and some of them genuinely were. The problem is that many of those solutions arrived alongside additional systems, mechanics and progression layers that gradually became just as important as the tanks themselves.

Modern World of Tanks is no longer a game where understanding tanks alone is enough. Players are expected to understand spotting mechanics, camouflage values, bush mechanics, crew skills, directives, equipment setups, field modifications, consumables and countless interactions between those systems. Individually these mechanics are not necessarily bad, but together they create a learning curve that becomes increasingly difficult for new players to overcome.

I noticed this whenever I introduced friends to the game. Over the years I used referral programs several times, helping new players start their journey while unlocking rewards together. Almost all of them eventually quit. The problem was not a lack of interest in tanks or military vehicles. The problem was that World of Tanks demanded an enormous amount of knowledge before it became enjoyable. Even with an experienced player explaining mechanics, many found the game overwhelming. If players who have guidance struggle to remain interested, it is difficult to imagine how newcomers are expected to learn everything on their own.

The game's monetization evolved alongside these systems. World of Tanks has always favored paying players, so this is not a criticism unique to the modern version. The difference is that older versions of the game primarily rewarded patience and knowledge once you were inside a battle. Progression was slow, but the gameplay itself remained relatively clean. Today the experience is surrounded by battle passes, premium vehicles, equipment advantages, crew progression systems, progression shortcuts and various forms of monetized convenience. Free-to-play progression remains possible, but the gap between players willing to spend money and players relying solely on time investment remains difficult to ignore.

The introduction of premium ammunition for credits also changed many vehicle interactions. Premium ammunition already existed in older versions of the game, but most players rarely used it because doing so required spending real money. As a result, knowledge of armor layouts and weak spots remained extremely important. Certain vehicles were difficult to fight because players genuinely needed to understand where to shoot them.

Once premium ammunition became widely accessible through credits, those interactions changed considerably. Vehicles that once rewarded knowledge and careful aiming became easier to deal with, while newer tanks increasingly relied on unusual armor layouts, tiny weak spots and additional mechanics to compensate. Instead of simplifying combat, the game often felt like it was adding new systems to solve problems created by previous systems.

Map design presents another challenge. Learning a map in World of Tanks is not simply a matter of memorizing terrain. Different vehicle classes often require completely different routes, positions and strategies. A heavy tank, medium tank, tank destroyer and light tank can effectively be playing different games on the same map. Returning after a long break often feels less like building upon existing knowledge and more like starting over.

Another issue is how heavily modern gameplay depends on mechanics that many players never fully understand. Spotting, camouflage and bush mechanics became increasingly important over the years, often determining engagements before the first shot is even fired. While these systems add depth, they also create situations where success feels less dependent on understanding tanks and more dependent on understanding invisible calculations happening behind the scenes. For veteran players this may simply be another system to learn. For newcomers it often becomes another barrier.

The situation becomes even more difficult because new players are not entering the same game that veterans learned years ago. They are entering a game with more than a decade of accumulated mechanics, systems and player knowledge. Experienced players continue to populate lower tiers, veteran crews remain active throughout the matchmaking pool and many battles place newcomers against players with thousands of hours of experience. Learning the game is no longer a gradual process. It often feels like trying to catch up to years of accumulated knowledge all at once.

What ultimately pushed me away was not a single update, vehicle or balance change. It was the gradual realization that I was spending more time learning systems than learning tanks. When I think about the years I enjoyed World of Tanks the most, I remember armor duels, vehicle matchups, memorable battles and learning the strengths and weaknesses of different tanks. When I think about the modern game, I find myself thinking about spotting ranges, equipment configurations, crew optimization, progression systems and monetization layers.

World of Tanks played an important role in my gaming history and introduced me to a genre that I still enjoy today. Unfortunately, after returning multiple times over the years, I no longer see the same game that originally captured my attention. There is more content than ever before, more vehicles than ever before and more progression systems than ever before, yet the core experience feels increasingly disconnected from the tank-focused gameplay that made the game special in the first place.

Guild Wars 2 sigue siendo, incluso después de más de 13 años, uno de los MMORPG más inteligentes y agradables que he jugado. No es solo otro juego de “subir niveles y farmear equipo mejor”, es una experiencia que entiende realmente lo que significa divertirse a largo plazo.

Monetización

Lo primero que más valoro es su modelo de monetización extremadamente amigable. El juego base se compra una sola vez y ya tienes acceso completo a un mundo enorme. No hay suscripción mensual obligatoria. Las expansiones se pagan una vez y añaden muchísimo contenido de calidad (historia, mapas, monturas, habilidades élite, etc.). En la tienda de gemas (la parte de microtransacciones) solo encontrarás cosméticos, ranuras de inventario/banco, mejoras de calidad de vida y cosméticos espectaculares. Nada de pay-to-win. Puedes ser completamente competitivo y tener el mejor equipo del juego sin gastar ni un euro extra. Eso es algo cada vez más raro en el género y ArenaNet merece todo el reconocimiento por mantener esta filosofía durante más de una década.

El sistema de monturas

El sistema de monturas introducido con Path of Fire es probablemente una de las mejores mecánicas jamás añadidas a un MMORPG. No son simples vehículos bonitos: cada montura tiene habilidades únicas que cambian radicalmente cómo exploras y resuelves el mundo. El Griffon te permite planear y hacer acrobacias increíbles. El Springer te ayuda a saltar alturas imposibles. El Skimmer flota sobre el agua y la lava. El Jackal te permite teletransportarte en arena. El Skyscale (mi favorito) combina varias mecánicas y te da libertad total.

Las monturas no solo son divertidas, sino que están perfectamente integradas en el diseño de mapas. Muchas colecciones, puzzles y exploraciones requieren usar la montura correcta en el momento correcto. Es de esas mecánicas que, una vez las pruebas, hacen que otros MMORPG se sientan anticuados.

Progresión horizontal

Lo que realmente mantiene enganchado a miles de jugadores durante años es su progresión horizontal. En Guild Wars 2 nunca sientes que estás “atrasado”. El equipo legendario es muy poderoso, pero la diferencia de poder no es tan abismal como en otros juegos. En su lugar, el endgame se centra en:
Dominios y maestrías, Colecciones épicas, Logros, Construcciones creativas, Participación en eventos mundiales masivos (World Bosses y metas), PvP y WvW

Puedes volver después de meses o incluso años y seguir disfrutando plenamente. Siempre hay algo nuevo que conseguir que mejora tu experiencia sin obligarte a tirar todo lo anterior a la basura. Esa sensación de “ya estoy donde quiero estar, ahora solo quiero disfrutar” es adictiva.

Guild Wars 2 es un juego generoso, profundo y sorprendentemente fresco para su edad. Tiene una de las mejores comunidades del género, un combate fluido y dinámico, una historia interesante y, sobre todo, respeta tu tiempo y tu bolsillo. Si estás cansado de los MMORPG que te exprimen con battle passes y pay-to-win, Guild Wars 2 es el soplo de aire fresco que estabas buscando. ¡Altamente recomendado!

Path of Exile is not a game for the faint of heart. It's a deep, complex, and brutally challenging action RPG that will consume your time and reward your dedication in equal measure. If you're looking for a game with one of the most intricate character customization systems ever created, look no further.

The Passive Skill Tree is legendary. It's a massive web of nodes that can be both incredibly exciting and absolutely daunting for new players. The sheer number of possible builds is staggering, allowing you to create a truly unique character.

The itemization and crafting system is another layer of insane depth. Every piece of gear can be modified in countless ways, turning the loot hunt into a complex puzzle. Finding a good base item is just the beginning of the journey.

The game is famous for its endgame, where you dive into the Atlas of Worlds, completing maps that get progressively harder and more rewarding. It's a true 'one more map' trap.

Path of Exile is free-to-play with a very fair model, but be warned: it has a steep learning curve. It's a masterpiece for those willing to put in the time to learn its systems.

Verdict: 9/10. A true masterpiece for hardcore ARPG fans.

I've been playing Guild Wars since the original game launched in the early 2000s. With all the recent excitement surrounding Guild Wars 3, I've found myself spending more time in Guild Wars 2 again. While Steam shows only 110.4 hours played, that number doesn't come close to representing my actual time with the game. I originally played through the ArenaNet launcher and later transitioned my account to Steam through a workaround some friends showed me. Everything transferred smoothly, though it means I can't make purchases through Steam—which honestly doesn't bother me.

One of the biggest reasons I've always appreciated Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2 is their business model. I've never been someone who can fully commit to subscription-based MMOs like World of Warcraft or Star Wars: The Old Republic. Guild Wars respected my time and wallet with a one-time purchase, and Guild Wars 2 eventually adopted a free-to-play model with paid expansions. Considering the sheer amount of content available, it's one of the best values in gaming. You can step away for months—or even years—and still come back to find plenty to do.

The gameplay can become repetitive at times, but that's true of virtually any MMO with this much content. Even after all these years, I'm still discovering new events, mechanics, and systems I had never experienced before. There are storylines I haven't completed, mounts I still haven't unlocked, and entire character classes I haven't properly explored. The game constantly gives you another goal to chase without making you feel rushed.

The music and sound design deserve special praise. I usually disable music in most games, but Guild Wars 2 is one of the few exceptions. The soundtrack adds tremendously to the atmosphere, and the sound effects make combat, achievements, and progression feel genuinely rewarding.

What truly sets Guild Wars 2 apart, however, is its community. In my experience, players are overwhelmingly friendly and willing to help newcomers and veterans alike. The ability to belong to multiple guilds at the same time is also a fantastic feature. You can have a guild for close friends, another for large-scale activities, and still participate in broader communities without feeling locked into a single group.

Overall, Guild Wars 2 is easy to recommend. Whether you're looking for a casual MMO to jump into occasionally or a massive world to invest hundreds of hours in, it offers an incredible amount of content, a welcoming community, and exceptional value for the price.

Suggestion for WoW and FFXIV-Style Camera Controls

Suggestion for WoW and FFXIV-Style Camera Controls

Hello ESO Online Team,

First of all, I would like to congratulate everyone involved in bringing this incredible game to life. I am extremely excited to see this new era of ESO Online evolve into one of the most promising MMORPGs in recent years. The anticipation within the community is very high, and I am confident that the updates and improvements you are developing will create something truly remarkable.

I would like to share a suggestion that I believe could benefit many players while significantly improving both immersion and accessibility.

I have been playing MMORPGs for over 20 years, including titles such as World of Warcraft, Final Fantasy XIV, TERA, and many others. One feature I have always appreciated in these games is the ability to control the camera using the WASD keys, allowing the character to turn based on camera direction, keep the camera centered, and create a more fluid and natural movement system.

This type of control provides a smoother and more dynamic gameplay experience, especially during combat, gathering activities, exploration, and general movement. More importantly, it serves as a valuable accessibility feature for players who rely on WASD-based camera controls due to physical limitations, disabilities, or personal comfort needs.

My suggestion is not to replace the current control system, but simply to add this as an optional camera and movement configuration. By offering multiple camera behavior options and fixed-camera presets, ESO Online would allow players to customize their experience according to their individual needs and preferences.

Accessibility and inclusion are becoming increasingly important in modern game development. Implementing an alternative WASD camera control option would help make ESO Online more welcoming to a broader audience, including players with disabilities and those who depend on alternative control schemes to enjoy the game comfortably.

I truly believe this feature would not only improve gameplay but also demonstrate a strong commitment to inclusivity. It could even become a compelling part of ESO Online's evolution into a modern, next-generation MMORPG:

"ESO Online – Updated for a New Generation, with modern, fluid, and accessible camera controls for everyone."

Thank you very much for your time, consideration, and for all the incredible work you are doing. I am excited to see what the future holds for ESO Online and look forward to continuing this journey with the community.

Sincerely,

A Long-Time MMO Player

This has been one of my favorite MMOs I have played over the years. The game is over 15 years old and still going strong. I highly recommend this game to anyone that has never experienced the action style combat system that Guild Wars 2 implemented.

Pros: 
- Game runs well, for the most part.
- Graphics are amazing.
- Building is amazing also.
- Biomes are interesting and somewhat diverse.

Cons:
- Equipment and weapons. Boy oh boy, where do I start with this one. You have dozen of different weapons, most of which will be completely useless for anything. I thought about running with pistols, seemed interesting, but that was the worst idea ever. They are slow to shoot, and when you attack you stop to a halt, and that start moving at a snail pace while shooting. But that stop every time you make a new attack is just infuriating. other weapons also have the similar mechanics, bows and crossbows need to be "channeled" before an attack, so you can use them only if you intend to sit there and take the free damage from everything, axes and hammers are useful only material gathering, which leaves you with swords only, which are fine, but you are force into melee combat with them, which means you have to either play perfectly or be able to take damage or heal with non existing abilities. Armors are for the most part useless, in a way that it does not matter what you use, The only purpose of the armor is to raise your level so you can fight higher level enemies. stats and bonuses are irrelevant as long as you have them at higher level.

- Sun burning is interesting only in the very beginning, but after that it becomes a time waster. There are no real mechanics behind it and no real danger from it. The moment you graze the shadows, the sun exposure nullifies. It is highly unlikely that you will ever die from the sun, so it only exists to exist.

- Bosses are mehh. Some are ok, and a few are amazing (surprisingly), but most are bosses with little to no mechanics, just lots of HP and DMG, while you have very little HP and DMG, which truly shows the "amazing" development of the game. The developers have obviously "worked" really hard to make bosses repeat the same cycle of actions over and over again, where you are forced to repeat the same actions over and over again. Groundbreaking indeed, die and repeat. over and over and over and over.....

- Transformations are also almost completely useless. Wolf one is ok, because it allows you to move a little bit faster on the ground, and a bat one to fly fast across the skies (even tho it says that you can not carry any materials with you while in the bat form, you actually ca, so I don't know if it's a bug, but that is one useful thing about it), you have the human form, that you will only use for the achievement, same as rat form, you can transform into a barrel, for the reasons, and you can transform into spider, for more reasons. You have also a bear form, with which you can take down 1 single gate in the game, and that is it, outside of that it serves no purpose.

- You will be stuck by having to play late-game like it is scripted. For the most part, especially with bosses, you are either forced to play in the exact certain way, with exactly intended abilities and weapons, or you will pay with your own blood. Because you are not allowed to just play the game however you want. I wanted to play the game as summoner/warlock, but for half of the bosses late-game that was not doable, and for other half it was just raising t he difficulty for no reason, so you are given bunch of summons, that can't really do anything for the most part. So if you are expecting that you will just be playing your own style, forget it.

- Fast travel is almost as useless as it can be. You have vampire teleports, through which you can't go through with about 90% of the loot that you would acquire across the map. Which means you are only able to teleport empty to a location, farm whatever you were farming, and that have to run back every single time, across the map, regardless of where your castle is, half of your game time will be just running back and forth for farming materials. There are also caves for fast travel, through which you can carry everything, but they are fixed at certain locations. You can only travel from point A to point B, which becomes completely useless also since you will be running all across the map.

- Movement speed. This is what I found most infuriating about the game. You are as slow as you can be, everything in the world will be faster than you, the slowest npc's will be faster than you are. In the beginning it is fine while everything is more or less as strong as you are, but when you start hunting down bosses, the speed starts showing, every single boss will fly across the map at high speed, while you are stuck to either do perfect dodges in pixels or use dash every 8 seconds. And on top of how slow you are, when you start attacking, you slow down even more, while boss has pretty much no cooldowns, you only have cooldowns, which means anything that can be used for movement, might as well have not been added at all.

- Abilities are just bad also. Half of them are made for co-op or teams, so if you are playing single-player, they will just be JPG's on the screen. Half of the other half is useless also even in solo mode, which means you are stuck only with quarter of useful abilities. Do not expect much diversity with spells.

- There are transmog functions, which are also useless if you are playing solo, because what? Is your life so sad that you just sit there and look at your character in different outfits and different look styles. There are also lots of emotes, which, sure....

- I have to add horses here, that, I do not know why were added into the game. They serve no purpose, The whole map is overflowing with enemies, anything that touches you ever so slightly takes you off the horse or transformation. You pretty much can not ride anywhere with a horse, which means it just becomes a gimmick, you have a horse that will sit in the stable just to exist. 

- Also the game will not detect inputs properly lots of times, you will be clicking the button for whatever, but the game will simply not register that properly or at all. And some of the spells that are half solo, half duo, instead of when playing solo, that you click the ability and it activates, you have to point at yourself and than click on it which in some bullet hell scenarios is plainly bad design.

- Of course I did not buy dlc's but what the hell is going on with the pricing of those!?

Disclaimer: I've only played this game as a PVE co-op game with a few of my friends so my review is based on my experiences with that. For what it's worth I think it's amazing I've sunk almost 70hrs into it without touching any of the massively multiplayer or PvP parts at all. 

As a PVE co-op game, I think it's great! The environments are well crafted with beautiful gothic touches but nothing that could be considered horror (which I personally liked). There's a lack of diversity in character customization and armour options in the base game but considering that the game is played top down it didn't bother me too much. 

There's a lot of bosses to go through with interesting mechanics especially if you play on Brutal but I would definitely have had trouble solo. Builds are based mainly on the different spell classes but I liked the variety. For example I enjoyed experimenting with  both an AOE builds and a more supportive healing build. However I dislike how limited we are in terms of active spells as well as weapon skills being on shared cooldown. Maybe it would be more relevant in PVP balance-wise, but I wish we could've had more spell slots considering how many we have access to. 

The gameplay loop is fairly basic and it can feel a little grindy especially in mid to end game but it helps if you're playing with others and everyone is pooling their resources into a shared base. There's not much in way of PVE endgame once you've defeated all the bosses. I think for me the highlight of the game and the true endgame is base building. Even with the limited variety of decorative pieces in the base game, there's so many different ways to build your castle. I loved designing mine and I love seeing how other people have made theirs. I think I'd go back after taking a break just to build more in the various different areas.

What's great about this game is the control you have over your personal servers, from shortening daylight hours to eliminating crafting costs for a true creative mode. And the best part is being able to change these settings at any time so you can adjust for a personalized gaming experience. But here lies also one of the biggest downsides of the game for me, which is server hosting. Either you pick a public dedicated server and hope it's the closest to the gameplay style you want or you and your friends pay to host your own private server so that nobody has to wait for the host to be online to access their progress. While this is not an issue for people playing solo, I do think this game is best experienced in co-op. 

All in all, I think it was a great co-op PVE experience and one I'd go back to for the creative mode alone but there are some limitations that make it hard to recommend to everyone. However, it's a game I'd definitely suggest checking out on a sale especially if you have a couple of friends interested in being shapeshifting vampires and/or gothic architects together.

V Rising is a top down survival game around vampires. I'm always surprised there aren't more vampire themed games out there, it's such a fun concept to make a game about. The survival aspect is really well done. You need to gather materials to upgrade everything. Your level is based on the level of your gear so if you are efficient hunting down materials, you can level up fairly quickly. You'll find bosses throughout the world which will unlock new things you can build. 

Building a base is also really intuitive and it's fun to make a castle in it. There are also some nice quality of life features to make your castle more efficient. You can make different rooms focused on certain aspects like a forging room to be faster and use fewer resources. It's all about being as efficient as possible!

Exploration and gathering materials is pretty fun. My main complaint is the controls can often times be confusing in the fast paced combat. I feel like the game was designed with a controller in mind and then the developers just kind of jammed together some keyboard controls as an after thought. I constantly found myself using the wrong abilities in a fight. Turning the camera mid fight is also a hassle. 

Overall though, I'm not even a big survival game fan, and I really enjoyed this one.

This was the first MMORPG I've played and, while the community is great, you'll soon see how the game in general has a lot of wasted potential.

First, the good: the map is HUGE, very detailed. Despite being over ten years old, it still has pretty decent graphics and it runs very very nice on my certainly not powerful machine. Simply taking a stroll down a city and talking to NPCs (which are *all* fully dubbed!) is fairly enjoyable and fun.

Now, the bad: most of the quests are fairly basic and boring. Few require exploring or thinking, you're merely following the compass and roaming from place A to place B while fighting the same clinically blind enemies with dumb AI: just crouch and you can kill anyone without anyone noticing. They don't communicate with each other, so you may be slaughtering enemies five meters away from their peers, and they will keep chitchatting like you're not even there.

Your choices don't matter - they don't have any long term consequences past the current quest either, which is certainly not great for a role playing game. Whether you kill or spare a baddie, you won't see them again and won't be ever make an appearance later or influence the gameplay anywhere else. This is I think a recurring issue with characters: playing as a Dominion soldier, other than Razum-Dar or Ayreen, you rarely talk with anyone more than a couple times so I don't feel any kind of attachment to them. Why should I risk my life saving this dumb dude from a cave, again?

The monetization is not bad - it's outright insane. You have first the overly expensive ESO+ subscription - we're talking circa 120€ per year. Just think about how full games you can purchase with that. But it gets even worse as that doesn't unlock the full experience - there's then the crown store (you want a house? pay real money for it then!) and the gambling with the crown crates.

Menus are a complete mess. I have to navigate through all of them every time I need to do something. You wanna add an item to the hotbar? Go to the inventory, then select quick access menu. But you want to add a *reaction*, where would you look for that? In the same reaction menu? Well, no, of course, in the Help page! Want to visit a stranger's house? You think it'd be in the map section? No, it's in the group menu, why not!

The game seems to suffer from many graphical issues, reported, and for which ZOS seems to not care at all. Every single female khajiit has their eyelids clip with the eyes whenever they blink, and it's been a known issue reported on the forum for almost half a decade now. They've acknowledged on their issue tracker "it's a known issue" but fixing it would take too much effort, so they'd rather not and spend the time adding new lootbox mechanics or something.

I would not recommend buying this game in 2026. The few players left are nice enough but it's quickly dying as people move to PoE 2. Also, the actual RPG story is not very good. This game's a lot of fun for a Survival/Base Building game. Off the bat I'd give it a 9/10 and encourage anyone considering it to pick it up.

The combat is fun similar to top down games like Grim Dawn or Path Of Exile. Each weapon starts fairly weak and as you upgrade them eventually get two skills such as throwing out a javelin and having it spin to return to you or dash attacks with the great sword. Each weapon has unique abilities, speeds of attack, and damage making for a unique experience with each one. Later they get enchantments that can apply magical effects like leeching their life, setting them on fire, or cursing them so on death they rise as undead. The armors, amulets and skills allow for several different builds like a necromancer, life leech, fire magic, ice magic, illusionist, and an additional build or two.

The bosses are likely to be the main draw for a lot of people to the game and they don't disappoint. Each boss plays a bit differently like a frost archer, vampires based around trapping you in an iron maiden and draining your blood, or nightmarish mutated monsters. Every time you kill them you unlock upgrades for your gear, castle, and companions in game. On brutal difficulty, the bosses also gain extra phases or attacks which makes a brutal run feel fresh if you've already played through it. Without spoiling too much Dracula is an awesome fight and while certain elements are bullethellish to some of the later game bosses including Dracula he's one of the most fun bosses I've killed in a game.

The castle building is awesome full stop. It's very easy to make something that looks good with the way pieces snap together and the aesthetics were designed with this in mind, so even if you make an "ugly stone shoebox" the interiors are very easy to light, decorate, and make look great. There are dozens of decorative textures to apply to interior and exterior walls, different furniture sets, and all kinds of plants and items to design any kind of vampiric fantasy castle you can imagine.

In regards to the survival elements of this game the survival can be as difficult, grindy, fast paced, or easy as you want it to be. You can modifier player health and damage, loot that drops, drop stacks, resources from your servants and so on even day and night length. The survival elements are also probably the best implemented I've seen in a Survival Game such that calling V Rising a Survival Game feels like a disservice. The sun is one of your primary foes in the early game and encourages players to only explore at night or in the shadows of trees (the game starts in a forest), so it makes it fun to explore and fight feeling that time limit you are always up against, eventually you get better capes, blood types and other ways to resist the influence of the sun. Blood types are a mechanic where enemies have different stat buffs they provide based on what kind of creature/fighter they are providing buffs to gathering resources, movement speed, crit damage, health leech, or spell power and cooldown. It makes eating not just a "mechanic you are forced to engage with" for the sake of the genre but something that feels believable and fun to do. Eventually you get prisons where you can kidnap people and drain their blood on tap to get your favorite buffs whenever you want them. 

The game is really good I've put almost 1000 hours in and played with several of my friends, check it out and if you made it this far thanks for reading.

For being my first vampire game, I think it's going to be hard to top this one. Almost everything was just mechanically sound and served a purpose; I couldn't even tell you if or when I encountered any bugs. [i]V Rising[/i] is just an incredibly competent game that allows you and your friends to go hunt bosses as a roving band of dashing vampires.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]I've really only played this and [i]Terraria[/i], but this is my new gold standard for crafting mechanics. The crafting progression and how it was tied to the next boss fight was incredibly streamlined and really well done.
    [*]I really admired the U.I. for the boss tier system. It would have been incredibly easy to add unnecessary fluff to that screen, but they kept it simple and it benefitted from that decision.
    [*]Everything. Has. A use. There is quite literally only [i]one[/i] item in the entire game that I always had too much of and not enough uses for: oil. Everything else was constantly being used.
    [*]Straightforward combat system with several flavors of magic to choose from. The boss fights were also varied and felt fair (outside of a few).
    [*]Beautiful and diverse environments. Want to build your vampire castle on a snowy mountainside? You can do that.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]The inability to lower the camera angle further was a frequent nuisance. This also prevented me from just enjoying more of the game's scenery.
    [*]PvE really felt like an afterthought. Needing to coordinate with multiple people just to ensure there aren't any spare prison cells open on the entire map so you can send your dominated victim to [i]only[/i] your castle was such a needless pain with Dusk Callers.
    [*]Disappointingly light on lore. I'm a sucker for backstory and the game only has two sources of any kind of narrative: the intro and each boss's text descriptions.
    [*]Some of the "snap" mechanics were kind of janky when in build mode.
    [*]It's easy to lose your mouse cursor in combat. I wish they had included a way to tweak that or at least change the color of the reticle.
    [*]No real replayability once you beat Dracula. You'll still get your money's worth out of that alone (in PvE), but PvP in this game sounds like you're just ripe for griefing attempts.
[/list]

Path of Exile 1 offers a huge amount of content, but for me, it ultimately becomes more frustrating than enjoyable.

One of its strengths is the freedom in the endgame. You can choose the type of content you want to engage with. For example, I personally enjoy tower defense mechanics, so I like playing Blighted Maps. The variety is definitely there, and compared to the campaign, which you have to replay over and over again, the endgame at least gives you some sense of control. The campaign itself is repetitive and annoying, but at least it is relatively short.

However, the real problem begins once you try to progress further into the endgame. At some point, the game becomes extremely difficult to push forward. I constantly hit the same invisible wall that I simply cannot overcome. Whether it is due to a lack of currency, inefficient builds, or just not being strong enough, progression feels blocked in a very discouraging way.

For example, I have never even managed to encounter Sirus, which highlights how inaccessible parts of the game can feel. No matter what I try, I end up stuck in the same loop without meaningful progress. It creates a sense that unless you invest an enormous amount of time or deeply optimize every detail, you cannot fully experience the game.

For a casual player, Path of Exile 1 is simply not very welcoming. While the game offers depth and freedom on the surface, in practice it can feel punishing, restrictive, and exhausting rather than fun.

V Rising honestly is one of the best survival experiences out there, in my opinion. It kind of builds on the usual foundations you already know from the genre but it also has this strong identity, the atmosphere, and a very clear dedication to the vampire fantasy so it never really feels like yet another copy, in a sea of overcrowded releases. In a genre where a lot of titles blend together, V Rising kind of slips through and finds its own spot, and it does it in a way that leaves a mark, for real.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Atmosphere & Identity[/h2]

What really, like instantly drew me into V Rising was the atmosphere. The game kind of fully commits to its gothic vampire vibe, building a world that feels elegant, dark, and honestly pretty immersive. Even the way the architecture sits, the environments look, and how the enemies are designed, it all adds up. Like, every little part helps the fantasy of being a rising vampire lord, not just another survivor wandering through some harsh world. Every region, every castle, even the enemies they all stack up into that fantasy of becoming a rising vampire lord, not merely another survivor running around, grabbing resources in some hostile place. And more, it really seems to understand who it is. A lot of survival games talk about freedom, but then they end up making you feel kinda aimless, like ok…now what?. V Rising goes another route, because it keeps throwing you a clear sense of purpose and steady progression, almost all the time.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Progression & Systems[/h2]

The progression system is honestly one of the stronger parts, like it really keeps pulling you forward. Each boss isn’t just… you know, another obstacle on the way. when you beat them you get worthwhile rewards that expand what you can do right away, and also push you into new directions. So it feels like this steady loop where every win matters, every little advance feels earned, not like it was handed to you. More importantly, most players almost always know what they’re supposed to do next and how to get there. So instead of spending all day digging through guides, and wikis, you can actually spend your time playing the game.
Also, the boss lineup is a great. They each bring their own vibe themes, mechanics, and combat rhythm, so progression doesn’t turn into the same routine over and over. The game keeps dropping fresh kinds of trouble, which means the whole experience stays interesting from beginning till the end, even when you think you’ve seen it all. And beyond fighting, the systems for prisoners and servants really add to the vampire fantasy. It’s not only about surviving anymore. You’re building influence, organizing power, and setting control over what’s happening around you. That makes you feel like an actual vampire ruler, which is basically exactly the goal the game is aiming for. Then there’s the building system, which honestly deserves credit too. Sure, it’s simpler than a lot of other survival games, but that simplicity works in its favor. It’s smooth to use, efficient, and it doesn’t usually turn into some annoying grind of frustration. 
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Boss Design & Endgame Frustrations[/h2]

That said, the game is not without a few flaws, it kind of shows. Some of the endgame bosses felt frustrating though, not really because they were straight up difficult. It was more that a number of these encounters seem to lean on mechanics, and odd little gimmicks that occasionally feel kind of disconnected from the boss overall design. Instead of actually testing mastery of the game combat systems, those moments sometimes manufacture frustration for reasons that feel… sort of artificial. Not the nice kind of challenge, the kind that you can’t quite tie back to anything. A tough boss can be incredibly satisfying, no question. But a frustrating boss leaves, a totally different, impression in your head.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]The Endgame Grind[/h2]

My biggest criticism, however, kinda lies with the endgame grind. I get that resource gathering is a basic part of the survival genre , and I dont really mind grinding when it feels meaningful. The issue is that a lot of the endgame asks players to keep repeatedly gathering resources they have already farmed like a hundred times throughout the whole game . At that point it stops feeling like real progression and starts feeling more like a chore , you know? What used to be engaging slowly turns into something repetitive, and then the pacing kinda suffers because of it.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Music[/h2]

One small thing I kinda wish the game had done differently is how it handles major boss themes. The soundtrack is fine, but honestly I would have loved unique musical themes for the most important encounters, like not just the same overall vibe. At the very least, the final boss of each act could have had its own signature track. Memorable music has this weird way to elevate the fights and stick in your head long after the battle ends. A special theme for those key moments could have made several of the great bosses feel truly unforgettable, like Simon Belmont, for example.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Despite a few frustrations with some boss mechanics, and the sheer amount of grinding that keeps popping up in the later parts of the game, V Rising stays a pretty exceptional experience.  
The whole atmosphere is captivating, the progression feels consistently rewarding, and the systems somehow just fit together like they belong there, to deliver one of the best survival experince out there. Very few survival games manage to balance approachability, real depth, and a clear identity, and as far as I can tell V Rising does.
9.5/10

I played World of Tanks as a kid and recently decided to give it another shot in 2026. I was surprised by what a shithole this game is, and I quickly remembered why I stopped playing it in the first place.

You start out and everything feels fine — the game is fun. You play low-tier tanks, get some kills, and start figuring things out. RNG shots don't bother you because you don't even need to aim at specific spots; you just aim at the tank and deal damage. But as the game gets harder, you have to start hitting specific weak spots to do any damage — and honestly, that part actually motivates you. The game gets more complex, more demanding, and you genuinely want to get better at it. The problem is that the whole time you're trying to improve, that fucking RNG keeps following you into every single match.

After battling with RNG, you head back to the garage — only to start battling the game's idiotic currency system. You have to pay for ammunition, consumables, equipment, and even your destroyed tanks. At the start it doesn't bother you, because the game is easy and you earn more than you lose. But as the game gets harder, the credit problem gets worse too. Shots become less profitable, and you reach a point where even good games barely make you any credits. You end up saving for higher-tier tanks, which are even less likely to turn a profit, which forces you to grind lower-tier tanks just to afford the higher ones. So you get stuck in a loop: playing dozens of games in low-tier tanks just to fund a handful of games in the high tiers.

[b] And the solution to the problem Wargaming created itself? You can, of course, fix it with real money. [/b]

At first glance, you think the premium tanks are just a bit different — different cosmetics and so on, like in other games. But then you realize that most premium tanks are flat-out better, and basically the only reasonable way to make credits, and they can cost up to €100 depending on tier. Or, if you want to make credits on a regular tank, you need to buy a Premium Account for better earnings — and you can combine that with WoT Plus for even more credits and bonuses, plus a Battle Pass on top.
Wargaming recommends a combination of all of these. Because that yacht isn't going to pay for itself, you know.
