This game is one of the most complete, coherent and exhaustive MMO worlds on the market in which you, as a player, can experience your own adventure at your own pace- exploring Tamriel and what it offers, ranging from awe-inspiring, breathtaking views to darkness within it, hiding ominous activity in which power-hungry vile individuals strive to make a name for themselves for all the wrong and appalling reasons.

There is a myriad of aspects a player can and likely will enjoy about the game.

1) Character Creation
Considering that The Elder Scrolls Online is now well over a decade old, its character creation system remains surprisingly impressive. While newer MMORPGs have entered the market boasting cutting-edge visuals and customization tools, ESO still offers players an extensive range of options to shape their characters exactly as they envision them.

From facial features and body proportions to hairstyles, markings, adornments, and race-specific details, the amount of customization available allows players to create characters that genuinely feel unique. Whether you want to roleplay a noble High Elf scholar, a battle-hardened Nord warrior, a mysterious Dark Elf mage, or something entirely your own, the tools are there to bring that vision to life.

Character creation in ESO serves as an excellent foundation for what the game does best: giving players the freedom to create their own story within the vast world of Tamriel.

2. Classes

ESO features a selection of classes that each possess a distinct identity and personality. Every class offers unique abilities, visual effects, and gameplay philosophies that cater to different types of players.

Whether you prefer commanding dark magic, summoning daedric powers, wielding holy light, manipulating nature, or mastering destructive elemental forces, there is likely a class that fits your preferred fantasy archetype. What makes the system even more appealing is its flexibility. Players are not locked into rigid class structures and can branch into numerous skill lines, weapon specializations, guild abilities, and other progression paths.

This freedom allows players to create highly personalized builds that often blur traditional MMO boundaries. You can remain faithful to your class fantasy or experiment with unconventional combinations that result in entirely unique playstyles. The result is a progression system that rewards creativity while still maintaining class identity.

3. Skills and Combat

ESO's combat may initially struggle to impress players who are accustomed to the lightning-fast, visually explosive action combat found in games such as Black Desert Online. Compared to some modern MMORPGs, ESO's combat can appear somewhat clunky or restrained during the first few hours of gameplay.

However, first impressions can be deceiving.

Once players begin unlocking additional abilities, understanding animation weaving, utilizing synergies, and experimenting with class combinations, the combat reveals a surprising amount of depth and fluidity. While it may not possess the same visual spectacle or technical flashiness as newer action MMOs, it remains responsive, intuitive, and satisfying.

Every class has access to a wide variety of abilities that can be combined into devastating rotations and visually impressive displays of power. As players progress, combat becomes increasingly dynamic, rewarding proper timing, positioning, resource management, and skill execution. What may initially appear simplistic gradually evolves into a system that is engaging and genuinely enjoyable.


4. The World

If there is one area where ESO truly excels, it is the world itself.

The sheer scale of Tamriel is staggering. Players can invest hundreds,if not thousands,of hours exploring its many regions before experiencing every major storyline the game has to offer. From ancient forests and bustling cities to deserts, swamps, mountains, islands, and forgotten ruins, every zone possesses its own atmosphere, culture, and history.

Perhaps even more impressive is the fact that virtually every quest in the game is fully voiced. This remains one of ESO's greatest achievements and significantly enhances immersion. Rather than simply reading blocks of text, players are able to engage with characters who feel alive and connected to the world around them.

The main storylines are surprisingly well-written for an MMORPG, featuring memorable characters, meaningful conflicts, and lore-rich narratives that rival many single-player RPGs. Even the smaller side quests often display a level of care and attention that exceeds what players might expect from optional content.

Tamriel feels alive. It feels inhabited. Every region offers stories waiting to be discovered, and that sense of adventure remains one of ESO's strongest qualities.

. Gameplay

It would be difficult to fully summarize everything ESO has to offer in a single review. There are newcomer guides on YouTube lasting multiple hours that merely scratch the surface of the game's systems, and that alone speaks volumes about the amount of content available.

At its core, ESO provides players with the opportunity to live a second life in Tamriel and experience the world however they choose.

You can immerse yourself in roleplay with friends or with strangers you meet along your journey. You can dedicate yourself to questing and uncover every storyline across the continent. You can become a master crafter whose equipment is sought after by countless players. You can challenge powerful dungeon and trial bosses that demand teamwork, coordination, and skill. You can simply wander the world, exploring hidden locations and discovering forgotten secrets.

For players who enjoy creativity and self-expression, housing offers another entire dimension of gameplay. Some players spend countless hours designing breathtaking homes that serve as personal sanctuaries, social hubs, or artistic showcases.

The beauty of ESO lies in its freedom. Few MMORPGs offer such a wide variety of activities while maintaining a world that feels cohesive and meaningful. Whether your goal is combat mastery, storytelling, exploration, crafting, roleplay, housing, or social interaction, there is a place for you within Tamriel.

That is ultimately why The Elder Scrolls Online remains one of the strongest MMORPGs available today. Despite its age, it continues to deliver an enormous amount of content, remarkable freedom, and an immersive world that invites players to lose themselves within it. Growing up playing the Elder Scrolls games, stepping into ESO felt less like starting a new MMO and more like coming home. The lore is one of the biggest reasons this game stands above so many others. If you’ve spent years exploring Tamriel through Morrowind, Oblivion, or Skyrim, you’ll immediately appreciate how faithfully ESO expands the universe. Every zone, questline, dungeon, and faction feels connected to the world so many of us grew up with, and the amount of storytelling packed into this game is honestly incredible.

What really blows me away is the sheer amount of content. There are literally thousands of hours worth of things to do. Whether you enjoy PvP in Cyrodiil and Battlegrounds, PvE questing, veteran dungeons, trials (raids), exploration, achievement hunting, or just roleplaying and collecting cosmetics, ESO gives you endless ways to play. It never feels like you’re forced into one path.

The character building is also one of the best systems I’ve seen in an MMO. The amount of weapon combinations, armor setups, class identities, guild skill lines, world skill lines, crafting skill lines, and ability morphs gives you so much freedom to experiment. You can make genuinely unique builds that fit your own playstyle instead of being locked into rigid archetypes. Combat feels fluid and active too, especially once you start mastering weaving, dodging, bar swapping, and synergies with other players.

Crafting deserves its own mention because it’s way deeper than most MMOs. Blacksmithing, enchanting, provisioning, alchemy, jewelry crafting, furnishing, and trait research all add long-term progression that actually feels meaningful. Housing and furnishing alone can consume hundreds of hours if you’re into creativity and collecting.

One of the coolest progression systems is the Champion Point system (CP). Once you hit level 50, progression doesn’t just stop. Instead, your account continues leveling through CP, giving you additional passive bonuses and long-term goals that make your character feel like it’s always growing stronger. It keeps the game rewarding long after the normal level cap.

Even free-to-play players have an insane amount of content available. There are mounts, pets, companions, events, collectibles, and countless zones to experience without feeling hard locked out of the game. But once you add ESO Plus and the newer seasonal content like the Tamriel Tome and the additions they’ve been making to seasons overall, the game really starts to shine. The amount of convenience, DLC access, and evolving content pipeline has helped ESO blossom into one of the best modern MMORPGs on the market.

At this point, ESO isn’t just surviving — it’s setting the standard for what a long-running MMO should look like. Consistent content, respect for lore, freedom in how you play, meaningful progression, and a world that genuinely feels alive. If you’re an Elder Scrolls fan, this game is absolutely worth experiencing.

V Rising is a tough one to rate fairly. That's why my review will only reflect the single-player aspect of the game, since I only played solo PvE on my own server.

On the one hand, the game has interesting boss fights, but on the other, it's an unbearable grind—even with server settings turned to maximum Quality of Life. The loop is always the same: Kill a boss (10%), grind ingredients for the next weapon, armor or castle upgrade (90%), rinse and repeat.

You are forced to build and maintain a castle, since it is mandatory to craft your aforementioned upgrades. Did I mention that you also need slaves? And speaking of them, you need to regularly drink their blood to avoid starving and to fully max out your vampire abilities. But don't forget to feed your slaves with fish or they die when you drain their blood. On top of that, the blood quality is pure RNG: you have to run around for hours just to find an enemy with very good, let alone 100% blood quality. If you are unlucky, you won't find one for days.

And watch out, don't stay in the sun too long because your pale skin will burn to death. This is especially annoying if day breaks during a long boss battle. On top of that, if you kite a boss too far away, it will run off and instantly regain its full health.

When you die, you have to run all the way back to your corpse to retrieve your gear and your goods. Don't forget to repair your gear all the time either, because if it breaks during a boss fight, you are in serious trouble. And surely, you need to grind even more ingredients just to keep your gear in shape. But watch out, you can't fast travel while carrying resources, because the game frames every trip from A to B to be a dangerous "adventure".

Yes, you can use servants to grind ingredients for you. But not without hunting and capturing them in the wild before, which is also a pain in the ass since you need to fit their perk for the specific missions. And finally, you are forced to craft and upgrade a completely separate set of gear just to equip them so they don't die on the job! Sure, you can spawn ingredients or even gear with the console, but if you don't like cheesing in a single-player game, you won't do it since it ruins the whole idea of the game. As I mentioned before: You can turn some settings on for QoL, but the game still has too many hassles and hurdles.

After 83 hours, I quit the game with five bosses remaining since I lost my patience because of dying over and over due to plain unfair boss mechanics. While the boss battles were the most interesting part of the game, especially the last bosses are a slap in the player's face. You can try uncountable times to beat them. Or you experiment with dozens of magic spells with ridiculously long cooldowns while the game lets you equip only three of them.

If you want to roleplay a vampire and have the mood and time to grind for resources and build a beautiful, eye-candy castle—fine, go for it, this could be your game. But if you just want to fight bosses on your own like I did, stay away from V Rising, because the repetitive and tedious game loop simply does not respect your time with its unbearable progression loop and sluggish player movement.

For an ancient vampire climbing your way back to your place as the apex predator and defacto ruler of the land, you feel awfully weak. The walk speed is abysmally slow and the only way to go faster is to transform into a wolf, but attacking puts you back into your sluggish vampire form which is what you'll have to contend with for the combat. Powers are all on cooldowns instead of having a mana bar and they all feel just a little too slow to recharge. Enemies, despite being mere mortals, are all damage sponges, and boss designs range from pretty good to tearing my hair out frustrating. Many bosses spawn adds, which would be fine if everything in this game didn't take more hits than Snoop Dogg at the blunt rotation. On top of that, some bosses can heal themselves, or will roam various areas where you are guaranteed to stumble into a dozen or so enemies, including another roaming boss who patrols the same roads despite being 15 levels above everything else in the area. And then when you finally get the boss down low, they've suddenly decided that they're too far away from where you aggro'd them and decide to run away, even though the boss is designed to be kited, and they instantly heal back to full HP. The base building is fun though, but I hardly feel like a badass vampire with this ludicrously overtuned combat. A challenge is fine, and I enjoy a game with challenging combat, but this game feels like its own mechanics were designed to smother any fun in the crib.

V Rising is a pretty good action RPG/survival crafting game that suffers from balancing around the PvP leading to a much worse experience for the PvE content.

I'm not a big fan of survival crafting games, and I had no interest in playing this as a PvP game, so i played on a PvE world with one friend, and I also cranked up the resource gain and lowered crafting times. Without those changes the game would have felt incredibly grindy, but with them it wasn't too bad.

Pros:
- Respects your time and money
- Solid story with uneven but occasionally incredible writing
- Even when the game is tackling world ending threats, the story still manages to feel personal with strong characters
- Action gameplay is genuinely fun without nearly the feeling of button bloat I've found in other games (In WoW, I had 2 full bars for all my myriad buttons between purges, stops, defensives, core rotation, cooldowns, movement, and other various utilities. This doesn't include all the extra bars I had for other purposes)
- Mounts aren't as much in the way of raw "power", but are so much more fun than the skyriding system that was derivative of GW2's already incredible mount system.
- Fashion wars is a ton of fun
- I ADORE the freeform achievements, and collections are genuinely amazing
- I can come back after 6 years without my gear all being worthless. No endless cycle of going from god to peon every couple of months
- All of the content in the game is still playable and fun. I had a guild from when I used to play focused on a single map meta event/worldboss called Triple Trouble. Years later, they are still thriving, still running Triple Trouble, and it's still tons of fun
- No stupid subscription to pay to play what you've already paid to play
- Economy is amazing. I had a few thousand gold when I took a years long break, and that few thousand gold was STILL as valuable as ever. Seriously, I could buy four of the chase Legendaries with gold, and if I did they would still be an awesome unlock for my account in another 4-6 years.
- I could honestly keep going, but I'm too lazy to keep listing them all out
- Oh, that reminds me, you can be pretty lazy and still have fun

Cons:
- Endgame doesn't have as much breadth as WoW
- Lower player numbers (though this doesn't end up feeling all that bad since there is usually more than enough people at peak hours)
- My friends still play WoW (poor bastards)
- Sometimes can be difficult to figure out "what to do" since it doesn't have traditional railroading or quests
- Collections and achievements are awesome for me, but aren't for everyone.
- Sometimes story feels locked behind metas. While metas are great fun, they do require enough people about at the time you are running them.
- Some of the coolest mounts are gated behind LONG achievements (I actually enjoy this, but seeing everyone running around on dragons while you are using a glider can feel bad. This is especially true when you find out that the easiest path to get them still requires a solid couple days of essentially achievement hunting)

Could I have formatted this better? Absolutely, but I want to get back to playing. Oh, this game also is great for people with responsibilities since it doesn't consume every waking moment of your time.

➤ Who This Game Is For

I do not recommend this game in the same way I do not fully recommend its competitor, War Thunder. I would only recommend it if you plan to play it as a casual free-to-play experience, with friends, or if you genuinely enjoy the tank warfare genre and simply want something relaxing to spend time on.

If you understand what multiplayer games involve — frustration, grind, repetition, and monetization — then you may still enjoy it. Compared to War Thunder, World of Tanks is more direct, accessible, and relaxing. However, its free-to-play monetization systems are extremely aggressive, and I cannot recommend those practices even if the core gameplay itself can still be enjoyable.

➤ Monetization and Grind

The game is built around systems that encourage spending money to reduce frustration, speed up progression, and maintain competitiveness.

Pay-to-progress, pay-to-fast, battle passes, premium accounts, premium tanks, accelerated crews, boosters — all of these systems exist not to improve gameplay, but to maximize retention and revenue.

At some point, multiplayer games stop feeling like games and begin feeling like money factories where a skin, commander, or vehicle becomes more valuable than the game itself as a product.

You can play it for free, but the game constantly pushes you toward premium convenience. Your progress depends heavily on battle performance, available time, and your in-game economy. Premium accounts and premium vehicles drastically accelerate progression and reduce grind, turning time into money.

Too often, games like this stop respecting the player's time and instead exploit attachment to the genre, progression, and competition.

➤ Progression System

The progression system revolves around national tech trees and tank classes. Unlike War Thunder, where you mainly progress through a nation's line, World of Tanks separates progression by tank roles such as light tanks, medium tanks, heavy tanks, tank destroyers, and artillery.

You must unlock previous vehicles to continue advancing through each branch. The higher the tier, the higher the repair costs, ammunition costs, and economic pressure become. This creates a system where free-to-play progression becomes intentionally slower and more frustrating over time.

Crew systems also create a major gap between veteran players and newcomers. Experienced crews with optimized perks, upgraded equipment, and years of accumulated resources create advantages that new players realistically cannot match without massive time investment or spending money.

➤ Gameplay and Tank Design

One of the game's strongest points is its massive variety of tanks. However, that is also one of its weaknesses. Many vehicles are fictional, blueprint-only projects, prototypes, or tanks that never entered production. For some players this is fun; for others it completely breaks immersion.

World of Tanks is ultimately an arcade game pretending to simulate realism aesthetically. It has realistic visuals and presentation, but mechanically it remains highly arcade-focused.

Unlike War Thunder, vehicles here operate with health bars rather than detailed crew and module destruction systems. In World of Tanks, you die when your HP reaches zero, not necessarily because your crew was eliminated or your tank was critically disabled.

While crew injuries and module damage exist, they have far less impact than in War Thunder. The gameplay is simpler in concept but still strategically complex due to spotting mechanics, vision systems, and predefined battlefield roles.

Light tanks scout. Tank destroyers ambush. Heavy tanks frontline. You cannot fully play vehicles however you want — you are heavily constrained by the role your class is designed around.

➤ Veteran Perspective

I have played this game since its early beta period over 10 years ago. Back then, premium ammunition literally required premium currency. That system was eventually removed because it was far too pay-to-win, and now premium shells cost regular credits instead.

I have seen the evolution of this game over time, and while some systems improved, the monetization philosophy remained fundamentally the same. If the game gives away premium rewards today, it is not generosity — it is because whales financially sustain the ecosystem.

➤ Final Thoughts

World of Tanks can still be enjoyable if you approach it casually and understand what it is. But I cannot personally recommend the monetization systems surrounding it.

TLDR: Don't play this like an MMO, and you'll be happy. This is a very bad mmo, but a fantastic co op game where you explore Elder Scrolls and get lost in mindless questing. 


The bad: 

The group finder is absolute crap and janky to use. The dungeons and raids are generally crap as well.  Playing with other players is an awkward experience of spamming abilities and hoping for the best, while chasing after them as they blitz through content with or without you. Tanking is fine, but healing is a frustrating experience chasing after people who have a death wish. Maybe the experience is better with a guild, but I've yet to see it. And I've tried. 

World bosses are a similar experience. Honestly, anything that involves actually doing content with other players is pretty awful to behold, and not just because the community can be toxic. It's no more toxic than any other game in my experience. 

It's like this playing with friends as well, and friend sessions usually devolve into each person playing their own quests and reporting in on occasion. That's just the way this game is designed, even if the devs themselves seem to disagree. Maybe it's because of Bethesda's influence on how the games were originally played, maybe it's down to Zenimax failing to understand what makes good group play and decent mmo content. But in my opinion, it's bad. Very bad, in fact. If you want to roll a support and play this like every other mmo, just don't. Go play something else instead, like GW2, FF14 or WoW. This is not an mmo, it's a co op game where you occasionally run with other players in the world's worst physics engine, and fail at basic mechanics that are badly telegraphed.

End game is bad. Ask anyone who plays end game if they're happy, and most will probably tell you they aren't. The rest are in denial. Balance issues, odd mechanics, meta slavery, fighting against the horrible physics engine, the natural incoherent way players fight together in this game--it's all there, a thousandfold. Sometimes a trial or two will be fun, and if you find a group willing to let you learn, that's great. For everyone else, I wouldn't recommend bothering. 

There are also a lot of loot crates and a big cash shop. The loot crates are bad because all loot crates are bad, but they come with a decent pity system that I actually appreciate. The cash shop is pretty generous as well, and not at all predatory imo. But I suppose that depends 
 both on your definition of predatory as well as your willpower, which is true for any game with a cash shop and loot crates. 

The good: 

Sub is optional, and with the most recent update, all future DLC are free (yes, even without a sub). The new seasons set up is fantastic and I think it's a very good direction for the game. Speaking of, this game is pay once and own forever. You do not need a sub to play unlike other mmos with a sub option, and in fact, there is countless hours of content possible without ever paying more than the base amount. The sub is mostly there to support the game if you like it, as well as give you access to conveniences like the craft bag and 1650 cash shop currency every month. I really like this system. You can enjoy thousands of hours of content in this game as a broke ass bitch, which I appreciate being that I am one.

If you want to craft, you'll have a harder time without a sub. But honestly? If you just do the solo thing, avoiding the absolute garbage content that is dungeons and raids, there are very few reasons to actually need to craft in this game. It's mostly there for end game content and a way to fill the boredom. And like I said, better to avoid end game.

Playing this on your own like any other Elder Scrolls, getting lost in side quests and avoiding the main quest like the plague is the way to go. The main quest is good too, though, as are the DLCs. There are a lot of really fun quests, characters, plot twists, and beautiful things to see. The side quests in particular shine a bit in this one, as there are tons of utterly psychotic characters and really hilarious moments that I'll remember for a while. The map is also HUGE and spans several different planes of existence. If you start questing now, you'll probably still be wandering around a year from now. Esp if you decide to sub (as it will give you access to all the dlc pre-seasons).

The gameplay itself is very good when it's just you on your own, with a dodge, block, interrupt, action-style combat, and a weapon swap. Builds are fun with every class using any weapon, and you level them the same way you do in any elder scrolls game--you pick up and shoot. If you avoid end game and just play everything else the way you want, this is a really fun way to operate. Don't be a meta slave!

There are also interesting companions which can heal you, damage, tank for you, and they all have quests with dialogue based on what you're doing, an approval/disapproval system and they can also hang out in your house. Most of them have pretty engaging stories of their own, which often serve as a mystery to uncover. I've had a lot of fun with this.

The housing system is a little janky at times, but absolutely fantastic as far as housing systems go. I got plenty of decos without buying them in the cash shop simply by playing the game over time. My only real criticism of the housing is that you can't travel to it for free, and you need a wayshrine close by it to really travel back to where you were. It's pretty inconvenient to use, but I've def seen worse systems out there.

And best of all (imo), your character is fully customizable at any time in the collectables tab (as you collect things!). You can literally change your hairstyle, costumes, ect, with the click of a button once you unlock them, and this is true account-wide. Unleash your inner barbie.


That's it. That's my two dimes. Avoid end game, don't be a meta slave, and have fun running around talking to random npcs. There's a lot out there worth seeing.

If you play this game, you need to know that the default settings are genuinely terrible. Change these right away to save your sanity:
⠀
• [b]Turn on "Show All Usable Object Names":[/b] By default, the game hides item names. Turning this on lets you see hidden or hard to see quest items, collection coins, and chests glowing with text from far away.
⠀
• [b]Change Ground Targeting to "Fast with Range Indicator", or "Instant":[/b] This cuts out the clunky double-clicking for ground spells and makes combat feel incredibly fluid.
⠀
• [b]Fusing your Inventory:[/b] Open your inventory, click the gear icon, and select "Hide Bags." This turns your inventory into one continuous, clean block instead of a disjointed mess of individual grids.
⠀
[b]You can also turn the game into a First or Third-Person Shooter:[/b]
Hit Escape -> Options -> Keybinds, and set a key for “Toggle Action Camera.” Combine this with disabling camera shake and enabling first-person zoom, and the game completely changes how it plays. 
⠀
[i]Note on camera view:[/i] Third-person plays significantly better than first-person here. Unlike games like ESO, GW2 doesn’t actually show your weapon or hands on-screen when you use skills in first-person, which can feel a bit odd, like my deadeye sniper is sneezing out sniper shots. Stick to third-person action camera for the best combat experience.
⠀
There are a ton more UI optimizations to make, but these developers really need to update their defaults. Strongly recommend the game, just fix the settings first!
⠀

[b]Some Bonus Gameplay Tips:[/b]
⠀
• [b]Hunt Yellow Mobs for 4x XP:[/b] Enemies / Neutral NPCs not killed for a long time give massive bonus XP. Story of how I lost three weeks of my real life to ESO's guild trader system.

I joined an Elsweyr trading guild in 2022 as "just a stockpile dump" — sell my mats, log out, normal MMO behavior. By month four I was the guild's #2 weekly seller. By month six I owned a spreadsheet with 47 columns tracking market price drift across patch cycles. By month eight I was the guild MASTER because the previous master quit, citing "burnout from running five traders." I had become him. The cycle was complete.

The ESO economy is the most psychotic player-driven market in any MMO. There's no auction house. Each guild owns ONE trader who sits in a specific city. Players race weekly to bid for the BEST trader location (Mournhold is god-tier, Nimalten is exile). Prices drift wildly based on patch notes, set drops, and what some Twitch streamer crafted on stream Tuesday.

I have personally made 14 million gold off a single Plague Doctor set arbitrage when Update 38 dropped. I have personally LOST 8 million gold sitting on Coral Riptide trash pieces when the meta shifted. I have FRIENDS now whose names I've never heard pronounced — they're "Crafter-Mike-from-Saturday-Bids" and "Mournhold-Stevie."

The actual game (dungeons, story, PvP) is great. The economy is the parallel dimension where 5% of the playerbase actually lives.

If you've ever wanted to play Wall Street with elves, this is the game. We have an ESO crew at discord.gg/uga — some of us still raid vet trials, most of us just compare guild trader bid sheets at 2 AM.

ESO. What to say.. I came back to the game after a 3 year hiatus. I started on PS4. I thoroughly enjoyed the game, got lots of cool cosmetics, housing, mounts, etc. I've spent countless hours and resources grinding out levels. My BIGGEST qualms with this game are a) There is no porting profiles between devices. I am starting a brand new profile and playthrough from scratch on PC. b) Cross platform is not a thing, at least that was the case when I last played. It does seem they've updated the UI and some other minor quality of life things, but these are the two BIG complaints I have with Zenimax currently. My level 500+ character and the shameful amount of money I've put into it seem a wash simply because I cannot get my profile from PS to PC (and PS4+ prices continue to rise, all just so I can play online, so it's no longer justifiable). There are also some things that are gatekept behind a paywall which is... frustrating to say the least. Prices continue to rise for intellectual property which is insane. Any DLC content, maps, quests, are all kept behind comparable prices of what it costs to buy the base game. So a $20 game can easily turn into a $100+ game with all the DLC content. 

With that being said, I've enjoyed the online community of ESO. This game is definitely better with friends and partaking in the social elements. It's one of my favorite things, honestly. I've had a lot of silly and fun interactions, and a lot of sweet ones with people who have been eager to help. I'm not saying everyone is like that, but it's pretty easy to ignore and filter out those who don't fit the vibe (so to speak). The events are generally pretty fun because they do often give you free items or ways to earn specialty items (like indrik mounts, non-combat pets, gear, etc). It can be a bit of a grind, but it's always better with friends. Despite my frustrations with Zenimax and what they could do better for the gamer/customer base, I do enjoy the game content and what it offers. I just wish it wasn't so expensive, the integrity of the profiles could be preserved between systems and that I could play with friends regardless of what system they are on.

------------------ OLD REVIEW   -------------
This is an amazing game full of stories, lore, action and events. The world is beautiful and exploration is rewarding.

The game runs perfectly fine on LINUX. 
THE GAME NEEDS around 200GBs of free space to install. You can delete some AUDIO files later to save space.

First thing first: AS YOU LEVEL UP, YOU GET WEAKER!

That's right. You were holding a weapon that did 1200 damage. You leveled up and now suddenly it does 600 damage. Your Health, Mana and stamina all decreased. So you will constantly need new weapon and armor. But don't worry, most quests keep giving you rewards based on your level and loot is plentiful. 

You are what you wear. I came to realize that classes are only a small part of the game. If you are holding a 2H sword, you are a two hand fighter and that skill line progress. If you are holding a Healing Staff, you are now a healer. I maxed them all and change accordingly. Well, you can say I am bad at every role equally but that's because I lack the gear. 

I loved the MAIN STORY. It very much fits the Elder Scrolls lore and all of the characters are fully polished. 

The game is fully voiced. Total of 80GBs of voice files is the proof of that. (I deleted everything else but English to save space)

If you explore, go where your hat shows, you'll find lots of quests, mostly unique. Some of them were really amazing little stories and I kinda regret some of the actions I have taken. Some choices change the landscape permanently (but only for you). They don't effect anything else. 

CRAFTING is weird. I maxed all crafting skills but still don't know how to use them properly. Crafting SET items require certain places and it is VERY expensive. You may need to read a guide on that. 

I bought all expansions on sale. The best thing that comes with them are the COMPANIONS. All companions can be customized for any role (HEALER, DPS, TANK) and although some are better than others at certain roles, all get the job done. They seem to lack DPS but me and my companion is able to finish any 4 person dungeon, albeit of course slower than a full group. 

Buying expansions is the only way to get a companion. Otherwise, you are on your own.

Speaking of dungeons, most old players speed run dungeons. Which can be annoying if you want to listen to the story. Worse is, if you pause to hear the story, they push up and you are instantly teleported to their location. Since I am slow at times, I even failed some quests because I couldn't talk to some NPCs in time and got teleported and couldn't return back. Even worse, if all other 3 members of the group leave the dungeon, the dungeon auto ends in 1 minute. 

I really wish there was an option "RP dungeon" in the dungeon queues for people who wants to enjoy the dungeon's story.

Community is one of the best and welcoming. People are mostly helpful. How many times I needed something and asked where I can find/buy it and people simply sent it to me. 

The world is HUGE. Very big. Very wide. And you can go anywhere anytime. The whole world is at your level always, (or you are at their level always). That means a Level 1 player and a Level 50+1600 can do the same event and Level 1 player won't be useless. 

The entire game is PVE. PVP is only on one special region that's at the center of the world. There are also some game modes that enable quick PVP battles. Try them, they are fun. 


Overall ESO is one of the best MMOs I have ever played and I played them all.

Great as a free game, if you like the style. It has issues with framerate on lower spec computer when the screen gets too busy. I feel like the game could just severely cut on the effects in lower end computers to maintain a decent framerate. 
Skill effects can overwhelm the screen and prevent the player from detecting threats and react in time. Some monsters and effects (Azurite Orb rares monsters and player phasing effect for example) are so similar that makes it hard to tell when the monster is in melee range and you need to move away. Some spectre minions create so many overlapping effects it becomes very difficult to see anything on the map. Other effects or minions even without crazy graphics accumulate around bosses and make reading the boss tells, facing direction and moves very difficult. Just a few examples. 
Crafting system could be fantastic, but instead relies too much on RNG and repetition. Making good items is basically a process of re-rolling your chances until you find by luck what you are looking for, for the most part. There is hardly any meaningful process of working on an item and incrementally making it better, and when that is possible it's still layered with too many dumb-luck RNG repetitive cycles. I find this extremely frustrating and disappointing, feels like a lot of lost potential in creating a truly engaging crafting system. These 2 aspects are particularly frustrating to me - the graphic effects incompatible with a game that requires good reads and quick reflexes + the casino crafting.
While the depth of the game is intimidating for a new player, it is fantastic.

​Do you love timers? Do you love waiting in real-time for artificial barriers to unlock basic gameplay features? Then boy, do I have the MMORPG for you.

​Let's talk about the absolute joke that is "Trait Researching" for Blacksmithing, Clothing, and Woodworking. When you start out, it takes a reasonable amount of time to learn a single item trait—maybe it was 7 hours for me to learn one thing early on. Fine. That makes sense. But the system scales exponentially like a predatory mobile game designed to frustrate you into spending real money.

​If you want to fully unlock a single item type (like a sword or a chest piece) to craft endgame gear sets, the time doubles for every trait you learn. By the time you get to the 9th and final trait on an item, it literally takes up to 30 days of REAL-TIME waiting just to finish researching ONE SINGLE TRAIT. If you don’t invest your hard-earned skill points into passive skills to reduce the timer, or if you don't have an ESO Plus subscription, it can take over a month or two just for a single slot. To fully master all blacksmithing and crafting skills across the board? You are looking at nearly a YEAR of real-world time ticking away.

​The game literally expects you to leave oven timers running for months just to be self-sufficient at endgame crafting. Why? Because they want you to get sick of waiting and go to the Crown Store to buy premium "Research Scrolls" with real money to skip the artificial wait times. It is disgusting mobile game monetization disguised as an MMO mechanic.

​And it doesn't stop there. If you look online, the community is shouting about the exact same predatory, time-wasting loops:

​The Inventory / Craft Bag Extortion: If you don't pay the monthly subscription fee ($15/month) for the "infinite craft bag," you will spend 50% of your actual playtime standing at a bank managing your inventory. The base inventory space is intentionally choking you to force you into paying a sub fee.

​Terrible Level Scaling: The progression feels totally backwards. Because of the way the world scales, you actually feel weaker as you level up unless you constantly replace your gear with exact level-equivalent items. You don't feel like a powerful hero; you feel like you're running on a treadmill.

​Endgame Paywalls: Want to stay relevant in the endgame or competitive PVP/PVE meta? Get ready to drop massive cash on yearly expansions and constant DLCs, or be locked out of the best gear dungeons and zones.
​Clunky Combat: The combat boils down to animation-canceling and spamming the exact same button sequence over and over again. It completely lacks the weight or immersion of a true Elder Scrolls game.

​Save your money and your time. If a game requires me to set a calendar alert for a month from now just to see a progress bar finish filling up for a blacksmithing passive, it doesn't respect me as a player. Go play something else.

Noita expects you to play shorter/carefree runs at first, so you can discover ways to consistently increase your health, earn gold, and test spells. Then, to turn the odds in your favor, you'll finally have to mix in a single run as much as you've discovered, which could result in a much longer run (unless you're lucky) with backtracking and micromanagement. It's similar to how The Outer Wilds expects you to explore and find information separately in each life cycle until you can finally sort out the mystery. In this case, the mystery is how to find enough resources to stay alive and go deep enough without risking it all.

That said, there are still a few situations you're bound to find unfair, such as enemies shooting you from off-screen or explosive barrels suddenly falling on your head. But honestly, that's how it is. Noita is that friend you both love and hate for being a jerk. Much of what I've said might not sound surprising since we're talking about a roguelike, but in truth, the pacing turns out to be quite different from what you'd commonly experience in the genre. 

It's also worth mentioning the game gets a lot more interesting in Nightmare mode, which gives you an initial perk and three extra wands in exchange for increased difficulty and a random map layout. Despite somewhat simple mechanics, Noita's environmental challenges give life to an experience that you will not find resistance in calling the hardest game you have ever played, or at the very least one of the hardest.

This is a great game for gamers who used to be into first-person shooters but whose reaction times have slowed down a bit. There was a time when I could play a game like *Titanfall*, step into a room with a sidearm, and clear it. Now I could not do it with a vest full of bombs strapped to me.

World of Tanks is a good solution for that. I still get the feel and action of a battle, but the pace is slower and places a much bigger premium on smart play. Understanding the game matters more than pure reaction time.

I am new to the game, so these are my early impressions. The game can definitely be a grind, but the nice thing is that while you are grinding, you are still playing the game. I do not mind that too much, especially because I am not eager to interfere with veteran players’ battles before I know what I am doing.

Your first several battles will be against bots. They will absolutely find you and shoot you, but they are not especially strategic. This is a great way to learn the basics: positioning, ammo types, tank classes, and the many creative ways you can get yourself destroyed. You also start to understand the different currencies, how to maximize them, and what might actually be worth spending real money on later.

I now have a couple of higher-level tanks and have started fighting mostly against human players. I win enough to stay encouraged, and I try to stay out of the veterans’ way while I learn. Sometimes I hang back and protect the back line. Other times I jump into a faster tank and scout for the team. Even with a weaker tank, skill and positioning can still win out. I am nowhere close to mastering the maps yet, so I am learning them in small pieces.

There is also plenty of PvE content that you can play solo or with a group, which helps you farm currencies and experience. That means there is almost always a way to make progress. The events are pretty cool too, and the community has mostly been helpful. You will always run into the occasional “mom’s basement” bro with no social skills who flames everyone, but they are easy enough to ignore. Overall, I have found that most players seem like mature adults. The veterans, in particular, are often happy to tell you how you can help the team.

I also like that people actually try to win in this game. So far, I have not run into obvious throwers, which is refreshing.

The game can be played for free, but I think many players will burn out quicker that way. My suggestion is to play for free for a while, and if you find yourself sticking with it, then figure out the best way to spend for your own needs. There is a ton of YouTube content about that and almost every other part of the game. Players are more than willing to give away their best techniques if it gets them a view.

I think I will play World of Tanks for several months before I burn out on it. I am not sure if there is a real spending ceiling, but some players say you eventually reach a point where you do not need to spend real money to keep progressing. So far, I have found that spending mostly gives you a “get there faster” advantage, which I personally do not mind. I generally do not mind spending money to reduce grind, so take that into consideration when reading my opinion.

Overall, World of Tanks is a slower paced, more tactical alternative to twitch shooters. It still gives me the action and satisfaction of a good battle, but it rewards patience, positioning, and game knowledge more than raw reflexes. For me, that makes it a great fit.

World of Tanks takes me back quite a few years. I spent countless hours grinding it long before it came to Steam, and I have tried to return several times since. Every time, though, I run into the same fundamental issues that keep me from enjoying it.

I’ll split this review into three sections: gameplay, historical tanks, and the premium model.

Let’s start with gameplay.

World of Tanks is built primarily around casual 15v15 battles. Competitive modes exist, and Wargaming has pushed them over the years, but the main gameplay loop is still random battles. For me, that is one of the game’s biggest problems.

Ever stomped your opponent in a MOBA, only to realize your bot lane is 0/10? Ever tried to buy an AWP in Counter-Strike, only to notice that every teammate bought one too? World of Tanks has a similar issue, except its entire default experience depends on fifteen random players somehow creating a coherent battle plan.

The game does have some well-designed maps, each with prominent positions that allow for tactical and strategic play, which rarely works in casual matches. A huge portion of many maps is effectively no-man’s-land: go there and you are exposed, helpless, and probably dead within seconds. You usually learn this by being instantly deleted after making one bad positional choice.

That leaves the same few key positions, where everyone else is also trying to drive their slow, clunky metal box. You end up shoving and squeezing through your own team just to reach a useful spot, only to realize that nobody went to the other side of the map and you are now being shot from the flank or rear.

Roughly half of my matches feel like camp fests. On one side, heavy tanks hide behind city blocks because nobody wants to be the first to peek and become the sacrifice. On the other, tank destroyers sit in forests and hills, waiting for light tanks to spot something they can erase. The other half of my matches feel lost from the start because of skill imbalance, poor tank composition, or simple herd mentality.

This is not unique to World of Tanks. Anyone who has played casual Counter-Strike should be familiar with the feeling to see four people trying to snipe down Dust2 long while the bomb is already planted on B. But World of Tanks suffers from it more because casual random battles are not just a side mode; they are the core experience.

Another major gameplay issue is the damage model.

Tanks have hit points, and if you penetrate the armor, you reduce those hit points. The issue is that the game often does not meaningfully care where you penetrated the tank. Some tanks are simply worse because they have a large commander’s hatch, an awkward turret weak spot, or some other exposed area that players can aim at to drain the entire vehicle’s health pool.

Again, this is not unique to World of Tanks. Shooters taught us long ago that repeatedly shooting someone in the foot will eventually kill them. But in WoT, the issue feels worse because there is often no satisfying damage reduction for hitting less critical parts. A tiny weak spot can decide the entire viability of a tank, even when the actual shot feels absurd.

Next are the historical tanks.

Coming from Company of Heroes, I fell into the same trap as many Wehraboos and went for the German line. German tanks are monsters in plenty of World War II games, but in World of Tanks they come with a lot of problems.

I am not here to argue about perfect historical accuracy. In fact, I am glad Wargaming lets me leave spawn in a Tiger II without immediately suffering transmission failure. But I do think there is a strange problem at the heart of World of Tanks as a World War II-themed tank game: the actual historical tanks often do not feel like the stars.

It is baffling to have iconic vehicles like the T-34, Panzer IV, Tiger, Pershing, Sherman, and many more, only for them to become stepping stones toward the “real” endgame: prototypes, blueprint vehicles, post-war concepts, and now Tier XI fantasy-style super tanks with special mechanics.

Why build so much of your game’s identity around World War II armor if the actual vehicles from that era are mostly something you pass through on your way to the real meta?

If you want to play seriously, you eventually need to reach the highest tiers. But those tiers are dominated by vehicles that either barely existed, never saw meaningful service, or exist mostly as speculative designs. Maybe this is just personal taste, but I never formed the same attachment to those clunky blueprint behemoths as I did to real, functional tanks — or even semi-functional ones like the Tiger II.

To Wargaming’s credit, they do sometimes try to represent historical strengths and weaknesses. The problem is that this creates an uneven playing field when real vehicles are balanced against paper tanks whose stats are untested or straight up propaganda. Historical limitations matter a lot more when your opponent is, by design, make-believe.

Finally, there is the premium model.

World of Tanks is not the worst free-to-play model out there. At least it is mostly clear what you are buying, unlike in many gacha systems. But the grind is brutal, and sooner or later the game pushes you hard toward a premium account if you want progression to feel reasonable.

The bigger issue for me is premium ammunition, still commonly called “gold ammo.” As far as I know, it got that name because it originally required gold, World of Tanks’ real-money currency. It has been purchasable with regular credits for many years now, but the design problem remains.

Premium ammo generally offers higher penetration, letting you punch through armor with far less effort. At higher tiers, it is so widely used that regular ammunition often feels like the exception rather than the norm. This reduces the importance of positioning, armor knowledge, and weak-spot targeting. It also feels terrible when your tank’s main strength is supposed to be armor, only for that armor to become much less relevant because the enemy loaded the expensive rounds.

This is especially frustrating for German tanks. Many of them rely on thick, relatively flat armor rather than extreme angles. Premium ammo naturally punishes that design, because higher penetration makes the “just have more armor” solution far less reliable. Tanks with obvious weak spots suffer even more, since premium ammo makes those shots easier and more consistent.

Typical Bethesda product with as many cons as pros, so make sure you understand (and comprehend) the already known pits before you undertake this journey yourself. This is my own cumulative review after nearly 2 years in their strange, wonderful, yet often frustrating land. Since there is not room for a fully detailed review to include the pros, which do exist, the old adage "doing your job is not an exceptional feat, and will rarely be commented on, but every screw up will be magnified and writ large' still applies, and in ZoS case the scales are about even... though barely. Though Steam does not allow for a middle ground recommendation, so pushing the issue has resulted in a NO that is only sometimes deserved.

ONE: Lack of visual control accuracy. For those with visual impairments that include light sensitivity, be aware that even with disabling of bloom, rays, etc and while keeping contrast as low as still playable - there is a persistent mulishness on ZoS part to have effects that are NOT properly affected by these settings. From full screen white/blue flash effects to flames and 'glows' that cause bleeding eyeballs even with those that have healthy 20/20 sight, bottom line here is they value their own 'preferences' well above the physical discomforts and damages they cause their players, and persistently ignore any related complaints. So if you suffer from such disabilities, ESO is NOT the game for you.

TWO being their craptastic UI, in conjunction with their marginal infrastructure. The existing UI, what there is of it, is very minimal and still based on their decades old framework - which is still top heavy and prone to a needed kick (/reloadui) once and a while to keep it working. The infrastructure is passable on a normal day, but issues do persist with inventory, bank, and guild bank access delays (waiting on previous action) being fairly regular - and gets appreciably worse during events with population spikes during events and new content releases. Random latency spikes and/or disconnects also persist, often with a 5 minute 'penalty timer' before one can get back in. The onscreen loot history, alerts, and other notifications have a significant delay, and some actions will have them so back logged that they will keep the screen/audio 'effects' going for several minutes unless you change zones to clear the buffer. Counter to this, the system alerts in the chat window are immediate, but this part of the UI is so atavistic and outdated that one can not have separate chat window(s) to keep things from crowding each other. There was an old add-on that allowed separate chat windows, but it was killed (by ZoS) very quickly and will FUBAR things if you try to use it today.

NOTES: One should pay close attention to disabling cloud sync services (ONEdrive especially) for the working ESO folder that resides in a given users documents folder). One should also clean out their Documents\Elder Scrolls Online\live\ShaderCache.cooked at each major update. Yes, you will have an appreciably longer character login when you first log back in, but as that will be the case after most updates anyway, a few more seconds to keep things healthy is a small price to pay. When ESO was first released, I thought I was disappointed. What I wanted was a new Skyrim, but instead ESO is kind of a generic MMO with an Elder Scrolls skin on it.

A couple years later I've had the itch to try some MMO. I feel like I'm way too late to WoW, so that's not happening. Final Fantasy XIV looks like it might be good, but I refuse to pay a subscription. The way content gets deleted from Destiny 2 is ridiculous. So by method of elimination I am left with ESO. It's cheap enough for the base game, so I thought why not give it a try?

I'm glad I tried it out because it scratches that MMO itch [i]perfectly[/i]. But, it's not a game that I enjoyed immediately, but it took a while to grow on me. The starting area kind of sucks (the jail breakout + Auridon + main story is all kind of boring). Combat is a bit floaty, but still ok, but not great. The UI is overwhelming and takes a while to get used too. The game starts getting good, when you start exploring more and get to see new parts of the Elder Scrolls world. Reading some of the lore on the unofficial ESO wiki also helps understand the world better. I like the other zones I've explored so far, like Grahtwood and Daggerfall. I liked the stuff with Apocrypha (the Oblivion realm of knowledge and fate). There's a quest that introduces you to it and there's a wave based co-op dungeon survival mode. Group dungoens are decent fun to run around and fight stuff with other players. The grind seems kind of pointless to me because everything scales anyway. It's just numbers going up. The "Golden Pursuits" (challenges) give you some much needed purpose and direction in the game. "Tomes" are like a battlepass. By doing those you unlock a lot of stuff, including some currency ("Seals") for better pets and mounts.

My point is, there is a lot to do and enjoy with just the base game. If you play to explore the world and try out the various in-game activities, it's easy to ignore the grind. There's a lot to see and do. It's fun to see other players running around, going about their business and sometimes teaming up for a dungeon run. I recommend it overall, even if it has it's flaws. With all the content in the game, the real challenge is finding out how you like to play it.

Noita is one of those games that feels almost impossible to describe to someone who hasn't played it. Every single pixel in the world is simulated, which sounds like a tech demo gimmick until you realize it actually shapes how you play. Water douses fire, lava melts steel, blood pools and freezes, and your own spells will absolutely kill you if you get reckless with them.

The wand crafting system is where the game truly shines. It starts off looking like a simple roguelike spell setup, but the deeper you go, the more you realize you're basically programming weapons of mass destruction. Some of the most satisfying moments come from cobbling together a wand that completely breaks the game in your favor, right before it ironically blows you up.

What really keeps Noita special is how much it refuses to explain itself. There is nothing like Noita.  It succeeds both as an unforgiving little game that you can pick up for a few hours on a weeknight, and as a highly complex ([i]highly[/i] complex) puzzle that rewards you for becoming hopelessly ([i]hopelessly[/i]) obsessed with it.

You remember when Elden Ring came out and everyone simultaneously experienced those [spoiler]trap chests that teleport you to Caelid and the Altus Plateau,[/spoiler] and the feeling was something like "this game is HOW BIG?". Well, Noita does something similar and better, over and over and over again.  This is a game of frankly psychotic depth and intricacy that allows for many things you can't even imagine before they happen right in front of your face.

The game is very hard but actually cools off quite a lot once you start to understand it.  I'd say you should expect to die frequently, often completely out of nowhere, often in new and interesting ways, for the first 50 hours or so.  If you approach it with curiosity and a sense of humor it is quite manageable and worth the investment of your time.

A lot has been said about the depth of the secret material in this game.  Most of the puzzles are at the top-end of what someone could reasonably be expected to sort out on their own without consulting a wiki, and there are [spoiler]a handful of puzzly things in the game that, to this day, nobody has figured out how to solve.[/spoiler]  I actually think the game is good both as something that you attempt to struggle through purely on your own, and also as something that you consult all available communal knowledge to work through.  I played for about 100 hours without really touching the wiki, but for the last 50 hours I've been grindin', and that has been a lot of fun too.  What I'm trying to say is that whatever you wanna do is cool.

It's also the best-sounding game I've ever played.  It is number one, and it's not close.  The audio is incredibly stylish while also being quite grounded and realistic (as much as you can be grounded and realistic in a game about magic wands), and it's all implemented with elegance in a program that is so complicated.  I have to imagine it was an enormous undertaking so I want to publicly express that when I kick a wooden box in this game and it clatters around in whatever environment it's in, the sound I hear could make me cry it is so good.  Shoutout Niilo and friends.

There is also now a fully functional multiplayer mod for this game.  It's not how I would start playing but dang if it doesn't add a whole extra layer to something that was already great.  Spending a few minutes away from a friend and returning to them only to find that they've created a wand that turns your entire screen pure white when they click left mouse (possibly killing you in the process) is good fun.  It's so fun that I'm starting to think this is something that Nolla games should holler at the mod makers about and get this functionality put into the base game.

So yeah, nothing but appreciation for this one.  I think it's probably the best indie game that has ever been made.

Online games are a plus for some players, but as a single player, for me this is not. If you have great internet and don't experience problems, I'm happy for you,

Every playthrough I check all the rock carvings, special locations and talk to all npcs about the subjects they tell. Its a masterpiece of art that should be experienced.

Sound, Music, animations, artwork and graphics are all top level. If you manage your game settings you can get it to run well on a modest system without turning your rig into a coal furnace, thus ending its lifespan prematurely because you read running the GPU at 90c is fine. Its is not.

Character customiztion. Some classes are better suited, or rather, positioned in the skill web, to access certian abilities better than others. But the replay value here is staggering because of it. You can make any and all sorts.

Highly not recommended. Boils down to Customer Service dealing with account bans, community toxicity around help and support for banned accounts, extremely aggressive behind the scenes monetization model, and general hostility towards Steam and players who play from Steam. 

Customer service and community toxicity revolving around banned accounts: To me, considering to start playing a MMORPGs is a massive decision, and because I'm gonna be potentially spending many many years in these games along with potential multiple purchases over the years, I'd have to consider the company that runs the MMORPG and if they're good candidates to be getting into this kind of relationship with. And specifically one of the criteria for my assessment revolves around how irresponsible or heavy handed a publisher is with regards to account bans (if its a possibility), the rules that trigger said account bans, how transparent the publisher is around these bans, and the process to reverse bans should they occur. 

And on that note, I have been spending quite a bit of time in the GW2 communities and paying special attention to topics of discussions revolving around this issue. From what it looks like, Arenanet (the publisher) generally provides good and decent service, but should your account gets banned for any of the more serious transgressions like RMT (real money transactions), you're not gonna get a good experience with regards to the customer service process in getting your account back. You'd be treated with contempt (not just by the CS but also the community), and in many cases I've seen, Arenanet will not be honest about them making a mistake (if they did) and will just blame the player anyways. Its quite frankly very disheartening to have on the back of my mind especially given the amount of commitment this game requires if you want to get serious. And mind you, you can get banned for receiving gold purchased via RMT. So if someone buys gold illegally, then uses the gold to buy stuff from you, or otherwise just hands the gold to you, you have the chance of getting your account permanently banned (I actually lost my first account this way 13 years ago, seems like nothing's changed since then). And this no-RMT rule (and how insanely it is implemented) is absurd given that Arenanet's official shop actually does allow you to purchase gold directly from Arenanet themselves. And with this, the community (that's portrayed to be a friendly and good one) can be extremely toxic and unsympathetic with regards to dealing with cases like these, so if you find yourself on the wrong end of a ban hammer, expect to have a horrible experience of it, regardless of whether or not you're innocent. 


Extremely aggressive behind the scenes monetization: Aside from these two points, the monetization for this game is actually extremely aggressive. You're extremely limited in terms of space whether it is inventory slots, bank slots, or character slots. The space provided by the game is sufficient for most players in their first 50 hours or so, but beyond that you'll need to start spending more money for gems to purchase more inventory slots with, and because these inventory slots are character specific and not account wide, it means each new character you buy will need to have that money spent on them as well. In the long term over a period of several years, you're going to find out very quickly that it can be extremely expensive to play this game despite its so called friendly monetization model. 

Last but not least. I strongly do not recommend playing from Steam. There is a lot of hostility from both Arenanet and players towards players playing on Steam accounts and Steam in general where any issues you have accessing the game is automatically blamed on Steam being the middleman, and I have seen several accounts of players being treated harshly by Arenanet Customer Service simply because they're a Steam platform player, but received immediate responses and solutions as soon as their friend or family member with a standalone account messages Arenanet on their behalf.

This game is amazing. It's inspired by the history and philosophy of alchemy, which is very secretive and mysterious by necessity. There are a lot of puzzles and hidden mechanics that are key to unlocking new areas, but the most interesting part to me is the wand-building. Art design is awesome, and interacting with the physics and chemistry sandbox is fun and rewarding, you can manipulate the environment A LOT.

It's a difficult game, but as you gain understanding it becomes much easier. Creativity and wisdom will take you far, and your curiosity will be rewarded. The initial learning curve is steep but once you get the hang of the fundamentals it gets really interesting. There are hundreds of spells that combine and interact in complex ways, and each wand you find has randomized stats that drastically change their characteristics and the behavior of spells you put on them. A huge chunk of my hours in the game have just been experimenting with wands and spells in the Holy Mountain. A small change in the spell combination / arrangement on a wand can have a tremendous impact on its performance, so discovery through experimentation is essential if you want to learn. You can get strong early with simple spells if you understand how the spells work together and you put them on the right wand. 

Noita wants you to 'break' the game, and think outside the box. FAFO is often the only way to learn and the reward is sometimes death. But to sacrifice oneself in the pursuit of knowledge is the highest tribute to the Gods. 10/10 outstanding game, I'm only just beginning to understand what's going on.

World of Tanks is a game that perfectly blends tactical gameplay with fast-paced action. At first glance, it might seem like just another shooter, but it quickly reveals a much deeper layer of strategy and teamwork.

The variety of tanks is impressive, ranging from light scouts to heavily armored giants, each with its own playstyle. This makes every match feel different, as you constantly adapt to your vehicle and team composition. The progression system is rewarding, giving you a real sense of achievement as you unlock new tanks and upgrades.

Visually, the game still holds up well, with detailed tank models and immersive maps. Sound design also deserves credit — every shot and engine roar adds to the battlefield atmosphere.

However, the game is not without its flaws. The grind can be quite heavy, especially at higher tiers, and matchmaking sometimes feels unbalanced. Additionally, premium content can give certain players an advantage, which might be frustrating for those who prefer a purely free-to-play experience.

Overall, World of Tanks is a solid and engaging game that offers both casual fun and competitive depth. If you enjoy strategy, teamwork, and historical military vehicles, it’s definitely worth trying.

I am a long-time, storied MMO player. I mostly play casual, because anything more than that required a lot of me to keep up, with item levels, story progression, character levels, evolving items.. Guild Wars 2 isn't like that. I found that I can play casually and still like, be included in what is considered core multiplayer content.
Firstly, while there is SO MUCH to do in GW2, there's still incentive to replay content or to play through legacy content, so there's still people playing through Group Events in every zone to the point where I can participate. There's also been the same level cap since base game, so I'm not having to catch up to folks level-wise. It took like 3 hours to max the skill tree on the character I am using right now to play through the story missions after I unlocked the glider & Springer on my first character, but I could have done different skill point things to not need those. Gearing also is easy, the stats are not based on RNG, it's possible to change stats on gearpieces or tear gear down to make your own with the right stats, and gearing stops at Ascended or Legendary, which have the same stats, so I'm able to just run into content and have a good time. There's a lot to do that doesn't feel like grinding, but there's also goals to work towards if I wanted to grind. Playing this game also sparked my interest for the previous title in the series.
I hope more people continue to play this game, and if I see you in Fractals, I'll be happy.

[hr][/hr][b] INTRO [/b][hr][/hr] 

There are things to love about the game. Seeing all of Tamriel in one game is a highlight that never gets old.

I will give the devs credit for taking a lot of positive steps in the last few updates. Many people seem to be happy with the overall trajectory of things, but for me this is still not enough. 

There are fundamental issues with the game that probably cannot be fixed at this point, which become increasingly evident and problematic the longer you play.

After years of playing (3000+ hours, not all via Steam), I had to stop for a few key reasons:


[hr][/hr][b] 1. ABUSIVE MONETISATION: [/b][hr][/hr] 

They create artificial problems to sell you the solutions (inventory space, mount training etc).

Most of the cool cosmetic stuff is locked behind overpriced loot boxes, while there is comparatively little worth earning through in-game achievements.

To circumvent gambling laws, they allow you to earn some of these top items in-game via seals (endeavors) + tomes, but it takes almost a year to grind out enough currency for one apex mount, and the best tome rewards are still locked behind paid premium passes.

Speaking of which... the season pass reward tiers should IMO automatically be available with ESO+ membership, but they still want you to pay separately for both; it's just blatant gouging at this point.


[hr][/hr][b] 2. HOUSING IS POINTLESS: [/b][hr][/hr] 

You are collecting all this junk for what? 

Housing is a major pillar of end-game content, but ultimately adds nothing of value to your character, nor has any practical impact on the game, aside from houses being usable as de-facto wayshrines and crafting stations.


[hr][/hr][b] 3. LACK OF ACTUAL BUILD VARIETY: [/b][hr][/hr] 

They want you to believe you can literally play as anything you want.

In reality, there are only a small handful of builds that are viable for end game content.

You will see the same cookie-cutter meta builds over and over again in end-game trial groups and PVP. 


[hr][/hr][b] 4. 95% OF ARMOR SETS ARE USELESS: [/b][hr][/hr] 

Mind-blowing that this has never been addressed by the devs (ever), since you spend such a huge amount of your time collecting set items in this game (currently 700+ sets), never to be used.

So many interesting builds could be possible if the devs would just update the stats on the older sets to keep them competitive. 

Instead, these are left to rot on the vine while everybody flocks to the latest BIS meta sets and ends up with the same boring cookie-cutter builds in every update cycle.


[hr][/hr][b] 5. CONSTANT NERFS:[/b][hr][/hr] 

Your time is not respected, as every update cycle, your previous build that you spent months putting together is now suddenly useless, often for reasons that seem totally arbitrary. 

Time to begin the grind all over again, chasing the next meta. Eventually I just couldn't anymore.
 

[hr][/hr][b] 6. THE WORLD IS TOO SMALL: [/b][hr][/hr] 

Yes, it's a large open world, but the scale of everything is off. 

In real terms, every region is only a few kilometres across, and can be traversed in a matter of minutes, making everything feel like a theme park instead of a living, breathing world inhabited by real people. 

Farms and actual industry (outside of crafting stations) are also conspicuously absent in most areas, adding to the pervasive feeling of a fake, empty world where everything merely exists as a quest location or harvesting node.

I guess this is fine if immersion is not important to you.


[hr][/hr][b] 7. DIALOG IS MEANINGLESS: [/b][hr][/hr] 

All dialog choices lead to the same outcomes. 

Your decisions have zero impact on the story. 

All quests are just unfolding on rails at all times. 

There is no reason to care about anything or anyone, thus you are incentivised to skip rapidly through all dialog and speed through every fetch quest as quickly as possible. 

(Particularly aggravating when having to repeat the tedious main quest on a new character.)


[hr][/hr][b] 8. COMBAT IS DULL + REPETITIVE: [/b][hr][/hr] 

Your build is ultimately meaningless because combat for everybody boils down to the same stale rotation of: 

- Cast buffs/debuffs
- Lay down dots/hots
- Spam your spammables until buffs/debuffs + dots/hots need to be refreshed
- Repeat

Majority of skills in the game are basically just themed re-skins for the above actions.


[hr][/hr][b]  9. GUILDS + TRADE: [/b][hr][/hr] 

The whole setup is just clumsy and poorly implemented, and requires a bunch of external add-ons to even be usable (like so many other aspects of the game). After more than a decade, this has not been addressed in any meaningful way. 

Also, pointless limits on guild memberships and items you can put up for sale at any given time. Just so unbelievably tedious. 


[hr][/hr][b] 10. FOMO: [/b][hr][/hr] 

Too much of the game is built around fomo and dark patterns. 

Everything in the crown store being a limited time offer. Daily writs (so incredibly tedious to grind out on multiple toons). Daily endeavours. Daily log-in rewards (Tomes have only partially solved some of this). Daily mount trainings. Daily job brokers. Daily pledges. Daily Tribute matches. Daily Thieves Guild heists. Daily Brotherhood contracts. 

At a certain point, you are just logging in to complete a laundry list of daily chores that quickly turn into a grindy slog, leading rapidly to burnout. It feels more like a second job that you are paying for the privilege of working at. 

Yes you can ignore all of it, if you don't mind the penalty of giving up those rewards and the creeping sense of 'falling behind'. 


[hr][/hr][b] CONCLUSION [/b][hr][/hr] 

I really want to recommend this game to new players, but I just can't in its current state. 

It's all very immersive in the early honeymoon stages, but eventually boils down to nothing of much substance or consequence. The longer you play, the more unsatisfying it becomes. Time for me to take a very long, perhaps permanent break.
