If, like me, you're here because you like Diablo 2, but haven't yet tried Path of Exile, I suggest reading below as this game may not be for you.

So, this game doesn't really have a story with cutscenes like Diablo 2 and most of the story you get interacting with the world feels like world building. If you're motivated by a good story, this game is not it.

Now, one of the first things you notice when you enter the game is the graphics. I'm usually not picky but Path of Exile graphics are not great. The problem isn't that the graphics are old. They lack identity and the only thing that really stands out is the dark tone they've tried to set for the game. Unfortunately, that dark tone means places like caves are really dark and there's no easy solution as the game doesn't let you adjust the gamma or brightness. My monitor is an M28U. Maybe with an OLED the game is more palatable.

Once the game actually starts, you'll feel tempted to check the abilities you can have based on the character you chose. Well, you can't. There's no 'active abilities' talent tree. You actually get abilities from gems that are socketed into gear. So, in order to know what abilities are out there, you have to either do research outside the game or play enough to acquire all those gems with abilities. There's a lot of them and you get them for all classes, not just yours. Moreover, you can technically use them all, but they do have attribute requirements, so not really. There's some more complexity to this system but the main point is: when you start the game, you're not given the information needed to plan out your active abilities based on the class you chose.

At level 2, I acquired a gem that gave me the Slam ability. An AOE damage ability. It's like the slam ability you'd expect in many other ARPGs. Usually, an endgame ability. For me, this really affects the sense of progression within the game. I personally don't like it, but maybe you like skipping introductions.

Another thing you might have noticed at the start of the game is that there is this immense 'passives' talent tree. Seems overwhelming, and that's probably the point, but to me it feels lackluster. There's over a 1,000 talents in that tree but you'll only have access to a bit over a 100 by the end of the game (I had to search this on the internet). Also, depending on the class you choose, you'll start closer to a different set of talents. Ultimately, it feels like there is a lot, but there isn't as much as is shown.

There are more issues with the 'passives' talent tree. If you do a quick scan of the talents, you'll find out there's a lot of bloat. For example, there's a talent that can increase your total health by 30. To get it, you have to spend quite a few talent points. However, as a marauder, before level 20, you can already have around 500 health. So 30 health feels like a trap for people who haven't taken the time to understand the game.

The bloat seen in the 'passives' talent tree is replicated in other systems, like the attributes system, the abilities system and the loot system. The game relies on you not knowing the value of things and so it doesn't provide you with the needed information. For example, within the 'passives' talent tree, at times you can choose between points to strength and extra % damage. But you don't know the values of these. In a game like Diablo 2, you get 5 attribute points a level and you can see attribute requirements on gear so early on you get a sense of the value of strength as well as the value of other attributes. In Path of Exile you don't really have this information and it has the added complexity of abilities also requiring attributes to be used.

Now, the thing that actually broke me and made me stop playing was the loot system. From the beginning you're bombarded with items. Mostly normal, magical and rare items. But Path of Exile has tried to make every type of item interesting so, along your way, you find these orbs or fragments or whatever they are that turn a normal item into magical or rare or give the item sockets (needed to put gems that give you abilities) or connect the sockets within an item (also needed for abilities) or change the properties of the items, etc. As a new player, you soon find that everything is potentially interesting and so nothing is interesting at all. Even the uniques I got were orbs that would turn a weapon or piece of armor into a unique with a couple of fixed properties and some other random properties. Basically, in 15 hours I didn't find a piece of gear that stood out, like a Leoric's crown or King Arthur's sword or gloves of Midas, you get the point. It was all 'random loot generator'...with the ability to modify anything that dropped.

Of course, carrying all those orbs and things occupies a lot of inventory space so you quickly get picky about what you grab from the floor. It's okay because, even though Path of Exile has gold, you can't really sell those items for gold to a vendor. Vendors exchange things. You give them items in exchange for fragments and scrolls and, you can imagine, another complex system. Moreover, if you sell the right combination of items to a vendor, you get better rewards in exchange. Think of it in these terms: if you sell a sword and an axe, you get standard fragments or scrolls. If you sell 2 swords, you get a special orb of something.

Ultimately, Path of Exile is not a tightly packaged game for the masses. It's a niche game for the people that like the min-maxing aspect of ARPGs and have endless hours to sink into the game. That's not to say it's bad. Like me, you may just not be the target audience.

"My Gaming Life" by Arensky and Jon Becker.

"Fear Not This Night" by Jeremy Soule and Asja Kadric.

Guild Wars 2 is easily one of the best MMORPGs ever made, and honestly, games like this just aren’t made anymore.

What sets it apart right away is how much it respects your time. There’s no forced grind, no subscription pressure, and no feeling that you’re falling behind if you take a break. Instead, it offers a massive open world that feels alive, with dynamic events replacing the usual boring quest chains. The world reacts to players, and exploration genuinely feels rewarding.

The combat is another highlight — fast, fluid, and skill-based. It doesn’t lock you into rigid roles, so every class feels flexible and fun to experiment with. Add to that deep character customization, tons of builds, and both PvE and PvP modes, and you get a system that stays engaging for hundreds (or thousands) of hours.

What really makes Guild Wars 2 special, though, is its design philosophy. It avoids many of the outdated MMO mechanics and instead focuses on freedom, cooperation, and discovery. It’s been praised as “one of the most exhaustively detailed and rewarding MMOs in existence” and “the best online role-playing game in years” — and even after all this time, that still holds true.

On top of that, it’s free-to-play with no subscription, constantly updated with expansions, and supported by a passionate community that keeps the world alive.

If you’re looking for an MMO that values your time, rewards exploration, and still feels fresh years later — this is it. A true classic, and sadly, a reminder that the genre doesn’t get games like this anymore.

If you are a f2p player and realistically cannot ever afford the Elder Dragon Saga Complete Collection, then do NOT play this game. However, for level 50-80 players who enjoy base game Tyria without mounts and can afford the Elder Dragon Saga Collection without stressing over $100 in the next 6 months, then this game may be for you. Nearly all content such as dungeons, fractals, and world events in Core Tyria are accessible to f2p accounts. Although for new accounts, purchasing exotic gear on the trading post to maximize damage can be a difficult endeavor due to Nika, Zhed, and Devona armor being locked behind account restrictions (you must own expansions). 

Note that the Collection mentioned above contains all 6 massive expansions and is a one-time purchase with no subscription fees. This is truly the easiest approach if you prefer to just own the game in its entirety; budgeting options exist too though. If you purchase ANY expansion for this game, the Elder Dragon Saga Complete Collection goes away and you will need to buy the Living World Seasons through the gem store as its not available on steam. This is the reason I absolutely recommend getting the Elder Dragon Saga Complete Collection as it saves the hassle. 

This game is highly P2W due to the trade post and gem store convenience issues; you can purchase legendary weapons for real money whaling, although the game incentivizes you to earn it through the crafting system--usually this can take players roughly 50-150 hours to complete a full trade mastery as you must reach level 500 crafting and your choice of world completion. However, due to the balanced gear scaling between exotic, ascended, and legendary equipment, this may not be an issue for most players as it will usually only provide a 10% stat increase and has QoL more than anything. Lastly, you must earn legendary armor which is a bulk of your build, so again this is not as serious of an issue.

All expansion content is relevant due to the level 80 gear cap, many endgame players will return and explore zones in Core Tyria, rarely will you see people not participating in world bosses and meta events. The MMORPG genre can be complex and confusing, so I suggest taking your time with a f2p account since its free anyway; change controls, graphic settings, use the wiki and YouTube, analyze inventory buttons, read tooltips, buffs, debuffs, by any means to learn the game and get a good starting point.

Most game content is locked behind expansions like Living World Seasons (2-5) and the 6 Major Expansions which includes locked content such as the Skyscale, Roller Beetle, class weapons, passives, subclassing, & elite specs, gliders, mounts, masteries, raids, fishing, 30 maps, and more. This game has PLENTY to offer though, which is why this review is positive. Overall, I think the Elder Dragon Saga is definitely worth it and will provide a bountiful amount of content to players wanting to enjoy a fresh MMO experience. Many content forums and YouTube explanations define Living World as "Story Content" which is very misleading, since there is tons of actual game changing content in these Title Updates as mentioned above and why I recommended the Elder Dragon Saga Collection.

I’m not new to Guild Wars 2. I played at launch, reached max level, and only came back recently because a friend insisted, especially after my time with Turtle WoW came to an end. It felt like a good moment to revisit older MMOs and see how they’ve evolved.

When I logged back in, my old character was gone. Honestly, I didn’t mind restarting, but it still felt like something that should have been better communicated.

The biggest issue is onboarding. The game throws a massive amount of systems, menus, and currencies at you almost immediately while only explaining the basics. Everything beyond that feels like you’re expected to figure it out alone.

Progression is the game’s biggest structural flaw. I reached level 80 after completing only a handful of starting and mid-level maps. That pacing is absurd. You massively outlevel content before truly understanding your class, the world, or the game’s systems.

This completely undermines combat learning. The combat mechanics are genuinely excellent, but the game never forces you to learn them properly during leveling. You unlock skills faster than you can process them, so early combat becomes little more than spamming cooldowns, swapping weapons randomly, and steamrolling everything anyway. It works, but it feels shallow for far too long.

Crafting progression is handled terribly. By the time I reached level cap, my professions were still far behind because the game provides no natural or satisfying way to level them alongside normal gameplay. Instead of being a meaningful parallel progression system, crafting becomes a separate grind after the fact. At that point, most of what you craft is already obsolete or irrelevant, which makes the whole process feel pointless and demotivating.

Inventory management remains one of the worst friction points, especially for free players. Bag space is extremely restrictive, forcing constant trips to the bank and turning basic item management into a chore. Combined with waypoint costs and travel time, the game often feels like it wastes more of your time on logistics than on actual gameplay.

Dungeon design may be fine mechanically, but the player culture around them ruined the experience for me. My first dungeon run was completely rushed by veterans sprinting through everything as fast as possible. Nobody waited, nobody explained anything, and if you fell behind, missed dialogue, loot, or map details, that was your problem. There was no opportunity to appreciate the dungeon itself, its atmosphere, or its story. It felt less like group content and more like being dragged behind people doing mandatory chores.

The post-80 gameplay loop did not improve my opinion. The game immediately pushes you toward dailies and weeklies centered around event grinding, but as someone without mounts, traversing the world for these objectives is tedious and slow. Worse, many event participants barely engage with the content. Players swoop in, contribute the bare minimum for credit, and leave instantly. The cooperative open-world design that sounds great on paper ends up feeling hollow and transactional in practice.

At no point did the game motivate me to push further into raids or deeper endgame systems. And that matters. If an MMO fails to convince a player to continue after they have reached level cap, tried dungeons, experienced open-world endgame loops, and sampled its progression systems, then “the real game starts later” is not a defense, it is an indictment.

To be clear: Guild Wars 2 has excellent combat fundamentals, an immersive world, and one of the most alive-feeling open worlds in the MMO genre. The foundation is strong.

But the actual player progression experience, from leveling to early endgame, feels fundamentally poorly structured. The game constantly gets in its own way through bad pacing, poor onboarding, disconnected progression systems, and community-driven optimization that strips the soul out of group content.

I wanted to like it more than I did.

But after giving it a fair chance, I simply do not think Guild Wars 2 respects a new or returning player’s time well enough to recommend it.

I’m still a relatively new World of Tanks player, but even in a short time I’ve already started noticing the cracks in the game.

At first the game feels really fun. You get fast progression, easy matches, and unlock tanks at a satisfying pace. But after a while the gameplay loop becomes very repetitive, and progression starts to feel noticeably slower.

When advancing through the higher tiers, the skill cap gets steeper. I would say it took me 1000 games to get a bit of an understanding of the gameplay on tier 8-10. The game simply isn´t beginner friendly. You really need to put the hours in and grind to get better. It´s a sweatfest.

Balance is also an issue. There are clearly overpowered tanks like the Ares and BZ-176.  I’ve had multiple frustrating sessions that just ended in rage quits because of how unbalanced some encounters feel.

The monetization also stands out more the longer you play. World of Tanks feels heavily pushed toward a cash-grab model. Premium tanks are often stronger than tech tree tanks, and many of the newer vehicles are locked behind lootboxes with very low drop rates. Realistically, you can end up spending 50€ or more just for a chance at what you actually want.

I also expected a more grounded, realistic tank experience, but the direction has shifted quite a bit. The game is increasingly filled with fantasy-like or gimmick mechanics such as double-barrel tanks, boosters, and now even tier 11 vehicles with ridiculous names like “Gorilla”, “Executor”, “Hacker” and similar over-the-top designs that completely break immersion.

On top of that, content updates feel limited. Game modes rarely change in meaningful ways, artillery-filled games are a pain in the butt, matchmaking can be inconsistent, and I honestly can’t remember the last time a new map was introduced.

Overall, the early experience is enjoyable, but once you get deeper into the game it becomes repetitive, heavily monetized, sweaty and increasingly disconnected from the more grounded style it used to have.

- Combat: Great
Every class can equip several main-hand and off-hand weapons. An elementalist can use scepter and/or dagger for mainhand. However, each class has their own skills for every weapon. So the combat spells for a Ranger Bow will be different compared to the combat spells of a Guardian (Dragonhunter Specialization) Bow.

You can chain your auto-attack combos to your spells as well. You can cater your slot and elite skills (not the weapon skills of the class) based on the build that you are aiming for.

Each class also has customiseable builds that you can select based on the build you are aiming for. An elementalist or guardian can select and mix-and-match different builds based on a certain playstyle they're aiming for (ex., dps, support, condi/quickness support). 

Meta events are dynamic events present in the world in which you or several players can partake into. These are usually aligned to the story of the region you are in, and the rewards are always generous. 

Even if you are <= Level 80, you can partake into any meta events and reap the their rewards with other players. You don't have to worry about loot being stolen or missed since Guild Wars 2 ensures every participant receives a reward based on their contribution to the event.

- Map: Great
Seriously, you can really observe and feel the love the game designers, artists, and developers poured into through the maps. The maps (especially core Tyria) contain so much details, features, and storybuilding. Narratives are presented just through what you see in the maps. 

There are also hidden entrances that lead to jumping puzzles. Jumping puzzles usually give rewards, but I find that the true reward you get is the journey you tread as you solve these puzzles. Sometimes, you are taken into a completely secret but beautiful place like Diadre's Steps, or you venture into hidden areas that provide much more lore to the game's worldbuilding. It's amazing.


- Storybuilding: Great
The game has excellent storybuilding without the use of the traditional questing system in MMOs. The world's story is presented to you through the meta and heart events that you can accomplish as you explore a multitude of zones in the world. The main story is also great so far (I am speaking as someone who has played up until End of Dragons as of writing this review). The lore of the world is truly fascinating since you are introduced to cultural differences between races and how they perceive certain civil-related matters. 

- Gearing: Fantastic
This game is very forgiving with gear. Even if you do not have Ascended gear, your gear is still very relevant to the end-game meta events as well as dungeons, raids, and fractals. Important to note is the collaboration of players during these events. Strategy and teamwork is emphasized rather than how robust or sick your gear is. 

Hence, the game respects your time and wouldn't demand much time from you just for you to be relevant in participating in any of the games' events.

- Expansions: Great
Once you buy an expansion, you will forever access any of its content. No monthly subscription.

I have been playing WoT since 2013.

Back then...
- I enjoyed the times when there was almost no physics in the game where you could not fall off of a cliff or deal any DMG through ramming other tanks.
- Gold ammunition was only available for gold, making it more special, rare, and precious to use. Today, everyone is using.
- Gold ammo, making your armour obsolete, unless you sidescrap 24/7 which is impossible unless you have no weak sposts on your turret and you camp in one place all game, where as we know, everyone wants to get that "special place" on the map and will ram you toward enemy just to get it...
- Crew perks, Crew training and Researching new tanks used to take months. I remember getting ~300 experience per 15 minute battle without the premium account bought, where to unlock the last or second to last tier arty i had to amass 300,000 points of experience, so you can imagine it took me almost a year to get that desired tank. And mind you i was doing my job on the battlefield, those were not bad games, it's just how the rates used to be back then. Same goes for the crew members and their perks. I remember the shock i was in, when a friend of mind told me he's got 6 perks on a crew member and he cannot level them up anymore. That friend used to play this game 18 hours a day, playing special mode on the "global map", so for a regular player it was impossible to reach that level.
- Artillery used to be max VIII tier and there were no "stun" mechanics. 
- The T92 SPG still has the biggest gun caliber from the entire game (topping FV215b 183) which is 240 mm yet it deals way less DMG than many other smaller caliber guns, which makes no sense unless you want to please people who despise "clickers" because they were barraged with thousands of DMG every 50 seconds so you had to "nerf" the arty.
- Russian tree still has the best tanks in the game (hidden favouritism), due to their armour shape which in some places has over 500mm (Medium tanks + Heavy Tanks [Hello Obj. 279e]), accuracy and gun reload (Arty),Damage / Penetration (Tank Destroyers, and premium Vehicles).

Nowadays...
- Artillery has been nerfed to the point where it's almost obsolete on the battlefield. The only thing that keeps them somewhat-useful is that if you stun someone who either ran out of first aid kit or forgot to buy it, because most of the times if you stun someone, they will auto-heal up and your hit for ~300 DMG does nothing to help the team, whereas stunning them actually weakens the crew, reload time etc, which is very helpful when you need to help your team with a high-priority target.
- They shove those battle-pass and weird game-modes down your throat every few weeks to keep veterans engaged in this game.
- After taking a few years break, i came back to nuances like double-barreled tanks. After composing myself from laughter at first i thought i was seeing things, or this tank was a unique, special, premium tank, but no, they've created an entire tree dedicated to this ridiculous double-barreled tanks.
- This may not be such a bad thing but it cuts down the time you spend in this game which keeps you engaged -- upgrading crew members and researching new tanks takes weeks now, if not days, whereas if you remember it took me several months to research 9-10 tier back in the day. It's not such a bad thing, but it makes "tomatoes" (bad players) obtain high-level tanks and play in the same match-making with other more advanced players who "maxed-out" their tanks, where the so called tomatoes not only do not know how to drive such a high tier but also they are mostly stock.
- Gold ammunition is available for credits now, which you basically can use auto-aim on X tier and still hit someone. This fact makes tanks purely dependable on armour (e.g. Japanese HTs, British TDs, American TDs...) obsolete, because they will always pen you (there are instances where some Heavy Tanks have so low penetration on gold ammo, that it's actually impossible to pen using only auto-aim, so thank you for that lol).
- To my liking, there are too many "new" special tanks / premium tanks. Most of the time when i play after taking a longer break, i see new tanks that are outside of the research-tree. Sometimes they change the tank's status to "special" or "premium" because all they did was put new camo on it. It's literally the same tank but with a different name and different camo on it. I guess some people are into it, i guess.
- In my opinion the new garage layout is furiously confusing and makes you open 5 different windows just to inspect your tank's stats, where in older patches it was displayed automatically next to the tank. I can't get used to it.
- Major changes to the tanks. On the top of making artillery a tier X now, they've changed some core meta of this game. Many tanks that i remember playing religiously, nowadays are forgotten and either nobody plays them, they are a different (lower) tier today or they were made a special vehicle with nerfed gun. Shoutout to KV-1S, T-150, Chaffee, Hellcat, Wolverine and many more...
- I have saved the worst change of them all for last. And those are Tier XI's...

The gameplay formula is overall great, it is addictive even! However I have a few things that drive me up a wall with this game:

1. You can't choose which map you play! It makes roles of different tanks useless in many scenarios and makes maps straight up garbage because they try to fit all playstyles and as a result fit none. Most of the maps are unbalanced and badly thought through. So out of all 40+ maps you will probably enjoy 2 or 3 and celebrate every time you randomly got that map you wanted.

2. The battles are not balanced based on any useful metric! You will be put in a round with 14 random players. No, their skill is not taken into account during matchmaking. So the people you have a potential to meet might have better stats then you and probably most of your teammates combined. It leads to "turbo" games quite often when all your team is slaughtered in less then three minutes without enemies even taking one loss.

3. The community is perhaps one of the most toxic out there. I suggest you turn off the in game chat as soon as you install the game because you won't see anything good being said in there. The players of this game hate each other and so will they hate you. Welcome to the family!

4. Developers are actively encouraging the passive and unskilled players with the systems they've made. Tanks can randomly miss, you can randomly bounce a shot off a vehicle that has next to no armor, you can deal no damage with your shot and so on. This game has mad RNG and you will become the victim of it. Therefore it is impossible to take any competitive play seriously here because even if you aimed your shot perfectly it can just miss based on the randomness of the game. Your aim, your skill and your reaction time don't matter much in this game.

SHORT SUMMARY: You can't choose which map you will be playing to play your tank role properly. You will encounter teams that will steamroll you, or you will steamroll them, no fun will be had in any of those games. You will randomly miss a perfectly aimed shot, or fail to penetrate the armor of the enemy tank, so no skill is required to play, just aim in their general direction and shoot, RNG will do the rest. You will feel like you are being punished for any initiative you take in battle, it's because you are. They want you to sit near your base and wait for the enemy to come, or for your time to run out, so you can find many nooks and cozy bushes there to do just that.

The Core Problem: A 2018 Engine in a 2026 World

When the Core graphics engine launched, it was a massive leap forward and essentially rebuilt the game’s visuals from scratch.
But that leap happened eight years ago. Today’s graphics standards have moved dramatically.
Modern game engines now feature:
real-time global illumination
hardware ray tracing
fully destructible environments (down to each individual brick!)
advanced physics simulations
procedural vegetation ecosystems
World of Tanks still looks good—but it rarely feels like it belongs in the same technological generation.

Final Verdict

World of Tanks in 2026 is visually impressive—but technically conservative. It remains a strong-looking game with:

✔ Beautiful tank models
✔ Large, well-designed battlefields
✔ Solid lighting and terrain systems
✔ Stable performance across many PCs

But it also feels like a game that has stopped pushing boundaries.

There is enormous potential still waiting inside this battlefield.

Imagine:

track physics that deform terrain

forests full of wildlife and dynamic ecosystems

true environmental destruction

deeper tank mechanical simulation

ultra-high-resolution terrain textures with no pop-in. Until those arrive, World of Tanks will remain visually good… yet strangely behind its time. A polished battlefield. But one that still feels like it’s waiting for its next real evolution.

What do I think about World of Tanks? It's one of the hardest games I've played, and the best. Why? There are over 700 tanks in the game, 43 maps, and that means a lot of situations. Plus, new tanks are constantly coming, sometimes even maps, but they're rare. In most video games, you can be a pro after 200-300 hours of playing, here it's not enough, you need at least 1000 hours. Really good players have played over 5000 hours and over 50,000 battles. Here you have to acquire a lot of knowledge and skills, for example, you have to know the damage per minute of most tanks, gun depression, weak points on the armor, armor thickness, their weaknesses and strengths, average damage, penetration, accuracy, aiming time, speed, camouflage value, terribly good map knowledge, you also have to learn to aim, you have to know how to use armor. It is worth using the site tanks.gg, here you can learn the statistics of tanks and get to know the armor of tanks. Patience and perseverance are important! I recommend it, WoT is not dead, in fact it is getting better! But this is a pay to win game, but so fun!

I’ve been playing this game for nearly nine years, though not through Steam but via Wargaming’s standalone client. I stopped early last year because the game has increasingly shifted toward loot boxes.

Without purchasing these overpriced loot boxes, you miss out on a significant amount of rewards and content. This practice isn’t limited to just one title—Wargaming applies the same model across all their games.
The result is a pay-to-win environment where premium vehicles outperform regular ones and generate far more in-game currency. What was once an enjoyable experience has devolved into a system designed to push players into spending money.

Instead of improving gameplay or adding new maps, Wargaming focuses on releasing premium vehicles tied to loot box events. The priority is clear: selling loot boxes, not enhancing the game.
I cannot recommend investing your time or hard-earned money here. What used to be a solid game has become a loot box-driven cash grab.

Overall, the game can be funny and occasionally enjoyable, but there are a number of huge downsides that completely ruin the experience:

Toxic game environment: Daily quests are frustrating and unfair (for example, “finish in the top 1–3 by rating”), which is extremely difficult for an average player. The streamer community often mocks bad players, which adds to the negativity. Special modes are also toxic or boring - for instance, the current Chinese New Year mode forces you to complete borinng quests just to earn rewards, instead of having fun. Some tanks feel extremely unbalanced: they can destroy you with one blind shot, while others just YOLO into you without any consequences. You can start a match and be sent back to the garage within a minute, with almost no chance to actually play.

Heavy reliance on RNG (random number generator): Each tank has an accuracy rating, but in practice, aiming feels completely unreliable due to RNG. I’ve hit moving targets while moving in tanks with poor accuracy - something that should be nearly impossible. Meanwhile, stationary sniper tanks with very high accuracy and full aim often fail to hit stationary targets even close. The shells just veer completely off course, with no explanation or reason.

World of Tanks is a free-to-play multiplayer tank combat MMO where players control armored vehicles from multiple nations, battle in team-based matches, and experience both tactical positioning and chaotic PvP firefights. (store.steampowered.com
)

Strengths:
✔️ Huge variety of tanks — light, medium, heavy, and tank destroyers, each with unique playstyles.
✔️ Tactical gameplay — positioning, angling, and teamwork are critical; matches are more strategic than run-and-gun shooters.
✔️ Historical detail — models and mechanics feel authentic, appealing to history buffs.
✔️ Regular updates — new tanks, maps, and events keep the game fresh.
✔️ Accessible free-to-play — easy to jump in and enjoy casual or competitive matches.

Weaknesses:
✖️ Grindy progression — unlocking high-tier tanks and equipment can take a lot of time or money.
✖️ Matchmaking imbalance — sometimes players face much stronger tanks or experienced opponents, which can be frustrating.
✖️ Slow-paced battles — matches can feel long, especially with heavy tank-heavy teams.
✖️ Pay-to-win temptation — premium tanks, ammo, and account boosts give advantages.
✖️ Steep learning curve for newcomers — understanding armor angling, shell types, and map strategy takes time.

Overall impression:
World of Tanks is a deep, strategic, and rewarding tank combat game. Ideal for players who enjoy teamwork, historical vehicles, and tactical battles, but casual players should be prepared for long matches and progression grind.
